Draw shell diagrams yourself: label the nucleus and count every dot.

faqs.q: What is the difference between atomic number and mass number?
faqs.a: The atomic number is the number of protons in an atom and identifies the element. The mass number is protons plus neutrons. Subtract the atomic number from the mass number to find the number of neutrons.

faqs.q: How many electrons fit in the first shell?
faqs.a: The first shell holds at most two electrons. The second and third shells each hold up to eight for the elements studied in early chemistry. Always fill inner shells before outer ones.

faqs.q: Why does a neutral atom have no charge?
faqs.a: A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons (positive) and electrons (negative), so the charges cancel out. Losing or gaining electrons creates a charged particle called an ion.

faqs.q: What are valence electrons?
faqs.a: Valence electrons are the electrons in the outermost shell. They control how an atom bonds. Atoms with a full outer shell are stable; others gain, lose, or share electrons to reach stability.

faqs.q: What should a shell diagram include?
faqs.a: A labelled nucleus showing protons and neutrons, circles for each shell, and dots for electrons adding up to the atomic number. Always count the dots at the end to check your work.

title: Reading the Periodic Table: Groups, Periods and Trends
desc: Learn to read the periodic table: groups, periods, metals, non-metals and trends, with colour-coding that makes patterns easy to remember.
intro: The periodic table looks complicated at first glance, but it is really a map — and like any map, it becomes easy once you know what the rows and columns mean. Reading the periodic table is about groups, periods, and trends: the vertical columns are groups, the horizontal rows are periods, and an element's position tells you how it is likely to behave. In this guide you will learn to read the table step by step, without memorising every element. We start with the layout: why elements sit where they do, what the group numbers mean, and how periods connect to electron shells. Then we look at the big regions of the table — metals on the left, non-metals on the right, and the metalloids in between — and the trends that run across and down the table. By the end you will be able to look at an element's position and predict useful facts about it, such as how many outer electrons it has and whether it is likely to lose or gain electrons. This skill pays off in every later chemistry topic, from bonding to reactions, so take the time to build it properly with a colour-coded table of your own.

paras: A group is a vertical column of the periodic table. Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in their outer shell, which is why they behave alike. Group 1 elements each have one outer electron, Group 2 elements have two, and Group 7 elements have seven. This single fact explains most of the similarities within a group: members react in similar ways, form similar compounds, and show a steady change in properties as you move down the column.

Some groups have special names worth knowing. Group 1 is the alkali metals (lithium, sodium, potassium and friends), soft reactive metals that form compounds with chlorine and oxygen. Group 7 is the halogens, reactive non-metals that include chlorine and bromine. Group 0 or 18 is the noble gases — helium, neon, argon — with full outer shells, which makes them very unreactive. When a question asks why two elements behave similarly, the answer is very often that they are in the same group.

A period is a horizontal row of the periodic table. The period number tells you how many electron shells the atom has: elements in Period 2 have two shells, elements in Period 3 have three shells, and so on. As you move across a period from left to right, the number of outer-shell electrons increases by one at each step, while the number of shells stays the same. This is why properties change gradually across a period — metals on the left give way to non-metals on the right.

Across a period, atoms gain protons, so the pull of the nucleus on the outer electrons grows stronger. This affects size and reactivity in ways you will study in more detail later. For now, remember the core pattern: down a group, shells increase; across a period, outer electrons increase. If you can say both of those sentences from memory, you already understand the skeleton of the table.

The periodic table divides roughly into two regions. Metals sit on the left and in the centre: they are shiny, good conductors of heat and electricity, and they tend to lose electrons in reactions. Non-metals sit on the right: they are dull in appearance, poor conductors, and they tend to gain or share electrons. A zig-zag staircase line near the right side separates the two regions, and the elements along that line are called metalloids — elements like silicon and boron that show a mix of metal and non-metal properties.

Knowing which region an element belongs to gives you a quick prediction about its behaviour. A metal on the left of the table, such as sodium, will usually form a positive ion by losing electrons. A non-metal on the right, such as chlorine, will usually form a negative ion by gaining an electron, or share electrons in a covalent bond. This left-right pattern is one of the most useful shortcuts in school chemistry, and it is worth colouring on your own copy of the table: one colour for metals, one for non-metals, and one for metalloids.

Colour-coding is a study technique, not decoration. When you shade each group in its own colour, the patterns jump out: the alkali metals marching down Group 1, the halogens down Group 7, the noble gases sitting quietly at the far right. For more on study methods that use visual organisation, see [How to Get A+ in Sindh Board Exams](/blog/how-to-get-a-plus-sindh-board-exams.html) and [Science Vocabulary Roots](/blog/english-medium-science-vocabulary-roots.html).

diagram.caption: The main regions of the periodic table and what each region predicts about behaviour.

sections.h2: Trends Across and Down the Table
paras: A trend is a pattern that repeats as you move in one direction across the table. Moving down a group, atoms get larger because each step adds a new electron shell, and the outer electrons sit further from the nucleus. Reactivity also changes down a group: Group 1 metals become more reactive as you go down, because the single outer electron is further from the nucleus and easier to lose. Group 7 halogens show the opposite pattern — they become less reactive down the group, because gaining an electron becomes harder as the atom grows.

Moving across a period from left to right, atoms get slightly smaller because the growing nuclear charge pulls the same number of shells inward. Metals become less reactive and non-metals become more reactive as you approach the right side. You do not need to memorise long lists of trend facts; if you can explain each trend with shells and nuclear pull, you can work out the answer in the exam. Practise by picking any group and predicting which member is largest, and any period and predicting which member is most metallic.

sections.h2: Using the Table in Exam Questions
paras: Most school questions about the periodic table follow a few familiar patterns. You may be asked to find an element's group and period from its electron arrangement: the number of outer electrons gives the group, and the number of shells gives the period. You may be asked to predict properties: an element in Group 2 will form a 2+ ion, while an element in Group 7 will form a 1- ion. Or you may be asked to compare two elements: explain why potassium is more reactive than lithium (same group, more shells, outer electron further out and easier to lose).

The safest exam method is to write the electron arrangement first, then read the group and period from it, then answer. This turns a memory question into a reasoning question. Keep a blank periodic table outline beside you while you revise, and fill it in from memory: group numbers across the top, period numbers down the side, and the names of the special groups. If you can rebuild the skeleton of the table without looking, the detail questions become much easier.

Periods are horizontal rows: the period number equals the number of shells.
Metals sit left, non-metals right, metalloids along the staircase line.
Down a group atoms get larger; across a period they get slightly smaller.

faqs.q: How do I find an element's group from its electron arrangement?
faqs.a: Count the electrons in the outer shell — that number is the group number (for the main groups). For example, an arrangement of 2,8,1 has one outer electron, so the element is in Group 1.

faqs.q: How do I find an element's period?
faqs.a: Count the number of shells in the electron arrangement. Two shells means Period 2, three shells means Period 3, and so on.

faqs.q: Why do elements in the same group behave alike?
faqs.a: They have the same number of outer electrons, and outer electrons control bonding and reactions. Group members therefore react in similar ways and form similar compounds.

faqs.q: Why are Group 1 metals more reactive going down the group?
faqs.a: Each step down adds a shell, so the single outer electron sits further from the nucleus and is held less tightly, making it easier to lose.

faqs.q: What are noble gases, and why are they unreactive?
faqs.a: Noble gases in Group 0/18 have full outer shells, so they have no need to gain, lose, or share electrons. That stability makes them very unreactive.

title: Chemical Bonding: Ionic vs Covalent, Explained Simply
desc: Ionic vs covalent bonding explained simply: electron transfer and sharing, dot-and-cross diagrams, and properties of each bond type.
intro: Atoms rarely live alone. Most atoms join together to form compounds, and the force that holds them together is called a chemical bond. Chemical bonding comes in two main types that every chemistry pupil must master: ionic bonding, where electrons are transferred from one atom to another, and covalent bonding, where electrons are shared between atoms. The reason atoms bond at all is stability: atoms with incomplete outer shells gain, lose, or share electrons to reach a full outer shell, usually of eight electrons. This drive toward a full outer shell explains why sodium and chlorine form a compound, why two hydrogen atoms pair up, and why water holds together. In this guide we compare ionic and covalent bonding side by side, using dot-and-cross diagrams — the standard drawing method that shows exactly which electrons move and which are shared. By the end you will be able to look at a pair of elements, predict the bond type, draw the diagram, and explain the properties of the compound that forms.

sections.h2: Why Atoms Bond: The Full Outer Shell
paras: An atom with a full outer shell is stable, like the noble gases helium, neon, and argon, which almost never react. Other atoms have outer shells that are partly empty, and bonding is how they complete them. A sodium atom has one outer electron; losing it leaves a full shell underneath. A chlorine atom has seven outer electrons; gaining one completes its shell. So sodium and chlorine are a natural pair: one wants to lose an electron, the other wants to gain one, and the compound they form gives both atoms stable arrangements.

The same idea explains sharing. A hydrogen atom has one electron and needs one more to fill its first shell, which holds only two. Two hydrogen atoms can each share their electron with the other, so both feel as if they have two. Sharing works when neither atom is willing to give up its electron completely — a common situation between two non-metals. Whether electrons are transferred or shared depends on which elements are involved, and that is the heart of the ionic-versus-covalent distinction.

Ionic bonding happens between a metal and a non-metal. The metal atom loses one or more electrons to become a positively charged ion, and the non-metal atom gains those electrons to become a negatively charged ion. The opposite charges then attract each other strongly, and that electrostatic attraction is the ionic bond. Sodium chloride, common table salt, is the classic example: sodium loses its outer electron to become Na+, chlorine gains it to become Cl-, and the ions pack together in a giant crystal lattice.

Ionic compounds have distinctive properties that follow from this structure. They are usually solids with high melting points, because breaking apart a lattice of strongly attracted ions takes a lot of energy. They conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water, because the ions are then free to move, but not as solids, because the ions are locked in place. They are often soluble in water. If an exam asks you to explain any of these properties, always link back to the ions and the lattice — that connection is what earns the marks.
bullets: Metal loses electrons to form a positive ion; non-metal gains electrons to form a negative ion.
The bond is the attraction between opposite charges.
Example: Na+ and Cl- in sodium chloride, held in a giant ionic lattice.
Properties: high melting point, conducts when molten or dissolved, brittle crystals.

paras: Covalent bonding happens between two non-metals, which share pairs of electrons so that each atom reaches a full outer shell. In a hydrogen molecule, one shared pair gives each atom two electrons. In a water molecule, the oxygen atom shares one pair with each hydrogen atom, giving oxygen eight outer electrons and each hydrogen two. In a methane molecule, carbon shares four pairs with four hydrogen atoms. A single shared pair is a single bond; two shared pairs make a double bond, as in oxygen gas, and three shared pairs make a triple bond, as in nitrogen gas.

Covalent substances have very different properties from ionic ones. Simple covalent molecules, like water or carbon dioxide, usually have low melting and boiling points because only weak forces hold the separate molecules together, even though the bonds inside each molecule are strong. They do not conduct electricity, because there are no free ions or electrons. Giant covalent structures like diamond are the exception: every atom is bonded into one huge network, making diamond extremely hard with a very high melting point. When you describe covalent properties in an exam, always say whether you mean simple molecules or a giant structure.

diagram.caption: A side-by-side comparison of electron transfer and electron sharing, with examples and properties.

paras: Dot-and-cross diagrams are the standard way to show bonding in school chemistry. Draw the symbol of each atom, then mark the electrons of one atom as dots and the electrons of the other atom as crosses, so the examiner can see which electron came from where. For ionic bonding, show the transfer with an arrow: the metal's outer electron moves to the non-metal, then draw the two ions in square brackets with their charges. For covalent bonding, draw the shared pairs between the atoms, with each pair containing one dot and one cross where possible.

Work through a few standard examples until the method is automatic: sodium chloride and magnesium oxide for ionic bonding; hydrogen, chlorine, water, methane, and carbon dioxide for covalent bonding. Always check your finished diagram: every atom should end with a full outer shell (two for hydrogen, eight for the rest), and the total number of dots and crosses must match the total electrons of the atoms involved. A diagram that fails either check has an error. For more on careful exam technique, see [How to Avoid Common Exam Mistakes](/blog/how-to-avoid-common-exam-mistakes.html).

sections.h2: Predicting Bond Type from the Elements
paras: The fastest way to predict bond type is to look at the two elements. Metal plus non-metal usually means ionic bonding: the metal loses electrons and the non-metal gains them. Non-metal plus non-metal usually means covalent bonding: the atoms share electrons. Two metals bond differently again, through metallic bonding, which you will meet separately. This simple rule answers most school-level questions, and the periodic table helps you decide which elements are metals: they sit on the left and in the centre, while non-metals sit on the right.

When you write an answer, follow a three-step pattern: name the bond type, explain what happens to the electrons, and link to a property. For example: sodium chloride is ionic because sodium transfers its outer electron to chlorine; the oppositely charged ions attract strongly, which is why the compound has a high melting point. That structure — type, electrons, property — works for almost every bonding question. You can revise supporting vocabulary in [Science Vocabulary Roots](/blog/english-medium-science-vocabulary-roots.html) and practise the mole concept in [Class 11 Chemistry Mole Concept](/blog/class-11-chemistry-mole-concept-stepwise.html).

Ionic bonding = electron transfer between a metal and a non-metal.
Covalent bonding = electron sharing between two non-metals.
Dot-and-cross diagrams show exactly which electrons move or are shared.
Bond type explains properties such as melting point and conductivity.

faqs.q: What is the difference between ionic and covalent bonding?
faqs.a: In ionic bonding, electrons are transferred from a metal to a non-metal, forming oppositely charged ions that attract. In covalent bonding, electrons are shared between two non-metals so each atom reaches a full outer shell.

faqs.q: Why does sodium chloride have a high melting point?
faqs.a: Sodium chloride is a giant lattice of Na+ and Cl- ions held by strong electrostatic attraction. A lot of energy is needed to break those attractions, so the melting point is high.

faqs.q: Why do simple covalent molecules have low melting points?
faqs.a: The bonds inside each molecule are strong, but only weak forces hold separate molecules together. Little energy is needed to separate the molecules, so melting and boiling points are low.

faqs.q: What does a dot-and-cross diagram show?
faqs.a: It shows the outer electrons of each atom, with dots for one atom's electrons and crosses for the other's, so the transfer or sharing of electrons is visible. Finished atoms should show full outer shells.

faqs.q: Can a metal bond with another metal ionically?
faqs.a: No. Ionic bonding needs a metal that loses electrons and a non-metal that gains them. Two metals form metallic bonding instead, where electrons move freely through the metal structure.

title: Acids, Bases and the pH Scale with Everyday Examples
desc: Acids, bases and the pH scale explained with safe household examples, indicators, neutralisation, and the colours that tell you the pH.
intro: Lemons taste sharp, soap feels slippery, and both of those everyday sensations are chemistry. Acids, bases, and the pH scale describe how acidic or alkaline a substance is, and once you understand the scale, you start noticing it everywhere: in food, in cleaning products, in soil, and even in your own body. This guide explains acids and bases using safe household substances, so you can learn the ideas without handling dangerous chemicals. We begin with what acids and bases are and how they behave, then move to the pH scale — a number line from 0 to 14 that tells you how acidic or alkaline a solution is. You will learn how indicators reveal pH through colour changes, and how acids and bases cancel each other out in neutralisation. By the end you will be able to classify common household substances, predict what happens when an acid meets a base, and explain why the pH scale is logarithmic. Everything here uses safe, everyday examples; leave concentrated laboratory acids and alkalis to your teacher's demonstrations.

paras: An acid is a substance that produces hydrogen ions (H+) when dissolved in water. Common acids include citric acid in lemons and oranges, ethanoic acid (acetic acid) in vinegar, and carbonic acid in fizzy drinks. Acids taste sour, and strong acids can sting skin and damage materials, which is why you should never taste or touch laboratory acids. A base is a substance that neutralises an acid. An alkali is a base that dissolves in water to produce hydroxide ions (OH-). Common alkalis include baking soda solution and the ammonia in some household cleaners, while soap is mildly alkaline, which is why it feels slippery.

The key point is that acids and bases are defined by their ions in water: acids add H+, alkalis add OH-. When the two meet, the H+ and OH- combine to form water, and that is the heart of neutralisation. Weak acids and weak bases produce only a few ions, so their effects are mild; strong acids and strong alkalis produce many ions and are far more hazardous. Household substances are almost always weak and dilute, which is what makes them safe to observe and useful as examples.

sections.h2: The pH Scale: A Number Line from 0 to 14
paras: The pH scale runs from 0 to 14 and measures how acidic or alkaline a solution is. A pH of 7 is neutral — pure water sits here. Numbers below 7 are acidic, and the lower the number, the stronger the acid: lemon juice is around pH 2, vinegar around pH 3. Numbers above 7 are alkaline, and the higher the number, the stronger the alkali: baking soda solution is around pH 8 to 9, and soap solution is around pH 9 to 10. Knowing these anchor points lets you estimate the pH of most household substances without memorising long tables.

The scale is logarithmic, which means each whole step is ten times stronger than the one before. A solution of pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4, and a hundred times more acidic than pH 5. This is why small pH changes matter so much in nature and in the body: a shift of one or two units can mean a huge change in the concentration of hydrogen ions. When you answer exam questions about pH, always state the number, say whether it is acidic, neutral, or alkaline, and, if asked, explain the ten-times rule.
bullets: pH 0-6: acidic — lemon juice (~2), vinegar (~3), fizzy drinks (~3-4).
pH 7: neutral — pure water.
pH 8-14: alkaline — baking soda (~9), soap (~9-10), oven cleaner (very high, hazardous).
Each whole pH step is a tenfold change in acidity or alkalinity.

paras: Indicators are dyes that change colour depending on pH. Litmus is the simplest: blue litmus paper turns red in acid, and red litmus paper turns blue in alkali. Universal indicator is more informative because it shows a rainbow of colours across the whole pH range — red for strong acid, orange and yellow for weak acid, green for neutral, blue and purple for alkali. In school you may use universal indicator solution or pH paper to estimate the pH of household liquids such as lemon juice, soap solution, and tap water.

Natural indicators work the same way. Red cabbage juice turns red-pink in acid, purple when neutral, and green-yellow in alkali, and making it is a classic safe classroom activity: chop red cabbage, soak it in hot water, strain, and test drops of household liquids. Whatever indicator you use, always record the colour you observed and the pH it indicates, and never taste the liquids you are testing. For safe, structured write-ups of such experiments, see [Lab Report Writing](/blog/english-medium-lab-report-writing.html).

diagram.caption: The colour sequence of universal indicator from strong acid to strong alkali.

paras: Neutralisation happens when an acid reacts with a base to produce a salt and water. The word equation is simple: acid + base -> salt + water. For example, hydrochloric acid plus sodium hydroxide gives sodium chloride (common salt) plus water. If the acid and base are mixed in the right amounts, the resulting solution is neutral, pH 7. This is why neutralisation is so useful: it cancels out acidity or alkalinity.

Everyday life is full of neutralisation. Antacid tablets neutralise excess stomach acid. Baking soda neutralises the acid in a bee sting or in sour milk spills. Gardeners add lime to neutralise acidic soil. In each case the same chemistry is at work: H+ from the acid and OH- from the base combine to make water, and the remaining ions form a salt. When you write about neutralisation in an exam, always give the word equation, name the salt formed, and explain the pH change.

sections.h2: Staying Safe with Acids and Alkalis
paras: Household acids and alkalis are weak and dilute, but laboratory ones can be dangerous. Never taste any chemical, never add water to a concentrated acid, and always wear eye protection when your teacher demonstrates with strong acids or alkalis. If a chemical splashes on skin, rinse with plenty of running water and tell your teacher at once. Strong acids burn, strong alkalis feel slippery and can also burn, and both can damage eyes, so goggles matter even for short demonstrations.

At home, the safe way to explore pH is with food substances: lemon juice, vinegar, baking soda solution, and soapy water, tested with litmus paper or red cabbage indicator. Keep cleaning products in their original labelled bottles, never mix bleach with acids or with other cleaners, and store everything out of reach of younger children. Good chemistry is careful chemistry — and the habits you build with safe substances now are the same habits that keep you safe in a real laboratory later.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a base and an alkali?
faqs.a: A base is any substance that neutralises an acid. An alkali is a base that dissolves in water to give hydroxide ions. All alkalis are bases, but not all bases are alkalis — some bases, like copper oxide, do not dissolve in water.

faqs.q: Why is the pH scale logarithmic?
faqs.a: Each whole-number step on the pH scale represents a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration. So pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4 and a hundred times more acidic than pH 5.

faqs.q: What colour does universal indicator turn in acid and alkali?
faqs.a: It turns red in strong acid, orange and yellow in weak acid, green at neutral pH 7, blue in weak alkali, and purple in strong alkali.

faqs.q: What is formed in neutralisation?
faqs.a: A salt and water. The H+ ions from the acid and OH- ions from the base combine to make water, and the remaining ions form the salt.

faqs.q: Is it safe to test household substances for pH?
faqs.a: Testing food substances like lemon juice, vinegar, and baking soda solution with litmus or cabbage indicator is safe. Never taste laboratory chemicals, never mix cleaning products, and always follow your teacher's safety instructions.

title: Types of Chemical Reactions with Everyday Examples
desc: Sort chemical reactions into combination, decomposition and displacement types, with kitchen and lab examples and word equations you can write.
intro: A chemical reaction happens when substances change into new substances with different properties. Rusting, burning, cooking, and the fizz of an antacid tablet are all chemical reactions, but they do not all work the same way. Chemists sort reactions into types so that each new reaction you meet can be recognised, predicted, and explained. In this guide we cover the three types you will meet first: combination, decomposition, and displacement reactions. Each type has a simple pattern, a word equation you can write in seconds, and everyday examples you already know. We also show how to tell a chemical change from a physical change, because that distinction sits behind many exam questions. By the end you will be able to look at a reaction description, name its type, write its word equation, and explain what evidence shows that a chemical change happened. Keep your examples concrete — kitchen and lab examples are the ones examiners love, because they prove you understand the chemistry rather than just the definition.

paras: A physical change alters appearance or state without making a new substance: melting ice, dissolving sugar, or tearing paper. The change can usually be reversed, and no new substance appears. A chemical change makes one or more new substances with different properties, and it is usually hard or impossible to reverse by simple means. Burning wood makes ash, smoke, and gases that cannot be turned back into wood. Cooking an egg changes its proteins permanently.

Five signs suggest a chemical reaction has taken place: a colour change, a gas being produced (bubbles or fizz), a temperature change without heating or cooling, a solid forming in a liquid (a precipitate), or a new smell. No single sign proves a reaction on its own — dissolving can also cause a temperature change — so look for the strongest evidence: a new substance with new properties. When you answer a question about this, always name the sign you observed and the new substance you think formed.

In a combination reaction, two or more substances join to form a single product. The pattern is A + B -> AB. A familiar example is the formation of water from hydrogen and oxygen. Another is magnesium burning in air: magnesium + oxygen -> magnesium oxide, seen as a bright white flame and a white powder product. The rusting of iron is also a combination reaction, though a slow one: iron + oxygen + water -> hydrated iron oxide, the flaky brown substance we call rust.

Combination reactions often release energy, especially heat. That is why burning is a combination reaction with oxygen: fuel + oxygen -> oxides + energy. In the kitchen, the browning of bread in a toaster involves combination reactions between sugars and proteins. When you write a combination word equation, check that the product is a single substance and that the reactants are the simpler substances that joined to make it.

Decomposition is the opposite of combination: one substance breaks down into two or more simpler substances. The pattern is AB -> A + B. The breakdown can be caused by heat, light, or electricity. Heating calcium carbonate (limestone) produces calcium oxide and carbon dioxide, a reaction used in making cement. Heating copper carbonate gives copper oxide and carbon dioxide, with a clear colour change from green to black. Electrolysis — passing electricity through a compound — decomposes water into hydrogen and oxygen.

Your own body uses decomposition too: when you eat, enzymes break down large food molecules into simpler ones your body can absorb. In the kitchen, baking powder decomposes when heated, releasing carbon dioxide gas that makes cakes rise. Look for the signature pattern in exam questions: one reactant on the left, two or more products on the right, and a cause such as heat, light, or electricity mentioned in the question.

diagram.caption: A decision flow for classifying any reaction as combination, decomposition, or displacement.

paras: In a displacement reaction, a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive element in a compound. The pattern is A + BC -> AC + B. A classic classroom example is iron displacing copper from copper sulfate solution: iron + copper sulfate -> iron sulfate + copper. The blue colour of the solution fades and a reddish-brown coating of copper appears on the iron — two clear signs of a chemical change. Zinc displaces copper in the same way, and magnesium displaces hydrogen from acids.

Displacement only works in one direction: a less reactive element cannot displace a more reactive one. Copper will not displace zinc from zinc sulfate, because zinc is more reactive than copper. The reactivity series — a ranking of metals from most to least reactive — predicts which displacements are possible, and it is one of the most useful reference tools in school chemistry. If a question asks whether a displacement will happen, compare the two metals in the reactivity series before you answer.

sections.h2: Writing Word Equations for Each Type
paras: Word equations are the simplest way to show a reaction: name the reactants on the left, an arrow, and the products on the right. For combination, practise: hydrogen + oxygen -> water; calcium + oxygen -> calcium oxide. For decomposition, practise: calcium carbonate -> calcium oxide + carbon dioxide; copper carbonate -> copper oxide + carbon dioxide. For displacement, practise: iron + copper sulfate -> iron sulfate + copper; magnesium + hydrochloric acid -> magnesium chloride + hydrogen.

Three habits make word equations reliable. First, use the correct names — say copper sulfate, not blue liquid. Second, include every product, including gases such as hydrogen or carbon dioxide. Third, check that your equation matches the reaction type you named: one product for combination, one reactant for decomposition, a swapped partner for displacement. Examiners often ask you to name the type and write the equation together, so practise both as a pair, not as separate skills. For careful exam habits, see [How to Avoid Common Exam Mistakes](/blog/how-to-avoid-common-exam-mistakes.html) and [Lab Report Writing](/blog/english-medium-lab-report-writing.html).

points: Chemical changes make new substances; physical changes do not.
Combination: two or more reactants join into one product.
Decomposition: one substance breaks into two or more products.
Displacement: a more reactive element replaces a less reactive one.
Write the word equation and check it matches the reaction type.

faqs.q: What is the pattern of a combination reaction?
faqs.a: Two or more substances join to form one product: A + B -> AB. Example: magnesium + oxygen -> magnesium oxide.

faqs.q: What is the pattern of a decomposition reaction?
faqs.a: One substance breaks into two or more simpler substances: AB -> A + B. The breakdown is usually caused by heat, light, or electricity.

faqs.q: What is the pattern of a displacement reaction?
faqs.a: A more reactive element replaces a less reactive element in a compound: A + BC -> AC + B. Example: iron + copper sulfate -> iron sulfate + copper.

faqs.q: Can copper displace zinc from zinc sulfate?
faqs.a: No, because zinc is more reactive than copper. Displacement only works when the free element is more reactive than the one it replaces, so check the reactivity series.

faqs.q: How do I know a chemical reaction happened?
faqs.a: Look for a colour change, gas production, temperature change, a precipitate forming, or a new smell — and check that a new substance with new properties has appeared.

title: Balancing Chemical Equations: The Counting Method
desc: Balance chemical equations with the atom-counting method: tally tables, step-by-step worked examples, and the mistakes to avoid.
intro: Balancing chemical equations is the skill that turns chemistry from word descriptions into precise science, and many pupils find it harder than it needs to be. The secret is that balancing is not guessing — it is counting. A balanced equation has the same number of each type of atom on both sides, because atoms are never created or destroyed in a chemical reaction; they only rearrange. In this guide you will learn the counting method: a systematic, step-by-step way to balance any equation you meet in school chemistry. We start with the one rule that matters, then work through examples of increasing difficulty using a tally table — a simple counting grid that keeps track of every atom. You will learn which elements to balance first, how to use brackets for groups like sulfate, and the mistakes that cost marks even when the chemistry is understood. By the end, balancing will feel like bookkeeping: slow and careful at first, then fast and automatic with practice.

sections.h2: The One Rule: Atoms Are Conserved
paras: In a chemical reaction, atoms are rearranged but never created or destroyed. This is the law of conservation of mass, and it is the reason equations must balance: if an equation shows three oxygen atoms on the left and only two on the right, it cannot describe a real reaction, because an oxygen atom has vanished. Balancing means adjusting the numbers in front of formulae — the coefficients — until every element has the same total on both sides. The coefficients tell you how many units of each substance react.

One rule must never be broken: you may change coefficients, but you may never change the formulae themselves. Turning H2O into H3O changes the substance from water to something else; writing 2H2O instead means two water molecules, which is allowed. This is the most common balancing error, and examiners check for it carefully. If you ever feel tempted to change a subscript, stop — the answer is to change a coefficient somewhere else instead.

sections.h2: The Tally Table: Count Before You Balance
paras: The counting method starts with a tally table: a small grid listing each element, how many atoms of it are on the left, and how many are on the right. Take the formation of water: H2 + O2 -> H2O. The tally shows hydrogen 2 on the left and 2 on the right — balanced — but oxygen 2 on the left and 1 on the right — not balanced. The table makes the problem visible: we need one more oxygen atom on the right.

To fix it, put a 2 in front of H2O: H2 + O2 -> 2H2O. Now oxygen balances at 2 each side, but hydrogen is now 2 on the left and 4 on the right. Put a 2 in front of H2: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O. The new tally shows hydrogen 4 and 4, oxygen 2 and 2 — balanced. Always rebuild the tally after every change, because fixing one element usually disturbs another. The tally table is your proof that the equation balances, and writing it out in rough work prevents the most common slips.
bullets: Step 1: Write the correct formulae for reactants and products.
Step 2: Draw a tally table: each element, left count, right count.
Step 3: Balance one element at a time by changing coefficients only.
Step 4: Rebuild the tally after every change.
Step 5: Check every element and simplify coefficients if they share a factor.

paras: Consider magnesium burning in oxygen: Mg + O2 -> MgO. The tally shows magnesium 1 and 1, balanced, but oxygen 2 on the left and 1 on the right. Put a 2 in front of MgO: Mg + O2 -> 2MgO. Now oxygen is 2 and 2, but magnesium is 1 on the left and 2 on the right. Put a 2 in front of Mg: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO. The final tally reads magnesium 2 and 2, oxygen 2 and 2 — balanced.

Notice the order of work: we balanced oxygen first because it appeared in only one compound on each side, and magnesium followed naturally. A good habit is to balance elements that appear in only one place on each side first, leave hydrogen and oxygen until later when they appear in several compounds, and leave elements that appear as pure elements (like O2 or Mg) until last. This order keeps the tally stable and reduces the number of corrections you need.

Some equations contain groups of atoms that stay together, such as sulfate (SO4) or nitrate (NO3). Treat a group as a single unit in your tally when it appears unchanged on both sides. For example, in zinc + sulfuric acid -> zinc sulfate + hydrogen, the sulfate group appears once on each side, so you can count it as one sulfate unit rather than counting sulfur and oxygen separately. This shortcut keeps tally tables short and reduces arithmetic errors.

Another useful habit is to finish by checking that the coefficients have no common factor. If an equation balances as 2H2 + 2O2 -> 2H2O, all coefficients share a factor of two, and the simplest form is H2 + O2 -> 2H2O — wait, that last form does not balance, which shows why you must recheck after simplifying. Only simplify when the balanced equation genuinely shares a factor across all coefficients, and always re-verify the tally afterwards. For more on presenting working clearly, see [How to Avoid Common Exam Mistakes](/blog/how-to-avoid-common-exam-mistakes.html).

diagram.alt: The Counting Method in Five Steps
diagram.caption: A repeatable flow for balancing any school-level chemical equation.

paras: The most damaging mistake is changing subscripts instead of coefficients — it changes the substance and makes the whole equation wrong. The second is forgetting that elements like oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, and chlorine exist as diatomic molecules (O2, H2, N2, Cl2) when written alone; writing O instead of O2 throws every count off. The third is stopping too early: balancing one element and forgetting to recheck the rest, which leaves the equation unbalanced somewhere else.

A fourth mistake is messy working. Balancing in your head feels faster but produces far more errors than a written tally table. Write the tally, cross it out, and rewrite it — examiners reward correct final equations, and clear working lets you spot your own slips. Practise with five equations a day for a week, mixing combination, decomposition, and displacement reactions, and the method will become automatic. You can build the underlying arithmetic confidence with [Maths Word Problem Language](/blog/english-medium-math-word-problem-language.html) and [Class 11 Chemistry Mole Concept](/blog/class-11-chemistry-mole-concept-stepwise.html).

Change coefficients only — never change a formula's subscripts.
A tally table makes unbalanced elements visible and checkable.
Balance elements in one place per side first; hydrogen and oxygen often last.
Rebuild the tally after every change and check every element at the end.

faqs.q: Why must chemical equations be balanced?
faqs.a: Because atoms are conserved in a reaction — none are created or destroyed. A balanced equation shows the same number of each type of atom on both sides, matching what actually happens.

faqs.q: Can I change a subscript to balance an equation?
faqs.a: No. Changing a subscript changes the substance itself — H2O becomes something else. Only change the coefficients, the numbers in front of the formulae.

faqs.q: What order should I balance elements in?
faqs.a: Balance elements that appear in only one compound on each side first, then the rest, leaving hydrogen and oxygen until later if they appear in several compounds, and pure elements until last.

faqs.q: What is a tally table?
faqs.a: A small grid listing each element with its atom count on the left and on the right of the equation. Rebuild it after every coefficient change so you can see what is balanced and what still needs fixing.

faqs.q: Why is oxygen written as O2 and not O?
faqs.a: Oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, and chlorine exist as diatomic molecules — two atoms joined together — when written as pure elements. Writing O instead of O2 makes every oxygen count wrong.

title: Metals vs Non-Metals: Properties and Everyday Uses
desc: Compare metals and non-metals: lustre, conductivity, malleability and uses, with objects pupils handle every day as examples.
intro: Pick up a steel spoon and a wooden pencil, and you are holding the two great families of elements in your hand — or at least their everyday representatives. Metals and non-metals are the two main groups into which the elements are divided, and their properties explain why we build bridges from steel, carry water in plastic bottles, and wire our homes with copper. In this guide we compare metals and non-metals property by property: appearance, hardness, conductivity, malleability, and how they behave in chemical reactions. Every property is tied to an object you handle daily, so the comparison is easy to remember and easy to use in exam answers. We also look at the exceptions that examiners love — the non-metal that conducts, the metal that is soft — because a good answer shows you know the pattern and its limits. By the end you will be able to classify an element from its properties, predict its uses, and explain each use in terms of a property.

paras: Metals are shiny — they have lustre — when freshly cut or polished. Think of a new coin, a steel spoon, or an aluminium pot. They are usually hard and strong, which is why tools, machines, and building frames are made from them. Non-metals are usually dull in appearance: sulfur is a yellow powder, carbon as charcoal is black and dull, and oxygen is a colourless gas. Most non-metals are soft or brittle when solid — sulfur crumbles, charcoal snaps — though diamond, a form of carbon, is the famous exception and the hardest natural substance known.

These differences come from atomic structure. In metals, outer electrons are free to move through the whole structure, which gives metals their shine and strength. In non-metals, electrons are held tightly in bonds between atoms, so the material is dull and brittle. When you describe appearance in an exam, use the technical words: metals have lustre, non-metals are dull; metals are hard and strong, most solid non-metals are soft and brittle.

Metals are good conductors of heat and electricity because their free electrons carry energy and charge through the material. Copper is used for electrical wires because it conducts electricity extremely well and is ductile enough to be drawn into thin wires. Aluminium and steel cooking pots conduct heat from the stove to the food. Non-metals are usually poor conductors, which makes them useful as insulators: plastic handles on pots stop heat reaching your hand, and rubber coatings on wires stop electricity reaching you.

The great exception is graphite, a form of carbon, which conducts electricity because of its layered structure with free electrons. It is used for electrodes and in pencils, where its softness leaves marks on paper. Examiners often ask about graphite precisely because it breaks the simple rule, so remember it as the non-metal that conducts. When you explain a use in an exam, always link property to purpose: copper is used for wires because it is a good conductor and ductile, not simply because it is a metal.
bullets: Metals: good conductors of heat and electricity (free electrons).
Non-metals: poor conductors, used as insulators (plastic, rubber, wood).
Exception: graphite, a non-metal form of carbon, conducts electricity.
Uses follow properties: copper for wires, plastic for handles and coatings.

paras: Malleable means can be hammered or rolled into sheets; ductile means can be drawn into wires. Metals are both: gold can be hammered into foil thinner than paper, and copper is drawn into the wires in your home. These properties come from the layers of metal atoms sliding over each other without breaking the metallic bond. Non-metals are neither malleable nor ductile — solid non-metals are brittle, meaning they break or shatter when hit rather than bending. Sulfur cracks under a hammer; charcoal snaps.

These mechanical properties decide how materials are shaped in industry. A jeweller hammers and rolls gold because it is malleable; an electrician pulls copper through dies because it is ductile; a builder never tries to hammer sulfur into a sheet, because it would shatter. In exam answers, use the three words precisely: malleable for sheets, ductile for wires, brittle for breaking. Confusing them is a common mark-loser.

Metals tend to lose electrons in reactions, forming positive ions. This is why metals react with acids to release hydrogen gas, and why sodium, a very reactive metal, must be stored away from air and water. Non-metals tend to gain or share electrons, forming negative ions or covalent molecules. Chlorine gains an electron to become chloride; oxygen shares electrons in water and carbon dioxide. The most reactive metals — potassium, sodium, calcium — sit on the left of the periodic table, and the most reactive non-metals — fluorine, chlorine, oxygen — sit on the right.

This difference also shows in oxides. Metal oxides are usually basic: magnesium oxide neutralises acids. Non-metal oxides are usually acidic: carbon dioxide dissolves in water to form a weak acid. These two facts explain many everyday observations, from why lime (a metal oxide) sweetens acidic soil to why fizzy drinks are slightly acidic. When a question asks you to predict reaction behaviour, start from the metal-or-non-metal identity, then apply the electron rule: metals lose, non-metals gain or share.

diagram.caption: A side-by-side comparison of the physical and chemical properties of metals and non-metals.

paras: Everyday objects make the properties concrete. The steel blade of a kitchen knife is hard and strong. The copper wire inside a charger is a good conductor and ductile. The aluminium pot conducts heat. The iron frame of a school gate is strong and can be welded. On the non-metal side, the plastic bottle is light, cheap, and an insulator; the rubber soles of your shoes grip and insulate; the oxygen you breathe and the carbon dioxide plants use are non-metal gases; the sulfur in matches and the iodine in antiseptic are non-metal solids and solutions.

Alloys — mixtures of metals, such as steel (iron plus carbon) and brass (copper plus zinc) — combine the best properties of their ingredients, which is why pure metals are often less useful than their alloys. When an exam asks why a material is used for a job, answer in three parts: name the property, explain why the job needs it, and name the material. For example: overhead cables use aluminium because it is a good conductor and light, so it carries current without weighing down the pylons. That property-to-purpose link is the whole skill. For more on how science vocabulary helps you write these answers, see [Science Vocabulary Roots](/blog/english-medium-science-vocabulary-roots.html).

points: Metals are shiny, hard, strong, and good conductors; non-metals are usually dull, brittle, and poor conductors.
Metals are malleable and ductile; solid non-metals are brittle.
Metals lose electrons to form positive ions; non-metals gain or share electrons.
Metal oxides are usually basic; non-metal oxides are usually acidic.
Uses follow properties — always link a use to the property that makes it work.

faqs.q: What is the difference between malleable and ductile?
faqs.a: Malleable means a material can be hammered or rolled into sheets; ductile means it can be drawn into wires. Metals are both. Solid non-metals are neither — they are brittle and break instead.

faqs.q: Which non-metal conducts electricity?
faqs.a: Graphite, a form of carbon, conducts electricity because of its layered structure with free electrons. It is the standard exception examiners ask about.

faqs.q: Why are metals good conductors?
faqs.a: Metals have free electrons that move through the whole structure, carrying electrical charge and heat energy as they go. Non-metals hold their electrons tightly in bonds, so they conduct poorly.

faqs.q: Are metal oxides acidic or basic?
faqs.a: Metal oxides are usually basic — magnesium oxide neutralises acids. Non-metal oxides are usually acidic — carbon dioxide forms a weak acid in water.

faqs.q: What is an alloy, and why are alloys used?
faqs.a: An alloy is a mixture of metals (sometimes with a non-metal), such as steel or brass. Alloys combine the best properties of their ingredients, so they are often stronger, harder, or more resistant than the pure metals.

title: What Air and Water Are Made Of: Composition Explained
desc: What air and water are made of: the gases in air, the composition of water, and simple experiments that show both clearly.
intro: Air and water are the two substances you use most and think about least. You breathe air every moment and drink water every day, yet most pupils cannot say what either one is actually made of. This guide answers both questions with simple, standard chemistry: air is a mixture of gases, mostly nitrogen and oxygen, and water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen. Understanding the difference between a mixture and a compound is the key to the whole topic, because air and water look similar — both are colourless and everywhere — but they are chemically opposite kinds of substance. We explain the composition of air with percentages, show how scientists proved what air contains, and describe the composition of water with the famous electrolysis experiment that splits it back into hydrogen and oxygen. Along the way you will learn why pure water is rare, why air pollution matters, and how the composition of both substances connects to life itself.

sections.h2: Air Is a Mixture, Not a Compound
paras: Air is a mixture of gases that are simply mixed together, not chemically bonded. The main gases are nitrogen, about 78 percent, and oxygen, about 21 percent, with the remaining 1 percent made up of argon, carbon dioxide, water vapour, and tiny amounts of other gases. Because air is a mixture, its composition varies slightly from place to place: humid air holds more water vapour, city air holds more carbon dioxide and pollutants, and the proportions can be separated by physical methods such as cooling and fractional distillation.

The mixture idea explains many observations. You can breathe air in and out all day without changing what air is, because your lungs do not split the mixture apart chemically — they simply take some oxygen from it and add carbon dioxide. The gases in air keep their own properties: oxygen still supports burning, nitrogen still dilutes it, carbon dioxide is still absorbed by plants. If air were a compound, its parts would lose those properties, and breathing would be a very different process.

sections.h2: Oxygen and Nitrogen: The Two Main Gases
paras: Oxygen, about a fifth of air, is the gas that supports burning and breathing. A glowing splint relights in oxygen, a test that proves its presence. All animals, including humans, need oxygen to release energy from food, and all fires need it to burn. Nitrogen, about four-fifths of air, is much less reactive. It dilutes the oxygen, slowing burning so fires stay manageable, and it is the raw material plants need to build proteins — though plants cannot use nitrogen gas directly and rely on nitrogen-fixing bacteria and fertilisers to convert it into usable forms.

A useful way to remember the proportions is that air is roughly four parts nitrogen to one part oxygen. A simple school experiment proves that oxygen is about a fifth of air: burning a candle or a piece of phosphorus inside an inverted jar over water removes the oxygen, and water rises to fill about one-fifth of the jar. This experiment is a classroom classic because it turns an invisible gas into a visible measurement, and it is worth being able to describe it step by step in an exam.
bullets: Nitrogen: about 78% of air, unreactive, dilutes oxygen, raw material for plant proteins.
Oxygen: about 21% of air, supports burning and breathing, tested with a glowing splint.
Argon and others: about 1%, including carbon dioxide and water vapour.
Air is a mixture: gases keep their own properties and can be separated physically.

sections.h2: Carbon Dioxide, Water Vapour and Argon
paras: Carbon dioxide is only a small fraction of air — roughly four hundredths of one percent — but it matters enormously. Plants absorb it for photosynthesis, and it is the gas we breathe out. Human activity, especially burning fossil fuels, has increased its concentration, which warms the planet. Water vapour is the gas form of water, and its amount varies with weather: humid days hold more, dry days less. It matters for clouds, rain, and how comfortable the air feels.

Argon, about 0.9 percent of air, is a noble gas that does almost nothing chemically. It is used in light bulbs, where its unreactive nature protects the filament, and in welding, where it shields hot metal from oxygen. The small gases in air are a good reminder that importance is not about quantity: carbon dioxide is tiny in proportion yet central to life and climate, while nitrogen is huge in proportion yet chemically quiet.

Water is not a mixture — it is a compound, a substance in which hydrogen and oxygen atoms are chemically bonded in a fixed ratio. Every water molecule is H2O: two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom. Unlike the gases in air, hydrogen and oxygen in water have lost their individual properties: hydrogen alone burns explosively and oxygen alone supports burning, but water puts out fires. That change of properties is the signature of a compound, and it is the strongest contrast you can draw between air and water.

The fixed ratio matters too. A mixture can vary — air can hold more or less water vapour — but a compound cannot: every pure water molecule is H2O, always. This is why chemists call water a compound and air a mixture, and why the two substances are separated by different methods. You can separate air physically; you can only split water chemically, by giving it enough energy to break its bonds.

diagram.caption: A water molecule: two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom in a bent shape.

paras: Electrolysis splits water into hydrogen and oxygen using electricity, and it is the classic proof of water's composition. When an electric current passes through slightly acidified water, bubbles of hydrogen appear at the negative electrode and bubbles of oxygen at the positive electrode. The hydrogen collects twice as fast as the oxygen — two volumes of hydrogen for every one volume of oxygen — matching the H2O ratio. The gases can be identified by their tests: hydrogen pops with a lighted splint, oxygen relights a glowing splint.

The experiment also proves that water is a compound rather than a mixture, because only a chemical change — breaking bonds with electrical energy — can split it. Pure water conducts electricity poorly, so a little acid or salt is added to help the current flow. Being able to describe this experiment — apparatus, observation, gas tests, and the 2:1 conclusion — is a standard exam question, and the ratio is the fact examiners most often check. For related life-science context, see [Photosynthesis Process Steps](/blog/biology-photosynthesis-process-steps.html) and [Ecosystem Energy Flow](/blog/biology-ecosystem-energy-flow.html).

Water is a compound: every molecule is H2O, two hydrogen to one oxygen.
Mixtures vary and keep their parts' properties; compounds are fixed and change them.
Electrolysis splits water into hydrogen and oxygen in a 2:1 volume ratio.

faqs.q: What is air made of?
faqs.a: Air is a mixture of gases: about 78% nitrogen, about 21% oxygen, and about 1% argon, carbon dioxide, water vapour, and other gases. The proportions vary slightly with place and weather.

faqs.q: What is water made of?
faqs.a: Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen with the formula H2O — two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom in every molecule.

faqs.q: Why is air a mixture but water a compound?
faqs.a: In air the gases are only mixed, keep their own properties, and can vary in proportion. In water the hydrogen and oxygen are chemically bonded in a fixed ratio and have lost their individual properties.

faqs.q: How does electrolysis prove water is H2O?
faqs.a: Electrolysis splits water into hydrogen and oxygen gases in a 2:1 volume ratio — two volumes of hydrogen for every one volume of oxygen — matching the two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom in each molecule.

faqs.q: How can I show oxygen is about a fifth of air?
faqs.a: Burn a candle or phosphorus in an inverted jar over water: the oxygen is used up, and water rises to fill about one-fifth of the jar, showing oxygen is roughly 20% of air.

title: Introduction to Organic Chemistry and Hydrocarbons
desc: Meet organic chemistry through hydrocarbons: carbon chains, methane, ethane, fuels, and models you can build from everyday materials.
intro: Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon, and carbon is the element that life is built from. Every living thing — plants, animals, and you — is made of carbon compounds, and so are fuels, plastics, medicines, and most of the food you eat. This guide introduces organic chemistry through its simplest family, the hydrocarbons: compounds made of carbon and hydrogen only. You will learn why carbon is special, how carbon atoms link into chains, and how the first few hydrocarbons are named and used. We keep the chemistry concrete: the gas in a kitchen stove, the petrol in a motorbike, and the wax in a candle are all hydrocarbons, and understanding them is understanding organic chemistry at its foundation. You will also build models from everyday materials — a hands-on method that makes molecular shapes easy to remember. By the end you will be able to name the first hydrocarbons, draw their structures, and explain why they burn the way they do.

paras: Carbon is special because each carbon atom can form four bonds, and carbon atoms can bond to each other in long chains, branches, and rings. No other element builds structures with such variety. A carbon atom with four bonds can link to four hydrogen atoms, or to other carbons, or to a mix of both, and each arrangement is a different compound with different properties. This is why there are millions of known carbon compounds — far more than compounds of any other element — and why organic chemistry is a whole branch of chemistry on its own.

Carbon's four bonds come from its electron arrangement, 2,4: four outer electrons, needing four more to complete its shell, which it gains by sharing. That sharing gives covalent bonds, the bond type of nearly all organic compounds. The other elements in organic compounds — hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen — fit around the carbon skeleton. Learn to see every organic molecule as a carbon skeleton with other atoms attached, and the whole subject becomes a matter of recognising skeletons.

Hydrocarbons are the simplest organic compounds: they contain only carbon and hydrogen. The family is named by the number of carbon atoms: one carbon is methane, two is ethane, three is propane, four is butane. The endings tell you about the bonds: -ane means all single bonds, -ene means one double bond, -yne means one triple bond. For school chemistry, the -ane family, the alkanes, matters most, and the first four alkanes are worth memorising with their formulae: methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8, butane C4H10.

Each alkane differs from the next by one carbon and two hydrogens — CH2 — a pattern called a homologous series. Members of a series show a steady change in properties: boiling points rise as molecules get larger, because bigger molecules need more energy to separate. The pattern means you can predict properties of a hydrocarbon you have never met, simply from its position in the series. That predictive power is one of the great satisfactions of organic chemistry.

The most familiar hydrocarbons are fuels. Natural gas is mostly methane, used for cooking and heating. LPG, the gas in cylinders used in many homes, is mostly propane and butane. Petrol is a mixture of larger hydrocarbons, and candle wax is a mixture of still larger ones. All of them burn in oxygen to release energy, producing carbon dioxide and water when burning is complete: hydrocarbon + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy. That word equation is the same for every hydrocarbon fuel, and it is one of the most useful equations in school chemistry.

Incomplete burning, when oxygen is short, produces carbon monoxide and soot instead of carbon dioxide — both dangerous. Carbon monoxide is a poisonous gas that stops blood carrying oxygen, which is why gas heaters and stoves need ventilation and why car exhausts are harmful in closed spaces. When you answer questions about fuels, always distinguish complete from incomplete combustion, name the products of each, and mention the safety consequence. For energy in living things, see [Ecosystem Energy Flow](/blog/biology-ecosystem-energy-flow.html).

diagram.caption: How hydrocarbons are organised: alkanes, their uses, and what happens when they burn.

paras: Molecular models make organic chemistry visible, and you do not need a bought kit. Use small balls of modelling clay or rolled paper for atoms — black for carbon, white for hydrogen — and matchsticks or toothpicks for bonds. Build methane first: one black ball with four toothpicks, a white ball on each end. Then build ethane: two black balls joined by a toothpick, with three white balls on each carbon. Then propane: three carbons in a chain. Counting the bonds at each carbon — always four — checks your model, and seeing the shapes makes the formulae memorable.

Models also show why structures matter. Butane's four carbons can form a straight chain or a branched shape, and the two arrangements are different compounds with different properties — a phenomenon called isomerism. You can discover this yourself by building butane two ways and seeing that both use four black and ten white balls. That discovery, made with your own hands, teaches more than any textbook paragraph, and it is exactly the kind of concrete learning that examiners reward when you describe it.

sections.h2: From Hydrocarbons to the Rest of Organic Chemistry
paras: Hydrocarbons are only the beginning. Replace one hydrogen atom in methane with an -OH group and you get methanol, an alcohol. Replace it with a -COOH group and you get an acid. Add oxygen, nitrogen, or other elements to the carbon skeleton and you get the other families of organic chemistry: alcohols, acids, esters, and the huge molecules of life such as sugars, fats, and proteins. Each family has its own ending and its own properties, but the carbon skeleton underneath follows the same rules you learned with hydrocarbons.

Keep two habits as you go deeper. First, always count bonds at each carbon — four, every time — because a carbon with three or five bonds has an error. Second, learn each family's functional group, the small group of atoms that gives the family its behaviour. Organic chemistry rewards pattern-spotters: once you see the skeleton-and-group pattern, each new family is a variation on a theme you already know. For vocabulary skills that help with naming, see [Science Vocabulary Roots](/blog/english-medium-science-vocabulary-roots.html) and [Lab Report Writing](/blog/english-medium-lab-report-writing.html).

points: Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon, the element of life and fuels.
Each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds and links into chains and rings.
Hydrocarbons contain carbon and hydrogen only; alkanes end in -ane.
Complete combustion gives carbon dioxide + water + energy; incomplete gives carbon monoxide and soot.
Build models with clay and matchsticks — count four bonds at every carbon.

faqs.q: What is a hydrocarbon?
faqs.a: A compound containing carbon and hydrogen only. Examples include methane, ethane, propane, and butane. Fuels such as natural gas, LPG, and petrol are hydrocarbons or mixtures of hydrocarbons.

faqs.q: Why can carbon form so many compounds?
faqs.a: Each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds and can bond to other carbon atoms in chains, branches, and rings, producing an enormous variety of skeletons with different atoms attached.

faqs.q: What are the first four alkanes?
faqs.a: Methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8, and butane C4H10. Each differs from the next by CH2, and their boiling points rise as the molecules get larger.

faqs.q: What is the difference between complete and incomplete combustion?
faqs.a: Complete combustion in plenty of oxygen gives carbon dioxide + water + energy. Incomplete combustion in limited oxygen gives carbon monoxide and soot, which are dangerous.

faqs.q: What is isomerism?
faqs.a: Isomerism is when two compounds share the same formula but have different structures — for example, butane's straight chain and branched forms. The different arrangements give different properties.

title: Solutions and Concentration: Solute, Solvent and Dilution
desc: Solutions and concentration explained: solute, solvent, dilution, and simple concentration calculations with a squash-drink analogy.
intro: Stir sugar into tea and you have made a solution — one of the most common things in chemistry, and one of the easiest to misunderstand. A solution is a mixture in which one substance is dissolved evenly through another, so every spoonful is the same as every other. In this guide we build the vocabulary of solutions step by step: solute, solvent, solution, and concentration. The squash-drink analogy carries the whole topic: a little squash in a lot of water tastes weak, a lot of squash in a little water tastes strong, and the difference is concentration. You will learn how to describe concentration in words and numbers, how to dilute a solution to make it weaker, and how to calculate how much solute a solution contains. These ideas appear in chemistry, biology, cooking, medicine, and farming, so the time you spend mastering them pays off far beyond one exam. By the end you will be able to make, describe, and dilute solutions with confidence.

paras: In any solution, the solute is the substance that dissolves, and the solvent is the substance it dissolves in. In sugary tea, sugar is the solute and water is the solvent. In salty water, salt is the solute and water is the solvent. In fizzy drinks, carbon dioxide gas is a solute dissolved in water. The product — the even mixture that results — is the solution. The solute is usually present in the smaller amount, and the solvent in the larger amount, though a solution can be solid, liquid, or gas: brass is a solution of zinc in copper, and air is a solution of gases in nitrogen.

Water is called the universal solvent because it dissolves more substances than any other liquid, which is why so much of chemistry and biology happens in water. But not everything dissolves: sand in water is not a solution, because the sand sits at the bottom unchanged. When a substance does not dissolve, we say it is insoluble. The test of a true solution is that it is uniform throughout — you cannot see the solute, and it will not settle out if you leave the mixture standing.

Concentration tells you how much solute is packed into a given amount of solution. Think of squash: one spoonful of squash in a full jug of water tastes weak — a dilute solution. Five spoonfuls in the same jug tastes strong — a concentrated solution. The same idea applies to salt water, medicines, and fertilisers. Concentration is a ratio, not just an amount: a jug with two spoonfuls in one litre is more concentrated than a jug with two spoonfuls in two litres, because the same solute is spread through less solvent.

This analogy also explains dilution: adding more solvent to a solution lowers its concentration without changing the amount of solute. If you add water to strong squash, the drink gets weaker, but the total squash stays the same — it is just spread thinner. Dilution is how chemists prepare weaker solutions from strong stock solutions, and it is why the instruction on a bottle of squash or medicine says to add a certain amount of water. When you describe concentration in an exam, always state both parts of the ratio: how much solute, in how much solution.
bullets: Dilute solution: little solute in a lot of solvent (weak squash).
Concentrated solution: a lot of solute in a little solvent (strong squash).
Dilution: adding solvent lowers concentration; the amount of solute stays the same.
Saturated solution: no more solute will dissolve at that temperature.

paras: Chemists measure concentration in grams per litre (g/L): the mass of solute dissolved in one litre of solution. If 20 grams of salt are dissolved to make one litre of solution, the concentration is 20 g/L. If 20 grams are dissolved to make two litres, the concentration is 10 g/L — the same solute spread through twice the volume. The formula is simple: concentration = mass of solute divided by volume of solution. Always use the volume of the whole solution, not just the water added, and always include the units.

Worked example: a pupil dissolves 15 g of sugar and adds water until the total volume is 500 mL, which is 0.5 L. Concentration = 15 / 0.5 = 30 g/L. Another example: how much salt is needed to make 2 L of a 25 g/L solution? Mass = concentration x volume = 25 x 2 = 50 g. Practise these two rearrangements — finding concentration, and finding mass — until both feel automatic, because exam questions use both directions and the arithmetic is simple once the formula is secure.

Dilution problems use one principle: the mass of solute does not change when you add solvent. So mass before = mass after, which means concentration x volume before = concentration x volume after. Suppose you have 100 mL of a 50 g/L solution and you add water until the volume is 500 mL. The new concentration is (50 x 100) / 500 = 10 g/L. The solution is five times more dilute because the volume is five times larger, and the answer can be checked by that simple ratio: volume up five times, concentration down five times.

A common mistake is to add the volumes wrongly: if you add 100 mL of water to 100 mL of solution, the final volume is 200 mL, not 100 mL. Always work with the final total volume. Another mistake is mixing units — millilitres and litres in the same calculation. Convert to one unit first, usually litres or millilitres consistently on both sides. Dilution questions are among the most reliable marks in chemistry exams, because they test one idea and one formula — so make them yours.

diagram.caption: A step-by-step flow for any dilution or concentration calculation.

sections.h2: Solubility: Why Some Things Dissolve and Others Do Not
paras: Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that will dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature. Sugar is very soluble in water; chalk is almost insoluble. Temperature matters: most solids dissolve better in hot water than in cold, which is why sugar dissolves faster in hot tea. A solution that holds as much solute as it possibly can is called saturated — add more and the extra simply sits undissolved at the bottom. A solution holding less than the maximum is unsaturated.

These ideas explain everyday observations. The sea is a solution of salts in water, but not a saturated one — it could hold more. A fizzy drink is a solution of carbon dioxide gas in water, and gases behave oppositely to solids: they dissolve better in cold water, which is why a warm fizzy drink goes flat faster than a cold one. When you write about solubility, always mention temperature, because a solubility figure without a temperature is incomplete.
