faqs.a: Under BISE Multan's condition, if the original paid bank challan does not reach the Assistant Controller (Secrecy) within the period, no action is taken on the application.

faqs.q: Can I apply for rechecking and prepare for the supplementary examination at the same time?
faqs.a: Yes, and for most students with a failed or strangely low paper, doing both is the sensible combination: rechecking covers a possible error, while preparation covers the paper itself.

title: BISE Lahore On-Screen Marking: What Changes for Inter Students
desc: BISE Lahore is moving to on-screen marking for four inter subjects. Find out what changes for students, who attends the workshops and which papers are not included.
kw: BISE Lahore on-screen marking inter subjects
intro: BISE Lahore has begun moving to on-screen marking, under letter No. 512-RCO/BISE LHR dated 7 October 2026, and the change matters for every intermediate student in the Lahore board's jurisdiction, even though most students will never attend a workshop or see the new system directly. On-screen marking means answer sheets are scanned and examiners mark them on a computer screen instead of on paper, and Lahore is starting with four intermediate subjects only: Chemistry, Biology, Computer Science and Statistics. Matric papers are not included in this first step, and the board has not yet named the first examination to be marked on screen. This guide explains what the change actually means, who is involved, what stays the same, and what students in the four subjects should and should not worry about.

paras: On-screen marking changes how examiners handle your answer sheet, not how you write it. You will still sit in an examination hall, receive a paper answer booklet, and write your answers by hand exactly as before, because the change happens after your booklet leaves the hall. Your booklet is scanned into a digital image, and examiners then view that image on a computer screen, award marks on screen, and record totals digitally. For students, the examination itself feels the same; the difference lies in the marking room, where the board gains tighter control over how marks are recorded, checked and totalled.

That distinction is worth holding on to, because it answers the most common student worry, which is whether they need to learn a new way of answering. You do not. Your job remains what it has always been: write clearly, show your working, label your diagrams, and answer every part of every question, because a scanned page rewards legible, well-organised writing just as a paper page does. If anything, on-screen marking raises the value of clear handwriting and clean layout, since an examiner reading a scanned image benefits even more from answers that are easy to follow. Prepare exactly as you would for any board paper, and let the board handle the change in how marking is done. For general board news and study guides, see the [blog](/blog/).

sections.h2: The Four Subjects in the First Step
paras: Lahore's first step covers four intermediate subjects only: Chemistry, Biology, Computer Science and Statistics. These are the subjects named in the board's 7 October 2026 letter, and no other intermediate subject is included at this stage. If your subject is not one of these four, this change does not affect your papers yet, and you should continue preparing under the existing marking arrangements without worrying about a system that does not apply to you. The board has chosen a limited first step deliberately, so that the new process can be tested and refined on a manageable set of subjects before any wider rollout is considered.

Equally important is what the letter does not include: matric papers are not part of this first step, so Class 9 and 10 students under BISE Lahore are unaffected for now. Students sometimes hear that marking is going digital and assume every paper changes at once, but the letter is specific and limited, and that specificity is good news for everyone else. A limited rollout means the board can train examiners, fix scanning and software problems, and learn from the first subjects before expanding, rather than risking disruption across all papers at once. If you study one of the four subjects, read the rest of this guide carefully; if you do not, you can set the topic aside until the board announces a further step.

diagram.alt: On-Screen Marking: What Changes and What Does Not
diagram.caption: The first step covers four inter subjects only; the student's examination experience stays the same.

sections.h2: Who Goes to the Workshops — and Who Does Not
paras: The letter arranges workshops to prepare colleges for the new system, and the invitation list is narrow by design. Each college sends one student per subject, chosen by the college, together with the principal and heads of department, which means a college offering all four subjects sends four students in total, one for each subject. Those students attend as their college's representatives, learn how the on-screen process works, and carry that understanding back to their classmates. The workshops are preparation for the system, not a new examination, and attending one does not change a student's own marks or standing.

Every other student does not attend, and that is not a disadvantage or an oversight. The workshops exist to prepare colleges and their representatives, not to teach the whole student body a new skill, because students do not need a new skill: they still write on paper in the hall. If you are not chosen, nothing is expected of you beyond your normal preparation, and you should not worry that classmates who attend have gained an advantage in marking. If you are chosen, treat it as a responsibility to your college: attend carefully, ask questions about anything unclear, and share what you learn accurately with your class, without exaggerating the change into something it is not.

sections.h2: Which Exam Comes First? What We Know and Do Not Know
paras: One question the letter leaves open is which examination will be the first to be marked on screen, and honest reporting requires saying that the board has not named it. The next intermediate examination on the calendar is the second annual examination beginning on 3 November 2026, which makes it the natural candidate in students' minds, but natural does not mean confirmed, and no student should treat the second annual as the first on-screen examination until the board says so. The gap between a reasonable guess and a board announcement is exactly where rumours grow, and this guide will not fill it with a claim the board has not made.

What students can do is watch for the board's own announcement through their college, which will receive official word before any website or chat group. If the board names the second annual examination, students in the four subjects will know in time to prepare with confidence, and if it names a later examination, nothing is lost by having prepared normally. Either way, the correct preparation is identical: study the syllabus, practise past papers, write clearly and answer completely. A marking system changes how marks are recorded, not what knowledge earns them, so the student who prepares well is ready for either system on any date the board chooses.

sections.h2: Rechecking Rules Stay Put Until the Board Says Otherwise
paras: The final point students should hold on to is that existing HSSC rechecking rules still apply until the board says otherwise. On-screen marking does not silently abolish rechecking, change its window, or alter its fee, and students who need rechecking for the 22 October 2026 result should follow the current procedure for their board without waiting for the new marking system to clarify itself. The rechecking window, counted as 15 days from 22 October, runs to about 6 November 2026, and if your board prints a different date, follow your board's date. A change in marking technology and a change in rechecking rules are two separate decisions, and only an explicit board notice can change the second.

That stability is reassuring, and it points to a general habit worth building: treat every board change as limited to what the board's letter actually says. The 7 October letter says four subjects, workshops for college representatives, and a move to on-screen marking; it does not say new syllabuses, new paper patterns, new rechecking rules or new examination dates, and none of those should be assumed. Students who read board letters this way, narrowly and literally, protect themselves from the exaggerated versions that circulate online, and they focus their energy on the one thing that has not changed at all: learning the subject well enough to earn the marks. For the current rechecking process, see [rechecking versus retotalling](/blog/board-rechecking-retotalling-difference.html), and for subject revision, see the [books section](/books.html).

title: Lighter Bags, Sharper Thinking: Study Habits for Sindh's Creative Turn
desc: Sindh's minister says pupils will be relieved of excessive book burden and guided toward creative thinking. Turn that vision into daily study habits you can start now.
kw: less book burden creative study habits Sindh
intro: In a statement reported around 20 October 2026, Sindh's Education Minister said pupils will be relieved of excessive book burden and guided toward creative thinking, as part of a revised curriculum planned for the next academic year. The revised curriculum's stated focus includes research, scientific thinking and creativity, modern trends in science, technology, mathematics, languages and social sciences, plus religious tolerance, mutual respect, gender studies and environmental protection. That is a direction, not a syllabus in force today, and this article does not pretend otherwise. What it does is translate the direction into daily study habits you can start now, with the books you already have, so that when the revised curriculum arrives, you are already the kind of learner it is designed for. Lighter bags are the minister's promise; sharper thinking is a habit you can build yourself, starting tonight.

paras: Before building habits on a statement, it is worth getting the statement right. The minister's words, as reported around 20 October 2026, were that pupils will be relieved of excessive book burden and guided toward creative thinking, within a revised curriculum from the next academic year that emphasises research, scientific thinking and creativity, modern trends across subjects, and values including tolerance, mutual respect, gender studies and environmental protection. Note the tense: this is a plan for the next academic year, not a description of the books in your bag today. Your current textbooks, examinations and syllabus remain what they are, and any habit you build should strengthen your performance in them, not distract you from them.

That distinction protects you from two mistakes. The first is waiting: students who hear that a lighter, more creative curriculum is coming sometimes relax, as though the change will do the learning for them, when in fact the next academic year rewards the students who arrive already curious and already practised in thinking. The second is discarding: students who throw away careful textbook study in the name of creativity usually lose marks in the examinations that still test the textbook, because creative thinking is an addition to knowledge, not a replacement for it. The habits below are designed to sit on top of your current study, making the same books yield more understanding, so that both today's examinations and tomorrow's curriculum find you ready.

sections.h2: From Lighter Bags to Sharper Habits
paras: A lighter bag does not automatically mean a lighter mind; it means the weight shifts from carrying many books to using one book well. The core habit is simple: for every lesson you study, do something with it beyond reading it. Explain it aloud in your own words, write a three-line summary without looking, invent one question the lesson raises, or connect it to something you saw outside school. Each of these moves forces your brain to process the material rather than merely pass your eyes over it, and processed material is remembered far longer than read material. Students who study this way often find they need fewer repeated readings, which is exactly the relief from burden the minister described, achieved by method rather than by waiting for policy.

Start small so the habit survives contact with homework and examinations. Choose one lesson a day for the full treatment: read it once, close the book, explain it aloud, and write down one question it leaves you with. Keep a small notebook for those questions and summaries, because a notebook of your own thinking becomes a revision resource no textbook can replace. Over weeks, the notebook grows into evidence of your own creative work, and revision becomes re-reading your own ideas rather than re-reading whole chapters under pressure. The habit costs ten extra minutes per lesson and returns hours of revision time later, which is a trade any student can afford.

diagram.alt: Six Daily Habits for Creative Study
diagram.caption: Small daily moves that turn the same textbook into sharper thinking.

sections.h2: Research and Scientific Thinking in Daily Study
paras: Research sounds like a university activity, but at school level it means a simple discipline: do not accept a claim until you have checked it against something. When your textbook states a fact, ask where it comes from and whether another source agrees; when a classmate states a fact, ask how they know; when a social media post states a fact, treat it as unproven until a reliable source confirms it. This is the same verification habit that protects students from fake result announcements, applied to everyday learning, and it is the foundation of scientific thinking. A student who checks claims habitually is harder to mislead in examinations, in admissions and in life, because misinformation depends on unquestioning readers.

Scientific thinking also means testing your own understanding rather than trusting your feeling of understanding. After studying a science or mathematics topic, solve a problem you have not seen before, predict an outcome before reading the answer, or explain why a wrong answer is wrong rather than merely noting the right one. Each test reveals gaps that reading alone hides, and each gap found in practice is a mark saved in the examination. Keep a list of the questions that stumped you and return to them weekly, because a question you struggled with once and then mastered is knowledge you will keep. The [solved notes](/solved.html) on this site are useful here: use them to check your working after you attempt a problem, not instead of attempting it.

sections.h2: Tolerance, Respect and the World Around You
paras: The revised curriculum's emphasis on tolerance, mutual respect, gender studies and environmental protection is sometimes dismissed as soft content beside mathematics and science, but that dismissal misunderstands what these topics teach. Tolerance and mutual respect are practised, not memorised: they show in how you discuss a classmate's different opinion, how you share credit in group work, and how you speak about people whose background differs from yours. Gender studies, at school level, means noticing who gets heard, who gets opportunities and who carries which burdens, in your classroom, your family and your community, and asking whether that distribution is fair. These are thinking skills, and they are tested in life far more often than in examinations.

Environmental protection offers the most concrete daily practice of all. Notice the water, electricity and paper your school and home use, and find one waste you can reduce this week; notice the plants, animals and open spaces in your neighbourhood, and learn the name of one you did not know. Small observations like these turn a curriculum theme into lived knowledge, and lived knowledge is what you remember and what you act on. When you discuss these topics with classmates, practise the respect the curriculum names: listen fully before replying, disagree with ideas rather than with people, and change your mind openly when a better argument appears. A classroom that practises that discipline is already living the revised curriculum, whatever year it formally arrives.

sections.h2: A Week of Creative Habits You Can Start Now
paras: Here is a week that puts the whole article into practice without overhauling your routine. On Monday, pick one lesson and explain it aloud to a family member or an empty room. On Tuesday, write three questions the lesson raises and try to answer one from another source. On Wednesday, find a real-life example of the lesson's idea and note it in your notebook. On Thursday, summarise a different lesson in three lines without looking, then check what you missed. On Friday, discuss a topic with a classmate and practise listening fully before replying. On Saturday, review your week's notebook and pick the idea you most want to remember. On Sunday, rest, because a rested mind is a creative mind, and the habit must survive the week to matter.

After a month of such weeks, judge the habit by its results, not by its intentions. Are your summaries getting sharper? Are you asking better questions? Are you remembering lessons with fewer re-readings? If yes, keep the habit and extend it to more lessons; if a particular move does not suit you, replace it with another from this article rather than abandoning the whole project. The revised curriculum, when it arrives next academic year, will ask for research, creativity, tolerance and environmental awareness, and you will already have a notebook proving you can do all four. That is the real meaning of a lighter bag: not fewer books to carry, but a stronger mind to carry what matters. For subject support alongside your habits, explore the [books section](/books.html) and the [blog](/blog/) for study guides.

It also emphasises tolerance, mutual respect, gender studies and environmental protection.

faqs.q: Is the new creative curriculum already in force?
faqs.a: No. The revised curriculum is planned for the next academic year, as stated in the minister's statement reported around 20 October 2026. Your current textbooks and syllabus remain in force.

faqs.q: What will the revised curriculum focus on?
faqs.a: Research, scientific thinking and creativity, modern trends in science, technology, mathematics, languages and social sciences, plus religious tolerance, mutual respect, gender studies and environmental protection.

faqs.q: How can I study creatively with my current books?
faqs.a: Do something with each lesson beyond reading: explain it aloud, write a three-line summary without looking, ask one question it raises, and connect it to a real-life example.

faqs.q: Does creative study mean I can skip textbook study?
faqs.a: No. Creative thinking adds to knowledge; it does not replace it. Your examinations still test the textbook, so habits must strengthen textbook learning, not distract from it.

faqs.q: What is one habit I can start today?
faqs.a: Pick one lesson, read it once, close the book, explain it aloud in your own words, and write down one question it leaves you with.

title: Waiting for BIEK Pre-Medical Part-I? Use the Wait as a Part-II Head Start
desc: No official date is published for BIEK Pre-Medical Part-I. Use the wait well: build Part-II foundations from your Part-I books with a weekly plan that keeps you moving.
kw: BIEK pre-medical part 1 waiting study plan
intro: If you are a BIEK Pre-Medical Part-I student, you are waiting for a result that has no official date. As of 26 October 2026, the Pre-Medical, Commerce and Humanities Part-I groups have not been officially announced, and the end-of-October expectation repeated by aggregator websites is an unverified guess, not a board date. Waiting without a plan is miserable: days blur, study stops, and anxiety grows with every rumour. This article offers a different use for the wait. Your Part-I books are not finished business; they are the foundations of Part-II, and every week you spend strengthening them now is a week you will not need to spend relearning them later. Here is a study plan that treats the wait as a head start, keeps you checking the right source, and keeps you moving toward Part-II regardless of when the result arrives.

sections.h2: The Wait Is Real — and So Is the Opportunity
paras: First, let the facts settle the waiting question so rumours stop running your days. BIEK announced Pre-Engineering Part-I on 2 October 2026, but Pre-Medical Part-I has no official announcement and no published date as of 26 October 2026, and BIEK releases each group separately, so one group's announcement says nothing about another group's timing. Checking the board portal, biek.edu.pk, once or twice a day is enough; checking it every hour does not bring the result sooner, and it steals the study time that would actually improve your future. Accept the wait as a fact, give it a fixed place in your day, and then get on with the work that the wait makes possible.

That work is more valuable than it looks, because the gap between Part-I and Part-II is where many strong students lose momentum. Students who stop studying while waiting often find that Part-II begins with relearning: formulas forgotten, diagrams blurred, definitions half-remembered, and the first weeks of the new class spent catching up rather than moving forward. Students who keep studying through the wait arrive at Part-II with their foundations warm, their notes organised and their confidence intact, and they learn new material faster because it lands on prepared ground. The wait is not wasted time unless you waste it, and the plan below is designed to make wasting it difficult.

Every Part-II subject grows out of Part-I, and the connection is closer than students usually realise. In Biology, the Part-I study of cells, tissues and life processes is the language in which Part-II topics are written, and a student who cannot explain a cell confidently will struggle with every system built upon it. In Chemistry, Part-I concepts such as atomic structure, bonding and periodicity return in more advanced forms, and the student who truly understands them finds Part-II far less intimidating. In Physics, the Part-I grounding in measurement, motion and forces underpins the more demanding Part-II work, and weak foundations there compound faster than anywhere else.

Use the wait to audit those foundations honestly, subject by subject. For each Part-I chapter, ask yourself whether you could explain its central idea to a classmate without the book, solve a typical problem from it, and draw its key diagram from memory. Chapters that pass all three tests need only light revision; chapters that fail any test are your waiting-period curriculum, and they deserve focused rebuilding now while there is no new class competing for your time. Work from your own Part-I textbooks and your class notes, because those are the verified sources for what you were actually taught, and avoid building foundations on guesswork about what Part-II might contain. The [solved notes](/solved.html) on this site can support your revision, and the status guide for [remaining BIEK Part-I groups](/blog/biek-part-1-remaining-groups-status-october-2026.html) keeps the waiting facts straight.

sections.h2: A Weekly Plan That Uses the Wait Well
paras: A waiting plan needs a shape, or the days will dissolve into good intentions. Divide your week into three kinds of days: foundation days for rebuilding weak Part-I chapters, practice days for solving problems and past-paper questions from those chapters, and one review day for testing yourself and organising notes. Keep the load realistic, around three to four focused hours a day, because a plan you abandon after three days is worse than a modest plan you keep for a month. Study in the morning when your mind is freshest, keep your phone away during study blocks, and end each day by writing down what you covered and what remains, so tomorrow starts with a clear task rather than a vague intention.

Protect one more element of the week: a rest day, or at least a rest half-day, in which you do no board study at all. Waiting is tiring in itself, and a student who studies seven days a week through an indefinite wait will burn out before the result even arrives. Rest is part of the plan, not a break from it, and it keeps the other six days sharp. If the result arrives mid-week, the plan adapts instantly: celebrate or regroup as needed, then carry your strengthened foundations straight into Part-II preparation, because the work you did while waiting belongs to you regardless of what the result says. That is the real point of the plan, which is that no announcement can waste it.

diagram.alt: Your Waiting Week: A Part-II Head Start
diagram.caption: A weekly shape that rebuilds Part-I foundations while the result is pending.

sections.h2: What Not to Trust While You Wait
paras: The waiting period attracts rumours the way a still pond attracts mosquitoes, and the most important waiting skill is refusing to drink from it. Do not trust any date for the Pre-Medical Part-I result that does not come from biek.edu.pk or your college, because as of 26 October 2026 no official date exists, and every date you see elsewhere is either an aggregator's expectation or an invention. Do not trust screenshots of result pages, forwarded messages claiming inside information, or coaching advertisements promising early access, because none of these can produce a result the board has not announced. Do not trust a friend's claim that their result is out unless you can find the same announcement on the board portal yourself.

Equally, do not trust the feeling that waiting means you should stop preparing. The students most damaged by a long wait are not the ones who studied through it, but the ones who paused everything and then faced Part-II cold, whether their result was good or bad. Keep your routine, keep your notes growing, and treat each rumour as a test of the verification habit: source, board notice, college confirmation, in that order. If a claim fails any step, discard it and return to your plan, because the plan is the one thing in this period that is fully under your control, and it is the thing that will still matter when the result finally arrives.

Checking well is a skill with two parts: checking the right place, and checking at the right frequency. The right place is biek.edu.pk, typed by yourself, plus your college notice board, which receives the board's word directly. The right frequency is once in the morning and once in the evening, at fixed times you choose in advance, so that checking becomes a brief errand rather than a compulsion. Between those fixed checks, put the result out of your mind deliberately: close the result pages, silence the chat groups that trade rumours, and return to the study block in front of you. A student who checks twice a day learns of the result within hours of its announcement, which is exactly as fast as anyone needs to know.

When the announcement does come, handle it calmly whatever it says. Read the board's notice in full, note which groups it covers, and confirm the news with your college before acting on it, because even real news is sometimes misread in excitement. If you passed, your waiting-period foundations become your Part-II advantage immediately. If you did not pass everything, your foundations are still stronger than they were, and the papers that remain are fewer and clearer for the work you did. Either way, the wait will have served you, because you refused to let an unpublished date run your life, and you used the empty weeks to build something no announcement can take away. For help reading your result when it arrives, see the guide to [reading a marksheet](/blog/board-marksheet-reading-codes-grades.html).

Part-I books are the foundations of Part-II, so rebuilding them now is a genuine head start.

faqs.q: Has BIEK announced the Pre-Medical Part-I result?
faqs.a: No. As of 26 October 2026, Pre-Medical, Commerce and Humanities Part-I have not been officially announced, and no official date has been published.

faqs.q: Should I stop studying until the result comes?
faqs.a: No. Use the wait to rebuild weak Part-I chapters, because those chapters are the foundations of Part-II, and students who stop studying lose momentum that is hard to recover.

faqs.q: How often should I check for the result?
faqs.a: Twice a day at fixed times, on biek.edu.pk and your college notice board. More frequent checking does not bring the result sooner.

faqs.q: Can I prepare for Part-II without knowing the Part-II syllabus?
faqs.a: Yes, by strengthening your Part-I foundations from your own textbooks and notes. Avoid inventing Part-II syllabus claims; solid Part-I understanding is what Part-II builds on.

faqs.q: What should I do when the result finally arrives?
faqs.a: Read the board's notice in full, confirm it with your college, and carry your strengthened foundations into Part-II preparation, whatever the result says.

title: After the October Results: What Happens Next for Sindh Board Students
desc: BIEK Pre-Engineering Part-I is out, BSEK 9th class is declared and other Sindh groups are pending. Here is what happens next, without borrowing Punjab's dates.
kw: Sindh boards after October results next steps
intro: October 2026 has been a busy month for Sindh's board students, but it has not been a tidy one: some results are out, some are pending, and the two situations demand different responses from different students. BIEK announced the Pre-Engineering Part-I result on 2 October 2026, BSEK declared the 9th class annual examination, reported on 12 October 2026, and the other BIEK Part-I groups remain unannounced with no official date published as of 26 October 2026. Meanwhile Punjab's second annual examinations begin on 3 November 2026, and some Sindh students have mistakenly applied Punjab's dates to their own plans. This article sorts the verified picture from the confusion, tells each group of students what happens next for them, and names the only sources that can tell you what comes after that.

sections.h2: October 2026: What Has Actually Been Announced
paras: Start with the verified record, because everything else in this article depends on it. BIEK, the Board of Intermediate Education Karachi, announced the HSC Part-I Science Pre-Engineering Group Annual Examination 2026 result on 2 October 2026, with 15,044 students registered, 14,683 appeared and 6,310 passing all six papers. Separately, BSEK, the Board of Secondary Education Karachi, declared the 9th class annual examination 2026 for Science and General groups, reported on 12 October 2026. These are two different boards handling two different levels: BSEK handles matric, Classes 9 and 10, while BIEK handles intermediate, Classes 11 and 12, and confusing the two boards is the first error students make when they hear result news.

For context, BIEK's Part-II groups for 2026 are already out, having been announced across July, August and September: Pre-Medical Part-II on 31 July, Humanities Part-II on 7 August, Pre-Engineering Part-II on 17 August, Science General Part-II on 27 August, Commerce Part-II on 14 September, and Home Economics, Humanities Private and Special Candidates on 31 July. That spread across three months is normal for BIEK, which releases each group separately, and it explains why October's picture looks uneven. A student whose group is out and a student whose group is pending are not experiencing a delay and an on-time result; they are experiencing the same system at different points in its ordinary schedule.

sections.h2: What Is Still Pending — and Why That Is Normal
paras: The pending list is short and specific: BIEK's Pre-Medical, Commerce and Humanities Part-I groups have no official announcement as of 26 October 2026, and no official date has been published for any of them. The end-of-October expectation repeated by aggregator websites is an unverified guess, not a board date, and students in these groups should plan as though the announcement could come at any time, without believing any particular day. That uncertainty is uncomfortable, but it is not unusual, and it is not evidence that anything has gone wrong with checking or compilation. Groups are released when their work is complete, and the board's silence about a date is simply the absence of a date, not a hidden problem.

If your group is pending, your next steps are the same as any waiting student's: keep studying, keep checking the board portal at fixed times, and refuse rumours. Do not pay for any service promising early access to your result, do not travel to the board office on the strength of a social media post, and do not let a classmate's different group result convince you that yours must be imminent. Your result will be announced on the board's schedule, and when it is, it will be visible to every student on the same portal at the same time. The status guide for [remaining BIEK Part-I groups](/blog/biek-part-1-remaining-groups-status-october-2026.html) tracks exactly which groups are out and which are pending, and it is the best companion to this waiting period.

diagram.caption: Three different October situations, three different next steps — start from your own board and group.

sections.h2: Do Not Borrow Punjab's Dates for Sindh
paras: The most consequential confusion this October is the borrowing of Punjab's dates by Sindh students. Punjab's HSSC Second Annual Examination begins on 3 November 2026, with Part-II papers from 3 to 16 November and Part-I papers from 17 to 28 November, and Punjab's rechecking window runs 15 days from its 22 October result. None of those dates belongs to Sindh. Sindh's boards run their own examinations, their own results and their own procedures, and a Sindh student who plans around 3 November as though it were a Sindh date will prepare for an examination that is not theirs, while missing whatever their own board actually announces.

The confusion is understandable, because Punjab's dates dominate national result websites and social media, and a student searching for second annual news will meet Punjab's schedule first. The defence is a simple question to ask of every date you encounter: which board announced this, and is it my board? If the answer is a Punjab board and you study under a Sindh board, the date is information about another province, not an instruction for you. Keep your own board's portal and your college notice as your only sources of dates, and treat every other date as background until your own board confirms it. Provinces share a country, not a date sheet, and remembering that distinction saves real mistakes.

sections.h2: Your Three Checkpoints: Portal, College, Gazette
paras: Whatever your situation, three checkpoints will carry you through the weeks after October's results. The first is your board's portal: biek.edu.pk for intermediate students in Karachi, bsek.edu.pk for matric students in Karachi, biselrk.edu.pk for Larkana board students, and bisesuksindh.edu.pk for Sukkur board students, each typed by yourself rather than clicked from a message. The second is your college or school notice board, which receives the board's word directly and can confirm anything you find online. The third is the gazette, for groups whose results are out, because it is the board's published record of roll numbers, marks and papers passed, and it settles disputes that online lookups cannot.

Use the three checkpoints in order whenever a claim reaches you: portal first, college second, gazette third where it applies. If the portal does not show it, it has not been announced; if the college cannot confirm it, it is unverified; if the gazette contradicts it, the gazette is the record to trust. Students who run every claim through these checkpoints rarely act on rumours, and they rarely miss genuine announcements either, because genuine announcements pass all three checks easily. Make the checkpoints a habit now, and they will serve you through every result season, admission cycle and board notice you meet in the years ahead. The guide to [which board handles what](/blog/bsek-biek-difference-which-board-handles-what.html) explains the board divisions behind these portals.

sections.h2: Planning the Next Weeks Without Invented Dates
paras: Planning without dates feels impossible, but it is actually the normal condition of student life between announcements, and it works when you plan around tasks instead of dates. If your result is out, your tasks are clear: read your gazette entry, list your papers passed, decide on recovery or Part-II preparation, and discuss both with a teacher. If your result is pending, your tasks are equally clear: keep studying your Part-I foundations, keep checking the portal twice a day, and keep rumours out of your schedule. In both cases, the next task does not depend on a date you do not have, and a student who completes today's task is better prepared than a student who waits for a date to tell them what to do.

Resist the temptation to fill the gap with invented dates of your own, whether that means assuming the result must come this week, or assuming it cannot come before next month. Both assumptions distort your planning: the first creates panic when the week passes without news, and the second creates complacency that wastes study time. Plan week by week, review your progress every Saturday, and let the board's announcement, when it arrives, interrupt a plan that is already working rather than rescue a plan that never started. October's results have given some Sindh students answers and others a wait, but both groups share the same next step, which is to keep learning, keep checking the right sources, and keep their plans anchored in verified facts. For study support in the meantime, see the [solved notes](/solved.html).

title: How Colleges Use Your Part-I Marks for Part-II Admission
desc: Your Part-I marks shape your Part-II subject choices and college conversations. Learn how colleges read them, what to ask and how to plan when marks disappoint.
intro: When Part-I results arrive, most students read them as a verdict on the past year, but colleges read them as a guide to the next one. Your Part-I marks shape the conversations you will have about Part-II subject choices, about which streams remain open to you, and about how much support you may need in the year ahead, and understanding that reading helps you walk into those conversations prepared rather than anxious. This guide explains, in general terms, how colleges use Part-I performance when they talk to students about Part-II admission, set against the October 2026 context in which BIEK's Pre-Engineering Part-I result is out since 2 October while other Part-I groups remain pending. It names no merit percentages, cut-offs or college policies, because those vary by college and must be confirmed with your own college, and it focuses instead on the habits and questions that help every student, whatever their marks.

sections.h2: Why Part-I Marks Matter Beyond the Result Card
paras: Part-I marks matter for Part-II because Part-II builds directly on Part-I, and colleges know that a student's Part-I record is the best available evidence of how they will handle the harder year ahead. A student with strong Part-I marks in a subject has shown they can handle its concepts, its workload and its examination style, which makes them a safer bet for the advanced version of the same subject. A student with weak Part-I marks in a subject has shown, at minimum, that the subject needs more work, and colleges will want to discuss whether that work is realistic alongside everything else Part-II demands. Neither reading is a judgement of worth; both are practical judgements about readiness, and students who understand that framing can discuss their marks without defensiveness.

Marks also matter because Part-II admission conversations happen quickly and often informally, in a teacher's office or a college corridor, rather than through a single formal announcement. A student who arrives with their marks organised, their strengths and weaknesses honestly assessed, and a clear idea of what they want to study will shape that conversation far better than a student who arrives with only a result slip and anxiety. Preparation for the conversation is therefore part of preparation for Part-II itself, and it costs nothing but an hour of honest reflection. Write down your marks subject by subject, mark the subjects you enjoyed and the subjects you struggled with, and note any subject where your mark surprised you in either direction, because those surprises are exactly what a good college conversation explores.

sections.h2: Subject Choices: Where Part-I Marks Speak Loudest
paras: The loudest voice Part-I marks have is in subject choice, because Part-II subjects are not chosen freely but in streams and combinations that presume certain foundations. A student who excelled in Biology and Chemistry will find the medical stream conversation straightforward, while a student who struggled in Mathematics will face a serious discussion before continuing with a mathematics-heavy combination. That discussion is not a punishment; it is the college protecting the student from a year of struggle in a subject whose foundations are shaky, and students who hear it that way make better decisions than students who hear it as rejection. The honest question to ask yourself is not which subjects sound impressive, but which subjects you can actually build on for another year.

Use your Part-I marks as a map of your foundations, not as a cage. A weak mark in a subject you love is a reason to plan extra work, not necessarily a reason to abandon the subject, provided you are honest about the effort that extra work requires. A strong mark in a subject you dislike is a reason to think carefully, because a year of studying something you dislike, even successfully, is a heavy cost. Talk to the teachers of the subjects in question, because they have seen your classwork as well as your examination marks, and their view of your readiness is often more complete than any single result. Bring your marks, your questions and your willingness to listen, and let the conversation, not the mark alone, decide the choice. For general guidance on reading results, see [reading a marksheet](/blog/board-marksheet-reading-codes-grades.html).

diagram.alt: How Part-I Marks Shape Part-II Conversations
diagram.caption: Your marks inform the conversation; your teachers and your own reflection complete it.

paras: Admission conversations for Part-II vary widely between colleges, and this guide deliberately describes them in general terms, because no single description fits every college's policy. Some colleges admit their own Part-I students into Part-II almost automatically, using marks mainly to guide subject choices and support. Others apply stricter internal criteria, particularly for popular streams, and use Part-I marks as one factor among several, alongside attendance, classwork and teacher recommendations. Still others treat Part-II admission as a fresh application, with its own forms and timelines. Because the range is so wide, the only reliable statement about your college's process is the one your college itself gives you, and asking early is always better than assuming.

Prepare for the conversation by preparing questions, not just answers. Ask which subjects your marks qualify you to continue, and what support exists if you want to continue a subject where your mark was weak. Ask about timelines, forms and any documents you need to bring, so that a missed paper does not delay your admission. Ask whether your college offers a probationary or conditional route for students on the borderline of a stream, and what conditions such a route carries. Write the answers down, because admission conversations are easily misremembered under stress, and a written record lets you compare what was said with what later happens. A student who asks clear questions signals seriousness, and colleges notice seriousness.

Disappointing Part-I marks hurt, and the first thing to say is that the hurt is legitimate and shared by thousands of students every year, including students who later do very well in Part-II. A weak Part-I result is information, not identity: it tells you where your preparation, your understanding or your examination technique fell short, and each of those causes has a remedy. Preparation gaps are fixed by steady study; understanding gaps are fixed by rebuilding concepts from the textbook with a teacher's help; examination technique gaps are fixed by practising timed answers and learning to read questions carefully. The remedy differs by cause, which is why the most useful response to a disappointing mark is diagnosis, not despair, and why a teacher's help in diagnosing it is worth seeking promptly.

It is also worth remembering, in the October 2026 context, that not every Part-I student even has a result yet: Pre-Engineering Part-I is out since 2 October, but other BIEK Part-I groups remain pending, so some of your classmates are still waiting while you plan. If your result disappointed you, do not let it also isolate you; talk to classmates, teachers and family, and treat the disappointment as a shared, solvable problem rather than a private shame. Students who recover best are usually those who act fastest: they identify the weak subjects within days, arrange support within a week, and start the rebuilding work while the disappointment is still fresh enough to motivate them. Time softens disappointment, but only action converts it into improvement, and the sooner action starts, the more of Part-II it can influence.

sections.h2: Questions to Ask Your College — and Yourself
paras: End your preparation with two lists of questions: one for your college, and one for yourself. For your college, ask how Part-I marks affect Part-II admission in your institution, which subject combinations your marks support, what the admission timeline and documents are, and what help exists for students who want to strengthen a weak subject. For yourself, ask which subjects you genuinely want to study for another year, which weak subjects you are willing to work hard to rebuild, and what kind of support you need to succeed, whether that means tutoring, study groups, or simply a better daily routine. The college's answers tell you what is possible; your answers tell you what is desirable, and a good Part-II choice sits where the two overlap.

Take both lists to your college conversation, and take notes during it, because the combination of a prepared student and a clear college process produces decisions that survive the pressure of results season. If the conversation goes badly, or if you feel pushed toward a choice you do not want, seek a second conversation with another teacher or a senior staff member, because one rushed discussion should not decide a year of your education. And if your result is still pending, use the waiting time to prepare both lists now, so that when your result arrives, you are ready to act within days rather than weeks. Part-I marks open the Part-II conversation, but they do not close it; the student who arrives prepared, honest and curious will always have more room to move than the mark alone suggests. title: Didn't Clear All Six Papers? Your BIEK Pre-Engineering Recovery Plan
desc: Cleared some BIEK Pre-Engineering papers but not all six? Plan your recovery by papers passed, understand the ungraded rule and use scrutiny wisely.
kw: BIEK pre-engineering recovery plan papers passed
intro: If your BIEK Pre-Engineering Part-I result, announced on 2 October 2026, shows fewer than six papers passed, you are far from alone, and you are far from finished. Out of 14,683 students who appeared, 6,310 passed all six papers, which means 8,373 students did not clear all six, spread across every possible count: 79 passed five papers, 747 passed four, 1,827 passed three, 1,864 passed two, and 1,783 passed one. Each of those groups faces a different recovery task, and the biggest mistake is treating them all as the same failure. This article builds your recovery plan from your own papers-passed count, explains the ungraded rule that may sit behind your result, and shows how scrutiny fits, or does not fit, into your next steps. Recovery is not a single road; it is a set of roads, and your count tells you which one is yours.

sections.h2: First, Read Your Result for What It Actually Says
paras: Recovery starts with an honest reading of your result, and the gazette is the best place to do it, because it groups candidates by papers passed and lists marks paper by paper. Find your entry, note your papers-passed group, and write down, for each paper, whether you passed it and what mark you received. That simple list is your recovery map: the papers on it that you passed are finished business, and the papers on it that you did not pass are the whole of your remaining task. Students who skip this step often carry a vague sense of failure into their recovery, studying everything a little and nothing properly, while students who make the list study only what remains, with full energy.

Separate two different kinds of remaining papers as you list them, because they need different responses. A paper you narrowly missed, where your mark sits close to the pass line, usually needs revision and practice rather than relearning, and it is the quickest win in your recovery. A paper where your mark is far below the line, or where you scored under 40 percent and therefore fall under the ungraded rule, needs rebuilding from the foundations, and it deserves the largest share of your study time. Be honest about which kind each paper is, and ask a teacher to check your sorting if you are unsure, because a recovery plan built on a misdiagnosis wastes the very weeks it is meant to save. Use your college's help and the board's own record to confirm your entry, and the [solved notes](/solved.html) can support your rebuilding work. The earlier guide on [reading a gazette](/blog/biek-pre-engineering-gazette-how-to-read-2026.html) explains the gazette's layout in general.

sections.h2: Planning by Papers Passed: From Five Down to One
paras: Your papers-passed count sets the scale of your recovery, and each count deserves its own plan. If you passed five papers, your task is narrow and focused: one paper stands between you and a complete result, so give that paper daily attention, practise its past papers intensively, and treat its examination as a single-paper campaign rather than a whole-year repeat. If you passed four papers, two papers remain, and your plan should split your time between them by weakness, giving the weaker paper more hours while keeping the stronger one warm with regular practice. In both cases, protect your passed papers by not neglecting them entirely in conversation, but do not waste study hours relearning what you have already passed.

If you passed three papers or fewer, your recovery is larger, and it needs a longer view and a steadier rhythm. With three papers passed, three remain, and the sensible approach is to rebuild them one at a time in order of difficulty, starting with the paper you came closest to passing, so that early progress builds confidence for the harder rebuilds. With two or one papers passed, the honest assessment is that your foundations need broad rebuilding, and you should discuss with your teachers whether your recovery runs alongside Part-II preparation, or whether a different sequence suits your situation better, since that decision depends on your college and your board's eligibility rules. Whatever your count, the principle is the same: the fewer papers you passed, the more your plan should emphasise foundations over shortcuts, and the more it should lean on teachers rather than on solitary struggle.

diagram.alt: Your Recovery Plan by Papers Passed
diagram.caption: Each papers-passed count faces a different task; start from your own count.

sections.h2: The Ungraded Rule: Under 40 Percent Means Reappear
paras: Behind many recovery plans sits the new grading rule that BIEK applies under the IBCC and Sindh Universities and Boards Department decision: a candidate who scores under 40 percent in any paper is graded as ungraded in that paper, which means the paper is not passed, and the candidate reappears in that paper subject to eligibility. This rule changes how you should read a low mark, because a mark in the thirties is not a narrow miss to be nudged over the line by rechecking, but a paper to be genuinely relearned and reappeared in. Students who misunderstand the rule sometimes spend their recovery window chasing a checking error in a paper that actually needs rebuilding, and they lose the time that rebuilding required.

If one or more of your papers falls under the ungraded rule, make those papers the centre of your plan, and be realistic about what rebuilding them takes. Return to the textbook chapters behind the paper, work through them with a teacher's guidance, and practise until you can solve typical questions without help, because a reappearance that repeats the same preparation usually repeats the same result. Check your eligibility for reappearing with your college, since reappearance is subject to eligibility and the conditions are the board's, not yours to assume. The guide to the [new grading system and the ungraded rule](/blog/biek-new-grading-system-ungraded-40-percent.html) explains the rule's background, and your teachers can confirm how it applies to your specific papers.

sections.h2: Scrutiny: What Rs 1,000 Per Paper Buys — and What It Does Not
paras: Scrutiny is the option students reach for first and understand least, so it deserves a plain explanation. BIEK's scrutiny fee is Rs 1,000 per paper, and no scrutiny deadline was published on BIEK's pages at the time of checking, which means you must confirm the current position with your college or the board rather than assuming a date. Scrutiny, like rechecking elsewhere, is a checking process: it verifies that your paper was handled correctly, and it does not re-mark your answers or rescue a paper whose answers were weak. It fits the student who has a specific reason to suspect a handling error in a particular paper, and it fits that student only.

Before paying Rs 1,000 for any paper, ask yourself whether you have such a reason. Did your mark in that paper fall far below your performance in class tests and your own sense of the examination? Did a teacher who knows your work find the mark surprising? Is there a specific anomaly, such as a paper whose total looks inconsistent with its parts? If you can answer yes with specifics, scrutiny may be worth the fee for that paper. If your honest answer is that the paper simply went badly, the fee is better spent on nothing at all, and the time is better spent rebuilding the paper for reappearance. Scrutiny and recovery are not alternatives; scrutiny checks the past result, while recovery builds the next one, and most students with papers to clear need the second far more than the first. For the Sindh process in detail, see [scrutiny and rechecking in Sindh](/blog/board-result-scrutiny-rechecking-sindh-how-to-apply.html).

sections.h2: Your Recovery Timetable Without Invented Dates
paras: A recovery plan needs a timetable, but this article will not invent one for you, because reappearance dates and second sittings depend on board eligibility and board announcements that this article does not presume. What you can timetable today is the preparation, and preparation timetabled well is what makes any future date workable. Divide your remaining papers into weekly blocks, giving each paper a set number of study days per week in proportion to its weakness, and end each week with a self-test on the papers you studied. Keep a simple log of what you covered and what you still cannot do, because that log becomes the evidence you show a teacher when you ask for help, and it keeps your recovery honest when motivation dips.

Alongside preparation, keep two administrative tasks on your list: confirming your eligibility for reappearance with your college, and confirming the current scrutiny position, including its fee and any deadline the board has since published, before you spend money on it. Both confirmations cost a single visit or message each, and both prevent the two costliest recovery mistakes, which are preparing for a sitting you are not eligible for, and paying for a process whose window has closed. Recovery is not glamorous work, and it rarely feels as good as a fresh start, but students who do it properly, paper by paper and week by week, routinely turn a partial result into a complete one. Your count tells you where you stand; your plan decides where you finish, and the plan starts with the next study session, not with the next announcement.

title: Karachi Board 11th Class Result 2026 Announced — BIEK HSC Part-I Pre-Medical, Commerce, Arts & More
desc: BIEK Karachi announced the remaining HSC Part-I 2026 results on 26 October 2026. Check by roll number, gazette and app, with group-wise pass percentages.
kw: Karachi board 11th class result 2026, BIEK HSC Part-I result 2026 announced, BIEK 1st year result 2026 check by roll number
intro: First-year students in Karachi have their results. The Board of Intermediate Education Karachi (BIEK) announced the Intermediate Part-I (Class XI / 1st Year) Annual Examination 2026 results for all remaining groups on Monday, 26 October 2026, on the instructions of BIEK Chairman Faqir Muhammad Lakho. The announcement, recorded in BIEK Press Release No. BIEK/PR/152/2026 dated 26 October 2026, covers Science Pre-Medical, Science General, Commerce (Regular and Private), Humanities/Arts (Regular and Private), Special Candidates (Arts Regular) and Home Economics. It completes the Karachi first-year picture for 2026: the Science Pre-Engineering group had already been announced separately earlier in October, on 2 October 2026, so this post is only about the groups declared on 26 October. This guide explains how to check your result by seat (roll) number on the board website and app, how to use the official gazette, what each group's pass percentage was, what the new 'Ungraded' rule means if you scored below 40 per cent in a paper, and what to do next.

sections.h2: The announcement: which groups were declared on 26 October 2026
paras: BIEK does not release all of its intermediate groups on a single day. For the HSC Part-I Annual Examination 2026, the Science Pre-Engineering group came first, on 2 October 2026. The 26 October 2026 announcement covers everything else: Science Pre-Medical, Science General, Commerce Regular, Commerce Private, Humanities/Arts Regular, Humanities/Arts Private, Special Candidates (Arts Regular) and Home Economics. If your group is Pre-Engineering, your result was already out weeks ago — do not wait for a second announcement for that group.

The results are published as gazette lists in which candidates are grouped by how many papers they passed, with the marks for each paper shown beside the seat number. That format matters for first-year students: unlike a simple pass-or-fail list, the gazette tells you exactly which papers you cleared and which ones still need work. Keep your seat number slip ready before you start searching, because every checking method — the website, the app and the gazette — is built around that number. The online copy of your result is provisional; the board's own record, issued through the board and your college, is the official one.

Students and parents should be careful about one common confusion. BIEK is Karachi's intermediate board, while the Board of Secondary Education Karachi (BSEK) handles Karachi's matric (SSC) examinations. A first-year result belongs to BIEK, not BSEK. Our guide to the [difference between BSEK and BIEK](/blog/bsek-biek-difference-which-board-handles-what.html) explains which board handles what, and the [books catalogue](/books.html) and [solved notes library](/solved.html) can help with the next class once you know your result.

sections.h2: How to check your Karachi 11th class result online
paras: The most direct way to see your result is the board's own website. On announcement day the site gets heavy traffic, so if a page does not load on the first try, wait a few minutes and try again rather than submitting the same search repeatedly. The steps below follow the method described in the announcement reports.

Before you begin, make sure you are looking at the HSC Part-I Annual 2026 result for your own group. Selecting the wrong group — for example, Commerce when you sat Pre-Medical — will simply return no record, even though your result has been announced. Double-check the group name on your admit card before searching.

Step 2: Select HSC Part-I Annual Examination 2026 and then your group (for example, Science Pre-Medical or Commerce Regular).
Step 3: Enter your seat (roll) number exactly as printed on your admit card.
Step 4: Submit the search and wait for your detailed result to appear.

sections.h2: Check by gazette and the official BIEK app
paras: The second method is the official result gazette: the complete PDF list of candidates' results published on the board website. For the Commerce Regular group, the board released a 172-page gazette containing the seat numbers and marks of candidates who passed one or more examination papers. Download the gazette PDF for your group, open it, and use your reader's search function — Ctrl+F on a computer, or the search option in a mobile PDF app — to find your seat number. The gazette is slower than the portal for a single student, but it is the best fallback when the website is busy, and it serves as the official record of the announcement.

BIEK also provides its results through its official Android app, available on the Google Play Store by searching for 'BIEK'. The app route uses the same seat-number search as the website. This guide uses only the checking methods confirmed in the announcement reports — the board website, the official app and the gazette. Do not pay for, or trust, result codes circulating on unofficial pages unless BIEK itself publishes one for this result. For help reading a gazette against an online result, see our guide on the [difference between a gazette and an online result](/blog/board-result-gazette-vs-online-result-difference.html).

sections.h2: Key statistics: pass percentages group by group
paras: Across the eight groups announced on 26 October 2026, 91,575 candidates appeared and 41,501 passed all of their papers, an overall pass rate of 45.32 per cent. The pass percentage here means candidates who cleared every paper of their group — six papers for Science and Arts groups, seven for Commerce and Home Economics — as reported from the board's figures. A candidate who passed some papers but not all of them is listed in the gazette under the number of papers passed, not counted in the 'passed all papers' total.

Science Pre-Medical saw 24,544 candidates appear out of 25,157 registered, with 11,966 passing all six papers — a pass rate of 48.75 per cent. Science General recorded 15,036 passes out of 30,386 who appeared, at 49.48 per cent, the highest rate among the large groups. Commerce Regular, the largest single group after Science General, had 22,693 appear and 9,332 pass all papers (41.12 per cent), while Commerce Private recorded 628 passes out of 1,413 who appeared (44.44 per cent).

Humanities (Arts) Regular recorded 3,748 passes out of 10,678 who appeared (35.10 per cent), and Humanities (Arts) Private recorded 692 passes out of 1,623 (42.64 per cent). Special Candidates (Arts Regular) had the highest pass rate of the announcement at 59.79 per cent (58 out of 97), while Home Economics recorded the lowest at 29.08 per cent (41 out of 141). These are group averages, not individual verdicts: a student who passed four of six papers is much closer to completing first year than the headline percentage suggests, because only the remaining papers need to be retaken.

sections.h2: The new grading rule: what 'Ungraded' means
paras: This year's Intermediate Part-I results use a new grading system introduced following decisions by the Inter Boards Coordination Commission (IBCC) and the Sindh government's Universities and Boards Department. Under it, a candidate who scores below 40 per cent in any paper is declared 'Ungraded' in that paper. An Ungraded paper is not counted as passed, even if the candidate's overall total looks comfortable.

The practical consequence is straightforward: you must reappear in any paper in which you were declared Ungraded, provided you meet the other eligibility conditions for taking that examination. Science groups' optional subjects in this cycle were checked through E-Assessment (OMR) and E-Marking, according to the announcement reports. If a paper shows as Ungraded on your result, do not assume it will be adjusted later — watch BIEK's official announcements for the improvement and supplementary examination schedule and form submission dates, and prepare for that paper as a separate examination.

sections.h2: What to do next: scrutiny, reappearing and 12th class
paras: First, verify your details. Compare your name, seat number and subject-wise marks against your admit card, and report any mismatch to your college and the board promptly — corrections become harder once the official record is finalised. Keep a saved copy of your online result, but remember it is provisional until the board's official record is issued.

If you believe a paper was not marked correctly, BIEK's scrutiny and rechecking route is separate from simply checking the result. Apply only through BIEK's official scrutiny notice for this examination, and confirm the fee and deadline in that notice before applying — this post does not state a fee or deadline because none was verified for this announcement. Our guide to [scrutiny and rechecking in Sindh](/blog/board-result-scrutiny-rechecking-sindh-how-to-apply.html) explains how the process works in general, but the board's own notice for HSC Part-I 2026 is the authority for your application.

If you have Ungraded papers, start preparing for those papers now rather than waiting for the supplementary schedule to be published. First-year marks feed into your composite intermediate total, so a strong 12th-class performance, combined with cleared first-year papers, still leaves you well placed for university and entry-test admissions. Students who cleared everything should turn their full attention to 12th class, where the Part-II result carries the decisive weight.

sections.h2: Reading your result: passed all papers, some papers, or not yet
paras: The headline pass percentage counts only candidates who passed all papers. That is why the board also published a breakdown by how many papers each candidate passed. A student who passed six papers, for example, is listed in that category — not in the 'passed all papers' total, and not simply as a failure. Understanding that breakdown is essential, because it tells you exactly how much work remains: only the papers you did not pass need to be cleared in the next examination, under the board's rules.

The reported breakdown, shared by the Controller of Examinations, is: 21,999 candidates passed six papers only, 11,006 passed five papers only, 7,431 passed four papers only, 4,409 passed three papers only, 3,101 passed two papers only, and 2,439 passed one paper only. Candidates who passed only some papers will need to clear the remaining papers in the next examination as per board rules. Do not treat a partial pass as a complete pass, and do not treat it as starting again from zero either — your passed papers stand, and your effort should focus on the remaining ones.

If your result shows a paper as not passed, check the marks in that paper carefully. Under the new grading system described below, a paper below 40 per cent is not counted as passed. If you believe there is an error in your name, roll number or marks, report it to your school and the board promptly, and keep a saved copy of your online result. For general guidance on how an online result differs from a gazette record, see our guide on the [difference between a gazette and an online result](/blog/board-result-gazette-vs-online-result-difference.html).

According to the board's press release of 28 October 2026, a total of 180,054 students registered for the Class 9 Science Group First Annual Examinations 2026, of whom 177,923 appeared and 2,131 remained absent. Of those who appeared, 123,757 candidates passed all subjects, giving the overall pass percentage of 69.56 per cent. The board reported that 53,849 candidates failed, as reported in the announcement coverage. These are the figures that were consistently reported across the announcement reports, and this post uses no other totals for this result.

The 69.56 per cent figure is lower than the previous year's Class IX Science Group pass rate. HUM English reported that in 2025, 137,350 of the 175,511 candidates who appeared passed all their papers, a pass rate of 78.26 per cent. The drop does not change any individual student's result, but it does put this year's result in context: a larger share of candidates this year will be clearing remaining papers in the next examination, and schools and students should plan revision for those papers now rather than waiting for a later announcement.

No position-holder list for this result was reported in the announcement coverage used for this post, so none is named here. If BSEK publishes a position list separately, it will be on the board's own website, and this post does not guess at any names or marks.

sections.h2: The new grading rule: passing marks raised to 40%
paras: This is the first year of a new grading system for Class 9, applied from the First Annual Examinations 2026 following a decision of the Inter Boards Coordination Commission (IBCC) and the Sindh government's Universities and Boards Department. Under the new scheme, BSEK has raised the passing marks from 33 per cent to 40 per cent for Class 9 from 2026 (and for Class 10 from 2027). In practical terms, a paper with less than 40 per cent marks is not counted as passed, even if the candidate's overall total looks comfortable.

That change explains why some students who expected to pass on the old 33 per cent threshold may find a paper marked as not passed this year. It is not a marking error: it is the new threshold. The same 40 per cent rule was applied in Karachi's intermediate results this year, where a paper below 40 per cent is declared 'Ungraded'. Our guide to the [new grading system and the 40 per cent rule](/blog/biek-new-grading-system-ungraded-40-percent.html) explains how that rule works at intermediate level; for Class 9, the key point is the same — every paper must individually reach 40 per cent to count as passed.

For revision, that means subject-by-subject preparation, not just total-marks preparation. A student who passed five papers and missed one by a small margin should focus revision on that one paper's syllabus, past papers and weak topics, rather than re-studying everything. The [books catalogue](/books.html) and [solved notes library](/solved.html) can help with that focused revision once you know which papers remain.

sections.h2: What to do next: reappearing, scrutiny and Class 10
paras: First, verify your details. If you passed all papers, your next step is Class 10. Start with the subjects you found hardest in Class 9, because Class 10 builds directly on them, and keep your Class 9 notes for revision. If you passed some papers only, make a short list of the remaining papers and start preparing for them now, under the board's next-examination rules — do not wait for a reminder. title: Active Recall: Testing Yourself with the Book Closed
desc: Close the book and test yourself before checking: a simple active recall routine that turns passive re-reading into real memory for school exams.
intro: Most pupils revise by reading a chapter again and again, and most pupils are surprised when the exam paper feels unfamiliar. The reason is simple: reading feels easy, so it feels like learning, but it only trains your eyes to recognise words that are already in front of you. Active recall works the opposite way. You close the book, ask yourself a question, and try to produce the answer from memory before you look. That effort of pulling an answer out of your head is what strengthens the memory itself, so the answer is there again when the exam asks for it. This article explains a closed-book routine you can use for any subject, starting tonight, with nothing more than your notebook and a pen.

sections.h2: Why Re-reading Feels Easy and Fails
paras: Re-reading creates a comfortable illusion. When the answer is sitting on the page, your brain recognises it and mistakes that recognition for knowledge, so you turn the page feeling confident. In the exam hall, though, there is no page to recognise: the question asks you to produce the answer, not to recognise it. That is a completely different mental job, and it is one that re-reading never practises. Pupils who only re-read often say the paper felt harder than their revision did, and this gap between recognition and recall is exactly why.

Active recall closes that gap by making revision match the exam. Every time you try to answer with the book closed, you practise the same skill the exam will demand: retrieving information without help. The attempt does not have to be perfect to be useful. Even a half-remembered answer that you then correct teaches your brain more than a smooth re-reading of the same page, because the struggle itself marks the information as important. Short, effortful attempts beat long, comfortable reading every time, and they take less time too.

sections.h2: The Closed-Book Routine, Step by Step
paras: Start with a small chunk, never a whole chapter at once. Read one section or one set of notes carefully, then close the book and write down everything you can remember about it, in your own words, without peeking. Use rough paper or the back of your notebook so the attempt feels low-pressure; this is practice, not a test, and messy recall is perfectly fine. Give yourself a few minutes of genuine effort before you open the book again, because the benefit comes from the trying, not from getting everything right first time.

Now open the book and check your recall against the original, marking what you missed or got wrong in a different colour. Do not just read the corrections: say them aloud or write them again from memory, so the corrected version gets its own retrieval attempt. Then move to the next small chunk and repeat the cycle. A single study session built this way covers less ground than a re-reading session, but what it covers actually stays with you, which is why it saves time over the whole week. You can find more study methods on the [blog](/blog/) and in the [book collection](/books.html).

diagram.caption: Repeat this cycle for each small chunk of a chapter.

sections.h2: What to Do When You Cannot Recall Anything
paras: A blank mind during recall is not a failure; it is useful information. It tells you exactly which part of the chapter has not been learned yet, and that is far more valuable than a vague feeling that you sort of know it. When you draw a blank, do not sit staring at the page for ten minutes. Open the book, re-read just that small part, close it again, and try once more. Two or three short attempts with checking in between will fix a fact far better than one long stare at the open page.

If the same point keeps slipping away, change how you store it instead of repeating the same failed attempt. Turn it into a question you can ask yourself, connect it to something you already know, or break it into smaller pieces. Pupils often find that the points they struggled most to recall are the ones they remember best in the exam, because the effort spent on them made the memory stronger. Keep a short list of your stubborn points and return to them first in your next session, rather than starting again from the beginning of the chapter.

sections.h2: Using Closed-Book Recall in Every Subject
paras: Active recall adapts to any subject because every subject has something to retrieve. In Islamiat or history, recall the main points of a lesson and the order in which events or ideas follow each other. In science, close the book and write the steps of a process, the parts of a diagram, or the meaning of a term from memory. In mathematics, cover the worked example and try to solve the problem yourself before looking at the solution, because reading a solution feels like understanding it even when you could not produce it alone.

For language subjects, recall works beautifully with vocabulary and grammar. Cover the meanings and try to write them, or read a sentence in one language and reproduce it in the other. The method also works in pairs: one pupil asks questions from the notes while the other answers with the book closed, then they swap roles. Pair recall adds a gentle pressure that feels like exam pressure, which makes it excellent preparation. Browse the [solved notes](/solved.html) for material to practise with, and start with short sessions of twenty minutes before building up.
bullets: Islamiat and history: recall lesson points and their order from memory.
Science: recall process steps, diagram parts, and term meanings with the book closed.
Mathematics: cover the worked example and solve the problem yourself first.
Languages: cover meanings and reproduce vocabulary or sentences from memory.
Pair work: take turns asking and answering questions with the book closed.

sections.h2: Building Recall Into Your Daily Revision
paras: Recall works best as a daily habit, not as a last-minute technique. Begin each study session by recalling yesterday's topic before opening today's chapter, because that short warm-up both revises old work and tells you what needs another look. End each session the same way: close everything and spend five minutes writing down the main points of what you just studied. Those two bookends turn every session into a recall session without adding much time, and they stop the common problem of learning a chapter and then never returning to it.

Keep the sessions short and regular rather than long and rare. Twenty to thirty minutes of closed-book recall, done most days, will beat a three-hour re-reading marathon before the exam, because memory grows through repeated retrieval spread over days. Track your progress simply: note which topics you recalled well and which needed checking, and let that list decide tomorrow's session. Over a few weeks, the list of weak topics shrinks, and that visible progress is one of the most motivating sights in revision. More practical guidance is on the [home page](/) and the [blog](/blog/).
