faqs.q: How long should a weekly review take?
faqs.a: Forty-five to sixty minutes for a normal school week: a quick notes review, a mistakes review, and a flashcard run. If it takes much longer, your week's notes are probably too long, and shortening them is itself useful.

faqs.q: When is the best time for a weekly review?
faqs.a: A fixed slot each week, such as Friday evening or Saturday morning, works best. A fixed slot removes the daily decision about whether to review, which is the decision most often answered with no.

faqs.q: What is a mistakes book and why does it matter?
faqs.a: It is a notebook where you copy each week's important mistakes, the correct version, and a one-line note about what went wrong. Over a term it becomes a map of your weaknesses, and revising from it targets exactly where you lose marks.

faqs.q: What if I am too busy for the full ritual one week?
faqs.a: Do a shortened ritual rather than skipping it. Ten minutes of mistakes review alone is worth far more than nothing, and a ritual kept imperfectly every week beats a perfect ritual kept once.

faqs.q: How does a weekly review reduce exam anxiety?
faqs.a: It replaces guessing about what you know with evidence. Each week shows which topics are solid and which are shaky, so by exam time you have a short list of known weak points instead of a vague fear of everything.

title: Class 6 Whole Numbers: Place Value Made Simple
desc: Learn place value in Class 6 maths: read, write and compare large numbers with charts, expanded form and simple worked examples.
intro: Every digit in a number has two values: its own face value and its place value, which depends on where it stands. In the number 45,678, the digit 4 is not just 4, because it stands in the ten-thousands place, so its value is 40,000. Pupils who understand this idea stop guessing at large numbers and start reading them with confidence. Place value is the key to adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing large numbers correctly, because every written method lines digits up by their places. This guide explains place value with charts, expanded form, comparing and ordering, so that numbers up to lakhs feel as friendly as numbers up to hundreds. You can find more Class 6 help in the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

paras: Place value means that the same digit is worth a different amount depending on its position in a number. In 45,678, the digits from the right are ones, tens, hundreds, thousands and ten-thousands, so 8 means 8 ones, 7 means 7 tens or 70, 6 means 6 hundreds or 600, 5 means 5 thousands or 5,000, and 4 means 4 ten-thousands or 40,000. Adding these values together, 40,000 + 5,000 + 600 + 70 + 8, gives back 45,678, which proves the breakdown is correct. This is why a zero matters so much: in 405, the zero in the tens place holds the place, so the 4 means 400, not 45. Without place value, we could not write large numbers at all.

A place-value chart is the best tool for seeing this clearly, because it puts each digit in its own labelled column. Write the number into the chart from the right, one digit per column, starting with ones, and read across to name the value of each digit. Try it with 304,050: the chart shows 3 in the hundred-thousands place, 0 in ten-thousands, 4 in thousands, 0 in hundreds, 5 in tens and 0 in ones, so the value of 3 is 300,000 and the value of 4 is 4,000. Practise with your own numbers every day, such as house numbers, page numbers and prices, and soon you will read the value of any digit at a glance. More maths guides are on the [blog](/blog/).

Large numbers are read in groups of three digits, counted from the right, and commas mark these groups to make reading easier. The number 304,050 is read as three hundred four thousand and fifty, because the group 304 stands for thousands and the group 050 stands for the rest. Read the thousands group first, say the word thousand, then read the last three digits as an ordinary three-digit number. The number 1,250,000 is read as one million two hundred fifty thousand, following the same grouping rule. Saying numbers aloud in this grouped way stops the common mistake of reading 304,050 as thirty thousand or three million.

Writing numbers from words needs the same grouping skill in reverse, and a chart helps again. To write fifty-six thousand three hundred twenty, first put 56 in the thousands group and 320 in the ones group, giving 56,320. Watch out for missing places: seventy thousand and four is written as 70,004, because the hundreds and tens places both need a zero to hold them. A useful check is to count the digits: thousands numbers have four to six digits, and hundred-thousands numbers have six digits. If your written number has the wrong number of digits, a place has been missed. Practise by writing the numbers you hear in class, then checking them with a chart.
bullets: Group digits in threes from the right before reading a large number.
Read the thousands group first, say thousand, then read the last three digits.
Use a zero to hold any empty place when writing numbers from words.
Count the digits as a final check: four digits means thousands, five or six means ten-thousands and above.

paras: Expanded form writes a number as the sum of the place values of its digits, and it is the clearest proof that you understand place value. The expanded form of 45,678 is 40,000 + 5,000 + 600 + 70 + 8, and adding those parts gives back the original number. Expanded form also explains written addition and subtraction: when we add 45,678 and 12,345, we really add ones with ones, tens with tens, hundreds with hundreds, and so on. Try the expanded form of 70,409, which is 70,000 + 0 + 400 + 0 + 9, or simply 70,000 + 400 + 9, since zero places add nothing. Leaving the zero places out is fine, as long as you know they were there.

Expanded form helps with mental maths too, because breaking a number apart makes it easier to work with. To add 300 + 45,678, think of 45,678 as 45,000 + 678, add 300 to the hundreds part to get 45,000 + 978, and the answer is 45,978. To subtract 5,000 from 45,678, take it from the thousands part: 5,000 minus 5,000 leaves 40,678. These tricks only work when you can see the place values inside a number, which is why teachers ask for expanded form so often. Make it a habit to expand any new large number before you calculate with it, and written methods will feel much more natural. See the [home page](/) for more study resources.

To compare two numbers, first count the digits: the number with more digits is always larger, because it reaches a higher place. So 10,234 is larger than 9,876, even though 9,876 starts with a bigger digit, because 10,234 has five digits and reaches ten-thousands while 9,876 has only four. When both numbers have the same number of digits, compare them place by place from the left until the digits differ, and the number with the larger digit at that first different place is larger. Compare 45,678 and 45,768: the ten-thousands are both 4 and the thousands are both 5, but the hundreds differ, 6 against 7, so 45,768 is larger. The first place where digits differ decides the whole comparison.

Ordering means arranging numbers from smallest to largest or largest to smallest, and the same two rules do all the work. Order 9,876, 10,234 and 9,999 from smallest to largest: first count digits, so 10,234 with five digits must be the largest, then compare the two four-digit numbers, where 9,876 is smaller than 9,999 because at the hundreds place 8 is less than 9, giving 9,876, 9,999, 10,234. The symbols help record this: 9,876 < 9,999 < 10,234, where the symbol opens towards the larger number. Always check your order by reading it back: each step from left to right should genuinely increase, or your ordering has a mistake hiding in it.

diagram.caption: The steps for deciding which of two numbers is larger.

paras: Rounding gives a nearby round number that is easier to use for estimates, and place value tells us which digit decides the rounding. To round 45,678 to the nearest thousand, look at the hundreds digit, which is 6, and since 6 is 5 or more, round the thousands digit up: 45,678 rounds to 46,000. To round 45,321 to the nearest thousand, the hundreds digit is 3, which is less than 5, so round down and keep the thousands digit as it is: 45,321 rounds to 45,000. The simple rule is to look at the digit just right of the place you are rounding to: 5 or more rounds up, 4 or less rounds down, and every digit to the right becomes zero.

Rounding is useful for checking answers and for quick estimates in daily life, such as estimating the total cost of shopping. If a school collects 45,678 rupees and 12,345 rupees in two terms, rounding both to the nearest thousand gives 46,000 and 12,000, whose sum is 58,000, close to the exact total of 58,023. If your exact answer is far from your rounded estimate, you probably made a place-value slip, so go back and check. Never round in the middle of a calculation that needs an exact answer, though: round only for estimates and checks, and keep exact digits for the real working. That habit keeps both your estimates and your exact answers trustworthy.

Read large numbers in groups of three digits from the right, using commas as guides.

faqs.q: What is the place value of 5 in 45,678?
faqs.a: The 5 stands in the thousands place, so its place value is 5,000. Its face value is 5, but its place value is 5 multiplied by 1,000.

faqs.q: How do I read 304,050?
faqs.a: Group it as 304 and 050 from the right, then read it as three hundred four thousand and fifty. The group 304 gives the thousands part and 050 gives the rest.

faqs.q: Why do we write zero in 70,004?
faqs.a: The zeros hold the hundreds and tens places, which are empty. Without them, 70,004 would collapse into 7,4, which is a different number entirely.

faqs.q: Which is larger, 9,876 or 10,234?
faqs.a: 10,234 is larger, because it has five digits and reaches the ten-thousands place, while 9,876 has only four digits. More digits always means a larger whole number.

faqs.q: How do I round 45,678 to the nearest thousand?
faqs.a: Look at the hundreds digit, which is 6. Since 6 is 5 or more, round the thousands digit up, giving 46,000.

title: Class 6 Factors and Multiples: HCF and LCM Without Fear
desc: Factors, multiples, HCF and LCM explained simply for Class 6, with prime factors and short worked examples you can follow step by step.
intro: Factors and multiples sound alike, but they point in opposite directions, and mixing them up is the most common Class 6 maths mistake. Factors divide into a number exactly, while multiples are what you get when you multiply a number by 1, 2, 3 and so on. From these two ideas come HCF, the highest common factor, and LCM, the lowest common multiple, which solve real problems like sharing things equally and finding when two repeating events happen together. This guide builds the ideas slowly, with short worked examples for the numbers 12 and 18, so that HCF and LCM stop feeling like tricks and start feeling like tools. Find more Class 6 guides in the [book collection](/books.html) and on the [blog](/blog/).

paras: A factor of a number is a whole number that divides it exactly, leaving no remainder. The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12, because each of these divides 12 exactly: 12 divided by 3 is 4, 12 divided by 4 is 3, and so on. A quick way to find all factors is to test numbers in pairs: 1 times 12 is 12, 2 times 6 is 12, and 3 times 4 is 12, and once the pairs start repeating, you have found them all. Every number has 1 and itself as factors, and every number except 1 has at least those two. A number with exactly two factors is called a prime number, like 7, whose only factors are 1 and 7, while a number with more than two factors, like 12, is composite.

Factors are useful whenever things must be shared equally, because the factors of a number are exactly the group sizes that share it with nothing left over. Twelve pencils can be shared equally among 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 or 12 pupils, but not among 5 pupils, because 5 is not a factor of 12 and 12 divided by 5 leaves a remainder of 2. When you list factors, always work in pairs and write both members of each pair, or you will miss one. A neat trick for checking your list is to count the pairs: if the number is not a perfect square, its factors come in an even count of pairs, and a missing partner means the list is incomplete. Practise with 18, 20 and 30 until listing factors feels automatic.

sections.h2: Multiples: The Times Table Going On Forever
paras: A multiple of a number is the result of multiplying that number by a whole number, so the multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36 and so on, without end. Unlike factors, which are limited, multiples never stop, which is why questions always ask for the first few multiples or for multiples within a range. The first five multiples of 8 are 8, 16, 24, 32 and 40, found by multiplying 8 by 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. A number is always a multiple of itself and of 1, and every multiple of a number is at least as large as the number itself. If you know your times tables, you already know multiples: the 6 times table is simply the multiples of 6.

Multiples appear in daily life whenever something repeats at regular steps, such as bus times, packet sizes and calendar patterns. If one shop sells pens in packs of 6 and another in packs of 8, the numbers of pens you could buy equally from either shop are the common multiples of 6 and 8, which are 24, 48, 72 and so on. Spotting multiples quickly comes from times-table fluency, so a few minutes of times-table practice each day pays off directly here. When a question asks for multiples up to a limit, write them in order and stop at the limit, rather than writing an endless list. That discipline keeps your work tidy and your answers complete. More study help is in the [solved notes](/solved.html).

sections.h2: Prime Factors: Breaking Numbers to Their Bones
paras: Every composite number can be broken down into prime factors, which are prime numbers that multiply to give the original number. The prime factors of 12 are 2, 2 and 3, because 2 times 2 times 3 is 12, written as 2 squared times 3. To find them, divide by the smallest prime that divides exactly, and keep dividing the result until only primes remain: 12 divided by 2 is 6, 6 divided by 2 is 3, and 3 is prime, so the work stops. The prime factors of 18 are 2, 3 and 3, because 18 divided by 2 is 9, and 9 divided by 3 is 3. Writing prime factors as a product, 12 = 2 x 2 x 3 and 18 = 2 x 3 x 3, is called prime factorisation.

Prime factorisation is worth learning because it makes HCF and LCM almost mechanical, as the next sections show. It also settles questions like whether a number is prime: try dividing it by primes in order, and if no prime up to its square root divides it, it is prime. For Class 6, the practical skill is a factor tree: write the number, split it into any factor pair, then keep splitting every composite branch until only primes are left at the ends. The primes at the ends are your prime factors, whatever pair you started with, which is a good check: if two pupils start with different pairs, they must still finish with the same prime factors. Try factor trees for 20, 30 and 36 and compare your endings with a friend.

sections.h2: HCF: The Biggest Number That Divides Both
paras: The highest common factor of two numbers is the largest number that divides both of them exactly. To find the HCF of 12 and 18, list their factors: the factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12, and the factors of 18 are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 18. The common factors are 1, 2, 3 and 6, and the highest of these is 6, so the HCF of 12 and 18 is 6. Using prime factors gives the same answer faster: 12 = 2 x 2 x 3 and 18 = 2 x 3 x 3, and the primes common to both, taking the smallest power of each, are 2 and 3, whose product is 6. Both methods agree, which is a useful way to check your work.

HCF solves sharing problems where the groups must be as large as possible. Suppose a teacher has 12 red pens and 18 blue pens and wants identical packets with no pens left over: the largest possible packet size is the HCF, 6, so she can make packets of 6 pens, using 2 red packets and 3 blue packets in each mixed set, or more simply, the greatest equal group size is 6. Another example: the HCF of 15 and 20 is 5, because the factors of 15 are 1, 3, 5 and 15, the factors of 20 are 1, 2, 4, 5, 10 and 20, and the highest common factor is 5. Always finish by checking that your HCF divides both original numbers exactly, or it is not a common factor at all. See the [home page](/) for more guides.

diagram.alt: Finding HCF and LCM by Prime Factors
diagram.caption: One prime factorisation gives both HCF and LCM.

sections.h2: LCM: The Smallest Number Both Divide Into
paras: The lowest common multiple of two numbers is the smallest number that is a multiple of both. To find the LCM of 12 and 18 by listing, write the multiples of 12, which are 12, 24, 36, 48, and the multiples of 18, which are 18, 36, 54, and the first number appearing in both lists is 36, so the LCM is 36. By prime factors, take the highest power of every prime that appears: 12 = 2 x 2 x 3 and 18 = 2 x 3 x 3, so the LCM is 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 = 36. Both methods agree again, and the prime-factor method is faster when the numbers are large. As a check, note that the LCM is never smaller than either number, and the HCF is never larger than either number.

LCM answers questions about things happening together again. If one bell rings every 12 minutes and another every 18 minutes, and they ring together now, they will ring together again after the LCM of 12 and 18 minutes, which is 36 minutes. Similarly, the LCM of 15 and 20 is 60, because 15 = 3 x 5 and 20 = 2 x 2 x 5, so the LCM is 2 x 2 x 3 x 5 = 60, and indeed 60 is the first number in both times tables. A quick check is that HCF times LCM equals the product of the two numbers: for 12 and 18, 6 times 36 is 216, and 12 times 18 is also 216. If your HCF and LCM fail this check, one of them is wrong, so redo the factorisation.

Multiples go on forever: the multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 and so on.
Prime factorisation breaks a number into primes: 12 = 2 x 2 x 3 and 18 = 2 x 3 x 3.
The HCF of 12 and 18 is 6, the largest number dividing both exactly.
The LCM of 12 and 18 is 36, the smallest number that is a multiple of both.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a factor and a multiple?
faqs.a: A factor divides into a number exactly, while a multiple is made by multiplying the number. Factors of 12 are limited, but multiples of 12 go on forever: 12, 24, 36, 48 and so on.

faqs.q: How do I find the HCF of 12 and 18?
faqs.a: List the factors of 12 (1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12) and of 18 (1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18). The common factors are 1, 2, 3 and 6, and the highest is 6, so the HCF is 6.

faqs.q: How do I find the LCM of 12 and 18?
faqs.a: List multiples of 12 (12, 24, 36) and of 18 (18, 36). The first number in both lists is 36, so the LCM is 36. By prime factors it is 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 = 36.

faqs.q: What is prime factorisation?
faqs.a: It is breaking a number into prime numbers that multiply to give it. For example, 12 = 2 x 2 x 3, because 2, 2 and 3 are all prime and their product is 12.

faqs.q: How can I check my HCF and LCM answers?
faqs.a: Multiply them: HCF times LCM should equal the product of the two numbers. For 12 and 18, 6 times 36 is 216, and 12 times 18 is also 216, so both answers check out.

title: Class 6 Fractions and Decimals: From Halves to Hundredths
desc: Class 6 fractions and decimals made easy: compare fractions, convert to decimals, and use halves, quarters and hundredths in daily life.
intro: Fractions and decimals are two ways of writing the same idea: a part of a whole. One half can be written as the fraction 1/2 or as the decimal 0.5, and three quarters can be written as 3/4 or 0.75. Pupils often treat them as two separate topics, but once you see how they convert into each other, both become much easier. This guide starts with simple fractions, shows how to compare them, converts them into decimals, and finishes with everyday examples like money and measuring, where decimals appear all the time. More Class 6 maths help is in the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

paras: A fraction has a numerator on top and a denominator below, and the denominator tells you how many equal parts the whole is split into, while the numerator tells you how many of those parts you have. In 3/4, the whole is split into 4 equal parts and you have 3 of them, so 3/4 is three quarters of the whole. In 1/2, the whole is split into 2 parts and you have 1, which is one half. Equal parts matter: if the parts are not equal, the fraction does not describe them properly, which is why fraction diagrams always show pieces of the same size. A fraction like 5/5 means the whole thing, because you have all 5 of the 5 parts.

Fractions also appear as parts of a group, not just parts of a shape. If a class has 20 pupils and 12 of them walk to school, the fraction that walks is 12/20, which simplifies to 3/5 by dividing numerator and denominator by 4. Simplifying means dividing both parts by their common factor, and a fraction is in simplest form when numerator and denominator share no common factor except 1. So 12/20 simplifies to 3/5, and 6/8 simplifies to 3/4 by dividing by 2. Always simplify your final answer unless the question asks otherwise, because simplest form is the standard way to present a fraction. Practise simplifying 10/15, which becomes 2/3, and 9/12, which becomes 3/4.

When fractions share the same denominator, comparing them is easy: the one with the larger numerator is larger, so 3/8 is larger than 2/8 because 3 parts out of 8 beat 2 parts out of 8. When the denominators differ, cross-multiplication gives a reliable comparison without finding a common denominator. To compare 2/3 and 3/5, multiply the numerator of each by the denominator of the other: 2 times 5 is 10, and 3 times 3 is 9, and since 10 is larger than 9, 2/3 is larger than 3/5. Write the products above the fractions they belong to, so you never mix up which product goes with which fraction, and the larger product marks the larger fraction.

Another way to compare is to convert both fractions to a common denominator, which works well when the denominators are small. To compare 1/2 and 3/4, convert 1/2 to 2/4, and then 3/4 is clearly larger than 2/4. For 2/3 and 3/4, the common denominator 12 gives 8/12 and 9/12, so 3/4 is larger. A quick sense check helps too: any fraction larger than 1/2 has a numerator more than half its denominator, so 5/8 is larger than 1/2 while 3/8 is smaller. Use whichever method you find clearest, but always show your working, because a bare answer to a comparison question earns little credit. Find more guides on the [blog](/blog/).

A fraction means division: 3/4 means 3 divided by 4, so dividing gives the decimal form. Three divided by 4 is 0.75, so 3/4 = 0.75, and one divided by 2 is 0.5, so 1/2 = 0.5. Fractions with denominator 10 or 100 convert by place value alone: 7/10 = 0.7, because the 7 sits in the tenths place, and 45/100 = 0.45, because 4 is in tenths and 5 is in hundredths. For other denominators, first convert to tenths or hundredths if you can: 3/5 becomes 6/10 by multiplying numerator and denominator by 2, so 3/5 = 0.6. The fractions worth memorising are 1/2 = 0.5, 1/4 = 0.25, 3/4 = 0.75, 1/5 = 0.2 and 1/10 = 0.1, because they appear constantly.

Decimals can also be turned back into fractions, which is useful for simplifying and comparing. The decimal 0.45 means 45 hundredths, so it equals 45/100, which simplifies to 9/20 by dividing by 5. The decimal 0.6 means 6 tenths, so it equals 6/10, which simplifies to 3/5. Read the decimal aloud to find its fraction: 0.25 is twenty-five hundredths, giving 25/100, which simplifies to 1/4. This two-way skill means you can always switch to whichever form makes a question easier: use decimals for money and measuring, and fractions for exact parts and sharing. Try converting 0.8, which is 8/10 or 4/5, and 0.35, which is 35/100 or 7/20.

diagram.caption: The same part of a whole, written two ways.

paras: Comparing decimals is easy once you line up the decimal points and compare place by place, just like whole numbers. To compare 0.45 and 0.5, first write 0.5 as 0.50 so both numbers have two decimal places, then compare the hundredths: 45 hundredths is less than 50 hundredths, so 0.45 is smaller than 0.5. The common mistake is to think 0.45 is larger because 45 is a bigger number than 5, but the place values decide, not the digits alone. Comparing 0.6 and 0.65 works the same way: write 0.6 as 0.60, and 60 hundredths is less than 65 hundredths, so 0.6 is smaller than 0.65. Padding with zeros never changes a decimal's value, so use it freely.

Ordering decimals follows the same method: pad them to the same number of decimal places, then order them like whole numbers. Order 0.5, 0.45 and 0.75: padded, they are 0.50, 0.45 and 0.75, so from smallest to largest they are 0.45, 0.5, 0.75. In money, this skill is used daily: Rs 12.50 is more than Rs 12.05, because at the tenths place both have 5, but at the hundredths place 0 is less than 5, so Rs 12.05 is the smaller amount. Always write decimals with their points lined up in a column when you compare them on paper, because a misaligned point is the usual cause of a wrong comparison. The [home page](/) has more study material.

sections.h2: Fractions and Decimals in Daily Life
paras: Fractions and decimals are everywhere once you start looking, especially in shopping, cooking and measuring. A shopkeeper who sells half a litre of milk sells 0.5 litres, and a bottle marked 0.25 litres holds one quarter of a litre. A discount of one quarter off a Rs 400 shirt saves Rs 100, because 1/4 of 400 is 100, leaving Rs 300 to pay. In cooking, half a cup is 0.5 cups, and three quarters of a cup is 0.75 cups, so recipes written either way describe the same amounts. Cricket fans meet decimals in run rates, and petrol is sold by the litre with two decimal places, so reading decimals correctly saves real money.

Marks and test scores use both forms too, and converting between them helps you understand your results. Scoring 15 out of 20 is the fraction 15/20, which simplifies to 3/4, which as a decimal is 0.75, which as a percentage is 75 percent. A pupil who scored 0.8 on a quiz scored 4/5, or 80 percent, which is a strong result. When you see a decimal in daily life, try naming its fraction: 0.5 litres is half a litre, 2.5 kilograms is two and a half kilograms, and Rs 7.25 is seven rupees and twenty-five paisa. This habit turns every price tag and measuring jug into fraction practice, and soon converting between the two forms will feel automatic rather than like a school exercise.

Compare fractions with the same denominator by numerator, or use cross-multiplication: 2/3 beats 3/5 because 10 beats 9.
Convert fractions to decimals by dividing: 3/4 = 0.75, 3/5 = 0.6, 7/10 = 0.7.
Compare decimals by lining up decimal points and padding with zeros: 0.45 is smaller than 0.50.
Simplify fractions by dividing numerator and denominator by their common factor: 12/20 = 3/5.

faqs.q: How do I convert 3/4 into a decimal?
faqs.a: Divide the numerator by the denominator: 3 divided by 4 is 0.75, so 3/4 = 0.75. You can also write 3/4 as 75/100, which is 0.75 by place value.

faqs.q: Which is larger, 2/3 or 3/5?
faqs.a: Cross-multiply: 2 times 5 is 10, and 3 times 3 is 9. Since 10 is larger than 9, 2/3 is larger than 3/5.

faqs.q: Is 0.45 larger than 0.5?
faqs.a: No. Write 0.5 as 0.50, then compare: 45 hundredths is less than 50 hundredths, so 0.45 is smaller than 0.5.

faqs.q: How do I simplify 12/20?
faqs.a: Divide numerator and denominator by their common factor 4: 12 divided by 4 is 3, and 20 divided by 4 is 5, so 12/20 simplifies to 3/5.

faqs.q: What is 0.25 as a fraction?
faqs.a: 0.25 means 25 hundredths, so it is 25/100, which simplifies to 1/4 by dividing numerator and denominator by 25.

title: Class 6 Percentages: A First Introduction With Shop Examples
desc: A first introduction to percentages for Class 6: per hundred made simple, with shop discounts, marks and easy worked examples.
intro: Percent means per hundred, and the symbol % is simply a short way of writing out of 100. When a shop says 25% off, it means 25 rupees off for every 100 rupees of price, and when a pupil scores 75%, it means 75 marks out of every 100. Percentages turn fractions and decimals into a single common scale, which is why shops, banks, exams and news reports all use them. This guide explains percentages from the beginning, with shop discounts and school marks as the main examples, so that the idea feels useful rather than abstract. More Class 6 maths guides are in the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

paras: The word percent comes from per centum, meaning per hundred, so 25% is simply another way of writing the fraction 25/100 and the decimal 0.25. This is why percentages are so easy to compare: every percentage is measured on the same scale of 100, so 60% is always larger than 45%, whatever the original totals were. Converting a fraction to a percentage means making its denominator 100: 1/2 becomes 50/100, which is 50%, and 3/4 becomes 75/100, which is 75%. Converting a decimal is even quicker: move the decimal point two places to the right and add the % sign, so 0.6 becomes 60% and 0.05 becomes 5%.

Percentages above 100 are possible too, and they simply mean more than the whole: 150% of Rs 200 is Rs 300, because 100% is Rs 200 and another 50% is Rs 100. Percentages below 1% are rare in Class 6 work, but the idea is the same: 1% means 1 out of every 100. A useful picture is a 10 by 10 grid of 100 small squares: shading 25 squares shows 25%, shading half the grid shows 50%, and shading the whole grid shows 100%. Drawing this grid for a few percentages makes the per-hundred idea concrete, and it also shows why 25% is the same as one quarter and 50% is the same as one half. Keep this grid picture in mind whenever a percentage question feels confusing.

sections.h2: Finding a Percentage of a Number
paras: To find a percentage of a number, turn the percentage into a fraction over 100 and multiply. To find 25% of 200, write 25/100 times 200, which is 25 times 200 divided by 100, giving 5,000 divided by 100, which is 50. A shorter method is to find 1% first and then multiply: 1% of 200 is 2, so 25% is 25 times 2, which is 50. Both methods agree, and the 1% method is especially handy for percentages like 30% or 45%, where the fraction method involves larger numbers. Try 20% of 500: 1% of 500 is 5, so 20% is 20 times 5, which is 100.

Some percentages have quick mental shortcuts worth memorising, because they appear constantly in shops and exams. Ten percent means divide by 10, so 10% of 800 is 80. Fifty percent means halve the number, so 50% of 800 is 400. Twenty-five percent means divide by 4, so 25% of 800 is 200. Seventy-five percent means three quarters, so 75% of 800 is 600. Combining shortcuts handles other percentages: 30% of 800 is three times 10%, which is 3 times 80, giving 240. Practise these shortcuts until they are instant, because they make discount and marks questions much faster, and they also give you a quick check on longer written methods. More guides are on the [blog](/blog/).

sections.h2: Shop Discounts: Percentages That Save Money
paras: A discount is a percentage taken off the marked price, and the steps are always the same: find the discount amount, then subtract it from the price. A shirt marked Rs 800 with 10% off has a discount of 10% of 800, which is 80, so the sale price is 800 minus 80, which is Rs 720. A school bag marked Rs 1,200 with 25% off has a discount of 25% of 1,200, which is 300, so the sale price is 1,200 minus 300, which is Rs 900. Always check that the sale price is less than the marked price and that the discount is a sensible fraction of it: a 10% discount on Rs 800 cannot be Rs 400, because that would be half the price, not a tenth.

Some shops show two discounts in words, such as 20% off plus an extra 10% off, and pupils often add them to get 30% off, which is wrong. The second discount applies to the already-reduced price, not the original price, so a Rs 1,000 item at 20% off costs Rs 800, and a further 10% off Rs 800 saves Rs 80, giving a final price of Rs 720, which is a total saving of Rs 280, or 28%, not 30%. This is a good example of why percentages need care: they always act on a particular amount, and changing the amount changes the result. When a question says percent off, first ask: percent of what? Answering that question correctly is half the problem solved.

diagram.caption: The same three steps solve every discount question.

paras: Exam percentages are found by dividing the marks obtained by the total marks and multiplying by 100. A pupil who scores 45 out of 60 has a percentage of 45 divided by 60 times 100, which is 0.75 times 100, giving 75%. A pupil who scores 36 out of 50 has 36 divided by 50 times 100, which is 0.72 times 100, giving 72%. The method never changes, whatever the total: divide by the total, multiply by 100, and add the % sign. Simplifying the fraction first often makes the division easier: 45/60 simplifies to 3/4, and 3/4 of 100 is 75, which matches the first answer.

Percentages let you compare results from tests with different totals, which raw marks cannot do fairly. Scoring 36 out of 50 beats scoring 45 out of 60 in percentage terms? No: 36 out of 50 is 72%, while 45 out of 60 is 75%, so the 45 out of 60 result is actually better, even though 45 is only 9 marks more than 36. This is the real power of percentages: they put different totals on the same 100-point scale. When you work out your own test percentages, always write the fraction first, then the division, then the multiplication by 100, so that a small arithmetic slip is easy to spot. A percentage above 100 in a test would mean scoring more than the total, which is impossible, so such an answer signals an error.

The most common percentage mistake is forgetting what the percentage is a percentage of, especially when a price changes twice. If a Rs 400 item rises by 25%, the increase is 25% of 400, which is 100, giving a new price of Rs 500. If it then falls by 25%, the decrease is 25% of 500, which is 125, giving Rs 375, not the original Rs 400, because the second percentage acted on a larger amount. Equal percentage rises and falls do not cancel out, and remembering this saves many marks. Another common slip is writing 0.5 as 5% instead of 50%: moving the decimal point two places, not one, is the rule for converting decimals to percentages.

A second mistake is confusing percentage points with percentages, though Class 6 pupils mainly need to avoid mixing up the percentage and the amount it produces. In the discount example, 10% is the rate and Rs 80 is the amount: the question may ask for either, so read it twice. If it asks how much you save, the answer is Rs 80; if it asks the sale price, the answer is Rs 720. Labelling your working helps: write discount = Rs 80 and sale price = Rs 720 as separate lines, so you can pick the one the question asked for. Finally, always finish with a sense check: a 10% discount should be a small part of the price, a 50% discount should be half, and a percentage of a number should never exceed the number itself unless the percentage exceeds 100%. The [home page](/) has more study help.

Find a percentage by multiplying by the fraction over 100, or by finding 1% first.
A discount is found first, then subtracted: 10% off Rs 800 gives a sale price of Rs 720.

faqs.q: What does 25% mean?
faqs.a: It means 25 out of every 100. As a fraction it is 25/100, which simplifies to 1/4, and as a decimal it is 0.25.

faqs.q: How do I find 25% of 200?
faqs.a: Multiply 25/100 by 200, which is 5,000 divided by 100, giving 50. Or find 1% of 200, which is 2, and multiply by 25 to get 50.

faqs.q: A shirt costs Rs 800 with 10% off. What is the sale price?
faqs.a: The discount is 10% of 800, which is 80. Subtract it from the price: 800 minus 80 is 720, so the sale price is Rs 720.

faqs.q: How do I turn 45 out of 60 into a percentage?
faqs.a: Divide 45 by 60 to get 0.75, then multiply by 100 to get 75%. So 45 out of 60 is 75%.

faqs.q: Why is 20% off then 10% off not 30% off?
faqs.a: The second discount applies to the reduced price, not the original. On Rs 1,000, 20% off gives Rs 800, and 10% off Rs 800 gives Rs 720, a total saving of 28%, not 30%.

title: Class 6 Geometry: Lines, Angles and Triangles
desc: Class 6 geometry made simple: lines, types of angles, triangle names, and how to draw and measure angles with a protractor.
intro: Geometry is the maths of shapes, and it starts with two simple ideas: lines and angles. Lines can run side by side forever without meeting, cross each other, or meet at a square corner, and the angle between two lines tells you how much one has turned from the other. Triangles, the simplest closed shape, are built entirely from three lines and three angles, and their names come straight from those angles and sides. This guide explains lines, angle types, triangle names, and how to use a protractor, with examples you can draw yourself. More Class 6 help is in the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

paras: A line goes on forever in both directions, while a line segment has two endpoints and a ray has one endpoint and goes on in one direction. The edges of your notebook page are line segments, a sunbeam is like a ray, and a road stretching to the horizon is like a line. Parallel lines are lines in the same plane that never meet, however far they are extended, like the two long edges of a ruler or railway tracks. Intersecting lines are lines that cross at a point, like the diagonals of a square, and perpendicular lines are intersecting lines that meet at a right angle of 90 degrees, like the corner of a page where its edges meet.

Spotting these lines in daily life makes the definitions stick. The lines of a ruled notebook page are parallel, the hands of a clock at 3 o'clock are perpendicular, and the letter X is made of two intersecting lines. In a rectangle, opposite sides are parallel and neighbouring sides are perpendicular, which is why rectangles look so neat. When you draw parallel lines, use a ruler and keep the distance between them the same all along; when you draw perpendicular lines, check the corner with the square corner of a book or a set square. Naming the lines you see around you, in doors, windows and floor tiles, turns the whole classroom into a geometry lesson. Find more guides on the [blog](/blog/).

An angle is formed when two rays meet at a point called the vertex, and its size is measured in degrees. An acute angle is smaller than 90 degrees, like the angle of a partly opened book or the hands of a clock at 2 o'clock, which show about 60 degrees. A right angle is exactly 90 degrees, like the corner of a page, and it is usually marked with a small square at the vertex. An obtuse angle is larger than 90 degrees but smaller than 180 degrees, like the hands of a clock at 4 o'clock, which show about 120 degrees. A straight angle is exactly 180 degrees, a flat line, like the hands of a clock at 6 o'clock.

A reflex angle is larger than 180 degrees but smaller than 360 degrees, and a full turn is 360 degrees, which brings a ray back to where it started. Pupils often confuse obtuse and reflex angles, so remember the boundary: anything under 180 degrees that is not acute or right is obtuse, while anything over 180 degrees is reflex. Estimating angles before measuring them is a good habit: look at the angle and guess whether it is acute, right or obtuse, then measure to check. If your guess and your measurement disagree wildly, you have probably read the wrong scale on the protractor, which is the most common measuring mistake. Practise estimating the angles of clock hands, open doors and roof slopes until your guesses are close.

sections.h2: Measuring and Drawing With a Protractor
paras: A protractor measures angles up to 180 degrees, and using it correctly needs three careful steps. First, place the centre mark of the protractor exactly on the vertex of the angle, so the protractor cannot slide. Second, line up the base line of the protractor with one arm of the angle, so that arm reads zero. Third, read the scale where the other arm crosses the protractor, choosing the scale that starts at zero on the arm you lined up: if the first arm is on the right, read the inner scale, and if it is on the left, read the outer scale. Reading the wrong scale gives the supplement of the angle, for example 120 degrees instead of 60 degrees, so your earlier estimate is your best protection.

Drawing an angle is the reverse process, and it also needs care. To draw a 60-degree angle, draw one arm with a ruler, place the protractor's centre on the endpoint and its base line on the arm, mark a small dot at 60 degrees on the correct scale, remove the protractor, and join the endpoint to the dot with a ruler. Check your drawing by measuring it back: the measured angle should match the angle you intended. Use a sharp pencil, because a thick pencil line can hide a few degrees of error, and draw arms long enough to read clearly. Pupils who rush protractor work usually lose marks on the scale choice, not on the drawing itself, so slow down at the reading step. The [home page](/) has more study resources.

diagram.alt: Measuring an Angle With a Protractor
diagram.caption: Four steps to a correct protractor reading.

sections.h2: Triangles by Their Angles and Sides
paras: Triangles are named by their angles and by their sides, and both naming systems are used together. By angles, a triangle with one right angle is right-angled, a triangle with one obtuse angle is obtuse-angled, and a triangle with all three angles acute is acute-angled. By sides, a triangle with all three sides equal is equilateral, a triangle with two sides equal is isosceles, and a triangle with no sides equal is scalene. An equilateral triangle is also acute-angled, because each of its angles is 60 degrees, and an isosceles triangle has two equal angles opposite its two equal sides. Learning both systems means you can describe any triangle fully, such as a right-angled isosceles triangle.

The angles of any triangle add up to 180 degrees, which is one of the most useful facts in geometry. If a triangle has angles of 60 degrees and 70 degrees, the third angle must be 180 minus 60 minus 70, which is 50 degrees, because 60 plus 70 is 130 and 180 minus 130 is 50. This rule lets you find a missing angle whenever you know the other two, and it also checks your protractor work: if your three measured angles add to much more or less than 180 degrees, at least one measurement is wrong. Try tearing the three corners off a paper triangle and placing them together: they form a straight line of 180 degrees, which is a convincing proof you can do at your desk. Triangles also appear in bridges and roofs because they are rigid shapes that do not wobble.

sections.h2: Drawing Triangles and Checking Your Work
paras: Drawing a triangle from given sides needs a ruler and a pair of compasses, and the method is satisfying once you practise it. To draw a triangle with sides 5 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm, first draw the 7 cm base with a ruler, then open the compasses to 5 cm, place the point on one end of the base and draw an arc, then open them to 6 cm, place the point on the other end and draw a second arc. The point where the arcs cross is the third vertex: join it to both ends of the base, and the triangle is complete. If the arcs do not cross, the three lengths cannot form a triangle, which happens when the longest side is longer than the other two sides added together.

Always check a drawn triangle by measuring its sides and angles back against the question. The sides should match the given lengths within a millimetre or two, and the angles should add to 180 degrees. Label the vertices with capital letters, usually A, B and C, and label the sides with their lengths, so that anyone reading your drawing can check it without asking. Neat construction lines, the light arcs left by the compasses, show your method and earn marks, so do not rub them out. Geometry rewards patience: a slow, careful drawing beats a quick, rough one every time, and the checking step is what turns a good drawing into a reliable one. See the [solved notes](/solved.html) for more practice.

points: Parallel lines never meet; perpendicular lines meet at a right angle of 90 degrees.
Acute angles are under 90 degrees, right angles are exactly 90, obtuse angles are between 90 and 180, and straight angles are 180.
Measure with a protractor by centring it on the vertex, lining up the base line, and reading the scale that starts at zero.
The three angles of any triangle add up to 180 degrees: 60 plus 70 leaves a third angle of 50 degrees.
Triangles are named by angles (acute, right, obtuse) and by sides (equilateral, isosceles, scalene).

faqs.q: What is the difference between parallel and perpendicular lines?
faqs.a: Parallel lines never meet, however far they are extended, like railway tracks. Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle of 90 degrees, like the corner of a page.

faqs.q: Is a 120-degree angle acute or obtuse?
faqs.a: It is obtuse, because obtuse angles are larger than 90 degrees and smaller than 180 degrees. Acute angles are smaller than 90 degrees.

faqs.q: Why do I sometimes read 120 degrees instead of 60 degrees on a protractor?
faqs.a: You read the wrong scale. Use the scale that starts at zero on the arm you lined up with the base line, and check your reading against your estimate of acute or obtuse.

faqs.q: A triangle has angles of 60 and 70 degrees. What is the third angle?
faqs.a: The angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees, so the third angle is 180 minus 60 minus 70, which is 50 degrees.

faqs.q: What is an isosceles triangle?
faqs.a: It is a triangle with two equal sides. The two angles opposite those equal sides are also equal.

title: Class 6 Ratio and Proportion in Simple Words
desc: Ratio and proportion in simple words for Class 6: recipes, class strength and the unitary method, with easy worked examples.
intro: A ratio compares two quantities of the same kind, and it tells you how many times one fits into the other. If a class has 24 boys and 16 girls, the ratio of boys to girls is 24 to 16, which simplifies to 3 to 2. Ratios appear in recipes, in maps, in mixing paint, and in sharing money fairly, and they are the doorway to proportion, which says that two ratios are equal. This guide explains ratios with recipes and class strength, shows how to simplify them, and teaches the unitary method, which solves a huge family of daily-life problems. More Class 6 maths is in the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

paras: A ratio is written with a colon, like 3:2, and it compares two quantities measured in the same unit. The order matters: the ratio of boys to girls in a class of 24 boys and 16 girls is 24:16, but the ratio of girls to boys is 16:24, which is a different comparison. Ratios have no units, because the units cancel when you compare like with like, and a ratio only makes sense when both quantities are in the same unit: comparing 2 metres with 50 centimetres needs a conversion first, giving 200 centimetres to 50 centimetres, or 4:1. Always check the units and the order before you write a ratio, because both mistakes are common and both change the answer.

A ratio is not a fraction of a whole, though the two ideas are related, and keeping them apart avoids confusion. In a class with 24 boys and 16 girls, the ratio of boys to girls is 24:16, but the fraction of the class that is boys is 24 out of 40, or 3/5, because the whole class is 40 pupils. The ratio compares one part with another part, while the fraction compares one part with the whole. Both are useful: the ratio tells you the mixture, and the fraction tells you the share. When a question asks for a ratio, give it with a colon and simplified; when it asks for a fraction, give it out of the total. Reading the question's exact words is the key to choosing correctly.

A ratio is simplified by dividing both parts by their highest common factor, just like simplifying a fraction. The ratio 24:16 simplifies by dividing both parts by 8, giving 3:2, because 24 divided by 8 is 3 and 16 divided by 8 is 2. The ratio 15:25 simplifies by dividing by 5, giving 3:5, and the ratio 12:18 simplifies by dividing by 6, giving 2:3. A simplified ratio is the standard answer, and it also makes the comparison easier to understand: 3:2 is clearer than 24:16, because it says that for every 3 boys there are 2 girls. If the two parts share no common factor except 1, the ratio is already in simplest form.

Simplifying also works when a ratio has more than two parts, which happens in recipes and mixtures. A mixture of 12 spoons of flour, 6 spoons of sugar and 3 spoons of cocoa simplifies by dividing all three parts by 3, giving 4:2:1. Decimal ratios should be converted to whole numbers first: the ratio 1.5:2.5 becomes 15:25 by multiplying both parts by 10, and then simplifies to 3:5 by dividing by 5. Always divide by the highest common factor in one step when you can, but dividing step by step also works if you keep going until no common factor remains. Check your simplified ratio by confirming that both parts divided by the same number give your answer, and that no further common factor exists.

Recipes are ratios in disguise, because they fix the proportions of ingredients whatever the batch size. A recipe that uses 2 cups of flour to 1 cup of sugar has the ratio 2:1, so doubling the recipe needs 4 cups of flour and 2 cups of sugar, keeping the same ratio, and halving it needs 1 cup of flour and half a cup of sugar. If a recipe for 4 people uses 3 cups of rice, then the same recipe for 8 people needs 6 cups, because the number of people has doubled and so must the rice. Scaling a recipe means multiplying every ingredient by the same number, which keeps the taste the same; changing only one ingredient changes the ratio and changes the dish.

Mixtures follow the same rule, from paint to squash to cement. A paint mixture in the ratio 3:1 of white to red paint means that for every 3 parts of white paint there is 1 part of red, so a batch of 12 litres contains 9 litres of white and 3 litres of red, because the mixture has 4 parts in total and each part is 3 litres. Finding the value of one part, by dividing the total by the number of parts, is the key step in mixture questions. A squash mixture in the ratio 1:4 of squash to water means 1 part squash and 4 parts water, so a 500 ml jug holds 100 ml of squash and 400 ml of water. Practise with your own kitchen: the ratio of rice to water in cooking is a ratio you already use every day. More guides are on the [blog](/blog/).

sections.h2: Proportion: When Two Ratios Are Equal
paras: Two ratios are in proportion when they are equal, even though their numbers look different. The ratios 2:3 and 4:6 are in proportion, because 4:6 simplifies to 2:3, and the ratios 3:5 and 6:10 are in proportion for the same reason. Proportion is written as 2:3 :: 4:6, and it can be checked by cross-multiplication: 2 times 6 is 12, and 3 times 4 is 12, and since both products are equal, the ratios are in proportion. If the cross products differ, the ratios are not in proportion: 2:3 and 3:5 give 2 times 5 is 10 and 3 times 3 is 9, which differ, so they are not in proportion. Cross-multiplication is the quickest proportion check, and it also finds missing values.

To find a missing value in a proportion, cross-multiply and solve the small equation that results. If 3 pencils cost Rs 30, how much do 7 pencils cost? The ratio of pencils to cost must stay in proportion, so 3:30 :: 7:x, cross-multiplying gives 3 times x is 210, so x is 210 divided by 3, which is 70, and 7 pencils cost Rs 70. This method works whenever two quantities grow together at a steady rate, which is called direct proportion: more pencils cost more money, more workers take more food, and more hours of work earn more pay. If the quantities move in opposite directions, such as more workers finishing a job faster, the proportion is inverse, and Class 6 questions usually stick to direct proportion, so check which kind you have before calculating.

diagram.caption: The ideas behind every ratio question.

sections.h2: The Unitary Method: Find One, Then Find Many
paras: The unitary method solves rate problems in two steps: first find the value of one unit, then multiply to find the value of many. If 5 pencils cost Rs 50, one pencil costs 50 divided by 5, which is Rs 10, and 8 pencils cost 8 times 10, which is Rs 80. If a car travels 180 km in 3 hours, it travels 180 divided by 3, which is 60 km in one hour, and in 5 hours it travels 5 times 60, which is 300 km. The method is called unitary because it goes through the unit, the value of one, and it works for any steady rate: price per item, speed per hour, or food per person. Always label the one-unit value clearly, because it is the bridge to every other answer.

The unitary method also handles division problems, where you need the value of one share. If 6 friends share Rs 720 equally, one friend gets 720 divided by 6, which is Rs 120. If 4 kg of rice costs Rs 480, one kilogram costs 480 divided by 4, which is Rs 120, and 7 kg costs 7 times 120, which is Rs 840. A common mistake is multiplying when you should divide in the first step: to find the value of one, you divide the total by the number of units, and only then do you multiply. Write both steps out, even when the numbers look easy, because the written steps earn method marks and make errors easy to find. The [home page](/) has more maths guides.

Simplify ratios by dividing both parts by their highest common factor: 24:16 becomes 3:2.
Scale a recipe by multiplying every ingredient by the same number, keeping the ratio unchanged.

faqs.q: What is the ratio of 24 boys to 16 girls?
faqs.a: It is 24:16, which simplifies by dividing both parts by 8 to give 3:2. The order matters: boys to girls is 3:2, while girls to boys is 2:3.

faqs.q: How do I simplify 15:25?
faqs.a: Divide both parts by their highest common factor, which is 5: 15 divided by 5 is 3, and 25 divided by 5 is 5, so the simplified ratio is 3:5.

faqs.q: How do I check if 2:3 and 4:6 are in proportion?
faqs.a: Cross-multiply: 2 times 6 is 12, and 3 times 4 is 12. Since both products are equal, the ratios are in proportion.

faqs.q: If 5 pencils cost Rs 50, how much do 8 pencils cost?
faqs.a: Use the unitary method: one pencil costs 50 divided by 5, which is Rs 10, so 8 pencils cost 8 times 10, which is Rs 80.

faqs.q: A paint mixture is 3:1 white to red. How much of each in 12 litres?
faqs.a: The mixture has 4 parts in total, so each part is 12 divided by 4, which is 3 litres. That gives 9 litres of white paint and 3 litres of red paint.

title: Class 6 Integers on the Number Line
desc: Positive and negative integers on the number line for Class 6: ordering, opposites, and adding with jumps, with simple examples.
intro: Integers are the whole numbers plus their negatives: ..., -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ... Positive numbers sit to the right of zero on the number line, negative numbers sit to the left, and zero sits in the middle, neither positive nor negative. Negative numbers describe real things: temperatures below zero, floors below ground level, money owed, and depths below sea level. This guide shows how to place integers on the number line, order them, find their opposites, and add and subtract them with jumps, so that negative numbers stop feeling strange and start feeling useful. More Class 6 maths is in the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

sections.h2: The Number Line and Where Integers Live
paras: A number line is a straight line marked with numbers at equal gaps, with zero in the middle, positive numbers marching to the right and negative numbers marching to the left. Moving right increases a number by one at each step, and moving left decreases it by one, so the number line is really a picture of counting in both directions. The integer -3 sits three steps left of zero, and the integer 4 sits four steps right of zero, and the distance of a number from zero is called its absolute value: the absolute value of -3 is 3, and the absolute value of 4 is 4. Drawing a number line is the first step for almost every integers question, because seeing the positions makes ordering and adding far easier than trying to do them in your head.

Equal gaps are essential on a number line, because the gaps are what make the picture honest: if the gap between 0 and 1 is wider than the gap between 1 and 2, the line lies about the numbers. Always mark zero first, then mark equal steps on both sides, and label at least the numbers you need for the question. A number line also shows why negative numbers behave as they do: -1 is greater than -5, even though 5 is greater than 1, because -1 sits closer to zero on the right side of the negative region. Pupils who draw the line rarely make this mistake, while pupils who guess from the digits alone often do. Keep a ruler handy and draw the line for every integers question until the picture lives in your head. More guides are on the [blog](/blog/).

On the number line, a number is larger when it sits further to the right, whatever its sign. So -5 is smaller than -2, because -5 sits further left, and -2 is smaller than 0, and 0 is smaller than 3, giving the order -5 < -2 < 0 < 3. A useful rule for negatives is that the larger the digits, the smaller the number: -8 is smaller than -3, because 8 is further from zero on the left. To order a mixed set like 4, -1, 0, -6 and 2, first separate the negatives and positives, order the negatives by closeness to zero in reverse, giving -6 then -1, then put zero, then the positives in order, giving -6, -1, 0, 2, 4. Checking your order by reading it left to right on a drawn number line catches most errors.

The opposite of a number is the number the same distance from zero on the other side, so the opposite of 5 is -5, the opposite of -3 is 3, and the opposite of 0 is 0. Opposites add to zero, which is why they are also called additive inverses: 5 plus -5 is 0, and -3 plus 3 is 0. Opposites appear in daily life as pairs that cancel: a lift that goes up 3 floors and then down 3 floors returns to its start, and a temperature that rises 4 degrees and then falls 4 degrees returns to its start. When a question asks for the opposite of an integer, simply change its sign, and leave zero unchanged. The symbol for the opposite of a number is a minus sign in front of it, so the opposite of -7 is written as -(-7), which equals 7.

Adding an integer means jumping on the number line: a positive addend means jump right, and a negative addend means jump left. To work out -3 + 5, start at -3 and jump 5 steps right: -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, landing on 2, so -3 + 5 = 2. To work out 4 + (-7), start at 4 and jump 7 steps left: 3, 2, 1, 0, -1, -2, -3, landing on -3, so 4 + (-7) = -3. The jump method never fails, and it explains the shortcut rules: when the signs are the same, add the absolute values and keep the sign, so (-2) + (-3) = -5, and when the signs differ, subtract the smaller absolute value from the larger and keep the sign of the larger, so -3 + 5 = 2 because 5 minus 3 is 2 and 5 is positive.

Adding integers is also how temperature and money problems work, which makes the jumps easy to picture. If the morning temperature is -2 degrees and it rises by 6 degrees, the new temperature is -2 + 6 = 4 degrees, found by jumping 6 steps right from -2. If a shopkeeper has Rs 100 and owes Rs 150, his balance is 100 + (-150) = -50, meaning he is Rs 50 short, found by jumping 150 steps left from 100, or more simply by the different-signs rule: 150 minus 100 is 50, and the larger absolute value belongs to the negative side. Practise jumps with small numbers first, saying each landing point aloud, and the shortcut rules will soon feel obvious rather than memorised. The [home page](/) has more study material.

diagram.caption: Start on the number line and jump in the direction of the sign.

paras: Subtracting an integer means jumping in the opposite direction to adding it: subtracting a positive number means jumping left, and subtracting a negative number means jumping right. To work out 3 - 5, start at 3 and jump 5 steps left, landing on -2, so 3 - 5 = -2. To work out -1 - 4, start at -1 and jump 4 steps left, landing on -5, so -1 - 4 = -5. The trickiest case is subtracting a negative: 5 - (-2) means jumping 2 steps right from 5, landing on 7, so 5 - (-2) = 7. This matches the rule that subtracting a negative is the same as adding its opposite: 5 - (-2) = 5 + 2 = 7, because taking away a debt is like gaining money.

A reliable shortcut turns every subtraction into an addition: keep the first number, change the minus to a plus, and change the sign of the second number, then use the addition rules. So 3 - 5 becomes 3 + (-5), which is -2, and -1 - 4 becomes -1 + (-4), which is -5, and 5 - (-2) becomes 5 + 2, which is 7. Write this conversion out for every subtraction until it is automatic, because skipping it is how sign errors creep in. Check each answer by adding back: if 5 - (-2) = 7, then 7 + (-2) should equal 5, and indeed it does, because 7 minus 2 is 5. This inverse check, adding the subtracted number back to the answer to recover the first number, works for every subtraction question. See the [solved notes](/solved.html) for more practice.

Integers describe any situation with two opposite directions, and recognising them is the first step to solving such problems. Temperatures use integers naturally: -4 degrees is 4 degrees below zero, and a rise from -4 degrees by 10 degrees gives -4 + 10 = 6 degrees. Buildings use integers too: ground floor is 0, floors above are positive, and basement floors are negative, so going from basement 2 up 5 floors reaches floor 3, because -2 + 5 = 3. Bank balances use integers: a balance of -Rs 500 means Rs 500 owed, and depositing Rs 800 gives -500 + 800 = Rs 300 in credit. Sea level works the same way: a submarine at -200 metres that rises 50 metres reaches -150 metres, because -200 + 50 = -150.

Sports and games also use integers, from golf scores below par to points lost in a quiz. A quiz team that scores 10 points, loses 4 points and then gains 7 points finishes on 10 - 4 + 7 = 13 points, worked left to right: 10 minus 4 is 6, and 6 plus 7 is 13. When a problem mixes gains and losses, write each gain as a positive number and each loss as a negative number, then add them in order on a number line. This turns a confusing story into a plain addition problem, which the jump method solves reliably. The habit of translating words into signed numbers, up as positive and down as negative, in as positive and out as negative, is the real skill of this chapter, and it transfers to every later topic that uses negative numbers.

points: Integers are whole numbers and their negatives: positives sit right of zero, negatives sit left, and zero is neither.
A number further right on the number line is larger: -5 < -2 < 0 < 3.
Add by jumping: positive addends jump right, negative addends jump left, so -3 + 5 = 2.
Subtract by converting to addition: change the sign of the second number, so 5 - (-2) = 5 + 2 = 7.
The opposite of a number is the same distance from zero on the other side: the opposite of -3 is 3.

faqs.q: Is -5 larger or smaller than -2?
faqs.a: Smaller, because -5 sits further left on the number line. For negative numbers, the larger the digits, the smaller the number.

faqs.q: How do I work out -3 + 5?
faqs.a: Start at -3 on the number line and jump 5 steps right: -2, -1, 0, 1, 2. You land on 2, so -3 + 5 = 2.

faqs.q: How do I work out 5 - (-2)?
faqs.a: Subtracting a negative is the same as adding its opposite, so 5 - (-2) = 5 + 2 = 7. On the number line, jump 2 steps right from 5.

faqs.q: What is the opposite of -7?
faqs.a: It is 7, because 7 is the same distance from zero on the opposite side. Opposites add to zero: -7 + 7 = 0.

faqs.q: Is zero positive or negative?
faqs.a: Neither. Zero sits between the positives and the negatives on the number line, and it is its own opposite.

title: Class 6 Averages: Mean, Median and Mode
desc: Mean, median and mode for Class 6: find averages from marks and heights with tables, and learn when to use each average.
intro: An average is a single number that represents a whole set of numbers, and Class 6 teaches three kinds: mean, median and mode. The mean is the total shared equally, the median is the middle value when the numbers are in order, and the mode is the value that appears most often. Each kind is useful in a different situation: the mean describes test scores, the median describes heights when one pupil is much taller than the rest, and the mode describes the most popular shoe size. This guide works through all three with marks and heights, shows how to use tables, and explains which average to choose. More Class 6 maths is in the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

sections.h2: The Mean: Sharing the Total Equally
paras: The mean is found by adding all the values and dividing by how many values there are, which is exactly like sharing a total equally. Five test scores of 70, 80, 90, 60 and 100 add to 400, because 70 plus 80 is 150, plus 90 is 240, plus 60 is 300, plus 100 is 400, and dividing 400 by 5 gives a mean of 80. The mean of 80 means that if all five pupils had scored equally, each would have scored 80, even though their real scores ranged from 60 to 100. The mean uses every value in the set, which is its strength and its weakness: one very high or very low value pulls the mean towards itself, so the mean of 10, 10, 10 and 90 is 30, which describes nobody in the group well.

Tables make mean calculations tidy, especially when values repeat. Suppose five pupils have heights of 120 cm, 130 cm, 140 cm, 150 cm and 160 cm: the total is 120 plus 130 plus 140 plus 150 plus 160, which is 700, and dividing by 5 gives a mean height of 140 cm. With a frequency table, multiply each value by how many times it appears, add those products, and divide by the total count: if the score 70 appears twice and 80 appears three times, the total is 2 times 70 plus 3 times 80, which is 140 plus 240, giving 380, and dividing by 5 pupils gives a mean of 76. Always check that your mean lies between the smallest and largest values: a mean outside that range is certainly wrong. Find more guides on the [blog](/blog/).

The median is the middle value when the numbers are arranged in order, smallest to largest, and ordering first is essential. The scores 55, 60, 70, 80 and 95 are already in order, and the middle value, with two values on each side, is 70, so the median is 70. The same set in a different order, 95, 55, 80, 70, 60, has the same median, because ordering it gives the same middle value. When there is an even number of values, there is no single middle value, so the median is the mean of the two middle values: for 60, 70, 80 and 90, the two middle values are 70 and 80, and their mean is 75, so the median is 75. Pupils who forget to order first, or who pick the middle of an unordered list, get the median wrong most of the time.

The median is the best average when an extreme value would distort the mean, which happens often with money and heights. The incomes 1,000, 1,200, 1,300, 1,500 and 20,000 have a mean of 5,000, because the total is 25,000 divided by 5, but the median is 1,300, which describes the typical income far better. Similarly, if one pupil in a class is much taller than the rest, the median height stays typical while the mean is pulled up. The median ignores the actual size of extreme values and cares only about their position in the order, which is why it stays steady when an outlier changes. When a question asks for a typical value and the data contains an outlier, choose the median and say why.

sections.h2: The Mode: The Most Frequent Value
paras: The mode is the value that appears most often in a set, and it is the only average that works for non-numerical data like favourite colours. The scores 60, 70, 70, 80 and 90 have the mode 70, because 70 appears twice while every other score appears once. A set can have two modes: the scores 60, 60, 70, 80 and 80 have two modes, 60 and 80, because both appear twice, and such a set is called bimodal. A set can also have no mode: the scores 60, 70, 80, 90 and 100 all appear once, so no value is most frequent. The mode is quick to find from a tally table, where the tallest tally column marks the mode at a glance, and it never needs division, which makes it the simplest average to calculate.

The mode is the right average when the question is about popularity or the most common choice. A shoe shop deciding which size to stock most of checks the mode of sizes sold, not the mean size, because a mean size of 6.5 might correspond to no shoe anyone wears. A teacher asking which question most pupils got wrong looks at the mode of the wrong answers. The mode's weakness is that it may ignore most of the data: in the set 70, 70, 70, 90, 95 and 100, the mode is 70, but the mean is 82.5, which better reflects the higher scores. Choosing between mean, median and mode means asking what the average is for, and the next section gives a simple guide to that choice. The [home page](/) has more study help.

Choosing the right average depends on the data and the question, and examiners often ask you to justify your choice. Use the mean when every value matters and there are no extreme outliers, such as ordinary test scores in a class, because the mean uses all the data. Use the median when an outlier would distort the mean, such as incomes or heights with one extreme value, because the median stays typical. Use the mode when you need the most common value or when the data is not numerical, such as favourite subjects or shoe sizes, because only the mode answers those questions. A strong answer names the average, gives its value, and explains the choice in one sentence, for example: the median is 70, chosen because one very low score would drag the mean down.

Sometimes a question asks for all three averages so that they can be compared, and the comparison itself is informative. For the scores 70, 80, 90, 60 and 100, the mean is 80, the median is 80, and there is no mode, because every score appears once, so the mean and median agree and the data looks balanced. For the scores 60, 70, 70, 80 and 90, the mean is 74, because the total is 370 divided by 5, the median is 70, and the mode is 70, so the mean sits above the median because of the high score of 90. Noticing whether the mean is above or below the median tells you which side the extreme values sit on, which is a useful skill for reading data in later classes.

diagram.caption: Three averages, three different jobs.

paras: Frequency tables organise data before averaging, and they are worth using whenever values repeat. A table of marks might show that 2 pupils scored 60, 3 pupils scored 70 and 1 pupil scored 80: the total number of pupils is 2 plus 3 plus 1, which is 6, and the total of the marks is 2 times 60 plus 3 times 70 plus 1 times 80, which is 120 plus 210 plus 80, giving 410, so the mean is 410 divided by 6, which is about 68.3. The mode is read straight from the table as the value with the highest frequency, which is 70, because 3 pupils scored it. The median needs the ordered list, which the table lets you rebuild: 60, 60, 70, 70, 70, 80, whose two middle values are both 70, so the median is 70.

Tally tables are the first step when raw data arrives as a list, because they turn counting into a table. Suppose the heights in centimetres are 130, 140, 130, 150, 140, 130 and 140: tallying gives 130 three times, 140 three times and 150 once, so the mode is shared between 130 and 140, the total is 3 times 130 plus 3 times 140 plus 1 times 150, which is 390 plus 420 plus 150, giving 960, and dividing by 7 pupils gives a mean of about 137.1 cm. Always check that your frequencies add to the number of data values, or your total will be wrong before you even divide. Tables also make checking easy: a classmate can recount your tallies and confirm your frequencies without redoing the whole calculation. See the [solved notes](/solved.html) for more practice.
