points: Mean = total divided by count: 70, 80, 90, 60 and 100 give a mean of 80.
Median = middle value in order: 55, 60, 70, 80 and 95 give a median of 70.
Mode = most frequent value: in 60, 70, 70, 80 and 90, the mode is 70.
With an even count, the median is the mean of the two middle values: 60, 70, 80, 90 give 75.
Use the mean for balanced data, the median when outliers distort, and the mode for popularity.

faqs.q: How do I find the mean of 70, 80, 90, 60 and 100?
faqs.a: Add them to get 400, then divide by 5, the number of values, giving a mean of 80.

faqs.q: How do I find the median of 60, 70, 80 and 90?
faqs.a: They are already in order, and with an even count there are two middle values, 70 and 80. Their mean is 75, so the median is 75.

faqs.q: What is the mode of 60, 70, 70, 80 and 90?
faqs.a: It is 70, because 70 appears twice while every other value appears once.

faqs.q: Can a set of numbers have no mode?
faqs.a: Yes. If every value appears the same number of times, such as 60, 70, 80, 90 and 100, there is no most frequent value and therefore no mode.

faqs.q: Why use the median instead of the mean sometimes?
faqs.a: Because one extreme value pulls the mean away from the typical value, while the median stays in the middle. For incomes 1,000, 1,200, 1,300, 1,500 and 20,000, the median 1,300 is far more typical than the mean 5,000.

title: Class 6 Perimeter and Area of Rectangles and Squares
desc: Perimeter and area of rectangles and squares for Class 6: fencing and flooring examples, formulas, and correct units explained.
intro: Perimeter is the distance around a shape, and area is the space inside it, and confusing the two is one of the most common Class 6 errors. A farmer fencing a field needs the perimeter, because fencing runs around the edge, while a farmer planting the field needs the area, because seeds cover the inside. Both are found from the same two measurements of a rectangle, its length and its width, but they use different formulas and different units: perimeter is measured in metres, while area is measured in square metres. This guide explains both formulas with fencing and flooring examples, so you always know which one a question is asking for. More Class 6 maths is in the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

paras: The perimeter of a shape is the total length of its boundary, found by adding the lengths of all its sides. A rectangle has two lengths and two widths, so its perimeter is length plus width plus length plus width, which shortens to 2 times (length + width). For a rectangle 12 m long and 8 m wide, the perimeter is 2 times (12 + 8), which is 2 times 20, giving 40 m. A square has four equal sides, so its perimeter is 4 times the side: a square with side 9 m has a perimeter of 4 times 9, which is 36 m. The brackets matter in the rectangle formula: 2 times (12 + 8) is 40, but 2 times 12 plus 8, without brackets, is 32, which is wrong, so always add length and width first.

Perimeter questions usually hide the sides in a story, and the first job is to find them. If a rectangular garden is 15 m long and its perimeter is 50 m, the width is found by working backwards: half the perimeter is 25 m, because 50 divided by 2 is 25, and half the perimeter equals length plus width, so the width is 25 minus 15, which is 10 m. Check it: 2 times (15 + 10) is 50 m, which matches. Perimeter is always measured in ordinary length units, metres, centimetres or kilometres, never in square units, because it is a length, not a surface. When a question mentions fencing, a border, a frame or walking around a field, it is asking for perimeter, and that word picture is your best clue.

The area of a rectangle is length times width, which counts how many unit squares fit inside it. A rectangle 12 m long and 8 m wide has an area of 12 times 8, which is 96 square metres, written as 96 m squared, because it holds 96 squares of 1 m by 1 m. A square with side 9 m has an area of 9 times 9, which is 81 square metres, because its length and width are both 9 m. Area units are always square units: square centimetres, square metres or square kilometres, and writing plain metres for an area is a unit error that loses marks. The picture behind the formula is simple: area counts squares, so its unit must be a square.

Area questions also hide in stories, and the clue words are covering, painting, tiling and planting. If a floor is 12 m by 8 m, its area is 96 square metres, and if each floor tile covers 1 square metre, the floor needs 96 tiles. If a wall 10 m long and 3 m high is to be painted, its area is 10 times 3, which is 30 square metres, and paint bought by the square metre can then be worked out. When the sides are in different units, convert first: a rectangle 2 m long and 50 cm wide must become 200 cm by 50 cm, giving 10,000 square centimetres, or 2 m by 0.5 m, giving 1 square metre, and both answers describe the same area. Converting before multiplying is the step pupils most often forget. More guides are on the [blog](/blog/).

sections.h2: Fencing a Field: A Worked Example
paras: A farmer wants to fence a rectangular field 12 m long and 8 m wide, with fencing that costs Rs 50 per metre, and the question asks for the total cost. First find the perimeter, because fencing runs around the edge: the perimeter is 2 times (12 + 8), which is 2 times 20, giving 40 m. Then multiply the perimeter by the cost per metre: 40 times 50 is Rs 2,000, so the fencing costs Rs 2,000. The two steps must stay in order: finding the area here would give 96 square metres, which cannot be multiplied by a per-metre price, and the units would not match. Checking units is a powerful habit: metres times rupees per metre gives rupees, which is the answer the question wants.

Fencing questions sometimes add a gate, which changes the length to be fenced. If the same field has a gate 2 m wide that needs no fencing, the length to fence is 40 minus 2, which is 38 m, and the cost is 38 times 50, which is Rs 1,900. If the field is fenced twice around, with a double row of wire, the length doubles to 80 m and the cost doubles to Rs 4,000. Read the story twice before calculating: does it mention a gate, a double row, or more than one field? Each detail changes the perimeter before the cost step, and catching it early saves redoing the whole question. A sketch of the field with its sides labelled makes these details visible instead of hiding them in words.

diagram.caption: Perimeter first, then multiply by the price per metre.

sections.h2: Flooring a Room: A Worked Example
paras: A room floor 12 m long and 8 m wide is to be covered with square tiles, each 1 m by 1 m, and the question asks how many tiles are needed. First find the area, because tiles cover the inside: the area is 12 times 8, which is 96 square metres. Each tile covers 1 times 1, which is 1 square metre, so the number of tiles is 96 divided by 1, which is 96 tiles. If the tiles were 2 m by 2 m instead, each would cover 4 square metres, and the room would need 96 divided by 4, which is 24 tiles. The method never changes: find the floor area, find one tile's area, and divide the first by the second.

Flooring questions sometimes ask for cost as well, which adds one more multiplication. If each 1-square-metre tile costs Rs 120, then 96 tiles cost 96 times 120, which is Rs 11,520, because 100 times 120 is 12,000 and 4 times 120 is 480, so 12,000 minus 480 is 11,520. Always allow a few spare tiles in real life for cutting and breakage, though exam questions usually ask for the exact count. A common error is dividing the perimeter by the tile size instead of the area, which gives 40 tiles for this room, a meaningless number, because tiles cover a surface, not a boundary. Asking yourself whether the question is about the edge or the inside, before choosing a formula, prevents this error every time. The [home page](/) has more study help.

sections.h2: Squares, Units and Checking Your Answers
paras: Squares are rectangles with all sides equal, so both formulas simplify: perimeter is 4 times the side, and area is side times side. A square garden with side 9 m has a perimeter of 36 m and an area of 81 square metres, and a square with side 15 cm has a perimeter of 60 cm and an area of 225 square centimetres, because 15 times 15 is 225. When a question gives only the area of a square, the side is found by asking which number multiplied by itself gives the area: an area of 81 square metres means a side of 9 m, because 9 times 9 is 81. This reverse skill, finding a square root for small perfect squares, appears often in perimeter and area questions.

Checking answers means checking numbers and units together. A perimeter answer in square metres is wrong, an area answer in plain metres is wrong, and an area smaller than the perimeter is possible but worth a second look, since area and perimeter measure different things. A quick estimate also helps: a 12 m by 8 m rectangle has an area near 100 square metres, because 12 times 8 is close to 10 times 10, so an answer of 960 or 9.6 signals a decimal or multiplication slip. Finally, remember that doubling the side of a square doubles its perimeter but quadruples its area: a 9 m square has area 81 square metres, while an 18 m square has area 324 square metres, which is 4 times 81. This is why area grows faster than perimeter, and why unit checks matter so much. See the [solved notes](/solved.html) for more practice.

Area is the space inside: the same rectangle has an area of 96 square metres.
Fencing uses perimeter: 40 m at Rs 50 per metre costs Rs 2,000.
Flooring uses area: a 96-square-metre floor needs 96 tiles of 1 square metre each.
Perimeter uses length units (m) and area uses square units (m squared) — never mix them up.

faqs.a: It is 2 times (12 + 8), which is 2 times 20, giving 40 m.

faqs.q: What is the area of a rectangle 12 m by 8 m?
faqs.a: It is 12 times 8, which is 96 square metres.

faqs.a: Multiply 40 by 50, which is Rs 2,000.

faqs.a: Fencing, borders, frames and walking around mean perimeter. Covering, painting, tiling and planting mean area.

title: Class 6 Maths Word Problems From Daily Life
desc: Turn market, pocket-money and sharing stories into sums: a four-step method for Class 6 maths word problems, with worked examples.
intro: Word problems feel hard because the maths is hidden inside a story, but every word problem is really an ordinary sum wearing a disguise. A market story about buying 3 kg of onions hides a multiplication, a pocket-money story about saving hides another, and a sharing story hides a division. The skill is not harder arithmetic: it is translating the story into numbers, choosing the right operation, and checking that the answer makes sense in the story. This guide teaches a four-step method and applies it to market, pocket-money, sharing and travel stories, so that word problems become the most satisfying questions on the paper. More Class 6 maths is in the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

paras: Step one is to read the problem twice, slowly, and underline the numbers and the question being asked. Many errors come from answering a different question than the one asked, such as giving the cost of the onions when the question asked for the change. Step two is to list what you know and what you need: the known numbers, the unknown, and any extra numbers that are not needed, because word problems sometimes include distractors. Step three is to choose the operation by the story's action: buying more of the same thing means multiplication, sharing equally means division, combining amounts means addition, and finding what is left means subtraction. Step four is to calculate carefully and then check the answer against the story.

Checking is a real step, not an optional extra, and it has two parts: checking the arithmetic and checking the sense. Check the arithmetic by redoing the calculation or by using the inverse operation: if you multiplied to get the cost, divide the cost by the quantity to recover the price. Check the sense by asking whether the answer fits the story: change cannot be larger than the money paid, a share cannot be larger than the whole, and a total cannot be smaller than any of its parts. Pupils who check both ways catch most of their own errors before the teacher ever sees them, and the four-step method, practised on easy problems, becomes fast enough to use under exam pressure. Find more guides on the [blog](/blog/).

diagram.caption: Four steps that work for market, money and sharing stories.

paras: Market problems combine multiplication for the cost and subtraction for the change, and doing them in order matters. A pupil buys 3 kg of onions at Rs 60 per kg and pays with a Rs 500 note: first find the cost, 3 times 60, which is Rs 180, then find the change, 500 minus 180, which is Rs 320. The two-step structure is the whole problem, and writing both steps as separate lines, cost = Rs 180 and change = Rs 320, makes the working easy to follow and easy to mark. A common error is subtracting before multiplying, such as 500 minus 60 times 3 worked left to right without brackets, so always finish the multiplication before the subtraction, or use brackets to show the order clearly.

Market problems with several items need a small table or a list before calculating, so that no item is forgotten. A shopping list of 2 kg of rice at Rs 120 per kg, 1 kg of sugar at Rs 90 per kg and 4 eggs at Rs 15 each costs 2 times 120, which is 240, plus 90, plus 4 times 15, which is 60, giving a total of 240 plus 90 plus 60, which is Rs 390. Paying with Rs 500 leaves change of 500 minus 390, which is Rs 110. Listing each item's cost on its own line, then adding the column, is slower than mental arithmetic but far more reliable, especially when the list grows. In a real shop, the shopkeeper's bill works exactly this way, line by line, and your school working should imitate a real bill.

Pocket-money problems are usually about saving the same amount repeatedly, which means multiplication, or about spending part of a total, which means subtraction or fractions. A pupil who saves Rs 20 every week will have 20 times 4, which is Rs 80, after 4 weeks, and 20 times 10, which is Rs 200, after 10 weeks, because saving steadily is repeated addition, which is multiplication. A pupil with Rs 500 who spends Rs 150 on a book and Rs 80 on a geometry set has spent 150 plus 80, which is Rs 230, and has 500 minus 230, which is Rs 270, left. Writing the spent total first, then subtracting once, is cleaner than subtracting twice, though both give the same answer.

Some pocket-money problems ask how long saving will take, which means division. If a bat costs Rs 600 and a pupil saves Rs 50 a week, the weeks needed are 600 divided by 50, which is 12 weeks. If the division leaves a remainder, the answer needs thought: saving Rs 50 a week towards a Rs 625 bat gives 625 divided by 50, which is 12 remainder 25, so 12 weeks give Rs 600, which is not enough, and a 13th week is needed, with Rs 25 to spare. Remainder problems are common in word problems, and the story decides whether to round up, round down or keep the remainder: weeks needed round up, full boxes round down, and money left over stays as a remainder. Always read the final question to see which kind of remainder answer it wants. The [home page](/) has more study help.

sections.h2: Sharing Problems: Equal Parts and Leftovers
paras: Sharing problems divide a total into equal parts, and the key question is whether the division is exact or leaves a remainder. Twenty-four sweets shared equally among 6 friends give 24 divided by 6, which is 4 sweets each, with nothing left over, because 6 times 4 is exactly 24. Thirty sweets shared among 7 friends give 30 divided by 7, which is 4 remainder 2, so each friend gets 4 sweets and 2 are left over, which might be kept by the host or shared differently. The multiplication check, 7 times 4 plus 2 is 30, confirms the division, and writing the remainder as part of the answer, not hiding it, earns full marks. Sharing money works the same way: Rs 720 shared among 6 friends gives Rs 120 each, because 6 times 120 is 720.

Sharing problems sometimes work backwards: given the share and the number of people, find the total, which means multiplication. If each of 8 pupils gets 5 pencils, the total is 8 times 5, which is 40 pencils, and if each of 12 guests gets 3 samosas, the total is 36 samosas. Another type shares by ratio rather than equally, which connects to the ratio chapter: Rs 300 shared in the ratio 2:1 gives 3 parts of Rs 100 each, so the shares are Rs 200 and Rs 100. The habit that unites all sharing problems is asking first whether the shares are equal or in a ratio, and second whether a remainder is possible, because those two answers choose the operation and the form of the answer. See the [solved notes](/solved.html) for more practice.

Travel problems use speed, distance and time, and in Class 6 they usually give two of these and ask for the third with simple numbers. A car travelling 60 km in one hour travels 60 times 3, which is 180 km, in 3 hours at the same speed, because equal hours cover equal distances. A cyclist who covers 120 km in 4 hours travels 120 divided by 4, which is 30 km, in one hour, which is the speed. Time problems also use timetables: a bus leaving at 9:15 and arriving at 11:45 travels for 2 hours and 30 minutes, found by counting from 9:15 to 11:15, which is 2 hours, and then 30 more minutes to 11:45. Drawing a small timeline for time problems prevents the common error of subtracting the clock readings as if they were ordinary numbers.

Mixed problems combine two operations, and the four-step method keeps them manageable. A pupil walks 2 km to school in 30 minutes and returns by bus in 10 minutes: the total travel time is 30 plus 10, which is 40 minutes, a simple addition hiding inside a travel story. A family drives 150 km in the morning and 90 km in the afternoon, covering 240 km in total, and if the car uses 1 litre of petrol for every 20 km, the petrol used is 240 divided by 20, which is 12 litres. The second example needs addition first and division second, and the order comes from the story: total distance first, then petrol from that total. When a problem has two steps, label each step's result before moving on, so the second step uses the right number and the examiner can follow your thinking.

title: Class 7 English Tenses: Present and Past in Real Sentences
desc: Learn Class 7 English tenses with real daily-routine sentences: present simple, present continuous, past simple and past continuous, explained clearly with examples.
intro: Tenses tell your reader when something happens, and getting them right makes your English clear at once. In Class 7, four tenses do most of the work in your writing: the present simple, the present continuous, the past simple, and the past continuous. Pupils often know the rules but still mix the tenses up in sentences, writing things like "I am go to school every day" when they mean "I go to school every day". This guide fixes that confusion with daily-routine sentences you can copy, change, and reuse. By the end, you will be able to choose the right tense for habits, actions happening now, finished past actions, and actions that were in progress.

sections.h2: Present Simple: Habits and Daily Routines
paras: We use the present simple for habits, routines, and facts that are generally true. Think of the things you do every day: "I wake up at six o'clock." "My mother cooks breakfast." "We walk to school together." The verb stays in its base form with I, we, you, and they, but with he, she, and it we add -s or -es: "He wakes up at six o'clock." "She watches the news after dinner." This small -s ending is the most common mark lost in Class 7 writing, so check every present simple sentence for it when the subject is he, she, or it.

Signal words help you spot the present simple: every day, always, usually, often, sometimes, and never. For example, "I always brush my teeth before breakfast" and "Ali sometimes plays cricket in the evening" both describe repeated actions, not actions happening right now. Negative sentences use do not or does not: "I do not like cold milk" and "She does not watch television at night." Questions use do or does: "Do you walk to school?" "Does your brother play football?" Practise by writing five sentences about your own morning routine, then read them aloud and check each verb ending.

We use the present continuous for actions happening at this moment or around now. The form is am, is, or are plus the verb with -ing: "I am writing my homework now." "She is reading a storybook." "They are playing in the garden." Compare this with the present simple: "I write in my diary every night" is a habit, but "I am writing in my diary now" is happening at this moment. That contrast is exactly what examiners test, so learn the pair together rather than learning each tense alone.

Signal words for the present continuous include now, right now, at the moment, today, and Look! or Listen! For example, "Look! The cat is climbing the tree" and "At the moment, we are preparing for the test." A common mistake is dropping the helping verb: "She reading a book" is wrong, while "She is reading a book" is correct. Another mistake is using the continuous for a habit: "I am going to school every day" is wrong, because every day signals a habit and needs the present simple, "I go to school every day." Keep the two uses separate and your sentences will sound natural.

sections.h2: Past Simple: Finished Actions in the Past
paras: We use the past simple for actions that started and finished in the past. Regular verbs add -ed: "We walked to the market yesterday." "She cleaned her room last Sunday." Irregular verbs change their form, and these must be learned by heart: "I went to school early." "He ate his lunch quickly." "They saw a beautiful rainbow." Time words such as yesterday, last night, last week, and two days ago are strong signals for the past simple, and they should always sit with a past verb, never a present one.

Negatives in the past simple use did not plus the base verb, not the past form: "I did not go to the park yesterday" is correct, while "I did not went to the park" is wrong. Questions work the same way: "Did you finish your homework?" not "Did you finished your homework?" This is the single most tested past-tense rule in Class 7, so practise it until it feels automatic. Write ten past simple sentences about yesterday, then turn five of them into negatives and five into questions, checking each time that the main verb is back in its base form after did.

sections.h2: Past Continuous: Actions in Progress in the Past
paras: We use the past continuous for an action that was in progress at a particular time in the past. The form is was or were plus verb-ing: "I was reading when the lights went out." "They were playing cricket at four o'clock." It often appears together with the past simple: the longer action takes the past continuous and the shorter, interrupting action takes the past simple. For example, "While I was walking home, it started to rain" — the walk was in progress and the rain interrupted it. Learning this pair of sentences together makes both tenses easier to remember.

The words while and when are your best guides here. While usually introduces the longer, continuing action: "While she was cooking dinner, her friend called." When usually introduces the shorter action: "She was cooking dinner when her friend called." Both orders are correct, and both mean the same thing, so choose the one that sounds smoother in your paragraph. Avoid the mistake of putting both verbs in the past simple — "While I walked home, it started to rain" loses the sense that the walk was still going on. The past continuous adds that background feeling, which is why story writers use it so often.

diagram.caption: Ask these questions in order to choose the correct tense for your sentence.

sections.h2: A Daily-Routine Drill You Can Reuse
paras: Here is a drill that practises all four tenses with one routine. First, write your morning in the present simple: "I wake up at six. I wash my face. I eat breakfast. I go to school." Second, rewrite the same morning as if it is happening now: "I am waking up. I am washing my face. I am eating breakfast." Third, rewrite it as yesterday: "I woke up at six. I washed my face. I ate breakfast. I went to school." Fourth, add a past continuous background: "While I was eating breakfast, my friend arrived." One routine, four tenses, and every sentence checked against its signal words — that is how tense sense becomes automatic.

Finally, build a self-check habit before you hand in any written work. Read each paragraph once only for verbs, underlining every verb and asking whether its tense matches its time words. If you see yesterday beside a present verb, or every day beside a continuous verb, fix it before the examiner finds it. Keep a small notebook list of irregular past forms — go and went, see and saw, eat and ate, write and wrote — and add one new verb each week. points: Present simple is for habits and routines, with -s or -es for he, she, and it.
Present continuous is am, is, or are plus verb-ing for actions happening now.
Past simple describes finished past actions; use did not plus the base verb for negatives.
Past continuous shows an action in progress in the past, often interrupted by a past simple action.
Practise all four tenses on one daily routine to learn the contrasts quickly.

faqs.q: When do I use the present simple instead of the present continuous?
faqs.a: Use the present simple for habits and routines, such as "I go to school every day", and the present continuous for actions happening now, such as "I am going to school now". Time words like every day and now usually tell you which one fits.

faqs.q: Why is "I did not went" wrong?
faqs.a: After did, the main verb returns to its base form, so the correct sentence is "I did not go". The past meaning is already carried by did, and adding a past verb as well doubles the past marking.

faqs.q: What is the difference between "I read yesterday" and "I was reading at six"?
faqs.a: "I read yesterday" reports a finished past action, while "I was reading at six" describes an action in progress at that past time. Use the past continuous when you want the background feeling of an action still going on.

faqs.q: How do I remember irregular past forms?
faqs.a: Learn them in small groups and use them in your own sentences: go and went, see and saw, eat and ate, write and wrote. A notebook list with one new verb added each week builds the set steadily without cramming.

faqs.q: Which tense goes with "while"?
faqs.a: While usually introduces the longer action in the past continuous, as in "While I was walking home, it started to rain". The shorter, interrupting action takes the past simple.

title: Class 7 Active and Passive Voice: A Simple Switch
desc: Master Class 7 active and passive voice: learn how subject and object switch places with be plus past participle, and when the passive actually sounds better.
intro: In an active sentence, the doer of the action comes first: "Ali kicked the ball." In a passive sentence, the action's receiver comes first: "The ball was kicked by Ali." Both sentences describe the same event, but they shine the light on different parts of it. Class 7 pupils often find the passive confusing because the verb changes shape and the subject and object seem to swap places. In fact, the switch follows one steady pattern — be plus the past participle — and once you can see that pattern, you can change sentences in both directions without fear. This guide shows the switch step by step, tense by tense.

sections.h2: Seeing the Switch: Subject and Object Change Places
paras: Start with a simple active sentence and name its three parts: subject, verb, and object. In "Sara wrote a letter", Sara is the subject who does the action, wrote is the verb, and a letter is the object that receives the action. To make it passive, move the object to the front, change the verb to be plus the past participle, and move the old subject to the end after by: "A letter was written by Sara." Nothing about the event has changed — only the spotlight has moved from Sara to the letter.

Try the same switch on other sentences and watch the pattern repeat. "The gardener waters the plants" becomes "The plants are watered by the gardener." "My father bought a new bicycle" becomes "A new bicycle was bought by my father." "The teacher praised the class" becomes "The class was praised by the teacher." In each case, the object moves to the front, the verb becomes a form of be plus the past participle, and the old subject follows by. Practise by taking five active sentences from your own notebook and switching each one, checking that the new subject agrees with its new verb.

sections.h2: The Key Formula: Be Plus Past Participle
paras: The heart of the passive is be plus the past participle, and the be verb changes with the tense while the past participle stays the same. In the present simple it is am, is, or are plus the past participle: "The room is cleaned every day." In the past simple it is was or were plus the past participle: "The room was cleaned yesterday." In the present continuous it is am, is, or are plus being plus the past participle: "The room is being cleaned now." The past participle is the third form of the verb — written, cleaned, bought, made — and learning it is the same work as learning irregular past forms.

The most common passive mistake is forgetting the be verb or using the wrong participle. "The letter written by Sara" is not a complete passive sentence; it needs was: "The letter was written by Sara." Likewise, "The plants are water" is wrong because water is not a past participle; the correct form is "The plants are watered." Build a habit of checking two things in every passive sentence: is there a form of be, and is the main verb in its past participle form? If both answers are yes, the skeleton of your passive is sound, and only the tense and agreement remain to check.

The passive is not just a grammar exercise; writers choose it when the receiver of the action matters more than the doer, or when the doer is unknown or unimportant. News reports use it for this reason: "The road was repaired last week" matters because of the road, not because of who repaired it. Science writing does the same: "The solution was heated slowly" focuses on the experiment, not on the person holding the burner. In your own writing, use the passive when the result is the news, and keep the active when the person matters, as in "Our teacher announced the result."

The passive also lets you leave the doer out entirely when it is unknown. "My bicycle was stolen last night" is natural because you do not know who stole it, and adding by someone would add nothing. But do not hide behind the passive to avoid naming a doer who matters: "Mistakes were made" sounds evasive beside "I made a mistake." Good writers switch voices on purpose. As a rule for Class 7, use the active as your default voice, and choose the passive when the receiver deserves the spotlight or the doer is unknown. That choice, made deliberately, is what examiners reward.

Each tense has its own passive form, but the pattern never changes: keep the tense in the be verb and keep the past participle fixed. Present simple: "She cleans the classroom" becomes "The classroom is cleaned by her." Past simple: "She cleaned the classroom" becomes "The classroom was cleaned by her." Present continuous: "She is cleaning the classroom" becomes "The classroom is being cleaned by her." Future with will: "She will clean the classroom" becomes "The classroom will be cleaned by her." Notice how the tense lives in is, was, is being, and will be, while cleaned never changes.

Pronouns also change their form when they move. The subject I becomes by me, he becomes by him, she becomes by her, we becomes by us, and they becomes by them: "They painted the hall" becomes "The hall was painted by them." Keep the new subject and verb in agreement too: "The books were collected" is correct, while "The books was collected" is wrong, because books is plural and needs were. Work through one tense at a time, writing five conversions for each, and the whole system will feel like one rule with different be verbs rather than four separate rules to memorise.

diagram.alt: Active Voice Compared with Passive Voice
diagram.caption: The same event told two ways: the active spotlights the doer, the passive spotlights the receiver.

sections.h2: Practice and Common Mistakes to Avoid
paras: Now put the whole switch into practice with a short drill. Take the paragraph of your day — "I opened my books. My mother packed my lunch. The teacher checked our homework" — and rewrite it in the passive: "My books were opened by me. My lunch was packed by my mother. Our homework was checked by the teacher." The passive version sounds odd for a diary, and that oddness is itself a lesson: the active is usually better for personal writing, while the passive suits reports and descriptions. Being able to convert is the skill; knowing when to convert is the judgement.

Watch for three mistakes that appear again and again. First, a missing be verb: "The work completed yesterday" needs was. Second, a wrong participle: "The door was broke" should be "The door was broken." Third, a subject-verb mismatch after the switch: "The letters was posted" should be "The letters were posted." Read every passive sentence backwards if you are unsure: find the past participle, check the be verb before it, and check that the new subject agrees with that be verb. points: Passive moves the object to the front and the old subject after by.
The passive verb is always a form of be plus the past participle.
The tense lives in the be verb; the past participle never changes.
Use the passive when the receiver matters more or the doer is unknown.
Check every passive for a be verb, a correct participle, and subject-verb agreement.

faqs.q: How do I change "Ali kicked the ball" into the passive?
faqs.a: Move the object to the front, use be plus the past participle, and put the old subject after by: "The ball was kicked by Ali." The past tense stays in was, and kicked becomes the participle kicked.

faqs.q: What is the past participle?
faqs.a: It is the third form of the verb, used after be in the passive and after have in perfect tenses: written, cleaned, bought, broken, made. For regular verbs it ends in -ed, while irregular ones must be learned, such as write, wrote, written.

faqs.q: Can I leave out "by Ali" in a passive sentence?
faqs.a: Yes, when the doer is unknown or unimportant, as in "My bicycle was stolen last night". Keep the by-phrase when the doer is important information, as in "The prize was won by Sara".

faqs.q: Why is "The plants are water" wrong?
faqs.a: Because the passive needs a past participle after be, and water is the base form. The correct sentence is "The plants are watered", with the participle watered.

faqs.q: Should I write everything in the passive?
faqs.a: No. Use the active as your default voice and choose the passive on purpose, when the receiver matters more than the doer or the doer is unknown. A paragraph of only passive sentences sounds heavy and dull.

title: Class 7 Direct and Indirect Speech Without Confusion
desc: Learn Class 7 direct and indirect speech step by step: reporting verbs, tense shifts, pronoun changes and time-word changes, with clear worked examples.
intro: Direct speech repeats a person's exact words inside quotation marks: Sara said, "I am happy today." Indirect speech reports the same meaning without the exact words: Sara said that she was happy that day. The meaning stays the same, but three things shift — the tense, the pronouns, and the time words — and pupils who miss one of those shifts lose marks. The good news is that the shifts follow a simple rule: move everything one step back in time, as if you are reporting from a later point. This guide walks through that rule with reporting verbs, tense shifts, pronoun changes, questions, and commands, so reported speech stops feeling like guesswork.

sections.h2: Direct and Indirect: What Actually Changes
paras: Direct speech shows the speaker's own words: Ali said, "I will come tomorrow." Indirect speech reports those words through a reporting verb: Ali said that he would come the next day. Four changes happened at once. The quotation marks and comma disappeared, the word that joined the two parts, the pronoun I became he, and the verbs shifted back — will became would and tomorrow became the next day. Once you can name those four changes, every reported-speech question becomes a checklist rather than a puzzle.

The reporting verb itself matters too. Said is the safe, neutral choice, but told needs an object: "She told me that she was busy" is correct, while "She told that she was busy" is incomplete. Other reporting verbs add meaning: asked for questions, requested for polite requests, and ordered for commands. Choosing the right reporting verb shows the examiner that you understood the speaker's intention, not just the words. Practise by taking five direct sentences from a storybook and reporting each one, checking off the four changes every time.

sections.h2: The Tense Shift: One Step Back
paras: The main tense rule is simple: when the reporting verb is in the past, shift the reported verb one step back. Present simple becomes past simple: "I like mangoes" becomes "He said that he liked mangoes." Present continuous becomes past continuous: "I am reading" becomes "She said that she was reading." Present perfect becomes past perfect: "I have finished my work" becomes "He said that he had finished his work." Future with will becomes would: "I will help you" becomes "She said that she would help me." Learn these four shifts as a set and most Class 7 questions are already covered.

Two exceptions are worth knowing. If the reported statement is a universal truth, the tense often stays: "The teacher said that the sun rises in the east" keeps rises, because the fact is still true. Also, if the reporting verb is in the present — "She says that she is busy" — no backshift happens at all, because the report is happening in the same time frame as the speech. Watch out for the most common error: shifting only half the sentence, as in "He said that he is busy" when the original was present and the report is in the past. The correct backshift is "He said that he was busy."

sections.h2: Pronouns and Time Words Change Too
paras: Pronouns change to match the new point of view, and this is where careless errors creep in. When Sara says, "I love my school," the report from someone else becomes "Sara said that she loved her school" — I becomes she and my becomes her. When Ali tells you, "I will help you," your report becomes "Ali said that he would help me" — you becomes me, because the report is now from your point of view. Always ask: who is speaking now, and who is being spoken about? The pronouns must answer from the reporter's position, not the original speaker's.

Time and place words shift as well, because the report happens later and usually somewhere else. Today becomes that day, tomorrow becomes the next day, yesterday becomes the previous day, now becomes then, here becomes there, and this becomes that. So "I am busy today" reported later becomes "She said that she was busy that day," and "I will come here tomorrow" becomes "He said that he would come there the next day." Pupils often shift the tense perfectly and then leave tomorrow unchanged, which breaks the logic of reporting from a later time. Check pronouns and time words as a pair at the end of every conversion.

Questions in indirect speech lose their question form: the word order returns to statement order and the question mark disappears. A yes-or-no question uses if or whether: "Are you ready?" asked by the teacher becomes "The teacher asked whether we were ready." A wh-question keeps its question word and takes statement order: "Where do you live?" becomes "She asked me where I lived" — not "where did I live," because the helping verb did disappears in the statement order. This return to statement order is the single most tested rule in reported questions, so drill it with ten examples until it feels natural.

Commands and requests use an infinitive with to, and the reporting verb tells the reader what kind of sentence it was. "Please sit down" becomes "The teacher asked us to sit down," while "Do not run" becomes "She told the boys not to run." Notice that not goes before to in a negative command. Requests with please usually take asked, while strict orders take ordered or told: "Open your books" becomes "The teacher told us to open our books." Keep the structure tight — reporting verb, object, to plus base verb — and commands become the easiest part of reported speech rather than the hardest.

diagram.alt: Converting Direct Speech to Indirect Speech
diagram.caption: Follow these five steps in order for every reported-speech conversion.

paras: Here is a drill that covers every rule in this guide in five minutes a day. Take one short dialogue from your English reader — even four lines is enough — and report the whole conversation in your notebook. Convert one statement, one question, one command, and one sentence with a time word, then check your work against the five-step list above. Do this for a week and you will have practised thirty-five conversions, which is more than most pupils do in a whole term. The goal is not speed but accuracy: a slow, correct conversion beats a fast, half-shifted one every time.

Before any test, run a final checklist over your reported sentences. Is the word order statement order in questions? Did the tense shift one step back? Do the pronouns match the reporter? Did today, tomorrow, and yesterday change? Did commands use to plus the base verb? If all five answers are yes, your reported speech is sound. With a past reporting verb, shift the reported tense one step back.
Pronouns change to match the reporter's point of view.
Time words shift too: today, tomorrow, and yesterday all move.
Questions return to statement order, and commands use to plus the base verb.

faqs.q: How do I report "I am happy today"?
faqs.a: Shift the tense, pronoun, and time word: "She said that she was happy that day." Present continuous becomes past continuous, I becomes she, and today becomes that day.

faqs.q: What is the difference between said and told?
faqs.a: Said does not need an object, as in "She said that she was busy", while told needs one: "She told me that she was busy". Using told without an object is incomplete.

faqs.q: How do I report a yes-or-no question?
faqs.a: Use if or whether and statement word order: "Are you ready?" becomes "The teacher asked whether we were ready." There is no question mark and no helping-verb inversion.

faqs.q: How do I report "Please sit down"?
faqs.a: Use asked plus an infinitive: "The teacher asked us to sit down." For a negative command, put not before to: "She told them not to run."

faqs.q: Does the tense always shift in indirect speech?
faqs.a: Not always. If the reporting verb is in the present, as in "She says that she is busy", no backshift happens. Universal truths also often keep their tense, as in "The teacher said that the sun rises in the east".

title: Class 7 Prepositions: In, On and At Explained
desc: Master Class 7 prepositions in, on and at for place and time: clear rules, picture examples and common mistakes, so you never mix them up again.
intro: In, on, and at are tiny words that cause big mistakes, because each one can describe both place and time, and the choice depends on size and precision. Pupils write "in Monday" or "at the table" when they mean something else entirely, and the error stands out to any examiner. The good news is that the rules follow a simple picture: at is a point, on is a surface, and in is a space you can be inside. Once that picture is fixed in your mind, most preposition questions answer themselves. This guide covers place and time separately, with picture examples and the fixed phrases you simply have to learn.

sections.h2: Place: At a Point, On a Surface, In a Space
paras: Picture the three prepositions as a target. At is the exact point: "We met at the gate." "She is waiting at the bus stop." Use at for small, specific places such as an address point, a station, or a corner. On is a surface something rests on: "The book is on the table." "The picture hangs on the wall." Use on whenever one thing touches the surface of another. In is an enclosed space: "The books are in the bag." "We live in Karachi." Use in for rooms, buildings, cities, and countries — any space with boundaries you can be inside.

The size rule helps with towns and addresses. We say "at the school gate" for the point, "on Main Street" for the street as a line, and "in Karachi" for the city as an area. The same building can take different prepositions depending on what you mean: "at school" for the point where you are, but "in the classroom" for the room you sit inside. Test yourself by picturing each sentence: point, surface, or enclosed space? If you can see the picture, the preposition usually follows. Draw the three pictures once in your notebook and the rule will stay with you far longer than a memorised list.

sections.h2: Time: At a Moment, On a Day, In a Period
paras: Time works the same way, with at for a point in time, on for a day, and in for a longer period. At takes clock times and single moments: "The class starts at eight o'clock." "We eat dinner at night." On takes days and dates: "We have a test on Monday." "Her birthday is on 14 August." In takes months, years, seasons, and parts of the day: "School opens in April." "He was born in 2013." "It rains in summer." "We study in the morning." The pattern is point, day, period — and it mirrors the place rule exactly, which makes both rules easier to remember together.

Three fixed time phrases break the pattern and must be learned as they are: at night, at the weekend, and in the morning, afternoon, and evening. Notice that night takes at even though morning takes in — English is not perfectly logical here, and examiners know it, which is why these phrases are tested so often. Also note at noon and at midnight, both points in time. A useful drill is to write your whole weekly timetable with prepositions: "I have English on Monday at nine o'clock in the morning" practises all three in one sentence. Read such sentences aloud until the combinations sound right, because the ear catches preposition errors faster than the eye.

Let us fix the rules with one picture you can replay in your head. Imagine a cat. The cat sits at the door when it waits at a point. The cat sleeps on the mat when it rests on a surface. The cat hides in the box when it is inside an enclosed space. Now imagine the same cat through a week: it visits the vet on Friday, it naps at noon, and it stays indoors in winter. Six sentences, and every preposition follows the point, surface, and space picture. When a test question confuses you, bring back the cat and ask which picture your sentence matches.

The same picture trick works for trickier sentences. "The keys are in the drawer" is a space, so in is right. "The keys are on the shelf" is a surface, so on is right. "Meet me at the library" is a point, so at is right — but "The books are in the library" is a space, so in is right, even for the same building. The building did not change; your way of picturing it did. That is the real secret of prepositions: they describe how you see the place or time, not the place or time itself. Practise by describing your own room with ten in, on, and at sentences, and check each one against its picture.

sections.h2: Fixed Phrases to Learn by Heart
paras: Some prepositions cannot be worked out from rules and must be learned as fixed phrases. We say in the morning but at night, on foot but by bus, at home but in the house, interested in, good at, afraid of, and arrive at a small place but arrive in a big city. "She arrived at the station" and "She arrived in Karachi" show the small-point versus large-area rule again, but many phrases are simply customs of English. The only way to master them is to collect them: keep a notebook page headed "Preposition phrases" and add every new phrase your teacher or reader gives you, with a full example sentence beside it.

Reading is the fastest way to grow that collection, because fixed phrases appear naturally in stories and lessons. When you meet one, underline the whole phrase, not just the preposition — "good at mathematics" is the unit to learn, not "at" alone. Then use the phrase in a sentence of your own the same day, so it moves from your reading memory into your writing memory. Ten phrases learned this way beat fifty phrases copied from a list and never used. Before a test, read your phrase page aloud twice; hearing the correct combinations is what stops you writing "in Monday" under pressure.

diagram.alt: In, On and At at a Glance
diagram.caption: One picture for place and time: at is a point, on is a surface or day, in is a space or period.

sections.h2: Common Mistakes and a Quick Test
paras: Here are the mistakes examiners see most often, with their corrections. "In Monday" should be "on Monday." "At the morning" should be "in the morning." "On Karachi" should be "in Karachi." "At the table" for a book resting on it should be "on the table." Each error comes from using the wrong picture — a day treated as a space, a morning treated as a point, a city treated as a surface. Run the picture test on every doubtful sentence and most errors vanish before you write them. Also watch for missing prepositions: "I go school" needs to: "I go to school."

Finish with this quick self-test, answering without looking back. Fill in the blanks: "We meet ___ the park ___ Sunday ___ five o'clock." "The cat is ___ the roof ___ the morning." "My birthday is ___ December." The answers are at, on, at; on, in; in. If you got them all, your picture sense is working. If any felt like a guess, return to the cat picture and the point, surface, and space rule. points: At is a point, on is a surface, and in is an enclosed space.
For time, at takes moments, on takes days and dates, and in takes longer periods.
Learn fixed phrases as whole units, such as in the morning and at night.
The same building can take at or in depending on how you picture it.

faqs.q: Why do we say "on Monday" but "in April"?
faqs.a: On takes days and dates, while in takes longer periods such as months, years, and seasons. Monday is a single day, so it takes on; April is a whole month, so it takes in.

faqs.q: Is it "at school" or "in school"?
faqs.a: Both are possible with different meanings. "At school" treats school as a point where you are, while "in the classroom" treats the room as an enclosed space. The preposition follows how you picture the place.

faqs.q: Why is "at night" correct but "in the morning"?
faqs.a: These are fixed phrases of English custom, not logic. Night takes at, while morning, afternoon, and evening take in. Learn them as phrases and they stop causing errors.

faqs.q: Do we say "arrive at" or "arrive in"?
faqs.a: Arrive at takes a small, specific place, as in "arrive at the station", while arrive in takes a large area, as in "arrive in Karachi". The size rule decides.

faqs.q: How can I stop mixing up in, on, and at?
faqs.a: Use the picture test: point means at, surface means on, and enclosed space means in. Practise by describing your room and your week with all three, and keep a notebook page of fixed phrases you meet in reading.

title: Class 7 Articles: A, An and The Rules That Stick
desc: Learn Class 7 articles a, an and the with a simple rule: first mention versus known things, plus vowel sounds, no-article cases and short drills.
intro: A, an, and the are the smallest words in English and some of the most tested, because a missing or wrong article makes a sentence feel off even when every other word is right. The whole system rests on one idea: a and an introduce something new or any one of a kind, while the points to something already known or the only one of its kind. Add one sound rule for choosing between a and an, and a short list of no-article cases, and you have the complete Class 7 article system. This guide explains each rule with short drills you can do in your notebook tonight.

sections.h2: A and An: First Mention of Something New
paras: Use a or an when you mention something for the first time, or when you mean any one of a kind rather than a particular one. "I saw a dog in the street" introduces a dog the reader has not met before. "She wants to be a teacher" means any teacher, not one specific teacher. "He bought an umbrella" introduces one umbrella out of many. In each case, the reader cannot yet point to which one you mean, and that newness is exactly what a and an signal. Once the thing has been introduced, you switch to the, as the next section explains.

The choice between a and an depends on sound, not spelling. Use an before a vowel sound: "an apple", "an egg", "an hour" — hour starts with the letter h but its first sound is a vowel, so it takes an. Use a before a consonant sound: "a book", "a university" — university starts with the letter u but its first sound is the consonant y, so it takes a. Say the word aloud and listen to its first sound; that sound decides. Practise with a list of tricky words — hour, honest, university, European, one — and the sound rule will replace the spelling guess that causes most errors.

sections.h2: The: Known Things and Only Ones
paras: Use the when the reader already knows which thing you mean. The most common way a thing becomes known is that you mentioned it before: "I saw a dog in the street. The dog was chasing a cat." The first mention takes a, and every later mention takes the, because now both writer and reader are thinking of the same dog. The also points to things known from the situation: "Please close the door" works because there is one obvious door in the room, and "The teacher asked us to sit down" works because the class knows which teacher is meant.

The also goes with things that are the only one of their kind: the sun, the moon, the earth, the sky. There is only one sun in our sky, so it is always the sun, never a sun, in ordinary writing. The same logic covers superlatives and firsts: "the best student", "the tallest boy", "the first chapter" — each one points to a single, identified thing. A useful test is to ask: can my reader point to exactly which one I mean? If yes, use the. If the reader would ask "which one?", you probably need a or an, or no article at all.

Some nouns take no article at all, and this is where many pupils add a or the by mistake. General plural and uncountable nouns take no article when you mean them in general: "Dogs are loyal animals" speaks about dogs in general, not particular dogs, so it needs no article. "Water is precious" and "Honesty is the best policy" work the same way. School subjects, languages, and most sports also take no article: "She studies mathematics", "He speaks Sindhi", "They play cricket." Meals follow the same pattern in general statements: "We eat breakfast at seven."

Names of most places take no article too: "She lives in Karachi", "He visited Pakistan", "We went to Murree." Exceptions with the include rivers, seas, and groups of islands — the Indus, the Arabian Sea — and country names that are plural or contain a common noun, such as the United States. Do not add the to a person's name or to a single mountain: "Ali", "Mount Everest". When you are unsure, ask whether you mean the thing in general or one particular thing. General meaning usually means no article, while particular meaning usually means the.

sections.h2: Short Drills That Fix the Rules
paras: Drill one: first mention versus known things. Read this paragraph and fill in the articles: "Ali found ___ old key in ___ garden. ___ key opened ___ small box." The answers are an, the, The, a — an old key is a first mention, the garden is known from the situation, The key is now known, and a small box is newly introduced. Cover the answers and repeat the paragraph until the pattern feels obvious. Then write your own four-sentence paragraph that introduces two new things and mentions them again, checking that every first mention takes a or an and every repeat takes the.

Drill two: sound, not spelling. Sort these words into a and an columns: apple, university, hour, egg, European, honest man, one rupee, orange. The an column holds apple, hour, egg, honest man, and orange, because each begins with a vowel sound. The a column holds university, European, and one rupee, because each begins with a consonant sound despite its spelling. Do this sorting aloud, listening to the first sound of each word, and the rule will hold under test pressure far better than a memorised spelling list ever could.

diagram.alt: Choosing A, An, The, or Nothing
diagram.caption: Ask these questions in order whenever you are unsure about an article.

paras: The most frequent article mistakes in Class 7 are easy to list and easy to fix. Using the for a first mention: "I saw the dog" when no dog has been mentioned is wrong unless the situation makes the dog obvious. Using a before a vowel sound: "a apple" should be "an apple." Adding the to a general statement: "The honesty is the best policy" should be "Honesty is the best policy." Adding the to school subjects: "the mathematics" should be "mathematics" in "She likes mathematics." Each of these errors comes from skipping one question in the flowchart above, so run the flowchart mentally on every doubtful noun.

Build a final checking habit for written work: read each paragraph once only for articles, underlining every a, an, and the and every bare noun. For each one, ask whether the thing is new, known, or general. This single slow read catches more article errors than any amount of fast re-reading, because articles are small and the eye skips them at normal speed. Keep a notebook page of your own article mistakes, with the corrected sentence beside each one, and review it before every test. The points to something already known, mentioned before, or the only one of its kind.

faqs.q: Why is it "an hour" but "a university"?
faqs.a: The choice follows sound, not spelling. Hour begins with a vowel sound, so it takes an, while university begins with a consonant y sound, so it takes a. Say the word aloud and listen to its first sound.

faqs.q: When do I switch from a to the?
faqs.a: Use a or an for the first mention of something new, then the for every later mention, because the thing is now known to the reader. For example: "I saw a dog. The dog was friendly."

faqs.q: Why is there no article in "She studies mathematics"?
faqs.a: School subjects take no article when named in general. Mathematics here means the subject in general, not a particular book or class, so no article is used.

faqs.q: Is it "the sun" or "a sun"?
faqs.a: It is the sun, because there is only one sun in our sky and it is known to everyone. Unique things take the.

faqs.q: Should I write "the honesty is the best policy"?
faqs.a: No. Honesty in general takes no article, so the sentence is "Honesty is the best policy". Adding the would suggest one particular honesty, which is not the meaning.

title: Class 7 Synonyms and Antonyms: Grow Your Vocabulary
desc: Grow your Class 7 vocabulary with synonyms and antonyms: learn word pairs in sentences, avoid near-synonym traps, and build a word notebook that lasts.
intro: A synonym is a word with a similar meaning, and an antonym is a word with an opposite meaning: happy and glad are synonyms, while happy and sad are antonyms. Class 7 tests love these pairs because they check whether you really know a word or only recognise it. Pupils who memorise long lists often fail anyway, because synonyms are rarely exact — glad and happy are close but not identical — and antonyms depend on context. This guide teaches word pairs the way they actually work: in sentences, in families, and in your own notebook, so your vocabulary grows in a way that survives tests and improves your writing.

sections.h2: What Synonyms and Antonyms Really Are
paras: A synonym shares meaning with another word but almost never matches it perfectly. Big, large, and huge all describe size, yet "a huge mistake" sounds stronger than "a big mistake," and "a large number" sounds more natural than "a huge number" in a report. Learning a synonym therefore means learning its strength and its usual company, not just its dictionary meaning. When you meet a new word, ask which words it can replace and which it cannot, and you will learn the word properly instead of collecting a false twin.

An antonym is the opposite of a word, but many words have more than one opposite depending on meaning. The antonym of light as a weight is heavy, but the antonym of light as brightness is dark. The antonym of right as a direction is left, but the antonym of right as correct is wrong. Context decides, which is why test questions always give the word in a sentence or ask for the opposite "in this sense." Always read the sentence before choosing an antonym, and never pick the first opposite that comes to mind without checking which meaning is in play.

sections.h2: Learning Words in Pairs and Families
paras: Words stick better in pairs and families than alone. Learn brave with its synonym courageous and its antonym cowardly together, in one group, and the three words support each other in memory. Learn families the same way: happy, glad, cheerful, joyful form a family of rising strength, while sad, unhappy, gloomy, and miserable form the opposite family. When you revise one word, the whole family comes back, and in a test you can reach for the exact strength you need instead of repeating happy in every sentence.

A word notebook makes this method work. Give each new word a small entry: the word, its meaning in your own words, one synonym, one antonym, and one sentence of your own. For example: "Ancient — very old. Synonym: old. Antonym: modern. Sentence: The ancient fort stands on the hill." Five words a day in this format beats fifty words copied from a list, because every entry forces you to use the word. Review the notebook every Sunday, covering the meanings and recalling them before you look, and your vocabulary will grow week by week without cramming.

sections.h2: Synonyms in Sentences: The Only Real Test
paras: A synonym is only learned when you can use it correctly in a sentence, so sentence practice is the heart of vocabulary work. Take the word begin and its synonym start, and write both in sentences: "The lesson begins at eight" and "The lesson starts at eight" both work, so these two are close twins. Now try rich and wealthy: "He is a rich man" and "He is a wealthy man" both work, but "a rich harvest" sounds natural while "a wealthy harvest" sounds odd. That oddness is the lesson: synonyms overlap but do not always swap, and only sentence practice reveals the edges.

Try this exercise with five words from your current lesson: rapid, clever, kind, honest, and brave. For each word, write one synonym sentence and one antonym sentence. For example: "The rapid river rushed past" and "The slow river moved gently." Then swap the synonym into a different sentence and check whether it still sounds natural. If it does not, note the restriction in your word notebook. This habit of testing words in sentences is what separates pupils who know words from pupils who only recognise them, and it directly improves composition marks, where varied, accurate vocabulary earns credit.

sections.h2: Antonym Traps and How to Avoid Them
paras: Antonym questions contain traps, and knowing them saves marks. The first trap is the near-opposite: the antonym of love is hate, not dislike, when the question wants the strongest opposite. The second trap is the wrong meaning: the antonym of hard as difficult is easy, but the antonym of hard as solid is soft. The third trap is the negative prefix that looks right but is not a real word or not the expected answer — unkind is the antonym of kind, but unbrave is not the antonym of brave; cowardly is. When a prefix answer feels invented, it probably is, and a real opposite word is expected.

Another trap is the antonym that changes the part of speech: the antonym of the adjective happy is sad, not sadness, because the answer must match the word's form. Keep the part of speech the same in every answer. A final trap is the sentence that flips the meaning: "He is not happy" does not make not happy the antonym; the antonym is still sad. Read the question stem carefully — does it ask for the opposite word, or the opposite meaning in this sentence? Answering the question actually asked, rather than the one you assumed, is a skill that protects marks across every subject, not just vocabulary.

diagram.alt: How to Learn a New Word Properly
diagram.caption: Five steps that turn a new word into vocabulary you can actually use.

sections.h2: Using New Words in Your Writing
paras: Vocabulary only counts when it appears in your writing, so set yourself a weekly target: use five notebook words in your compositions and answers that week. Replace a repeated word deliberately — instead of writing good three times, use excellent once, pleasant once, and fine once, where each fits. Do not force a difficult word into a sentence where a simple word is better; examiners reward accurate variety, not decoration. A well-chosen simple word always beats a misused impressive one, and a misused synonym is worse than a repeated correct word.

Finally, read widely, because reading is where vocabulary grows fastest. Storybooks, lesson texts, and even newspaper headlines expose you to words in their natural company, which is exactly the knowledge tests check. When you meet an unknown word, do not skip it: guess its meaning from the sentence, check it in a dictionary, and add it to your notebook with a synonym, an antonym, and your own sentence. Ten minutes of this habit after each reading session will do more for your vocabulary than any list. Antonyms depend on which meaning of the word is in play.

faqs.q: Are synonyms always interchangeable?
faqs.a: No. Synonyms overlap but have different strengths and usual company. "A big mistake" and "a huge mistake" differ in strength, and "a wealthy harvest" sounds odd beside "a rich harvest". Test every synonym in a sentence before using it.

faqs.q: What is the antonym of light?
faqs.a: It depends on the meaning. As a weight, the antonym is heavy; as brightness, the antonym is dark. Always read the sentence to find which meaning is in play before choosing.

faqs.q: How many new words should I learn each day?
faqs.a: Five words a day, learned properly with a meaning, synonym, antonym, and your own sentence, beats fifty words copied from a list. Review them weekly from memory.

faqs.q: Why is "unbrave" not the antonym of brave?
faqs.a: Because the real opposite word is cowardly. Not every word forms its antonym with a prefix, and an invented prefix word is not an acceptable answer even if its meaning is guessable.

faqs.q: Does the antonym have to match the part of speech?
faqs.a: Yes. The antonym of the adjective happy is the adjective sad, not the noun sadness. Keep the word form the same in every vocabulary answer.

title: Class 7 Letter Writing: The Format Examiners Want
desc: Learn Class 7 letter writing format: formal and informal letters with address, date, greeting, body and ending, plus a model outline and common errors.
intro: Letter writing earns easy marks when the format is right, and loses them just as easily when it is wrong, because examiners check the layout before they read a single sentence. A letter has a fixed skeleton — address, date, greeting, body, and ending — and formal and informal letters differ mainly in how polite and distant their language is. Pupils who learn the skeleton once can write any letter the exam sets, from a letter to a friend to a letter to a headteacher. This guide gives you both formats, a clear body plan, and the errors to avoid, so your next letter starts with full format marks already secured.

paras: Every letter, formal or informal, follows the same order from top to bottom. First comes the sender's address at the top, then the date below it, then the greeting on the left, then the body in paragraphs, then the ending and signature. In a formal letter, the receiver's address also appears, placed after the date and before the greeting, along with a subject line that states the purpose in a few words. Learning this order as a picture — top to bottom, address to signature — means you never have to reconstruct it under exam pressure; you simply fill in the parts.

The date format matters: write it in full, such as "12 March 2026", rather than in figures alone, which can be misread. The greeting in a formal letter is "Dear Sir," or "Dear Madam," or "Dear Mr Ahmed," when you know the name, while an informal letter uses "Dear Ali," or "My dear Mother,". The ending matches the greeting in formality: formal letters close with "Yours faithfully," when you used Dear Sir or Madam, and "Yours sincerely," when you used the person's name. Informal letters close with "Yours lovingly," or "Your loving friend,". Matching greeting to ending is a small detail examiners notice at once.

sections.h2: Formal Letters: Polite, Clear, and to the Point
paras: A formal letter is written to someone you do not know well — a headteacher, an editor, a manager — so its language is polite, direct, and free of slang. The body usually has three paragraphs. The first states the purpose plainly: "I am writing to request permission to visit the library during the holidays." The middle paragraph gives the reason and the necessary details, such as dates and names, in clear sentences. The last paragraph states what you hope will happen and thanks the reader: "I would be grateful if you could grant this permission. Thank you for your time." No paragraph should wander; every sentence should serve the purpose.

Formal language has its own habits. Use full forms, not contractions: "I am" rather than "I'm", and "I do not" rather than "don't". Avoid exclamation marks and chatty phrases such as "By the way". Keep sentences complete and respectful, even when you are complaining: "I wish to draw your attention to the broken fans in our classroom" is far stronger than an angry complaint. Remember that a formal letter is a piece of official communication; it should sound like something you would be comfortable having read aloud in an office. Practise by writing a formal letter requesting a school transfer certificate, and check every sentence for politeness and purpose.

sections.h2: Informal Letters: Warm, Natural, and Personal
paras: An informal letter goes to family and friends, so it can be warm, relaxed, and full of personal news. The body still needs paragraphs, but the tone changes completely. Open with a friendly line: "I hope you are well. I was delighted to receive your letter." Then share your news in the middle paragraphs — your studies, a match you played, a visit you enjoyed — in the order that feels natural, as if you were talking. Close with a warm line: "Please convey my regards to everyone at home. I look forward to your reply." The reader should feel your personality in the letter, not a stiff template.

Informal does not mean careless. Contractions such as "I'm" and "don't" are fine here, but spelling, punctuation, and paragraphing still count, and slang should stay light. A common mistake is writing one giant paragraph of news with no breaks; instead, start a new paragraph for each topic — health and greetings, then your news, then questions about the reader, then the closing. Another mistake is copying a formal opening into a friendly letter: "I am writing to inform you" sounds absurd to a cousin. Match the voice to the reader, and the letter will feel genuine rather than memorised.

sections.h2: Building the Body Paragraph by Paragraph
paras: The body is where most letter marks are won or lost, so plan it before you write. For any letter, jot down three points: the purpose, the details, and the closing request or message. Then give each point its own paragraph. A letter to a friend about a school trip might run: paragraph one, thanks for the last letter and the trip news; paragraph two, what you saw and enjoyed most; paragraph three, a question about your friend's own trip and a warm close. Three paragraphs, three jobs, no repetition — that structure works for almost every Class 7 letter topic.

Link your paragraphs with natural connectors rather than jumping between topics. Phrases such as "Besides this", "Another thing I enjoyed", and "Before I close" guide the reader smoothly from one point to the next. Keep each paragraph to four or five sentences; very long paragraphs tire the reader, while one-sentence paragraphs look unfinished. Read the finished letter aloud: if it sounds like a real person talking to a real reader, the body is working. If it sounds like a list of memorised lines, rewrite the stiffest sentences in your own words before handing it in.

diagram.alt: The Parts of a Complete Letter
diagram.caption: Every letter runs in this order from top to bottom; formal letters add the receiver's address and a subject line.

paras: These errors appear in letter after letter, and avoiding them is worth several marks on its own. Missing the date or the address loses format marks before the body is even read. Using "Yours faithfully" with a named greeting, or "Yours sincerely" with Dear Sir, mixes the formal pairings. Forgetting the subject line in a formal letter leaves the reader guessing at the purpose. Writing the whole letter as one paragraph, or forgetting paragraphs entirely, makes even good content look unplanned. Signing with your full name in an informal letter to a friend looks odd; a first name is enough.

Other errors are about tone: slang in a formal letter, stiff official language in a friendly letter, and exclamation marks everywhere in both. Spelling of the receiver's name and title matters too — check them twice. Finally, never leave a letter unfinished: a letter without an ending and signature looks abandoned, however good its body was. Before you hand in any letter, run down the skeleton from top to bottom — address, date, greeting, body paragraphs, ending, signature — and tick each part off.
