title: BIEK Pre-Medical Part-I Result 2026: 11,966 Passed All Six — Reading the Numbers
desc: BIEK Pre-Medical Part-I 2026: 11,966 of 24,544 appeared students passed all six papers. Read what the 48.75% figure means, how marking worked, and what it does not say.
intro: Pre-Medical is the largest and most watched group in the BIEK HSC Part-I examination, and its 2026 result, announced on 26 October 2026, gives students a useful case study in how to read board figures honestly. Of 25,157 registered students, 24,544 appeared, and 11,966 passed all six papers — 48.75% of those who appeared. That single percentage has already been quoted as proof of many things, from the difficulty of the papers to the quality of teaching, but a careful reading shows both less and more than the headlines suggest. This article works through the Pre-Medical numbers step by step, explains how the science papers were marked, compares the group with its neighbours, and separates what the figures genuinely show from what they cannot show at all.

sections.h2: The Pre-Medical Numbers, Step by Step
paras: Start with the three counts, because each one answers a different question. Registered students numbered 25,157, which is the size of the cohort that entered for the examination. Appeared students numbered 24,544, which means 613 registered students did not sit the examination, a gap that usually reflects illness, changed plans, or registration problems rather than academic failure. Passed-all-six students numbered 11,966, and the headline rate of 48.75% is simply 11,966 divided by 24,544, the appeared total. Students who passed some papers but not all sit outside that headline figure, just as they do in the BSEK result, so the 48.75% describes full passes only, not the share of students who passed most of their papers.

The complement of the headline figure is equally important: 12,578 appeared students did not pass all six papers, a group that includes both partial passes and students who passed none. That large remainder is the reason this result matters so much for guidance work, because more than half the cohort now needs a plan for open papers. It is also the reason the percentage should not be read as a verdict on individual students. A cohort rate describes a whole group of nearly 25,000 young people across hundreds of colleges; it cannot tell you whether your own 42% in chemistry was good, bad, or typical, and it certainly cannot tell you whether you are suited to a medical career. Your own mark sheet, paper by paper, is the only result that describes you. For textbooks behind these subjects, see the [book collection](/books.html).

sections.h2: How the Science Papers Were Marked
paras: One verified feature of this year's marking deserves attention: science-group optional subjects were assessed through E-Assessment using OMR sheets, together with E-Marking. In practical terms, this means objective portions of the science papers were captured and marked electronically rather than by hand, which the boards present as a step towards faster and more consistent marking. For students, the main implication is about how to answer: objective sections reward careful, complete filling of the answer sheet and penalise careless slips, such as marking two options or leaving a question blank by accident, in ways that a human marker might have forgiven.

Electronic marking also changes what scrutiny can and cannot do. If you believe an objective answer was misread, the formal scrutiny route exists — the fee is Rs 1,000 per paper — but students should understand that electronic capture leaves less room for the kinds of addition errors that scrutiny used to catch in hand-marked papers. That does not make scrutiny useless, but it does mean the strongest response to a disappointing science result is usually better preparation for reappearance rather than a dispute about marking. Practise objective questions under timed conditions, learn to manage the answer sheet calmly, and treat every multiple-choice question as a mark that is fully within your control. The [solved notes](/solved.html) include practice material for science subjects.

diagram.caption: Five distinctions that keep the 48.75% figure from misleading you.

paras: Pre-Medical's 48.75% sits close to Science General's 49.48%, the highest full-pass rate among the groups announced on 26 October, and clearly above Commerce Regular at 41.12%, Commerce Private at 44.44%, Arts Regular at 35.10%, Arts Private at 42.63%, and Home Economics at 29.07%. It also sits above the Pre-Engineering full-pass figure from 2 October, where 6,310 of 14,683 appeared students passed all six papers, about 43%. The honest summary is therefore that Pre-Medical performed near the top of this year's groups, roughly level with Science General and ahead of the commerce, arts, and home economics groups.

These comparisons have limits that students should respect. Different groups take different subjects, so a higher rate in one group does not mean its students worked harder or its papers were easier in any simple sense. Pre-Medical students take biology, chemistry, and physics alongside compulsory subjects, while Commerce students take a different seven-paper combination, and the difficulty of each combination cannot be reduced to a single percentage. The comparison is useful for one purpose only: it shows that a full-pass rate below half was normal across the whole Part-I examination this year, not a peculiar failure of Pre-Medical students. That context should reassure students with open papers without excusing the need to clear them. More result analysis is on the [blog](/blog/).

sections.h2: What the Figures Do Not Say
paras: The published figures do not include a subject-wise breakdown for Pre-Medical, so nobody can say from them whether biology, chemistry, or physics pulled the rate down, or whether the pattern was even. Claims online that name a single difficult subject as the cause of the result are therefore unverified, however widely they are shared. The figures also do not show how many students passed five papers, four papers, or fewer, so the size of each partial-pass band within Pre-Medical is unknown from the release reporting. Without that breakdown, advice must stay at the level of the individual mark sheet: your open papers are known to you, even if the group's bands are not published.

The figures also say nothing about why any individual student scored as they did. A cohort rate cannot distinguish between a student who missed the threshold in one paper by two marks and a student who struggled across all six, and it cannot measure teaching quality, paper difficulty, or preparation in any direct way. Students who treat 48.75% as a judgement on their own ability are making a statistical error, and parents who do the same risk pressuring a child for a result that mostly reflects a new threshold applied to a very large cohort. The right response to the number is practical: check your own papers against the 40% line, clear what is open, and start Part-II with a study method that leaves a margin above the threshold.

sections.h2: What Pre-Medical Students Should Do Now
paras: If you passed all six papers, your task is simple: begin Part-II with the same seriousness, knowing that the 40% standard applies there too, and that Part-II biology, chemistry, and physics build directly on Part-I foundations. Do not let a comfortable Part-I result breed complacency, because Part-II papers are longer and the competition for professional-college entry only sharpens. Revise Part-I chapters that Part-II assumes, keep a steady weekly test routine, and use the months before Part-II examinations for depth rather than last-minute cramming.

If you have open papers, treat them as a defined project with a deadline set by the board's next notice. List each open paper, note the gap to 40%, and revise from the textbook with timed practice, asking teachers to mark sample answers. Check biek.edu.pk for the official reappearance procedure and confirm any scrutiny decision — Rs 1,000 per paper — from the board's own notice, since no scrutiny deadline is stated in the release reporting used here. And whatever your result, remember that Part-I is one stage of a longer path: students who clear open papers promptly and study Part-II steadily are in a far stronger position than students who spend the year worrying about a percentage that described a cohort, not a person. The [home page](/) links to further guides for intermediate students.

The 48.75% counts full passes only; partial passes sit outside it.
Science optional subjects used E-Assessment (OMR) and E-Marking.
Pre-Medical sits near the top of the 2026 groups, roughly level with Science General.
No subject-wise breakdown is published, so single-subject causes are unverified.

faqs.q: What was the BIEK Pre-Medical Part-I 2026 pass rate?
faqs.a: 11,966 of the 24,544 students who appeared passed all six papers, which is 48.75%. The rate counts full passes only; students who passed some papers are not included in it.

faqs.q: How many Pre-Medical students registered and appeared?
faqs.a: 25,157 students registered and 24,544 appeared, so 613 registered students did not sit the examination.

faqs.q: How were the science papers marked in 2026?
faqs.a: Science-group optional subjects were assessed through E-Assessment using OMR sheets, together with E-Marking, which means objective portions were captured and marked electronically.

faqs.q: Is Pre-Medical's rate higher than other groups?
faqs.a: It is close to Science General's 49.48% and above Commerce, Arts and Home Economics, but different groups take different subjects, so the rates are not a direct measure of difficulty or effort.

faqs.q: I passed five Pre-Medical papers. What should I do?
faqs.a: Identify your one open paper, check its gap to the 40% threshold, and prepare to reappear in it when the board announces the procedure on biek.edu.pk, while starting Part-II work in parallel.

title: BISE Hyderabad Result Inquiry 2026: What Students Need to Know
desc: A three-member committee is inquiring into alleged irregularities in BISE Hyderabad's Class XII 2026 results. Learn what is confirmed, what is only alleged, and what students should do.
kw: BISE Hyderabad result inquiry 2026 students guide
intro: On 23 October 2026, the Sindh government suspended the Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education Hyderabad's Deputy Controller of the Top Secret Branch and formed a three-member inquiry committee to examine alleged irregularities in the Class XII annual examination 2026 results. The story has since travelled fast on social media, and with it a great deal of speculation that goes far beyond what is actually known. This guide sets out the confirmed facts, explains what an inquiry of this kind can and cannot do, and tells students plainly what they should and should not do while it runs. The most important point comes first: the allegations are allegations, not proven findings, the announced results have not been cancelled, and no student has been named as a beneficiary of manipulation.

paras: The confirmed sequence is as follows. The Sindh government suspended BISE Hyderabad Deputy Controller (Top Secret Branch) Ijaz Ali Kaka — spelled Ejaz Ali Kaka in some reports — on the orders of Provincial Minister for Universities and Boards Muhammad Ismail Rahoo. At the same time, a three-member inquiry committee was formed through a notification issued by Universities Secretary Abbas Baloch. A suspension in these circumstances is an administrative step taken while an inquiry runs; it is not itself a finding of guilt, and students should not treat it as one. Officials are suspended pending inquiry precisely so that the examination of records can proceed without interference, and the outcome depends on what the committee finds.

The inquiry's scope, as reported, covers alleged irregularities in the Class XII (Intermediate Part-II) annual examination 2026 results, specifically in the pre-medical and pre-engineering groups. The committee is examining position holders, top-10 candidates, and students with A-1 and A grades, and it is looking at the checking, tabulation, and announcement processes behind the results. The allegations themselves circulated through social media and public complaints; that is how they reached the authorities, but circulation is not proof. Until the committee reports, every claim about what happened in the marking or tabulation process remains an allegation, and responsible coverage must keep saying so.

sections.h2: Who Is on the Committee and When It Reports
paras: The committee is headed by Professor Dr Arbeela Bhutto, Vice Chancellor of the Sindh Agriculture and Business University (SIBA Jamshoro). Its members are Additional Secretary Amir Fazal Owaisi — spelled Ameer Fazal Owaisi in some reports — and Mehran University Registrar Dr Nasrullah Pirzada. The composition matters because it places the inquiry in the hands of senior academics and administrators from outside the board under inquiry, which is the normal way to give such a process credibility. Students do not need to follow the committee's internal workings, but knowing who is responsible helps distinguish genuine updates from rumours that invent new names or new findings.

The committee's report is due within 30 days of 23 October 2026, which this guide describes only as within 30 days rather than as a confirmed calendar date. That window means students should expect news during November, but they should not treat any particular day as fixed, and they should not trust social media posts that claim the report has already been delivered before any official announcement. If the committee needs longer, or if its findings lead to further steps, those developments will come through official channels, not through forwarded messages. Patience during this window is not passivity; it is the sensible course while a formal process runs. For general board guidance, see the [blog](/blog/) and the [home page](/).

diagram.alt: BISE Hyderabad Inquiry: What Is Confirmed So Far
diagram.caption: Only the confirmed steps are shown; findings are not yet known and must not be guessed.

sections.h2: What the Inquiry Does Not Mean
paras: Three misunderstandings need correcting clearly. First, the announced results have not been cancelled. Reports confirm that the results stand as announced while the inquiry proceeds, so a student holding a Class XII mark sheet still holds a valid result unless and until an official decision changes it. Second, the inquiry does not mean every position holder or A-1 grade student did something wrong; the committee is examining those categories because that is where irregularities, if any, would show up, not because every student in them is suspect. Third, no student has been named in the published reporting as a beneficiary of manipulation, and this guide names nobody; any social media post that names a student in that connection is unverified and potentially defamatory, and sharing it helps nobody.

It is also worth understanding what an inquiry can actually establish. A committee examining checking, tabulation, and announcement processes can find procedural errors, inconsistencies in records, or evidence of wrongdoing, and it can recommend action, but it does not itself rewrite results on the spot. Any change to an individual student's result, if one were ever recommended, would follow a formal decision by the competent authority, with its own process. Students should therefore ignore claims that results have already been changed, that particular grades have been withdrawn, or that a new merit list exists, unless such a claim comes from the board or the Universities and Boards Department itself.

The practical advice for Hyderabad board students is short and calm. Keep your official transcript and mark sheet safe, together with your admit card and any result documents your college issued, because these are the records any future process would refer to. If you are a Class XII student who believes there is a genuine discrepancy in your own mark sheet — for example, marks that do not match your answer sheet as you remember it — use the board's formal rechecking route rather than joining public speculation. Rechecking deals with your own paper through a defined process; it does not depend on the inquiry, and it does not require you to prove anything about other students.

Students applying for further study should proceed with their applications using the result they hold, since it has not been cancelled. Colleges and universities deal with board results as announced, and an inquiry in progress does not suspend admissions based on those results unless an authority formally says so. If an institution asks about the inquiry, the accurate answer is that a committee is examining allegations and is due to report within 30 days of 23 October 2026, and that no findings have been published yet. That answer is honest, it protects you from repeating rumours, and it leaves you free to focus on your studies rather than on a process you cannot control. The [book collection](/books.html) and [solved notes](/solved.html) remain available for students preparing for the next stage.

sections.h2: How to Spot Rumours About the Inquiry
paras: Inquiry stories attract rumours because they combine official action with unanswered questions, and students need a simple test for what they read. Ask three questions of any claim: does it name an official source, such as the Universities and Boards Department or the board itself; does it distinguish between an allegation and a finding; and does it name a student or a grade change without evidence? If the answer to the first is no, or if the claim presents allegations as proven facts or names a student, treat it as unverified and do not forward it. Forwarding an unverified claim about a named student can cause real harm to a young person who may have done nothing wrong, and it can also expose the forwarder to trouble.

The same test applies to screenshots of supposed official letters. A genuine notification will be traceable to the issuing authority and will usually be reported by established news outlets as well as shared on social media; a screenshot circulating alone, with no news report and no official posting behind it, should be treated with suspicion. During the inquiry window, the safest information habit is to check one or two established news sources and the board's own communications, and to ignore the rest. When the committee's report is genuinely published, it will be news everywhere at once; you will not miss it by ignoring the rumours, but you may be misled badly by believing them.

faqs.a: No. The announced results have not been cancelled. The inquiry is examining allegations about the results, but until an official decision follows the committee's report, the results stand as announced.

faqs.q: Who is heading the inquiry committee?
faqs.a: Professor Dr Arbeela Bhutto, Vice Chancellor of the Sindh Agriculture and Business University (SIBA Jamshoro), heads the committee. The members are Additional Secretary Amir Fazal Owaisi and Mehran University Registrar Dr Nasrullah Pirzada.

faqs.a: The report is due within 30 days of 23 October 2026. This guide does not claim a confirmed calendar date; watch official announcements rather than social media claims about a delivery date.

faqs.q: Does the inquiry mean position holders cheated?
faqs.a: No. The committee is examining position holders, top-10 candidates and A-1/A grade students because that is where irregularities would show up, not because every student in those categories is suspect. The allegations remain unproven.

faqs.q: What should I do if I suspect an error in my own mark sheet?
faqs.a: Use the board's formal rechecking route for your own paper, and keep your official transcript, mark sheet and admit card safe. Do not rely on social media claims or name other students.

title: Punjab Second Annual Exams Start 3 November 2026: Final 5-Day Checklist
desc: Punjab's HSSC second annual exams begin 3 November 2026. Use this final five-day checklist: timings, documents, centre rules, and revision priorities for Part-II and Part-I.
kw: Punjab second annual exams November 2026 checklist
intro: Punjab's HSSC second annual (supplementary) examinations begin on 3 November 2026, just five days from today, and the province-wide schedule set by the Punjab Boards Committee of Chairpersons is now the document every candidate should be working from. Part-II (12th class) theory papers run from 3 to 16 November 2026, and Part-I (11th class) theory papers follow from 17 to 28 November 2026. With so little time left, the difference between a calm candidate and a panicked one is rarely knowledge; it is preparation — knowing your timings, having your documents ready, and spending the remaining days on the revision that actually earns marks. This checklist covers all three, in the order you should deal with them.

sections.h2: Know Your Dates: Part-II First, Then Part-I
paras: The first thing to fix in your mind is which window you belong to. If you are a Part-II candidate, your theory papers run from 3 to 16 November 2026; if you are a Part-I candidate, yours run from 17 to 28 November 2026. Part-I candidates therefore have about two extra weeks, but that is not a reason to relax: the Part-I window is just as compressed once it starts, and the same daily discipline applies. Do not confuse the two windows, and do not rely on a friend's timetable if your class differs from theirs. Your own board's date sheet and your roll number slip are the final authority for your subjects, and where they differ from any general schedule, your own documents win.

One published example shows how specific the date sheets are: Rawalpindi board's second-annual sheet lists 3 November with Psychology and Commercial Geography in the morning and History in the evening, 4 November with English compulsory in two groups, and 16 November with Physics in first and second groups. Your board's sheet will have its own subject order, so read it paper by paper and write your personal timetable from it, not from a summary. Note that BISE Lahore had not posted its second-annual intermediate date sheet as of 24 October 2026, so Lahore candidates in particular should confirm that their board's sheet is now available and work from it directly. The [blog](/blog/) has further examination guides for Punjab board students.

sections.h2: Timings: Morning, Evening, and the Friday Change
paras: Morning papers follow a fixed pattern across the province: report at 8:30 AM and the paper begins at 9:00 AM. Evening papers normally require reporting at 1:30 PM with the paper at 2:00 PM, but Fridays are different: on Fridays only, reporting is at 2:00 PM and the paper begins at 2:30 PM, allowing for Jummah prayers. That Friday change is the single most common timing mistake in the second annual examinations, because a candidate who arrives at the normal evening time on a Friday will still be in time, while a candidate who confuses the two patterns and arrives late risks missing the paper entirely. Write the Friday timing separately on your personal timetable so it stands out.

Plan your travel around the reporting time, not the paper time. Reporting half an hour before the paper leaves room for identity checks, seat allocation, and the unexpected — a traffic delay, a wrong turn to an unfamiliar centre, or a queue at the gate. Aim to reach the centre at least 45 minutes before reporting time on your first paper, and at least 30 minutes early on later papers once you know the route. Candidates who arrive exactly at paper time start the examination already stressed, and stress is the enemy of clear answers. A calm arrival is part of the examination, not a luxury before it. For study material to revise in these final days, see the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

Gather your documents now, not on the morning of 3 November. You need your roll number slip, your original national identity card or B-Form as applicable, and your previous result or registration documents if your board asks for them. Regular candidates normally collect their roll number slips from their college, while private candidates obtain them from their board's website, and you should confirm which route applies to you today so there is still time to fix a problem. Check every detail on the slip the moment you receive it: your name's spelling, your subjects, your centre, and your paper dates. An error found today can be corrected; an error found at the centre gate usually cannot.

Keep a small examination kit ready beside the documents: pens that you have already tested, a geometry box if your subjects need one, a transparent pouch, and a bottle of water if your centre allows it. Do not carry a mobile phone into the examination hall unless your centre's rules explicitly permit it in a designated place, because possession of a phone in the hall can lead to an unfair-means case even if you never use it. Photocopy or photograph your roll number slip and keep the copy at home, so that losing the original does not leave you with nothing to show. These are small tasks, but each one removes a risk that has genuinely cost candidates their papers in past sessions.

diagram.caption: Work through these steps in order; each one removes a risk before the first paper.

sections.h2: Revision Priorities for the Last Five Days
paras: Five days is enough time to raise your marks significantly, provided you spend it on the right things. First, stop starting new topics; new material learned now is rarely retained well enough to earn marks, and it steals time from the topics you can actually strengthen. Instead, list the chapters in each paper where you lost marks last time, or where your preparation is thinnest, and work through those chapters from the textbook, making short notes as you go. Second, practise writing full answers under time, because second annual candidates most often lose marks through incomplete answers and poor time allocation rather than through total ignorance.

Third, use past papers as your main practice tool. Work through at least one past paper per subject under examination conditions, mark it honestly, and spend the next session only on the questions you got wrong or left incomplete. Fourth, protect your sleep and your health: a candidate who revises until 3 AM the night before a 9 AM paper will perform worse than a candidate who stopped at a reasonable hour and slept properly. Eat normally, avoid heavy unfamiliar food on examination days, and keep one evening hour free for rest so that revision does not become exhaustion. The examination rewards steady preparation, not heroic last nights.

sections.h2: What Not to Do in the Final Days
paras: Do not spend the final days chasing rumours about leaked papers, changed dates, or grace marks. Second annual examinations attract exactly these rumours, and every hour spent forwarding or worrying about them is an hour stolen from revision that genuinely earns marks. If a date or centre changes, your board will announce it through official channels and your college will pass it on; anything else should be treated as unverified. Similarly, do not pay anyone who promises a pass, a leaked paper, or a changed result — these are frauds, and involvement in them can end a candidate's examination career far more surely than a failed paper.

Also note what is already closed: the second annual admission windows, which ran from 24 September to 17 October with single, double, and triple fee stages, are now closed, so do not waste time looking for a late admission route that does not exist. Your task now is to sit the papers you are already entered for, and to sit them as well as you can. Candidates who entered for the second annual examination have already taken the hardest step, which is deciding to improve their result rather than accepting it; the remaining step is simply to prepare calmly, arrive on time, and write the best answers they can. The [home page](/) gathers further examination preparation guides.

faqs.a: Part-II (12th class) theory papers run from 3 to 16 November 2026, and Part-I (11th class) theory papers run from 17 to 28 November 2026, under the province-wide PBCC schedule.

faqs.q: What are the morning and evening paper timings?
faqs.a: Morning papers require reporting at 8:30 AM with the paper at 9:00 AM. Evening papers normally require reporting at 1:30 PM with the paper at 2:00 PM, except on Fridays, when reporting is at 2:00 PM and the paper is at 2:30 PM.

faqs.q: Why is the Friday evening timing different?
faqs.a: The Friday evening schedule is adjusted for Jummah prayers: reporting at 2:00 PM and the paper at 2:30 PM, half an hour later than the normal evening pattern.

faqs.q: Can I still apply for the second annual exams?
faqs.a: No. The admission windows ran from 24 September to 17 October 2026 with single, double and triple fee stages, and they are now closed. Candidates should focus on the papers they have already entered for.

faqs.a: Check your name's spelling, your subjects, your examination centre, and your paper dates as soon as you receive the slip. Report any error to your college or board immediately, while there is still time to correct it.

desc: Where to get your Punjab second annual roll number slip, how centres work, the exact morning, evening and Friday timings, and why Multan practicals are a separate schedule.
kw: Punjab second annual roll number slip centre guide
intro: For Punjab's second annual candidates, the roll number slip is the single most important document of the examination, because it settles every practical question — where you sit, when you report, and which papers you take on which dates. Yet every year, candidates lose marks or even papers through slip problems that were entirely avoidable: a slip collected too late, a centre never visited in advance, or a timing confused with another session's. This guide explains where regular and private candidates get their slips, how examination centres work, the exact timings for morning, evening, and Friday papers, and one important local exception — the Multan practical schedule — that must not be mistaken for a province-wide rule. Read it once, check your own slip against it, and the examination days become far simpler.

sections.h2: Where to Get Your Roll Number Slip
paras: Regular candidates normally receive their roll number slips from their college, while private candidates obtain theirs from their board's website. That distinction is the first thing to get right, because a private candidate waiting for a college to hand over a slip, or a regular candidate hunting a website for a slip the college already holds, both waste the final days before the examination. If you are a regular candidate and your college has not issued slips yet, ask the college office directly and promptly; if you are a private candidate, download your slip from your own board's official website, print it, and keep a digital copy as backup. Do not rely on a slip forwarded by a friend or a screenshot from a group chat, since only your own slip, checked against your identity details, is reliable.

The moment you hold your slip, check it line by line: your full name and its spelling, your father's name if printed, your registration or roll number, your subjects, your examination centre and its address, and the date and session of every paper. Errors are rare but real, and they are correctable only if found early. If anything is wrong, report it to your college or to your board's relevant branch immediately, and keep a written record of whom you spoke to and what was promised. A candidate who discovers a wrong subject or a wrong centre on the morning of the paper has almost no remedy; a candidate who finds it a week early usually has a simple one. The [blog](/blog/) carries more examination-day guides.

Your centre is assigned by the board, not chosen by you, and it may be a different school or college from your own. Visit the centre in advance if you possibly can, so that you know the route, the travel time, and the entrance you will use; candidates who arrive at an unfamiliar centre for the first time on examination morning commonly lose ten to twenty minutes to confusion that a single advance visit would have prevented. On the day, follow the centre staff's directions for seating and identity checks without argument, even if the arrangements differ from what you expected, because the centre superintendent's authority in the hall is final for practical purposes.

Centre rules are strict on a few points that candidates sometimes underestimate. You must sit in your allotted seat, not wherever you prefer; you must not carry a mobile phone or other electronic device into the hall unless the centre's rules explicitly provide a deposit arrangement; and you must not exchange anything with another candidate during the paper. Breach of these rules can lead to an unfair-means case, which is a far heavier consequence than the loss of a single paper. If you are unwell on an examination day, inform the centre staff at once rather than struggling silently, since centres have procedures for illness that are far better than a paper abandoned without explanation. For revision material to take into the final days, see the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

sections.h2: Exact Timings: Morning, Evening, and Friday
paras: The province-wide timings for the second annual examinations are fixed and worth memorising. Morning papers: report at 8:30 AM, paper begins at 9:00 AM. Evening papers: report at 1:30 PM, paper begins at 2:00 PM. Fridays only: evening reporting moves to 2:00 PM and the paper begins at 2:30 PM, the adjustment being for Jummah prayers. These timings apply to the theory papers in the Part-II window of 3 to 16 November 2026 and the Part-I window of 17 to 28 November 2026. Write them on your personal timetable, and mark every Friday evening paper separately, because the Friday change is the timing error that catches candidates most often.

Reporting time is not a suggestion; it is the time by which you should be present for checking and seating, and candidates who arrive after the paper has begun may be refused entry or admitted only at the centre's discretion, with lost time not restored. Treat the reporting time as your deadline and aim earlier: 30 to 45 minutes before reporting time for your first paper at a new centre, and at least 15 to 30 minutes early thereafter. If your journey involves public transport, add a margin for delays, and on your first paper, travel the route the day before if you can. Punctuality is the cheapest insurance in the whole examination, and it costs nothing but a slightly earlier alarm.

sections.h2: The Multan Practicals: A Local Schedule, Not a Provincial One
paras: One schedule in the second annual season is frequently misread as province-wide, and it deserves a clear warning. The practical examinations scheduled from 1 to 11 December 2026 are the Multan board's schedule, as read from the Multan date sheet, and they should be presented and understood as Multan's schedule only until other boards confirm their own practical dates. A candidate under another board who plans around the Multan dates risks missing their own board's practicals entirely, or revising practical work weeks too early. The safe rule is simple: practical dates come from your own board's date sheet and your own roll number slip, and no other board's dates substitute for them.

The same caution applies to the theory date sheets. Rawalpindi board's published second-annual sheet confirms the province-wide windows with its own subject dates, but each board publishes its own subject order, and BISE Lahore had not posted its second-annual intermediate date sheet as of 24 October 2026. Candidates under any board should therefore confirm that their own board's sheet is available and read their personal paper order from it. General schedules tell you the windows; only your board's sheet and your slip tell you your papers. If either document is missing or unclear, raise it with your college or board now, while correction is still possible.

Build a simple exam-day routine and repeat it for every paper. The night before, lay out your slip, identity card, pens, and instruments, and check the next day's paper, centre, and reporting time against your slip one final time. In the morning, eat normally, leave early, and reach the centre with time to spare. In the hall, read the whole question paper first, allocate time to each question before writing, and keep the last ten minutes for checking rather than starting a new answer you cannot finish. After the paper, do not spend hours dissecting it with friends; note any lesson for the next paper, then move on to revising the next subject.

Two final cautions complete the routine. First, the second annual admission windows of 24 September to 17 October are closed, so ignore anyone offering a late entry route; your only task is the papers you have entered. Second, the second annual result is expected around 12 January 2027 according to the reported schedule, but that is a reported expectation rather than a board guarantee, so do not plan admissions or commitments as if it were fixed. Between the last paper and the result, the most useful thing a candidate can do is rest properly and then return to regular study, because the next academic step will arrive whether or not the result date moves. points: Regular candidates get slips from their college; private candidates from their board's website.
Check name, subjects, centre, and paper dates on your slip the day you receive it.
Morning: report 8:30 AM, paper 9:00 AM; evening: report 1:30 PM, paper 2:00 PM.

faqs.q: Where do private candidates get their roll number slip?
faqs.a: Private candidates obtain their roll number slip from their board's official website, print it, and keep a digital backup. Regular candidates normally collect theirs from their college.

faqs.q: What time must I report for a morning paper?
faqs.a: Morning papers require reporting at 8:30 AM, with the paper beginning at 9:00 AM. Aim to arrive 30 to 45 minutes before reporting time at an unfamiliar centre.

faqs.q: What is the Friday evening timing?
faqs.a: On Fridays only, evening papers require reporting at 2:00 PM and begin at 2:30 PM, adjusted for Jummah prayers. On other days, evening reporting is 1:30 PM and the paper begins at 2:00 PM.

faqs.q: Are the 1–11 December practicals for all Punjab boards?
faqs.a: No. The 1–11 December 2026 practical schedule is the Multan board's schedule. Other boards' practical dates must be confirmed from their own date sheets and roll number slips.

faqs.q: What should I do if my slip has an error?
faqs.a: Report it to your college if you are a regular candidate, or to your board's relevant branch if you are a private candidate, immediately. Errors found early can usually be corrected; errors found on examination morning usually cannot.

title: Sindh Boards in November 2026: What Students Should Watch For
desc: November 2026 brings the Hyderabad inquiry report window, Punjab's second annual exams, and the road to Class 10's new 40% rule. Here is what Sindh students should watch, without invented dates.
intro: November 2026 is a month of consequences for Sindh's students: the results announced in late October will turn into reappearance plans, an inquiry report will fall due, and the new 40% grading rule will move one step closer to Class 10. It is also a month in which rumours thrive, because several processes are running at once and students are eager for dates that have not yet been announced. This forward look separates what is genuinely on the calendar from what is merely expected, so students can plan around confirmed events and watch for official announcements without being misled by invented ones. No date in this article is claimed unless it comes from the verified record.

paras: The most closely watched Sindh event of November is the report of the three-member inquiry committee into alleged irregularities in BISE Hyderabad's Class XII annual examination 2026 results. The committee, headed by Professor Dr Arbeela Bhutto with members Additional Secretary Amir Fazal Owaisi and Mehran University Registrar Dr Nasrullah Pirzada, was formed on 23 October 2026, and its report is due within 30 days of that date. This guide deliberately does not convert that window into a single calendar date, because the reporting states the window, not a confirmed date, and students should distrust any post that claims the report will land on a particular day before the authorities say so.

What should students do while waiting? In practical terms, very little changes. The announced Class XII results have not been cancelled, so students applying for further study should proceed on the results they hold. Students who believe their own mark sheet contains an error should use the board's formal rechecking route rather than waiting for the inquiry, since rechecking addresses an individual paper through a defined process. And everyone should treat the inquiry's subject matter — the allegations about pre-medical and pre-engineering results — as allegations until the committee reports. The report, when it genuinely appears, will be news everywhere at once; until then, patience and official sources are the best policy. The [blog](/blog/) will carry further guidance when the report is published.

sections.h2: After the Karachi Results: Reappearance Notices to Watch
paras: The second November watch item is quieter but affects far more students: the reappearance and scrutiny notices that should follow the late-October Karachi results. BSEK announced the Class 9 Science Group result on 28 October 2026, with 123,757 full passes and tens of thousands of partial passes, and BIEK completed its HSC Part-I results on 26 October 2026, with full-pass rates below half in every group. Students with ungraded or failed papers in either result now need the boards' next notices — the procedure, eligibility, fee, and dates for reappearing — and those notices have not yet been published in the reporting used for this guide. Students should therefore check bsek.edu.pk and biek.edu.pk regularly, and their school or college notice boards, rather than trusting dates from social media.

While waiting, the useful work is revision, not speculation. Students with open papers should already be revising them from their textbooks, paper by paper, aiming comfortably above the 40% threshold rather than at it. The BIEK scrutiny fee is Rs 1,000 per paper for students who believe a paper was marked wrongly, but no scrutiny deadline is stated in the release reporting used here, so confirm any deadline from the board's own notice. The pattern to avoid is the familiar one: waiting passively for a notice, then discovering that the gap between notice and examination is too short for real preparation. Revision started now is revision that counts whenever the notice arrives. For textbooks and solved exercises, see the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

diagram.alt: Sindh Boards: November 2026 at a Glance
diagram.caption: Confirmed windows and events only; unannounced dates are marked as such, not invented.

sections.h2: Next Door in Punjab: The Second Annual Examinations
paras: Although this is a Sindh calendar, Punjab's second annual examinations running through November matter to Sindh students too, because many families follow both provinces' boards and because the same rumours cross provincial lines. Punjab's Part-II theory papers run from 3 to 16 November 2026, and Part-I theory papers from 17 to 28 November 2026, with morning reporting at 8:30 AM and papers at 9:00 AM, evening reporting at 1:30 PM and papers at 2:00 PM, and Friday evenings adjusted to 2:00 PM reporting and 2:30 PM papers. Sindh students should not confuse these dates with their own boards' schedules, but they should understand them if they have relatives or friends sitting the Punjab examinations, and they should be alert to rumours that mix the two provinces' timetables.

One Punjab detail deserves a warning for the same reason: the practical examinations scheduled from 1 to 11 December 2026 are the Multan board's schedule only, not a province-wide or national one. Posts that present Multan's practical dates as applying everywhere are a reliable sign of an unreliable source, and the same scepticism should be applied to any post that claims a Sindh practical or supplementary date without naming the board that published it. Keeping the provinces' calendars separate is a small discipline, but it prevents the most common calendar confusion of the examination season.

sections.h2: The Road to Class 10 Under the 40% Rule
paras: November is also the month to look ahead to what the 40% rule means for the next examination cycle. Class 9 has used the new threshold since the 2026 annual examinations, and Class 10 follows from 2027, which means the current Class 9 cohort will sit its Class 10 examinations under the higher bar. Students now in Class 10 preparation, and students now in Class 9, should therefore treat 40% as the floor in every paper and build a margin above it, rather than aiming at the line and hoping the paper is kind. The habit that matters is regular testing: short weekly tests in each subject reveal weak chapters while there is still time to fix them, whereas a single pre-examination cram reveals them too late.

The curriculum itself is also set to change. The Sindh Textbook Board's 2026-27 textbooks — the Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Textbook Series, covering Early Childhood to Grade 10 with 195 titles in Sindhi, Urdu, and English and 52 million sets — were distributed from 19 February 2026, and a ministerial statement in about October 2026 described a revised curriculum from the next academic year, emphasising research, scientific thinking, creativity, modern science, technology, mathematics, languages, and social sciences, together with religious tolerance, mutual respect, gender studies, and environmental protection, and a promise to relieve pupils of excessive book burden. No new STBB announcement was verified on 29 October 2026 itself, so students should treat the curriculum change as a next-academic-year development to watch, not as a change already in force. The [home page](/) gathers the site's curriculum and textbook guides.

sections.h2: A Sensible November Routine for Sindh Students
paras: Pulling the month together, a sensible November routine has four parts. First, check the official board websites weekly — bsek.edu.pk and biek.edu.pk — for reappearance and scrutiny notices, and check your school or college notice board just as often, since some notices reach institutions first. Second, keep revising open papers from the textbook, with timed practice, so that any notice finds you prepared rather than starting from scratch. Third, follow the Hyderabad inquiry only through established news sources and official announcements, ignoring social media claims that present allegations as findings or name students without evidence. Fourth, plan Class 10, or Part-II, study around the 40% standard from the start of the month, not from the eve of the examinations.

Above all, resist the temptation to fill every gap in the calendar with a rumoured date. The verified November calendar is genuinely busy — an inquiry report window, reappearance notices to come, a neighbouring province's examinations, and a grading rule moving towards Class 10 — and it needs no invented additions to be worth planning around. Students who work from the confirmed calendar, revise steadily, and check official sources weekly will be ready for whatever November actually brings, while students who chase rumours will spend the month anxious about dates that never existed. That difference, more than any single examination result, is what a well-managed November looks like.

Watch bsek.edu.pk and biek.edu.pk for reappearance and scrutiny notices after the October results.
Punjab second annual theory: Part-II 3–16 November, Part-I 17–28 November 2026.

faqs.q: When is the Hyderabad inquiry report due?
faqs.a: The three-member committee's report is due within 30 days of 23 October 2026. No confirmed calendar date is claimed here; watch official announcements rather than social media claims about a specific day.

faqs.q: Have BSEK and BIEK announced reappearance dates for October's results?
faqs.a: No reappearance dates are stated in the reporting used for this guide. Students with ungraded or failed papers should check bsek.edu.pk and biek.edu.pk and their institution's notice board regularly.

faqs.q: Does the 40% rule apply to Class 10 yet?
faqs.a: Class 9 has used the 40% threshold since the 2026 annual examinations, and Class 10 follows from 2027. Current Class 9 students will therefore sit Class 10 under the new rule.

faqs.q: Is there a new STBB announcement in November 2026?
faqs.a: No new STBB announcement was verified on 29 October 2026. The revised curriculum described in the ministerial statement is a next-academic-year development, not a change already in force.

faqs.q: Should Sindh students follow Punjab's second annual dates?
faqs.a: No, except to understand them for family or friends. Punjab's dates — Part-II 3–16 November and Part-I 17–28 November — belong to Punjab's boards, and Sindh students should plan from their own boards' schedules.

title: Karachi Boards Result Season 2026: The Big Lessons for Class 10 and 12 Students
desc: Karachi's 2026 result season is complete: BIEK Part-I and BSEK Class 9 Science are both out. Here are the big lessons — the 40% rule, partial passes, and study habits that work.
intro: With the BIEK HSC Part-I results completed on 26 October 2026 and the BSEK Class 9 Science Group result announced on 28 October 2026, Karachi's 2026 result season is now complete, and it is worth stepping back to ask what the whole season actually taught us. The two results share a defining feature — the new 40% grading rule — and they share a pattern: full-pass rates below the levels of previous years, large partial-pass groups, and a great deal of public confusion about what the numbers mean. This wrap-up draws the lessons together for the students who matter most now: those moving into Class 10 and those moving into Part-II. It makes no new claims and invents no new figures; every number here comes from the two announcements themselves.

paras: BIEK announced its HSC Part-I results in two stages: Pre-Engineering on 2 October 2026, with 15,044 registered, 14,683 appeared, and 6,310 passing all six papers, followed by all remaining groups on 26 October 2026 under Press Release No. BIEK/PR/152/2026. The 26 October groups ranged from Pre-Medical, with 11,966 of 24,544 appeared students passing all six papers (48.75%), and Science General at 49.48%, down through Commerce, Arts, and Home Economics at 29.07%. Two days later, BSEK announced the Class 9 Science Group result, with 180,054 registered, 177,923 appeared, 123,757 passing all papers, 53,849 failed, and an overall pass percentage of 69.56%, down from 78.26% in 2025. Together, the two announcements cover hundreds of thousands of Karachi students, and together they tell one story above all others.

That story is the new grading rule. Class 9 from the 2026 annual examinations, and the intermediate examinations under the same system, now require 40% in a paper to pass, raised from 33%, and anything below 40% is recorded as ungraded. The rule was decided by the Inter Board Coordination Commission together with the Sindh Universities and Boards Department, and Class 10 follows from 2027. Every other lesson of the season flows from this single change, because it redefines what a pass is, what a partial pass means, and how students should study. Students who understand the rule understand the season; students who still think in terms of 33% will keep misreading their own results.

sections.h2: Lesson One: The Bar Moved, So Study Must Move Too
paras: The most practical lesson of the season is also the simplest: aiming at the pass line no longer works, because the line is higher and the margin for error is thinner. Under the old 33% rule, a student could pass a paper with patchy preparation; under the 40% rule, the same preparation leaves the paper ungraded. The students who fared best this season were not necessarily the most talented but the most consistent — those who revised every chapter, practised full answers under time, and tested themselves regularly enough to find weak spots early. For Class 10 and Part-II students, the implication is direct: build a study routine that leaves a comfortable margin above 40% in every subject, and treat any subject where you hover near the line as an urgent priority, not a safe pass.

This lesson also reframes what a good study method looks like. Rote memorisation of a few expected questions is a fragile strategy under a higher threshold, because it collapses when the paper asks something unexpected. Textbook-first study, by contrast, covers the whole syllabus and survives surprises. Students moving into Class 10 should work through their Sindh Textbook Board books chapter by chapter, use solved exercises to check understanding, and take timed practice tests that mimic examination conditions. The [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html) exist for exactly this kind of steady, complete preparation, and the students who use them systematically will be the ones who clear 40% with room to spare.

sections.h2: Lesson Two: Partial Passes Are Normal — and Manageable
paras: The second lesson is about the large middle of both results. BSEK's breakdown shows 21,999 students passing six papers, 11,006 passing five, 7,431 passing four, and thousands more in the lower bands, while BIEK's group figures imply similarly large numbers of students with some papers open, since no group's full-pass rate reached half of appeared students. A partial pass is therefore not an exceptional disaster; it is the normal outcome for a large share of the cohort under the new rule, and it should be treated as a defined task — clear a known list of papers — rather than as a verdict on a student's ability. Schools and families can help enormously by saying this plainly, because shame is the main reason partial-pass students hide their open papers instead of working on them.

Manageability has a practical side too. A student with one or two open papers can clear them while keeping up with the next class, provided the revision is regular and targeted at the chapters where marks were lost. A student with more open papers needs a sequenced plan, starting with the paper closest to 40%, and honest conversations with teachers about priorities. In both cases, the next step is the same: watch the board's official website — bsek.edu.pk or biek.edu.pk — for the reappearance notice, keep all documents safe, and revise in the meantime rather than waiting passively. The [blog](/blog/) carries step-by-step guides for students clearing individual papers.

diagram.alt: Five Lessons From the 2026 Result Season
diagram.caption: What Karachi's two big results teach students entering Class 10 and Part-II.

paras: The third lesson is about information itself. This season produced a flood of confident claims — subject-wise failure rates, reasons for the BSEK pass rate falling from 78.26% to 69.56%, and lists of toppers — most of which the boards never published. The board has published no single official reason for the BSEK fall, no subject-wise breakdown for either result in the reporting used here, and no position-holder or topper names for the BIEK or BSEK 2026 results. Students who learned to ask for a source before believing a claim were protected from all of this; students who forwarded every dramatic post were not. The habit of checking whether a claim names the board's release or a named official is a study skill in its own right, and it will matter even more in future seasons.

The same discipline applies to the Hyderabad inquiry, the season's other major story. A three-member committee formed on 23 October 2026 is examining allegations about BISE Hyderabad's Class XII 2026 pre-medical and pre-engineering results, with a report due within 30 days, and the announced results have not been cancelled. The allegations remain allegations, no student has been named as a beneficiary of manipulation, and the responsible response is to wait for the official report rather than to repeat rumours. Karachi's students have now seen, in one season, both how results work and how result stories can mislead; carrying that scepticism forward is itself one of the season's most valuable lessons.

sections.h2: Lesson Four: The Next Year Starts Now
paras: The final lesson is about timing. Class 10 students will sit their examinations under the 40% rule from 2027, and Part-II students face the same standard, so the preparation that matters is the preparation that starts now, not the preparation that starts a month before the examinations. November is the right month to set the pattern: a weekly timetable that covers every subject, short regular tests, textbook-first revision, and a standing habit of checking official board websites for notices. Students with open papers from this season should fold those papers into the same timetable, giving the closest-to-passing paper the first slot, so that the new year and the old papers move forward together rather than competing.

There is also a wider reason for optimism. The Sindh Textbook Board's 2026-27 textbook series, with 195 titles and 52 million sets distributed from 19 February 2026, means the books students need are available, and the promised revised curriculum from the next academic year aims to reduce excessive book burden while emphasising research, scientific thinking, and creativity. No new STBB announcement was verified on 29 October 2026, so the curriculum change remains a next-year development to watch, but the direction is towards study that rewards understanding over memorisation — exactly the kind of study the 40% rule demands. Students who build that habit now, in Class 10 and Part-II, will be ready for whatever the next result season brings. The [home page](/) gathers the site's guides for the year ahead.

The defining change is the 40% pass threshold, up from 33%; below 40% is ungraded.

faqs.q: Which Karachi results completed the 2026 season?
faqs.a: BIEK completed HSC Part-I on 26 October 2026, following Pre-Engineering on 2 October, and BSEK announced the Class 9 Science Group result on 28 October 2026. Together these complete Karachi's main 2026 result season.

faqs.q: What is the single biggest lesson of the season?
faqs.a: The pass threshold is now 40%, not 33%. Students must aim comfortably above 40% in every paper, because a mark below 40% is recorded as ungraded and the paper must be reappeared in.

faqs.q: Why did the BSEK pass rate fall to 69.56%?
faqs.a: The board has published no single official reason for the fall from 78.26% in 2025. The threshold change mechanically moves some students from full pass to partial pass, but the board has not attributed the whole fall to it.

faqs.q: Are partial passes something to be ashamed of?
faqs.a: No. Tens of thousands of students hold partial passes this year under the new rule. A partial pass is a defined list of papers to clear, not a verdict on ability, and teachers deal with it every year.

faqs.q: What should Class 10 students do differently now?
faqs.a: Study textbook-first, chapter by chapter, test yourself weekly, and build a margin above 40% in every subject, since Class 10 comes under the new grading scheme from 2027.

title: Class 9 Islamiat: Tawheed and the Attributes of Allah
desc: Learn Tawheed and the attributes of Allah in simple words: oneness, beautiful names, and how belief in one God shapes a Muslim's daily life.
kw: Tawheed attributes of Allah Class 9 Islamiat
intro: Tawheed is the first and most important belief in Islam, and it means that Allah alone is worthy of worship. For a Class 9 student, Tawheed is not just a word to memorise for an examination; it is the foundation on which every other belief stands. When a Muslim says that Allah is One, it means that no one shares His power, His knowledge, or His right to be worshipped. This belief gives life a clear direction, because a person who truly believes in one God does not bow before idols, superstitions, or human beings. In this guide, we explain Tawheed and the attributes of Allah in simple words, with examples that students can remember and use in their own answers and daily conduct.

sections.h2: What Tawheed Means in Simple Words
paras: Tawheed comes from the Arabic word for making something one, and in Islamic belief it means affirming that Allah is One in His being, His lordship, and His right to worship. A Muslim believes that Allah created the heavens and the earth, gives life and death, and provides for every creature, and that no partner helps Him in any of these works. This is why the first part of the Shahadah declares that there is no god but Allah. For students, the simplest way to remember Tawheed is this: one Creator, one Sustainer, and one God worthy of worship, without any partner, equal, or rival in any sense at all.

Tawheed also protects a believer from confusion and fear, because it teaches that help should be sought from Allah alone. A person who believes in Tawheed does not believe that stars, charms, graves, or powerful people control destiny by themselves. Instead, such a person works hard, uses lawful means, and trusts Allah for the result. This balance between effort and trust is one of the most practical lessons of Tawheed. It keeps faith pure, keeps hope alive in difficulty, and keeps a student honest, because Allah sees every action even when no teacher or parent is watching.
bullets: One Creator and Sustainer of everything that exists
No partner, equal, or rival in worship or power
Help and trust belong to Allah alone, alongside honest human effort

sections.h2: Allah Is One, Without Partner or Equal
paras: The Quran describes Allah as One, Eternal, and unlike anything else, and this description answers a natural question that students often ask: if Allah is One, why do people worship many things? The answer is that human beings sometimes turn to visible objects or powerful personalities because they want quick help or approval. Islam teaches that these things are themselves created and limited, so they cannot give what only Allah can give. Worshipping them alongside Allah is called shirk, and it is the opposite of Tawheed. Understanding this difference helps students recognise pure worship and avoid practices that mix Allah's rights with the rights of created things.

Belief in one God also brings unity to a Muslim's life, because the same Allah is worshipped at home, at school, and in the mosque. A student does not need one set of values for examinations and another for friendships; honesty, kindness, and justice are duties everywhere. This unity of purpose is a great strength in student life. When a young person knows that Allah alone is the judge of deeds, it becomes easier to resist cheating, to admit mistakes, and to treat classmates fairly. Tawheed is therefore not only a belief about God, but also a guide for character in every place and situation.

sections.h2: The Beautiful Names and Attributes of Allah
paras: Allah has beautiful names, called Asma-ul-Husna, and each name describes an attribute such as mercy, knowledge, power, and justice. When students learn names like Ar-Rahman, the Most Merciful, and Al-Alim, the All-Knowing, they are learning something real about how Allah relates to His creation. These names are not empty titles; they tell us that Allah's mercy covers His servants, His knowledge includes everything hidden and open, and His justice never wrongs anyone. Learning the names with their meanings, rather than only memorising a list, makes the lesson deeper and helps students explain each attribute in their own words during class discussion or written work.

A helpful study habit is to connect each attribute with a daily example that makes sense to a student. Allah's provision, Ar-Razzaq, can be seen in the food, rain, and opportunities that reach people in ways they did not plan. Allah's wisdom, Al-Hakim, can be seen in the order of nature and the balance of the human body. When students practise this kind of reflection, the attributes stop being abstract definitions and become reasons for gratitude and trust. It also builds a respectful attitude, because a person who remembers that Allah is All-Seeing will think twice before harming another person or wasting a blessing.

diagram.caption: Each attribute describes Allah's perfection and guides how a believer should live.

paras: Islam teaches that Allah's attributes are perfect and unique, so believers affirm them without comparing Allah to created beings. For example, when we say that Allah hears and sees, we do not mean hearing and seeing like human hearing and seeing, which depend on ears, eyes, distance, and light. Allah's hearing and seeing are perfect and complete, without weakness or limit. This rule protects students from two mistakes: denying the attributes altogether, or imagining Allah in human form. The safe and correct path is to accept what the Quran and authentic teachings affirm, and to leave the exact nature of those attributes to Allah's perfect knowledge.

This point matters for examinations as well as for belief, because many students lose marks by writing confused or exaggerated explanations. A clear answer states the attribute, gives its simple meaning, and adds that it belongs to Allah in a perfect way unlike creation. For instance, a student can write that Allah is Ever-Living and Self-Sustaining, while every living creature depends on food, rest, and help from others. Such comparisons show understanding without claiming that Allah resembles His creation. Teachers appreciate answers that are precise, respectful, and free from guesswork about matters beyond human knowledge.

Tawheed becomes visible when a student prays only to Allah, asks Allah for help in difficulty, and thanks Allah for success instead of boasting about personal ability. It also appears in small daily choices, such as refusing to cheat even when no one would notice, returning a lost item, and speaking truthfully when a lie would be easier. These actions show that belief has moved from the tongue into the heart and then into behaviour. Parents and teachers notice this change quickly, because a student grounded in Tawheed is steadier under pressure and kinder in dealings with others, whether the matter is big or small.

Students can strengthen Tawheed through simple daily habits that take only a few minutes but build lasting faith. Reading a short passage of the Quran with translation, learning one beautiful name with its meaning each week, and pausing before an action to ask whether it pleases Allah are all practical steps. Keeping company with honest friends and avoiding gatherings where false beliefs are promoted also protects faith. For more solved notes and study material, students can explore the solved notes collection on [Solved Notes](/solved.html) and browse the full book list on [Books](/books.html) to support their Islamiat preparation.

points: Tawheed means Allah alone is worthy of worship, with no partner or equal.
Allah's beautiful names describe His perfect mercy, knowledge, power, and justice.
Attributes are affirmed without comparing Allah to created beings.
True Tawheed shows in honest actions, prayer, and trust in Allah alone.
Daily reflection on one name at a time makes the lesson easy to remember.

faqs.q: What is Tawheed in one simple sentence?
faqs.a: Tawheed is the belief that Allah is One in His being, His lordship, and His right to be worshipped, with no partner, equal, or rival. It is the foundation of Islamic faith, and every other belief in Islam rests on this oneness. A student can remember it as one Creator, one Sustainer, and one God worthy of worship.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Tawheed and shirk?
faqs.a: Tawheed is worshipping Allah alone, while shirk is giving any part of worship, or Allah's unique powers, to someone or something else. Shirk is the opposite of Tawheed because it treats a created thing as if it shared Allah's rights. Islam teaches that only Allah creates, sustains, and deserves worship, so a believer avoids directing prayer or ultimate trust to anyone else.

faqs.q: How should students explain Allah's attributes in an answer?
faqs.a: A good answer names the attribute, gives its simple meaning, and adds that it belongs to Allah in a perfect way unlike creation. For example, Allah's knowledge is complete and covers everything hidden and open, while human knowledge is limited and learned step by step. This method is clear, respectful, and avoids comparing Allah to human beings.

faqs.q: Why do Muslims learn the Asma-ul-Husna?
faqs.a: Learning the beautiful names helps Muslims know Allah better and live by that knowledge. A name like Ar-Rahman reminds a believer of Allah's mercy, while Al-Adl reminds them of His perfect justice. When students connect each name with a daily example, such as provision or forgiveness, the names become practical guidance for gratitude, honesty, and hope.

faqs.q: How can a student practise Tawheed in daily life?
faqs.a: A student practises Tawheed by praying only to Allah, asking Allah for help, thanking Allah for blessings, and acting honestly even when no one is watching. Small habits help, such as reading the Quran with translation, learning one name each week, and choosing honest friends. These habits turn belief into character that teachers, parents, and classmates can see.

title: Class 9 Islamiat: Risalat and the Finality of Prophethood
desc: Understand Risalat and Khatm-e-Nubuwwat in simple words: why Allah sent prophets, their common message, and the finality of prophethood.
kw: Risalat finality of prophethood Khatm-e-Nubuwwat Class 9 Islamiat
intro: Risalat means the sending of prophets by Allah to guide human beings, and it is one of the central beliefs in Islam. Allah did not leave people without guidance; He sent messengers in different times and places to teach the same basic message of worshipping one God and living justly. The chain of prophethood reached its completion with Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, who is the final prophet, and this belief is called Khatm-e-Nubuwwat. For Class 9 students, understanding Risalat means understanding both the role of prophets and why no prophet comes after the final prophet. This guide explains the idea step by step, in clear and simple language.

sections.h2: Why Allah Sent Prophets to People
paras: Human beings have reason and conscience, but they still need clear guidance about the purpose of life, right and wrong, and the life after death. Allah sent prophets to provide that guidance in a form people could understand and follow. A prophet was a human being chosen by Allah, known for truthfulness and good character, who received revelation and conveyed it to his people. This is why prophets are described as guides and warners: they showed the straight path, warned against wrongdoing, and gave glad news of reward for those who obey Allah and live righteously in this world.

Prophets also served as living examples, because their followers could watch how they prayed, treated neighbours, kept promises, and faced hardship with patience. A book alone might be misunderstood, but a prophet's life showed how its teachings worked in real situations. For students, this is an important point: Risalat is not only about receiving a message, but also about demonstrating it. When a prophet forgave an enemy, helped the poor, or stood firm for truth, he was teaching his community through action, and that practical example is part of why prophethood was necessary for human guidance.

sections.h2: The Common Message of All Prophets
paras: Although prophets came to different peoples and times, their core message was the same: worship Allah alone, avoid shirk, live justly, and prepare for accountability after death. The Quran mentions many prophets, including Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, peace be upon them all, and presents them as part of one continuous chain of guidance. Their laws and practices differed in details according to their communities, but the foundation never changed. Recognising this unity helps students avoid the mistake of thinking that each prophet brought a completely different religion; instead, they all called people to the same Tawheed and the same moral values.

This unity also teaches respect, because Muslims believe in all the prophets sent by Allah and do not reject any of them. A Muslim honours earlier prophets while following the final message given to Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. For classroom answers, students can explain this point clearly: earlier scriptures and prophets are respected, and the final revelation completes and confirms the guidance that came before. This balanced view keeps faith firm without disrespecting the beliefs of others, and it shows why Risalat is described as a mercy, since guidance reached people again and again through history.

Khatm-e-Nubuwwat means that prophethood ended with Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and that no prophet will come after him. The word Khatm means a seal, and just as a seal closes a document, the final prophet sealed the chain of prophethood. The Quran describes him as the Seal of the Prophets, and his message, the Quran, is preserved as guidance for all people until the end of time. For students, the key idea is simple: earlier prophets were sent to particular peoples, but the final prophet was sent as a mercy to all worlds, so his guidance is complete and does not need a successor prophet.

The finality of prophethood also has a practical meaning for Muslims today. When a question about faith or practice arises, Muslims turn to the Quran and the Sunnah of the final prophet, rather than expecting a new prophet or a new revelation. Scholars explain and apply these sources, but they do not claim prophethood, and no new scripture can replace the Quran. Understanding this distinction helps students answer examination questions accurately and avoid confusion. It also gives confidence, because the guidance Muslims follow is complete, preserved, and available to every generation without waiting for another messenger.

diagram.alt: From the First Prophet to the Final Prophet
diagram.caption: One chain of guidance, completed by the final prophet.

sections.h2: What Finality Means for Believers Today
paras: Belief in finality protects the Muslim community from false claims and confusion, because any person who claims prophethood after the final prophet contradicts a clear and settled belief. Students should understand that this is not a minor detail; it is part of the core faith, and that is why teachers treat it with such seriousness. At the same time, finality does not mean that learning has stopped. Scholars, teachers, and students continue to study, explain, and apply the Quran and Sunnah to new situations, such as modern science, business, and social life, without adding new revelation or claiming prophetic authority for themselves.

Finality also brings a sense of responsibility, because Muslims are the carriers of the final message and are expected to present it through good character. When a student is honest in examinations, kind to classmates, and respectful to elders, that behaviour reflects the teachings of the final prophet. In this way, Khatm-e-Nubuwwat is not only a belief to state in an answer, but also a trust to live by. Students who understand this connection write stronger answers, because they can explain both the belief itself and its effect on daily conduct in their school and community.

Loving and following the final prophet means studying his Seerat, adopting his manners, and obeying his teachings in practical matters. His honesty earned him the title Al-Amin, the Trustworthy, even before prophethood, and his kindness extended to family, neighbours, children, and even those who opposed him. Students can take simple lessons from this example: keep promises, speak gently, help those in need, and remain patient when treated unfairly. These qualities are not separate from worship; they are part of what it means to follow a prophet whose character the Quran describes as a great and noble example for believers.

A good study method is to learn one aspect of the Seerat each week and practise it consciously, such as truthfulness in speech or punctuality in prayer. Students can also use solved notes and guides to revise the topic, and the solved notes collection on [Solved Notes](/solved.html) offers helpful revision material for Islamiat. For the full list of books and subjects, visit [Books](/books.html) and choose the relevant class. Revising with a clear structure, belief, evidence, and daily application, will help students write confident answers about Risalat and the finality of prophethood in examinations.
