points: Rozmarra is natural everyday usage; a muhavara is a fixed phrase with figurative meaning.
Learn idioms in theme groups of five, with words, meaning, and sentence together.
A good sentence uses the idiom naturally and makes its meaning clear from context.
Recognise four question forms: meaning, sentence use, correction, and choice.
Revise little and often with spaced tests instead of cramming long lists.

faqs.q: What is the difference between rozmarra and muhavara in one sentence?
faqs.a: Rozmarra is the natural, everyday way of expressing something in Urdu, while a muhavara is a fixed phrase whose figurative meaning differs from its literal words. For example, a rozmarra question tests whether your sentence sounds natural to a fluent speaker, while a muhavara question tests whether you know the special meaning of a set phrase. Keeping the two categories separate in your notes prevents confusion when a paper mixes both types. Revise them with different methods: rozmarra by noticing natural usage, muhavare by learning meaning plus sentence.

faqs.q: Should I write the literal meaning of a muhavara in the exam?
faqs.a: No, unless the question specifically asks for it. Examiners want the figurative, real meaning of the idiom, not a word-by-word translation, which is often misleading or funny. Write the figurative meaning in clear, simple words, and if you add a sentence, make sure it demonstrates that meaning naturally. A literal translation as your answer shows that you do not know the idiom, even if every word is translated correctly. When in doubt, write the sense the idiom carries in real usage.

faqs.q: Can I change the words of a muhavara to fit my sentence?
faqs.a: Generally no, because a muhavara is a fixed expression and changing its words can break it or change its meaning. You may adjust grammatical endings where the language naturally allows it, but the core words and their order should stay as the idiom is normally used. If you are unsure whether a change is acceptable, use the idiom in its standard form in a sentence built around it, rather than reshaping the idiom itself. Your teacher can confirm the standard form of idioms you practise.

faqs.q: How many muhavare should I learn for Class 10?
faqs.a: Quality matters more than quantity: it is better to know forty idioms with meanings and sentences perfectly than to half-know a hundred. Start with the idioms your teacher emphasises and those in your textbook exercises, then expand gradually by theme. A steady pace of five per week builds a strong stock over a term without overwhelming you. Before the exam, consolidate your known set with self-tests rather than adding a large new list at the last moment.

faqs.q: How do I answer a rozmarra correction question?
faqs.a: First, identify what sounds unnatural in the given sentence: a wrong word choice, an unnatural phrase, or a literal translation from another language. Then rewrite the whole sentence correctly, using the natural Urdu expression. Do not only underline the error or explain it without giving the corrected sentence, since the corrected sentence earns the marks. Practise correction questions regularly, because they train your ear for natural usage in a way that memorising lists alone cannot.

title: Class 10 Urdu Tazkira: Poets of Your Course
desc: Learn Class 10 Urdu tazkira writing: how to write a poet's life sketch, what to include, and how to answer tazkira questions well.
kw: Class 10 Urdu tazkira poets life sketch
intro: A tazkira is a short life sketch of a poet, and in the Class 10 Urdu paper it tests whether you know the important facts of a poet's life and can present them in an organised, readable form. Many students either write a long, unfocused biography or list a few dates without explaining why the poet matters. A good tazkira sits between these extremes: it gives the essential facts, mentions the poet's major work and style briefly, and explains the poet's importance in clear paragraphs. This guide teaches the general method for writing any tazkira, without claiming a list of poets for any particular course. Always base your facts on your own textbook and your teacher, since they are the authority for your exam.

sections.h2: What a Tazkira Is and Why It Is Asked
paras: The word tazkira comes from the tradition of writing about poets and scholars, recording their lives, their work, and their place in literary history. In a school exam, a tazkira is a short, structured life sketch, not a full biography: it selects the facts that help a reader understand the poet and the poetry. Examiners ask for tazkira writing because it tests several skills at once: factual knowledge, selection of important details, organisation into paragraphs, and clear, respectful language. A student who can write a good tazkira shows that they have studied the poet as a person, not merely memorised a few verses.

A tazkira also helps you understand poetry better, because knowing a poet's time, environment, and concerns often explains the themes in the poems. A poet who lived through a period of change may write about hope or loss in ways that make more sense once you know the background. However, a tazkira must stay factual and balanced: it should present the poet's life and work honestly, without exaggerated praise or invented stories. When you study a poet, separate what your textbook states from what guidebooks claim, and trust your textbook when they differ. Further study material is available on [Solved Notes](/solved.html) and the [Blog](/blog/).

sections.h2: What to Include: The Essential Facts
paras: A complete school tazkira usually includes the poet's name and pen name, or takhallus, the dates and place of birth and death where these are known, and a brief note on education and life circumstances. Next, it mentions the poet's major works or collections, the type of poetry associated with the poet, such as ghazal or nazam, and one or two distinctive features of style. Finally, it states the poet's importance: what contribution the poet made to Urdu literature and why the poet is still read. This structure, life, work, style, importance, covers everything an examiner expects, and it keeps your answer organised even under time pressure.

Select facts carefully: include only those that are relevant and verified in your textbook, and leave out minor anecdotes that add length without adding marks. If a date is uncertain in your sources, do not guess it; either omit it or write it as your textbook gives it. Similarly, do not attribute a famous verse to a poet unless you are sure it belongs to that poet, because misattribution is a clear factual error. Keep the language respectful and simple, avoiding both exaggerated praise and casual slang. A tazkira written in calm, factual Urdu, with correct names and dates, always scores better than a flowery one full of uncertain claims.

sections.h2: How to Study a Poet Before Writing
paras: Studying a poet well means going beyond the tazkira paragraph itself and understanding the poet through the poetry in your textbook. Start by reading the poet's poems in your course slowly, noting their themes, mood, and any distinctive images or devices. Then read the biographical note in your textbook and underline the facts that fit the life, work, style, and importance structure. Next, make a small fact card for the poet with these headings and only the verified facts under each, leaving blank any heading your textbook does not cover. This fact card becomes your revision tool and prevents the invention of details during the exam.

Also listen carefully to your teacher's explanation of each poet, because teachers often clarify which facts examiners emphasise and which stories are unreliable. If your teacher corrects a guidebook fact, follow your teacher. Discuss poets with classmates too, but verify anything a classmate tells you against your textbook before writing it in an answer. Finally, practise writing the tazkira from your fact card without looking, then compare your draft with the card and correct any errors. This write-and-compare routine builds accurate recall far better than repeated reading alone, and it reveals exactly which facts you still confuse.

diagram.alt: How to Prepare and Write a Tazkira
diagram.caption: Follow these steps for every poet you study.

sections.h2: Writing the Tazkira in the Exam
paras: In the exam, structure your tazkira in three or four short paragraphs. Paragraph one introduces the poet: name, pen name, birth and death details, and a brief note on life and education. Paragraph two discusses the poet's work: major collections or types of poetry, and the themes the poet is known for. Paragraph three covers style and importance: what makes the poet's poetry distinctive and why the poet matters in Urdu literature. This shape is easy for the examiner to follow and ensures you cover all the expected points without wandering into irrelevant stories.

Keep the length moderate, roughly three-quarters of a page to a page, and write in your own words rather than copying a guidebook paragraph. Use correct spellings for names and places, since errors in proper names are easy for examiners to spot. If the question asks for a tazkira of a specific poet, write only about that poet, and do not add material about others. If it asks for a short note, shorten each paragraph rather than omitting a whole section, so the answer stays balanced. After writing, check names, dates, and the order of paragraphs once before moving on to the next question.

The most damaging mistake is inventing facts: guessing dates, inventing a birthplace, or attributing a famous verse to the wrong poet. Such errors suggest the answer was not studied, and they can cost marks even when the rest is correct. The second mistake is writing only praise without facts, producing a paragraph of admiration that tells the examiner nothing about the poet's life or work. The third is copying a long memorised paragraph that does not match the question, for example writing a full biography when only a short note was asked. The fourth is confusing two poets, mixing one's dates with another's works, which happens when poets are revised together without fact cards.

Prevent these errors with disciplined revision: one fact card per poet, studied separately, with write-and-compare practice for each. Revise poets in small sets, and test yourself by writing the name, pen name, dates, and one major work from memory for each poet in the set. In the final week, revise only your fact cards, not new guidebook material, so your recall stays clean. If you forget a date in the exam, omit it calmly and write the facts you do know correctly, rather than guessing. Accurate, well-organised partial knowledge always outscores confident invention. More exam guidance is on the [Blog](/blog/) and book details on [Books](/books.html).

You can ask it to check whether your draft covers all four parts. Join Muse with invite code LTGSWD — in the Muse app, go to Settings > Redeem token and enter the code. points: A tazkira is a short, structured life sketch, not a full biography.
Include life, work, style, and importance, using only verified textbook facts.
Study poets through their poems plus textbook notes, made into fact cards.
Write in three or four paragraphs: introduction, work, style and importance.
Never guess dates or attribute verses you are not sure about.

faqs.q: How long should a tazkira answer be in Class 10?
faqs.a: Roughly three-quarters of a page to a full page is right for a standard tazkira question: enough for introduction, work, style, and importance paragraphs. A much shorter answer usually misses facts, while a much longer one often adds irrelevant stories. If the question asks for a short note, write a compact version keeping all four parts but with fewer details in each. Always follow your teacher's guidance on the marks allocated, since higher-mark questions deserve fuller answers.

faqs.q: What should I do if I forget a poet's date in the exam?
faqs.a: Omit the date calmly and write the facts you know correctly, rather than guessing. A guessed date that is wrong is a factual error, while an omitted date is only a small gap. You can still earn most of the marks with correct information about the poet's work, style, and importance. To reduce this risk, practise dates with write-and-compare drills during revision, testing yourself on one poet at a time from your fact cards.

faqs.q: Should a tazkira include the poet's famous verses?
faqs.a: Only if you are certain the verse belongs to that poet and it illustrates a point about style or theme. Quoting a verse does not by itself earn marks; explaining what it shows about the poet does. Never attribute a well-known verse to a poet on a guess, since misattribution is a clear error. In most school tazkira answers, a brief mention of themes and style, without quotation, is safer and fully sufficient.

faqs.q: How is a tazkira different from a khaka (character sketch)?
faqs.a: A tazkira is a factual life sketch of a real poet or author, based on biographical facts and literary work. A khaka is a literary portrait of a person, often written with humour, observation, and personal impression, and it may describe a fictional or everyday character. The tazkira values accuracy and organisation, while the khaka values vivid description and style. Keep the two forms separate in revision, since examiners may ask for either.

faqs.q: How can I avoid confusing two poets during revision?
faqs.a: Study one poet at a time with a separate fact card, and test yourself on that poet alone before moving to the next. When you revise two poets together, compare them deliberately: note what is different about their periods, themes, and styles, rather than only what is similar. Write-and-compare practice, where you draft from memory and then check against the card, exposes confusion early. In the final week, revise fact cards in small sets with short breaks between poets.

title: Class 10 Urdu Nasr: How Urdu Prose Developed
desc: Trace Class 10 Urdu nasr ka irtiqa: early prose, its growth through essays, stories and criticism, and how to answer history questions.
kw: Class 10 Urdu nasr irtiqa prose development
intro: Urdu prose, or nasr, did not appear in its modern form overnight: it grew over time as writers, translators, reformers, and institutions shaped it for new purposes. For Class 10 students, the history of prose can feel like a list of periods and names to memorise, but it becomes much easier when you understand it as a story of changing needs. Early prose served religious and educational purposes, later prose served reform and journalism, and modern prose serves fiction, criticism, and personal expression. This guide traces that development in broad, general stages and shows how to answer exam questions about it. It teaches the pattern of development, not a list of unverified claims, so confirm period details with your own textbook.

sections.h2: What Nasr Means and Why Its History Matters
paras: Nasr is prose writing that is not bound by the metre and rhyme of poetry, and it includes essays, stories, letters, biographies, criticism, and journalism. Its history matters because the forms you study in Class 10, such as the mazmoon, afsana, inshaiya, and khutut, all developed at different times for different reasons. Understanding when and why each form grew helps you answer questions about prose development without memorising isolated facts. For example, knowing that the essay grew with education and journalism explains why essays discuss social issues, while knowing that the short story grew later explains its focus on character and incident.

A useful way to study nasr ka irtiqa is to ask, at each stage, three questions: who was writing, for whom were they writing, and what purpose did the writing serve? Early writers often wrote for education and moral instruction, while later writers wrote for newspapers, magazines, and a growing reading public. As the readership changed, the language, subjects, and forms changed too. Keep this three-question habit in mind as you read the stages below, because it turns a timeline into a story you can retell. General histories agree on this broad pattern, but your textbook remains the authority for the specific periods and emphasis your exam expects. More background is available on [Solved Notes](/solved.html) and the [Blog](/blog/).

sections.h2: Early Urdu Prose: Translation, Religion and Education
paras: The earliest Urdu prose grew largely from practical needs: translating religious and educational material so that ordinary readers could understand it, and writing simple explanatory prose for teaching. This early prose was often straightforward and functional, valuing clarity over literary decoration, because its purpose was to inform rather than to impress. Over time, writers began to use prose for storytelling and for discussing everyday life, and the language gradually became more flexible and expressive. These early stages are important not because of individual famous works, which your textbook will name, but because they established prose as a serious medium alongside poetry.

A common exam question asks why early prose was simple in style, and the answer lies in its purpose: it was written to be understood by common readers, not to display literary skill. Another useful point is that early prose developed alongside the growth of printing and education, which created more readers and more reasons to write. When you revise this stage, note its purpose, its audience, and its style in three short phrases, and you will have a complete answer. Do not invent specific titles or dates for this stage unless your textbook gives them; general, accurate statements about purpose and audience earn marks without risking factual errors.

sections.h2: Growth Through Reform, Journalism and the Essay
paras: A major turning point in Urdu prose came when writers began using it for social reform and public discussion, especially through newspapers, magazines, and essays. Reform-minded writers argued about education, social customs, and progress, and they needed a prose style that could persuade ordinary readers. The essay, or mazmoon, became the natural form for this purpose, because it could present an argument clearly and at length. Journalism added speed and topicality: writers responded to current events and debates, which made prose more direct, more varied, and more connected to daily life than before.

This stage also improved the language of prose itself, as writers developed a clearer, more standard style suited to argument and explanation. Vocabulary expanded, sentence structure became more organised, and writers learned to support opinions with reasons and examples. For exam answers, the key points are the new purposes of prose, reform and public debate, the new platforms, newspapers and magazines, and the resulting style, clear and persuasive. If your textbook names particular movements or writers for this stage, learn those names from the textbook itself, and link each one to one contribution you can state confidently. Avoid adding names from general knowledge that your course may not include.

diagram.alt: Broad Stages in the Development of Urdu Prose
diagram.caption: A general pattern to organise your revision; confirm period details in your textbook.

sections.h2: Fiction, Criticism and the Modern Short Story
paras: As Urdu prose matured, fiction became one of its most important branches, with novels and later short stories exploring character, society, and human psychology. The novel allowed writers to follow characters over a long period and to describe social change in detail, while the afsana, which developed later, focused on a single incident or character with intensity. Literary criticism grew alongside fiction, as writers and scholars began to discuss what makes prose good, how stories work, and how literature reflects society. This critical discussion raised the standard of prose writing itself, because writers now wrote with an awareness of form and technique.

For Class 10 answers, connect each form to its strength: the novel for breadth and social detail, the afsana for focus and intensity, and criticism for understanding and judgement. When a question asks about the development of fiction, describe this progression from longer, broader forms to shorter, more focused ones, and mention the growing attention to character and realism. Again, use only the names and works your textbook provides for this stage, and describe the general pattern confidently. A clear account of how forms changed, with reasons for each change, scores better than a list of names without explanation.

sections.h2: Modern Prose and How to Answer Irtiqa Questions
paras: Modern Urdu prose is marked by variety: personal essays, humour writing, travel writing, biographies, and many kinds of fiction now exist side by side. Writers today mix forms freely, and the language of prose continues to change with new media and new readers. For exam purposes, the important point is not to list every modern form, but to show that prose kept developing because readers, purposes, and platforms kept changing. The story of nasr ka irtiqa is therefore a story of adaptation: each new need produced a new form or a new style, and each new form expanded what prose could do.

When answering an irtiqa question, use a simple structure: begin with a one-sentence overview, then describe three or four stages in order, giving the purpose, platform, and style of each, and end with a concluding sentence about modern variety. Give each stage roughly equal space, and link stages with words like then, as a result, and later, so the answer reads as development rather than a list. Revise by drawing the timeline from memory and labelling each stage with its purpose, which is faster and more reliable than memorising paragraphs. Check your timeline against your textbook before the exam, and confirm names or dates only from that source. Further history guidance is on the [Blog](/blog/) and book lists on [Books](/books.html).

Muse AI is Meta's personal AI assistant, and it can help with nasr ka irtiqa by helping you turn a timeline into a short summary, or by quizzing you on the purpose and style of each stage of prose development. You can ask it to check a paragraph you wrote about one stage. Join Muse with invite code LTGSWD — in the Muse app, go to Settings > Redeem token and enter the code. Disclosure: LTGSWD is the author's Muse invite code. Muse AI does not give official STBB answers — always verify against your STBB book and your teacher. Remember to verify against your Sindh Textbook Board book before writing any prose-history answer in your exam.

points: Nasr includes essays, stories, letters, biographies, criticism, and journalism.
Early prose served translation and education, favouring clarity over decoration.
Reform and journalism made prose persuasive, clear, and topical through essays.
Fiction matured from novels to focused short stories, with criticism alongside.
Answer irtiqa questions as stages linked by purpose, platform, and style.

faqs.q: What is nasr ka irtiqa in simple words?
faqs.a: Nasr ka irtiqa means the development of Urdu prose over time: how prose forms, styles, and purposes changed from early simple writing to the varied modern forms we have today. It is best understood as a story of changing needs, since each stage of development responded to new readers, new platforms, or new purposes. For exam answers, describe the stages in order, giving the purpose and style of each, rather than memorising a list of names. Your textbook gives the specific periods and emphasis your exam expects.

faqs.q: Why did Urdu prose develop later than Urdu poetry?
faqs.a: Poetry was the dominant literary form for a long time, valued for its beauty, memorability, and performance, while prose was mainly used for practical purposes like teaching and translation. Prose grew as a literary form when education, printing, newspapers, and reform movements created new readers and new purposes for writing. This is a general pattern: forms develop when readers and purposes for them appear. State this explanation in general terms, and use only the specific details your textbook provides for your course.

faqs.q: What role did journalism play in prose development?
faqs.a: Journalism gave prose new platforms, newspapers and magazines, and new purposes: informing readers, debating social issues, and responding to current events. It made prose more direct, topical, and varied, and it helped standardise a clear style suited to argument and explanation. The essay flourished in this environment because it could present reasoned views at length. In answers, link journalism to clarity, topicality, and public debate, since those are the qualities it most clearly encouraged.

faqs.q: How should I structure a long answer on nasr ka irtiqa?
faqs.a: Begin with a one-sentence overview of prose development, then describe three or four stages in order, giving each stage's purpose, platform, and style. Use linking words to show development rather than listing disconnected facts, and end with a sentence on modern variety. Give each stage roughly equal space, and include only names and works that your textbook provides. Practise by drawing the timeline from memory, since a timeline you can reproduce is the backbone of a strong answer.

faqs.q: Do I need to memorise many writer names for irtiqa questions?
faqs.a: No. Learn thoroughly the names your textbook and teacher emphasise for each stage, with one contribution each that you can state confidently. A few well-understood names linked to clear contributions score better than a long list of names without explanation. If you are unsure about a name or its contribution, leave it out rather than guessing, and focus on the general pattern of development, which carries most of the marks. Confirm all names from your textbook, not from general knowledge or guidebooks.

title: Class 10 Urdu Imla and Qawaid: Exam-Focused Rules
desc: Master Class 10 Urdu imla and qawaid: common spelling errors, grammar rules, and board-paper patterns with a daily practice drill.
kw: Class 10 Urdu imla qawaid spelling grammar rules
intro: Imla, or spelling, and qawaid, or grammar, are the quiet mark-earners of the Class 10 Urdu paper: they appear in short questions, in sentence correction, and in the quality of everything else you write. A student with good ideas but weak spelling loses marks in every section, while a student with solid imla and qawaid gains marks in every section. The rules that appear most often are surprisingly few, and they can be mastered with short daily practice rather than last-minute cramming. This guide covers the most common spelling errors, the essential grammar rules, and the question patterns board papers use. All rules here are general language rules, so confirm specific syllabus points with your teacher.

sections.h2: Why Imla Matters More Than Students Think
paras: Imla matters because spelling errors change meaning, distract the examiner, and suggest carelessness even when the ideas are good. In Urdu, many spelling mistakes come from confusing similar-sounding letters, from wrongly joining or separating words, or from misplacing dots and marks. A single wrong letter can turn one word into another, and in a short answer that error stands out sharply. Examiners therefore treat imla as evidence of language command, not as a minor detail, and they deduct marks for repeated errors across a paper. Improving imla is one of the fastest ways to raise your total score, because it lifts every answer you write.

The good news is that most imla errors come from a small set of confusions that you can learn systematically. Keep a personal error diary: every time your teacher marks a spelling mistake, write the correct spelling, the wrong version, and one sentence using the word. Revise this diary five minutes daily, and test yourself by writing the words from memory each week. Over a term, your error diary becomes a personal list of exactly the words you used to misspell, which is far more valuable than a generic list. Never be embarrassed by the diary; every strong writer built accuracy by correcting mistakes, not by avoiding them. Spelling help and study notes are on [Solved Notes](/solved.html) and the [Blog](/blog/).

sections.h2: Common Spelling Errors and How to Fix Them
paras: The most common Urdu spelling errors involve letters that sound similar but are written differently, and words whose correct form must simply be learned by sight and practice. Another frequent error is the wrong use of hamza and related marks, especially in words borrowed from Arabic or Persian, where the spelling follows the original form. A third error is joining words that should stay separate, or separating a compound word that should stay joined. A fourth is misspelling everyday words through carelessness, because students write quickly in exams and do not proofread. Each type of error needs a different fix, so identify which type you make most often before choosing a remedy.

For similar-sounding letters, learn words in pairs that contrast the two letters, and practise writing both words correctly side by side. For hamza and borrowed words, learn the standard spellings of the most common examples from your textbook, and check uncertain words in a dictionary rather than guessing. For joining and separation, read your sentences aloud after writing, because unnatural joins often sound wrong even when they look plausible. For careless errors, build a proofreading habit: after finishing each answer, read it once slowly, looking only at spelling, before moving on. That one extra minute catches many errors that speed creates.

sections.h2: Essential Qawaid: The Rules Papers Test Most
paras: Qawaid questions most often test the basics: correct use of gender and number agreement, correct verb forms and tenses, proper use of particles and postpositions, and correct sentence structure. Agreement errors are common because the subject and verb must match in gender and number, and long sentences make it easy to lose track of the subject. Tense errors appear when a student mixes past and present in one sentence, or uses the wrong verb form for the intended time. Particle errors involve small words that change meaning, so using the wrong one can alter a whole sentence. Sentence structure errors include incomplete sentences, run-on sentences, and misplaced phrases that confuse the meaning.

Master these rules one at a time instead of trying to revise all grammar at once. For one week, focus only on agreement, and check every sentence you write for subject-verb matching. The next week, focus on tense consistency, and the following week on particles. This focused rotation builds each skill properly, and by the end of the rotation you will have covered the main rules with real practice. Use your textbook grammar section and your teacher's explanations as your authority, and practise with exercises that require you to correct sentences, since correction practice directly matches exam questions. Always verify a doubtful rule with your teacher rather than trusting a guidebook blindly.

diagram.caption: Fifteen minutes a day, rotating through the four skills.

sections.h2: Board Paper Patterns: What Questions Look Like
paras: Board papers typically test imla and qawaid through short, focused questions: correct the spelling of given words, correct the grammar of given sentences, fill in blanks with the correct form, or choose the correct option among given choices. Each form rewards a different skill, so practise all of them rather than only one. Spelling questions reward visual memory and your error diary. Sentence correction rewards rule knowledge and careful reading. Fill-in-the-blank questions reward knowledge of the exact form a context requires. Choice questions reward elimination: rule out the clearly wrong options first, then choose between the remaining ones.

Time management for this section is simple: these questions are short, so answer them first or early in the paper, while your mind is fresh, and do not spend long on any single item. If you are unsure about one item, mark it, move on, and return to it after finishing the rest, because a fresh look often resolves a doubt. Read every given sentence completely before correcting it, since the error may be at the end rather than where you first look. Finally, never leave a short question blank: a reasoned guess, based on the rules you know, has a chance of earning the mark, while a blank guarantees none.

sections.h2: A Daily Drill and Exam-Day Checklist
paras: A fifteen-minute daily drill is enough to build lasting accuracy. Spend five minutes revising your error diary, five minutes correcting sentences or practising one grammar rule, and five minutes writing a short paragraph and proofreading it for spelling only. Rotate the grammar focus weekly as described earlier, and take a short self-test every Friday covering the week's words and rules. This routine works because it is short enough to sustain daily, yet frequent enough to build automatic accuracy. Students who follow it for a term usually find that spelling and grammar stop being a source of lost marks.

On exam day, use a simple checklist for every answer: check the spelling of difficult words, check subject-verb agreement, check tense consistency, and check that each sentence is complete. Proofread each answer once before moving on, looking only at language rather than content, since content checking and language checking need separate readings. Write at a steady pace rather than rushing, because most careless errors come from speed, not ignorance. If you finish early, use the remaining time to proofread the whole paper again, starting with the shortest answers where errors are most visible. More exam preparation is on the [Blog](/blog/) and book information on [Books](/books.html).

Muse AI is Meta's personal AI assistant, and it can help with imla and qawaid by quizzing you on spelling words from your error diary, or by explaining a grammar rule like agreement in simple words with an example. You can ask it to check a short paragraph you wrote for tense consistency. Join Muse with invite code LTGSWD — in the Muse app, go to Settings > Redeem token and enter the code. Disclosure: LTGSWD is the author's Muse invite code. Muse AI does not give official STBB answers — always verify against your STBB book and your teacher. Remember to verify against your Sindh Textbook Board book before writing any grammar answer in your exam.

points: Imla and qawaid marks appear in every section, not just in short questions.
Keep a personal error diary of words you misspell, with correct sentences.
Learn confusable letters in pairs and borrowed spellings from the textbook.
Rotate grammar focus weekly: agreement, tenses, particles, sentence structure.
Proofread every answer once for language alone before moving on.

faqs.q: How can I improve Urdu spelling quickly before the exam?
faqs.a: Focus on your own error diary rather than a generic list, since your repeated mistakes are the ones most likely to recur. Revise the diary daily for five minutes and test yourself weekly by writing the words from memory. Add a proofreading pass to every practice answer, reading slowly and looking only at spelling. In the final weeks, consolidate known words instead of learning many new ones, because confident recall of your common words prevents the most frequent errors.

faqs.q: What is the most common grammar mistake in Class 10 Urdu papers?
faqs.a: Subject-verb agreement is among the most common, because students lose track of the subject in long sentences and mismatch gender or number. Tense inconsistency is another frequent error, especially when narrating past events with mixed past and present verbs. Both improve with focused practice: check agreement in every sentence for one week, then tense consistency the next. Correction exercises are the best practice, since they match the exam question form directly.

faqs.q: Should I memorise grammar rules or practise exercises?
faqs.a: Both, but practice matters more. Learn each rule in simple words, then apply it immediately in correction and sentence-writing exercises, because rules without application fade quickly. After exercises, review your errors and note which rule each error broke, so revision targets your weak rules. A rule you can state and apply correctly is learned; a rule you can only recite is not yet ready for the exam. Ask your teacher to check your understanding of rules you find confusing.

faqs.q: How do I handle a sentence correction question I am unsure about?
faqs.a: Read the whole sentence first, identify the most likely error type, such as agreement, tense, or particle, and apply the relevant rule. If two corrections seem possible, choose the one that makes the sentence most natural and grammatically consistent. Rewrite the whole sentence correctly rather than only underlining the error. If still unsure, make your best reasoned attempt and move on, returning later if time allows, since a blank answer earns nothing.

faqs.q: Does handwriting affect imla and qawaid marks?
faqs.a: Indirectly, yes. Unclear handwriting can make correct spellings look wrong, especially where dots and marks distinguish letters in Urdu script. Write slowly enough to form letters and dots clearly, and leave proper spacing between words. Examiners cannot award marks for what they cannot read, so legibility protects your spelling and grammar marks. Practise writing at exam speed with neat formation, rather than writing fast drafts that you cannot read back yourself.

title: Class 10 Urdu Sabaq-wise Khulase: All Lessons in Brief
desc: Learn Class 10 Urdu sabaq-wise khulase: write one-paragraph summaries of every prose lesson and revise the whole course efficiently.
kw: Class 10 Urdu sabaq wise khulase lesson summaries
intro: When the Class 10 Urdu course feels too large to revise, sabaq-wise khulase, or lesson-wise summaries, are the tool that makes it manageable: one clear paragraph per lesson, capturing its subject, main points, and lesson. Many students revise by re-reading whole lessons, which takes hours and leaves little in memory, while others rely on memorised summaries they do not understand. The right method is to write your own one-paragraph summary for every prose lesson, using a fixed template, and then to revise from those paragraphs. This guide teaches that template, shows how to cover every lesson, and explains how to use summaries for final revision. Summaries here describe the method only; your own summaries must come from your textbook lessons.

sections.h2: Why One Paragraph Per Lesson Works
paras: A one-paragraph summary forces you to decide what matters most in a lesson, and that decision is itself powerful learning. When you must compress a whole lesson into five or six sentences, you cannot hide behind copying: you must identify the subject, the main points, and the conclusion or lesson. This active selection builds understanding far better than passive re-reading, and the resulting paragraph is short enough to revise in two minutes. Over a course of many lessons, a complete set of one-paragraph summaries becomes a revision book you wrote yourself, which you trust and remember far better than any guidebook.

The method also reveals gaps honestly: if you cannot summarise a lesson in one paragraph, you have not yet understood it, and you know exactly which lesson needs more work. That diagnosis is valuable, because it directs your remaining study time to the weakest lessons instead of the ones you already know. Write summaries during the term, lesson by lesson, rather than leaving them all for the final month, since writing them is itself a form of study. Keep them in a dedicated notebook, one lesson per page, so you can add corrections and teacher feedback without rewriting the whole set. Lesson summaries and study help are on [Solved Notes](/solved.html) and the [Blog](/blog/).

sections.h2: The Five-Sentence Template for Every Lesson
paras: A reliable template for a prose lesson summary has five sentences. Sentence one states the lesson's subject and type, such as an essay, a story, or a biographical piece, and what it is about. Sentences two and three give the main points in order, covering the central discussion, events, or arguments without minor details. Sentence four notes any distinctive feature worth remembering, such as the writer's style, a memorable example, or an important quotation in your own words. Sentence five states the conclusion or lesson the piece teaches or suggests. This template works across lesson types with small adjustments, which makes writing summaries fast once you practise it.

For a story lesson, adapt the middle sentences to plot: sentence two covers the situation and conflict, and sentence three covers the turning point and ending. For an essay lesson, the middle sentences cover the main arguments in order. For a biographical lesson, they cover the person's important life stages and contribution. Keep each sentence focused on one idea, and avoid copying sentences from the lesson itself, since the summary must be in your own words to prove understanding. After writing a summary, read it aloud and check that a classmate who had not read the lesson could understand its subject, points, and lesson from your paragraph alone.

diagram.caption: Five sentences that capture any prose lesson.

sections.h2: Covering Every Lesson Without Missing Any
paras: Completeness matters: a summary set that skips difficult lessons leaves exactly the gaps examiners can test. Start by listing every prose lesson in your textbook in order, using the contents page, and tick each one off as you summarise it. Work through the list steadily, one or two lessons per week, rather than rushing at the end. If a lesson is long or difficult, split the work: read and note its main points one day, and write the summary the next day, so the task stays manageable. Keep the list visible in your notebook, because a visible checklist motivates you to finish the remaining lessons.

For lessons you find hard, use extra help before summarising: re-read the lesson slowly, discuss it with your teacher or a classmate, and note the main points in rough form first. Only then shape those notes into the five-sentence summary, because summarising a lesson you have not understood produces a vague paragraph that helps nobody. After writing, compare your summary with the lesson's headings or exercises to check you covered the main points. If your teacher provides lesson summaries or notes, use them to check your own, not to replace them, since your own wording is what you will remember in the exam.

sections.h2: Using Summaries for Revision and Exam Answers
paras: Summaries are revision tools first: in the weeks before an exam, read through your summary notebook lesson by lesson, covering each paragraph and recalling its points from memory before reading it. Test yourself by writing the subject and lesson of each prose piece from memory, then checking against your summaries. This active recall strengthens memory far more than re-reading, and it quickly shows which lessons need another look. In the final week, revise the summaries of the lessons you find hardest twice, and the rest once, so your time goes where it helps most.

Summaries also help you answer exam questions, because many questions ask for a lesson's central idea, its main points, or its moral, all of which your summary already contains. When such a question appears, expand the relevant sentence of your summary into a full answer, adding one or two supporting details from the lesson. Do not, however, copy a summary word for word when a question asks for something specific, such as a character sketch or a style analysis; adapt your knowledge to the question asked. The summary gives you the material, and your judgement shapes it into the answer the examiner wants.

The most common mistake is writing summaries that are too long, essentially copying the lesson in shorter form instead of selecting its main points. A summary longer than a paragraph defeats its purpose, because it takes as long to revise as the lesson itself. The second mistake is writing summaries that are too vague, using general phrases that could describe any lesson, without the specific points that make this lesson distinct. The third is copying guidebook summaries without understanding them, which fails when the exam asks a question the guidebook did not cover. The fourth is leaving summaries unfinished, with the difficult lessons missing from the set.

Avoid all four by following the template strictly: five sentences, specific points, your own words, and a complete checklist. After writing each summary, test it with two questions: could a reader identify this lesson from the summary alone, and could you expand it into an exam answer? If either answer is no, revise the summary before moving on. Show your summaries to your teacher periodically, because feedback at this stage corrects misunderstandings while there is still time to fix them. A complete, tested set of summaries is one of the most valuable revision resources you can own. More revision strategies are on the [Blog](/blog/) and book lists on [Books](/books.html).

points: One paragraph per lesson forces selection of what truly matters.
Use the five-sentence template: subject, main points, feature, conclusion.
List every lesson from the contents page and tick each off as summarised.
Revise by active recall from summaries, not by passive re-reading.
Expand summary sentences into exam answers, adapted to each question.

faqs.q: How long should a sabaq-wise khulasa be?
faqs.a: One paragraph of about five or six sentences is ideal: long enough to cover the subject, main points, a distinctive feature, and the conclusion, but short enough to revise in two minutes. Longer summaries take as long to revise as the lesson itself, while shorter ones usually miss essential points. If a lesson is unusually rich, allow a sixth sentence for an extra main point, but keep the paragraph tight. The test of a good summary is whether you can expand it into a full exam answer when needed.

faqs.q: Should summaries be in Urdu or in my own simpler words?
faqs.a: Write summaries in the language of your exam answers, which for Urdu lessons means simple, correct Urdu in your own words. Using your own words proves understanding and makes the summary easier to remember and expand in the exam. Avoid copying sentences from the lesson or from guidebooks, since copied summaries do not build the understanding you need when questions vary. If a technical term must appear, use it correctly and make sure you understand it.

faqs.q: What if I cannot summarise a lesson I find difficult?
faqs.a: That difficulty is useful information: it tells you the lesson needs more study before summarising. Re-read the lesson slowly, note its main points in rough form, and discuss it with your teacher or a classmate. Then shape those rough notes into the five-sentence template, and check the result against the lesson's headings. Do not skip the lesson or copy someone else's summary; working through the difficulty is exactly how understanding is built. Ask your teacher to check your summary once it is written.

faqs.q: How do I use summaries in the last week before the exam?
faqs.a: Read through your summary notebook lesson by lesson, testing recall by covering each paragraph and reciting its points before reading it. Revise the hardest lessons twice and the rest once, and practise expanding one summary sentence into a full answer each day. Do not start new summaries in the last week; instead, consolidate the set you already have. If a summary reveals a gap, re-read that lesson briefly rather than rewriting the whole summary.

faqs.q: Can summaries replace reading the actual lessons?
faqs.a: No. Summaries are revision tools that help you recall and organise what you have already studied, not substitutes for reading the lessons themselves. Read each lesson fully at least once, understand its language and details, and then write your summary from that understanding. Students who only read summaries miss the language, examples, and details that exam questions often test. Use summaries to revise efficiently, and return to the full lesson whenever a summary reveals uncertainty.

title: Sindhi Grammar: Ism, Fail and Harf Explained
desc: Learn Sindhi grammar word classes: ism, fail and harf explained simply with clear Sindhi examples, sentence patterns and easy practice tips for students.
intro: Sindhi grammar ism fail harf is the starting point for every student who wants to read, write and speak Sindhi correctly. Every word in a Sindhi sentence belongs to one of three main classes: ism, which names a person, place, thing or idea; fail, which shows an action or state; and harf, which joins words and shows a relationship between them. Once you can tell these three apart, sentences stop looking like a jumble of words and start looking like a clear pattern. This guide explains each class with illustrative Sindhi examples in Roman transliteration, so you can practise without a dictionary. You will also learn quick tests for identifying each word, common confusions, and how to use all three classes together in your own sentences for classwork and exams.

sections.h2: Why Sindhi Words Fall Into Three Classes
paras: Sindhi, like many languages, groups words by the job they do in a sentence, and the three traditional classes are ism, fail and harf. An ism names something, so it can stand as the subject or object of a sentence. A fail tells us what happens, what someone does, or what state something is in, and it usually changes with tense. A harf does not name or act on its own; instead, it connects an ism to another word and shows direction, place, possession or a similar relationship. Learning these classes first saves time later, because rules about gender, number, case and tense all build on knowing which class a word belongs to.

A useful habit is to ask a simple question about each word you meet. If the word answers who or what, it is probably an ism. If it answers what is happening or what was done, it is probably a fail. If it only makes sense beside another word, joining or relating it to the rest of the sentence, it is probably a harf. Try this test on short sentences from your reading book, and underline each word in a different colour. After a few days of practice, you will begin to spot the pattern at a glance, and longer sentences will feel much less confusing. For extra reading material, explore the [book list](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html) pages.

sections.h2: Ism: Words That Name People, Places and Things
paras: An ism is a naming word. It can name a person, such as chhokro (boy) or ustad (teacher); a place, such as goth (village) or school; a thing, such as kitab (book) or qalam (pen); or an idea, such as mohabbat (love) or sachai (truth). Isms can be common, naming any member of a group, or proper, naming one particular person or place, such as Ali or Hyderabad. In a sentence, an ism often comes first as the subject, or after the fail as the object. Recognising the ism is the first step in understanding who the sentence is about and what it is discussing.

Isms in Sindhi also carry gender and number, which is why later lessons on muzakkar and muannas and wahid and jama matter so much. For example, the illustrative sentence Chhokro kitab parhi tho (The boy is reading a book) contains two isms, chhokro and kitab, and one fail, parhi tho. Change the ism and the sentence changes its meaning completely, while the structure stays the same. When you write, choose your ism carefully, check its spelling, and make sure the rest of the sentence agrees with it. Practise by listing ten isms from your own classroom and sorting them into people, places, things and ideas.
bullets: Person: ustad, shagird, amma, abba
Place: goth, sheher, school, ghar
Thing: kitab, qalam, kursi, mez
Idea: mohabbat, himmat, sachai, khushi

sections.h2: Fail: Words That Show Action and State
paras: A fail is an action word or a state word. It tells the reader what the subject does, did, or will do, or what condition the subject is in. Common illustrative examples include parhan (to read), likhan (to write), khaen (to eat), wanjen (to go) and vehn (to sit). Unlike an ism, a fail changes its form with time: the same action looks different in the past, present and future. That is why verb lessons often come with tables, and why practising one fail in all three tenses is such a useful exercise for building confidence in Sindhi writing.

To find the fail in a sentence, ask what is happening. In the illustrative sentence Shagird sabak likhi tho (The student is writing the lesson), the fail is likhi tho, because it shows the action being done. In Chhokri khushi aahe (The girl is happy), the word aahe works like a state word, telling us about the subject's condition rather than a physical action. Some students confuse an ism and a fail when a word can appear in both roles, so always check the job the word does in that particular sentence, not just its dictionary meaning. Keep a small notebook of new fails with one example sentence each.

sections.h2: Harf: Small Words That Join and Relate
paras: A harf is a small joining or relating word, and it rarely makes full sense standing alone. Common illustrative examples include me (in), te (on), kha (from), saan (with) and lae (for). In the sentence Kitab mez te aahe (The book is on the table), the harf te links kitab and mez and shows where the book is. Remove te and the sentence falls apart, because the relationship between the two isms disappears. Harf words may look unimportant because they are short, but they carry the direction, place, time and possession that make a sentence precise.

Students often skip harf words when reading quickly, and that is where meaning gets lost. Compare two illustrative sentences: Ali ghar me aahe (Ali is in the house) and Ali ghar kha aayo (Ali came from the house). The only change is the harf, yet the meaning changes completely. When you write, pause after each harf and ask whether it says exactly what you mean: in, on, from, with, for and to are not interchangeable. Practise by taking one sentence and swapping only its harf, then explaining how the meaning changes. This single exercise sharpens both reading comprehension and writing accuracy.

diagram.alt: How to Identify Ism, Fail and Harf
diagram.caption: Ask these questions in order to classify any Sindhi word in a sentence.

sections.h2: Using Ism, Fail and Harf Together in Sentences
paras: A complete Sindhi sentence usually needs at least an ism and a fail, and often a harf as well. Start simple: choose one ism as your subject, one fail as your action, and add an object ism if the action needs one. For example, the illustrative sentence Ustad sabak parhae tho (The teacher is teaching the lesson) has ustad as subject ism, sabak as object ism, and parhae tho as fail. Once that core feels easy, add a harf phrase for extra detail, such as school me (in school) or subuh jo (in the morning), and the sentence becomes richer without becoming confusing.

Build up gradually rather than writing very long sentences at once. Write five short sentences using one new ism, one new fail and one harf each, then read them aloud to check that they sound natural. Ask a classmate or teacher to mark the ism, fail and harf in each sentence, and correct any word you misclassified. Over time, try joining two short sentences with a conjunction, but keep the ism-fail core of each part clear. This steady practice is exactly what examiners reward: clear subjects, correct verbs and precise joining words. You can find more study help on the [blog](/blog/) and the [home page](/) of this site.

Fail shows an action or state and changes form with past, present and future tense.
Harf joins words and shows relationships such as place, direction, time and possession.
Classify a word by the job it does in that sentence, not only by its dictionary meaning.
Practise with short sentences first, then add harf phrases and conjunctions gradually.

faqs.q: What is an ism in Sindhi grammar?
faqs.a: An ism is a naming word. It names a person like ustad, a place like goth, a thing like kitab, or an idea like mohabbat. In a sentence it usually works as the subject or the object. If a word answers the question who or what, it is very likely an ism. Proper isms name one particular person or place, while common isms name any member of a group.

faqs.q: How is a fail different from an ism?
faqs.a: A fail shows action or state, while an ism names something. In the illustrative sentence Chhokro kitab parhi tho, chhokro and kitab are isms and parhi tho is the fail, because it tells us what the boy is doing. A fail also changes with tense, so the same action looks different in the past, present and future, whereas an ism changes mainly for gender and number.

faqs.q: Why are harf words important if they are so small?
faqs.a: Harf words carry relationships that change meaning. In Kitab mez te aahe, te tells us the book is on the table. Change the harf and the meaning changes, even though the isms stay the same. Without harf words, sentences lose place, direction, time and possession, so readers have to guess what the writer meant.

faqs.q: Can one Sindhi word be more than one class?
faqs.a: Yes, sometimes the same word can act as an ism in one sentence and part of a fail phrase in another, depending on its job. That is why grammar teaches you to check the word in context. Always ask what the word is doing in this particular sentence before deciding whether it is an ism, a fail or a harf.

faqs.q: How can I practise ism, fail and harf at home?
faqs.a: Take five short sentences from your reading book, underline each word, and label it as ism, fail or harf. Then write five sentences of your own using one new word from each class. Read them aloud, swap only the harf in one sentence, and notice how the meaning changes. Ask your teacher to check your labels once a week until the pattern feels automatic.

title: Sindhi Grammar: Zamir and Its Types
desc: Understand Sindhi zamir types: personal, demonstrative and relative pronouns explained with clear examples, sentence patterns and common student mistakes.
intro: Sindhi grammar zamir types matter because zamir words let us avoid repeating the same name again and again in every sentence. A zamir is a pronoun: a word that stands in place of an ism, such as a person, place or thing already mentioned. Instead of writing Ali went, Ali sat and Ali read in three sentences, we can write Ali went, he sat and he read, using a zamir for the second and third mention. This guide explains the main types of zamir in Sindhi, including personal, demonstrative and relative pronouns, with illustrative examples in Roman transliteration. You will learn how each type works, how to choose the right form, and which mistakes students make most often in writing.

sections.h2: What Is a Zamir and Why Do We Need It
paras: A zamir replaces an ism so that speech and writing stay smooth and natural. Without zamir words, even a short paragraph would sound repetitive and clumsy, because every sentence would have to repeat full names and nouns. With zamir words, a writer can introduce a person or thing once, then refer back to it briefly in the sentences that follow. That is why zamir is one of the first grammar topics taught after ism, fail and harf: it builds directly on knowing what an ism is, and it makes longer writing possible without constant repetition.

The key rule is that a zamir must point clearly to something the reader already knows. If you write He is reading, the reader must be able to tell who he refers to, either from an earlier sentence or from the situation. A vague zamir confuses the reader just as much as a missing word does. Good writers therefore introduce the ism first, then use the zamir, and they switch back to the full name whenever a new person enters the story. Practise this by rewriting a short paragraph: replace repeated names with zamir words, then read it aloud to check that every reference is still clear.

Personal zamir words refer to people in the first, second or third person. First-person forms include maan (I) and asaan (we), used when the speaker talks about himself or herself or a group including the speaker. Second-person forms include tuhin (you, singular familiar) and tawhaan (you, respectful or plural), used when speaking directly to someone. Third-person forms include hu (he or she, near or general) and uh (that one), used when talking about someone who is not part of the conversation. Choosing between tuhin and tawhaan also shows respect, so students should notice how adults address elders and teachers.

Personal zamir forms change with case and number, so the same person may appear as maan, muhinjo (my) or mukhe (to me) depending on the sentence. For example, the illustrative sentences Maan kitab parhi tho (I am reading a book) and Ustad mukhe sabak dino (The teacher gave me the lesson) both refer to the speaker, but the form changes because the role in the sentence changes. The best way to learn these forms is to practise one person at a time: write five sentences using maan, then five using asaan, then five using tawhaan, and compare the forms. For more solved material, visit the [solved notes](/solved.html) and [book list](/books.html) pages.
bullets: First person: maan (I), asaan (we)
Second person: tuhin (you, familiar), tawhaan (you, respectful)
Third person: hu (he or she), uh (that person)
Possessive: muhinjo (my), tuhinjo (your), hunjo (his or her)

sections.h2: Demonstrative Zamir: Pointing to Near and Far
paras: Demonstrative zamir words point to something, showing whether it is near the speaker or farther away. Sindhi uses hi (this) for things that are near and hu or uh for things that are farther away, although the exact form depends on gender, number and case in the full sentence. For example, the illustrative sentence Hi kitab muhinji aahe (This book is mine) points to a book close at hand, while Hu kitab ustad ji aahe (That book is the teacher's) points to one farther away. Learning this near and far contrast helps students describe objects, choose items in a shop, and follow directions accurately.

A common confusion is mixing demonstrative zamir with demonstrative sifat, which is a describing word used before an ism. In Hi kitab suthi aahe (This book is good), hi points to the book and works with the ism kitab. The test is simple: if the word stands alone in place of the ism, it is a zamir; if it stands before the ism and describes which one, it is closer to a sifat. Students should practise pairs of sentences, one with the word alone and one with the word before an ism, and explain the difference. This small distinction earns marks in grammar exercises and improves clarity in everyday writing.

sections.h2: Relative Zamir: Joining Two Ideas Together
paras: Relative zamir words join two clauses by referring back to a person or thing already mentioned. The most important Sindhi relative word is jehro or jo (who, which, that), used in sentences where one part describes another. For example, the illustrative sentence Chhokro jehro mehnat kare tho, so kamyab thindo (The boy who works hard will succeed) uses jehro to link the description of hard work to the boy. Without the relative zamir, the sentence would split into two short, disconnected statements, and the link between effort and success would feel weaker.

Relative zamir sentences need care with word order and agreement, because the relative clause sits inside the main sentence. A useful method is to build the sentence in two steps: first write the main statement, then add the describing clause with jo or jehro. For example, start with Kitab suthi aahe (The book is good), then expand it to Kitab jo maan parhi, so suthi aahe (The book which I read is good). Read the full sentence aloud and check that the relative word still points to the right ism. If the sentence sounds tangled, split it again and rebuild it slowly. This patient method prevents the long, confusing sentences that lose marks.

diagram.caption: Personal, demonstrative and relative zamir each do a different job in a sentence.

sections.h2: Common Zamir Mistakes and How to Fix Them
paras: The most common zamir mistake is a unclear reference: the reader cannot tell who he or she means because two people were mentioned. For example, if Ali and Ahmed are both in a paragraph and the next sentence says Hu aayo (He came), the reader cannot know which boy came. The fix is simple: repeat the name when a new person appears, or rewrite the sentence so only one person is possible. Another frequent mistake is mixing respectful and familiar forms, such as using tuhin for a teacher, which sounds rude in Sindhi. Always use tawhaan for elders, teachers and strangers, and keep tuhin for close friends and younger children.

A third mistake is changing the zamir halfway through a paragraph without reason, jumping from maan to asaan or from hu to uh. Consistency matters: once you choose a form for a person, keep it unless the person or distance genuinely changes. Before submitting written work, read it once just for zamir words: circle each one, draw an arrow to the ism it replaces, and check that every arrow is clear. This five-minute check catches most errors and is one of the fastest ways to raise the quality of Sindhi composition. More practice ideas are available on the [blog](/blog/) and the [home page](/) of this site.

points: A zamir stands in place of an ism so writing avoids repeating the same name.
Personal zamir covers first, second and third person, including respectful tawhaan.
Demonstrative zamir points near with hi and farther away with hu or uh.
Relative zamir words like jo and jehro join a description to the main sentence.
Every zamir must point clearly to one ism, or the reader will be confused.

faqs.q: What is the difference between ism and zamir?
faqs.a: An ism names a person, place or thing directly, such as Ali or kitab. A zamir replaces that ism after it has been introduced, such as hu for Ali. You introduce the ism first so the reader knows who you mean, then use the zamir in later sentences to avoid repetition. If the zamir could point to two different people, repeat the name instead.

faqs.q: When should I use tuhin and when tawhaan?
faqs.a: Use tuhin for close friends, younger children and people you know very well. Use tawhaan for teachers, elders, strangers and anyone you should address respectfully, and also when speaking to more than one person. Using tuhin for a teacher sounds disrespectful in Sindhi, so this choice is about manners as well as grammar.

faqs.q: What is a demonstrative zamir with an example?
faqs.a: A demonstrative zamir points to something near or far. Hi means this and points to something close, as in Hi kitab muhinji aahe (This book is mine). Hu or uh means that and points to something farther away, as in Hu kitab ustad ji aahe (That book is the teacher's). The contrast between near and far is the key idea to remember.

faqs.q: How does a relative zamir work in a sentence?
faqs.a: A relative zamir joins a describing clause to a main sentence. In Chhokro jehro mehnat kare tho, so kamyab thindo, jehro links the description of hard work to the boy. Build such sentences in two steps: write the main statement first, then add the clause with jo or jehro, and read the result aloud to check the word order.

faqs.q: Why is my zamir marked wrong even when the word is correct?
faqs.a: Often the word itself is right but the reference is unclear. If two people appear in a paragraph and you write hu, the examiner cannot tell which person you mean. Fix it by repeating the name when a new person enters, keeping one form consistently for each person, and circling each zamir to check it points to exactly one ism before you submit your work.

title: Sindhi Grammar: Sifat and Adverbs in Sentences
desc: Learn Sindhi sifat and adverbs: describing words for nouns and verbs, their position in sentences, agreement rules and easy examples for students.
intro: Sindhi grammar sifat adverbs are the words that add colour and precision to a sentence, telling us what kind of thing something is and how an action is done. A sifat is a describing word that tells us more about an ism, such as whether a book is new, big or interesting. An adverb, often called a fail jo sifat in simple terms, tells us more about a fail, such as whether someone reads slowly, carefully or every day. Without these words, sentences are correct but flat: The boy reads becomes a picture only when we know which boy and how he reads. This guide explains sifat and adverbs separately, shows where each one sits in a sentence, and gives illustrative Sindhi examples in Roman transliteration for practice.

sections.h2: What Is a Sifat in Sindhi Grammar
paras: A sifat is a word that describes an ism, giving information about its quality, size, colour, number or condition. In the illustrative sentence Sutho chhokro school wanji tho (The good boy is going to school), sutho is the sifat because it describes chhokro. Other common sifat words include wado (big), nandho (small), lal (red), navo (new) and purano (old). A sifat usually comes before the ism it describes in Sindhi, which makes it easy to spot once you look for the describing word just before a noun. Students should practise by adding one sifat to a plain noun and noticing how much clearer the picture becomes.

Sifat words also agree with the ism they describe in gender and number, and this agreement is where many students lose marks. A sifat used with a muzakkar ism may look different from the same sifat used with a muannas ism, and the plural form may change again. The rule is simple to state but needs practice: always check the ism first, then choose the sifat form that matches it. When you write, underline each sifat and its ism together, and ask whether they match. This pairing habit, repeated daily with five new sentences, builds agreement into your writing so that it becomes automatic rather than a last-minute worry.

sections.h2: Types of Sifat Students Should Know
paras: Sifat words fall into useful groups that help students choose the right description. Quality sifat words describe character or condition, such as sutho (good), kharab (bad) and bahadur (brave). Quantity sifat words tell how many or how much, such as ghanan (many), thora (few) and sab (all). Colour and size sifat words describe appearance, such as lal (red), sawo (green), wado (big) and nandho (small). Number sifat words give an exact count or order, such as pehriyon (first), be (two) and teen (three). Knowing these groups helps you find a precise word instead of repeating sutho for everything.

Demonstrative and possessive words sometimes act like sifat when they stand before an ism, such as hi kitab (this book) or muhinji kitab (my book). In those cases the word points to or claims the ism rather than describing its quality, but it still sits in the sifat position. Students do not need to argue about the label in every case; what matters is recognising that the word belongs with the ism and agrees with it. A practical exercise is to take ten isms from your classroom, write two different sifat words for each, and sort them into quality, quantity, colour, size and number groups. For more reading, see the [book list](/books.html) and [solved notes](/solved.html).
bullets: Quality: sutho, kharab, bahadur, mehnati
Quantity: ghanan, thora, sab, kuch
Colour and size: lal, sawo, wado, nandho
Number: pehriyon, be, teen, chauthon

sections.h2: What Is an Adverb and How Does It Differ
paras: An adverb describes a fail, not an ism, and it answers questions like how, when, where and how often an action happens. In the illustrative sentence Chhokro ahista parhi tho (The boy is reading slowly), ahista is the adverb because it tells us how the boy reads. In Chhokri roz school wanji thi (The girl goes to school every day), roz is an adverb of time, telling us how often she goes. In Ustad bahar betho aahe (The teacher is sitting outside), bahar is an adverb of place. The test is reliable: if the word describes the action, it is an adverb; if it describes a noun, it is a sifat.

Confusion arises because some words can act as sifat in one sentence and adverb in another. For example, ahista can describe a slow boy in one sentence and slow reading in another, and only the job in that sentence decides the label. Students should therefore ask two questions for every describing word: what does it describe, and is that thing an ism or a fail? Answering those questions correctly is more important than memorising long lists. Practise with pairs of sentences that use the same describing word in both roles, and explain the difference in your own words to a classmate.

sections.h2: Where Sifat and Adverbs Sit in a Sentence
paras: Position helps the reader understand a sentence quickly, so placing sifat and adverbs correctly matters. A sifat normally comes before the ism it describes, as in navo kitab (new book) or suthi chhokri (good girl). An adverb is more flexible: it often comes before the fail, as in ahista parhi tho, or at the start of the sentence for emphasis, as in Roz, chhokri school wanji thi. Adverbs of place often come after the object or before the fail, depending on what the writer wants to stress. Reading sentences aloud is the best test: a well-placed describing word sounds smooth, while a misplaced one sounds awkward.

Word order mistakes usually come from translating directly from another language or from piling too many describing words into one sentence. Keep it simple: one sifat before the ism and one adverb near the fail is enough for most school sentences. If you want a second description, put it in a new sentence or join it with a conjunction. For example, instead of writing a long chain of adjectives, write Kitab navo aahe (The book is new) and then add So sutho bhi aahe (It is also good). Short, well-placed descriptions impress examiners far more than long, tangled ones. More guidance is available on the [blog](/blog/) and the [home page](/).

diagram.caption: Use this comparison to decide whether a describing word is a sifat or an adverb.

paras: Describing skills grow fastest when students practise with real objects and actions around them. Start with five objects in your classroom: write the ism, add a sifat for colour or size, and then write a full sentence using it. Next, choose five actions you do every day, add an adverb for how or when, and write a sentence for each. For example, Maan ahista likhan tho (I am writing slowly) practises an adverb, while Maan navo qalam kharidyo (I bought a new pen) practises a sifat. Doing both exercises in one session teaches the contrast far better than memorising definitions alone.

A second useful exercise is editing: take a plain paragraph of five sentences and add exactly one sifat and one adverb to each sentence, without changing the facts. Then read the edited paragraph aloud and ask whether every addition helps or whether some additions feel forced. Good description adds information the reader needs; extra description that repeats what is already known only makes the paragraph heavy. Ask your teacher to mark one edited paragraph each week, focusing only on sifat and adverb choice and position. Within a month, your descriptions will become sharper, and your composition marks will usually rise with them.
