An adverb describes a fail, telling how, when, where or how often an action happens.
Sifat usually comes before its ism and agrees with it in gender and number.
Adverbs sit near the fail and are more flexible in position than sifat words.
One well-chosen description beats a long chain of vague describing words.

faqs.q: How do I tell a sifat from an adverb quickly?
faqs.a: Ask what the word describes. If it describes an ism, such as a boy, book or girl, it is a sifat. If it describes a fail, such as reading, writing or going, it is an adverb. In Sutho chhokro, sutho describes the boy, so it is a sifat. In Ahista parhi tho, ahista describes the reading, so it is an adverb. This question works for almost every school sentence.

faqs.q: Does a sifat change with the ism it describes?
faqs.a: Yes, a sifat usually agrees with its ism in gender and number. That means the same describing idea may take a different form with a muzakkar ism, a muannas ism, or a plural ism. Always check the ism first, then choose the matching sifat form, and underline the pair when you revise so mismatches stand out.

faqs.q: What are the main kinds of adverb in Sindhi?
faqs.a: The main kinds are manner, time, place and frequency. Manner tells how an action is done, such as ahista (slowly). Time tells when, such as aj (today). Place tells where, such as bahar (outside). Frequency tells how often, such as roz (every day). Naming the kind helps you place the adverb and check that it answers the right question.

faqs.q: Can the same word be both a sifat and an adverb?
faqs.a: Yes, some describing words can do both jobs in different sentences. The label depends on the job in that sentence, not on the word alone. If the word describes a noun, call it a sifat; if it describes a verb, call it an adverb. Practise with sentence pairs that use the same word in both roles to make this distinction clear.

faqs.q: How many describing words should I use in one sentence?
faqs.a: For school writing, one sifat before the ism and one adverb near the fail is usually enough. Adding more descriptions can help if each one adds new information, but a long chain of adjectives makes sentences heavy and hard to read. If a sentence feels crowded, split it into two sentences or move the extra description into the next sentence.

title: Sindhi Grammar: Jumla and Its Kinds
desc: Learn Sindhi jumla kinds: simple, compound and complex sentences explained with structure, examples and tips for writing clear Sindhi sentences.
intro: Sindhi grammar jumla kinds give students a map for building sentences that are clear, correct and varied. A jumla is a group of words that makes complete sense on its own, usually containing at least a subject and a fail. Sindhi sentences can be simple, with one main idea; compound, with two equal ideas joined together; or complex, with one main idea plus a describing or dependent clause. Knowing which kind you are writing helps you control length, punctuation and meaning, and it helps examiners see that you can do more than repeat one short pattern. This guide explains each kind with illustrative Sindhi examples in Roman transliteration, plus practical advice for choosing the right kind for each purpose.

sections.h2: What Makes a Group of Words a Jumla
paras: A jumla must make complete sense by itself. It needs a subject, usually an ism or zamir, and a fail that says what the subject does or what state it is in. The illustrative sentence Chhokro parhi tho (The boy is reading) is a complete jumla because it has both parts and leaves the reader with no unanswered question. A group like Parhi tho alone is not a complete jumla, because the reader does not know who is reading. Similarly, a group like Chhokro kitab without a fail is only a phrase, not a sentence, because it states no action or condition.

Students should test every sentence they write with two questions: who or what is this about, and what is said about it? If both answers are clear, the jumla is probably complete. If one answer is missing, add the missing part before moving on. This test is especially useful in exams, where incomplete sentences lose marks even when the vocabulary is good. Practise by taking five phrases from your textbook, turning each one into a complete jumla by adding a subject or a fail, and then reading the results aloud. For extra solved material, visit the [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [book list](/books.html).

sections.h2: Simple Jumla: One Idea, Clearly Stated
paras: A simple jumla, called jumla-e-sada in grammar terms, expresses one main idea with one subject and one fail, even if it also contains objects and describing phrases. Examples include Ali school wanji tho (Ali is going to school) and Chhokri kitab parhi thi (The girl is reading a book). Simple sentences are the backbone of clear writing: they are easy to read, easy to check for agreement, and easy to correct. Young writers should master simple sentences before attempting longer ones, because every longer sentence is built from simple cores joined or expanded carefully.

Simple does not mean weak or childish. Many strong sentences in essays and stories are simple, because they state one idea with force and leave no room for confusion. A paragraph of well-chosen simple sentences often reads better than a paragraph of tangled long sentences. To practise, write ten simple sentences about your school day, each with a different subject and fail, and check each one for a complete subject and fail. Then choose two of them to expand later with a harf phrase, such as subuh jo (in the morning) or school me (in school), without changing the core idea.
bullets: One subject and one fail form the core of a simple jumla.
Objects and harf phrases can expand it without changing its kind.
Simple sentences are easiest to check for gender and tense agreement.
Strong writing often mixes simple sentences with longer ones.

sections.h2: Compound Jumla: Two Equal Ideas Joined
paras: A compound jumla joins two simple sentences of equal importance with a conjunction such as ain (and), par (but) or ya (or). For example, the illustrative sentence Ali parhi tho ain Ahmed likhi tho (Ali is reading and Ahmed is writing) contains two complete ideas, each with its own subject and fail, joined by ain. Neither part depends on the other for its meaning; each could stand alone as a simple sentence. Compound sentences are useful when two actions happen together, when two facts belong side by side, or when a contrast needs to be shown in one breath.

The most common compound-sentence mistake is joining two ideas without a conjunction, creating a run-on sentence that confuses the reader. Another mistake is joining ideas that do not belong together, such as a sentence about school and a sentence about food, just because both are true. Before joining, ask whether the two ideas share a topic and whether the conjunction says the right relationship: ain adds, par contrasts, and ya offers a choice. Practise by taking pairs of simple sentences on the same topic, joining them with each conjunction in turn, and explaining how the meaning changes with each choice.

sections.h2: Complex Jumla: A Main Idea Plus a Dependent Clause
paras: A complex jumla contains one main clause that makes sense alone, plus one or more dependent clauses that add information but cannot stand alone. Relative words such as jo or jehro (who, which) and time words such as jadhen (when) often introduce the dependent clause. For example, the illustrative sentence Chhokro jehro mehnat kare tho, so kamyab thindo (The boy who works hard will succeed) has a main idea about success and a dependent clause describing which boy. The dependent clause adds meaning, but on its own it would leave the reader asking who succeeds.

Complex sentences let writers explain causes, conditions and descriptions without breaking the flow into many short sentences. They also carry a risk: if the dependent clause is placed badly or the relative word points to the wrong ism, the sentence becomes confusing. Build complex sentences slowly, starting from the main clause, then adding one dependent clause at a time. Read the whole sentence aloud and check that the main idea is still clear and that the dependent clause points to the right word. One well-built complex sentence per paragraph is usually enough for school writing; the rest can be simple or compound.

diagram.alt: From Simple to Complex: Building Longer Sentences
diagram.caption: Build sentences in stages so each longer form stays clear and correct.

sections.h2: Choosing the Right Kind for Your Writing
paras: Good writers do not use one kind of sentence for everything; they mix kinds to match their purpose. Simple sentences work best for instructions, facts and strong statements. Compound sentences work well for listing related actions, showing contrast, or offering choices. Complex sentences work best for explanations, reasons and descriptions that need extra detail. A paragraph that mixes all three kinds feels natural and mature, while a paragraph of only one kind feels flat or exhausting. When revising, read your paragraph aloud and notice whether the rhythm changes; if every sentence feels the same length, try joining two short ones or splitting one long one.

In exams, variety matters, but correctness matters more. Never write a complex sentence you cannot control just to impress the examiner; a correct simple sentence earns more marks than a tangled complex one. A safe plan is to write most sentences as simple or compound, and to include one or two careful complex sentences where explanation is genuinely needed. After writing, check each sentence for a subject and fail, check each conjunction for the right relationship, and check each dependent clause for a clear reference. More study help is available on the [blog](/blog/) and the [home page](/).

A simple jumla has one main idea with one subject and one fail.
A compound jumla joins two equal ideas with ain, par or ya.
A complex jumla adds a dependent clause to a main clause.
Mix sentence kinds for natural rhythm, but never sacrifice correctness for length.

faqs.q: What is a jumla in Sindhi grammar?
faqs.a: A jumla is a group of words that makes complete sense on its own. It usually has a subject, such as an ism or zamir, and a fail that says what the subject does or what state it is in. Chhokro parhi tho is a jumla, but Parhi tho alone is not, because the reader does not know who is reading.

faqs.q: How is a compound jumla different from a complex jumla?
faqs.a: In a compound jumla, two ideas of equal importance are joined, and each could stand alone as a simple sentence. In a complex jumla, one main clause stands alone while a dependent clause adds information but cannot stand alone. The test is to cover each part in turn and ask whether it makes complete sense by itself.

faqs.q: Which conjunctions join compound sentences in Sindhi?
faqs.a: The most common are ain (and) for adding, par (but) for contrast, and ya (or) for choice. Choose the conjunction that matches the relationship between the ideas. Joining two unrelated ideas with ain, or using par where no contrast exists, confuses the reader even when both parts are grammatically correct.

faqs.q: What introduces a dependent clause in a complex sentence?
faqs.a: Relative words such as jo or jehro (who, which, that) and time words such as jadhen (when) often introduce dependent clauses. For example, in Chhokro jehro mehnat kare tho, so kamyab thindo, jehro introduces the clause describing which boy. Check that the relative word points to the right ism in the main clause.

faqs.q: How many complex sentences should I use in an exam answer?
faqs.a: One or two careful complex sentences per paragraph is usually enough. Most of your writing can be simple or compound sentences, which are easier to keep correct. A correct simple sentence always earns more marks than a tangled complex sentence, so build complex sentences slowly and read them aloud before submitting your work.

title: Sindhi Grammar: Wahid and Jama Rules
desc: Master Sindhi wahid and jama: singular to plural rules, common patterns, irregular plurals and agreement tips with clear examples for students.
intro: Sindhi grammar wahid and jama rules decide whether a word refers to one thing or to more than one, and getting them right changes the whole sentence. Wahid means singular, one person, place or thing, while jama means plural, more than one. In Sindhi, changing a noun from wahid to jama often changes its ending, and the verb, sifat and zamir in the sentence must change to match. This guide explains the most common singular-to-plural patterns, the irregular forms students meet most, and the agreement checks that keep sentences correct. All Sindhi examples are illustrative, given in Roman transliteration, so you can practise the patterns without memorising whole lists blindly.

sections.h2: Wahid and Jama: The Basic Idea
paras: Wahid refers to one item, such as hik kitab (one book) or hik chhokro (one boy). Jama refers to more than one, such as be kitaba (two books) or ghanan chhokra (many boys). The change from wahid to jama is not just about the noun itself: in a correct sentence, the verb and any describing words must also agree with the new number. For example, the illustrative pair Chhokro parhi tho (The boy is reading) and Chhokra parhin tha (The boys are reading) shows the noun, the verb form and the overall pattern changing together. Students who change only the noun often produce sentences that sound wrong to a Sindhi reader.

Number also interacts with gender, because muzakkar and muannas nouns may form their plurals differently. That is why grammar lessons teach wahid and jama alongside gender: the two systems work together in every sentence. A practical starting habit is to learn each new ism in a pair, wahid and jama together, rather than learning the singular alone and guessing the plural later. Write the pair in your notebook, add one example sentence for each form, and revise the pairs weekly. This small habit prevents a large number of agreement errors in composition and translation exercises.

Many Sindhi nouns form their jama by changing or adding an ending, and recognising the pattern makes new words easier. One common pattern changes a final vowel, so a noun ending in a certain sound takes a different ending in the plural. Another pattern adds a plural marker to the stem, keeping the base word recognisable. A third pattern changes an internal vowel or uses a form borrowed from Arabic or Persian patterns, which students meet in more formal vocabulary. Rather than memorising a rule for every word, learn the pattern groups with three examples each, and then sort new words into the group they resemble.

Counting words also help signal jama: be (two), teen (three) and ghanan (many) almost always appear with plural nouns, and they give the reader an early clue about number. When you read, underline the noun and its number word together, and notice the verb form that follows. When you write, decide the number before you choose the verb: if the subject is jama, the verb must be jama too. Teachers often mark number agreement first because it is easy to check and because it affects the whole sentence. Keep a list of pattern groups in the back of your notebook and add each new plural you meet to the group. For more material, see the [book list](/books.html) and [solved notes](/solved.html).
bullets: Pattern 1: final vowel change in the noun ending
Pattern 2: plural marker added to the noun stem
Pattern 3: internal vowel change or borrowed plural form
Number words like be, teen and ghanan signal a plural noun

sections.h2: Irregular Plurals and Words That Stay the Same
paras: Not every noun follows a neat pattern, and irregular plurals are where students need extra care. Some nouns have a plural form that looks quite different from the singular, often because the word came from Arabic or Persian with its own plural system. Others are collective or uncountable, such as pani (water) or khorak (food), and they do not take a normal plural because they name a substance rather than countable items. A third group stays the same in form for singular and plural, and only the verb or number word shows whether one or many is meant. These exceptions cannot be guessed reliably, so they must be learned as pairs.

The best approach to irregular forms is to collect them deliberately instead of hoping to absorb them by chance. Keep a separate page titled irregular plurals, and write each pair with a short example sentence in both forms. Revise that page more often than the regular patterns, because irregular forms are forgotten fastest. In exams, if you are unsure of a plural, choose a different noun you know well rather than guessing a form that may be wrong. Examiners reward correct, confident vocabulary more than risky guesses, and a safe word used correctly always beats an impressive word used incorrectly.

sections.h2: Agreement: Making the Whole Sentence Match
paras: Agreement means that the noun, sifat, zamir and fail in a sentence all match in number, and often in gender as well. If the subject is jama, the verb must be jama, the sifat describing it must be jama, and any zamir referring back to it must be plural too. For example, the illustrative sentence Sutha chhokra parhin tha (The good boys are reading) keeps sifat, noun and verb all plural. Change one part back to singular and the sentence breaks: a careful reader notices the mismatch immediately, even if the meaning is still understandable. Agreement is therefore a matter of correctness, not just style.

A reliable revision check is to read each sentence and ask, one by one, whether the subject is wahid or jama, and then whether every related word matches that answer. Circle the subject, draw lines to the sifat, verb and zamir that belong to it, and check each line for agreement. This check takes only a minute per paragraph, but it catches errors that spellcheckers and quick rereads miss. Students who do this check before submitting work consistently score higher on grammar, because number agreement is one of the first things a marker notices. Practise the check on old compositions as well as new ones. More tips are on the [blog](/blog/) and the [home page](/).

diagram.alt: From Wahid to a Correct Jama Sentence
diagram.caption: Follow these steps whenever you change a sentence from singular to plural.

sections.h2: Practice Plan for Wahid and Jama Mastery
paras: A short daily practice plan works better than one long cramming session for wahid and jama. Each day, choose ten nouns from your lesson, write their jama forms, and then write one sentence using each plural correctly. On the second day, return to the same ten words without looking, and write new sentences with them. On the third day, mix those words with ten new ones, so that older forms stay fresh while new ones are added. This spaced repetition mirrors how memory actually works, and it turns plural patterns from a list to be memorised into a skill you can use under exam pressure.

Pair work also helps: one student says a wahid sentence and the partner must convert the whole sentence to jama, changing noun, sifat and verb together. The first student checks every change, and the pair swaps roles after five sentences. This game exposes the common mistake of changing only the noun, because the partner must catch it to score a point. Keep a record of words your class finds hardest, and revise those words most often. Within a few weeks, most students find that plural agreement becomes a habit rather than a calculation, and their writing gains a noticeable smoothness and confidence.

Changing a noun to jama usually requires changing its verb and sifat too.
Common plural patterns include ending changes, added markers and internal vowel changes.
Irregular and uncountable nouns must be learned as pairs, not guessed.
Check every sentence for number agreement before submitting written work.

faqs.q: What is the difference between wahid and jama?
faqs.a: Wahid means singular, one person, place or thing, such as hik kitab. Jama means plural, more than one, such as be kitaba. The difference matters because the verb, sifat and zamir in the sentence must match the number of the subject. A sentence with a plural subject but a singular verb sounds wrong to a Sindhi reader.

faqs.q: How do I know the plural form of a new Sindhi word?
faqs.a: First, look for the pattern group the word belongs to, such as an ending change or an added plural marker. Then check whether the word is irregular or uncountable, in which case the plural must be learned as a pair. Learn each new noun with its plural in your notebook, and use number words like be or ghanan as clues when you read.

faqs.q: Why does my verb change when the noun becomes plural?
faqs.a: Because Sindhi verbs agree with their subjects in number. A singular subject takes a singular verb form, and a plural subject takes a plural verb form. In Chhokro parhi tho and Chhokra parhin tha, both the noun and the verb change. Changing only the noun leaves a mismatch that markers notice immediately.

faqs.q: Are there Sindhi nouns with no normal plural?
faqs.a: Yes, uncountable nouns naming substances, such as pani (water), do not take a normal plural because they are not counted as separate items. Some nouns also keep the same form for singular and plural, with only the verb or number word showing the difference. Learn these words individually and use quantity words like thoro or ghanan with them instead of a plural ending.

faqs.q: What is the fastest way to improve plural agreement?
faqs.a: Practise ten nouns a day in wahid and jama pairs, write a sentence for each plural, and revise the same words over three days. Then use the circle-and-check method: circle the subject in each sentence and check that its sifat, verb and zamir all match in number. Pair work, where a partner converts your singular sentences to plural, also catches the habit of changing only the noun.

title: Sindhi Grammar: Muzakkar and Muannas
desc: Learn Sindhi muzakkar and muannas: gender rules, how to identify masculine and feminine nouns, agreement, and words that break the usual rules.
intro: Sindhi grammar muzakkar and muannas rules tell us whether a noun is treated as masculine or feminine, and that choice affects verbs, sifat words and zamir words throughout the sentence. Muzakkar means masculine gender and muannas means feminine gender in Sindhi grammar. For people and animals, gender often follows natural sex, but for things and ideas, gender is grammatical: a book, a table or a feeling is muzakkar or muannas by convention, not by nature. This guide explains how to identify gender, how agreement works, and which common words break the patterns students expect in everyday classroom writing. All Sindhi examples are illustrative, given in Roman transliteration for easy practice.

sections.h2: Muzakkar and Muannas: What Gender Means in Grammar
paras: In Sindhi grammar, every ism belongs to one of two genders: muzakkar (masculine) or muannas (feminine). For living beings, the gender usually matches the being itself: chhokro (boy) is muzakkar and chhokri (girl) is muannas. For non-living things, gender is a property of the word, learned with the word itself: kitab (book) is muannas in Sindhi usage, while qalam (pen) is muzakkar. There is no physical reason why one object is masculine and another feminine; the language simply assigns each noun a gender, and speakers must learn the assignment along with the meaning.

Gender matters because it controls agreement across the sentence. A muzakkar subject takes a muzakkar verb form and muzakkar sifat forms, while a muannas subject takes muannas forms. For example, the illustrative pair Chhokro sutho aahe (The boy is good) and Chhokri suthi aahe (The girl is good) shows the sifat changing from sutho to suthi to match the subject. Students who ignore gender produce sentences that are understandable but clearly incorrect, and examiners mark gender agreement closely. Learn each new noun with its gender, just as you learn its plural, and gender errors will fall sharply.

Although gender must ultimately be learned word by word, several clues help students guess correctly more often. Nouns ending in certain vowels are more likely to be muannas, while nouns ending in other sounds are more likely to be muzakkar, and these tendencies cover a large share of everyday vocabulary. Words borrowed from Arabic or Persian often keep the gender they had in the source language, which creates another pattern for formal words. Words naming male people and male animals are muzakkar, and words naming female people and female animals are muannas, which is the most reliable clue of all for living beings.

Clues are tendencies, not guarantees, and that is why they must be used with a dictionary or teacher check, not as a substitute for learning. A student who relies only on endings will still meet exceptions, especially among common household words and abstract ideas. A practical method is to note the clue beside each new word in your notebook, such as ending pattern or source language, and then confirm the gender with your teacher. Over time, the clues become a useful first guess, and the confirmed list in your notebook becomes the reliable record. For more solved material, see the [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [book list](/books.html).
bullets: People and animals: gender usually follows natural sex
Word endings: certain final vowels lean muzakkar or muannas
Borrowed words: Arabic and Persian words often keep source gender
Always confirm: clues guide a guess, they do not replace learning

paras: Gender agreement works like number agreement: once the subject's gender is known, the sifat, fail and zamir that belong to it must match. In the illustrative sentence Suthi kitab mez te aahe (The good book is on the table), the sifat suthi and the verb form match the muannas noun kitab. If the subject were a muzakkar noun, the sifat and verb forms would change accordingly. Zamir words referring back to the subject must also match: a muannas subject is referred to with muannas pronoun forms in later sentences, and the same holds for muzakkar subjects. Agreement is checked as a whole, not word by word in isolation.

A common error is to match the verb to the nearest noun instead of to the real subject. For example, in a sentence where a harf phrase sits between the subject and the verb, the verb must still agree with the subject, not with the noun inside the harf phrase. To avoid this, find the subject first, cover the middle of the sentence with your finger, and then choose the verb form. Then uncover the sentence and check the sifat and zamir as well. This subject-first method is simple, but it prevents a large share of gender errors in longer sentences, where the nearest noun is often a trap.

sections.h2: Words That Break the Rules Students Expect
paras: Every language has words that surprise learners, and Sindhi gender has its share. Some words look muzakkar by their ending but are treated as muannas, and some look muannas but are treated as muzakkar. Some words naming professions or roles have both a muzakkar and a muannas form, such as ustad and ustani, and students must learn the pair rather than using one form for both. Other words, especially abstract ideas like mohabbat (love) or himmat (courage), have a fixed gender that cannot be guessed from meaning, because ideas have no natural sex at all.

The right response to rule-breakers is to collect them, not to argue with them. Keep a page in your notebook titled gender surprises, and write each surprising word with its gender and one example sentence. Revise that page before tests, because examiners often choose exactly these words to test whether students have learned real usage rather than just rules. When you meet a new word whose gender surprises you, add it to the page the same day, while the surprise is fresh. Over a term, this page becomes a personal dictionary of the hardest words, and it is far more valuable than a generic rule list. More guidance is on the [blog](/blog/) and the [home page](/).

diagram.alt: How Gender Spreads Through a Sentence
diagram.caption: The subject's gender controls the forms of the words that belong to it.

paras: Gender confidence comes from daily contact with nouns in full sentences, not from reading a rule once. Each day, take ten nouns from your lesson, write muzakkar or muannas beside each one, and write a sentence for each noun that includes a sifat and a verb. The sentence forces you to use the gender, which is the only way to test whether you really know it. If you only write the label without a sentence, you may recognise the gender on a list but still fail to use it correctly in writing, which is where marks are actually earned.

A second exercise is gender swapping: take a correct sentence with a muzakkar subject, replace the subject with a muannas noun of similar meaning, and change every agreeing word to match. For example, change a sentence about a boy to a sentence about a girl, changing sifat, verb and zamir as needed. This exercise makes agreement visible, because every word that must change stands out. Ask a partner to check your swapped sentence, and keep a list of the words you most often forget to change. With steady practice, gender agreement becomes a habit, and your Sindhi writing will read as natural and correct.

points: Muzakkar means masculine gender and muannas means feminine gender in Sindhi grammar.
For things and ideas, gender is grammatical convention, not natural sex.
Word endings and source language give useful clues but never guarantee gender.
Sifat, fail and zamir must all agree with the subject's gender.
Collect surprising words in a personal list and revise them before tests.

faqs.q: How do I know if a Sindhi noun is muzakkar or muannas?
faqs.a: For people and animals, gender usually follows natural sex. For things and ideas, gender is a property of the word that must be learned with the word itself. Word endings and source language give useful clues, but the reliable method is to learn each noun with its gender in your notebook and confirm doubtful words with your teacher or dictionary.

faqs.q: Why does gender change the verb in a sentence?
faqs.a: Because Sindhi verbs agree with their subjects in gender as well as number. A muzakkar subject takes a muzakkar verb form and a muannas subject takes a muannas form. If the verb does not match the subject, the sentence sounds incorrect even when the meaning is clear, so markers check gender agreement closely.

faqs.q: Do sifat words change for gender too?
faqs.a: Yes, sifat words describing a noun usually change to match that noun's gender. For example, sutho is used with a muzakkar noun and suthi with a muannas noun in the illustrative pair about a good boy and a good girl. Always check the noun first, then choose the sifat form that matches it.

faqs.q: What should I do with a word whose gender surprises me?
faqs.a: Write it on a special page for gender surprises, with its correct gender and one example sentence. Revise that page before tests, because examiners often choose surprising words. Do not try to force the word to follow the pattern you expected; learn its real usage and use it confidently from then on.

faqs.q: Can one profession word have both genders?
faqs.a: Yes, many role words have a muzakkar form and a muannas form, such as ustad and ustani. Learn the pair together and use the form that matches the person described. Using the muzakkar form for a female teacher, or the reverse, is a gender agreement error even when the rest of the sentence is correct.

title: Sindhi Grammar: Fail and Tense Forms
desc: Learn Sindhi fail tense forms: past, present and future verb tables, how tense changes verb endings, and tips for choosing the right tense.
intro: Sindhi grammar fail tense forms show when an action happens: in the past, in the present, or in the future. The fail is the action word of the sentence, and its form changes with time, with the subject's gender and number, and sometimes with the kind of sentence. Students who master tense can tell a story in order, describe daily routines, and make plans clearly and confidently, while students who mix tenses confuse the reader about when events happened. This guide explains past, present and future forms with illustrative Sindhi verb examples in Roman transliteration, shows how tables help you learn them, and gives practice methods that make tense choice automatic.

sections.h2: What Tense Means for a Fail
paras: Tense is the part of grammar that places an action in time. Present tense describes actions happening now or happening regularly, such as Maan parhan tho (I am reading) or Maan roz parhan tho (I read every day). Past tense describes actions already finished, such as Maan parhiyo (I read, past). Future tense describes actions not yet done, such as Maan parhandus (I will read). The same fail, parhan (to read), appears in three different forms, and the reader learns the time of the action from the form alone, without needing extra words like yesterday or tomorrow, although those words often help.

Tense also works together with gender and number, so a complete verb form carries several pieces of information at once: what the action is, when it happens, and who is doing it. That is why verb tables are so useful: a table shows one fail across persons, genders, numbers and tenses, so students can see the whole system instead of memorising isolated forms. When you meet a new fail, do not learn only its present form; learn its past and future forms in the same session, and write one sentence for each tense. This triple learning prevents the common problem of knowing a verb in one tense only.

sections.h2: Present Tense: Now and Every Day
paras: Present tense covers two related uses: actions happening right now and actions that happen regularly. The illustrative sentence Chhokro parhi tho (The boy is reading) describes an action in progress at this moment. The sentence Chhokro roz parhi tho (The boy reads every day) uses a similar form but adds roz (every day) to show a habit. Students should notice that the time word changes the meaning from a single moment to a routine, even when the verb form looks similar. Context and time words therefore matter as much as the verb form itself.

A frequent present-tense mistake is using a present form for a finished action, which makes a story sound as if everything is happening now. Another mistake is forgetting agreement: a present verb must still match its subject in gender and number, so a muannas subject and a plural subject need different forms from a muzakkar singular subject. Practise present tense by writing a diary paragraph about today, using only present forms, and then underlining each verb and its subject to check agreement. For more solved material, see the [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [book list](/books.html).
bullets: Action now: Chhokro parhi tho (The boy is reading)
Daily habit: Chhokro roz parhi tho (The boy reads every day)
Always check gender and number agreement in present forms
Time words like roz, aj and hane clarify present meaning

paras: Past tense describes actions that are complete, and Sindhi past forms often look quite different from present forms. The illustrative sentence Chhokro kitab parhi (The boy read the book) places the action firmly in the past, while Chhokri kitab parhi (The girl read the book) shows how gender can affect the past form. Past tense is the backbone of storytelling: once a story moves into the past, most of its verbs should stay in the past unless a character speaks in the present or a habit is described. Mixing past and present without reason is one of the most noticeable errors in student stories.

To learn past forms, practise with a timeline: write five things you did yesterday, in order, using past verbs only. Then write five things you did last week, and notice whether the same verbs keep the same past forms. Some verbs are regular in the past, following a clear pattern, while others are irregular and must be learned individually. Keep a list of irregular past forms in your notebook, with the present form beside each one, and revise that list weekly. Storytelling practice, even a short paragraph a day, teaches past tense faster than memorising tables alone, because the forms are used for a real purpose.

Future tense describes actions that will happen, including plans, promises, predictions and intentions. The illustrative sentence Maan subhane school wendus (I will go to school tomorrow) combines a future verb form with the time word subhane (tomorrow) to make the timing unmistakable. Future forms are also used for offers and requests in polite speech, such as asking whether someone will help. Students should practise future tense by writing plans for tomorrow, next week and next year, because each plan naturally needs a future verb and a time word together.

A common future-tense error is using a present form for a future plan without a time word, leaving the reader unsure whether the action is happening now or later. Always pair a future intention with either a future verb form or a clear time word, and preferably both in school writing. Another error is promising in the future tense but describing the steps in the present tense without signalling the change, which breaks the timeline. Before submitting a paragraph about plans, underline every verb, label its tense, and check that the timeline moves in a sensible order from now to later. More help is available on the [blog](/blog/) and the [home page](/).

diagram.alt: Past, Present and Future on a Timeline
diagram.caption: Place each verb form on the timeline to check that your story stays in order.

sections.h2: Using Verb Tables Without Memorising Blindly
paras: Verb tables look intimidating, but they are simply a map of one fail across persons, genders, numbers and tenses. Read a table row by row, not all at once: first learn the three tenses for maan (I), then for tuhin and tawhaan (you), then for hu (he or she), and so on. Say each form aloud as you write it, because hearing the ending helps memory far more than silent copying. After studying a row, cover the table and write the forms from memory, then check and correct only the forms you missed. This cover-and-recall method beats copying the whole table five times.

Tables should also be used for checking, not just for learning. When you write a paragraph, keep the table for your main verbs open beside you, and check each verb form against it before submitting. Over time, you will need the table less and less, because the forms you use most often will become automatic. Do not try to learn ten verbs at once; master one common fail fully, including all three tenses and both genders, before adding the next. Depth with a few verbs builds a pattern sense that transfers to new verbs, while shallow knowledge of many verbs fades quickly under exam pressure.

For this topic, ask it to show one verb in past, present and future forms with new examples, then try writing your own sentences in each tense before checking its answers.

points: Tense places a fail in the past, present or future.
Present tense covers actions happening now and regular habits.
Past tense describes finished actions and carries most storytelling.
Future tense covers plans, promises, predictions and intentions.
Verb tables work best when studied row by row with cover-and-recall practice.

faqs.q: How do I choose between past, present and future tense?
faqs.a: Ask when the action happens. If it is already finished, use past tense. If it is happening now or happens regularly, use present tense. If it has not happened yet, use future tense. Time words like kal (yesterday), aj (today) and subhane (tomorrow) help, but the verb form itself should also show the tense clearly.

faqs.q: Why does the same verb look different in each tense?
faqs.a: Because Sindhi verb forms change their endings to show time, and they also agree with the subject in gender and number. The base meaning stays the same, but the form carries extra information about when and by whom the action is done. Verb tables show these changes systematically for each person, gender and number.

faqs.q: What is the most common tense mistake in stories?
faqs.a: Mixing past and present without reason is the most common mistake. Once a story moves into the past, most verbs should stay in the past unless a character speaks in the present or a habit is described. Before submitting a story, underline every verb, label its tense, and fix any verb that breaks the timeline without a good reason.

faqs.q: How should I use a verb table for revision?
faqs.a: Study one row at a time, starting with maan, then tuhin and tawhaan, then hu. Say each form aloud, cover the table, write the forms from memory, and correct only the ones you missed. Use the table to check your writing as well, keeping it open beside your paragraph until the most common forms become automatic.

faqs.q: Are some past forms irregular in Sindhi?
faqs.a: Yes, some verbs have past forms that do not follow the regular pattern and must be learned individually. Keep a list of irregular past forms with their present forms beside them, and revise that list weekly. In exams, prefer a verb whose past form you know confidently over a verb whose past form you would have to guess.

title: Sindhi Grammar: Murakkab Jumle Made Easy
desc: Learn Sindhi murakkab jumle: joining sentences with conjunctions correctly, choosing ain, par, ya and jo, and avoiding run-on sentences.
intro: Sindhi grammar murakkab jumle are sentences made by joining two or more simpler sentences into one longer, connected sentence. Murakkab means compound or joined, and these sentences let writers show relationships between ideas: adding information, showing contrast, offering a choice, or explaining a cause. Students often write only short simple sentences because longer ones feel risky, but murakkab jumle, used carefully, make writing sound mature and connected. This guide explains the main conjunctions for joining sentences, shows how to choose the right one, and warns against the run-on sentences that lose marks for classwork, homework and exams in Sindhi. All Sindhi examples are illustrative, given in Roman transliteration for practice.

paras: A murakkab jumla joins two clauses, each of which could often stand alone, into a single sentence with a conjunction or a relative word. For example, the illustrative sentence Ali parhi tho ain Ahmed likhi tho (Ali is reading and Ahmed is writing) joins two simple sentences with ain (and). The result is one sentence with two subjects and two verbs, but the reader can still see both ideas clearly. Murakkab jumle are different from simple jumle, which carry one idea, and they are the natural next step once simple sentences feel comfortable.

The purpose of joining is not to make sentences longer for its own sake, but to show how ideas relate. Joining with ain shows addition, joining with par shows contrast, joining with ya shows choice, and joining with jo or jehro adds a description. A writer who joins sentences thoughtfully guides the reader through the logic of a paragraph, while a writer who joins randomly only creates confusion. Before joining two sentences, always ask what relationship exists between them, and choose the joining word that names that relationship exactly. For more solved material, see the [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [book list](/books.html).

The most used joining words are ain (and) for adding and par (but) for contrasting. Ain joins ideas that belong together: Ali school wanji tho ain sabak parhi tho (Ali goes to school and studies his lesson). Par joins ideas that pull in different directions: Ali mehnat kare tho par kamyab na thiyo (Ali works hard but did not succeed). The difference matters, because swapping ain and par changes the logic of the sentence even when both parts are correct. Students should practise pairs of sentences where only the conjunction changes, and explain how the meaning changes with each choice.

Other useful conjunctions include ya (or) for choice, je (if) for condition, and chho jo (because) for cause. Each one answers a different question: ya asks which option, je asks under what condition, and chho jo asks why. A paragraph that uses only ain sounds flat, because every relationship is presented as addition, even when contrast or cause is meant. Varying conjunctions, but only where the meaning genuinely calls for variety, is a mark of mature writing. Keep a list of conjunctions with one example sentence each, and check your list before writing a long composition. More tips are on the [blog](/blog/) and the [home page](/).
bullets: Ain (and): adds a related idea to the first one
Par (but): shows contrast or an unexpected result
Ya (or): offers a choice between two ideas
Chho jo (because): gives the reason for the first idea

sections.h2: Joining With Jo, Jehro and Jadhen
paras: Relative and time words also create murakkab jumle, but they work differently from ain and par. Words like jo and jehro (who, which, that) attach a describing clause to a noun, as in Kitab jo maan parhi, so suthi aahe (The book which I read is good). The describing clause cannot stand alone, so the whole sentence is complex as well as compound in the broad sense of joined. Time words like jadhen (when) attach a clause that says when something happens, as in Jadhen ustad aayo, shagird khara thi waya (When the teacher came, the students stood up). These joining words add detail without adding a second equal idea.

The danger with jo, jehro and jadhen is placing the clause so that it points to the wrong word. In a long sentence, a relative clause should sit as close as possible to the noun it describes, or the reader may attach it to a nearer noun by mistake. A safe method is to build the sentence in two steps: write the main sentence first, then insert the describing clause right after the noun it describes, and read the result aloud. If the sentence still sounds clear, keep it; if it sounds tangled, split it back into two sentences and try again. Clarity always beats length in school writing.

A run-on sentence joins two ideas without any conjunction or punctuation, leaving the reader to guess where one idea ends and the next begins. For example, writing Ali parhi tho Ahmed likhi tho without ain or a full stop is a run-on, even though both parts are correct on their own. The fix is simple: add a conjunction, add a full stop and start a new sentence, or use a semicolon-like pause if your teacher allows it. Students should check every long sentence in their work for a joining word, and split any sentence that has two subjects and two verbs but no conjunction.

Tangled sentences are the opposite problem: too many clauses joined in a chain, so the reader loses track of the main idea. A sentence with three or four conjunctions usually needs splitting into two sentences, even if it is grammatically correct. A practical limit for school writing is two clauses per sentence in most cases, with an occasional third clause only when the relationship is very clear. After writing, read each sentence aloud in one breath: if you run out of breath or lose the thread, split the sentence. Short, joined sentences that the reader can follow always earn more marks than impressive sentences that confuse.

diagram.caption: Ask what relationship links the two ideas, then pick the conjunction that names it.

sections.h2: Practice: From Simple Sentences to Murakkab Jumle
paras: The best practice for murakkab jumle starts with simple sentences you already know. Write five pairs of simple sentences on the same topic, such as your school day or a story you read. Then join each pair once with ain, once with par, and once with ya, and note which joining makes sense and which sounds wrong. This exercise teaches that conjunction choice is a meaning choice, not a decoration: the same two facts can add, contrast or offer a choice depending on the word you choose. Discuss your joined sentences with a partner, and defend each conjunction choice in one sentence.

A second exercise is editing a paragraph: take a paragraph written only in simple sentences, and join two or three pairs where the relationship is genuinely addition, contrast or cause. Leave the other sentences simple, so the paragraph gains variety without becoming tangled. Then read the edited paragraph aloud and ask whether every joined sentence is clearer than the two separate sentences were. If a joined sentence is not clearer, undo it. This editing habit is exactly what good writers do, and it teaches murakkab jumle as a tool for clarity rather than as a trick for length.

Remember to verify against your Sindh Textbook Board book before using any explanation in classwork or exams.

points: A murakkab jumla joins two or more clauses into one connected sentence.
Ain adds, par contrasts, ya offers a choice, and chho jo gives a reason.
Jo, jehro and jadhen attach describing or time clauses to a main sentence.
A run-on sentence joins ideas without a conjunction or full stop.
Split any joined sentence that sounds tangled when read aloud.

faqs.q: What is a murakkab jumla in simple words?
faqs.a: A murakkab jumla is a joined sentence made from two or more simpler sentences or clauses. For example, Ali parhi tho ain Ahmed likhi tho joins two simple sentences with ain. The joined sentence shows how the ideas relate, such as addition, contrast, choice or cause, instead of leaving them as separate statements.

faqs.q: How do I choose between ain and par?
faqs.a: Use ain when the second idea adds to the first, and par when the second idea contrasts with it or gives an unexpected result. Test by swapping the conjunctions and noticing how the meaning changes. If the second idea is surprising after the first, par is usually right; if it simply continues the first, ain is right.

faqs.q: What is a run-on sentence and how do I fix it?
faqs.a: A run-on sentence joins two complete ideas without a conjunction or punctuation, such as Ali parhi tho Ahmed likhi tho. Fix it by adding a conjunction like ain, or by adding a full stop and starting a new sentence. Check every long sentence for a joining word, and split any sentence with two subjects and verbs but no conjunction.

faqs.q: When should I use jo or jehro instead of ain?
faqs.a: Use jo or jehro when you want to describe a noun with extra information, not when you want to add an equal idea. In Kitab jo maan parhi, so suthi aahe, the clause describes which book is meant. Use ain when the second idea is equal in importance and could stand alone as its own sentence.

faqs.q: How long should a murakkab jumla be in school writing?
faqs.a: Two clauses per sentence is a safe limit for most school writing, with an occasional third clause only when the relationship is very clear. If a sentence has three or four conjunctions, it usually needs splitting. Read the sentence aloud in one breath: if you lose the thread, split it into two clear sentences.

title: Sindhi Grammar: Tashkeel-e-Alfaaz (Word Formation)
desc: Learn Sindhi tashkeel-e-alfaaz: word formation with prefixes, suffixes and root words, how new words are built, and how to guess meanings.
intro: Sindhi grammar tashkeel-e-alfaaz is the study of how words are formed, and it explains why so many Sindhi words look like families sharing a common root. A root word carries the core meaning, a prefix is added at the beginning to change or refine that meaning, and a suffix is added at the end to change the word's job or shade of meaning. Once students recognise roots, prefixes and suffixes, they can guess the meaning of unfamiliar words, spell new words more accurately, and build their vocabulary far faster than by memorising isolated words. This guide explains word formation with illustrative Sindhi examples in Roman transliteration and practical exercises for the classroom.

sections.h2: Root Words: The Core of a Word Family
paras: A root word is the smallest meaningful part of a word, carrying its core idea. For example, the root parh relates to reading, and it appears in parhan (to read), parhae (teaching, as a verb form) and parhaee (study or reading, as a noun idea) in illustrative usage. Recognising the root lets a student see that these words are related, even when their endings differ. Root words are the anchor of vocabulary learning: instead of memorising ten separate words, a student can learn one root and understand the family that grows from it, which saves time and builds confidence with unfamiliar texts.

Roots also help with spelling, because the root usually keeps its shape while prefixes and suffixes change around it. When a student is unsure how to spell a long word, breaking it into root plus affixes often reveals the correct spelling of each part. Practise by choosing five common roots from your lessons, such as likh for writing, parh for reading, and kha for eating, and listing every word you know that contains each root. Compare lists with classmates, and notice how many words share a root. This root-first habit turns vocabulary revision from random memorisation into organised family learning.

sections.h2: Prefixes: Meaning Added at the Beginning
paras: A prefix is a small part added before a root to change or refine its meaning. In Sindhi, prefixes borrowed from Persian and Arabic are common, such as be- for without or lack of, as in be-waqoof used illustratively for a lack of sense, and na- for not, as in na-mumkin (impossible). Other prefixes add ideas like again, together, or against, depending on the root they join. A prefix does not usually change the word's class on its own; it shades the meaning, often turning a positive idea negative or adding a sense of absence, repetition or opposition.

Students should learn prefixes as meaning units, not as random letters. When you meet an unfamiliar word, check whether it begins with a known prefix, remove that prefix mentally, and see whether the remaining root is familiar. If the root is familiar, the prefix will often explain the new meaning: be- plus a quality often means without that quality, and na- plus a possibility often means not possible. Keep a prefix table with three examples for each prefix, and add new examples as you meet them. This guessing skill is especially useful in reading comprehension, where unfamiliar words appear in context and must be understood quickly. For more material, see the [book list](/books.html) and [solved notes](/solved.html).
bullets: Be-: often means without or lacking, as in be-waqoof
Na-: often means not, as in na-mumkin (impossible)
Prefixes shade meaning; they rarely change word class alone
Strip a known prefix to reveal a familiar root underneath

sections.h2: Suffixes: Meaning and Job Added at the End
paras: A suffix is a part added after a root, and it can change both meaning and grammatical job. For example, adding a suffix to a verb root can turn an action into a person who does it, a place where it happens, or an abstract idea. Illustrative patterns include forming a doer word from an action root, or forming an abstract noun from a quality word, such as turning a description of goodness into the idea of goodness itself. Suffixes also mark gender, number and tense in Sindhi, so the same root with different suffixes can appear as a verb, a noun or a describing word in different sentences.

Because suffixes do so much work, they are a common source of spelling and agreement errors. A student who adds the wrong suffix may produce a word that looks close to correct but belongs to the wrong class or gender. The remedy is to learn suffixes in pairs with their function: this suffix makes a person, that suffix makes a place, this suffix makes an abstract idea. Practise by taking five roots and adding a different suffix to each, then writing a sentence that shows the new word's job. If the sentence does not work, the suffix choice is probably wrong, and the exercise itself teaches the correction.

sections.h2: Compound Words: Two Roots Joined Together
paras: Compound words join two roots or two full words into one new word with a combined meaning. Sindhi, like many languages, builds compounds for everyday ideas, such as joining a word for school with a word for book, or a word for day with a word for time, to name a familiar object or occasion. The meaning of a compound is often close to the sum of its parts, but sometimes it becomes a fixed expression with a special meaning that cannot be guessed from the parts alone. Students should therefore treat compounds as vocabulary to learn, while still using the parts as a first clue to meaning.

Compounds also teach spelling discipline, because the two parts keep their own shapes when joined, and a missing or doubled letter changes the word. When writing a compound, write each part separately first, check its spelling, and then join them carefully. When reading a compound, split it into its parts and ask what each part contributes to the whole meaning. This split-and-join exercise is excellent pair work: one student says a compound, the partner splits it and explains both parts, and the pair checks whether the combined meaning matches the dictionary meaning. More guidance is available on the [blog](/blog/) and the [home page](/).

diagram.alt: How a Sindhi Word Is Built
diagram.caption: A complete word can combine a prefix, a root and a suffix around its core meaning.

sections.h2: Using Word Formation to Guess Unknown Words
paras: Word formation is most valuable when you meet a word you have never seen before in a reading passage. Instead of stopping or guessing wildly, break the word into prefix, root and suffix, recall the meaning of each part, and combine them into a sensible guess. Then check your guess against the sentence: does it fit the subject, the verb and the overall topic? If it fits, you have probably understood the word well enough to continue reading. If it does not fit, try a different split, because some words can be divided in more than one way, and only one division matches the context.

This guessing method should be practised deliberately, not only used in emergencies. Each week, choose five unfamiliar words from your reading, break each one into parts, write your guessed meaning, and then check it with a dictionary or teacher. Record how often your guess was close, and which prefixes or suffixes helped most. Over time, your guesses will become more accurate, and your reading speed will rise, because you will stop at fewer words. Word formation thus connects grammar to real reading skill, and it is one of the most practical topics in the whole Sindhi grammar course.

A prefix is added before a root to shade, reverse or refine meaning.
A suffix is added after a root and can change meaning and word class.
Compound words join two roots or words into one combined meaning.
Breaking a word into parts is the best way to guess an unknown word.

faqs.q: What is tashkeel-e-alfaaz in Sindhi grammar?
faqs.a: Tashkeel-e-alfaaz is word formation: how new words are built from roots, prefixes, suffixes and compounds. A root carries the core meaning, a prefix adds meaning at the beginning, and a suffix adds meaning or changes the word's job at the end. Learning word formation helps students guess unfamiliar words, spell correctly and grow vocabulary faster.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a prefix and a suffix?
faqs.a: A prefix comes before the root, such as be- or na- at the start of a word, and it usually shades or reverses the meaning. A suffix comes after the root, and it can change the word's job, such as turning an action into a person or an abstract idea, as well as marking gender, number or tense. Position is the simplest way to tell them apart.

faqs.q: How does knowing a root help with vocabulary?
faqs.a: One root appears in many related words, so learning the root unlocks the whole family. For example, the root parh relates to reading and appears in several reading words. Instead of memorising each word separately, you learn the root once and recognise its family members in new texts, which makes revision organised rather than random.

faqs.q: Can I always guess a word from its parts?
faqs.a: Not always, but parts give a strong first guess that you can check against the sentence. Split the word into prefix, root and suffix, combine their meanings, and ask whether the result fits the subject and topic. If it fits, continue reading; if it does not fit, try a different split or check a dictionary. Compounds with special fixed meanings are the main exception.

faqs.q: How should I revise prefixes and suffixes for exams?
faqs.a: Keep a table with each prefix or suffix, its meaning or function, and three example words. Revise one group at a time, covering the examples and recalling them from memory. Then practise with five unfamiliar words each week, breaking them into parts and guessing their meanings before checking. This combination of table revision and guessing practice builds lasting skill.

title: Sindhi Grammar: Imla Mistakes Students Make Most
desc: Fix Sindhi imla mistakes: common spelling errors, confusing letter pairs, silent letters and proofreading habits that help students write correctly.
intro: Sindhi grammar imla mistakes cost students marks even when their ideas are good, because spelling errors distract the reader and sometimes change the meaning of a word. Imla means spelling and orthography: the correct written form of a word, including its letters, dots and joins. Sindhi spelling is challenging because some letters sound similar, some words differ by a single dot, and some borrowed words keep spellings from Arabic or Persian. This guide covers the most common imla mistakes students make, explains why each one happens, and gives proofreading habits that catch errors before work is submitted. All Sindhi examples are illustrative, given in Roman transliteration with the error described in words.

paras: Sindhi uses a script with many letters that share shapes and differ only by dots or small marks, so a single missed dot can turn one word into another. Several letters also sound alike in fast speech, especially for students who speak a different language at home, so they write the letter they hear rather than the letter the word actually uses. Borrowed words add another layer, because Arabic and Persian spellings do not always follow the sound patterns of everyday Sindhi speech. Together, these factors mean that imla cannot be learned by sound alone; it must be learned by eye, through reading and careful copying of correct forms.

The good news is that imla improves quickly once students treat spelling as a skill with patterns, not as a talent they either have or lack. Most errors fall into a small number of groups: similar-sounding letters, similar-looking letters, missing or extra dots, and borrowed-word spellings. If a student learns the pattern behind each group and practises the words in that group together, the error rate falls fast. Teachers can help by marking imla errors by group, not just by circling words, so students see which pattern they need to practise next. For more solved material, see the [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [book list](/books.html).

sections.h2: Confusing Letter Pairs That Sound Alike
paras: The largest group of imla mistakes comes from letters that sound similar but are written differently. Students often choose the letter that matches their pronunciation, especially when two letters share a sound in their home dialect. For example, pairs of letters for similar s, z, t and h sounds are frequent sources of confusion, and the wrong choice produces a word that looks almost right but is marked wrong. The only reliable cure is to learn each word's correct spelling as a visual picture, not as a sound, and to revise confusing pairs side by side so the difference becomes visible.

A practical exercise is to make minimal-pair cards: write two words that differ by only one letter on opposite sides of a card, with a picture or example sentence for each. Revise five cards a day, saying the word, visualising its letters, and writing it from memory. Another exercise is dictation with a partner: one student reads a list of confusing words slowly, the other writes them, and both check the spellings together, discussing each error by letter, not just by word. Over weeks, the visual memory of correct forms strengthens, and the similar-sound trap loses its power. Students should also read aloud from correct texts daily, because seeing correct spellings repeatedly builds the same visual memory.
bullets: Similar sounds: learn the word as a visual picture, not only by sound
Similar shapes: check dots and small marks letter by letter
Minimal pairs: revise words differing by one letter side by side
Dictation: practise confusing words with a partner weekly

sections.h2: Dots, Joins and Letters That Look Alike
paras: A second group of mistakes involves letters that look alike and differ only by dots or by how they join to neighbours. In handwriting, a dot placed hastily above the wrong letter, or a join written too loosely, can change the word completely. Students writing quickly in exams are especially vulnerable, because speed tempts them to skip dots or to join letters carelessly. The result is a word that the student meant correctly but the marker reads incorrectly, which is frustrating because the knowledge was present but the writing hid it.

The remedy is slow, deliberate handwriting practice, not just more writing. Set aside ten minutes a day to copy a short paragraph slowly, focusing on dots, joins and letter shapes, and compare your copy letter by letter with the original. In exams, reserve the last five minutes for a dot check: read your work once looking only at dots and joins, not at meaning, and fix any letter that looks doubtful. Writing slightly larger also helps, because small, cramped writing hides dot errors. Teachers often advise students to write clearly rather than quickly, because a readable answer with correct dots earns more than a fast answer full of dot mistakes.

Borrowed words from Arabic, Persian and English often keep spellings that do not match their Sindhi pronunciation, and these words trap even good spellers. A letter that is silent in speech may still be written, or a word may keep a double letter from its source language that Sindhi speech does not emphasise. Students who spell borrowed words purely by sound will therefore miss letters that must be present in writing. The solution is to learn borrowed words as whole written units, with attention to their source spelling, rather than trying to rebuild them from sound each time.

A useful method is to keep a borrowed-words page in your notebook, divided by source language where known, with the correct spelling and one example sentence for each word. Revise that page before tests, because borrowed words are common in formal Sindhi passages and in exam texts. When you meet a new borrowed word, copy it three times slowly, say it aloud, and write it once from memory the next day. If you still miss a letter, copy it three more times and test again the following day. This spaced copying method, though simple, is remarkably effective for words whose spelling cannot be guessed from sound alone. More help is on the [blog](/blog/) and the [home page](/).

diagram.caption: Run this check on every piece of written work before you submit it.

sections.h2: Building a Personal Imla Improvement Plan
paras: A personal imla plan turns random errors into steady improvement. Start by collecting your last five marked pieces of writing and sorting every spelling error into groups: similar sounds, similar shapes, dots and joins, and borrowed words. Count the errors in each group, and you will usually find that one or two groups account for most of your mistakes. Focus your practice on those groups first, because fixing the largest group gives the biggest improvement for the least effort. Set a simple goal, such as halving errors in your largest group within a month, and track it by counting errors in each new piece of work.

Daily habits support the plan: read a correct Sindhi text for ten minutes, copy a short paragraph slowly, and revise five minimal-pair or borrowed-word cards. Weekly habits add dictation with a partner and a dot-check of one old composition. Monthly, repeat the error count and adjust your focus to the group that is now largest. Students who follow this cycle often report that spelling stops feeling like luck and starts feeling like a system they control. Imla is not about being naturally good at spelling; it is about noticing patterns, practising the right words, and proofreading with a clear checklist every single time.

Similar-sounding letters cause the largest group of spelling errors.
Similar-looking letters and missed dots change words in handwriting.
Borrowed words keep source spellings that cannot be guessed from sound.
A five-minute proofreading check catches most errors before submission.

faqs.q: Why do I spell Sindhi words wrong even when I know what I mean?
faqs.a: Because Sindhi spelling depends on visual memory as well as sound. Some letters sound alike, some look alike apart from dots, and borrowed words keep source spellings. Knowing the meaning does not guarantee knowing the letters, so you must also learn each word's written picture through reading, slow copying and dictation practice.

faqs.q: How can I remember which similar-sounding letter is correct?
faqs.a: Use minimal-pair cards: write two words differing by one letter, with a picture or sentence for each, and revise five cards a day by writing each word from memory. Reading correct texts daily also builds visual memory. Over time, the correct letter for each word becomes a picture you recognise, not a sound you guess.

faqs.q: What is the best proofreading check for imla?
faqs.a: Read your work slowly aloud first, then read it once looking only at dots, joins and letter shapes, then circle similar-sound words and borrowed words and verify each spelling. Reserve the last five minutes of exam time for this check. Writing slightly larger also helps, because cramped writing hides dot errors from both writer and marker.

faqs.q: Why are borrowed words harder to spell in Sindhi?
faqs.a: Borrowed words from Arabic, Persian and English often keep spellings from their source language, including silent letters or double letters that Sindhi speech does not emphasise. Spelling them purely by sound therefore misses letters. Learn borrowed words as whole written units, keep a borrowed-words page, and copy each new word slowly three times before testing yourself the next day.

faqs.q: How long does it take to improve Sindhi spelling?
faqs.a: Most students see clear improvement within a month of focused practice, because errors usually cluster in one or two groups. Sort your recent errors by group, practise the largest group daily with cards and dictation, and count errors in each new piece of work to track progress. Spelling improves like any skill: steady, patterned practice beats occasional long sessions.

title: Urdu Grammar: Ism and Its Kinds
desc: Learn Urdu grammar ism and its kinds — ism-e-zaat, ism-e-sifat, zamir and more — with clear definitions, simple examples and exam tips for Sindh board students.
intro: An ism is simply a word that names a person, place, thing, quality or idea, and once you can spot the ism in a sentence, the rest of grammar becomes much easier to understand. In this Urdu grammar ism kinds guide you will learn the main kinds of ism — ism-e-zaat, ism-e-sifat and zamir — with plain definitions and everyday examples you can practise at home. We will also show you how examiners test this topic, which mistakes students make most often, and a simple method for identifying the ism in any sentence within seconds. By the end, you will be able to classify naming words confidently in your textbook lessons and in your exam paper.

sections.h2: What Is an Ism in Urdu Grammar?
paras: Whenever you point at something and give it a name, you are using an ism, which is why grammarians call it the naming part of speech. In the sentence about a boy reading a book, both the boy and the book are isms, because each one names a person or a thing taking part in the action. Without isms, a sentence would have no subject and no object, and the listener would not know who did what or to whom it was done. That is why every Urdu grammar course starts here: the ism is the foundation on which verbs, adjectives and pronouns all depend.

Ask yourself whether the word names something or does something: if it names, it is an ism, and if it shows action, it is a fail. For example, in a sentence about a girl writing a letter, the girl and the letter are isms, while writing is the fail that connects them. Another useful test is to place a word like mera or yeh before it: if the phrase still makes sense, the word is very likely an ism. Practise this test on ten sentences from your Urdu reader every day, and spotting the ism will soon feel automatic rather than difficult.

A city name, a person's name or the name of a particular river belongs to the khaas group, because it points to one single thing and to nothing else. A word like city, boy or river belongs to the aam group, because it can describe any member of that class rather than one special member. Examiners love this distinction, so they often give a mixed list of words and ask you to sort them into khaas and aam columns. Remember that khaas names are usually written with a capital idea in mind, even though Urdu script has no capital letters, and they never take a plural in the same way common nouns do.

Write down five khaas names from your family, your street and your school, and beside each one write the aam word that describes its class, such as a teacher's name beside the word teacher. Then reverse the exercise: take an aam word like darya and list three khaas rivers you know, which trains your brain to move between the two levels. In exams, read the full sentence before deciding, because a word like school can be aam in one sentence and khaas when it is part of a school's full name. This habit of checking the context will protect you from the most common marking trap in this topic.
bullets: Ism-e-zaat-e-khaas: names one specific person, place or thing.
Ism-e-zaat-e-aam: names a whole class of similar things.
Test: if only one thing in the world carries that name, it is khaas.

sections.h2: Ism-e-Sifat: When a Name Describes a Quality
paras: Words for goodness, bravery, beauty, wisdom and patience all belong to this group, because they name qualities that live inside people and actions rather than things you can hold. In a sentence about an honest trader, the word for honesty is the ism-e-sifat, while the trader himself is the ism-e-zaat, and the two work together to give a fuller picture. Students often mistake ism-e-sifat for sifat itself, but the difference is simple: sifat describes a noun directly, while ism-e-sifat names the quality as an independent idea that can itself become the subject of a sentence.

Honesty is the best policy is a perfect example, because honesty sits in the subject position and the sentence talks about the quality itself. Compare that with an honest boy, where honest only describes the boy and cannot stand alone as the subject, so it is a sifat rather than an ism-e-sifat. Examiners frequently test exactly this contrast, so practise converting sifat phrases into ism-e-sifat sentences and back again. Five conversions a day will make the distinction permanent, and it will also improve your essay writing, where quality words carry much of the meaning.

sections.h2: Zamir: The Pronoun Family of Ism
paras: Instead of repeating a person's name five times in a paragraph, you use words like woh, uska, tum and hum, and the listener still understands exactly who is meant. Zamir is divided by person: first person for the speaker, second person for the listener, and third person for someone being talked about, and each group changes its form with number and respect. Because zamir replaces an ism-e-zaat, grammarians count it among the kinds of ism, and exam papers often ask you to underline the zamir and name the ism it replaces. Mastering zamir therefore improves both your grammar marks and the natural flow of your writing.

If the noun is a single feminine word, the zamir that refers back to it must also be feminine, and the same rule applies to plural nouns, which need plural zamair. To practise, take a paragraph from your Urdu textbook, circle every ism-e-zaat, and then underline each zamir and draw an arrow to the noun it stands for. When every arrow points to a matching noun, your paragraph is correct, and when an arrow points to a mismatched noun, you have found an error to fix. This arrow exercise is quick, visual and very close to how examiners check your answers.

diagram.alt: The Kinds of Ism at a Glance
diagram.caption: Ism divides into ism-e-zaat, ism-e-sifat and zamir, each with its own job in a sentence.

sections.h2: How to Identify the Ism in Any Sentence
paras: First, find the fail, because the action word tells you that something must be doing it and something must be receiving it. Second, ask kaun or kya before the fail: the answer to kaun is usually the ism doing the action, and the answer to kya is usually the ism receiving it. Third, check whether the word you found names something, describes a quality, or stands in place of a name, which tells you its kind. Fourth, test it with mera or yeh in front: if the phrase still sounds natural, your identification is almost certainly right, and you can write the answer with confidence.

Take one lesson, pick ten sentences, and apply the four steps to each, writing the ism, its kind and your reason in a notebook. After a week of this habit you will notice that you no longer need all four steps, because your eye will jump straight to the naming words. In the exam hall, spend the first minute of the grammar section scanning for isms in this way, and underline them lightly before answering, so that later questions about fail and sifat become easier too. For more study help, visit the [solved notes](/solved.html) and [books](/books.html) pages, and browse the [blog](/blog/) for other grammar guides.
