points: Zamir replaces a noun to avoid repetition and to link sentences smoothly.
First person is the speaker, second the listener, third the person talked about.
Respect matters: aap is respectful, tum is familiar — choose by situation.
A zamir must agree with its noun in gender, number and person.
Use the arrow test to trace each zamir to its noun and check clarity.

faqs.q: What is the arrow test for zamir?
faqs.a: Draw an arrow from each zamir back to the noun it replaces, then check gender, number and person along the arrow. If any link fails, the zamir is wrong or the arrow points to the wrong noun. The test also exposes unclear antecedents: if two nouns could both claim the zamir, the arrow is ambiguous and the sentence needs a repeated noun instead.

faqs.q: When should I repeat a noun instead of using zamir?
faqs.a: Repeat the noun when a zamir would be ambiguous — for example, when two people of the same gender and number appear in the previous sentence and a bare zamir could refer to either. Clarity matters more than economy, and examiners reward a clear sentence over a smooth-sounding but confusing one. One repeated noun restores clarity at once.

faqs.q: How do I choose between tum and aap?
faqs.a: Choose by respect and situation: aap is the respectful form for teachers, elders and formal situations, while tum is familiar and fits friends and peers. Using a familiar form where respect is required sounds disrespectful even when the grammar is correct, so examiners notice the choice. When in doubt in formal writing, choose aap.

faqs.q: Why does my paragraph drift between first and third person?
faqs.a: Person drift happens when you change perspective mid-paragraph without noticing, often while converting ideas from notes into full sentences. The cure is a final person check: read the paragraph and confirm that every zamir and fail belongs to the same person throughout. Person conversion exercises — rewriting a diary entry in third person — train this consistency directly.

faqs.q: How far can a zamir sit from its noun?
faqs.a: As close as possible: a zamir many sentences after its noun becomes a distant zamir, and the reader may forget the connection. If the gap grows beyond one or two sentences, repeat the noun once to refresh the connection. In exam answers, keep zamir near their nouns, especially when new people or things enter the paragraph.

title: Urdu Grammar: Muhavare and Rozmarra
desc: Learn Urdu grammar muhavare and rozmarra — idioms versus everyday phrases, with meanings — plus clear examples and exam tips for Sindh board students.
intro: Urdu grammar muhavare rozmarra is the chapter where language becomes colourful, because muhavare carry wisdom in a few words and rozmarra phrases keep daily conversation natural and fluent. A muhavara says much more than its literal words suggest, while a rozmarra phrase is an everyday expression whose meaning is close to its words but polished by common use. In this guide you will learn how muhavare and rozmarra differ, how to understand a muhavara from its story, and how to use both correctly in exams and essays. You will also learn the mistakes that make idiom use sound forced or wrong. By the end, you will use idioms with the confidence of a fluent speaker.

paras: A muhavara is a fixed phrase whose meaning cannot be guessed from its individual words, because the phrase as a whole has taken on a figurative sense through long use. When someone uses a muhavara about the heart or the eyes, they are rarely talking about body parts at all: they are expressing courage, fear, love or wisdom through an image the whole language community understands. This figurative leap is what makes muhavare powerful: a single phrase can express a complex feeling or situation that would otherwise need a whole sentence. It is also what makes them difficult for learners, because translating the words literally gives nonsense, and only learning the accepted meaning unlocks the phrase.

Muhavare are fixed, which means their words cannot be freely changed or rearranged without breaking the idiom: swapping a word for a synonym usually destroys the phrase, even when the synonym means the same thing alone. This fixedness is a useful exam clue: if changing a word breaks the meaning, you are probably dealing with a muhavara rather than an ordinary phrase. Examiners test muhavare by asking for meanings, by asking students to use them in sentences, or by giving a sentence and asking which muhavara it illustrates. All three question types reward learning muhavare as whole units with their meanings, not as collections of separate words.

Rozmarra means the everyday language of daily life: the common phrases, greetings, polite forms and routine expressions that fluent speakers use without thinking. Unlike a muhavara, a rozmarra phrase usually means something close to its literal words, but it is polished by habit into a standard form that sounds natural, while a word-by-word translation might sound stiff or foreign. Greetings, thanks, apologies, requests and farewells all belong to rozmarra, and mastering them is what makes a learner sound fluent rather than bookish. Examiners value rozmarra because it shows living command of Urdu, not merely grammar knowledge, and it appears in dialogue writing, letters and comprehension passages.

The best way to learn rozmarra is to listen and collect: notice the phrases your family, teachers and shopkeepers use in daily situations, and write them down with the situation they belong to. A phrase learned with its situation — a greeting for the morning, a polite request in a shop, an apology after a mistake — is remembered far better than a phrase learned from a list. Practise by using one new rozmarra phrase in real conversation each day, because a phrase used once in real life sticks better than a phrase read ten times. In exams, rozmarra knowledge shines in dialogue and letter questions, where natural phrasing earns impression marks that grammar alone cannot.
bullets: Rozmarra phrases mean something close to their literal words.
They are polished by daily habit into standard natural forms.
Learn each phrase with the situation where it belongs.

sections.h2: Muhavare Versus Rozmarra: The Key Differences
paras: The key difference between muhavare and rozmarra is figurativeness: a muhavara means something different from its literal words, while a rozmarra phrase means roughly what its words say, in a polished everyday form. A second difference is fixedness: muhavare resist word changes, while rozmarra phrases allow some variation, since their meaning lives in the words themselves rather than in the whole phrase. A third difference is purpose: muhavare add colour, wisdom and emphasis to writing, while rozmarra keeps daily communication smooth and polite. Examiners often ask students to distinguish the two, giving a phrase and asking whether it is a muhavara or rozmarra, so the figurativeness test is the fastest answer: if the literal meaning fails, it is a muhavara.

A practical classification exercise is to take ten phrases from your lessons and sort them into two columns, testing each with the literal-meaning question. For each phrase, ask whether a stranger hearing only the words would understand it: if yes, it is probably rozmarra, and if no, it is probably a muhavara. Then check fixedness by trying a synonym swap: if the phrase breaks, that confirms muhavara, and if it survives, that confirms rozmarra. Doing this exercise weekly builds a reliable instinct for the distinction, and it also deepens your vocabulary, because each sorted phrase is learned with its meaning, its type and an example sentence at the same time.

sections.h2: How to Learn and Use Muhavare Correctly
paras: Learning muhavare correctly means learning three things together: the exact words, the accepted meaning, and a sentence that shows the muhavara in action, because any one of the three alone is not enough for exam use. A student who knows the meaning but changes the words will be marked wrong, and a student who knows the words but uses the muhavara in the wrong situation will sound odd. The best notebook format has three columns — muhavara, meaning, sentence — and five new entries a week, reviewed regularly, will build a strong stock over a term. Choose muhavare from your textbook first, because examiners draw their questions from textbook idioms far more often than from rare or regional ones.

Using muhavare in essays requires restraint: one well-placed muhavara lifts a paragraph, while five crowded together make writing sound artificial, as if the student is showing off rather than communicating. Place a muhavara where its meaning genuinely fits the idea, not where it merely fills space, and check that its tone suits the paragraph: a humorous muhavara in a serious essay about a tragedy would be a serious misjudgement. In exam answers, use muhavare you are sure of, because a misused idiom loses more marks than a plain sentence would, while a correctly used one earns clear credit. Confidence comes from the three-column notebook and from using each new muhavara in homework before trusting it in an exam.

diagram.caption: One test separates them: does the literal meaning work, or does the phrase mean something else?

paras: The commonest idiom mistake is literal translation: writing a muhavara's words in another language or explaining it word by word, which destroys its figurative meaning and confuses the reader. A second mistake is word substitution, replacing one word of a muhavara with a synonym and assuming the idiom survives, when in fact the fixed phrase has been broken. A third mistake is overuse, crowding an essay with idioms until the writing sounds like a list rather than an argument, which examiners penalise as poor style. A fourth is wrong-situation use, placing a light or humorous muhavara in a serious context, which shows that the student knows the words but not the meaning's weight.

Avoid all four mistakes with a simple rule: use only muhavare you have learned as whole units with their meanings and example sentences, and use each one only where its meaning genuinely fits. Before an exam, review your three-column notebook and mark the ten muhavare you know best, because those are the ones to trust under pressure. In the exam, if you are unsure of a muhavara's exact words or meaning, write a plain sentence instead: a correct plain sentence always beats a broken idiom. This discipline — confidence with a few, caution with the rest — is what separates strong idiom users from students who lose marks showing off. For more guides, see the [blog](/blog/) and [solved notes](/solved.html) pages.

Rozmarra is everyday polished language: greetings, requests, thanks and farewells.
Literal meaning test: if literal sense fails, the phrase is probably a muhavara.
Learn each muhavara as words plus meaning plus an example sentence.
Use idioms sparingly and only where their meaning genuinely fits the context.

faqs.q: How can I tell a muhavara from an ordinary phrase?
faqs.a: Apply the literal-meaning test: if the phrase's words, taken literally, do not explain its meaning, it is a muhavara. Then apply the fixedness test: try swapping a word for a synonym, and if the phrase breaks, that confirms it is a muhavara. Ordinary phrases and rozmarra pass the literal test and usually survive a synonym swap.

faqs.q: Why must muhavara words not be changed?
faqs.a: Because a muhavara's meaning lives in the whole fixed phrase, not in its separate words, so changing a word breaks the unit the language community recognises. Even a synonym with the same individual meaning destroys the idiom, since listeners recognise the exact phrase, not a paraphrase of it. Always learn and use a muhavara's exact words.

faqs.q: How many muhavare should I use in an essay?
faqs.a: One well-placed muhavara per paragraph is plenty, and sometimes one per essay is enough. Overuse makes writing sound artificial, as if the student is showing off rather than communicating, and examiners penalise it as poor style. Choose muhavare that genuinely fit the idea, and prefer a plain sentence to a forced idiom.

faqs.q: What is the best way to memorise muhavare?
faqs.a: Use a three-column notebook — muhavara, meaning, example sentence — with five new entries a week, reviewed regularly. Learning the words, meaning and sentence together prepares you for all three exam question types: giving meanings, using idioms in sentences, and identifying the muhavara a sentence illustrates. Start with textbook muhavare, since examiners draw from them most.

faqs.q: How is rozmarra tested in exams?
faqs.a: Rozmarra appears mainly in dialogue writing, letters and comprehension passages, where natural phrasing earns impression marks. It is rarely tested by direct definition questions; instead, examiners reward students whose dialogues and letters sound like real Urdu rather than translated English. Collect phrases with their situations from daily life to build this skill.

title: Urdu Grammar: Imla Ki Ghaltiyan Aur Islah
desc: Learn Urdu grammar imla ki ghaltiyan aur islah — the spelling errors examiners notice first — with clear rules, examples and proofreading tips for students.
intro: Urdu grammar imla ghaltiyan aur islah is the topic that protects marks in every written answer, because spelling errors are the first thing an examiner notices and the easiest fault to penalise. Urdu imla is challenging because the script has several letters for similar sounds, silent letters, and joining rules that change a word's shape, so even good students make spelling mistakes under exam pressure. In this guide you will learn the error types examiners notice first, the rules behind correct imla, and a proofreading routine that catches mistakes before submission. You will also learn how to build a personal error list that targets your own weak words. By the end, your written Urdu will look as careful as your ideas deserve.

sections.h2: Why Imla Matters More Than Students Think
paras: A single spelling mistake in a heading or a first sentence is especially costly, because it shapes the examiner's first impression, while repeated errors in a paragraph suggest that the student did not re-read their work. Beyond impression, spelling errors can change meaning: two Urdu words that differ by one letter or one dot can mean entirely different things, so a spelling slip can turn a correct answer into a wrong one. That is why imla is tested both directly, through dictation and correction questions, and indirectly, through the language marks on every written answer.

Students often treat spelling as a matter of talent, believing that good spellers are born rather than made, but imla is a learnable skill built on patterns, attention and proofreading habits. Most spelling errors come from a small set of causes — similar-sounding letters, silent letters, joining mistakes and careless copying — and each cause has a rule or a habit that prevents it. A student who learns those causes and checks for them will spell better than a student who merely reads a lot and hopes, because reading alone does not train the eye to notice letter-level detail. Treat imla as a system to master, and your spelling will improve measurably within a single term.

Urdu has several groups of letters that sound similar but are spelled differently, and choosing the wrong member of such a group is the single commonest imla error in student writing. These letters differ in origin — some come from Arabic, some from Persian, some from native Urdu words — and each word's spelling preserves its origin, so the correct letter must be learned with the word rather than guessed from sound. Sound alone cannot decide, because the similar letters sound alike in normal speech, which is exactly why the trap works: a student writing by ear will choose the wrong letter half the time. Examiners know this, and they deliberately include similar-letter words in dictation and correction questions.

The cure is to learn similar-letter words visually, as pictures, rather than by sound: when you learn a new word, look at its letters carefully and notice which similar letter it uses, then write the word three times while looking at it, and once from memory. A dictation partner is even better: one student reads words aloud, the other writes them, and the pair checks the similar letters together, which turns a solitary chore into a quick game. After a few weeks, the correct letter will feel visually right, and the wrong one will look strange, which is the instinct good spellers rely on.

sections.h2: Silent Letters, Do-Chashmi He and Joining Rules
paras: Silent letters survive in spelling because of a word's history, even though modern speech has dropped them, and students writing by ear naturally omit them, producing a word that sounds right but is spelled wrong. Do-chashmi he causes the opposite error: students either omit it, changing an aspirated sound into a plain one, or add it where it does not belong, creating a sound the word never had. Joining rules add a third trap: Urdu letters change shape depending on their position, and a word copied with the wrong join looks broken even when its letters are correct.

Master these rules through slow, visual copying rather than fast writing: copy a paragraph from your textbook slowly, paying attention to every silent letter, every do-chashmi he and every join, and compare your copy letter by letter with the original. The comparison step is essential, because copying without comparing trains speed but not accuracy, while comparing trains the eye to notice exactly the details that exams test. Keep a list of the words you misspell in copying practice, with the correct spelling beside the wrong one, and review that list before tests. Most students find that ten to twenty personal trap words account for most of their errors, and fixing those few words transforms their imla marks.
bullets: Silent letters are written but not pronounced — learn them visually.
Do-chashmi he aspirates the letter before it; never guess its presence.
Joining shapes change by position; copy slowly and compare letter by letter.

sections.h2: The Proofreading Routine That Catches Errors
paras: Proofreading is the highest-value imla habit, because it catches errors that knowledge alone misses, especially under exam pressure when the hand moves faster than the eye. An effective routine has three passes: first read for meaning, checking that each sentence says what you intended; then read slowly word by word, checking spelling, dots and joins, which is the pass that catches imla errors; then read the first and last lines once more, because errors there shape the examiner's impression most. The word-by-word pass must be genuinely slow: point at each word if you must, because the eye skips familiar words at normal reading speed, and skipping is how errors survive.

Two proofreading tricks make the slow pass more effective: reading backwards, from the last word to the first, which breaks the meaning flow and forces the eye to see each word as a spelling unit; and reading aloud softly, which makes similar-letter errors audible when the written letter does not match the spoken sound. Use the backwards trick for short answers and the aloud trick for longer ones, and always leave time for proofreading in your exam plan: reserve the last five minutes of the paper for it, and never submit a paper you have not re-read.

diagram.alt: Proofread Every Answer in Three Passes
diagram.caption: Meaning first, spelling second, first and last lines last — five minutes that save many marks.

paras: Build it from your real mistakes: every time a teacher marks a spelling error in your homework, copy the wrong version and the correct version into your list, with the sentence it came from, so the word is learned in context. Review the list for two minutes before every Urdu test, and test yourself by covering the correct column and writing each word from memory, correcting mistakes at once. Words that leave the list after three correct recalls can be retired, and new mistakes take their place, so the list stays short, current and personal.

Pair the error list with a daily habit that prevents new errors: write five difficult words from your lessons each day, slowly and visually, checking each letter against the textbook before moving on. Difficult means words with similar letters, silent letters or do-chashmi he, because those are the words that will appear in dictation questions. Over a term, this habit builds a visual memory of correct spellings that survives exam pressure far better than last-minute cramming, which fades quickly. Combine the error list, the daily five words and the proofreading routine, and imla will change from your weakest area into a reliable source of marks. For more study guides, see the [blog](/blog/) and [solved notes](/solved.html) pages.

points: Spelling errors shape the examiner's first impression and can even change meaning.
Similar-sounding letters are the biggest trap: learn words visually, not by ear.
Silent letters and do-chashmi he must be learned as part of each word's spelling.
Proofread in three passes: meaning, word-by-word spelling, then first and last lines.
A personal error list of twenty to thirty words targets your own weak spots.

faqs.q: Why do I spell correctly at home but wrongly in exams?
faqs.a: Because exam pressure makes the hand move faster than the eye, turning attention gaps into errors even when you know the correct spelling. The cure is a proofreading routine with time reserved for it: read word by word, check dots and joins, and re-read first and last lines. Most home-versus-exam gaps close once proofreading becomes a habit, because the errors were never knowledge gaps.

faqs.q: How can I learn similar-sounding letters?
faqs.a: Learn them visually as pictures: look at each word's letters carefully, notice which similar letter it uses, write it three times while looking and once from memory. Group words by their similar letter into separate lists and compare the lists side by side. A dictation partner who reads words aloud while you write and check together makes this practice faster and more enjoyable.

faqs.q: What is do-chashmi he and why does it cause errors?
faqs.a: Do-chashmi he is the letter that aspirates the letter before it, changing its sound, and it causes errors because students either omit it, losing the aspiration, or add it where it does not belong. Learn it as part of each word's spelling through slow visual copying, not by guessing from sound, and keep aspirated words on your personal error list until they are certain.

faqs.q: Does reading backwards really help proofreading?
faqs.a: Yes, because reading from the last word to the first breaks the meaning flow and forces the eye to see each word as a spelling unit instead of skipping familiar words. It is most useful for short answers; for longer answers, reading aloud softly works similarly by making letter-sound mismatches audible. Both tricks turn passive re-reading into active error hunting.

faqs.q: How long should proofreading take in an exam?
faqs.a: Reserve the last five minutes of the paper for proofreading, and use it for the three passes: meaning, word-by-word spelling, then first and last lines. Five minutes is enough for most papers if the passes are practised beforehand, and it saves more marks than attempting one extra question in a rush. Never submit a paper you have not re-read.

title: BSEK 40% Pass Rule 2026: What Changed for Class 9 Science Students
desc: BSEK raised the Class 9 pass mark from 33% to 40% in 2026. Learn what ungraded means, how the new rule works, and what it means for Class 10 from 2027.
kw: BSEK 40 percent pass rule 2026 Class 9 science ungraded
intro: The Board of Secondary Education Karachi changed the rules of the game for Class 9 students in 2026, and many families only discovered the change when the result arrived. From the 2026 annual examinations, the pass threshold for Class 9 was raised from 33% to 40%, which means a paper scored below 40% is now recorded as ungraded rather than passed. The Board of Secondary Education Karachi announced the Class 9 Science Group result on 28 October 2026, and the new rule shaped that result in ways students and parents need to understand clearly. This guide explains exactly what changed, what ungraded means for your mark sheet, how the rule differs from the old 33% system, and what happens when Class 10 comes under the same scheme from 2027.

paras: For years, Sindh board students grew up with a simple number in their heads: 33% was the pass mark. A student who scored 35% in a paper passed it, and a student who scored 30% failed it, and everyone understood where the line stood. From the 2026 annual examinations, that line moved for Class 9. The pass threshold is now 40%, so a paper must be scored at 40% or above to count as passed, and anything below 40% is recorded as ungraded. This is not a small administrative adjustment; it changes the outcome for every student whose marks fall in the 33% to 39% band, because papers that would have passed under the old rule now stand open and must be cleared.

The change applies to Class 9 from the 2026 annual examinations, and Class 10 follows from 2027, so current Class 9 students will meet the same standard again next year. That timing matters for planning, because it means there is no point in treating 40% as a one-year hurdle to scrape past and forget. Students who build study habits that aim comfortably above 40% this year will carry that margin into Class 10, while students who aim only at the borderline risk falling below it again when a paper turns out harder than expected. The sensible response is to treat 40% as the floor and to aim for a clear pass in every paper, using the [book collection](/books.html) and [solved notes](/solved.html) to strengthen weak chapters rather than relying on guesswork.

sections.h2: What Ungraded Really Means on Your Mark Sheet
paras: The word ungraded causes confusion because it sounds softer than failed, but students should understand it precisely. Under the new grading scheme, a paper in which a student scores below 40% is marked ungraded, which means the student is unsuccessful in that paper and has not passed it. It does not mean the paper is ignored, and it does not mean the marks disappear; it means the paper remains open and the student reappears in it subject to eligibility, following the board's official process. Parents sometimes read ungraded as a partial credit or a near pass, but the practical meaning is straightforward: that paper still needs to be cleared before the student's record for the class is complete.

Ungraded also changes how a student should read the rest of the mark sheet. A student who passed some papers and has one or two ungraded papers is in a different position from a student who failed everything, and the plan for each case is different. The first step is always to list every paper, mark each one as passed or ungraded, and note how far below 40% each ungraded paper fell, because a gap of two marks needs a different revision plan from a gap of twenty marks. Students should check their result on the board's official website and keep a printed or saved copy of the mark sheet, since every later step, from reappearance to admission, will ask for exactly what that sheet shows.

diagram.caption: How the same marks are treated under the old and new Class 9 pass thresholds.

sections.h2: How the New Rule Shaped the 28 October 2026 Result
paras: The Class 9 Science Group result announced on 28 October 2026 gives the first full picture of the new rule in action. According to the figures shared by Controller of Examinations Ahmed Khan Chhutto, 180,054 students registered and 177,923 appeared, while 123,757 passed all papers and 53,849 failed. The overall pass percentage was 69.56%, compared with 78.26% in 2025, when 137,350 of 175,511 students who appeared passed all papers. That is a fall of about 8.7 percentage points, and it is tempting to blame the new threshold alone, but the board has published no single official reason for the fall, and this guide does not present one cause as fact. Several factors can move a pass rate, and students should be careful about explanations circulating without an official source.

What can be said safely is that the higher threshold mechanically changes outcomes for students in the 33% to 39% band, and that the large partial-pass groups in the 2026 figures show how many students were affected at the margins. The board reported 21,999 students passing six papers, 11,006 passing five, 7,431 passing four, 4,409 passing three, 3,101 passing two and 2,439 passing one paper, which together describe a very large group of students with open papers. Chairman Professor Musharraf Ali Rajput congratulated students who passed all papers and said transparency remained among the board's top priorities, and the result was available on the board's official website from 5:30 PM on 28 October 2026. For students, the lesson is practical rather than statistical: read your own mark sheet against the 40% line, not against last year's headlines.

sections.h2: What Class 9 Students Should Do Now
paras: The first task after the result is a careful, paper-by-paper review. Take your mark sheet and write down every paper with its marks, marking each one passed or ungraded against the 40% threshold, and calculate the gap for each ungraded paper. Papers missed by a few marks need focused revision of the chapters where marks were lost, while papers with a wide gap need a fresh study plan built from the textbook. Keep your admit card, mark sheet and registration details safe, because the reappearance process will require them, and watch the board's official website for the next official notice rather than trusting dates shared on social media, since no reappearance date for these papers was stated in the 28 October announcement.

The second task is to set a revision target with a margin of safety. Aiming for exactly 40% leaves no room for a hard paper, an off day, or a strict marking scheme, so aim for a comfortable pass well above the line in every open paper. Work from your Sindh Textbook Board book, use solved exercises to check your method, and test yourself under timed conditions so that exam pressure does not eat into your margin. If your school offers extra classes for students clearing papers, attend them and ask teachers which chapters carried the most marks. The [blog](/blog/) carries study guides for revising science subjects chapter by chapter, and building that margin now also prepares you for Class 10, where the same 40% standard will apply from 2027.

sections.h2: Class 10 From 2027: Preparing Under the Same Standard
paras: Class 10 comes under the new grading scheme from 2027, which means the current Class 9 cohort will face the 40% threshold again in their matric year. This is genuinely useful information, because it turns this year's result into a rehearsal rather than a one-off event. Students who learn now how to revise to a comfortable pass, how to read a mark sheet paper by paper, and how to close a gap in a weak subject will use exactly those skills next year, when the stakes are higher because Class 10 results feed into college admission. There is no separate trick for Class 10 under the new rule; the same habits of textbook-based revision, timed practice and honest gap measurement apply, only with more syllabus to cover.

Parents can help by treating the threshold as a planning tool rather than a source of panic. Ask your child to show you the mark sheet, go through the open papers together, and agree on a weekly revision timetable that protects time for both Class 10 schoolwork and the open Class 9 papers. Encourage your child to talk to subject teachers about the chapters that cost the most marks, and avoid agents or unofficial channels that promise shortcuts around the board's process. The board's official website remains the only reliable source for notices about reappearance, fees and dates, and the [about page](/about.html) of this site explains how our study guides are organised for Sindh board students working under the new grading scheme.

faqs.q: What is the new pass mark for BSEK Class 9 in 2026?
faqs.a: The pass threshold for Class 9 from the 2026 annual examinations is 40%. A paper scored below 40% is recorded as ungraded rather than passed. This replaces the old 33% threshold for Class 9.

faqs.q: I scored 35% in one paper. Did I pass it?
faqs.a: No. Under the new rule, 35% is below the 40% threshold, so the paper is marked ungraded and remains open. You will need to reappear in that paper subject to eligibility, following the board's official notice on its website.

faqs.q: Does the 40% rule apply to Class 10 as well?
faqs.a: Class 10 comes under the new grading scheme from 2027. Current Class 9 students will therefore meet the same 40% standard in their matric year, which is why building a margin above 40% now is so important.

faqs.q: Why did the Class 9 Science pass rate fall in 2026?
faqs.a: The overall pass percentage was 69.56% in 2026, compared with 78.26% in 2025, a fall of about 8.7 percentage points. The board has published no single official reason for the fall, so no single cause should be presented as fact. The higher threshold does change outcomes for students in the 33% to 39% band.

faqs.q: Where do I check official notices about reappearing in ungraded papers?
faqs.a: On the Board of Secondary Education Karachi official website, bsek.edu.pk, and your school notice board. No reappearance date for these papers was stated in the 28 October 2026 announcement, so treat dates circulating on social media as unverified.

title: BSEK 9th Science: Failed Papers? What to Do Next After the 2026 Result
desc: 53,849 students failed in the BSEK Class 9 Science result of 28 October 2026. Read what the figures mean, how partial passes work, and the next steps without invented dates.
kw: BSEK 9th science failed papers what next 2026 result
intro: The Board of Secondary Education Karachi announced the Class 9 Science Group result on 28 October 2026, and one figure has worried thousands of families: 53,849 students failed. That number sits alongside a much larger and more hopeful picture, because the board's own breakdown shows tens of thousands of students who passed some papers but not all of them, and each of those students has a different, manageable path forward. This guide explains what the 28 October figures actually mean for a student who failed or passed only some papers, how the new 40% rule affects the result, and what practical steps to take now, without inventing supplementary dates or promises the board has not made.

paras: Start with the board's own numbers, shared by Controller of Examinations Ahmed Khan Chhutto. Of 180,054 students who registered, 177,923 appeared and 2,131 were absent. A total of 123,757 students passed all papers, while the remaining appeared students fall into two groups that are often confused: the partial-pass bands and the failed group. The partial-pass bands are 21,999 students passing six papers, 11,006 passing five, 7,431 passing four, 4,409 passing three, 3,101 passing two and 2,439 passing one paper, and separately 53,849 students are recorded as failed. The overall pass percentage was 69.56%, down from 78.26% in 2025, but the board has published no single official reason for that fall, and families should not accept any single explanation presented as fact.

Why does this breakdown matter to you? Because the label on your own mark sheet decides your next step, and the headline figure does not. A student who passed six papers has one or two open papers and a short, focused job ahead, while a student in the failed group has a bigger job that still starts the same way: by listing every paper and its marks. Do not let the size of the failed figure convince you that your case is hopeless, and do not let a partial pass convince you that nothing more is needed. Both situations are common this year, both are dealt with through the board's formal processes, and both improve fastest when the student knows exactly which papers are open and by how many marks each one was missed.

sections.h2: Failed vs Partial Pass: Know Which Group You Are In
paras: The distinction between a partial pass and a failed result is practical, not just a label. A partial pass means you have passed at least one paper and have specific open papers left to clear, so your plan can be built paper by paper, starting with the paper closest to passing. A failed result means no paper was passed or the result is recorded as failed overall, so the plan must be broader: a fresh, full revision of the subjects, usually with the school's guidance on whether to reappear in the papers or repeat the class as the board's rules allow. In both cases the new 40% rule applies, because from the 2026 annual examinations a paper scored below 40% is recorded as ungraded rather than passed, and Class 10 follows the same scheme from 2027.

The first action is identical for both groups: read your official mark sheet, not a summary from a friend or a social media post. Write down each paper, the marks obtained, and whether it is passed or ungraded, and calculate the gap below 40% for each open paper. This list becomes your study plan, because it tells you where to spend time and where not to. A student who failed by narrow margins in several papers needs steady revision across those subjects, while a student with one wide gap needs to rebuild that subject from the textbook. For subject-wise study material, see the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html), and talk to your subject teachers about which chapters carried the most marks in the papers you missed.

sections.h2: What to Do This Week: Practical First Steps
paras: This week, do four concrete things. First, save and print your result from the board's official website, bsek.edu.pk, where the result has been available since 5:30 PM on 28 October 2026, and keep your admit card and registration details with it. Second, make the paper-by-paper list described above and share it with a parent and a teacher, because an adult who sees the exact gaps can help you plan realistically. Third, ask your school what support exists for students clearing papers, such as extra classes or remedial sessions, and whether the school expects you to continue into Class 10 while clearing open papers or to follow another route under the board's rules. Fourth, set a daily study slot for the open papers immediately, even before any official notice arrives, because revision started now is worth far more than revision started in a panic later.

At the same time, avoid the traps that waste this week. Do not pay any agent who promises to change a result or arrange a pass, because the board's process is formal and no unofficial channel can alter a mark sheet. Do not trust supplementary examination dates, fee figures or form links shared on social media unless they appear on the board's official website or your school notice board, since no reappearance date for these papers was stated in the 28 October announcement. Do not hide the result from your parents or teachers out of embarrassment; the board's figures show that tens of thousands of students are in the same position this year, and teachers deal with clearing papers every year. A result shared early gets help early, while a result hidden until the next examination becomes a crisis.

sections.h2: Building a Revision Plan That Actually Closes the Gaps
paras: A good revision plan for failed or ungraded papers starts from the textbook, not from short notes or guess papers. For each open paper, list the chapters, mark the ones where you lost the most marks, and work through them in order of marks weight, using solved exercises to check that your method is correct. Study in short, daily sessions rather than rare marathon sessions, and test yourself after each chapter with questions answered under timed conditions, because the examination rewards students who can produce answers under pressure, not students who have merely read the chapter. Keep a weekly checklist of chapters completed and practice tests taken, and review it every weekend so that slippage shows up while there is still time to correct it.

Balance is the hardest part of this plan, because Class 10 schoolwork continues at the same time for most students. Protect Class 10 school hours and homework time, and give the open Class 9 papers one or two focused hours a day, starting with the paper closest to passing so that an early success builds momentum. Science subjects overlap heavily between Class 9 and Class 10, so revising a Class 9 physics or chemistry chapter often strengthens the Class 10 chapter built on it, and that overlap should be used deliberately. If the number of open papers is large, be honest about the load: prioritise the papers closest to passing, talk to teachers about a realistic sequence, and remember that clearing papers properly, even if it takes longer, is far better than facing the next examination unprepared.

sections.h2: Staying Steady: Results, Rumours and the Next Examination
paras: A failed or partial result is emotionally hard, and students should be honest about that instead of pretending it does not matter. It is normal to feel disappointed, especially when classmates passed everything, but the board's figures prove that this year's result was difficult for a very large number of students, and a single examination does not fix a student's ability or future. Chairman Professor Musharraf Ali Rajput congratulated students who passed all papers and said transparency remained among the board's top priorities, and the fair way to read that message is that the system is meant to be navigable: open papers can be cleared through the board's own process, and students who follow that process do move forward. Comparing yourself with toppers helps no one; comparing today's marks with your own next attempt is the comparison that matters.

The steady approach is to keep two habits running until the next opportunity arrives: daily revision of the open papers, and weekly checks of the board's official website and your school notice board for the reappearance notice. When that notice appears, read it fully, noting eligibility, fee, last date and examination centre instructions, and complete the process through your school or the board's official channel as the notice directs. Until then, treat every unofficial date, fee claim or shortcut offer as unverified, keep your documents safe, and keep studying. The [blog](/blog/) carries further study guides for Sindh board students, and the [contact page](/contact.html) explains how to reach this site with questions about study material.

intro: The Board of Intermediate Education Karachi completed its HSC Part-I Annual Examination 2026 results on Monday, 26 October 2026, when it announced the remaining groups on the instructions of Chairman Faqir Muhammad Lakho, with Controller Zarina Rashid overseeing the release. The groups announced that day were Science Pre-Medical, Science General, Commerce in both Regular and Private categories, Humanities and Arts in both Regular and Private categories, Special Candidates in Arts Regular, and Home Economics, while Pre-Engineering had already been announced on 2 October 2026. This guide focuses on the Commerce and Arts students among that release: what the board's figures show, how to read your own result paper by paper, and what the new ungraded rule means if any paper falls below 40%.

paras: The 26 October announcement completed the HSC Part-I picture for 2026, because it covered every remaining group after Pre-Engineering had already been announced on 2 October 2026. For Commerce and Arts students, the important point is that both Regular and Private categories were included, so private candidates should read this guide alongside regular students rather than assuming it covers only college students. The results were published on the board's official website, www.biek.edu.pk, and on the official BIEK Android app, and students should check their result through those official channels rather than through screenshots or unofficial result pages, which can carry errors or outdated data. Keep a saved or printed copy of your result, because every later step, from scrutiny to reappearance, will ask for exactly what it shows.

Students should also note what this announcement was not. It was the HSC Part-I result, meaning Class XI or first year, and it should not be confused with Part-II results or with any supplementary examination. The announcement itself has already been covered by this site's result post, so this guide is written as a reading and next-steps guide rather than another announcement: it helps you understand the figures, interpret your own mark sheet, and decide what to do next. If you are a Science Pre-Medical or Science General student, the same 26 October release covers you too, but the figures and subject combinations in this guide focus on Commerce and Arts, with Science General covered in a companion guide.

sections.h2: Commerce Regular Figures: What the Numbers Show
paras: For Commerce Regular, the board's release gives a complete set of figures that students can use to understand their group. A total of 23,549 students registered, 22,693 appeared, and 9,332 passed all seven papers. That means a large share of Commerce Regular students did not pass all seven papers, and many of them passed some papers while leaving others open, which is a normal and manageable outcome under the board's system. The Commerce course has seven papers rather than six, so passing all seven is a bigger task than in a six-paper group, and students should judge their own result paper by paper instead of comparing themselves with students in groups that have fewer papers or different subjects.

If you are a Commerce student, your first job is to read your own mark sheet against the 40% line for each of the seven papers. List the papers you passed, list the papers marked ungraded, and note how far below 40% each ungraded paper fell, because that gap decides your revision plan. A paper missed by a few marks needs targeted revision of weak chapters, while a paper with a wide gap needs a fresh study plan from the textbook. Commerce subjects such as accounting and business mathematics reward regular practice, so daily worked examples matter more than last-minute reading. For study material matched to your subjects, browse the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html), and ask your college teachers which chapters carried the most marks in the papers you missed.

sections.h2: Arts and Humanities: What We Know From the Release
paras: Humanities and Arts students in both Regular and Private categories were part of the 26 October announcement, and the release also gives a small, complete set of figures for Special Candidates in Arts Regular: 99 registered, 97 appeared, and 58 passed all six papers. Those figures are useful because they show the same pattern as the larger groups: a substantial share of students passed all papers, and the rest have open papers to deal with, which is a normal outcome rather than a disaster. Students in the general Arts and Humanities groups should read their own mark sheets in exactly the same way, paper by paper against the 40% line, rather than judging themselves by group totals that were not published in the release this guide is based on.

Arts students sometimes feel their result matters less than a science result, but that is a mistake, because Part-I papers feed directly into Part-II and into the final intermediate certificate. An ungraded paper left unattended in Part-I becomes a problem carried into the second year, while an ungraded paper dealt with promptly through revision and the board's formal process becomes a closed chapter. Arts subjects reward regular writing practice, so students with open papers should write answers daily, not merely read notes, and should ask teachers to mark a sample answer so that weak points are visible. Keep your result, admit card and registration details safe, and watch the board's official website for any notice about reappearance or scrutiny rather than trusting social media claims.

sections.h2: The Ungraded Rule: What Below 40% Means for You
paras: The new grading system, decided by the Inter Board Committee of Chairmen together with the Sindh Universities and Boards Department, changes what a low mark means. Under this system, scoring below 40% in any paper means the paper is ungraded, which means the candidate is unsuccessful in that paper and reappears in it subject to eligibility. This replaces the older understanding in which 33% could pass a paper, and it applies across the groups announced on 26 October, including Commerce and Arts. Students should therefore read every paper on their mark sheet against the 40% line, and should not assume that a paper scored in the thirties is passed because it would have passed under an older scheme.

The practical consequence is that a student with one or two ungraded papers has a clear, limited job: revise those papers, aim comfortably above 40%, and reappear when the board's process allows. A student with several ungraded papers has a bigger job and should talk to college teachers about a realistic sequence, prioritising the papers closest to passing. In both cases, the board's official website is the only reliable source for notices about reappearance, eligibility and fees, and no reappearance date should be treated as confirmed unless it appears there. The [blog](/blog/) carries further guides for intermediate students, including how to revise commerce and arts subjects chapter by chapter.

sections.h2: Next Steps: Scrutiny, Revision and Second Year Planning
paras: If you believe a paper has been marked incorrectly, the board offers scrutiny, and the fee reported from the board's scrutiny form is Rs 1,000 per paper. No scrutiny deadline is stated in the material this guide is based on, so do not invent or trust an unofficial deadline; check the board's official website and your college notice board for the current scrutiny notice and its last date, and apply only through the official channel. Scrutiny is worth considering when your marks in a paper are far below what your class performance suggested, but it is not a substitute for revision, and students should revise the paper in parallel rather than waiting for a scrutiny outcome before opening the book.

Alongside any scrutiny decision, set up a revision routine for every open paper and protect time for second-year study as well, because Part-II work begins whether or not Part-I papers are fully cleared. Give Part-II its college hours and homework time, and protect a focused daily slot for the open Part-I papers, starting with the paper closest to passing so that an early success builds momentum. Tell your teachers which papers are open, because they can point you to the right chapters and practice material, and keep a weekly checklist of chapters revised and practice answers written. intro: Science General is one of the largest groups in Karachi's intermediate system, and its HSC Part-I Annual Examination 2026 result arrived with the remaining groups on Monday, 26 October 2026, announced on the instructions of Board of Intermediate Education Karachi Chairman Faqir Muhammad Lakho, with Controller Zarina Rashid overseeing the release. sections.h2: Science General Figures: Reading the Group Result
paras: The three numbers for Science General tell a story that every student in the group should understand. Of 30,991 registered students, 30,386 appeared, which means about six hundred registered students did not sit the examination, and 15,036 of those who appeared passed all six papers. Put simply, just under half of the students who appeared cleared every paper, while just over half have at least one open paper, whether that means a single ungraded paper or several. That is not a reason for panic, because intermediate results routinely leave a large group with open papers, but it is a reason for honest self-assessment: if you have open papers, you are in the majority group, not an exception, and the board's formal processes exist precisely for your situation.

The comparison that matters most is not with other groups but with your own mark sheet. Science General students take six papers, and passing all six means clearing every one of them at or above the 40% threshold, because under the new grading system any paper below 40% is recorded as ungraded. A student who passed five papers and missed one by a few marks is in a very different position from a student who passed two papers, and the board's group figures cannot tell you which one you are. Read your own result paper by paper, list the passed and ungraded papers, and measure the gap below 40% for each open paper, because that list becomes your revision plan. For subject-wise study material, see the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

sections.h2: E-Assessment and OMR: How Science Papers Were Marked
paras: One distinctive feature of the science groups' assessment in 2026 was the use of E-Assessment through OMR sheets together with E-Marking for the science-group optional subjects. In plain terms, the objective parts of those papers were answered on machine-readable OMR sheets and marked electronically, which is designed to make marking faster and more consistent than hand-marking thousands of objective answers. For students, the practical meaning is that the objective section rewards careful sheet-filling as much as subject knowledge: a correctly known answer marked in the wrong bubble, or a half-filled bubble, can cost marks that knowledge alone would have earned, so students preparing for the next attempt should practise OMR-style answering as part of their revision.

E-Marking also changes how students should think about scrutiny and rechecking. Because the objective marking is electronic, a scrutiny request is more likely to be useful when there is a clear discrepancy, such as marks far below class performance or a suspected error in the subjective section, than when a student simply hopes for a few extra marks. The scrutiny fee reported from the board's scrutiny form is Rs 1,000 per paper, and no scrutiny deadline is stated in the material this guide is based on, so students should check the board's official website for the current notice. Whether or not you apply for scrutiny, revise the open paper in parallel, because waiting for a scrutiny outcome before opening the book wastes the most valuable resource you have, which is time.

sections.h2: What Passing All Six Papers Really Means
paras: Passing all six papers sounds simple, but under the new grading system it has a precise meaning that students should understand. It means scoring at or above 40% in every one of the six papers, with no paper left ungraded, because a single paper below 40% breaks the full pass even if the other five are strong. This is why the 15,036 figure matters: those are the students who cleared every paper, while every other appeared student has at least one paper still open. Students sometimes add up their total marks and assume a high total compensates for a weak paper, but the system works paper by paper, and a strong performance in one subject does not rescue an ungraded paper in another.

For students who passed all six, the message is straightforward: congratulations, and carry the same standard into Part-II, where the same 40% logic applies. For students with open papers, the message is equally clear: your job is defined by the list of open papers, not by your total, and it should be tackled paper by paper, starting with the paper closest to 40%. Work from the textbook, practise objective questions in OMR style where relevant, and write subjective answers under timed conditions, because both halves of a science paper need practice. The [blog](/blog/) carries study guides for intermediate science subjects, and your college teachers can identify which chapters carried the most marks in the papers you missed.

sections.h2: If You Have Open Papers: A Practical Plan
paras: Begin by making the paper-by-paper list and sharing it with a parent and a teacher, because adults who see the exact gaps can help you plan realistically and can tell you what support your college offers, such as extra classes or remedial sessions. Then set a daily revision slot for the open papers alongside your Part-II study, protecting Part-II college hours while giving the open papers focused time each day. Start with the paper closest to passing so that an early success builds momentum, and use the overlap between Part-I and Part-II science chapters deliberately, since revising a Part-I concept often strengthens the Part-II chapter built on it. Keep a weekly checklist of chapters revised and practice tests completed, and review it every weekend.

Avoid the two most common mistakes. The second is stopping study while waiting for a notice, which turns a small gap into a forgotten subject by the time the examination arrives. Keep your result, admit card and registration details safe, because the reappearance process will require them, and treat every claim about dates or fees that does not come from the board as unverified until you have checked it yourself.

title: BIEK Ungraded Papers: Scrutiny or Supplementary? How to Choose
desc: One or more BIEK papers ungraded? Compare scrutiny at Rs 1,000 per paper with reappearing subject to eligibility, and learn how to decide which route fits your result.

intro: For thousands of Karachi intermediate students, the HSC Part-I results announced on 26 October 2026 brought a word that is still new to many families: ungraded. Under the new grading system decided by the Inter Board Committee of Chairmen together with the Sindh Universities and Boards Department, scoring below 40% in any paper means the paper is ungraded, so the candidate is unsuccessful in that paper and reappears in it subject to eligibility. Once that fact is clear, two questions follow, and students often confuse them: should I apply for scrutiny of the paper, or should I prepare to reappear in it? This guide explains what each route does, what scrutiny costs, and how to choose between them.

sections.h2: Ungraded Means One Thing: The Paper Is Still Open
paras: Before choosing any route, be precise about what ungraded means. It does not mean the paper is ignored, and it does not mean partial credit has been given; it means the student scored below 40% in that paper and is therefore unsuccessful in it, so the paper remains open until it is cleared through the board's formal process. This applies across the groups announced on 26 October 2026, including Science Pre-Medical, Science General, Commerce in Regular and Private categories, Humanities and Arts in Regular and Private categories, Special Candidates in Arts Regular, and Home Economics. A student with one ungraded paper and a student with four ungraded papers are both in the same formal position for each open paper, even though the size of their workload is very different, and both should start from the same place: a paper-by-paper list of passed and ungraded papers with the gap below 40% measured for each one.

That list is the foundation for every later decision, because scrutiny and reappearance answer different questions. Scrutiny asks whether the marks already awarded were recorded correctly, while reappearance asks whether you can earn a pass by sitting the paper again. If you do not know your exact marks and gaps, you cannot judge which question matters for your paper, and you risk spending money on scrutiny for a paper that actually needs revision, or spending months revising a paper whose marks were simply recorded wrongly. Read your official result on the board's website, www.biek.edu.pk, or the official BIEK Android app, keep a saved copy, and write the list down before you decide anything. For study material while you decide, see the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

sections.h2: Scrutiny: What It Does, What It Costs, What It Cannot Do
paras: Scrutiny is the board's formal rechecking process, and the fee reported from the board's scrutiny form is Rs 1,000 per paper. In practical terms, scrutiny means the board re-examines the paper's marking and totalling to check for errors, and it is worth considering when your marks in a paper are far below what your class performance, college tests or preparation suggested. A student who consistently scored well in a subject through the year and then received a surprisingly low board mark has a reasonable case for scrutiny, because a recording or totalling error, while uncommon, is exactly what scrutiny exists to catch. Apply only through the board's official channel, and check the board's official website and your college notice board for the current scrutiny notice, because no scrutiny deadline is stated in the material this guide is based on and no unofficial date should be trusted.

Students must also understand what scrutiny cannot do. It cannot turn a genuinely weak performance into a pass, it cannot award marks for answers that were not written, and it cannot replace revision, so a paper that was failed because the syllabus was not covered will almost certainly come back with the same result. Scrutiny also costs Rs 1,000 for each paper, so applying for every paper at once, without thinking about which papers show a genuine discrepancy, wastes money that could have gone to books or extra classes. The sensible approach is to shortlist only the papers where the gap between expected and awarded marks is large and hard to explain, apply for those, and revise all open papers in parallel while waiting, so that no time is lost whichever way the scrutiny outcome goes.

diagram.caption: How a BIEK Part-I student should choose between scrutiny and reappearing for each ungraded paper.

sections.h2: Reappearing: Clearing the Paper by Sitting It Again
paras: Reappearing is the route most ungraded students will ultimately use, because it addresses the commonest cause of an ungraded paper, which is that the student's preparation or performance on the day fell short of the 40% line. Under the new grading system, a candidate who is ungraded in a paper reappears in it subject to eligibility, which means the board's rules decide who may reappear and when, and students must follow the board's official notice for the next opportunity rather than assuming a date. No reappearance date for these papers is stated in the material this guide is based on, so any date circulating on social media should be treated as unverified until it appears on the board's official website or your college notice board. Keep your result, admit card and registration details safe, because the reappearance process will require them.

Preparation for a reappearance should be built around the gap you measured. A paper missed by a few marks needs focused revision of the chapters where marks were lost, with timed practice answers to fix exam technique, while a paper with a wide gap needs a fresh study plan from the textbook, chapter by chapter, with solved exercises used to check method. Science students should also practise OMR-style objective questions, since the science-group optional subjects were assessed through E-Assessment and OMR with E-Marking. Set a daily slot for the open papers alongside Part-II study, start with the paper closest to passing, and keep a weekly checklist so slippage shows up early. The [blog](/blog/) carries revision guides for intermediate subjects that can structure this work.

sections.h2: How to Choose: A Simple Decision Guide
paras: The choice becomes simple once it is made paper by paper rather than for the whole result at once. For each ungraded paper, ask two questions. First, were my marks surprisingly low compared with my class performance and preparation? If yes, scrutiny is worth considering for that paper, at Rs 1,000, through the official channel, while you revise it in parallel. Second, did I actually struggle with the syllabus or the paper itself? If yes, revision and reappearance are the answer, and scrutiny is unlikely to change anything. Many students will find that the two answers point to different routes for different papers, and that is perfectly normal: you might apply for scrutiny in one paper where the marks look wrong, and simply revise and reappear in another where you know the preparation was weak.

There are also cases where both routes apply to the same paper, and students should not feel forced to pick only one. Applying for scrutiny does not prevent you from revising, and revising does not prevent you from applying for scrutiny, so the safest combination for a paper with surprisingly low marks is to do both: apply officially, and keep studying as if the scrutiny will change nothing. What students should not do is apply for scrutiny in every paper without discrimination, pay an agent who promises a changed result, or wait idle for either a scrutiny outcome or a reappearance notice. Money spent on indiscriminate scrutiny is money lost, and time spent waiting is the one resource that cannot be recovered before the next examination.

sections.h2: Planning Second Year While Papers Are Open
paras: Whatever route you choose for each paper, Part-II study continues, and the timetable must carry both. Give Part-II its college hours and homework time, and protect a focused daily slot for the open Part-I papers, with the heaviest weight on the paper you will reappear in first. This balance is easier than it looks, because Part-I and Part-II syllabuses overlap heavily in most subjects, so revising a Part-I chapter often strengthens the Part-II chapter built on it. Tell your college teachers which papers are open, because they can point you to the right chapters, mark a sample answer, and advise on the board's eligibility rules for your case, which is far more useful than revising blindly or relying on friends' advice.

Finally, keep your paperwork and your information sources clean. Save your official result, your scrutiny receipt if you apply, your admit card and your registration details in one place, and check the board's official website regularly for notices about scrutiny and reappearance. Treat every unofficial date, fee claim or shortcut offer as unverified, and remember that the board's process is formal: no unofficial channel can alter a mark sheet. The [about page](/about.html) explains how this site's guides are organised for Sindh board students, and the [contact page](/contact.html) explains how to reach us with questions about study material for your open papers.

faqs.a: Under the new grading system, scoring below 40% in any paper means the paper is ungraded, so the candidate is unsuccessful in that paper and reappears in it subject to eligibility. The paper remains open until it is cleared through the board's formal process.

faqs.a: Decide paper by paper. If your marks in a paper are far below what your class performance suggested, consider scrutiny for that paper while revising it in parallel. If you know your preparation was weak, revision and reappearance are the answer, since scrutiny cannot award marks for answers that were not written.

title: Punjab Second Annual Exams 2026: Your 4-Day Countdown Checklist
desc: Punjab HSSC second annual exams start 3 November 2026, just four days away. Use this checklist for timings, roll number slips, centres and what to carry and confirm.
kw: Punjab second annual exams 2026 checklist 3 November
intro: Punjab's HSSC second annual, or supplementary, examinations begin on 3 November 2026, four days away, and for students across the province's nine boards this is the final stretch. The province-wide schedule set by the Punjab Boards Committee of Chairmen runs Part-II, or 12th class, theory papers from 3 to 16 November 2026, followed by Part-I, or 11th class, theory papers from 17 to 28 November 2026, with practical examinations from 1 to 11 December 2026. This checklist covers everything a student should confirm in the next four days: timings, roll number slip and centre, documents to carry, and the honest limits of what is already closed. Admission windows for these examinations are closed, so this guide does not present them as open.

sections.h2: The Schedule at a Glance: What Starts When
paras: The first fact to fix in your mind is the order of the examinations. Part-II theory papers come first, running from 3 to 16 November 2026, and Part-I theory papers follow from 17 to 28 November 2026, with practical examinations scheduled from 1 to 11 December 2026. That order matters for revision planning, because 12th class students have four days left while 11th class students have a longer runway, and each group should plan differently: 12th class students should now be in final revision and past-paper practice, while 11th class students can still use the gap during the Part-II window for structured revision, provided they do not let it drift into idle waiting. All nine Punjab boards share the 3 November start, but students must confirm their own board's subject-wise date sheet, because subject dates can differ between boards even when the overall window is shared.

Timings are fixed across the province and worth memorising now. Morning papers begin at 9:00 AM and evening papers at 2:00 PM, with Friday evening papers starting at 2:30 PM. Practical examinations run in two batches, from 9:00 AM to 12:00 PM and from 1:00 PM to 4:00 PM, with the Friday second batch adjusted to a 2:30 PM start. Arrive early for every paper, because centres close their gates before the paper begins and late arrival is the most preventable way to lose an examination. Set two alarms for each paper day, keep your transport plan ready the night before, and check whether your paper is a morning or evening session so you do not turn up at the wrong time. For general study help in these final days, see the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

sections.h2: Roll Number Slip and Centre: Confirm These First
paras: Your roll number slip is the single most important document for these examinations, and confirming it is the first item on the four-day checklist. Check that your name, photograph, subjects, centre name and centre address are all correct, and confirm the centre's location in advance rather than discovering it on the morning of the paper. If any detail on the slip looks wrong, contact your board or your institution immediately, because corrections made on the day of the paper are difficult and stressful, and in some cases impossible. Students appearing through an institution should collect the slip from their school or college, while private candidates should follow their board's official instructions for obtaining it, and every student should keep a photocopy or photograph of the slip separate from the original.

Visit or at least map your centre before the first paper if you possibly can, noting the travel time, the route, and a backup route in case of traffic or road closures. On the day, aim to reach the centre at least thirty minutes before the paper begins, because that buffer absorbs transport delays and gives you time to find your room and settle. Keep your board's official website and helpline details saved on your phone, and confirm your own board's subject-wise date sheet rather than relying on another board's sheet, since the Multan subject dates quoted in news coverage are examples from one board's sheet, not a guarantee for every board. The [blog](/blog/) carries further examination-day guides for Punjab board students.

diagram.caption: The province-wide schedule for the HSSC second annual examinations.

sections.h2: What to Carry, and What to Leave at Home
paras: Pack your examination bag the night before each paper, not on the morning of it. The essentials are your original roll number slip, your national identity card or the board's accepted identity document, pens in blue or black as your board directs, and the subject-specific items your paper allows, such as a geometry box for mathematics or an approved calculator where the board permits one. Carry water if your centre allows it, and keep your bag simple so that checking at the gate is quick. Do not carry a mobile phone into the examination hall, because boards treat possession of a phone or any unfair-means material as a serious offence with consequences that can extend far beyond one paper, and the safest approach is to leave the phone at home or with a trusted person outside the centre.

Dress and behaviour matter too, in ways students sometimes underestimate. Follow your centre's instructions about seating, keep your slip visible for invigilators, and read the instructions on the question paper before writing anything, because a few minutes spent understanding the paper's structure saves far more time than it costs. If a question is unclear, ask the invigilator rather than guessing at the instruction, and manage your time by allocating minutes per question before you start writing. Students who have prepared with past papers will find this easier, because they already know how long each question type takes, and the final four days are best spent on timed practice rather than on reading new material for the first time.

sections.h2: Admission Windows Are Closed: What That Means
paras: An important honesty note for this checklist: the admission windows for the second annual examinations, which ran from 24 September to 17 October 2026 across single, double and triple fee stages, are now closed, and this guide does not present them as open. Students who are already admitted should focus entirely on the checklist above, while students who missed admission should contact their board directly for advice about the next available opportunity rather than trusting agents or social media posts that claim late admission is still possible. No unofficial channel can create an admission that the board has closed, and money paid to such a channel is money lost, so the only safe advice for a missed admission is the board's own guidance.

The same caution applies to every other claim about these examinations. Subject dates quoted from the Multan date sheet, such as 12th class English on 4 November or Physics on 16 November, are examples from one board's sheet, and your own board's sheet is the document that governs your papers. Rechecking information from the earlier Part-I result, where all nine boards announced on 22 October 2026 at 10:00 AM with a rechecking window of about fifteen days, is a separate process from the second annual examinations and should not be confused with them. When in doubt, check your board's official website, ask your institution, and treat any claim that cannot be confirmed officially as unverified.

sections.h2: Final Four Days: A Revision Plan That Works
paras: With four days left, the best revision plan is narrow, timed and honest. List your papers in order, identify the chapters that carry the most marks in each, and give each paper a fixed daily slot, with the heaviest weight on the paper that comes first. Work through past papers under timed conditions, mark your own answers strictly, and spend the remaining time only on the chapters where marks were lost, rather than re-reading chapters you already know. Sleep properly the night before each paper, because a tired mind loses more marks than a missed chapter, and eat and travel on a plan made the night before so that the morning of the paper holds no surprises.

For 11th class students, whose papers begin on 17 November, the same discipline applies over a longer period, with one extra warning: do not waste the Part-II window. Use those two weeks for structured revision, chapter by chapter, with weekly self-tests, and resist the temptation to treat the gap as a holiday that will somehow be recovered later. For both groups, the [about page](/about.html) explains how this site's study guides are organised, and the [contact page](/contact.html) explains how to reach us with questions. Four days, or two weeks, is enough time to turn preparation into performance, provided the plan is followed daily and the official date sheet, not rumour, governs every decision.
