title: Punjab Second Annual 12th Class 2026: Subject Dates Guide and Warnings
desc: 12th class second annual papers run 3-16 November 2026. Read the Multan-sheet subject windows for English, Maths, Biology, Computer Science, Chemistry and Physics.
kw: Punjab second annual 12th class subject dates 2026 guide
intro: For 12th class students in Punjab, the second annual examinations are now only days away, with Part-II theory papers running from 3 to 16 November 2026 under the province-wide schedule. Subject-wise planning matters enormously in such a short window, because the gap between two papers decides how much revision each subject gets, and students who know their subject dates can plan backwards from each paper instead of revising blindly. This guide sets out the subject windows from the BISE Multan date sheet, including English Compulsory on 4 November, Mathematics and Biology on 6 November, Computer Science on 10 November, Chemistry on 12 November and Physics on 16 November, with a warning to confirm your own board's sheet.

sections.h2: The Multan Sheet: 12th Class Subject Windows
paras: The BISE Multan date sheet gives 12th class students a concrete sequence to plan around. English Compulsory falls on 4 November, very early in the window, which means English revision must be finished before the examinations begin rather than fitted in afterwards. Mathematics and Biology fall on 6 November, giving students two days after English to switch subjects and revise, while Computer Science follows on 10 November, Chemistry on 12 November, and Physics on 16 November, which is the last day of the Part-II window. That sequence is the backbone of a revision plan: work backwards from each date, giving the earliest papers the most attention now, and letting later papers take a lighter daily slot until their turn approaches.

It is worth noting what this sequence implies about workload. A student taking Mathematics, Chemistry and Physics faces papers on 6, 12 and 16 November, with gaps of six and four days between them, which is workable if revision is already underway but punishing if it starts from scratch. A student taking Biology instead of Mathematics faces Biology on 6 November and then a longer run to Chemistry and Physics, which changes the balance of the plan. Whatever your combination, write your own subject dates on a single page, mark the gaps between papers, and assign revision hours in proportion to both the gap and your weakness in each subject. For subject-wise study help, see the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

sections.h2: The Warning That Matters Most: Confirm Your Own Board's Sheet
paras: Every subject date in this guide comes from the BISE Multan date sheet, and that fact must be stated plainly, because Punjab has nine boards and subject-wise dates can differ between them. All nine boards share the 3 November start and the overall Part-II window of 3 to 16 November 2026, but a student under BISE Lahore, Rawalpindi, Gujranwala or any other board cannot safely assume that English falls on 4 November or Physics on 16 November for their board. Using another board's sheet as if it were your own is one of the most expensive mistakes a student can make, because it can mean revising the wrong subject for a paper, or worse, missing a paper entirely through a wrong date.

Confirming your own sheet takes ten minutes and should be done today. Check your board's official website, collect the date sheet from your school or college, and compare it paper by paper with the Multan windows given here, noting every difference on your own revision page. If your board's sheet shows a different date for any subject, your board's sheet governs, full stop, and the Multan dates become irrelevant for you. Save a copy of your own sheet on your phone and keep a printed copy with your roll number slip, so that both are checked together the night before each paper. The [blog](/blog/) carries further examination guides, but no guide can replace your own board's official date sheet.

diagram.caption: Subject dates from the Multan date sheet; confirm your own board's sheet before planning.

paras: With the subject dates known, the most effective planning method is to work backwards. Take the first paper, English on 4 November in the Multan sheet, and ask what must be finished by 3 November: essay and precis practice, grammar revision, and at least one timed past paper. Then do the same for 6 November, whether your subject is Mathematics or Biology, assigning the days after English to that subject's heaviest chapters and to timed numerical or diagram practice. Repeat the process for Computer Science on 10 November, Chemistry on 12 November and Physics on 16 November, so that every paper has a defined finish line and no subject is left to chance. This method works because it forces decisions about priority, and priority is exactly what a short examination window demands.

Within each subject's slot, follow a simple pattern: revise the highest-mark chapters first, practise past-paper questions under timed conditions, mark your answers strictly, and spend the remaining time only on the chapters where marks were lost. Do not start new, low-weight chapters in the final days, and do not re-read chapters you already know well, because both habits feel productive while adding few marks. Sleep properly before each paper, travel on a plan made the night before, and arrive at the centre at least thirty minutes early, since morning papers begin at 9:00 AM and evening papers at 2:00 PM, with Friday evening papers at 2:30 PM. A plan followed daily beats a perfect plan followed once.

sections.h2: Subject Tips for the Five Key Papers
paras: English Compulsory rewards practice over reading, so spend the remaining days writing essays, precis and comprehension answers under time limits, and revising grammar rules through examples rather than through rules alone. Mathematics rewards worked examples, so solve past-paper numericals by hand, check each step, and keep a short list of formulas you tend to forget, revising that list every evening. Biology rewards labelled diagrams and precise definitions, so practise drawing and labelling diagrams from memory and writing definitions in the textbook's language, because examiners award marks for accuracy in both. Computer Science rewards logic practice, so trace programs by hand, practise short questions on data and networks, and revise definitions until they can be written without hesitation.

Chemistry rewards balanced equations and numerical practice, so work through reaction types, practise mole and concentration calculations, and revise the chapters that carry the most marks first. Physics rewards numerical method, so practise past-paper numericals with units and significant figures, revise derivations by writing them out rather than reading them, and keep a formula sheet that you test yourself on daily. In every subject, the same principle holds: marks come from answers written under timed conditions, not from hours spent reading. If a chapter is weak, study it from the textbook, attempt its questions, and move on, because the examination rewards coverage of the whole syllabus more than perfection in one chapter.

sections.h2: After the Last Paper: Practicals and Results Thinking
paras: Physics on 16 November closes the Part-II theory window in the Multan sheet, but the examination season is not over, because practical examinations follow from 1 to 11 December 2026 in two batches each day, from 9:00 AM to 12:00 PM and from 1:00 PM to 4:00 PM, with the Friday second batch adjusted to a 2:30 PM start. Students should therefore keep their practical notebooks, apparatus familiarity and viva preparation ready during the theory window, rather than treating practicals as an afterthought once theory ends. Confirm your practical date, batch and centre from your own board's sheet as soon as it is published, and keep your practical record complete and signed, because an incomplete record is a preventable loss of marks.

Once the examinations end, resist the urge to chase rumours about results, marking or expected dates, and instead keep your roll number slip, admit card and date sheet safe until the result process is complete. If you later feel a paper was marked incorrectly, your board will publish a formal rechecking process, and the earlier Part-I result context, where all nine boards announced on 22 October 2026 at 10:00 AM with a rechecking window of about fifteen days, shows how such processes normally work, though the second annual rechecking notice must be checked on its own terms. title: Punjab Second Annual 11th Class 2026: After the 12th Papers, Your Turn
desc: 11th class second annual papers run 17-28 November 2026, after the 12th papers. Read the Multan-sheet subject windows, practical dates and a revision plan for the gap.
kw: Punjab second annual 11th class papers 17 November 2026 revision
intro: While 12th class students sit their second annual papers from 3 to 16 November 2026, 11th class students across Punjab have a different challenge: a waiting period that must be used, not wasted. Part-I, or 11th class, theory papers run from 17 to 28 November 2026 under the province-wide schedule, followed by practical examinations from 1 to 11 December 2026, and the gap before the first paper must be used well. This guide sets out the 11th class subject windows from the BISE Multan date sheet, including English Compulsory on 18 November, Computer Science on 23 November, Mathematics and Biology on 25 November, and Physics on 27 November, with a revision plan for the gap and a warning to confirm your own board's sheet.

sections.h2: Your Window: 17 to 28 November, After the 12th Papers
paras: The order of the second annual examinations is deliberate: Part-II papers come first, from 3 to 16 November 2026, and Part-I papers follow from 17 to 28 November 2026, so that centres, invigilators and marking can move from one group to the next in an orderly way. For 11th class students, this order creates both an opportunity and a trap. The opportunity is nearly three weeks of revision time from today, 30 October 2026, before the first paper, which is enough to cover a syllabus properly if it is used daily. The trap is that a long runway feels comfortable, so revision drifts, days slip, and the first paper arrives with chapters still unrevised. Treat the gap as a working period from today, not as a holiday that ends on 16 November, and the window becomes an advantage rather than a risk.

Timings for the Part-I papers follow the same province-wide pattern as Part-II: morning papers begin at 9:00 AM and evening papers at 2:00 PM, with Friday evening papers starting at 2:30 PM. Practical examinations follow from 1 to 11 December 2026 in two batches, from 9:00 AM to 12:00 PM and from 1:00 PM to 4:00 PM, with the Friday second batch adjusted to a 2:30 PM start. Write your own papers, timings and centre details on a single page as soon as your board's sheet is confirmed, and keep that page with your roll number slip, because a plan written down is far harder to drift away from than a plan kept only in your head. For subject-wise study help during the gap, see the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

sections.h2: The Multan Sheet: 11th Class Subject Windows
paras: The BISE Multan date sheet gives 11th class students a concrete sequence to plan around. English Compulsory falls on 18 November, the day after the Part-I window opens, which means English revision must be complete before the window begins, not fitted in during it. Computer Science follows on 23 November, giving five days after English to switch subjects, while Mathematics and Biology fall on 25 November, and Physics on 27 November, one day before the window closes on 28 November. That sequence shapes the whole revision plan: English first and finished early, then a focused block for Computer Science, then the science subjects in the final stretch, with the gaps between papers used for the next subject rather than for rest.

As with the 12th class guide, the warning about boards must be stated plainly: these dates come from the Multan sheet, and all nine Punjab boards share the overall windows but can differ on subject-wise dates. A student under any other board must confirm their own board's sheet and follow it wherever it differs from the Multan dates, because your board's sheet is the document that governs your papers. Check your board's official website, collect the sheet from your school or college, and mark every difference on your own revision page before you plan a single day. The [blog](/blog/) carries further examination guides, but no guide can replace your own board's official date sheet.

sections.h2: Using the Gap: A Revision Plan From 30 October to 17 November
paras: The gap from 30 October to 17 November should be divided into three phases. In the first phase, from now until about 10 November, cover the full syllabus chapter by chapter, working from the textbook, making short notes, and attempting solved exercises to check your method. In the second phase, from about 11 to 16 November, switch to timed past papers, marking your answers strictly and spending the remaining time only on chapters where marks were lost. In the third phase, the examination window itself, revise one subject at a time in the order of your papers, using the gaps between papers for the next subject and keeping each day's work narrow and timed. This structure works because it separates learning from testing, and testing from final polishing, instead of mixing all three into a confused final week.

Within each phase, keep the daily pattern simple and repeatable: a fixed number of study hours, a chapter list for the day, timed practice, and a short evening review of what was actually completed. Track completion on paper, not in your head, because a checklist reveals slippage while there is still time to correct it, while memory hides it until the paper arrives. English deserves early attention, since it falls on 18 November and cannot be crammed in a single day, while Mathematics, Biology and Physics reward daily numerical and diagram practice that should run through the whole gap rather than starting in the final week. Sleep properly throughout, because a tired mind in the examination hall loses more marks than a missed chapter.

sections.h2: Subject Tips for the 11th Class Papers
paras: English Compulsory rewards writing practice, so write essays, precis and comprehension answers under time limits through the gap, and revise grammar through examples rather than through rules alone. Computer Science rewards logic and definitions, so trace programs by hand, practise short questions, and revise definitions until they can be written without hesitation. Mathematics rewards worked examples, so solve past-paper numericals by hand, check each step, and keep a short list of formulas you tend to forget, revising that list every evening. Biology rewards labelled diagrams and precise definitions, so practise drawing diagrams from memory and writing definitions in the textbook's language.

Physics rewards numerical method, so practise past-paper numericals with units and significant figures, revise derivations by writing them out rather than reading them, and test yourself on a formula sheet daily. In every subject, marks come from answers written under timed conditions, not from hours spent reading, so the gap should be filled with practice, not with re-reading. If a chapter is weak, study it from the textbook, attempt its questions, and move on, because the examination rewards coverage of the whole syllabus more than perfection in one chapter. Ask your teachers which chapters carried the most marks in past papers, and give those chapters the heaviest weight in your plan.

sections.h2: After Theory: Practicals, and Keeping Documents Safe
paras: Practical examinations follow the theory window, running from 1 to 11 December 2026 in two batches each day, and 11th class students should keep practical preparation running alongside theory revision rather than leaving it until theory ends. Keep your practical notebook complete and signed, revise the experiments for your subjects, and practise viva answers, because practical marks are often the easiest marks to secure and the easiest to lose through an incomplete record. Confirm your practical date, batch and centre from your own board's sheet as soon as it is published, and arrive with the same punctuality as for theory papers, since the batch timings are fixed and late arrival disrupts the whole batch.

Once the examinations end, keep your roll number slip, admit card, date sheet and practical record safe until the result process is complete, and resist chasing rumours about results or marking. If you later feel a paper was marked incorrectly, your board will publish a formal rechecking process, and you should follow that notice on its own terms rather than trusting social media claims. The earlier Part-I result context, where all nine boards announced on 22 October 2026 at 10:00 AM with a rechecking window of about fifteen days, shows how such processes normally work, but each notice must be checked separately. The [about page](/about.html) explains how this site's guides are organised, and the [contact page](/contact.html) explains how to reach us with questions.

title: BISE Hyderabad Inquiry: 30-Day Report and What Students Should Do
desc: After the 23 October 2026 Hyderabad inquiry order, students ask what changes for them. Learn what the committee must report, why results stand, and what to keep safe.
kw: BISE Hyderabad inquiry 30 day report students what to do
intro: On 23 October 2026, the Sindh government suspended the BISE Hyderabad Deputy Controller of the Top Secret Branch and formed a three-member inquiry committee to examine alleged irregularities in the Class XII annual examination 2026 results, and students have asked what it means for their results. The short answer, based on the verified facts, is that the announced results have not been cancelled, the allegations are allegations and not proven findings, and no student has been named as a beneficiary of manipulation. This guide explains what the committee was asked to do, what its 30-day reporting window means, what students should and should not do while the inquiry runs, and how to protect your own record through formal channels rather than rumour.

paras: The action began with two linked decisions by the Sindh government. First, the Deputy Controller of the Top Secret Branch at the Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education Hyderabad, Ijaz Ali Kaka, was suspended on the orders of the Provincial Minister for Universities and Boards, Muhammad Ismail Rahoo. Second, a three-member inquiry committee was formed through a notification issued by Universities Secretary Abbas Baloch, headed by Professor Dr Arbeela Bhutto, with members Additional Secretary Amir, also reported as Ameer, Fazal Owaisi and Mehran University Registrar Dr Nasrullah Pirzada. These are the verified facts of the order, and they should be reported exactly as stated, without adding motives, outcomes or names that were not published.

The scope of the inquiry is also defined, and students should understand its limits. The committee is examining alleged irregularities in the Class XII, or Intermediate Part-II, annual examination 2026 results, specifically in the pre-medical and pre-engineering groups, looking at position holders, top-ten candidates and A-1 grade students, and at the checking, tabulation and announcement processes behind those results. The allegations themselves circulated through social media and public complaints, which is how they reached the authorities, but circulation is not proof, and this guide treats them strictly as allegations until the committee reports. No student has been named publicly as a beneficiary of manipulation, and no article should name any student in that connection.

sections.h2: The 30-Day Report: What It Means and What It Does Not
paras: The committee's report is due within 30 days of 23 October 2026, and that wording matters. This guide presents the window as within 30 days, not as a confirmed calendar date, because the verified material states the window in those terms and converting it into a specific date would add a claim the source does not make. Students should therefore watch for the report during that window without treating any particular day as a deadline, and should be suspicious of social media posts that announce a specific reporting date, a leaked outcome, or a decision that the committee has not yet published. The report, when it arrives, will go to the authorities that ordered the inquiry, and any action that follows will be announced through official channels, not through rumour.

It is equally important to understand what the 30-day window does not mean. It does not mean results are suspended while the committee works, it does not mean every Class XII result is under question, and it does not mean students must take any action before the report appears. The inquiry's scope is the pre-medical and pre-engineering groups' position holders, top-ten candidates and A-1 grade students and the processes behind those results, which is a defined subset, not the entire result. Students outside that scope have no reason to worry about their own results on the basis of this inquiry, and students inside it should still wait for an official outcome rather than acting on speculation about what the committee might find.

diagram.alt: Hyderabad Inquiry: What Students Should Do
diagram.caption: The verified facts of the inquiry and the safe steps for students while it runs.

sections.h2: Your Result Stands: Why There Is No Need to Panic
paras: The single most reassuring verified fact in this story is that the announced results have not been cancelled. Students who passed, students who hold positions, and students now in college or preparing for the next stage can continue on the basis of their announced results, because no cancellation has been ordered and no official notice has withdrawn any result. Panic helps no one, and it actively harms students who let rumour disrupt their studies or who pay agents promising to protect a result that is not actually under threat. If your result was announced and you hold an official transcript, that transcript remains your record unless and until an official notice says otherwise, and no social media post can change that.

Students should also resist the temptation to treat the inquiry as a judgement on every high-achieving student. Position holders and A-1 grade students are part of the inquiry's scope because the allegations concerned the processes behind top results, not because every top result is suspect, and the committee's job is to examine processes, including checking, tabulation and announcement, rather than to presume guilt. High achievers should continue their studies normally, keep their documents safe, and respond only to official communications, while other students should avoid speculating about named classmates, since no student has been named and speculation about individuals is both unfair and unverified. The [blog](/blog/) carries further guides for Sindh board students on reading results and using formal processes.

sections.h2: If You Suspect a Problem With Your Own Mark Sheet
paras: The inquiry does not replace the normal, individual route for a student who suspects a discrepancy in their own mark sheet, and that route is formal rechecking. If your marks in a paper look inconsistent with your class performance, or if you believe a totalling or recording error has occurred, apply for rechecking through your board's official process, following the notice published by the board, and keep the receipt and any reference number safe. Rechecking is an individual remedy for an individual mark sheet, and it works whether or not a wider inquiry is running, so students should not wait for the committee's report before using it if they have a genuine concern about their own result. Check your board's official website for the current rechecking notice, fee and last date, and apply only through the official channel.

At the same time, keep your paperwork in order, because every formal process asks for the same documents. Keep your official transcript, mark sheet, admit card, registration details and any rechecking receipt together, in both original and photocopy or photograph form, so that nothing is lost while the inquiry runs or afterwards. If your college or institution asks for documents for admission or verification, provide copies and keep the originals safe, and note down the dates and reference numbers of anything you submit. Students who keep clean records never have to reconstruct their case from memory, and that is the best protection available while any inquiry is unresolved. For general study material, see the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

sections.h2: Rumours, Social Media and Responsible Reading
paras: The Hyderabad allegations reached the authorities partly through social media and public complaints, which shows both the power and the danger of online discussion about board results. Social media can surface genuine concerns, but it can also amplify unverified claims, name students without evidence, and invent outcomes that no authority has announced, and students should read every post about this inquiry with that distinction in mind. A post that cites an official notification, names the committee and its reporting window, and states that results have not been cancelled is reporting verified facts, while a post that names a student, claims a result has been changed, or announces a leaked committee finding is speculation and should be ignored and not shared. Sharing an unverified claim about a named student can harm that student and can spread confusion that no later correction fully undoes.

The responsible habit for the coming weeks is simple: check one official source before believing or sharing any claim about the inquiry, whether that source is the board's official website, the Universities and Boards Department, or your institution's notice board. If a claim cannot be confirmed officially, treat it as unverified and do not act on it, whether it concerns your own result, a classmate's result, or the committee's findings. Continue your studies normally, keep your documents safe, and use formal rechecking for any individual concern, because those three habits protect you regardless of what the committee eventually reports. The [about page](/about.html) explains how this site verifies board news, and the [contact page](/contact.html) explains how to reach us with questions.

The committee is headed by Professor Dr Arbeela Bhutto; its report is due within 30 days.
The allegations concern Class XII pre-medical and pre-engineering results; they are ALLEGATIONS, not proven findings.
The announced results have NOT been cancelled, and no student has been named.

faqs.q: Has the BISE Hyderabad Class XII result been cancelled?
faqs.a: No. The announced results have not been cancelled. The inquiry examines alleged irregularities in the Class XII annual examination 2026 results for pre-medical and pre-engineering groups, but no cancellation has been ordered, so students should continue on the basis of their announced results.

faqs.q: What is the inquiry committee, and when does it report?
faqs.a: A three-member committee headed by Professor Dr Arbeela Bhutto, with members Additional Secretary Amir/Ameer Fazal Owaisi and Mehran University Registrar Dr Nasrullah Pirzada, was formed on 23 October 2026. Its report is due within 30 days of that date, presented here as a window rather than a confirmed calendar date.

faqs.q: Are the allegations against BISE Hyderabad proven?
faqs.a: No. The allegations circulated on social media and through public complaints and are allegations, not proven findings. The committee's job is to examine the checking, tabulation and announcement processes, and no outcome should be treated as decided before it reports.

faqs.q: Has any student been named in the inquiry?
faqs.a: No student has been named publicly as a beneficiary of manipulation. Students should not speculate about named classmates, and should ignore social media posts that name individuals without an official source.

faqs.q: What should I do if I suspect an error in my own mark sheet?
faqs.a: Use formal rechecking through your board's official process, following the board's published notice for fee and last date, and keep your official transcript, mark sheet, admit card and rechecking receipt safe. Do not wait for the committee's report before using this individual remedy if you have a genuine concern.

title: Sindh Boards November 2026 Calendar: What to Watch, Date by Date
desc: Your November 2026 watchlist for Sindh boards: Punjab second annual windows, the Hyderabad inquiry report window, official board sites, and what is not yet announced.
intro: November 2026 is a busy month for board students in and around Sindh, with an honest note that no new STBB announcement was verified on 30 October 2026. The month's confirmed landmarks come from neighbouring Punjab's second annual examinations, which run through November, and from the BISE Hyderabad inquiry, whose report is due within 30 days of 23 October 2026, while Sindh's own boards continue their normal post-result processes for the Karachi results announced in late October. This guide pulls those threads into one calendar, gives you the official websites to check, and marks clearly which items are confirmed, which are windows rather than single dates, and which announcements have not yet been made, so that you can plan November without chasing rumours.

sections.h2: The Headline Windows: Punjab Second Annual Examinations
paras: The largest dated item on the November calendar is the Punjab HSSC second annual examination programme, which matters directly to Punjab students and indirectly to Sindh students watching how supplementary examinations are run. Part-II, or 12th class, theory papers run from 3 to 16 November 2026, followed by Part-I, or 11th class, theory papers from 17 to 28 November 2026, with practical examinations from 1 to 11 December 2026. Morning papers begin at 9:00 AM and evening papers at 2:00 PM, with Friday evening papers at 2:30 PM, and practical batches run from 9:00 AM to 12:00 PM and from 1:00 PM to 4:00 PM, with the Friday second batch adjusted to a 2:30 PM start. Sindh students with friends or family in Punjab can use these dates to understand the provincial timetable, but they should not confuse Punjab's schedule with any Sindh board schedule, which follows its own notices.

Subject windows from the BISE Multan date sheet give the programme its shape, and they are worth noting as examples, with the usual warning that other boards' sheets can differ. For 12th class, English Compulsory falls on 4 November, Mathematics and Biology on 6 November, Computer Science on 10 November, Chemistry on 12 November and Physics on 16 November, while for 11th class, English Compulsory falls on 18 November, Computer Science on 23 November, Mathematics and Biology on 25 November and Physics on 27 November. Admission windows for these examinations, which ran from 24 September to 17 October 2026, are closed, so November is examination time, not application time, for Punjab students. For study material during examination season, see the [book collection](/books.html) and the [solved notes](/solved.html).

The second item to watch in November is the report of the three-member committee formed on 23 October 2026 to examine alleged irregularities in the BISE Hyderabad Class XII annual examination 2026 results for pre-medical and pre-engineering groups. The committee, headed by Professor Dr Arbeela Bhutto, with members Additional Secretary Amir, also reported as Ameer, Fazal Owaisi and Mehran University Registrar Dr Nasrullah Pirzada, must report within 30 days of 23 October 2026, which places its reporting window inside November. This guide deliberately presents the window as within 30 days rather than as a confirmed calendar date, because the verified material states it in those terms, and students should watch official channels during that window without treating any particular day as a deadline or believing social media claims of a leaked outcome.

While waiting, the verified position remains unchanged and reassuring: the announced results have not been cancelled, the allegations are allegations and not proven findings, and no student has been named as a beneficiary of manipulation. Students should therefore continue their studies normally, keep official transcripts and mark sheets safe, and use formal rechecking for any individual discrepancy in their own mark sheet rather than waiting for the committee. If the committee's report leads to any action, that action will be announced through official channels, and this site will report it only once it is officially confirmed. Until then, every claim about the inquiry's outcome that cannot be confirmed officially should be treated as unverified and not shared.

sections.h2: Sindh Boards: Post-Result Work After the October Results
paras: For Sindh students themselves, November is principally a post-result month, following two major Karachi announcements in late October. The Board of Secondary Education Karachi announced the Class 9 Science Group result on 28 October 2026, with 123,757 students passing all papers, 53,849 failing, and large partial-pass groups in between, under the new rule that a paper below 40% is ungraded. The Board of Intermediate Education Karachi announced HSC Part-I results for all remaining groups on 26 October 2026, including Science Pre-Medical, Science General, Commerce in Regular and Private categories, Humanities and Arts in Regular and Private categories, Special Candidates in Arts Regular, and Home Economics. Students from both results should spend November on the practical follow-up those results require: reading mark sheets paper by paper, revising open papers, considering scrutiny where marks look surprisingly low, and watching official websites for reappearance notices.

Scrutiny is the most time-sensitive of those follow-ups, and it illustrates why November requires weekly checks of official sources. The BIEK scrutiny fee reported from the board's scrutiny form is Rs 1,000 per paper, but no scrutiny deadline is stated in the verified material used here, so students must check the board's official website and their college notice board for the current notice rather than trusting an unofficial date. BSEK students in the same position should check bsek.edu.pk for their board's notices, since no reappearance date for the Class 9 Science open papers was stated in the 28 October announcement. A weekly habit of checking both official sites takes ten minutes and prevents the commonest November mistake, which is missing a genuine deadline while following a rumoured one.

sections.h2: Official Websites: Your November Checklist of Sources
paras: November is also a good month to save the official websites that govern every item on this calendar, because every rumour in board season can be settled by checking one of them. For Karachi, the Board of Secondary Education Karachi is at bsek.edu.pk and the Board of Intermediate Education Karachi is at biek.edu.pk, with results also available on the official BIEK Android app. For the other Sindh boards, the Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education Sukkur is at bisesuksindh.edu.pk and the Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education Larkana is at biselrk.edu.pk. Punjab students should use their own board's official website for date sheets, roll number slips and notices, and should confirm their own board's subject-wise sheet rather than relying on another board's sheet, since subject dates can differ between boards.

Make a simple November routine around these sources: check your board's website once a week, read your institution's notice board on the same day, and note anything new in a diary with the date you saw it. That routine catches genuine notices early, whether they concern scrutiny, reappearance, practical examinations or the Hyderabad inquiry, and it protects you from the opposite error of acting on a screenshot whose source cannot be verified. Keep your result, admit card, registration details and any scrutiny or rechecking receipts together, so that any process you need to join can be joined immediately. The [blog](/blog/) carries further board guides, and the [about page](/about.html) explains how this site verifies the board news it reports.

sections.h2: What Has NOT Been Announced: An Honesty Note
paras: A watchlist is only trustworthy if it says what is missing as clearly as what is present, so this section states the gaps plainly. No new announcement from the Sindh Textbook Board itself was verified on 30 October 2026, so this guide claims no new STBB book, curriculum or examination announcement for that date, and students should treat any such claim circulating online as unverified unless it appears on an official STBB or board channel. The standing STBB context remains the 2026-27 textbooks for Early Childhood to Grade 10, under the Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Textbook Series, with 195 titles in Sindhi, Urdu and English and 52 million sets, whose distribution was inaugurated on 19 February 2026, and a revised curriculum from the next academic year focusing on research, scientific thinking, creativity and related goals, with pupils to be relieved of excessive book burden.

Other gaps matter too, and students should know them before they plan around rumours. No confirmed BSEK General Group or private Science result beyond the 28 October Science Group announcement is part of the verified material, no BIEK Part-II supplementary dates for 2026 beyond what is listed here are confirmed, and no position-holder or topper names for the BIEK or BSEK 2026 results were published in the verified sources. Punjab's second annual admission windows are closed, not open, and the Hyderabad inquiry's outcome is not yet known. November will bring genuine news, but until it arrives through official channels, the honest position is to plan around the confirmed windows above, check official websites weekly, and keep studying. title: Arabic Alphabet and Harakat for Beginners
desc: Learn the Arabic alphabet and harakat step by step: letter shapes, sounds, short vowels, and simple reading practice for complete beginners.
kw: Arabic alphabet harakat beginners learn Arabic letters
intro: The Arabic alphabet is the doorway to reading Arabic, and it is also the doorway to reading the Quran with understanding. Arabic has 28 letters, written from right to left, and most letters change shape depending on whether they stand alone, join to the letter before them, or join to the letters on both sides. This sounds difficult at first, but the system is regular, and students who learn a small group of letters at a time usually make fast progress. Harakat are the short vowel marks placed above or below a letter, and they tell the reader which vowel sound to pronounce. In this guide, we explain the alphabet, the letter shapes, and the harakat in simple steps, with a practice method that any beginner can follow at home or in class.

sections.h2: The 28 Letters and the Right-to-Left Direction
paras: Arabic is written and read from right to left, which is the first habit a beginner must build. Start at the right side of the page and move leftwards, and practise by pointing at each letter as you read it. The 28 letters are alif, ba, ta, tha, jeem, ha, kha, dal, dhal, ra, zay, seen, sheen, saad, daad, ta, za, ain, ghain, fa, qaf, kaf, lam, meem, noon, ha, waw, and ya. Do not try to memorise all 28 in one sitting; learn them in groups of four or five, saying each name aloud and writing it several times. When you can name and write one group without hesitation, add the next group.

Many Arabic letters come in pairs that look alike but differ by dots. Ba has one dot below, ta has two dots above, and tha has three dots above, yet all three share the same basic shape. Seen and sheen are another pair, differing only by three dots, and the same pattern repeats with several other letters. This is good news for beginners, because learning one shape often means learning two or three letters at once. Pay close attention to the dots from the very first day, because a misplaced dot changes both the letter and the meaning of the word.
bullets: Learn letters in small groups of four or five, not all 28 at once
Read and write from right to left, pointing at each letter as you read
Watch the dots carefully: ba, ta, and tha share one shape but differ by dots

sections.h2: How Letter Shapes Change When Letters Join
paras: Most Arabic letters join to the letter that follows them, so a letter can look different at the beginning, middle, and end of a word. For example, the letter ba looks like a small boat with a dot below when it stands alone, but when it joins to the next letter it loses its tail and stretches into a connecting stroke. This is normal and regular, and once you learn the four forms of a few common letters, the rest become easy to predict. Practise by writing the same letter in all its forms on one line, and say the form aloud as you write it: isolated, initial, medial, and final.

Six letters do not join to the letter that follows them: alif, dal, dhal, ra, zay, and waw. When one of these letters appears in a word, the next letter must start afresh, which creates a small break inside the word. Beginners often mistake this break for the end of a word, so it is worth learning these six non-joining letters early. A simple memory trick is to call them the letters that refuse to hold hands with the next letter. Once you know them, you will read joined words more confidently, because you will expect the break instead of being surprised by it.

sections.h2: Harakat: The Short Vowels That Guide Pronunciation
paras: Harakat are small marks that show the short vowel sound of a letter. Fatha is a small slant above the letter and gives an short a sound, as in ba. Kasra is a small slant below the letter and gives an short i sound, as in bi. Damma is a small curl above the letter and gives an short u sound, as in bu. These three marks are the foundation of Arabic reading, and a beginner who masters them can sound out most simple words. Practise by taking one letter, such as ba, and reading it with all three harakat in turn: ba, bi, bu, until the sounds come without thinking.

Two more marks complete the beginner's toolkit. Sukun is a small circle above a letter and means that the letter carries no vowel, so it joins its sound to the vowel before it. Tanween doubles the fatha, kasra, or damma and adds an n sound at the end, giving an, in, or un. Shadda, which looks like a small w shape, means the letter is doubled and pronounced with extra strength. You do not need to master all of these in the first week, but you should recognise them when you see them. Reading practice with harakat marked, as in school textbooks and beginners' Quran copies, makes all of these marks familiar step by step.

diagram.alt: Reading an Arabic Letter in Four Steps
diagram.caption: Name the letter, note its shape, add the harakat, then blend the sound.

sections.h2: Long Vowels and the Letters Alif, Waw, and Ya
paras: After the short vowels, the next step is the long vowels, which stretch a sound for about twice as long. Alif after a fatha stretches the a sound, waw after a damma stretches the u sound, and ya after a kasra stretches the i sound. For example, ba with fatha and alif becomes baa, a longer sound that is easy to hear when a teacher reads it aloud. The difference between short and long vowels matters for meaning, so listen carefully when your teacher reads and copy the length of each vowel. Reading aloud every day, even for ten minutes, trains your ear faster than silent reading alone.

A common beginner mistake is to rush past long vowels and pronounce them as short vowels, which makes words hard to recognise. Another mistake is to add a long vowel where none is written, which changes the word. The cure for both mistakes is slow, loud reading with a finger under each word. Read the word letter by letter first, then read it again as a whole word, and finally read the whole sentence smoothly. This three-pass method feels slow at first, but it builds accuracy, and accuracy is what turns a struggling reader into a confident one within a few weeks.

sections.h2: A Simple Daily Practice Plan for Beginners
paras: A short daily routine beats a long weekly session, because Arabic reading is a skill that grows with repetition. Spend five minutes writing the letter group you are learning, five minutes reading words that use those letters, and five minutes listening to a teacher or a reliable recording and repeating after it. Keep a small notebook in which you copy five new words each day with their harakat and meanings, and review yesterday's words before adding new ones. If you miss a day, simply resume the next day without trying to double the work, because steady practice always beats hurried catch-up.

Use the resources around you to stay on track. Your class textbook and your teacher's pronunciation are your best guides, and solved notes can help you check your understanding of a lesson. For extra reading material and revision help, explore the collection on [Solved Notes](/solved.html), browse the full book list on [Books](/books.html), and visit the article index on [Blog](/blog/) for more study guides. Remember that every fluent Arabic reader once struggled with the first letters, so patience and daily practice will carry you further than any shortcut.

points: Arabic has 28 letters, written and read from right to left.
Most letters change shape when they join, but six letters never join forwards.
Fatha, kasra, and damma give the short a, i, and u sounds.
Dots change the letter, so ba, ta, and tha must be told apart carefully.
Fifteen minutes of daily reading, writing, and listening beats occasional long sessions.

faqs.q: How many letters are in the Arabic alphabet?
faqs.a: The Arabic alphabet has 28 letters, from alif to ya. Beginners should learn them in small groups of four or five, saying each name aloud and writing it several times. Learning the groups in order, with daily review, makes the full alphabet manageable within a few weeks.

faqs.q: What are harakat in Arabic?
faqs.a: Harakat are short vowel marks placed above or below a letter. Fatha gives an a sound, kasra gives an i sound, and damma gives an u sound, while sukun marks a vowelless letter and tanween adds an n sound. These marks guide pronunciation, especially in textbooks and beginners' reading material.

faqs.q: Why do Arabic letters look different inside words?
faqs.a: Most Arabic letters join to the following letter, so their shape changes at the beginning, middle, and end of a word. The basic shape stays recognisable, but tails are dropped and connecting strokes are added. Learning the four forms of a few common letters makes the pattern predictable across the whole alphabet.

faqs.q: Which Arabic letters do not join to the next letter?
faqs.a: Six letters do not join forwards: alif, dal, dhal, ra, zay, and waw. When one of these appears in a word, the next letter starts afresh, creating a small break inside the word. Knowing these six letters early prevents the common mistake of treating that break as the end of a word.

faqs.q: How long does it take a beginner to read Arabic words?
faqs.a: With fifteen minutes of daily practice, most beginners can sound out simple marked words within a few weeks. Progress depends on regular reading aloud, writing the letters, and listening to correct pronunciation. Slow and accurate reading at first is better than fast guessing, because accuracy builds the confidence that later brings speed.

title: Arabic Greetings and Daily Phrases
desc: Learn Arabic greetings and daily phrases with correct pronunciation and manners: salam, replies, thanks, and polite classroom expressions.
kw: Arabic greetings daily phrases salam learn Arabic speaking
intro: Greetings are the friendliest way to begin learning spoken Arabic, because they are short, useful, and used every single day. A student who can greet, thank, apologise, and ask politely in Arabic has already taken a real step into the language, and has also learnt something about Arab manners and Islamic etiquette. The most important greeting is Assalamu Alaikum, peace be upon you, and its reply is Wa Alaikum Assalam, and upon you be peace. In this guide, we explain the common greetings and daily phrases, how to pronounce them, when to use each one, and how to practise them until they come naturally in conversation.

paras: Assalamu Alaikum is the Islamic greeting, and it means peace be upon you. It is used when meeting someone, entering a room, starting a phone call, or greeting a teacher or elder. The reply, Wa Alaikum Assalam, returns the same wish of peace to the speaker, and a fuller reply adds Wa Rahmatullahi Wa Barakatuh, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings. Muslims are encouraged to greet warmly and to reply with an equal or better greeting, so learning both the greeting and the reply together is the correct approach. Practise them as a pair, not as separate words, so that the reply comes automatically when you hear the greeting.

Pronunciation matters, so break the greeting into parts and practise slowly: As-sa-la-mu A-lai-kum. Listen to your teacher's pronunciation and copy the sounds, especially the long vowel in salam and the clear k sound at the end. A common mistake is to rush the greeting into a mumbled single word, which loses both clarity and courtesy. Speak it clearly, with a smile, and look at the person you are greeting, because a greeting is a social act as much as a language exercise. When you greet your teacher or classmates in Arabic each morning, you turn a lesson into a daily habit.

Arabic also has time-based greetings that students will hear in conversations, stories, and lessons. Sabah Al-Khair means good morning, and its reply is Sabah An-Noor, morning of light. Masa Al-Khair means good evening, with the reply Masa An-Noor. These greetings are polite and common, but Assalamu Alaikum remains the greeting Muslims use most, and it can be used at any time of day. Knowing both kinds helps students understand dialogues in their textbook, because a character might greet with Sabah Al-Khair in a morning scene and reply with Sabah An-Noor.

For parting, Ma'a Salama means with safety, or goodbye, and it is a kind wish for a safe journey. Another useful parting phrase is Ila Al-Liqa, until we meet again, which suits classmates and friends. When leaving a teacher, students often combine politeness with gratitude, saying thank you before Ma'a Salama. Learning greetings in pairs, greeting and reply, morning and evening, meeting and parting, gives students a complete small toolkit that covers almost every everyday situation they will meet in class or at home.
bullets: Sabah Al-Khair means good morning; reply with Sabah An-Noor
Masa Al-Khair means good evening; reply with Masa An-Noor
Ma'a Salama means goodbye, literally with safety

sections.h2: Polite Phrases: Thanks, Apology, and Permission
paras: Polite phrases make a beginner sound respectful, and they are used constantly in Arabic-speaking settings. Shukran means thank you, and Jazak Allahu Khairan, may Allah reward you with good, is a warmer Islamic way to thank someone. The reply to thanks is Afwan, which means you are welcome. When you need to apologise, say Afwan can also mean pardon, but the clearer apology is Ana Asif, I am sorry, for a boy, and Ana Asifa for a girl. These small gender differences appear throughout Arabic, and noticing them early helps students speak correctly rather than repeating one form for everyone.

Asking permission politely is another essential skill. Min Fadlik means please, said to a boy or man, and Min Fadlik is the same phrase addressed to a girl or woman, with a different ending sound. To ask a question, you can begin with Hal, which turns a statement into a yes-or-no question, as in Hal tafham, do you understand? Learning these polite frames first means that even a beginner with a small vocabulary can ask, thank, and apologise gracefully. Manners and language grow together, and teachers notice both when a student speaks politely in Arabic.

sections.h2: Classroom Phrases Every Student Should Know
paras: Classroom Arabic is immediately useful, because students can use it in every lesson. Ana fahimt means I understood, and Ana lam afham means I did not understand, and both are better than silence when a lesson is unclear. A student who wants the teacher to repeat can say A'id min fadlik, please repeat. To ask the meaning of a word, say Ma ma'na hadhihi al-kalima, what is the meaning of this word? These four sentences alone can transform a student's participation, because they let the student ask for help in the language being learnt, which is exactly how language learning works best.

Other classroom phrases include Iftah al-kitab, open the book, and Ighliq al-kitab, close the book, which teachers use as instructions. Students answering a question might begin with Na'am, yes, or La, no, before giving their answer. Practise classroom phrases by role-playing with a partner: one student plays the teacher giving instructions, and the other responds and asks questions. After a few rounds, swap roles. This kind of paired speaking practice is more effective than memorising a list silently, because speaking aloud builds the mouth memory that silent study cannot give.

diagram.alt: A Polite Arabic Conversation in Five Steps
diagram.caption: Follow this order to greet, ask, thank, and part politely.

sections.h2: Practising Phrases Until They Become Natural
paras: The secret to speaking phrases naturally is to use them in real moments, not only in study time. Greet your family with Assalamu Alaikum in the morning, thank your mother with Jazak Allahu Khairan after a meal, and say Ma'a Salama when a guest leaves. Each real use strengthens the phrase far more than ten silent repetitions from a list. Keep a small phrase diary in which you write one new phrase each day with its meaning and a sentence showing when you used it. At the end of the week, read the diary aloud and check which phrases you now use without thinking.

Pair practice also helps a great deal. Find a classmate and agree to greet each other in Arabic every day for a week, then add one new phrase each week, such as a thanks, an apology, or a classroom question. Mistakes are part of the process, and a good partner corrects gently and keeps the conversation going. For more study guides and revision material, visit [Solved Notes](/solved.html), browse [Books](/books.html) for your class, and explore the article index on [Blog](/blog/). Speaking a language is a habit, and habits are built one greeting at a time.

points: Assalamu Alaikum means peace be upon you; reply with Wa Alaikum Assalam.
Sabah Al-Khair and Masa Al-Khair cover morning and evening greetings.
Shukran and Jazak Allahu Khairan are two ways to say thank you.
Classroom phrases like Ana fahimt help students ask for help in Arabic.
Daily real use turns memorised phrases into natural speech.

faqs.q: What does Assalamu Alaikum mean, and how do I reply?
faqs.a: Assalamu Alaikum means peace be upon you, and the reply is Wa Alaikum Assalam, and upon you be peace. A fuller reply adds Wa Rahmatullahi Wa Barakatuh, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings. Muslims reply with an equal or better greeting, so learning the pair together is the correct method.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Sabah Al-Khair and Assalamu Alaikum?
faqs.a: Sabah Al-Khair means good morning and is a time-based greeting, while Assalamu Alaikum is the Islamic greeting of peace that can be used at any time of day. Both are polite, but Assalamu Alaikum is the greeting Muslims use most. In a morning dialogue, a character might use either, and the replies are Sabah An-Noor and Wa Alaikum Assalam.

faqs.q: How do I say thank you and you are welcome in Arabic?
faqs.a: Shukran means thank you, and Jazak Allahu Khairan, may Allah reward you with good, is a warmer Islamic thanks. The reply is Afwan, which means you are welcome. Students should learn the thanks and the reply as a pair, so that they can respond politely when someone thanks them.

faqs.q: How do I say I did not understand in Arabic?
faqs.a: Ana lam afham means I did not understand, and it is one of the most useful classroom phrases a student can learn. Saying it honestly is much better than staying silent, because it lets the teacher explain again. A student can also ask A'id min fadlik, please repeat, to hear the point a second time.

faqs.q: What is a good way to practise Arabic phrases every day?
faqs.a: Use the phrases in real moments: greet your family in Arabic, thank people with Shukran, and say Ma'a Salama when someone leaves. Keep a small phrase diary with one new phrase per day and review it weekly. Pair practice with a classmate, greeting each other in Arabic daily, also turns memorised phrases into natural speech.

title: Arabic Numbers, Days and Months
desc: Learn Arabic numbers, days of the week, and months in order: counting, dates, and everyday sentences students use in class and at home.
kw: Arabic numbers days months counting learn Arabic vocabulary
intro: Numbers, days, and months are among the most useful Arabic vocabulary a student can learn, because they appear in dates, timetables, prices, ages, and everyday conversation. A student who can count in Arabic, name the days of the week, and say the months can already read a calendar, give the date, and understand a large part of classroom instructions. Arabic numbers from one to ten are the foundation, and once they are firm, the teens, tens, and hundreds follow clear patterns. In this guide, we teach the numbers, the days, and the months in order, with pronunciation tips and simple sentences that put the new words to work at once.

paras: The numbers from one to ten are wahid (one), ithnan (two), thalatha (three), arba'a (four), khamsa (five), sitta (six), sab'a (seven), thamaniya (eight), tis'a (nine), and ashara (ten). Learn them in order first, counting on your fingers as you say them, and then practise them out of order, so that you truly know each number rather than only the sequence. A useful drill is to count objects around you in Arabic: books on a desk, students in a row, or steps on a staircase. When the numbers are tied to real things, they stick much faster than when they are repeated from a list alone.

Pay attention to pronunciation, especially the sounds that are new to Urdu or Sindhi speakers. The th in thalatha is soft, like the th in think, and the kh in khamsa is a throaty sound like clearing the throat gently. The ain in ashara is a deep throat sound that takes practice, so listen to your teacher and imitate without embarrassment. Do not worry if these sounds feel strange at first; every learner's mouth needs time to learn new positions. Short daily repetition, five minutes of counting aloud, will make these sounds natural within a couple of weeks.
bullets: Wahid, ithnan, thalatha, arba'a, khamsa are one to five
Sitta, sab'a, thamaniya, tis'a, ashara are six to ten
Count real objects aloud to fix the numbers in memory

sections.h2: Teens, Tens, and Hundreds by Pattern
paras: After ten, Arabic numbers follow patterns that make counting further much easier than it first appears. Eleven is ahada ashar and twelve is ithna ashar, and the teens continue with the unit number followed by ashar. The tens are twenty ishroon, thirty thalathoon, forty arba'oon, fifty khamsoon, sixty sittoon, seventy sab'oon, eighty thamanoon, ninety tis'oon, and one hundred is mi'a. Once you know the units and the tens, you can build numbers like twenty-three by combining twenty and three, following the order your teacher shows you in class. Patterns, not memorising every number separately, are the key to counting confidently.

A common classroom use of numbers is telling age and class counts. Ana umri ithna ashar sana means my age is twelve years, using ithna ashar for twelve and sana for year. Fi safi thalathoon tilmeedh means in my class there are thirty students. Practise by making true sentences about yourself: your age, the number of students in your class, the number of books in your bag. True sentences are easier to remember than invented ones, because they connect the number to something you already know. Check your sentences with your teacher, who can correct the word order and pronunciation gently.

sections.h2: Days of the Week in Order
paras: The Arabic week begins on Sunday, which is an important difference from the Monday-start week many students are used to. The days are Al-Ahad (Sunday), Al-Ithnain (Monday), Al-Thulatha (Tuesday), Al-Arbi'a (Wednesday), Al-Khamees (Thursday), Al-Jumu'a (Friday), and As-Sabt (Saturday). Notice how several day names contain the numbers: Ithnain relates to two, Thulatha to three, Arbi'a to four, and Khamees to five, which makes the middle days of the week easier to remember once the numbers are known. Friday, Al-Jumu'a, is the day of congregational prayer, and it is a special day for Muslims.

To use the days in sentences, learn the question Ma al-yawm, what day is it today, and the answer Al-yawm Al-Ahad, today is Sunday, changing the day name as needed. Practise by saying the day in Arabic every morning before school, and by writing the day and date at the top of your notebook in Arabic. A weekly routine works well: on each day, say that day's name, yesterday's name, and tomorrow's name, so that you learn the days as a moving sequence rather than a fixed list. Within two weeks, naming the days will feel automatic.

diagram.alt: The Arabic Week from Sunday to Saturday
diagram.caption: The week begins on Sunday, and Friday is the congregational day.

paras: Arabic students meet two sets of month names: the Hijri months of the Islamic calendar and the Gregorian months used in everyday civil life. The Hijri months begin with Muharram, then Safar, Rabi al-Awwal, Rabi al-Thani, Jumada al-Ula, Jumada al-Akhira, Rajab, Shaban, Ramadan, Shawwal, Dhul-Qada, and Dhul-Hijja. Ramadan is the month of fasting, and Dhul-Hijja is the month of Hajj, so these two months are already familiar to most students. Learning the Hijri months in order is worthwhile, because Islamic dates, festivals, and history lessons all use them.

The Gregorian months in Arabic are Yanayir (January), Fibrayir (February), Mars (March), Abril (April), Mayu (May), Yunyu (June), Yulyu (July), Aghustus (August), Sibtambir (September), Uktubar (October), Nufambir (November), and Disambir (December). These names are borrowed and adapted, so they are easier to recognise than they first appear. Practise by writing your birthday month, the current month, and the month of Ramadan in Arabic. Combining a month with a number, such as the fifth of Ramadan, gives you a complete date, which is a genuinely useful skill for reading Islamic history and school notices.

sections.h2: Putting Numbers, Days, and Months Together
paras: The real test of this vocabulary is combining it into dates and everyday sentences. Al-yawm Al-Ithnain means today is Monday, and adding a date gives a full sentence, such as today is Monday, the tenth of Ramadan. Asking Ma at-tareekh al-yawm, what is the date today, is a question students can ask every morning in class. Timetables also become good practice: say your school subjects with their days, for example Arabic on Monday and mathematics on Tuesday, using the day names you have learnt. Each combination is a small act of real communication, not just a vocabulary drill.

Keep the learning alive by using it outside the lesson. Write the date in Arabic at the top of your homework, count your pocket money or your steps in Arabic, and name the day aloud each morning. Small daily uses keep the words fresh, while a list studied once and forgotten helps nobody. For more vocabulary guides and revision material, explore [Solved Notes](/solved.html), browse [Books](/books.html) for your class, and visit the article index on [Blog](/blog/). Numbers, days, and months are the kind of vocabulary that repays every minute spent on it, because you will use it for the rest of your life.

Tens follow patterns: ishroon is twenty, thalathoon is thirty, mi'a is one hundred.
The Arabic week begins on Sunday, Al-Ahad, and Friday is Al-Jumu'a.
Hijri months include Muharram, Ramadan, and Dhul-Hijja.

faqs.q: What are the Arabic numbers from one to ten?
faqs.a: One to ten are wahid, ithnan, thalatha, arba'a, khamsa, sitta, sab'a, thamaniya, tis'a, and ashara. Learn them in order first, then out of order, and practise by counting real objects aloud. Tying numbers to things you can see makes them stick much faster than repeating a list silently.

faqs.q: Which day does the Arabic week begin on?
faqs.a: The Arabic week begins on Sunday, Al-Ahad. The days then run Al-Ithnain (Monday), Al-Thulatha (Tuesday), Al-Arbi'a (Wednesday), Al-Khamees (Thursday), Al-Jumu'a (Friday), and As-Sabt (Saturday). Several day names come from numbers, which helps students remember the middle days of the week.

faqs.q: How do I ask what day it is in Arabic?
faqs.a: Ask Ma al-yawm, which means what day is it today, and answer with Al-yawm followed by the day name, for example Al-yawm Al-Ahad for today is Sunday. Practise this question every morning, saying the day, yesterday, and tomorrow, so the days become a moving sequence rather than a fixed list.

faqs.q: What are the Hijri months in order?
faqs.a: The Hijri months are Muharram, Safar, Rabi al-Awwal, Rabi al-Thani, Jumada al-Ula, Jumada al-Akhira, Rajab, Shaban, Ramadan, Shawwal, Dhul-Qada, and Dhul-Hijja. Ramadan is the month of fasting and Dhul-Hijja is the month of Hajj. Learning them in order helps students read Islamic dates and history lessons.

faqs.q: How can I practise Arabic numbers every day?
faqs.a: Count real things in Arabic: books on your desk, students in a row, or steps on a staircase. Write the date in Arabic on your homework, say your age in Arabic, and count your steps on the way to school. Short daily counting, even five minutes, fixes the numbers far better than one long weekly session.

title: Arabic: Ism, Fail and Harf — A First Introduction
desc: Meet the three kinds of Arabic words: ism, fail, and harf. Learn to tell nouns, verbs, and particles apart with clear examples for beginners.
kw: Arabic ism fail harf parts of speech Arabic grammar beginners
intro: Every Arabic word belongs to one of three families: ism, fail, or harf. Ism is a noun or naming word, fail is a verb or doing word, and harf is a particle, a small word that connects other words and has no complete meaning on its own. This three-way division is the foundation of all Arabic grammar, and students who learn it early find every later grammar lesson easier, because they can sort new words into families before trying to use them. In this guide, we introduce each family with clear signs and examples, and we show a simple test that helps you decide which family any word belongs to.

paras: An ism names a person, place, thing, quality, or idea, and it does not carry the idea of time. Examples include Muhammad (a person), madrasa (a school), kitab (a book), and ilm (knowledge). A useful sign of an ism is that it can take al, the definite article, as in al-kitab, the book, or it can take tanween, the doubled vowel ending that adds an n sound. If a word can take al or tanween, it is almost certainly an ism. Another sign is that an ism can follow a harf such as fi (in) or min (from), as in fi al-madrasa, in the school.

Ism words also change for gender and number, which is a feature students meet early. Kitab is masculine and singular, kutub is its plural, books, and madrasa is feminine, marked by the ta marbuta ending. Learning an ism together with its plural is a wise habit, because Arabic plurals are often irregular and cannot always be guessed. When you meet a new ism, write it with its meaning, its plural, and one short sentence using it. This four-part note, word, meaning, plural, sentence, is one of the best vocabulary habits a beginner can build.

sections.h2: Fail: The Doing Word With Time
paras: A fail is a verb, a word that shows an action together with time: past, present, or command. Kataba means he wrote, in the past, yaktubu means he writes or is writing, in the present, and uktub means write, as a command. The time element is the key difference from ism: an ism names something without time, while a fail always places its action in time. The root of most Arabic verbs is three letters, and kataba comes from the root k-t-b, which carries the idea of writing. Recognising the three-letter root helps students see the family links between words like kataba (he wrote), kitab (book), and maktaba (library).

Beginners often confuse fail and ism when a word looks similar in both families. The test is to ask whether the word shows an action in time. Kataba shows a past action, so it is a fail, while kitab names a thing, so it is an ism. Another test is to try adding al: al-kitab works, but al-kataba does not, because verbs do not take al. Practise this test on ten words from your textbook each week, sorting them into ism and fail columns, and check your answers with your teacher. Sorting practice is the fastest way to make the distinction automatic.
bullets: Fail always carries time: past, present, or command
Kataba means he wrote; yaktubu means he writes; uktub means write
Verbs do not take al, while nouns often do

paras: A harf is a particle, a small word that has no complete meaning on its own but gives meaning when it connects other words. Examples include fi (in), min (from), ila (to), ala (on), and an (that). On its own, fi means little, but fi al-bayt, in the house, is a complete and useful phrase. Harf words are usually short, often one or two letters, and they do not change for gender or number the way ism and fail do. They also do not take al or tanween, and they do not show time, which helps students tell them apart from the other two families.

Although harf words are small, they change the meaning of a sentence greatly. Kataba fi al-daftar means he wrote in the notebook, while kataba ala al-daftar means he wrote on the notebook, and the only difference is the harf. This is why teachers insist that students learn harf words with a full phrase, never alone. When you learn fi, learn fi al-madrasa, in the school; when you learn min, learn min al-bayt, from the house. A harf learnt inside a phrase is a harf you will use correctly, while a harf learnt alone is easily forgotten or misused.

sections.h2: A Simple Test for Sorting Any Word
paras: When you meet a new word and are unsure of its family, apply three quick tests in order. First, ask whether it shows an action in time; if yes, it is a fail. Second, try adding al; if al fits naturally, it is an ism. Third, check whether the word only makes sense when joined to another word; if yes, it is probably a harf. This test does not solve every difficult case, and some words need a teacher's help, but it correctly sorts the great majority of beginner words. Keep a sorting notebook with three columns, ism, fail, and harf, and add five new words to it after each lesson.

Sorting practice also improves reading, because a reader who knows the families can predict what comes next. After a harf like fi, an ism usually follows, and after an ism that is the subject, a fail often follows. These expectations make sentences feel less like random strings of words and more like patterns. Students who practise sorting for a few minutes each week usually report that their textbook sentences suddenly look clearer, as if the words have fallen into groups. That clarity is the real reward of learning ism, fail, and harf early.

diagram.alt: The Three Families of Arabic Words
diagram.caption: Every Arabic word is an ism, a fail, or a harf.

sections.h2: Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
paras: One common mistake is to call every word that ends in a vowel an ism, but verbs also end in vowels, so endings alone do not decide the family. Another mistake is to treat harf words as unimportant because they are small, and then to mistranslate sentences because a harf was ignored. A third mistake is to memorise grammar terms without examples, which leaves students able to recite definitions but unable to sort real words. The cure for all three mistakes is the same: always learn a grammar point with five real examples from your textbook, and always test yourself by sorting new words.

Build a steady routine around this topic. Each week, choose one ism, one fail, and one harf from your lesson, write each with its meaning and a sentence, and ask your teacher to check your sorting. Over a term, this routine builds a personal grammar collection of dozens of words that you truly understand. For more grammar guides and revision material, explore [Solved Notes](/solved.html), browse [Books](/books.html) for your class, and visit the article index on [Blog](/blog/). Grammar learnt word by word, week by week, is grammar that lasts.

You can give it ten words from your lesson and ask it to sort them, or ask it for five new examples of each family to practise on.
