faqs.q: When will the BIEK supplementary result 2026 be announced?
faqs.a: No date has been announced by BIEK, so there is no honest answer beyond that. The result can only come after the last paper on 21 November 2026, and the board will publish the genuine announcement on its website. Students should ignore dates shared by unofficial pages and check biek.edu.pk for the real announcement.

faqs.q: Where will the genuine result announcement appear?
faqs.a: Annual results appear on the board's Recent Result Declaration page at biek.edu.pk, and that is where a supplementary announcement should be expected. For annual results, the official BIEK Android app is also a channel. Any claim that does not come from the board itself should be treated as a rumour, however confidently it is written.

faqs.q: What should I keep safe after my last paper?
faqs.a: Keep your admit card and roll number safe, because the roll number will be needed to check the result. Store the card in a fixed place at home and keep a photograph of it as a backup, and write the roll number down separately as well. These small steps prevent a stressful search on result day.

faqs.q: How should I spend the waiting period?
faqs.a: Rest first, then use short daily study to strengthen the subjects that needed a supplementary attempt, since those gaps will matter again in the next class. Organising books and notes for the next stage is also valuable. Avoid spending the whole period refreshing unofficial pages, which produces anxiety without information.

faqs.q: What should I do if a paper is still not cleared in the supplementary result?
faqs.a: Note exactly which papers remain outstanding, then ask your school, college, or the board office what the next available route is, rather than assuming the worst. The supplementary attempt itself was a constructive step, and the right response to a remaining paper is a calm, practical plan for the next opportunity, not panic.

title: BIEK Pre-Engineering Scrutiny 2026: The 19 Oct – 18 Nov Window Explained
desc: BIEK HSC Part-I Pre-Engineering scrutiny is open from 19 October to 18 November 2026 at Rs 1,000 per paper. Who can apply, what scrutiny means, and the deadline.
kw: BIEK Pre-Engineering scrutiny 2026 fee last date
intro: If you are a BIEK Pre-Engineering student who feels your HSC Part-I marks do not reflect what you wrote, there is a formal route open right now: scrutiny. The submission window for HSC Part-I Pre-Engineering scrutiny runs from 19 October to 18 November 2026, with a fee of Rs 1,000 per paper, according to the BIEK scrutiny notification 2026. This guide explains what scrutiny actually means, who should consider it, how to decide which papers to put in, and why the 18 November deadline must be treated as fixed. It covers the Pre-Engineering window only, because that is the window the notification covers, and students of other groups should not assume the same dates apply to them without a board notice of their own.

sections.h2: What Scrutiny Means, and What It Does Not Mean
paras: Scrutiny is a re-checking of the marks already awarded: the board verifies that every answer was marked, that the marks were totalled correctly, and that the total was transferred correctly to the result. It is not a re-marking by a new examiner, and it is not a chance to have answers judged more generously. That distinction matters, because students who apply expecting a fresh evaluation will be disappointed, while students who apply because they suspect a totalling or transfer error are using the route for its real purpose. Understanding scrutiny correctly is the first step to using it well.

Because scrutiny checks the process rather than re-judging the answers, the outcome is usually confirmation of the original marks, with changes only where a genuine error is found. That is not a reason to avoid it when a real doubt exists, but it is a reason to apply with realistic expectations. A student who is confident about a paper and simply unhappy with the grade is unlikely to gain from scrutiny, while a student whose total looks inconsistent with their own careful estimate of the paper may have a genuine case. The fee of Rs 1,000 per paper also means the decision should be made paper by paper, not as a blanket application for everything.

diagram.alt: Deciding Whether to Apply for Scrutiny
diagram.caption: A practical decision path for Pre-Engineering students in the scrutiny window.

sections.h2: The Window and the Fee: 19 October to 18 November, Rs 1,000 Per Paper
paras: The scrutiny submission window opened on 19 October 2026 and closes on 18 November 2026, and the fee is Rs 1,000 per paper. Both facts should shape the decision: the window is generous but not open-ended, and the per-paper fee makes careful selection important. A student applying for three papers pays three times the single-paper fee, so applying for every paper on the off chance is an expensive way to express general disappointment. The sensible approach is to list the papers, rank them by strength of doubt, and apply for those where the doubt is specific, such as a total that does not match the student's own addition of the awarded marks.

The deadline deserves particular respect because it falls inside the supplementary examination window, when many students are focused on papers rather than paperwork. A Pre-Engineering student who is also sitting supplementary papers could easily let 18 November pass while preparing for the next paper, so the scrutiny application, if it is to be made at all, should be submitted early in the window rather than left to the final days. Marking the deadline on a calendar, and treating it as fixed, is the simplest protection against losing the opportunity through distraction.

sections.h2: Why Pre-Engineering Students Have This Window Now
paras: Pre-Engineering results were announced earlier than the remaining groups: BIEK announced the HSC Part-I Pre-Engineering result on 2 October 2026, while the remaining groups, including Science Pre-Medical, Science General, Commerce, Arts, Special Candidates, and Home Economics, followed on 26 October 2026. The scrutiny window follows the Pre-Engineering announcement, which is why it opened on 19 October, before the other groups' results were even declared. Students of other groups should therefore not read this window as applying to them; their own scrutiny arrangements, if any, would come through their own board notices, and assuming otherwise could lead to missed deadlines or wrong applications.

The timing also means Pre-Engineering students have had several weeks since 2 October to consider their results and decide. That is an advantage if it is used well: the decision can be made calmly, with time to recheck estimates and discuss with teachers, rather than in the rush of result week. Students who are still undecided should use the remaining days before 18 November to talk to a subject teacher, who can give an honest view of whether a paper's marks look out of line. A teacher who marked similar papers or who knows the student's work can often tell quickly whether a doubt is worth pursuing.

sections.h2: How to Choose Which Papers to Put In
paras: The best method is a paper-by-paper review. For each paper, the student should recall the answers written, estimate the marks each answer deserved under the marking scheme, and compare that estimate with the awarded marks. A large gap on its own is not proof of an error, because self-estimates are often generous, but a gap combined with a specific suspicion, such as a question the student is sure was answered well receiving no credit, or a total that does not add up, is a genuine reason to apply. Papers where the student knows the answers were weak should not be put in, because scrutiny will not turn weak answers into strong marks.

Students should also weigh the fee against the value of the outcome. If a paper's marks affect an important threshold, such as passing the paper or reaching a grade that matters for the next stage, then Rs 1,000 for a genuine check is a reasonable step. If the paper is already passed and the only question is a few marks either way, the student should think harder about whether the check is worth it. Discussing the choice with parents is wise, since they are usually paying the fee, and a joint decision made on specific reasons is better than a hurried application made alone. Further study support for Pre-Engineering subjects is available on [Solved Notes](/solved.html) and [Books](/books.html).

sections.h2: After You Apply: What to Expect
paras: After applying within the window and paying the fee per paper, the student should keep the application receipt safe and wait for the board's scrutiny outcome, which will either confirm the original marks or correct them where an error is found. There is no shortcut to the outcome, and students should not expect daily updates; the board processes scrutiny applications in its own order. While waiting, the best use of time is to continue with current studies, including any supplementary papers still to be sat, rather than pausing everything for the scrutiny result. The scrutiny outcome, when it comes, will be a correction or a confirmation, and either way the student's studies should have kept moving.

It is also worth remembering that scrutiny is one route among several, and it does not replace other options where they exist. A student with a failed paper may also be sitting the supplementary examinations, which run until 21 November 2026, and the two routes serve different purposes: supplementary examinations give a fresh chance to pass, while scrutiny checks whether the original marks were recorded correctly. Students should not confuse the two or assume that applying for one removes the need for the other. If in doubt, a teacher or the college office can explain which route fits the student's situation. More board guides are listed on [Blog](/blog/).

Fee is Rs 1,000 per paper, so choose papers with a genuine, specific doubt.

This window covers Pre-Engineering only; other groups need their own board notice.

faqs.q: What are the dates and fee for BIEK Pre-Engineering scrutiny 2026?
faqs.a: The submission window runs from 19 October to 18 November 2026, and the fee is Rs 1,000 per paper, according to the BIEK scrutiny notification 2026. Students should apply early rather than leaving it to the final days, since the deadline falls inside the supplementary examination window when attention is elsewhere.

faqs.q: Does scrutiny mean my paper will be marked again by a new examiner?
faqs.a: No, scrutiny is a re-checking of the process: that every answer was marked, that marks were totalled correctly, and that the total was transferred correctly to the result. It is not a fresh evaluation of the answers, so it will not turn weak answers into strong marks. It corrects genuine errors where they exist.

faqs.a: This window covers HSC Part-I Pre-Engineering only, because Pre-Engineering results were announced on 2 October 2026, ahead of the remaining groups on 26 October 2026. Students of other groups should not assume these dates apply to them and should wait for their own board notice before acting.

faqs.a: Review each paper against your own estimate of the marks, and apply only where there is a specific doubt, such as a total that does not add up or a well-answered question receiving no credit. faqs.a: Yes, the two routes serve different purposes and do not replace each other. If you are unsure which route fits your situation, ask a teacher or your college office.

title: BSEK Class 9 Science Result: How to Read Your Marksheet and Partial-Pass Categories
desc: BSEK Class 9 Science result was announced on 28 October 2026. How to read your marksheet, what each pass category means, and what to do about failed papers.
kw: BSEK Class 9 Science result marksheet pass categories
intro: The Board of Secondary Education Karachi (BSEK) announced the Class 9 Science Group (Regular) First Annual Examinations 2026 result on Wednesday 28 October 2026, and it was available on bsek.edu.pk from 5:30 PM that day. For many students, the result page raises as many questions as it answers: what does it mean to have passed six papers but not all, what happens to a paper marked ungraded, and what comes next for a paper that is failed? This guide explains how to read the marksheet, what each partial-pass category means in plain language, and what the new 40 percent pass threshold changes. It is written for students and parents looking at a real result, not for announcing the result itself, which is already three days old.

sections.h2: The Headline Numbers Behind Your Result
paras: The board's figures give useful context for reading an individual result. Of 180,054 registered students, 177,923 appeared and 2,131 were absent, while 123,757 passed all papers and 53,849 failed. The overall pass percentage was 69.56 percent, compared with 78.26 percent for the Science Group in 2025, a fall of about 8.7 percentage points. The board has published no single official reason for the fall, so students should not accept any one claimed cause as fact, whether it is blamed on the new threshold, the papers, or preparation. What matters for an individual student is not the overall percentage but their own combination of passed and failed papers, which decides their exact next step.

The partial-pass figures show how common it is to pass most papers but not all: 21,999 students passed six papers, 11,006 passed five, 7,431 passed four, 4,409 passed three, 3,101 passed two, and 2,439 passed one. A student in any of these categories has not failed everything, and that distinction matters, because the next step is about clearing the remaining papers, not about starting again from zero. Parents reading a marksheet should therefore look first at which papers are cleared and which are not, rather than reacting to the overall label alone. The marksheet is a list of subjects with individual outcomes, and each subject has its own next step.

sections.h2: What Each Pass Category Actually Means
paras: Passing all papers means the student has cleared Class 9 Science completely and moves forward without any outstanding subject from this examination. Passing six papers, the largest partial category with 21,999 students, means one paper remains, and the student's task is now focused entirely on that one subject. Passing five papers means two remain, and so on down the categories, with each step down meaning one more subject to clear. The smaller the number of passed papers, the broader the revision task, but the principle stays the same: only the outstanding papers need to be addressed, and the passed papers are already banked.

The category of 53,849 failed students needs careful reading too, because it sits alongside the partial-pass categories in the board's figures and can be misread as meaning every paper failed. A student's own marksheet is the authority, not the headline figure: it shows subject by subject what was passed and what was not. Whatever the category, the response should be subject-specific, starting with the weakest papers and the subjects where the gap is smallest and therefore quickest to close. A student who passed five papers and needs one more push in a single subject is in a very different position from a student with several papers to clear, and the plan should reflect that.

sections.h2: The New 40 Percent Rule and Ungraded Papers
paras: From the 2026 annual examinations, the pass threshold was raised from 33 percent to 40 percent, and scoring under 40 percent in a paper means the paper is marked ungraded, which means not passed in that paper. This is the single most important change for students reading a 2026 marksheet, because a score that would have passed under the old 33 percent rule may now fall short. Students who scored in the 33 to 39 percent range in a paper should therefore understand their position clearly: under the new grading, that paper is not passed, and it needs to be cleared through the board's next available route, even though the score looks close to a pass.

The new grading also changes how students should prepare for the next attempt. Revision should aim comfortably above 40 percent, not at the line itself, because a paper prepared to just scrape the threshold is vulnerable to a single difficult question or a marking variation. Building a margin, by mastering the core chapters and practising past papers, is the practical response to a higher threshold. Class 10 follows the same 40 percent rule from 2027, so Class 9 students who learn this lesson now will carry it into their next class, where the same standard will apply. Solved notes for Class 9 subjects are available on [Solved Notes](/solved.html) for targeted revision.

sections.h2: What to Do About Failed or Ungraded Papers
paras: The first step is to list the outstanding papers honestly and rank them by how close each one is to passing. A paper at 38 percent needs a different plan from a paper at 20 percent: the first needs consolidation and exam technique, while the second needs a fuller re-study of the subject's core chapters. Students should also ask a subject teacher to look at the marksheet with them, because a teacher can often spot whether the weakness is in a particular chapter, in presentation, or in time management during the paper. That diagnosis is worth more than simply re-reading the whole book from the first page.

The second step is to build a short, focused plan for each outstanding paper, with daily study slots and regular self-testing, rather than vague promises to study harder. Past papers are especially useful here, because they show the question patterns and the standard of answer the paper requires. Parents can help by keeping the plan realistic and by checking progress weekly, not daily, so that the student feels supported rather than pressured. The full book collection for revision is on [Books](/books.html), and further result guides are listed on [Blog](/blog/).

sections.h2: What This Result Does Not Cover
paras: It is important to be precise about the scope of the 28 October announcement, because confusion here leads to wasted worry. The announcement covers the Class 9 Science Group (Regular) First Annual Examinations 2026 only. The Class 9 General Group result came earlier, on 10 September 2026, and General Group and Private Science results are not part of the 28 October announcement. A student in one of those categories should therefore not expect their result to be explained by the Science Regular figures, and should check the board's own announcements for their category instead of drawing conclusions from this one.

Students should also avoid two common mistakes when discussing the result. The first is accepting a single claimed reason for the overall pass percentage fall, when the board has published no single official reason. The second is comparing a 2026 result directly with an older sibling's or friend's result from a different grading system, since the threshold change means the two results were judged by different standards. The fair comparison is within the 2026 system: which papers are passed, which are ungraded, and what the next step is for each. That is the reading that actually helps a student move forward.

title: The 40% Rule Reaches Class 10 in 2027: What Class 9 Students Must Learn Now
desc: The 40 percent pass threshold reaches Class 10 in 2027. What Class 9 students learned from the 2026 change, and how to prepare for the higher standard now.
intro: The pass threshold in Karachi's secondary examinations has changed, and Class 9 students are the first to feel it in full. From the 2026 annual examinations, the pass threshold rose from 33 percent to 40 percent, with under 40 percent in a paper marked ungraded, and Class 10 follows the same rule from 2027. That means today's Class 9 students will sit their Class 10 examinations under the higher standard, and the habits they build now will decide how smoothly they make that transition. This guide explains what changed, what the Class 9 Science result already teaches about the new standard, and how students can prepare for Class 10 so that the 40 percent rule is a comfortable bar rather than a barrier.

sections.h2: What Changed: From 33 Percent to 40 Percent
paras: Under the old system, a student needed 33 percent in a paper to pass it. From the 2026 annual examinations, the threshold is 40 percent, and a paper scored under 40 percent is marked ungraded, meaning not passed in that paper. The change is part of the new grading introduced with the IBCC and the Sindh Universities and Boards Department framework, and it applies across the board's examinations as each class transitions. For students, the practical meaning is straightforward: the margin for a weak paper has shrunk, and scores in the 33 to 39 percent range, which once passed, now fall short and leave the paper outstanding.

The change should not be read as a punishment, but as a higher expectation that rewards solid preparation. A student who genuinely understands the core chapters of a subject will usually clear 40 percent without difficulty, while a student who relied on scraping through with partial knowledge will now find that strategy failing. That is the lesson of the transition: preparation must aim at understanding, not at the minimum. Students who adjust their study habits now, in Class 9, will find Class 10 under the same rule far less daunting than students who wait until Class 10 to discover the new standard.

diagram.caption: How the higher pass threshold reaches each class in turn.

sections.h2: What the Class 9 Science Result Already Shows
paras: The Class 9 Science Group (Regular) result announced on 28 October 2026 gives the first large-scale picture of the new rule in action. The overall pass percentage was 69.56 percent, compared with 78.26 percent in 2025, a fall of about 8.7 percentage points, and 123,757 students passed all papers out of 177,923 who appeared. The board has published no single official reason for the fall, so it would be wrong to attribute it entirely to the threshold change, but the direction is clear: under a higher bar, weak preparation is more likely to show up as an ungraded paper. Students reading their own 2026 marksheet should check whether any paper fell in the 33 to 39 percent range, because those are the papers the new rule caught.

The partial-pass figures also show that many students were close: 21,999 passed six papers, 11,006 passed five, and thousands more passed four or fewer. For those students, the gap to a full pass is often one or two papers, and the lesson is that a small improvement in a weak subject would have changed the outcome. That is encouraging, because it means the next attempt does not require starting over; it requires targeted work on the specific papers that fell short. Class 9 students heading into Class 10 should carry that lesson with them: identify weak subjects early, fix them while there is time, and do not let a borderline subject drift until examination season.

sections.h2: Why Class 10 in 2027 Needs Preparation Now
paras: Class 10 follows the 40 percent rule from 2027, which means the students currently in Class 9 will face the higher threshold in their board class. Board classes carry extra weight because their results shape the next stage of education, so a student who enters Class 10 with weak foundations and a habit of scraping through will face the new standard at the worst possible moment. The time to build stronger habits is now, while Class 9 is still in progress and the stakes of each test are lower. Teachers, parents, and students should treat the rest of Class 9 as preparation for Class 10, not as a separate year that can be coasted through.

Preparation now also means using the Class 9 experience honestly. A student who received an ungraded paper in 2026 already knows which subject needs work, and that knowledge is more valuable than any general advice. Rather than forgetting the weak paper once the result is absorbed, the student should keep working on that subject alongside current studies, so that the gap closes before Class 10 begins. Solved notes can support that steady work, and the collection on [Solved Notes](/solved.html) covers Class 9 subjects for targeted revision, while [Books](/books.html) lists the full range of available books.

sections.h2: Study Habits That Clear 40 Percent Comfortably
paras: The habits that clear the new threshold are not exotic; they are the basics done consistently. First, master the core chapters of each subject rather than memorising summaries of everything, because core chapters carry the marks that push a score past 40 percent. Second, practise past papers under timed conditions, since examination technique, writing complete answers, managing time, and attempting every question, often accounts for the difference between 35 and 45 percent. Third, test yourself regularly with short quizzes instead of only re-reading notes, because self-testing reveals gaps while there is still time to fix them.

Fourth, treat borderline subjects as the priority, not the afterthought. Students naturally prefer subjects they are good at, but under a 40 percent rule, the subject closest to the line deserves the most attention, because it is the one most likely to become ungraded. A weekly slot dedicated to the weakest subject, with a teacher's help where needed, will do more for the overall result than extra hours on an already strong subject. Finally, keep attendance and homework steady throughout the year, since the 40 percent rule punishes the student who only starts serious study in the final month, when there is no longer time to build real understanding.

sections.h2: A Message for Parents and Teachers
paras: Parents and teachers have a role in this transition that goes beyond telling students to work harder. The first task is to explain the rule itself clearly, so that families understand that under 40 percent means ungraded and that a score in the high thirties is no longer a pass. Many families still think in terms of the old 33 percent line, and that misunderstanding leads to false reassurance when a child scores 35 percent in a test. Once the rule is understood, families can set realistic expectations: a test score of 45 percent is a pass with a thin margin, not a comfortable result, and the goal should be to build well above the line.

The second task is to respond to ungraded papers with a plan rather than blame. A student who has just learned that a paper is ungraded needs help diagnosing the weakness and a schedule for fixing it, not a lecture that adds anxiety to an already difficult moment. Teachers can help by identifying the chapters where marks were lost, and parents can help by protecting study time and checking progress calmly each week. The 40 percent rule, handled this way, becomes a prompt for better preparation rather than a source of fear, and students who experience that support in Class 9 will enter Class 10 in 2027 ready for the standard. Further guidance for families is listed on [Blog](/blog/).

title: Punjab Second Annual Exams: The Final 72 Hours Before 3 November
desc: Punjab second annual exams start 3 November 2026. A calm, practical 72-hour plan for the last three days: revision, papers, timings, and exam-day basics.
kw: Punjab second annual exams 2026 final preparation
intro: Punjab's HSSC Second Annual (supplementary) examinations begin on 3 November 2026, which means students have just three days left, the final 72 hours, to turn preparation into performance. Part-II (12th class) theory papers run from 3 to 16 November 2026, followed by Part-I (11th class) theory from 17 to 28 November, with practical examinations from 1 to 11 December on the Multan schedule. This guide is a practical plan for the last three days: what to revise, what to stop doing, how the paper timings work, and how to walk into the hall calm and ready. It is written for students who have prepared through the year and now need to finish well, not for students starting from zero.

sections.h2: The Schedule You Are Working Towards
paras: The province-wide picture, set by the Punjab Boards Committee of Chairpersons, is clear: Part-II theory from 3 to 16 November 2026, then Part-I theory from 17 to 28 November 2026. Morning papers begin at 9:00 AM, evening papers at 2:00 PM, and on Fridays the evening paper begins at 2:30 PM. The Multan date sheet gives subject examples that many students will recognise: for 12th class, English Compulsory on 4 November, Mathematics or Biology on 6 November, Computer Science on 10 November, Chemistry on 12 November, and Physics on 16 November; for 11th class, English Compulsory on 18 November, Computer Science on 23 November, Mathematics or Biology on 25 November, and Physics on 27 November. Other boards share the 3 November start, but every student must confirm their own board's subject-wise sheet, because subject dates can differ between boards.

Knowing the schedule matters for the final 72 hours because it tells you exactly which paper comes first and how much gap you have before the second. A 12th class student whose first paper is English Compulsory on 4 November should spend the largest share of the final three days on English, with lighter review of the next subject, rather than dividing time equally across all subjects. A student whose first paper is later in the window has more room, but the principle is the same: revise in the order of the papers, front-loading the first paper, and keep the later subjects warm with short daily review rather than full study sessions. The full picture for November is also covered in the wider boards calendar on [Blog](/blog/).

diagram.alt: Punjab Second Annual: The Final 72 Hours
diagram.caption: A three-day countdown to the 3 November start, in order.

sections.h2: Day One: Audit Everything, Then Revise the First Paper
paras: The first of the final three days should begin with an audit, not with opening a book at random. Check your own board's subject-wise date sheet, confirm the date, time, and centre for each of your papers, and make sure your admit card and stationery are ready. Confirm whether your first paper is a morning paper at 9:00 AM or an evening paper at 2:00 PM, because the two require different routines on the day. This audit takes less than an hour, but it removes the small uncertainties that cause the most anxiety on paper day, such as not knowing the centre or the shift.

After the audit, the rest of day one belongs to the first paper. Work through its most important chapters, practise writing full answers rather than only reading notes, and test yourself on the topics that carry the most marks. Avoid the temptation to start a new topic on day one; the final days are for consolidating what you know, not for learning what you never studied. If a chapter is genuinely unprepared, give it a single focused hour for its key points, then move on, because a weak chapter given three hours will still be weak, while a strong chapter given those hours becomes stronger.

sections.h2: Day Two: Practise Answers and Prepare for the Hall
paras: Day two is for practice and preparation. Write at least one full answer for each major question type in your first paper, under timed conditions if possible, because writing under time pressure is a different skill from knowing the material. Check your answers for the common faults that cost marks: incomplete introductions, missing steps in numerical work, diagrams without labels, and answers that stop halfway. Correcting these faults in practice is worth more than learning another chapter, because presentation and completeness decide a large share of the marks in board papers.

Day two is also when the practical side should be finished: pack your bag with the admit card, pens, pencils, ruler, and any permitted instruments, confirm your transport and route to the centre, and decide what time you will leave. If your first paper is a morning paper at 9:00 AM, plan to arrive well before the reporting time, allowing for traffic. If it is an evening paper, plan a calm morning with light revision and an early departure. Students can find further revision support on [Solved Notes](/solved.html) and the book collection on [Books](/books.html) for last-minute reference.

sections.h2: Day Three: Light Review, Early Rest, No New Material
paras: The day before the first paper should be the lightest study day of the three, not the heaviest. A short review of key formulas, definitions, and important points in the morning, followed by a relaxed afternoon and an early night, will serve a student better than a late-night cramming session. Sleep is not wasted time in the final 24 hours; it is what turns revision into recall. A student who sleeps well will remember more in the hall than a student who studied until midnight and arrives exhausted, however many extra pages the tired student read.

The evening before the paper should be kept calm and free of new material. Re-reading a short summary, glancing at a diagram, or testing yourself with a few flashcards is enough, and anything that causes confusion at this stage should be set aside rather than chased. Families can help by keeping the house quiet, avoiding discussions about expected marks, and confirming the morning routine. The goal of day three is to arrive at the paper rested, organised, and confident, not to add one more chapter to an already full preparation.

sections.h2: One Warning: Admission Windows Are Closed
paras: A point that needs stating plainly is that the admission windows for these examinations, which ran from 24 September to 17 October, are closed, and they must not be presented or understood as open. Students who are already registered and hold admit cards are the ones sitting from 3 November, and anyone who missed the window cannot join at this stage through these examinations. This matters because rumours sometimes suggest that late admission is still possible, which wastes the time of students who should instead be planning their next available opportunity through the proper channel.

For registered students, the closed window is simply background: your place is secured, your papers are scheduled, and the only task left is to sit them well. For students who missed registration, the constructive step is to ask their school, college, or board office about the next examination opportunity and to use the intervening time to prepare properly, rather than chasing a closed window. Either way, the final 72 hours belong to preparation and calm, not to paperwork that can no longer change. More board examination guides are available on [Blog](/blog/) for students planning their next step.

title: Sindh Boards in November 2026: Supplementary Exams, Punjab Papers and the Hyderabad Report
desc: November 2026 brings BIEK supplementary papers, Punjab second annual exams, and the Hyderabad inquiry report window. A clear month guide for Sindh students.
kw: Sindh boards November 2026 exams calendar BIEK BSEK
intro: November 2026 is a crowded month for board students connected to Sindh. In Karachi, the BIEK supplementary examinations that began on 28 October continue until 21 November, while next door in Punjab, second annual examinations run through the whole month, affecting Sindh students with family or admission links across the province border. Meanwhile, the inquiry into alleged irregularities at BISE Hyderabad, ordered on 23 October, is due to report within 30 days, which places its report in late November. This guide puts the month together in one place: what is happening, when, and what students should watch, without guessing at anything that has not been announced.

sections.h2: BIEK Supplementary Examinations Run Until 21 November
paras: The main Sindh event of November is the continuation of the BIEK supplementary examinations, which began on Wednesday 28 October 2026 and run until Saturday 21 November 2026. All papers are held in a single afternoon shift from 2:00 PM to 5:00 PM, with reporting at 1:30 PM, covering Pre-Medical, Pre-Engineering, Science General, Commerce, Arts and Humanities, and Home Economics. For Karachi intermediate students, November is therefore largely a month of sitting papers, with the rhythm of afternoon papers and gap-day revision continuing from late October. Students should keep their admit cards safe and their paper dates marked, because a three-week window is long enough for a date to be forgotten.

Two related BIEK dates also fall in November and deserve attention. The HSC Part-I Pre-Engineering scrutiny window, which opened on 19 October, closes on 18 November 2026, with a fee of Rs 1,000 per paper, so Pre-Engineering students considering scrutiny must act before that deadline passes. And no supplementary result date has been announced by BIEK, which means November will end without a result for supplementary candidates, however much they may hope otherwise. The result can only follow the last paper, and the board's Recent Result Declaration page at biek.edu.pk is where a genuine announcement will appear when it is ready.

diagram.caption: The verified November dates for board students, in order.

sections.h2: Punjab Papers Through November: Why Sindh Students Should Know
paras: Punjab's second annual examinations run through almost the whole of November: Part-II theory from 3 to 16 November, then Part-I theory from 17 to 28 November, with morning papers at 9:00 AM, evening papers at 2:00 PM, and Friday evening papers at 2:30 PM. Practical examinations follow from 1 to 11 December on the Multan schedule. Subject examples from the Multan sheet include 12th English Compulsory on 4 November, Mathematics or Biology on 6 November, Computer Science on 10 November, Chemistry on 12 November, and Physics on 16 November, followed by 11th English Compulsory on 18 November, Computer Science on 23 November, Mathematics or Biology on 25 November, and Physics on 27 November. Other boards share the 3 November start but students must confirm their own board's sheet.

Sindh students may wonder why Punjab dates belong in a Sindh calendar, and the answer is practical: families, admissions, and academic plans cross provincial lines, and many Sindh households follow both provinces' schedules. A student in Karachi with a sibling in Punjab, or a student considering an institution that follows the Punjab calendar, needs both pictures to plan the month. The admission windows for the Punjab examinations, 24 September to 17 October, are closed, so November is purely an examination month there, not a registration month. Students can read the detailed Punjab preparation guide on [Blog](/blog/) for the final-days plan.

sections.h2: The Hyderabad Inquiry Report Falls Due in Late November
paras: The third November item is the BISE Hyderabad inquiry, and it must be described with care. On 23 October 2026, the Sindh government suspended the BISE Hyderabad Deputy Controller of the Top Secret Branch, Ijaz Ali Kaka, on the orders of Provincial Minister for Universities and Boards Muhammad Ismail Rahoo, and a three-member inquiry committee was formed, headed by Professor Dr Arbeela Bhutto, with Additional Secretary Amir, also reported as Ameer, Fazal Owaisi and Mehran University Registrar Dr Nasrullah Pirzada as members. The committee's report is due within 30 days of 23 October, which places it in late November, and this guide deliberately does not name a confirmed calendar date, because the notification gives a window, not a day.

Equally important is the status of the matter: the inquiry concerns alleged irregularities in the Class XII annual examination 2026 results for pre-medical and pre-engineering groups, covering position holders, top-10, and A-1 and A grade students, and the checking, tabulation, and announcement of results. These are allegations, not proven findings, and the results have not been cancelled. Students should therefore not treat the inquiry as a change to any result, and no student names should be circulated in connection with it. The sensible stance for November is to watch for the report through proper news and board channels, and to continue normal studies in the meantime. Solved notes for ongoing study are on [Solved Notes](/solved.html).

sections.h2: What November Does Not Bring: A Supplementary Result Date
paras: It is worth saying plainly what November does not bring, because false expectations cause the most disappointment. November does not bring a BIEK supplementary result date, since none has been announced, and it should not be expected simply because the papers end on 21 November. Marking and compilation take time after the last paper, and the board will announce the result when it is ready, on its own channels. Students who spend late November refreshing unofficial pages for a date that does not exist will only add anxiety to an already long month, and families should be wary of any page that claims a date without a board source.

November also does not bring any new STBB textbook announcement that has been verified as of 31 October. The standing context is that STBB's 2026-27 textbooks, the Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Textbook Series from Early Childhood to Grade 10, comprise 195 titles in Sindhi, Urdu, and English, with 52 million sets, distribution inaugurated on 19 February 2026, and a revised curriculum from the next academic year. That background matters for the school year, but it is not a November event, and students should not confuse it with the month's examination activity. Keeping the month's real events separate from background context is part of reading board news accurately.

sections.h2: Planning the Month: One Calendar, Three Tracks
paras: The practical way to handle November is to keep one calendar with three tracks. Track one is your own papers: every BIEK supplementary date you must sit, with the 1:30 PM reporting time and the 2:00 PM start, plus the 18 November scrutiny deadline if it applies to you. Track two is any Punjab date that affects your household, such as a sibling's papers, so that family travel and study routines do not clash. Track three is the Hyderabad report window in late November, marked as something to watch, not something to act on, since it does not change any student's own result unless an official decision follows it.

With the calendar in place, the month becomes manageable: revise in paper order, protect sleep during the examination weeks, and use the days after 21 November to rest and then prepare for the next class, rather than waiting anxiously for an unannounced result. Students who plan this way will finish November having sat their papers well, met the scrutiny deadline if relevant, and kept their studies moving. That is a good month by any measure, regardless of what the report window brings. The full book collection for continued study is on [Books](/books.html), and further month guides are listed on [Blog](/blog/).

title: How BIEK Marks Science Papers: E-Assessment, OMR and E-Marking Explained
desc: BIEK uses E-Assessment with OMR and E-Marking for science-group optional subjects. How the system works, what it means for students, and how to fill an OMR sheet.
kw: BIEK E-Assessment OMR E-Marking science papers
intro: When BIEK announced the HSC Part-I results for the remaining groups on 26 October 2026, one technical detail stood out for science students: science-group optional subjects are assessed through E-Assessment, using OMR and E-Marking. Many students have heard these terms without knowing what they actually mean, and some worry that a machine decides their marks. This guide explains the system in plain language: what OMR sheets are, how E-Marking works, what it changes for students, and how to fill an OMR sheet correctly so that technology records the answers you actually intended. No part of this guide guesses at board procedures beyond what has been verified; where the board has not published a detail, this guide says so.

sections.h2: What E-Assessment Means for Science Students
paras: E-Assessment means that parts of the assessment process are handled electronically rather than entirely on paper. For BIEK's science-group optional subjects, the verified fact is that assessment runs through E-Assessment with OMR and E-Marking, and that fact was noted in the board's 26 October 2026 announcement for the remaining HSC Part-I groups, which included Science Pre-Medical and Science General. The practical meaning for students is that their answers in the affected subjects pass through a digital stage, whether that is machine reading of an answer sheet or on-screen marking of scanned scripts, rather than every step happening by hand on paper alone.

Students should understand that E-Assessment is a method of processing, not a different syllabus or a different standard. The questions, the marking scheme, and the knowledge required are the same; what changes is how answers are captured and checked. That distinction matters because it answers the most common worry: the system does not invent marks or change the difficulty of the paper. It records and processes what the student wrote, and the student's job remains what it always was, to write correct, complete answers. The verified context here is the 26 October announcement itself, and students should not assume details about the system that the board has not published.

diagram.caption: The general path of a science-group optional paper under E-Assessment, as verified.

sections.h2: OMR Sheets: What They Are and Why They Need Care
paras: OMR stands for Optical Mark Recognition, and an OMR sheet is an answer sheet on which students darken bubbles or marks to indicate their choices, usually for objective or multiple-choice questions. A machine reads the darkened marks, which makes the capture of objective answers fast and consistent, and removes the variation that comes from different people reading handwriting. For science students, OMR is most relevant to the objective sections of their papers, where a single darkened bubble carries the answer, and where a careless mark can therefore cost a mark just as surely as a wrong answer.

The care OMR requires is simple but strict: darken the chosen bubble completely, use the writing instrument the instructions specify, avoid stray marks on the sheet, and never darken two bubbles for one question. Students should also double-check the question number against the bubble row before darkening, because a slipped row, answering question 12 in row 13, is one of the most common and most avoidable OMR errors. Reading the sheet's instructions before starting, rather than assuming they match a previous paper's, is part of the discipline, because formats can differ between subjects and sessions.

sections.h2: E-Marking: What Happens After the Paper
paras: E-Marking means that marking is carried out through an electronic system, in which scripts or answer data are presented to markers on screen, and marks are entered digitally rather than written by hand on paper. The advantage is consistency and traceability: marks are recorded in a structured way, totals can be checked by the system, and the path from a marked answer to a published result has fewer manual transcription steps. For students, the practical consequence is that the system is designed to reduce the very errors, missed totals and wrong transfers, that the scrutiny process exists to catch.

It is important not to overclaim what E-Marking guarantees. It does not mean a paper is marked by a machine instead of a human examiner, and this guide does not claim that, because the board's verified statement is that science-group optional subjects are assessed through E-Assessment with OMR and E-Marking, without publishing a fuller procedural breakdown. What can fairly be said is that electronic capture and entry reduce transcription risk and make the checking process more systematic. Students who want the board's own detail should look to BIEK's official announcements rather than to unofficial explanations that invent steps the board has not described.

sections.h2: How Students Should Prepare for E-Assessed Papers
paras: Preparation for an E-assessed paper is mostly the same as for any paper, with a few extra habits for the objective sections. First, practise objective questions regularly, because multiple-choice and short objective items reward quick, accurate recall, and a student who only practises long answers may be slow on the objective section. Second, practise filling a sample OMR-style sheet if one is available from school or college, so that the real sheet feels familiar rather than strange. Third, during the paper, keep track of time separately for the objective and subjective sections, so that neither is starved by the other.

Fourth, keep written answers neat and complete even where marking is electronic, because scanned scripts must still be readable, and a cramped or faint answer helps nobody. Fifth, attempt every objective question unless the instructions penalise guessing, because an unanswered question is a certain zero while an attempted one has a chance. These habits are small, but together they protect the marks a student has earned through study, which is exactly what an assessment system, electronic or otherwise, is meant to record. Further study material is available on [Solved Notes](/solved.html) and [Books](/books.html).

sections.h2: E-Assessment and the 26 October Results in Context
paras: The E-Assessment note belongs to a specific announcement: the HSC Part-I results for remaining groups on 26 October 2026, announced by Controller of Examinations Zarina Rashid under Chairman Faqir Muhammad Lakho, covering Science Pre-Medical, Science General, Commerce (Regular and Private), Arts (Regular and Private), Special Candidates (Arts Regular), and Home Economics. The verified figures from that announcement include Pre-Medical with 25,157 registered, 24,544 appeared, and 11,966 passing all six papers, and Science General with 30,991 registered, 30,386 appeared, and 15,036 passing all six. Pre-Engineering had already been announced on 2 October 2026, and results are available on biek.edu.pk and the official BIEK Android app.

The same announcement introduced the new grading under which under 40 percent in any paper means ungraded, not passed in that paper, and students reading those results should keep the two facts separate: E-Assessment describes how papers are processed, while the 40 percent rule describes the standard for passing. Confusing the two leads to wrong conclusions, such as blaming a result on the marking method when the standard is the actual cause, or vice versa. Keeping method and standard distinct is part of reading board announcements accurately, and it helps students direct their effort correctly, towards stronger preparation rather than suspicion of the system. More board result guides are on [Blog](/blog/).

faqs.q: What is E-Assessment at BIEK?
faqs.a: E-Assessment means parts of the assessment process are handled electronically rather than entirely on paper. For BIEK, science-group optional subjects are assessed through E-Assessment with OMR and E-Marking, as noted in the 26 October 2026 HSC Part-I announcement. The syllabus and standard are unchanged; what changes is how answers are captured and processed.

faqs.q: What is an OMR sheet?
faqs.a: An OMR (Optical Mark Recognition) sheet is an answer sheet on which students darken bubbles to indicate their choices, usually for objective questions. A machine reads the darkened marks, making capture fast and consistent. Students must darken one bubble completely per question, match the question number to the row, and avoid stray marks.

faqs.q: Does a machine mark my whole science paper?
faqs.a: This guide does not claim that, because the board's verified statement is that science-group optional subjects are assessed through E-Assessment with OMR and E-Marking, without a fuller published breakdown. E-Marking means marks are entered through an electronic system, which reduces transcription risk. Students should rely on the board's own announcements for further procedural detail.

faqs.q: How can I avoid losing marks on an OMR sheet?
faqs.a: Darken the chosen bubble completely, use the instrument the instructions specify, check the question number against the row before marking, and never darken two bubbles for one question. Read the sheet's instructions before starting, since formats can differ between subjects. A slipped row is one of the most common and avoidable OMR errors.

faqs.q: What is the difference between E-Assessment and the 40 percent rule?
faqs.a: E-Assessment describes how papers are processed, through OMR and E-Marking, while the 40 percent rule describes the passing standard: under 40 percent in a paper means ungraded, not passed. The two facts come from the same 26 October 2026 announcement but answer different questions, and confusing them leads to wrong conclusions about a result.

title: Sindh's New Hindu Religious Books for Grades 3–5: What the 2026–27 Decision Means
desc: Sindh approved dedicated Hindu religious textbooks for Grades 3-5 in government schools for 2026-27. What was decided, who publishes them, and why it matters.
kw: Sindh Hindu religious textbooks Grades 3 4 5 STBB
intro: In a first for Sindh's government schools, dedicated religious textbooks for Hindu students in Grades 3, 4, and 5 have been approved for the academic year 2026-27. The decision was taken at the Sindh Curriculum Council Executive Committee meeting on 20 April 2026, followed by a letter to the STBB chairman on 29 April 2026, and reported by Dawn on 30 April and 2 May 2026 and by The Nation on 1 May 2026. The Sindh Textbook Board oversees distribution, while publication costs for 2026-27 are borne by Prem Sagar Sanstha Karachi, with STBB to fund publication from the next academic year. This guide explains what was decided, how the arrangement works, and why the decision matters for students, families, and schools.

paras: The decision is specific: the Sindh Education Department approved dedicated religious textbooks for Hindu students in government schools, for Grades 3, 4, and 5, for the academic year 2026-27. It was taken at the Sindh Curriculum Council Executive Committee meeting on 20 April 2026, and a letter followed to the STBB chairman on 29 April 2026, setting the arrangement in motion. The decision was then reported in the press, by Dawn on 30 April and 2 May 2026, and by The Nation on 1 May 2026, which is how the public record of the decision is dated. Students and families reading about the books should note these dates, because they show a decision made months before the school year, not a sudden announcement.

The scope of the decision is equally specific and worth stating plainly: it covers Grades 3 to 5, it covers government schools, and it covers Hindu students' religious education. It does not, on the verified record, extend to other grades or to other school types, and this guide does not claim otherwise. Keeping the scope exact matters, because a decision that is described more broadly than it was taken creates false expectations for families outside its range. The verified facts describe a focused first step, and that focus is itself part of the story.

diagram.caption: The verified dates behind the Grades 3-5 Hindu religious books.

sections.h2: Who Does What: STBB and Prem Sagar Sanstha
paras: The arrangement divides responsibilities clearly. The Sindh Textbook Board oversees distribution of the books, which fits its role as the province's textbook body, while Prem Sagar Sanstha Karachi bears the publication cost for the 2026-27 academic year. From the next academic year onwards, STBB itself is to fund publication. That funding sequence is important to understand: the first year is carried by a community organisation, and the board takes over funding afterwards, which means the books' continuation does not depend on a single year's private support. Families and schools can therefore treat the books as a lasting part of the curriculum, not as a one-year experiment.

The division of roles also shows how curriculum decisions move from approval to classroom. Approval came from the Education Department through the Curriculum Council, distribution sits with STBB, and the first year's publication cost sits with Prem Sagar Sanstha. Each step has a named owner, which makes the arrangement accountable: if a school has not received the books, the question of who to ask has a clear answer in the distribution role. Schools that are still waiting should raise the matter through their normal departmental channels rather than assuming the books do not exist, since the decision and the distribution arrangement are both on the public record.

sections.h2: Why This Is a First for Sindh Government Schools
paras: The decision is described as the first time such books are introduced for Hindu students in Sindh government schools, and that first is significant. Until now, Hindu students in government schools did not have dedicated religious textbooks of their own within the provincial system, which meant their religious education lacked the structured, grade-wise material that other subjects and other religious curricula provide. A dedicated textbook for Grades 3 to 5 gives young students age-appropriate material in their own religious tradition, taught in school rather than left entirely to home or community instruction, and that recognition within the formal system is itself meaningful for families.

The grade range also matters educationally. Grades 3 to 5 are the years when children move from learning to read to reading to learn, and when early ideas about faith, values, and community take shape. Providing structured religious material at exactly those ages means the books can support both religious knowledge and the broader values the curriculum emphasises, such as tolerance and respect for others. The STBB's wider 2026-27 textbook programme, the Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Textbook Series with 195 titles in Sindhi, Urdu, and English and 52 million sets, already emphasises tolerance among its revised curriculum themes, and the Hindu textbooks sit naturally alongside that direction.

sections.h2: What It Means for Students and Classrooms
paras: For a Hindu student in Grade 3, 4, or 5 in a government school, the practical meaning is simple: there is now a textbook for their religious education, provided through the school system like other textbooks. That means lessons can follow a planned sequence, teachers have material to teach from, and students can revise from a book rather than from scattered notes. It also means Hindu students are visible in the curriculum in the same way as other students, which matters for a child's sense of belonging at school. A textbook is a small object, but its presence on a desk sends a message about whose learning counts.

For teachers, the books bring both an opportunity and a responsibility: to teach the material accurately and respectfully, and to handle classroom discussion with the sensitivity that religious topics deserve. Teachers who have not taught this material before may need time and support to use it well, and schools should make sure the books reach classrooms together with whatever guidance the department provides. For classmates of other faiths, the books are also a chance to learn respect in practice, since a classroom where every child's tradition is treated seriously is a classroom where tolerance is lived, not just listed as a curriculum theme. The wider solved-notes collection on [Solved Notes](/solved.html) supports classroom learning across subjects.

The honest position on what comes next is that the verified record covers the 2026-27 arrangement and the funding change from the next academic year, and nothing beyond that has been verified for this guide. Families and schools should watch for two things: whether distribution reaches all intended government schools for Grades 3 to 5 during 2026-27, and how the STBB-funded publication from the next academic year is arranged. Those are practical questions with observable answers, and they are the right things to track, rather than speculation about grades or subjects that no verified decision currently covers.

Students and parents who want to follow the story should rely on the Education Department, STBB, and reputable press reporting, as with the Dawn and Nation reports that documented the original decision, rather than on social media claims that expand the decision beyond its verified scope. A first step as significant as this one deserves accurate reporting, and accuracy means keeping the grade range, the school type, and the funding arrangement exactly as decided. The full book collection, including STBB textbooks, is listed on [Books](/books.html), and further board and curriculum news is covered on [Blog](/blog/).

title: Shaheed Benazirabad Board 9th Class Result 2026 Announced — Check by Roll Number, SMS & Gazette
desc: BISE Shaheed Benazirabad announced the Class 9 Annual Examinations 2026 result on 31 October 2026, with a 79.02% Science Group pass rate. Check by roll number on bisesba.edu.pk.
kw: Shaheed Benazirabad board 9th class result 2026, BISE SBA class 9 result 2026 announced, Nawabshah board SSC Part-I result 2026 check by roll number
intro: Class 9 students of the Shaheed Benazirabad division have their result. The Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education Shaheed Benazirabad (BISE SBA), based in Nawabshah, announced the results of the Annual Examinations 2026 for Class IX (SSC Part-I) Science and General Groups on 31 October 2026. The announcement was made with the approval of Chairman Dr Asif Ali Memon and Controller of Examinations Shah Muhammad Farooq Rashdi, and was reported the same evening by the Associated Press of Pakistan (APP) through UrduPoint. This is the board's own Class 9 annual result: it is not the Karachi result, which was announced by a different board on 28 October, and it is not an intermediate result. Students can check their result on the board's official website, www.bisesba.edu.pk, and through the board's Android application, according to the board officials quoted in the announcement report. This guide explains exactly what was announced, how to check your result by roll number step by step, what the new grading rule means for your marks, and what to do next whether you passed all your papers, passed some of them, or need to appear again.

sections.h2: The announcement: BISE Shaheed Benazirabad Class 9 result, 31 October 2026
paras: The Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education Shaheed Benazirabad announced the results of its Annual Examinations 2026 for Class IX Science and General Groups on 31 October 2026. The announcement covers the SSC Part-I (Class 9) annual examinations conducted by the board for students in its jurisdiction in Sindh, centred on Nawabshah. The board's chairman, Dr Asif Ali Memon, and its Controller of Examinations, Shah Muhammad Farooq Rashdi, approved the result, according to the APP report carried by UrduPoint on the evening of 31 October 2026.

This announcement arrived later than many students expected. Sindh's boards do not announce on a single shared date the way Punjab's boards do; each Sindh board declares its result when its own marking and tabulation are complete. Karachi's secondary board, BSEK, announced its Class 9 Science Group result on 28 October 2026, and Shaheed Benazirabad followed three days later with its own Class 9 result. Students should therefore check only the Shaheed Benazirabad board's own website and app, not another board's portal, because each board holds only its own students' records. Our earlier post on the [Karachi Board 9th Class Result 2026](/blog/karachi-board-9th-class-science-result-2026-announced.html) explains how a neighbouring Sindh board's announcement worked, but your roll number will only work on the BISE SBA system.

No position-holder names were given in the announcement report for this Class 9 result, so this post names none. If the board publishes a separate position-holder list, it will appear through the board's own channels. The headline figures, however, are clear and come straight from the board's released results: the Science Group pass percentage is 79.02 per cent, and the General Group pass percentage is 52 per cent. The sections below break those figures down, explain the new grading system that applies to this year's Class 9 examinations, and walk you through checking your own result.

sections.h2: How to check your result online by roll number
paras: The simplest way to check your result is on the board's official website, www.bisesba.edu.pk. The board officials quoted in the announcement report confirmed that results can be checked through the official website and the board's Android application. Keep your roll number slip or admit card beside you before you start, because the portal asks for your roll number, and a single wrong digit will show no record or somebody else's result. If the website is slow in the first hours after the announcement, wait a few minutes and try again rather than re-entering different numbers; heavy traffic on result day is normal and does not mean your result is missing.

Follow these steps in order. First, open the board's official website, www.bisesba.edu.pk, on your phone or computer. Second, look for the results section on the homepage and choose the SSC Part-I (Class IX) Annual Examination 2026. Third, enter your roll number exactly as printed on your admit card. Fourth, submit the form and wait for your result card to load, then read every subject's grade carefully and note any paper marked Ungraded, which is explained in the grading section below. Fifth, save or print a copy of the online result for your own record, and collect your original result card from your school when the board issues it, because the online printout is for information while the school-issued card is your formal record.

sections.h2: SMS, app and gazette: the other ways to check
paras: If you cannot open the website, the board's Android application is the second official route named in the announcement report. Install the board's app, open its results section, and enter your roll number in the same way as on the website. The app and the website draw on the same board record, so a result shown on one should match the other; if the two ever disagree, trust the board's website and ask your school to confirm, because a typing error in one entry is the usual cause of a mismatch.

Result portals for this board also list an SMS method: type your roll number and send it to 800299. That code is reported by result portals rather than by the APP announcement report, so confirm the code on the board's own website or app before you send any message, and never pay anyone who offers to fetch your result for a fee. The board also publishes a result gazette, which is the complete published list of results; your school can help you look up your roll number in the gazette if the online portal is unreachable. Whichever method you use, check the result once carefully, write your grades down, and keep the copy safe for admission and record purposes.

sections.h2: Key statistics: Science Group 79.02 per cent, General Group 52 per cent
paras: The Science Group is by far the larger of the two groups in this announcement. A total of 52,260 candidates registered for the Science Group examinations, of whom 51,546 appeared. Of those who appeared, 41,425 students were declared successful, giving an overall pass percentage of 79.02 per cent. The board's breakdown shows that the 41,425 successful candidates passed all subjects, while other candidates passed some papers: 4,353 passed six subjects, 1,517 passed five subjects, 1,380 passed four subjects, 704 passed three subjects, 342 passed two subjects, and 286 passed only one subject. If you passed some papers but not all, you have not failed outright; your passed papers stand, and the remaining papers are the ones to plan for next, as explained in the final guidance section.

Of these, 26 students were declared successful, recording an overall pass percentage of 52 per cent. Because the General Group entry is so small, its percentage moves sharply with just a few students either way, so it should not be compared directly with the Science Group percentage as if the two groups were the same size. sections.h2: The new grading system and what your result means
paras: This year's Class 9 examinations follow a new grading system introduced under a decision of the Government of Sindh's Universities and Boards Department. Under the new system, a candidate securing less than 40 per cent marks in a paper will be declared Ungraded in that paper and will not be considered successful in it. That is the key change to understand when you read your result: a paper marked Ungraded is a paper you have not passed, even if your overall total looks reasonable, and it is the paper you must deal with in your next step.

Read your result subject by subject, not just as a total. If every paper shows a grade, you have passed all subjects and can move on to Class 10 with your school's admission process. If one or more papers show Ungraded, note exactly which subjects they are, because your plan depends on those subjects alone; your passed papers do not need to be repeated. Students sometimes panic when they see a single Ungraded paper, but the system is designed so that you can address the remaining papers through the board's next examination opportunity rather than repeating the whole class. Your school's examination office can confirm which route applies to you and the exact dates and fees.

The bi-annual (supplementary) session is the route for supplementary and improvement papers, so a student with Ungraded papers should ask their school immediately about registration for it, rather than waiting until the session has started. sections.h2: What to do next: rechecking, result card and supplementary exams
paras: First, collect your result card. The online result tells you your grades, but your school-issued result card is the document you will need for Class 10 admission and for your academic record, so ask your school when it will be available and check that your name, roll number, and subject grades on it match the online result. If you spot a spelling mistake in your name or a mismatch in a grade, report it to your school at once so the correction can be raised with the board; small errors are far easier to fix early than months later.

Second, decide about rechecking only after reading your result carefully. If a paper's grade looks far below what you expected, ask your teacher whether rechecking is open for this examination and what it costs and covers, because rechecking re-examines the marking of that paper rather than re-teaching the subject. If instead you have Ungraded papers, the practical route is usually the board's bi-annual (supplementary) session, confirm the registration deadline with your school, because missing it can cost you a whole session.

Third, plan your Class 10 year around the subjects that need work. Students who passed everything should start Class 10 reading early, while students retaking papers should split their time between keeping up with Class 10 and revising the Ungraded subjects, with a teacher's help to prioritise. Either way, keep your admit card, your printed online result, and your result card together in one folder, and do not share your roll number publicly or pay any agent who claims to change a result, because no genuine result change happens outside the board's own rechecking and examination process.
