title: Class 10 Physics: Speed and Velocity Numericals
desc: Master class 10 physics speed velocity numericals with step-by-step worked examples, unit conversions, and the difference between speed and velocity explained clearly.
intro: Class 10 physics speed velocity numericals appear in almost every test on motion, and they are also some of the easiest marks available if you handle the basics correctly. Most students lose marks not because the physics is hard, but because they mix up distance with displacement, forget to convert minutes to seconds or kilometres per hour to metres per second, or write an answer without a unit. This guide fixes all three problems with a clear method and original worked examples you can practise on your own. The keyword for this chapter is simple: write the formula, substitute with units, and only then calculate. Speed is a scalar quantity, which means it has magnitude but no direction, while velocity is a vector quantity, which means it has both magnitude and direction. A car travelling at 60 kilometres per hour has a speed of 60 kilometres per hour, but its velocity is 60 kilometres per hour east only if you also state the direction. In numerical problems, speed equals total distance divided by total time, and velocity equals displacement divided by time. Displacement is the straight-line distance from the starting point to the finishing point, together with its direction, so a runner who returns to the starting point has zero displacement and therefore zero average velocity, even though the speed was not zero. Keep that distinction in front of you for every question, and half the chapter becomes straightforward.

paras: Speed is defined as the distance travelled per unit time, and its formula is speed equals distance divided by time, written as v = s / t. The SI unit of speed is metres per second, written m/s, although kilometres per hour is common in everyday life and in many textbook questions. Average speed is total distance divided by total time, which is not the same as the average of two speeds unless the times are equal. For example, a cyclist who covers 30 kilometres in one hour and then 30 kilometres in two hours has an average speed of 60 kilometres divided by 3 hours, which is 20 kilometres per hour, not the simple average of 30 and 15. Always add up the distances and add up the times separately before dividing.

Velocity is displacement divided by time, so its formula looks the same, v = d / t, but d now means displacement rather than distance. Because displacement can be negative in a chosen direction, velocity can also be negative, and that sign simply tells you the direction of motion. A car moving backwards at 5 m/s has a velocity of negative 5 m/s if forward is taken as positive. In most Class 10 numericals the motion is in a straight line in one direction, so speed and velocity have the same numerical value and the difference only matters when direction changes or when the object returns towards its start. Read every question twice and underline whether it asks for distance or displacement before you begin.
bullets: Speed = distance / time; velocity = displacement / time.
SI unit for both: metres per second (m/s).
Speed is scalar; velocity is a vector with direction.
Average speed = total distance / total time, never just the average of speeds.

sections.h2: Unit Conversions You Must Get Right
paras: Unit conversion is where most numerical marks are lost, so learn two conversions by heart. To convert kilometres per hour to metres per second, multiply by 5/18, and to convert metres per second to kilometres per hour, multiply by 18/5. So 72 km/h becomes 72 times 5/18, which is 20 m/s, and 15 m/s becomes 15 times 18/5, which is 54 km/h. Time conversions matter just as much: one hour is 3600 seconds, one minute is 60 seconds, and a time given as 2 hours 30 minutes is 2.5 hours or 9000 seconds. Always convert every quantity to one consistent set of units before substituting into a formula, and state the conversion step in your answer so the examiner can follow your working.

A second common trap is mixing units inside one formula, for example dividing kilometres by seconds. If distance is in kilometres and time is in minutes, either convert distance to metres and time to seconds, or convert time to hours and keep distance in kilometres. Both routes are correct, but the SI route is safer because the answer then comes out in m/s, which is what most marking schemes expect. Check your final answer for sense: a walking person moves at about 1 to 2 m/s, a bicycle at about 5 m/s, and a car on a highway at about 20 to 30 m/s. If your answer says a cyclist travels at 200 m/s, you have made a conversion error and should go back and find it.

sections.h2: Worked Example 1: Speed and Average Speed
paras: Example: A bus travels 120 km in 2 hours and then 60 km in 1 hour. Find its average speed in km/h and in m/s. Solution: total distance = 120 + 60 = 180 km. Total time = 2 + 1 = 3 hours. Average speed = 180 / 3 = 60 km/h. To convert to m/s, multiply by 5/18: 60 times 5/18 = 300/18 = 16.7 m/s. Notice that we did not average 60 km/h and 60 km/h from the two parts separately by accident here, but the method of totals works in every case, even when the two part-speeds differ. Writing the totals as their own step makes your working clear and earns method marks even if a later arithmetic slip occurs.

Example: A student walks 400 m to school in 5 minutes. Find the speed in m/s. Solution: time = 5 minutes = 5 times 60 = 300 s. Speed = 400 / 300 = 1.33 m/s. This is a sensible walking speed, which confirms the conversion was done correctly. If you had forgotten to convert minutes to seconds and divided 400 by 5, you would have obtained 80, a meaningless answer with no correct unit. The habit of converting time first, before touching the formula, prevents this entire class of error. For more solved study material, browse the [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [books section](/books.html) on this site.

Example: A boy runs 100 m east in 20 s, then runs 60 m west in 10 s. Find his average speed and his average velocity. Solution: total distance = 100 + 60 = 160 m. Total time = 20 + 10 = 30 s. Average speed = 160 / 30 = 5.33 m/s. Displacement: taking east as positive, displacement = 100 + (negative 60) = 40 m east. Average velocity = 40 / 30 = 1.33 m/s east. The two answers are very different, and the difference is the whole point of the question: distance adds up, displacement partly cancels. Examiners love this pattern, so practise it until the distinction is automatic.

Example: A car travels around a circular track and returns to its starting point after 60 s, covering 600 m. Its average speed is 600 / 60 = 10 m/s, but its displacement is zero because start and finish are the same point, so its average velocity is 0 m/s. Students often find this result surprising, but it follows directly from the definitions. Whenever a question mentions a round trip or a return to the start, expect the displacement or average velocity to be zero or much smaller than the distance-based answer. Underline the words distance and displacement in the question so you never confuse them under exam pressure.

diagram.caption: Speed uses total distance; velocity uses displacement and direction.

paras: The most common mistake is writing an answer without a unit, which can cost the final mark even when the number is correct. Always write the unit, and check that it matches the quantities you used: metres and seconds give m/s, kilometres and hours give km/h. The second mistake is using the wrong time: average speed needs total time, including any rest time mentioned in the question, unless the question explicitly says to exclude it. If a bus stops for 30 minutes during a journey, that half hour belongs in the total time for average speed. The third mistake is rounding too early: keep two or three decimal places through the working and round only the final answer.

Build a short routine for every numerical: read the question and list the given quantities with units, convert units to a consistent set, write the formula in symbols, substitute the numbers with units, calculate, and finish with the answer plus unit and a quick sense check. Practise this routine on ten mixed problems and it becomes automatic, which is exactly what you need when exam time is short. Worked examples in this guide are original practice problems designed to teach the method; they are not copied from any textbook exercise. For more study help across subjects, visit the [blog](/blog/) and read the [about page](/about.html) to see what this site offers.
bullets: Always write the unit with the final answer.
Include rest time in total time for average speed.
Convert all units before substituting into the formula.
Do a sense check: walking about 1-2 m/s, cycling about 5 m/s.

points: Speed = distance / time; velocity = displacement / time.
Convert km/h to m/s by multiplying by 5/18, and m/s to km/h by 18/5.
Average speed uses total distance divided by total time.
A round trip has zero displacement and therefore zero average velocity.
Always write the unit and do a sense check on your final answer.

faqs.q: What is the difference between speed and velocity?
faqs.a: Speed is distance divided by time and has no direction, while velocity is displacement divided by time and includes direction. For motion in one straight direction they have the same value, but when direction changes or the object returns to its start, they differ.

faqs.q: How do I convert 72 km/h to m/s?
faqs.a: Multiply by 5/18. So 72 times 5/18 equals 20 m/s. The reverse conversion, m/s to km/h, uses 18/5: 20 m/s times 18/5 equals 72 km/h.

faqs.q: Why is average speed not the average of two speeds?
faqs.a: Because average speed is total distance divided by total time. Averaging two speeds only works if the time spent at each speed is equal. When the times differ, you must add the distances and add the times separately, then divide.

faqs.q: Can velocity be zero while speed is not zero?
faqs.a: Yes. If an object returns to its starting point, its displacement is zero, so its average velocity is zero, even though it travelled a real distance and its average speed is not zero.

faqs.q: What unit should I use for time in speed numericals?
faqs.a: Use seconds with metres to get m/s, or hours with kilometres to get km/h. Convert minutes and mixed times (like 2 hours 30 minutes) before substituting into the formula.

title: Class 10 Physics: Force, Mass and Acceleration Numericals
desc: Learn class 10 physics force mass acceleration numericals with F = ma worked examples, unit checks, and step-by-step solutions for every question type.
intro: Class 10 physics force mass acceleration numericals all rest on one relationship: Newton's second law, force equals mass times acceleration, written F = ma. If you can rearrange this one formula confidently and keep your units in kilograms, metres per second squared, and newtons, you can solve almost every question in this chapter. The difficulty is rarely the physics itself; it is unit conversion, especially grams to kilograms and kilometres per hour to metres per second, and knowing which of the three quantities the question is asking for. This guide teaches a fixed routine: identify the known quantities, convert the units, write the formula, substitute, and check the answer. Force is measured in newtons, where one newton is the force needed to accelerate a mass of one kilogram at one metre per second squared. Mass is measured in kilograms, and acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, measured in metres per second squared. A larger force produces a larger acceleration for the same mass, and a larger mass needs a larger force for the same acceleration. That everyday intuition is exactly what the formula says, and it is a useful sense check: if your calculated force for a bicycle is thousands of newtons, something has gone wrong.

sections.h2: Newton's Second Law in Plain Words
paras: Newton's second law states that the acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass. In symbols, F = ma, where F is the net force in newtons, m is the mass in kilograms, and a is the acceleration in metres per second squared. Net force matters: if two forces act in opposite directions, you must subtract the smaller from the larger before using the formula. A car engine pushing forward with 2000 N against 500 N of friction has a net force of 1500 N, and it is 1500 N, not 2000 N, that goes into F = ma. Many exam questions hide a friction or opposing force in the wording, so always ask yourself whether the stated force is the net force.

Rearranging the formula gives the other two forms you will need: a = F / m when acceleration is unknown, and m = F / a when mass is unknown. Practise all three arrangements so you never waste time rearranging under pressure. The triangle method helps some students: cover the quantity you want, and the remaining two show the operation, with F on top meaning F = ma, and covering F leaving m times a. Whichever memory aid you use, the physics is the same, and the units must always match: mass in kilograms, acceleration in m/s squared, force in newtons.
bullets: F = ma: force in newtons, mass in kilograms, acceleration in m/s squared.
Use net force: subtract opposing forces like friction first.
Rearranged forms: a = F / m and m = F / a.
One newton = 1 kg times 1 m/s squared.

sections.h2: Units and Conversions Before You Calculate
paras: Mass is often given in grams in exam questions, and forgetting to convert is the single most common error in this chapter. Divide grams by 1000 to get kilograms: 500 g is 0.5 kg, and 250 g is 0.25 kg. Acceleration may need to be calculated first from a change in velocity over time, using a = (v minus u) / t, where u is initial velocity, v is final velocity, and t is time in seconds. If velocities are given in km/h, convert them to m/s by multiplying by 5/18 before finding the acceleration. A question that gives a car speeding up from 36 km/h to 72 km/h in 10 seconds therefore needs two conversions before F = ma can even be used.

Work through that example fully: 36 km/h is 10 m/s, and 72 km/h is 20 m/s. Acceleration = (20 minus 10) / 10 = 1 m/s squared. If the car has a mass of 1000 kg, the net force is 1000 times 1 = 1000 N. Notice how each step is written separately: conversion, acceleration, then force. This layered working is what earns full marks, because an examiner can award method marks for each correct step even if one arithmetic step slips. Never jump straight from the question to a final number with no working shown.

Example: A force accelerates a 4 kg trolley at 3 m/s squared. Find the force. Solution: F = ma = 4 times 3 = 12 N. This is the simplest question type, and it should take under a minute. The only traps are unit traps: if the mass had been given as 4000 g, you would convert to 4 kg first, and the answer would still be 12 N. Always scan the question for grams, and convert before you substitute. A second example with a twist: a 2 kg object is pushed with 10 N but friction of 4 N opposes the motion. Net force = 10 minus 4 = 6 N, so acceleration = 6 / 2 = 3 m/s squared. The twist is the friction, and missing it gives the wrong answer of 5 m/s squared.

Example: A cricket ball of mass 150 g is hit and accelerates at 200 m/s squared. Find the force. Solution: mass = 150 / 1000 = 0.15 kg. Force = 0.15 times 200 = 30 N. The small mass and large acceleration combine into a very reasonable force, which is a good sense check. If you had forgotten the gram conversion and used 150 kg, you would have calculated 30,000 N, which is obviously absurd for a cricket ball. Sense checks like this catch errors fast: compare your answer with everyday forces, where lifting a 1 kg bag needs about 10 N and a car engine produces thousands of newtons.

sections.h2: Worked Example 2: Finding Mass and Acceleration
paras: Example: A force of 60 N produces an acceleration of 4 m/s squared in an object. Find its mass. Solution: m = F / a = 60 / 4 = 15 kg. Example: A 5 kg box is pulled with a force of 25 N. Find its acceleration. Solution: a = F / m = 25 / 5 = 5 m/s squared. These two question types are mirror images of each other, and the only skill is rearranging the formula correctly. A reliable check is to substitute your answer back into F = ma: 15 kg times 4 m/s squared is 60 N, which matches the question, so the mass is correct. This back-substitution takes five seconds and catches rearrangement slips, especially under exam stress.

Example: A 1200 kg car accelerates from rest to 30 m/s in 15 s. Find the net force. Solution: acceleration = (30 minus 0) / 15 = 2 m/s squared. Force = 1200 times 2 = 2400 N. This two-stage question combines the acceleration formula with F = ma, and it is a favourite exam pattern. Practise two-stage questions deliberately: first find acceleration from the velocity change, then find force. Students who try to do both stages in one line often mix up the numbers. For extra solved material, explore the [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [books section](/books.html).

diagram.caption: Follow these steps in order for every force, mass and acceleration numerical.

paras: The top three mistakes in this chapter are using grams instead of kilograms, using the applied force instead of the net force when friction is present, and forgetting that acceleration must be calculated from a velocity change when it is not given directly. A fourth mistake is writing the answer without a unit: a bare number like 12 earns no final mark, while 12 N does. A fifth is confusing mass and weight: mass in kilograms is the m in F = ma, while weight is a force equal to mass times gravity, about 10 N per kilogram. If a question gives weight in newtons, divide by 10 to get mass in kilograms before using F = ma.

Exam technique matters as much as physics here. Write the formula in symbols first, then the substitution with units, then the answer. Show net-force subtraction as its own line. Keep the same routine for every question so that easy questions stay easy and hard questions break into manageable steps. Practise mixed question types, where sometimes force is unknown, sometimes mass, sometimes acceleration, and sometimes acceleration must be found first. The examples in this guide are original practice problems for teaching the method, not reproductions of textbook exercises. More guidance is available on the [blog](/blog/) and the [about page](/about.html).
bullets: Convert grams to kilograms before substituting.
Subtract friction to get net force.
Mass and weight are different: weight = mass times gravity.
Back-substitute your answer into F = ma as a check.

Ask it to quiz you on all three arrangements of the formula until each one feels automatic. Join Muse with invite code LTGSWD — in the Muse app, go to Settings > Redeem token and enter the code. points: F = ma, with force in newtons, mass in kilograms, acceleration in m/s squared.
Always use net force: subtract friction and opposing forces first.
Convert grams to kilograms by dividing by 1000.
If acceleration is not given, find it from a = (v - u) / t.
Back-substitute your answer into F = ma to check it.

faqs.q: What is one newton?
faqs.a: One newton is the force needed to accelerate a mass of one kilogram at one metre per second squared. That is why 1 N equals 1 kg times 1 m/s squared, and why the units must always be kilograms and m/s squared.

faqs.q: Do I use the applied force or the net force in F = ma?
faqs.a: Always the net force. If friction or another force opposes the motion, subtract it from the applied force first, then use the result in F = ma.

faqs.q: How do I solve a question where mass is given in grams?
faqs.a: Divide the grams by 1000 to get kilograms before substituting. For example, 250 g becomes 0.25 kg. Using grams directly gives an answer 1000 times too large.

faqs.q: What is the difference between mass and weight?
faqs.a: Mass is the amount of matter in kilograms and does not change with location. Weight is a force, equal to mass times gravity, measured in newtons. On Earth, weight is roughly mass times 10.

faqs.q: How do I find acceleration when it is not given?
faqs.a: Use a = (v - u) / t, where u is initial velocity, v is final velocity, and t is time in seconds. Convert velocities to m/s first if they are given in km/h.

title: Class 10 Physics: Work, Energy and Power Numericals
desc: Master class 10 physics work energy power numericals with joules and watts, step-by-step solutions, and everyday examples that make the formulas stick.
intro: Class 10 physics work energy power numericals test three linked ideas: work done, energy transferred, and the rate at which that transfer happens. The formulas are short, work equals force times distance, kinetic energy equals half mass times velocity squared, potential energy equals mass times gravity times height, and power equals work divided by time, but students still lose marks by mixing up the formulas, forgetting the half in kinetic energy, or using the wrong unit for time. This guide separates the three ideas clearly, works through original examples with full steps, and shows how joules and watts connect to everyday life, from lifting a school bag to running up stairs. Work in physics has a precise meaning: work is done when a force moves an object in the direction of the force, and it is measured in joules. Pushing a wall that does not move does no work in the physics sense, however tiring it feels. Energy is the capacity to do work, and it is also measured in joules, which is why work and energy share a unit and why the work-energy idea is so useful: the work done on an object equals its change in energy. Power is different again: it measures how fast the work is done, and its unit is the watt, where one watt is one joule per second.

paras: Work is calculated as W = F times s, where F is the force in newtons and s is the distance moved in the direction of the force, in metres. The unit is the joule, where one joule equals one newton times one metre. The direction condition matters: if you carry a bag horizontally while walking, the lifting force is vertical but the movement is horizontal, so that force does no work in the physics sense during the walk. Exam questions test this by giving a force at an angle or a movement perpendicular to the force, and the correct answer for that component is zero work. When the force and movement are in the same direction, as in pushing a box along the floor, the full formula applies directly.

Work can also be found from a force that is not stated directly. If a question gives mass and acceleration, first find force with F = ma, then find work with W = F times s. If it gives weight and height, as in lifting problems, the force is the weight, mass times gravity, and the distance is the height lifted. Lifting a 5 kg bag through 2 metres needs a force of about 50 N (5 times 10) and work of 50 times 2 = 100 J. Writing both stages separately keeps the method visible and earns marks at each stage, which is exactly how exam marking works.
bullets: Work W = F x s, in joules (J).
Distance must be in the direction of the force.
No movement means no work, however hard you push.
Lifting work uses weight as the force and height as the distance.

paras: Kinetic energy is the energy of a moving object, given by KE = half times m times v squared, where m is mass in kilograms and v is velocity in metres per second. The half is essential and is the most commonly forgotten part of this chapter: a 2 kg object moving at 4 m/s has kinetic energy of half times 2 times 16, which is 16 J, not 32 J. Because velocity is squared, doubling the speed multiplies kinetic energy by four, which is why fast vehicles need much longer stopping distances. If a question gives speed in km/h, convert to m/s first by multiplying by 5/18, or the squared term will magnify the error enormously.

Potential energy is stored energy due to position, and for height above the ground it is PE = m times g times h, where g is about 10 m/s squared and h is height in metres. A 2 kg book on a shelf 3 metres high has potential energy of 2 times 10 times 3 = 60 J relative to the floor. The reference level matters: the same book has zero potential energy relative to the shelf itself. Exam questions usually take the ground as the reference, but always check the wording. The link between work and energy is direct: lifting the book did 60 J of work against gravity, and that work is now stored as 60 J of potential energy.

sections.h2: Worked Example 1: Work and Energy Together
paras: Example: A boy pushes a box with a force of 40 N over a distance of 5 m. Find the work done. Solution: W = F times s = 40 times 5 = 200 J. Example: A car of mass 1000 kg moves at 20 m/s. Find its kinetic energy. Solution: KE = half times 1000 times 20 squared = half times 1000 times 400 = 200,000 J, or 200 kJ. Note the size of the answer: moving vehicles carry large kinetic energies, which is why the kilojoule is often used. If your answer for a car came out as 200 J, you would know immediately that you had forgotten the square or the mass conversion.

Example: A 4 kg object is lifted to a height of 2.5 m. Find the work done against gravity and its potential energy at that height. Solution: weight = 4 times 10 = 40 N. Work = 40 times 2.5 = 100 J. Potential energy = m times g times h = 4 times 10 times 2.5 = 100 J. The two answers agree, as they must, because the work done lifting the object becomes its potential energy. Questions that ask for both are really asking one question twice, and recognising that saves time. For more solved study content, see the [solved notes](/solved.html) and [books section](/books.html).

sections.h2: Power: How Fast Work Is Done
paras: Power is the rate of doing work, P = W / t, where W is work in joules and t is time in seconds. Its unit is the watt, where one watt equals one joule per second. A machine that does 1000 J of work in 10 seconds has a power of 100 W, while the same work done in 2 seconds needs 500 W. This is why power, not just energy, decides how strong an engine feels: two motors can deliver the same energy, but the one that delivers it faster has the higher power. Time must be in seconds: a time given in minutes must be multiplied by 60 before dividing, and this is the most common error in power numericals.

Example: A motor lifts 200 kg of water through 10 m in 20 s. Find its power. Solution: weight = 200 times 10 = 2000 N. Work = 2000 times 10 = 20,000 J. Power = 20,000 / 20 = 1000 W, or 1 kW. Example: A student of mass 50 kg runs up stairs 4 m high in 5 s. Find the power developed. Solution: work = 50 times 10 times 4 = 2000 J. Power = 2000 / 5 = 400 W. Notice how the same three-step pattern, weight, work, power, solves both questions. Learn the pattern, not individual answers.

diagram.alt: Solving Work, Energy and Power Problems
diagram.caption: Identify the quantity asked, then follow the matching route.

paras: The most frequent mistakes are forgetting the half in kinetic energy, forgetting to square the velocity, using time in minutes instead of seconds for power, and using mass instead of weight when lifting work is asked. A second group of errors comes from unit mixing: mass in grams must be converted to kilograms, and speed in km/h to m/s, before either formula is used. A third trap is the perpendicular-force case: carrying an object horizontally does no work against gravity, and pushing a stationary wall does no work at all. Read the question for movement and direction before choosing a formula.

Write your working in stages: force or weight first, then work or energy, then power if asked. Each stage earns marks and makes errors easy to spot. End with a sense check: lifting a school bag a couple of metres is tens or hundreds of joules, a moving car is tens of thousands of joules, and a light bulb is tens of watts while a motor is hundreds or thousands. If your answer is wildly outside these ranges, recheck the conversions. The examples here are original practice problems for teaching the method. More help is on the [blog](/blog/) and the [about page](/about.html).
bullets: Never forget the half in KE = 1/2 m v squared.
Square the velocity, and convert km/h to m/s first.
Power needs time in seconds, not minutes.
Lifting work uses weight (mass times gravity), not mass alone.

points: Work W = F x s, measured in joules; distance must be in the force direction.
Kinetic energy KE = 1/2 m v squared; doubling speed quadruples KE.
Potential energy PE = m g h, with height above the reference level.
Power P = W / t, in watts; time must be in seconds.
Lifting work equals the gain in potential energy.

faqs.q: What is the difference between work and power?
faqs.a: Work is the energy transferred when a force moves an object, measured in joules. Power is how fast that work is done, measured in watts. The same work done in less time means higher power.

faqs.q: Why is there a half in the kinetic energy formula?
faqs.a: Kinetic energy equals half mass times velocity squared, KE = 1/2 m v squared. The half comes from the physics of accelerating an object from rest. Forgetting it doubles your answer, which is a common exam error.

faqs.q: Does carrying a bag horizontally do work against gravity?
faqs.a: No. The lifting force acts vertically while the movement is horizontal, so no work is done by that force in the direction of movement. Work needs movement in the direction of the force.

faqs.q: How do I convert watts to kilowatts?
faqs.a: Divide watts by 1000. So 1000 W is 1 kW. Large powers like motors are usually stated in kilowatts, while small devices use watts.

faqs.q: What value should I use for g?
faqs.a: Use g = 10 m/s squared unless the question gives another value. Some questions use 9.8, and then you should use 9.8 exactly as given.

title: Class 10 Physics: Pressure Numericals
desc: Learn class 10 physics pressure numericals with force per unit area, pressure in solids and liquids, and step-by-step worked examples with correct units.
intro: Class 10 physics pressure numericals are built on one short formula, pressure equals force divided by area, P = F / A, but they test whether you can apply it to very different situations: a person standing on one foot, a sharp knife, a dam wall, or a diver under water. The unit of pressure is the pascal, where one pascal is one newton per square metre, and the most common student errors are using area in square centimetres instead of square metres, and confusing pressure with force itself. This guide teaches the formula, the unit conversions, liquid pressure, and original worked examples for both solids and liquids. Pressure tells you how concentrated a force is. The same force spread over a large area gives low pressure, which is why tractors have wide tyres and why lying on a bed of nails does not hurt: the force is shared across many points. The same force concentrated on a tiny area gives high pressure, which is why a sharp knife cuts and a nail pierces. Whenever a question asks why something is wide, flat, sharp, or pointed, the answer almost always involves pressure, and the numerical part is simply P = F / A with careful units.

sections.h2: Pressure in Solids: P = F / A
paras: Pressure is force per unit area: P = F / A, where F is force in newtons and A is area in square metres. The SI unit is the pascal (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N/m squared. Force here is usually weight, mass times gravity, when an object rests on a surface. A 60 kg person standing on both feet exerts a force of about 600 N on the ground. If the total contact area of both shoes is 0.03 m squared, the pressure is 600 / 0.03 = 20,000 Pa, or 20 kPa. Standing on one foot halves the area and doubles the pressure to 40,000 Pa, which is why balancing on one foot on soft ground sinks deeper.

Area conversion is the critical skill. One square metre equals 10,000 square centimetres, so an area given as 50 cm squared must be divided by 10,000 to give 0.005 m squared. Students who divide by 100 instead, confusing length conversion with area conversion, get answers 100 times wrong. If the area is given as length times width, for example a rectangular block 0.2 m by 0.1 m, multiply first to get 0.02 m squared, then divide the force by it. Always convert area to square metres before using the formula, and write the conversion as its own step.
bullets: P = F / A, in pascals (Pa = N/m squared).
Force on a surface is usually weight: mass times gravity.
Convert cm squared to m squared by dividing by 10,000.
Smaller area means larger pressure for the same force.

sections.h2: Liquid Pressure: Depth Matters, Not Volume
paras: Pressure in a liquid at a depth h is given by P = rho times g times h, where rho is the density of the liquid in kg/m cubed, g is about 10 m/s squared, and h is depth in metres. This pressure acts in all directions and increases with depth, which is why dams are thicker at the bottom and why divers feel more pressure deeper down. A surprising result students must remember is that liquid pressure depends on depth and density only, not on the shape of the container or the total volume of liquid. Two containers with the same depth but different shapes have the same pressure at the bottom.

Total pressure at a depth under water is the liquid pressure plus atmospheric pressure acting on the surface, but many Class 10 questions ask only for the pressure due to the liquid, so read the wording carefully. If the question says pressure due to water at a depth, use rho times g times h alone. If it says total pressure, add atmospheric pressure, about 100,000 Pa. Density of water is 1000 kg/m cubed, which makes water calculations tidy: at 10 m depth, water pressure is 1000 times 10 times 10 = 100,000 Pa, exactly one atmosphere. That tidy result is a useful memory anchor.

sections.h2: Worked Example 1: Pressure Under a Block and a Person
paras: Example: A block of mass 20 kg rests on a face of area 0.1 m squared. Find the pressure it exerts. Solution: force = 20 times 10 = 200 N. Pressure = 200 / 0.1 = 2000 Pa. If the block is turned onto a smaller face of area 0.05 m squared, the pressure becomes 200 / 0.05 = 4000 Pa. The force did not change, but the pressure doubled because the area halved. This is the classic exam pattern: same object, different face, compare the pressures. Always state which face you used, and show the area for each case.

Example: A girl of mass 50 kg stands on one heel of area 1 cm squared. Find the pressure. Solution: force = 50 times 10 = 500 N. Area = 1 cm squared = 1 / 10,000 = 0.0001 m squared. Pressure = 500 / 0.0001 = 5,000,000 Pa, or 5 MPa. This huge pressure explains why a heel dents soft floors. The area conversion is the whole question: a student who uses 1 cm squared as 0.01 m squared gets 50,000 Pa, which is 100 times too small. For more solved material, visit the [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [books section](/books.html).

Example: Find the water pressure at a depth of 5 m. Solution: P = rho times g times h = 1000 times 10 times 5 = 50,000 Pa. Example: A tank holds oil of density 800 kg/m cubed to a depth of 2 m. Find the pressure at the bottom due to the oil. Solution: P = 800 times 10 times 2 = 16,000 Pa. Notice that the oil gives lower pressure than water at the same depth because its density is lower. Density is the only liquid property in the formula, so questions often give two liquids at the same depth and ask which gives higher pressure: the denser liquid always wins.

Example: A diver experiences water pressure of 200,000 Pa. How deep is the diver? Solution: rearrange to h = P / (rho times g) = 200,000 / (1000 times 10) = 20 m. Rearranging the liquid pressure formula is a common question type, so practise all three forms: P = rho g h, h = P / (rho g), and rho = P / (g h). As always, check units: density in kg/m cubed, depth in metres, pressure in pascals. A depth answer in metres for a diver should be a sensible number, not thousands of metres.

diagram.caption: Pressure depends on force and area for solids, and on density and depth for liquids.

paras: The biggest mistakes are using area in cm squared without converting, confusing pressure with force by forgetting to divide by area, and using mass instead of weight for the force. A second trap is liquid pressure questions that give the volume of the container or its shape: both are irrelevant, and only depth and density matter. A third trap is forgetting atmospheric pressure when total pressure is asked, or adding it when only liquid pressure is asked. Underline the words due to and total in the question to decide which one is wanted.

Follow a fixed routine: decide whether the question is about a solid or a liquid, pick the matching formula, convert area or depth to SI units, substitute, and finish with pascals. For comparison questions, calculate both pressures and state which is larger and why. The examples in this guide are original practice problems for teaching the method. More study guidance is available on the [blog](/blog/) and the [about page](/about.html).
bullets: Convert cm squared to m squared by dividing by 10,000.
Force on a surface is usually weight, not mass.
Liquid pressure depends on depth and density, not container shape.
Check whether total pressure or liquid pressure alone is asked.

Ask it to quiz you on both P = F / A and P = rho g h until you can pick the right formula instantly. points: Pressure P = F / A, measured in pascals (N/m squared).
Smaller contact area gives larger pressure for the same force.
Convert cm squared to m squared by dividing by 10,000.
Liquid pressure P = rho g h depends on depth and density only.
Total pressure includes atmospheric pressure; liquid pressure alone does not.

faqs.q: Why does a sharp knife cut better than a blunt one?
faqs.a: A sharp knife has a much smaller contact area, so the same force produces much higher pressure, which cuts through material more easily. Pressure is force divided by area.

faqs.q: How do I convert 50 cm squared to m squared?
faqs.a: Divide by 10,000, because 1 m squared equals 10,000 cm squared. So 50 cm squared is 0.005 m squared. Dividing by 100 is a common error: that converts length, not area.

faqs.q: Does the shape of a container affect liquid pressure?
faqs.a: No. Liquid pressure at a depth depends only on the liquid density and the depth, not on the container shape or the total volume. Two containers with the same depth have the same bottom pressure.

faqs.q: Why are dams thicker at the bottom?
faqs.a: Water pressure increases with depth, so the bottom of a dam faces much higher pressure than the top. The extra thickness at the bottom withstands that higher pressure.

faqs.q: What is the difference between pressure and force?
faqs.a: Force is a push measured in newtons. Pressure is force per unit area, measured in pascals. The same force can give very different pressures depending on the area it acts on.

title: Class 10 Physics: Ohm's Law Electricity Numericals
desc: Master class 10 physics ohm law electricity numericals with V = IR worked examples, circuit diagrams, and step-by-step solutions for current, voltage and resistance.
intro: Class 10 physics ohm law electricity numericals all come from one relationship: voltage equals current times resistance, V = IR. If you can rearrange this formula confidently and keep current in amperes, voltage in volts, and resistance in ohms, you can solve the majority of electricity questions in this chapter. The traps are unit conversions, especially milliamperes to amperes and kilo-ohms to ohms, and questions that give two quantities in a different order than you expect. This guide teaches a fixed method with original worked examples and explains how to read simple circuit diagrams so you know what each question is really asking. Ohm's law states that the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the voltage across it, provided the temperature stays constant. In practical terms, doubling the voltage across a fixed resistor doubles the current, and doubling the resistance halves the current for a fixed voltage. Resistance is the opposition to current flow, measured in ohms, and it depends on the material, length, and thickness of the conductor. A long thin wire has more resistance than a short thick wire of the same material, which is why household wiring uses thick copper and why heating elements use thin high-resistance wire.

sections.h2: Ohm's Law and Its Three Forms
paras: Ohm's law is V = IR, where V is potential difference in volts, I is current in amperes, and R is resistance in ohms. Rearranged, it gives I = V / R when current is unknown, and R = V / I when resistance is unknown. Practise all three forms until rearranging is instant, because exam questions rotate which quantity is missing. A quick check after every answer is to substitute back: if you found R = 10 ohms from V = 20 V and I = 2 A, check that 2 times 10 equals 20, which confirms the answer. This five-second check catches most rearrangement slips.

The condition for Ohm's law matters for theory questions: it holds when temperature is constant. A filament bulb does not obey Ohm's law strictly because its filament heats up and its resistance rises as current increases, so its current-voltage graph curves instead of staying straight. Metal wires at steady temperature do obey it, and their graphs are straight lines through the origin. When a question asks whether a component obeys Ohm's law, look for a straight-line graph or a constant resistance value across different voltages.
bullets: V = IR: volts, amperes, ohms.
Rearranged: I = V / R and R = V / I.
Ohm's law needs constant temperature.
Filament bulbs do not obey it strictly; metal wires do.

paras: Current is often given in milliamperes in exam questions, and 1 A equals 1000 mA, so 500 mA is 0.5 A and 250 mA is 0.25 A. Resistance is often given in kilo-ohms, and 1 kilo-ohm equals 1000 ohms, so 2 kilo-ohms is 2000 ohms. Forgetting either conversion throws the answer off by a factor of 1000, which is easy to spot if you sense-check: household circuits carry currents of a few amperes, and a small torch bulb may carry 0.3 A, not 300 A. If your answer is 300 A for a torch bulb, you forgot to convert milliamperes.

Work through a conversion example: a resistor of 2 kilo-ohms carries a current of 5 mA. Find the voltage. Convert first: R = 2000 ohms, I = 0.005 A. Voltage = 0.005 times 2000 = 10 V. The large resistance and tiny current combine into an ordinary voltage, which is a good sense check. Students who skip the conversions and multiply 5 times 2 get 10 as well by accident here, but with the wrong reasoning, and in most questions the accident does not happen. Convert first, every time, and write the conversion as its own step.

sections.h2: Worked Example 1: Finding Voltage and Current
paras: Example: A current of 2 A flows through a resistor of 15 ohms. Find the voltage across it. Solution: V = IR = 2 times 15 = 30 V. Example: A 12 V battery is connected across a 4 ohm resistor. Find the current. Solution: I = V / R = 12 / 4 = 3 A. These are the two simplest question types, and they should each take under a minute. The skill is recognising which quantity is missing and picking the matching rearrangement without hesitation, then writing the substitution with units before calculating.

Example: A bulb connected to a 6 V battery draws 0.5 A. Find its resistance. Solution: R = V / I = 6 / 0.5 = 12 ohms. Example: A resistor of 20 ohms is connected to a battery, and the current is 250 mA. Find the voltage. Solution: I = 250 / 1000 = 0.25 A. Voltage = 0.25 times 20 = 5 V. Notice how the conversion step is written before the formula step in both examples. That ordering is the habit that protects your marks. For more solved study material, see the [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [books section](/books.html).

sections.h2: Worked Example 2: Circuit Diagrams and Two-Stage Problems
paras: Example: In a simple circuit, a 9 V battery drives a current of 0.3 A through a resistor. The resistor is then replaced by one of double the resistance. Find the new current. Solution: original resistance = 9 / 0.3 = 30 ohms. New resistance = 60 ohms. New current = 9 / 60 = 0.15 A. Doubling the resistance halves the current, exactly as Ohm's law predicts, and this reasoning check confirms the calculation. Two-stage questions like this are common: first find a hidden quantity, then use it in a second step. Write each stage separately and label it.

Example: A circuit has a 12 V battery and two resistors in series, 2 ohms and 4 ohms. Find the current. Solution: total resistance in series = 2 + 4 = 6 ohms. Current = 12 / 6 = 2 A. This question previews the series rule covered in the next guide, but the Ohm's law step is the same: find total resistance first, then apply V = IR to the whole circuit. When reading a circuit diagram, trace the single loop for series circuits and confirm there is only one path for the current. A diagram that shows the battery, the resistors, and the connecting wires with no branches is a series circuit.

diagram.alt: A Simple Circuit for Ohm's Law
diagram.caption: One loop, one battery, one resistor: V = IR applies directly.

paras: The top mistakes are forgetting milliampere and kilo-ohm conversions, rearranging the formula incorrectly, and confusing voltage across a component with the battery voltage in a circuit with several components. In a series circuit, the battery voltage is shared between components, so the voltage across one resistor is only part of the total. Always check whether the question gives the voltage across the resistor itself or the whole battery, and if it gives the battery voltage for a multi-resistor circuit, find the total resistance first. A second trap is writing the answer without a unit: 30 is not an answer, 30 V is.

Build this routine: list V, I, and R with their units, convert mA and kilo-ohms, pick the rearrangement for the missing quantity, substitute with units, calculate, and back-substitute to check. Practise mixed questions where each of the three quantities is missing in turn, and include conversion questions deliberately, because they are the ones that separate full marks from partial marks. The examples here are original practice problems for teaching the method. More guidance is on the [blog](/blog/) and the [about page](/about.html).
bullets: Convert mA to A by dividing by 1000.
Convert kilo-ohms to ohms by multiplying by 1000.
In series circuits, battery voltage is shared between resistors.
Back-substitute your answer into V = IR to check it.

Ask it to quiz you on all three rearrangements of V = IR until each one is instant. Join Muse with invite code LTGSWD — in the Muse app, go to Settings > Redeem token and enter the code. points: Ohm's law: V = IR, with volts, amperes, and ohms.
Rearranged forms: I = V / R and R = V / I.
Convert mA to A by dividing by 1000; kilo-ohms to ohms by multiplying by 1000.
Ohm's law holds at constant temperature.
Back-substitute your answer to check every calculation.

faqs.q: What is Ohm's law?
faqs.a: Ohm's law states that current through a conductor is directly proportional to the voltage across it at constant temperature. In symbols, V = IR, where V is voltage, I is current, and R is resistance.

faqs.q: How do I convert 250 mA to amperes?
faqs.a: Divide by 1000. So 250 mA is 0.25 A. Similarly, 2 kilo-ohms is 2000 ohms, found by multiplying by 1000.

faqs.q: Does a filament bulb obey Ohm's law?
faqs.a: Not strictly. As current increases, the filament heats up and its resistance rises, so the current-voltage graph curves. Metal wires at steady temperature do obey Ohm's law.

faqs.q: How do I find resistance if I know voltage and current?
faqs.a: Use R = V / I. For example, 12 V divided by 3 A gives 4 ohms. Always check the answer by multiplying current times resistance to recover the voltage.

faqs.q: What happens to current if resistance doubles at fixed voltage?
faqs.a: The current halves, because I = V / R. Doubling the denominator halves the result when voltage stays the same.

title: Class 10 Physics: Series and Parallel Circuit Numericals
desc: Learn class 10 physics series parallel circuits numericals with equivalent resistance, current and voltage sharing, and step-by-step worked examples.
intro: Class 10 physics series parallel circuits numericals test whether you can tell the two combinations apart and apply the right rule for equivalent resistance. In series, resistances add directly. In parallel, reciprocals add, and the equivalent resistance is always smaller than the smallest individual resistor. Students lose marks mainly by using the series rule for a parallel circuit, by forgetting to invert the final reciprocal, and by mixing up how current and voltage behave in each combination. This guide teaches both combinations side by side with original worked examples, so the contrast itself becomes your memory aid. In a series circuit there is only one path for current, so the same current flows through every component, while the voltage is shared between components. In a parallel circuit there are branches, so the voltage across every branch is the same, while the current splits between branches. These two sentences are the key to almost every question: series means same current, shared voltage; parallel means same voltage, shared current. Household wiring uses parallel circuits precisely because every appliance then gets the full supply voltage, while old-style decorative lights in series dimmed or failed together because one break stopped the whole loop.

paras: For resistors in series, the equivalent resistance is the sum: R = R1 + R2 + R3, and so on. The current is the same through every resistor, and the total voltage divides in proportion to resistance: the larger resistor gets the larger share of voltage. Example: resistors of 2 ohms, 3 ohms, and 5 ohms in series have an equivalent resistance of 10 ohms. Connected to a 20 V battery, the current is 20 / 10 = 2 A through every resistor. The voltages are 2 times 2 = 4 V, 2 times 3 = 6 V, and 2 times 5 = 10 V, which add up to 20 V, confirming the calculation. Checking that branch voltages add to the battery voltage is a powerful verification step for series questions.

Series circuits have a practical weakness: if one component breaks, the whole circuit stops, because there is only one path. That is why series wiring is avoided for household lights but used where a single current through every component is wanted, such as in some decorative strings and in simple experimental circuits. In exam questions, a diagram with one loop and no branches is series, even if the components are drawn in different positions around the loop. Trace the path: if the current has no choice of route, it is series.
bullets: Series: R = R1 + R2 + R3.
Same current through every resistor.
Voltage shared in proportion to resistance.
One break stops the whole circuit.

paras: For resistors in parallel, the rule is 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3. The voltage across every branch is the same, and the total current splits between branches in inverse proportion to resistance: the smaller resistor carries the larger current. Example: resistors of 6 ohms and 3 ohms in parallel have 1/R = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/6 + 2/6 = 3/6 = 1/2, so R = 2 ohms. Notice that the equivalent resistance, 2 ohms, is smaller than both 6 and 3. This is always true for parallel combinations and is your best sense check: if your parallel answer is larger than the smallest resistor, you have made an error.

For two resistors only, a shortcut exists: R = (R1 times R2) / (R1 + R2). For 6 ohms and 3 ohms, that gives 18 / 9 = 2 ohms, matching the reciprocal method. The shortcut works only for two resistors, so do not use it for three or more. The final and most common error is forgetting the last step: after finding 1/R, you must invert it to get R. A student who stops at 1/R = 1/2 and writes 0.5 ohms has the reciprocal of the right answer. Circle the inversion step in your working until it is automatic.

Example: Resistors of 4 ohms and 6 ohms are connected in series to a 20 V battery. Find the total resistance, the current, and the voltage across each resistor. Solution: total resistance = 4 + 6 = 10 ohms. Current = 20 / 10 = 2 A, the same through both resistors. Voltage across 4 ohms = 2 times 4 = 8 V. Voltage across 6 ohms = 2 times 6 = 12 V. Check: 8 + 12 = 20 V, the battery voltage, so the answer is consistent. Writing the check line takes seconds and confirms all three answers at once.

Example: Three resistors, 2 ohms, 2 ohms, and 2 ohms, are connected in series to a 12 V battery. Find the current. Solution: total resistance = 6 ohms. Current = 12 / 6 = 2 A. Equal resistors share the voltage equally, so each gets 4 V. Equal-resistor questions are quick if you spot the pattern, but still write the total-resistance step, because examiners award marks for method even on short questions. For more solved material, see the [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [books section](/books.html).

Example: Resistors of 4 ohms and 4 ohms are connected in parallel to a 12 V battery. Find the equivalent resistance and the total current. Solution: 1/R = 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/4 = 1/2, so R = 2 ohms. Total current = 12 / 2 = 6 A. Each branch carries 12 / 4 = 3 A, and 3 + 3 = 6 A, confirming the total. Equal resistors in parallel halve the resistance, which is a useful pattern to recognise: two equal resistors in parallel give half of one resistor's value.

Example: Resistors of 10 ohms and 15 ohms are connected in parallel. Find the equivalent resistance. Solution: 1/R = 1/10 + 1/15 = 3/30 + 2/30 = 5/30 = 1/6, so R = 6 ohms. The answer is smaller than 10, as it must be. A common alternative is the product-over-sum shortcut for two resistors: (10 times 15) / (10 + 15) = 150 / 25 = 6 ohms. Both methods agree, so use whichever you find more reliable, but always finish with the sense check that the result is smaller than the smallest resistor.

diagram.caption: Same current in series, same voltage in parallel — the contrast to memorise.

paras: The most damaging mistakes are applying the series rule to a parallel circuit, forgetting to invert the final reciprocal, and using the battery voltage as the voltage across one resistor in a series circuit. A fourth mistake is misreading the diagram: resistors drawn side by side are not automatically parallel, and resistors drawn in a line are not automatically series. What matters is the wiring: branches mean parallel, a single path means series. Trace the current path with your finger on the diagram before choosing a rule, and label each branch or loop as you go.

For combined circuits, where some resistors are in series and some in parallel, work in stages: first reduce each parallel group to its equivalent resistance, then add the series parts. Write each reduction as its own line with a small diagram note, such as parallel pair equals 2 ohms, so the examiner can follow the stages. The examples here are original practice problems for teaching the method. More guidance is on the [blog](/blog/) and the [about page](/about.html).
bullets: Trace the current path before choosing series or parallel.
Parallel: invert the final reciprocal to get R.
Parallel equivalent resistance is always smaller than the smallest resistor.
Reduce parallel groups first in combined circuits.

points: Series: R = R1 + R2 + R3; same current, shared voltage.
Parallel: 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2; same voltage, split current.
Parallel equivalent resistance is always smaller than the smallest resistor.
For two resistors in parallel, R = (R1 x R2) / (R1 + R2).
Always invert the final reciprocal in parallel calculations.

faqs.q: How do I know if resistors are in series or parallel?
faqs.a: Trace the current path. If there is only one path through all resistors, they are in series. If the current splits into branches that rejoin, the resistors on different branches are in parallel.

faqs.q: Why is parallel resistance smaller than each resistor?
faqs.a: Parallel branches give current extra paths, so more total current flows for the same voltage. By Ohm's law, more current at the same voltage means lower equivalent resistance.

faqs.q: What is the shortcut for two resistors in parallel?
faqs.a: R = (R1 times R2) / (R1 + R2). It works only for two resistors. For three or more, use the reciprocal rule 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3.

faqs.q: Why are household appliances wired in parallel?
faqs.a: In parallel, every appliance gets the full supply voltage, and switching one off does not affect the others. In series, voltage would be shared and one failure would stop everything.

faqs.q: In series, does the larger resistor get more voltage?
faqs.a: Yes. Voltage divides in proportion to resistance, so V = IR with the same current gives a larger voltage across the larger resistor. The branch voltages add up to the battery voltage.

title: Class 10 Physics: Waves, Frequency and Wavelength
desc: Master class 10 physics waves frequency numericals with v = f times lambda, sound and water wave examples, and step-by-step solutions with correct units.
intro: Class 10 physics waves frequency numericals all rest on one wave equation: wave speed equals frequency times wavelength, written v = f times lambda. Frequency tells you how many waves pass a point per second, wavelength is the distance between two matching points on neighbouring waves, and wave speed is how fast the wave pattern travels. Students lose marks mainly by confusing frequency with time period, by using wavelength in centimetres instead of metres, and by mixing up wave speed with the speed of the vibrating source. This guide separates the three quantities clearly, works through sound and water wave examples, and gives you a routine that works for every question type. A wave transfers energy without transferring matter: water particles in a ripple bob up and down while the ripple pattern moves outward, and air particles in a sound wave vibrate back and forth while the sound travels forward. Frequency is measured in hertz, where one hertz is one wave per second. Time period is the time for one complete wave, measured in seconds, and it is the reciprocal of frequency: T = 1 / f. Wavelength is measured in metres. Wave speed in metres per second follows from these definitions: in one second, f waves pass, each of length lambda, so the pattern advances f times lambda metres, giving v = f times lambda.

paras: Frequency, f, is the number of complete waves produced per second, measured in hertz (Hz). A source vibrating 50 times per second produces waves of frequency 50 Hz. Time period, T, is the time taken for one complete wave, measured in seconds, and the two are linked by f = 1 / T and T = 1 / f. So a frequency of 50 Hz means a time period of 1 / 50 = 0.02 s. Exam questions often give the time period and ask for frequency, or give the number of vibrations in a given time: if a source makes 200 vibrations in 4 seconds, the frequency is 200 / 4 = 50 Hz. Always convert the vibration count into a per-second rate before using the wave equation.

Wavelength, lambda, is the distance between two adjacent crests, two adjacent troughs, or any two matching points on neighbouring waves. It is a length, so it must be in metres for the wave equation: a wavelength given as 25 cm is 0.25 m. Amplitude is different again: it is the maximum displacement of a particle from its rest position, and it controls loudness for sound or brightness for light, not wave speed. Questions that mention amplitude are usually testing whether you know it does not enter v = f times lambda at all, so do not force it into the calculation.
bullets: Frequency f in hertz: waves per second.
Time period T = 1 / f, in seconds.
Wavelength lambda in metres: crest to crest distance.
Amplitude affects loudness, not wave speed.

sections.h2: The Wave Equation: v = f Times Lambda
paras: The wave equation, v = f times lambda, links all three quantities, and it rearranges into f = v / lambda and lambda = v / f. Practise all three forms so you can answer whichever quantity is missing. Units must match: speed in m/s, frequency in Hz (which is per second), and wavelength in metres. A quick unit check confirms the equation: hertz times metres gives (1/s) times m, which is m/s, exactly the unit of speed. If your units do not combine to m/s, something is wrong before you even calculate.

Wave speed depends on the medium, not on frequency or wavelength alone. Sound travels at about 340 m/s in air but about 1500 m/s in water, so the same frequency has a much longer wavelength in water. In exam questions, wave speed is usually given or is a known value like the speed of sound in air, and you use it to find the missing quantity. When a wave moves from one medium to another, its frequency stays the same because it is set by the source, while its speed and wavelength change together. That fact answers many theory questions and prevents a common error: never change the frequency when a wave changes medium.

Example: A sound wave of frequency 500 Hz travels at 340 m/s in air. Find its wavelength. Solution: lambda = v / f = 340 / 500 = 0.68 m. Example: A tuning fork vibrates at 256 Hz and produces waves of wavelength 1.33 m. Find the speed of sound. Solution: v = f times lambda = 256 times 1.33 = 340.5 m/s, approximately the known speed of sound in air, which confirms the calculation. Notice how the known speed of sound acts as a built-in sense check for sound questions: answers near 340 m/s in air are plausible, while answers like 34 m/s or 3400 m/s signal a unit error.

Example: A source makes 120 vibrations in 3 seconds and produces waves of wavelength 2 m. Find the wave speed. Solution: frequency = 120 / 3 = 40 Hz. Speed = 40 times 2 = 80 m/s. This two-stage pattern, frequency first, then speed, is very common. Students who multiply 120 directly by 2 get 240, which is wrong because 120 is a count, not a frequency. Always convert counts to per-second rates first. For more solved study material, see the [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [books section](/books.html).

sections.h2: Worked Example 2: Water Waves and Time Period
paras: Example: Water waves have a wavelength of 0.5 m and a time period of 0.25 s. Find their frequency and speed. Solution: frequency = 1 / T = 1 / 0.25 = 4 Hz. Speed = 4 times 0.5 = 2 m/s. Example: A wave has a speed of 12 m/s and a frequency of 6 Hz. Find its wavelength and time period. Solution: wavelength = 12 / 6 = 2 m. Time period = 1 / 6 = 0.167 s. Working through both parts shows how the three formulas connect: frequency and time period are reciprocals, and the wave equation links them to speed and wavelength.

Example: A boy counts 20 water waves passing a point in 10 seconds. The distance between two adjacent crests is 40 cm. Find the wave speed. Solution: frequency = 20 / 10 = 2 Hz. Wavelength = 40 cm = 0.4 m. Speed = 2 times 0.4 = 0.8 m/s. This question combines all three traps: count to frequency, centimetres to metres, and then the wave equation. Questions that combine traps are exactly where a written routine pays off: convert first, then substitute, then calculate.

diagram.caption: Wavelength is crest to crest; amplitude is height from the rest position.

paras: The most common mistakes are using time period instead of frequency in the wave equation, using wavelength in centimetres, and using a vibration count as if it were frequency. A fourth mistake is changing frequency when a wave enters a new medium: frequency is set by the source and stays constant, while speed and wavelength change. A fifth is confusing wave speed with particle speed: particles vibrate in place, while the wave pattern travels at v. Exam theory questions often test exactly this distinction, so state it clearly in words when asked.

Follow this routine: list f, T, lambda, and v with units, convert counts to frequency and centimetres to metres, pick the rearrangement for the missing quantity, substitute, and sense-check. For sound in air, expect speeds near 340 m/s; for water ripples in a tank, expect speeds well under 1 m/s. The examples here are original practice problems for teaching the method. More guidance is on the [blog](/blog/) and the [about page](/about.html).
bullets: Convert vibration counts to frequency per second first.
Convert wavelength to metres before using v = f times lambda.
Frequency stays constant when a wave changes medium.
Do not confuse wave speed with particle vibration speed.

points: Wave equation: v = f times lambda, with m/s, Hz, and metres.
Frequency f = 1 / T; time period T = 1 / f.
Convert vibration counts to per-second frequency before calculating.
Wavelength must be in metres; convert centimetres by dividing by 100.
Frequency stays constant when a wave changes medium.

faqs.q: What is the difference between frequency and time period?
faqs.a: Frequency is the number of waves per second, measured in hertz. Time period is the time for one complete wave, measured in seconds. They are reciprocals: f = 1 / T.

faqs.q: How do I find frequency from a vibration count?
faqs.a: Divide the number of vibrations by the time in seconds. For example, 200 vibrations in 4 seconds gives 200 / 4 = 50 Hz.

faqs.q: Does wave speed change when frequency changes?
faqs.a: In the same medium, wave speed stays constant, so changing frequency changes wavelength instead. Speed changes only when the medium changes, and then frequency stays constant while wavelength changes.

faqs.q: What is wavelength, exactly?
faqs.a: Wavelength is the distance between two matching points on neighbouring waves, such as crest to crest or trough to trough, measured in metres.

faqs.q: Why does sound travel faster in water than in air?
faqs.a: Wave speed depends on the medium. Particles in water transmit vibrations more efficiently than air particles, so sound travels at about 1500 m/s in water compared with about 340 m/s in air.

title: Class 10 Physics: Light Reflection Numericals
desc: Learn class 10 physics light reflection numericals with the mirror formula, magnification, and step-by-step worked examples for concave and convex mirrors.
intro: Class 10 physics light reflection numericals centre on the mirror formula, 1/f = 1/v + 1/u, and magnification, m = negative v/u, together with the sign convention that makes them work. Students find this chapter hard not because the algebra is difficult, but because sign errors flip answers and because image nature, real or virtual, upright or inverted, magnified or diminished, must be read from the signs. This guide teaches the sign convention first, then the formulas, then original worked examples for concave and convex mirrors, so you can answer both the number and the description of the image. Reflection is the bouncing back of light when it strikes a smooth surface, and the laws of reflection state that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, with both angles measured from the normal, the line perpendicular to the surface. Mirrors form images by reflection: a plane mirror gives a virtual, upright, same-size image as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, while spherical mirrors, concave and convex, can magnify, diminish, and invert images depending on where the object stands. The mirror formula connects object distance, image distance, and focal length, and magnification tells you how large the image is compared with the object.

sections.h2: The Sign Convention You Must Memorise
paras: The sign convention used here is the standard one for Class 10: all distances are measured from the pole of the mirror. Distances measured in the direction of incident light, that is, in front of a mirror, are taken as negative, while distances behind the mirror are positive. Object distance u is therefore almost always negative, because the object stands in front of the mirror. Focal length f is negative for a concave mirror and positive for a convex mirror. Image distance v is negative for a real image formed in front of the mirror, and positive for a virtual image formed behind it. Height of the object is positive above the axis, and image height is positive if upright and negative if inverted.

This convention feels backwards at first, because the object distance you measure with a ruler is positive, but you must enter it as negative in the formula. The most reliable habit is to write u = negative value as the first line of every solution, before touching the mirror formula. If you skip that line, sign errors follow. A second habit is to interpret the sign of your answer at the end: a negative v means a real image in front of the mirror, a positive v means a virtual image behind it, and the sign of magnification tells you upright (positive) or inverted (negative). The number alone is only half the answer; the description completes it.
bullets: Object distance u is negative (object in front of mirror).
Concave f is negative; convex f is positive.
Negative v means real image; positive v means virtual image.
Magnification sign: positive upright, negative inverted.

paras: The mirror formula is 1/f = 1/v + 1/u, where f is focal length, v is image distance, and u is object distance, all in the same unit, usually centimetres. Focal length is half the radius of curvature: f = R / 2. Magnification is m = negative v / u, and it also equals image height divided by object height, m = h image / h object. The magnitude of m tells you size: m larger than 1 means magnified, m smaller than 1 means diminished, and m equal to 1 means same size. To find an unknown, rearrange the formula: 1/v = 1/f minus 1/u, then invert to get v. The inversion step is where many students stop early, so circle it in your working.

A worked pattern helps: for a concave mirror with f = negative 20 cm and an object at u = negative 30 cm, 1/v = 1/(negative 20) minus 1/(negative 30) = negative 1/20 + 1/30 = negative 3/60 + 2/60 = negative 1/60, so v = negative 60 cm. The negative sign means a real image 60 cm in front of the mirror. Magnification = negative (negative 60) / (negative 30) = negative 2, so the image is inverted and magnified twice. Every mirror question follows this same pattern: substitute with signs, solve for v, invert, then find m and describe the image.

Example: An object is placed 15 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find the image distance and magnification, and describe the image. Solution: f = negative 10 cm, u = negative 15 cm. 1/v = 1/f minus 1/u = 1/(negative 10) minus 1/(negative 15) = negative 1/10 + 1/15 = negative 3/30 + 2/30 = negative 1/30. So v = negative 30 cm. Magnification = negative (negative 30) / (negative 15) = negative 2. The image is real (negative v), inverted (negative m), and magnified 2 times, formed 30 cm in front of the mirror. This matches the known behaviour of a concave mirror when the object is between the focal point and the centre of curvature.

Example: An object 4 cm tall is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm. Find the image height. Solution: f = negative 20 cm, u = negative 30 cm. 1/v = 1/(negative 20) minus 1/(negative 30) = negative 1/20 + 1/30 = negative 1/60, so v = negative 60 cm. Magnification = negative (negative 60) / (negative 30) = negative 2. Image height = m times object height = negative 2 times 4 = negative 8 cm. The negative sign means inverted, and the height is 8 cm. Always include the sign in the image height, because it carries the upright or inverted information.

Example: An object is placed 20 cm in front of a convex mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find the image distance and magnification, and describe the image. Solution: f = positive 10 cm, u = negative 20 cm. 1/v = 1/10 minus 1/(negative 20) = 1/10 + 1/20 = 3/20, so v = positive 6.67 cm. Magnification = negative (positive 6.67) / (negative 20) = positive 0.33. The image is virtual (positive v), upright (positive m), and diminished (m less than 1), formed 6.67 cm behind the mirror. Convex mirrors always give this kind of image, whatever the object distance, which is why they are used as rear-view mirrors: they show a wide, upright, if smaller, view.

Example: A convex mirror has a radius of curvature of 40 cm. Find its focal length. Solution: f = R / 2 = 40 / 2 = 20 cm, and because the mirror is convex, f = positive 20 cm. Radius questions are easy marks, but remember the sign: concave mirrors take negative f, convex mirrors positive f, and the radius sign follows the same rule. For more solved study material, see the [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [books section](/books.html).

diagram.caption: Follow these steps in order and the signs take care of themselves.

paras: The dominant mistakes are entering u as positive, using the wrong sign for f, forgetting to invert after finding 1/v, and describing the image from the number alone without reading the signs. A second group of errors comes from mixing up magnification formulas: m = negative v / u uses distances, while m = image height / object height uses heights, and both give the same value. A third trap is unit mixing: object distance in metres and focal length in centimetres must be converted to the same unit before substituting. Convert everything to centimetres first, since mirror questions almost always use centimetres.

Exam technique: write the sign convention line first, substitute with signs visible, show the inversion step, and finish with a full image description in words, not just numbers. A complete answer reads: v = negative 30 cm, m = negative 2, so the image is real, inverted, and magnified 2 times, formed 30 cm in front of the mirror. That sentence earns the description marks that a bare number cannot. The examples here are original practice problems for teaching the method. More guidance is on the [blog](/blog/) and the [about page](/about.html).
bullets: Always write u as negative for an object in front of the mirror.
Concave f negative, convex f positive.
Invert 1/v to get v; do not stop at the reciprocal.
Describe the image fully: real or virtual, upright or inverted, size.

Ask it to quiz you on reading image nature from the signs of v and m. Join Muse with invite code LTGSWD — in the Muse app, go to Settings > Redeem token and enter the code.
