Always verify against your Sindh Textbook Board book and your teacher before using anything in classwork.

points: Mirror formula: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u, all distances in the same unit.
Object distance u is negative; concave f negative, convex f positive.
Magnification m = negative v / u = image height / object height.
Negative v means real image; positive v means virtual image.
Always describe the image: real or virtual, upright or inverted, size.

faqs.q: Why is object distance negative in the mirror formula?
faqs.a: By the sign convention, distances measured in front of the mirror, in the direction of incident light, are negative. Since the object stands in front of the mirror, u is entered as negative.

faqs.q: How do I know if an image is real or virtual?
faqs.a: Look at the sign of v. A negative v means the image forms in front of the mirror and is real. A positive v means it forms behind the mirror and is virtual.

faqs.q: What does a magnification of negative 2 mean?
faqs.a: The negative sign means inverted, and the magnitude 2 means the image is twice the size of the object. So the image is inverted and magnified 2 times.

faqs.q: Do convex mirrors ever give real images?
faqs.a: No, for a real object a convex mirror always gives a virtual, upright, diminished image behind the mirror, whatever the object distance.

faqs.q: How is focal length related to radius of curvature?
faqs.a: Focal length is half the radius of curvature: f = R / 2. Remember the sign: negative for concave mirrors, positive for convex mirrors.

title: Class 10 Physics: Heat and Temperature Conversions
desc: Master class 10 physics heat temperature conversions with Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin formulas, step-by-step worked examples, and common exam traps explained.
intro: Class 10 physics heat temperature conversion numericals ask you to move between three scales, Celsius, Fahrenheit, and Kelvin, and to connect temperature change with heat energy where needed. The conversion formulas are short, but students lose marks by adding 273 instead of 273.15 in the wrong direction, by forgetting to subtract 32 before multiplying in the Fahrenheit formula, and by using a temperature change in Celsius as if it were an absolute temperature. This guide teaches all three scales, the conversion formulas with original worked examples, and the difference between heat and temperature that theory questions love to test. Heat and temperature are not the same thing. Temperature measures how hot or cold a body is, related to the average kinetic energy of its particles, while heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference, measured in joules. A cup of boiling water and a bath of warm water can have very different temperatures and very different total heat energies: the bath holds far more heat energy because it has far more particles, even though its temperature is lower. Temperature is measured with a thermometer in degrees Celsius, degrees Fahrenheit, or kelvin, while heat is measured in joules, and the two are linked by specific heat capacity when a temperature change is involved.

paras: The Celsius scale sets the freezing point of water at 0 degrees and the boiling point at 100 degrees, dividing the range into 100 equal parts. The Fahrenheit scale sets freezing at 32 degrees and boiling at 212 degrees, dividing the same range into 180 parts, which is why each Celsius degree equals 1.8 Fahrenheit degrees. The Kelvin scale is the SI scale: it starts at absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature, and its degree is the same size as a Celsius degree, so converting between Celsius and Kelvin is a simple shift. Water freezes at 273.15 K and boils at 373.15 K, although Class 10 work usually rounds to 273 K and 373 K. Kelvin never takes a degree symbol: write 300 K, not 300 degrees K.

Absolute zero, 0 K or negative 273.15 degrees Celsius, is the temperature at which particle motion is at its minimum, and no temperature can be lower. This is why Kelvin values are always positive, and why a negative Kelvin temperature in your answer means an error. The three scales agree on the physics but differ in zero point and degree size, and every conversion formula simply accounts for those two differences. Memorise the fixed points of each scale, because they let you check any conversion: if your formula says water boils at 100 degrees Fahrenheit, the formula has been applied backwards.
bullets: Celsius: water freezes 0, boils 100.
Fahrenheit: water freezes 32, boils 212.
Kelvin: water freezes 273 K, boils 373 K; no degree symbol.
One kelvin equals one Celsius degree in size.

sections.h2: Conversion Formulas and How to Use Them
paras: The formulas are: K = C + 273, and C = K minus 273, for Celsius and Kelvin. For Celsius and Fahrenheit: F = (C times 9/5) + 32, and C = (F minus 32) times 5/9. The order of operations in the Fahrenheit formulas is critical: to go from Celsius to Fahrenheit, multiply first, then add 32; to go from Fahrenheit to Celsius, subtract 32 first, then multiply by 5/9. Reversing the order gives a wrong answer that often looks plausible, so write the subtraction or addition as its own step. For combined conversions, such as Fahrenheit to Kelvin, convert to Celsius first and then to Kelvin: it is two easy steps instead of one error-prone formula.

A worked pattern: convert 25 degrees Celsius to Fahrenheit. F = (25 times 9/5) + 32 = 45 + 32 = 77 degrees Fahrenheit. Reverse: convert 77 degrees Fahrenheit to Celsius. C = (77 minus 32) times 5/9 = 45 times 5/9 = 25 degrees Celsius. The round trip back to 25 confirms both formulas. Another anchor: 0 degrees Celsius is 32 degrees Fahrenheit and 273 K, and 100 degrees Celsius is 212 degrees Fahrenheit and 373 K. If you remember these two anchor points, you can check any conversion by asking whether your answer sits sensibly between them.

sections.h2: Worked Example 1: Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin
paras: Example: Convert 37 degrees Celsius (normal body temperature) to Fahrenheit and Kelvin. Solution: F = (37 times 9/5) + 32 = 66.6 + 32 = 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit. K = 37 + 273 = 310 K. Example: Convert 300 K to Celsius and Fahrenheit. Solution: C = 300 minus 273 = 27 degrees Celsius. F = (27 times 9/5) + 32 = 48.6 + 32 = 80.6 degrees Fahrenheit. Notice that the Kelvin-to-Celsius step is just a subtraction, while the Celsius-to-Fahrenheit step needs multiplication before addition. Writing each step separately prevents order-of-operations errors.

Example: A winter morning is negative 4 degrees Celsius. Express it in Fahrenheit and Kelvin. Solution: F = (negative 4 times 9/5) + 32 = negative 7.2 + 32 = 24.8 degrees Fahrenheit. K = negative 4 + 273 = 269 K. Negative Celsius values are normal, but the Kelvin result must stay positive: if you get a negative Kelvin value, you have subtracted instead of adding, or the Celsius value is below negative 273, which is impossible. For more solved study material, see the [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [books section](/books.html).

sections.h2: Worked Example 2: Temperature Change and Heat
paras: Example: A metal block warms from 20 degrees Celsius to 60 degrees Celsius. What is the temperature change in Celsius and in kelvin? Solution: change in Celsius = 60 minus 20 = 40 degrees Celsius. Because a kelvin and a Celsius degree are the same size, the change in kelvin is also 40 K. This is an important distinction: absolute temperatures differ by 273 between the scales, but temperature changes are identical. Students who add 273 to a temperature change get a wildly wrong answer, so underline the word change in the question whenever it appears.

Example: How much heat is needed to raise 2 kg of water by 10 degrees Celsius? The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg per degree Celsius. Solution: heat Q = m times c times temperature change = 2 times 4200 times 10 = 84,000 J. The temperature change here is 10 degrees, and it does not matter whether it is stated in Celsius or kelvin, because the change is the same. Specific heat capacity questions always use temperature change, never absolute temperature, which is another reason to keep the two ideas separate.

diagram.caption: Same physical points, different numbers: freezing and boiling of water on each scale.

paras: The most common mistakes are adding 32 before multiplying when converting Celsius to Fahrenheit, subtracting 32 after multiplying when converting the other way, adding 273 to a temperature change instead of an absolute temperature, and writing Kelvin with a degree symbol. A second trap is rounding: 273.15 versus 273 rarely changes a Class 10 answer by a mark, but be consistent with the value your question or teacher uses. A third trap is confusing heat with temperature in theory questions: temperature is average particle energy, heat is energy transferred, and a large cool body can hold more heat than a small hot one.

Exam routine: identify the starting scale and target scale, write the formula in symbols, substitute with the correct order of operations, and check against anchor points (0 C = 32 F = 273 K; 100 C = 212 F = 373 K). For heat questions, confirm you are using temperature change, not absolute temperature, and that mass is in kilograms and specific heat capacity matches the units given. The examples here are original practice problems for teaching the method. More guidance is on the [blog](/blog/) and the [about page](/about.html).
bullets: Celsius to Fahrenheit: multiply first, then add 32.
Fahrenheit to Celsius: subtract 32 first, then multiply by 5/9.
Temperature changes are the same in Celsius and kelvin.
Kelvin values are always positive; never write a degree symbol with K.

points: K = C + 273; C = K minus 273.
F = (C times 9/5) + 32; C = (F minus 32) times 5/9.
Anchor points: 0 C = 32 F = 273 K; 100 C = 212 F = 373 K.
Temperature changes are identical in Celsius and kelvin.
Heat Q = m c times temperature change, in joules.

faqs.q: What is the difference between heat and temperature?
faqs.a: Temperature measures how hot a body is, related to average particle energy. Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference, measured in joules. A large cool body can hold more heat energy than a small hot body.

faqs.q: Why is Kelvin never written with a degree symbol?
faqs.a: Kelvin is the SI unit of temperature and is written simply as K, for example 300 K. The degree symbol belongs to Celsius and Fahrenheit only.

faqs.q: Is a temperature change of 10 degrees Celsius the same as 10 K?
faqs.a: Yes. A kelvin and a Celsius degree are the same size, so temperature changes are identical on both scales, even though absolute values differ by 273.

faqs.q: What is absolute zero?
faqs.a: Absolute zero is 0 K, or negative 273.15 degrees Celsius, the lowest possible temperature, where particle motion is at its minimum. No temperature can be lower.

faqs.q: How do I convert Fahrenheit directly to Kelvin?
faqs.a: Convert to Celsius first: C = (F minus 32) times 5/9, then add 273 to get kelvin. Two easy steps beat one complicated formula.

title: Class 10 Physics: Gravitational Force Numericals
desc: Learn class 10 physics gravitational force numericals with Newton's law of gravitation, worked values, weight versus mass, and step-by-step solutions.
intro: Class 10 physics gravitational force numericals test Newton's law of universal gravitation: every mass attracts every other mass with a force proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. The formula, F = G times m1 times m2 divided by r squared, looks intimidating because of the gravitational constant and the large powers of ten, but the questions follow a small number of patterns: force between two masses, weight on Earth or another planet, and how force changes when mass or distance changes. This guide teaches each pattern with original worked values, careful powers of ten, and the weight-versus-mass distinction that theory questions always probe. Gravity is the weakest of the familiar forces, yet it governs planets, moons, and tides, because masses like the Earth are enormous. The gravitational constant G is 6.67 times 10 to the power negative 11, in units of N m squared per kg squared, which is why the force between everyday objects is too tiny to notice: two 1 kg masses 1 metre apart attract each other with a force of only 6.67 times 10 to the power negative 11 newtons. The same law gives the familiar weight of an object on Earth, because the Earth's mass is about 6 times 10 to the power 24 kg, and that enormous number compensates for the tiny constant.

paras: Newton's law states that the gravitational force between two masses is F = G times m1 times m2 divided by r squared, where m1 and m2 are the masses in kilograms, r is the distance between their centres in metres, and G is 6.67 times 10 to the power negative 11 N m squared per kg squared. The force is attractive, acting along the line joining the centres, and it obeys Newton's third law: each mass pulls the other with an equal and opposite force. The inverse-square part is the key idea: doubling the distance divides the force by four, tripling it divides the force by nine, and halving it multiplies the force by four. Many exam questions test only this scaling, with no numbers at all, so learn it as a sentence, not just as a formula.

The distance r is measured between centres, not between surfaces, which matters for planets and stars where the radius is large. For an object on Earth's surface, r is Earth's radius, about 6.4 times 10 to the power 6 m, plus any height above the surface, which is usually negligible. For two small objects on a bench, r is the distance between their centres. Reading the question for whether it gives centre distance or surface distance prevents a subtle error, although most Class 10 questions give r directly and expect you to use it as stated.
bullets: F = G m1 m2 / r squared, with G = 6.67 x 10^-11.
Force is attractive and equal on both masses.
Doubling distance divides force by four (inverse square).
Distance r is measured between centres.

paras: Weight is the gravitational force on an object, W = m times g, where g is the acceleration due to gravity, about 10 m/s squared on Earth. This formula is actually Newton's law applied to Earth: g equals G times Earth's mass divided by Earth's radius squared, which works out to about 9.8 m/s squared. That connection explains why g differs on other planets: a planet with larger mass or smaller radius has a larger g, and a smaller or larger planet has a smaller g. Mass never changes with location, but weight does, because weight depends on the planet's mass and radius through g.

Example: an astronaut of mass 70 kg has a weight on Earth of 70 times 10 = 700 N. On the Moon, where g is about 1.7 m/s squared, the same astronaut weighs 70 times 1.7 = 119 N, but the mass is still 70 kg. This mass-versus-weight distinction is the single most tested theory point in the gravitation chapter, so state it explicitly whenever a question asks about the Moon or another planet. A question that gives weight in newtons and asks for mass needs division by g: mass = weight / g, and the planet's g must be used, not Earth's, if the weight was measured there.

sections.h2: Worked Example 1: Force Between Two Masses
paras: Example: Find the gravitational force between two masses of 10 kg and 20 kg placed 2 m apart. Solution: F = G times m1 times m2 / r squared = 6.67 times 10 to the power negative 11 times 10 times 20 / (2 squared) = 6.67 times 10 to the power negative 11 times 200 / 4 = 6.67 times 10 to the power negative 11 times 50 = 3.34 times 10 to the power negative 9 N. The answer is tiny, as expected for everyday masses, and the working shows each step: product of masses, square of distance, then the constant. Keeping powers of ten separate from the main number prevents the most common arithmetic error in this chapter.

Example: Two masses attract each other with a force F. If the distance between them is doubled, what is the new force? Solution: force is inversely proportional to distance squared, so doubling distance gives F / 4. If the distance is halved instead, the new force is 4F. If one mass is doubled and the distance is doubled, the new force is 2F / 4 = F / 2, because the doubled mass multiplies the force by 2 while the doubled distance divides it by 4. Scaling questions reward reasoning over calculation, so write the scaling factor for each change before combining them.

sections.h2: Worked Example 2: Weight on Earth and Other Planets
paras: Example: A rock of mass 5 kg is taken to a planet where g is 4 m/s squared. Find its weight there and on Earth. Solution: weight on the planet = 5 times 4 = 20 N. Weight on Earth = 5 times 10 = 50 N. Mass stays 5 kg in both places. Example: An object weighs 600 N on Earth. Find its mass, and its weight on a planet where g is 5 m/s squared. Solution: mass = 600 / 10 = 60 kg. Weight on the planet = 60 times 5 = 300 N. Two-stage questions like this are standard: find mass from Earth weight first, then apply the new g. Always use the g of the place where the weight is being found.

Example: The mass of Earth is 6 times 10 to the power 24 kg and its radius is 6.4 times 10 to the power 6 m. Estimate g on Earth's surface. Solution: g = G times M / R squared = 6.67 times 10 to the power negative 11 times 6 times 10 to the power 24 / (6.4 times 10 to the power 6) squared. The numerator is about 4.0 times 10 to the power 14, and the denominator is about 4.1 times 10 to the power 13, giving g of about 9.8 m/s squared, matching the known value. This derivation question connects the two formulas and confirms that weight really is gravitation in action. For more solved study material, see the [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [books section](/books.html).

diagram.caption: Pick the pattern first: two masses, weight, or scaling.

paras: The most common mistakes are forgetting to square the distance, using surface distance instead of centre distance for planets, confusing mass with weight, and mishandling powers of ten, especially the negative exponent of G. A second trap is using Earth's g for a weight on another planet: always read which planet the question names. A third trap is scaling errors: doubling distance quarters the force, it does not halve it, because the distance is squared. Write the scaling as a fraction, new force = old force times (old distance / new distance) squared, to make the square visible.

Exam routine: decide which of the three patterns the question fits, write the matching formula, handle powers of ten separately, and sense-check the size of the answer. Forces between laboratory masses are extremely small, weights of people are hundreds of newtons, and g values for planets are single or double digits. The examples here are original practice problems for teaching the method. More guidance is on the [blog](/blog/) and the [about page](/about.html).
bullets: Square the distance: doubling distance quarters the force.
Mass is constant; weight changes with the planet's g.
Handle powers of ten separately from the main number.
Use the local g for weight on any planet or moon.

Ask it to quiz you on how force changes when distance doubles or triples. Join Muse with invite code LTGSWD — in the Muse app, go to Settings > Redeem token and enter the code. points: Newton's law: F = G m1 m2 / r squared, G = 6.67 x 10^-11.
Doubling distance divides force by four; halving distance multiplies it by four.
Weight W = m g; mass is constant, weight depends on local g.
Distance r is measured between the centres of the masses.
g on a planet = G times planet mass / radius squared.

faqs.q: What happens to gravitational force if distance doubles?
faqs.a: It becomes one quarter, because force is inversely proportional to distance squared. Doubling distance gives 1 / (2 squared) = 1/4 of the original force.

faqs.q: Does an astronaut's mass change on the Moon?
faqs.a: No. Mass is the amount of matter and never changes with location. Only weight changes, because the Moon's gravity is weaker, so the same mass weighs about one sixth as much there.

faqs.q: Why is the force between everyday objects so tiny?
faqs.a: Because the gravitational constant G is extremely small, 6.67 times 10 to the power negative 11. Only enormous masses like planets produce noticeable gravitational forces.

faqs.q: Is distance measured between surfaces or centres?
faqs.a: Between centres. For planets, r is the distance from the planet's centre, which is why Earth's radius appears in the calculation of g.

faqs.q: How is g related to Newton's law of gravitation?
faqs.a: Weight is the gravitational force, so m times g equals G times m times planet mass divided by radius squared. Cancelling m gives g = G times planet mass / radius squared.

title: Class 9 Chemistry: Atomic Mass and Mole Numericals
desc: Learn class 9 chemistry atomic mass mole concepts with clear gram-to-mole conversions, worked numericals, and common mistakes to avoid in exams.
intro: The class 9 chemistry atomic mass mole topic becomes easy once you see the mole as a counting unit, just like a dozen counts twelve items. One mole of any substance contains the same number of particles, and its mass in grams equals its atomic or molecular mass. This guide explains atomic mass, molecular mass, and the mole with simple gram-to-mole conversions that you can use in class tests and board-style questions. Work through each example slowly, write every unit, and check whether your answer makes sense before moving on.

paras: Atomic mass tells you how heavy one atom of an element is compared with a standard reference atom. In Class 9 chemistry, you usually use the rounded atomic masses given in your textbook table, for example hydrogen is 1, carbon is 12, oxygen is 16, sodium is 23, and calcium is 40. These numbers are not weights you can measure with a balance for a single atom, because one atom is far too light. Instead, they tell you the relative mass, so an oxygen atom is sixteen times heavier than a hydrogen atom. When you add the atomic masses in a compound, you get its molecular mass or formula mass, which is the bridge to real, weighable amounts in the laboratory.

A common confusion is mixing up atomic mass, mass number, and atomic number. Atomic number is the number of protons, mass number is protons plus neutrons in one isotope, and atomic mass is the average relative mass shown in the periodic table. For numericals, use the atomic mass from the table unless the question gives a different value. Always write the unit carefully: atomic mass itself is relative and has no unit, but molar mass is expressed in grams per mole. Keeping this distinction clear prevents the most frequent early mistakes, and it makes later mole calculations much smoother. Visit the [solved notes](/solved.html) for more Class 9 guides.

One mole is a fixed number of particles, just as one dozen is twelve items and one gross is 144 items. Chemists use the mole because atoms are too small to count one by one, so they count them in huge groups instead. One mole of hydrogen atoms, one mole of water molecules, and one mole of sodium ions all contain the same number of particles, but they have different masses because each particle has a different mass. That is why one mole of hydrogen gas has a mass of about 2 grams while one mole of oxygen gas has a mass of about 32 grams, even though both contain the same number of molecules.

The key formula is simple: number of moles equals given mass divided by molar mass. Molar mass is the mass of one mole, found by adding atomic masses, and it is written in grams per mole. If you are given moles and asked for mass, rearrange the formula to mass equals moles multiplied by molar mass. Always start by writing what is given, what is asked, and the molar mass you will use. This three-line habit catches unit errors early and turns a long question into a short, safe calculation. See the [books page](/books.html) for the textbooks these methods support.

diagram.caption: Follow these steps for every gram-to-mole numerical.

paras: Question: How many moles are present in 46 grams of sodium? Solution: The atomic mass of sodium is 23, so its molar mass is 23 grams per mole. Number of moles equals given mass divided by molar mass, which is 46 divided by 23, giving 2 moles. Notice how the grams cancel and leave moles behind. This cancelling of units is your best check: if grams do not cancel, you have divided the wrong way round. Try the same idea with 8 grams of oxygen atoms, where the molar mass is 16 grams per mole, giving 8 divided by 16, which is 0.5 mole. A value below one mole simply means less than a full mole, and that is perfectly normal.

Now try a compound. Question: How many moles are in 36 grams of water? First find the molar mass of water, H2O: two hydrogen atoms give 2 times 1, plus one oxygen atom at 16, making 18 grams per mole. Then divide 36 by 18 to get 2 moles of water. Many students forget to multiply by the subscript, so they use 17 instead of 18 and get the wrong answer. Always write the formula, put the atomic mass under each symbol, multiply by the subscript, and only then add. That slow, visible working is exactly what earns full marks, even if the final number is simple.
bullets: Sodium: 46 g divided by 23 g/mol equals 2 mol.
Water: molar mass 18 g/mol, so 36 g equals 2 mol.
Oxygen atoms: 8 g divided by 16 g/mol equals 0.5 mol.

sections.h2: Worked Example 2: Moles to Grams and Particles
paras: Question: What is the mass of 3 moles of calcium carbonate, CaCO3? First find its molar mass: calcium 40, plus carbon 12, plus three oxygen atoms at 16 each, which is 48, giving a total of 100 grams per mole. Then mass equals moles multiplied by molar mass, so 3 multiplied by 100 gives 300 grams. This reverse direction is just as common in exams, so practise both directions until neither feels new. If a question gives 0.25 mole of carbon dioxide, CO2, its molar mass is 12 plus 32, which is 44 grams per mole, and the mass is 0.25 multiplied by 44, giving 11 grams.

Questions about particles use the same mole idea: one mole always contains the same number of particles, so two moles contain twice that number and half a mole contains half. You do not need to memorise a huge number for most Class 9 numericals; the point is the comparison. For example, 2 moles of hydrogen molecules contain twice as many molecules as 1 mole, and 0.5 mole of water contains half as many molecules as 1 mole. When a question mixes mass and particles, convert mass to moles first, then compare moles. That two-step order keeps the working tidy and avoids jumping straight to a guessed number.
bullets: CaCO3: molar mass 100 g/mol, so 3 mol equals 300 g.
CO2: molar mass 44 g/mol, so 0.25 mol equals 11 g.
Always convert mass to moles before comparing particle counts.

paras: The most common mistake is using the atomic mass of one atom when the formula contains two or more of that atom, especially in H2, O2, H2O, and CO2. Another frequent error is dividing molar mass by given mass instead of the other way round, which gives an answer with the wrong unit and usually a strange size. A third error is forgetting that diatomic gases such as hydrogen and oxygen exist as H2 and O2 molecules, so their molar masses are 2 and 32 grams per mole, not 1 and 16, when the question is about the gas. Read the question twice: does it say oxygen atoms or oxygen gas? That one word changes the molar mass completely.

For exams, write the formula, the molar mass working, the substitution, and the final answer with its unit on separate lines. Show the division or multiplication clearly rather than writing only the answer, because method marks are often awarded even when a small arithmetic slip occurs. Practise five numericals a day for a week, mixing grams to moles, moles to grams, and compounds with subscripts, and the method will become automatic. End your revision by explaining the mole to a classmate in your own words, since teaching a concept is the fastest way to find the part you still need to practise. Browse more guides on the [blog](/blog/).

points: Atomic mass is relative mass; molar mass is grams per mole.
Moles equal given mass divided by molar mass.
Always multiply atomic mass by the subscript in a formula.
Diatomic gases H2 and O2 have molar masses 2 and 32 g/mol.
Write formula, molar mass, substitution, and unit for full marks.

faqs.q: What is the difference between atomic mass and molar mass?
faqs.a: Atomic mass is the relative mass of one atom compared with a standard atom. Molar mass is the mass of one mole of that substance in grams per mole, and it has the same number as the atomic or molecular mass.

faqs.q: How do I find the molar mass of water?
faqs.a: Water is H2O, so add two hydrogen atoms at 1 each plus one oxygen atom at 16, giving 18 grams per mole. Always multiply by the subscript before adding.

faqs.q: How many moles are in 46 grams of sodium?
faqs.a: Sodium has a molar mass of 23 grams per mole, so 46 divided by 23 gives 2 moles. The grams cancel and leave moles as the unit.

faqs.q: Why is 0.5 mole a valid answer?
faqs.a: A mole is a counting unit, so half a mole simply means half the particles in a full mole. Many real samples are smaller than one mole, so answers below one are common and correct.

title: Class 9 Chemistry: Balancing Chemical Equations
desc: Master class 9 chemistry balancing equations with the hit-and-trial method, five worked examples, and the mistakes that cost marks in exams.
intro: The class 9 chemistry balancing equations skill is really about counting atoms honestly: a balanced equation must have the same number of each atom on both sides, because atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. The hit-and-trial method means you try coefficients, count again, and adjust until both sides match. This guide teaches a calm order for balancing, then works through five examples from easy to harder, so you can handle the equations that appear in class tests with confidence.

paras: A chemical equation is a shorthand story of a reaction: reactants on the left, products on the right, and an arrow showing the change. If the numbers of atoms do not match, the story is claiming that atoms appeared or vanished, which never happens in an ordinary chemical reaction. Balancing does not change the substances involved; it only changes how many molecules or formula units of each substance take part. That is why you may change coefficients, the big numbers in front of formulas, but you must never change subscripts inside a formula, because that would invent a different substance altogether.

Unbalanced equations also hide useful information. A balanced equation tells you the reacting ratio, so you can see, for example, that two molecules of hydrogen react with one molecule of oxygen to make two molecules of water. This ratio is the starting point for later mole calculations, so balancing well now pays off in every later chapter. Examiners check balancing carefully, and a single unbalanced atom can lose the mark for the whole equation, so treat counting as part of the answer, not as an optional extra. Find more study help on the [solved notes](/solved.html) page.

Start by writing the correct formulas for every reactant and product, then count the atoms of each element on both sides in a small table. Balance metals first, then non-metals other than hydrogen and oxygen, then hydrogen, and finally oxygen, because hydrogen and oxygen appear in many compounds and are easier to fix last. Choose the element that appears in the fewest compounds first, and use the smallest whole-number coefficient that fixes it. After each change, recount everything, because fixing one element often disturbs another.

Work with whole numbers only, and if you end up with a fraction, multiply the whole equation by the denominator to clear it. Never change a subscript to make the numbers fit, and never add a new substance that was not in the original reaction. When you think you are finished, do a final count of every element on both sides and write the counts beside the equation in rough work. This final check takes less than a minute and catches most slips, especially with oxygen in combustion equations. The [books page](/books.html) lists the books this method supports.

diagram.caption: Balance in this order and recount after every change.

paras: Example 1: H2 plus O2 gives H2O. Count first: left has 2 hydrogen and 2 oxygen, right has 2 hydrogen and 1 oxygen. Oxygen is short on the right, so put 2 in front of H2O, giving 2 hydrogen on the left and 4 hydrogen on the right, and 2 oxygen on both sides. Now fix hydrogen by putting 2 in front of H2 on the left. The balanced equation is 2H2 plus O2 gives 2H2O, with 4 hydrogen and 2 oxygen on each side. Notice that balancing oxygen first forced a change in hydrogen, which is exactly why you must recount after every step.

Example 2: Methane combustion, CH4 plus O2 gives CO2 plus H2O. Carbon is already balanced with one on each side. Hydrogen has 4 on the left and 2 on the right, so put 2 in front of H2O, giving 4 hydrogen and 2 oxygen from water plus 2 oxygen from carbon dioxide on the right. Oxygen on the right is now 4 in total, so put 2 in front of O2 on the left. The balanced equation is CH4 plus 2O2 gives CO2 plus 2H2O. Check: 1 carbon, 4 hydrogen, and 4 oxygen on both sides, so the equation is complete.
bullets: 2H2 + O2 gives 2H2O: 4 H and 2 O on each side.
CH4 + 2O2 gives CO2 + 2H2O: 1 C, 4 H, 4 O each side.
Recount every element after each coefficient change.

paras: Example 3: Iron plus oxygen gives iron oxide, Fe plus O2 gives Fe2O3. Iron has 1 on the left and 2 on the right, oxygen has 2 on the left and 3 on the right. Balance iron with 2Fe and oxygen with 3O2 on the left and 2Fe2O3 on the right, then fix iron again: 4Fe plus 3O2 gives 2Fe2O3, with 4 iron and 6 oxygen on each side. Example 4: Aluminium plus hydrochloric acid gives aluminium chloride plus hydrogen, Al plus HCl gives AlCl3 plus H2. Chlorine needs 3HCl, hydrogen then needs 3H2 on the right, and aluminium needs 2Al and 2AlCl3 to balance: 2Al plus 6HCl gives 2AlCl3 plus 3H2, with 2 aluminium, 6 hydrogen, and 6 chlorine on each side.

Example 5: Calcium carbonate plus hydrochloric acid gives calcium chloride plus water plus carbon dioxide, CaCO3 plus HCl gives CaCl2 plus H2O plus CO2. Carbon and calcium are already balanced at one each. Chlorine needs 2HCl, which gives 2 hydrogen on the left, matching the 2 hydrogen in H2O on the right. Oxygen has 3 on the left and 3 on the right, one in water and two in carbon dioxide. The balanced equation is CaCO3 plus 2HCl gives CaCl2 plus H2O plus CO2. Practise these five until the order feels natural, then try similar equations without looking at the solutions.
bullets: 4Fe + 3O2 gives 2Fe2O3: 4 Fe and 6 O each side.
2Al + 6HCl gives 2AlCl3 + 3H2: all elements balanced.
CaCO3 + 2HCl gives CaCl2 + H2O + CO2: check oxygen last.

paras: The worst mistake is changing a subscript, for example writing H2O2 instead of H2O to balance oxygen, because that changes water into a different substance. Another common slip is balancing only one element and forgetting to recount the rest, which leaves hydrogen or oxygen unbalanced in the final answer. Students also forget that some elements exist as diatomic molecules, so O2 counts as two oxygen atoms and H2 counts as two hydrogen atoms, not one. Finally, do not leave a coefficient of one unwritten in the wrong place: an unwritten coefficient means one, and that is fine, but it must still be counted.

In exams, write the unbalanced equation first, then do your counting table in the margin, then write the balanced equation cleanly. If time is short, balance the equation that looks easiest first to secure marks, then return to the harder one. After balancing, read the equation aloud as a sentence: two molecules of hydrogen react with one molecule of oxygen to form two molecules of water. If the sentence sounds balanced in numbers, your counting is probably right. More revision guides are on the [blog](/blog/).

points: Balanced means equal atoms of each element on both sides.
Change coefficients only, never subscripts.
Balance metals first, hydrogen and oxygen last.
Recount every element after each change.
Clear fractions by multiplying the whole equation.

faqs.q: What is the hit-and-trial method?
faqs.a: You try coefficients, count the atoms on both sides, and adjust the numbers until every element matches. It is called hit-and-trial because you test and correct, rather than using a formula.

faqs.q: Can I change H2O to H2O2 to balance oxygen?
faqs.a: No, because that changes water into hydrogen peroxide, a different substance. You may only change the coefficient in front of the formula, never the subscript inside it.

faqs.q: Why do we balance oxygen last?
faqs.a: Oxygen appears in many reactants and products, so fixing it early often gets disturbed when you fix other elements. Balancing it last usually needs fewer corrections.

faqs.q: What should I do if I get a fraction?
faqs.a: Multiply every coefficient in the whole equation by the denominator of the fraction. This clears the fraction while keeping the ratios exactly the same.

title: Class 9 Chemistry: Acids, Bases and pH
desc: Understand class 9 chemistry acids bases ph with the pH scale, indicators, neutralisation reactions, and everyday examples explained simply.
intro: The class 9 chemistry acids bases ph topic explains why lemon juice tastes sour, soap feels slippery, and a pH strip changes colour. Acids release hydrogen ions in water, bases release hydroxide ions, and the pH scale measures how acidic or basic a solution is. This guide explains definitions, the pH scale, indicators, and neutralisation with everyday examples, so you can answer definition, comparison, and reaction questions confidently without memorising long lists blindly.

sections.h2: What Makes a Substance Acidic or Basic
paras: An acid is a substance that produces hydrogen ions when dissolved in water, while a base produces hydroxide ions in water. Common laboratory acids include hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, and nitric acid, and common bases include sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide, and calcium hydroxide. Many everyday substances fit the same pattern: vinegar contains acetic acid, citrus fruits contain citric acid, and washing soda and soap solutions are basic. The strength of an acid depends on how completely it releases hydrogen ions, so a strong acid releases almost all of them while a weak acid releases only a small fraction.

Bases are often described as the chemical opposites of acids, but they are not simply the absence of acid. A base reacts with an acid to form a salt and water, which is why basic substances can neutralise acidity. Alkalis are a special group of bases that dissolve in water, so all alkalis are bases but not all bases are alkalis. For example, sodium hydroxide dissolves and is an alkali, while copper oxide is a base that does not dissolve well in water. Keeping this distinction clear helps in questions that ask whether a substance is an acid, a base, or an alkali. See the [solved notes](/solved.html) for more guides.

The pH scale runs from 0 to 14 and measures the concentration of hydrogen ions in a solution. A pH of 7 is neutral, values below 7 are acidic, and values above 7 are basic or alkaline. The lower the number, the stronger the acid, and the higher the number, the stronger the base, so pH 1 is a strong acid, pH 4 is a weak acid, pH 10 is a weak base, and pH 13 is a strong base. Pure water is neutral at pH 7 because it contains equal, very small amounts of hydrogen and hydroxide ions. Remember that pH is a scale, not a substance, so you should always say the pH of a solution, not the pH of a solid on its own.

Each whole-number step on the pH scale represents a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration, which is why a small pH difference can mean a large chemical difference. A solution at pH 3 has ten times more hydrogen ions than a solution at pH 4, and one hundred times more than a solution at pH 5. This is why strong acids must be handled with care even in dilute form, and why a small amount of acid can change the pH of a weakly protected solution sharply. In exams, always place the value correctly: below 7 means acidic, 7 means neutral, and above 7 means basic, and never write pH 7 as weakly acidic or weakly basic. Check the [books page](/books.html) for supporting textbooks.

diagram.alt: The pH Scale at a Glance
diagram.caption: Use this map to place any solution on the pH scale.

paras: An indicator is a substance that changes colour in acids and bases, giving a quick visual test without measuring pH exactly. Litmus is the classic school indicator: blue litmus turns red in acid and stays blue in base, while red litmus turns blue in base and stays red in acid. Neutral solutions do not change either colour. Universal indicator is more informative because it shows a range of colours across the pH scale, from red in strong acid through green at neutral to purple in strong base. A pH strip soaked in universal indicator can therefore estimate pH, not just tell acid from base.

Natural indicators work the same way and make good home observations, though they are not used for precise measurement. Red cabbage juice turns pink-red in acid and green-yellow in base, and turmeric turns reddish-brown in base while staying yellow in acid. When using any indicator, always test a small sample, record the starting colour, and compare after adding the solution. A common exam mistake is claiming that an indicator proves strength exactly; litmus only shows acid, base, or neutral, while universal indicator gives an approximate pH value. State which indicator you used and what it showed, and your answer will be precise.
bullets: Blue litmus turns red in acid; red litmus turns blue in base.
Universal indicator gives an approximate pH by colour.
Neutral solutions cause no litmus colour change.

paras: Neutralisation happens when an acid reacts with a base to form a salt and water. The hydrogen ions from the acid join with hydroxide ions from the base to make water, while the remaining ions join to form the salt. A classic example is hydrochloric acid plus sodium hydroxide giving sodium chloride plus water: HCl plus NaOH gives NaCl plus H2O. Another example is sulphuric acid plus potassium hydroxide giving potassium sulphate plus water, where the coefficients must be balanced so that hydrogen and hydroxide match. The product is called a salt even when it is not table salt, because salt is the general name for the compound formed from an acid and a base.

Neutralisation is useful far beyond the laboratory. Farmers add lime, a base, to soil that is too acidic, so crops can grow better. Antacid tablets contain a mild base that neutralises excess stomach acid and relieves acidity. Bee stings are acidic and are often treated with a mild base, while wasp stings are basic and are treated with a mild acid such as vinegar, though you should always follow medical advice for real stings. In exams, always name the salt and water products, balance the equation, and explain neutralisation as hydrogen plus hydroxide forming water, not simply as mixing two liquids together.
bullets: Acid + base gives salt + water.
HCl + NaOH gives NaCl + H2O.
Lime neutralises acidic soil; antacids neutralise stomach acid.

sections.h2: Everyday Acids, Bases and Exam Tips
paras: Everyday revision works best when you sort substances into three columns: acid, neutral, and base, with one example and one pH idea for each. Acids include lemon juice, vinegar, and fizzy drinks; neutral substances include pure water and table salt solution; bases include soap solution, baking soda solution, and oven cleaner. Do not taste laboratory chemicals to test them, and never guess from appearance alone, because many acids and bases are colourless liquids. The safe school test is an indicator or a pH strip, with safety glasses and teacher supervision, and any spill should be reported at once rather than cleaned up casually.

For exam answers, define the term first, give the pH rule, then give an example and a reaction if asked. A strong answer to a neutralisation question names the acid, the base, the salt, and water, and shows the balanced equation. A strong answer to a pH question states the number, says acidic, neutral, or basic, and explains what that means for hydrogen ions. Avoid vague phrases such as very acidic without a pH value or indicator result, because examiners award marks for evidence. Finish by practising ten quick classifications a day until the pH scale feels like a number line you can picture. More tips are on the [blog](/blog/).

pH below 7 is acidic, pH 7 is neutral, pH above 7 is basic.

faqs.q: Is pH 6 acidic or basic?
faqs.a: pH 6 is weakly acidic because it is below 7. It has more hydrogen ions than neutral water, but far fewer than a strong acid at pH 1 or 2.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a base and an alkali?
faqs.a: All alkalis are bases, but only bases that dissolve in water are called alkalis. Sodium hydroxide is an alkali, while insoluble copper oxide is a base but not an alkali.

faqs.q: What are the products of neutralisation?
faqs.a: The products are a salt and water. Hydrogen ions from the acid join hydroxide ions from the base to make water, and the other ions form the salt.

faqs.q: Why does universal indicator help more than litmus?
faqs.a: Litmus only shows acid, base, or neutral by two colours. Universal indicator shows a range of colours, so it gives an approximate pH value across the whole scale.

title: Class 9 Chemistry: Percentage Composition Numericals
desc: Learn class 9 chemistry percentage composition with a clear formula, worked examples for water, carbon dioxide, and calcium carbonate.
intro: The class 9 chemistry percentage composition topic asks a simple question: what fraction of a compound's mass comes from each element? If you know the formula and the atomic masses, you can find the percent of every element with one reliable method. This guide explains the formula, works through water, carbon dioxide, calcium carbonate, and ammonia, and shows the mistakes that turn an easy numerical into a lost mark. Keep your working visible and your units clear, and these questions become quick, safe marks.

paras: Percentage composition means the mass of one element in a compound expressed as a percentage of the total mass of the compound. The formula is: percentage of an element equals the total mass of that element in one mole of the compound divided by the molar mass of the compound, multiplied by 100. The total mass of the element is its atomic mass multiplied by how many atoms of it appear in the formula, which is the subscript. For example, in water, H2O, hydrogen appears twice, so its total mass is 2 multiplied by 1, which is 2, while oxygen appears once at 16.

This method works because one mole of a compound always contains the same ratio of atoms, so the mass ratio is fixed no matter how large the sample is. Whether you have 18 grams or 180 grams of water, hydrogen still makes up the same percentage of the mass. Always calculate the molar mass first and write it down, because every percentage in the question will divide by that same total. If your percentages do not add up to 100, or very close to 100 after rounding, you have made an arithmetic error somewhere, and that check alone can save a question. Find more methods on the [solved notes](/solved.html) page.

First, write the chemical formula and list each element with its subscript. Second, multiply each atomic mass by its subscript to get the mass contributed by that element. Third, add all the contributions to get the molar mass of the compound. Fourth, for each element, divide its contribution by the molar mass and multiply by 100. Fifth, add the percentages together to check that they total 100. This five-step order never changes, whether the compound has two elements or four, so you can use it under exam pressure without deciding on a new plan each time.

Rounding needs care: keep at least one decimal place during the working and round only at the end, because early rounding can push the total away from 100. If a question asks only for one element, you still need the molar mass, so do not skip that step. Also watch for brackets in formulas such as calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)2, where the subscript 2 outside the bracket applies to both oxygen and hydrogen inside it. That gives two oxygen atoms and two hydrogen atoms, not one of each, and missing the bracket is one of the most common percentage errors. See the [books page](/books.html) for the books behind these examples.

diagram.caption: Use this fixed order for every percentage composition numerical.

paras: Question: Find the percentage composition of water, H2O. Molar mass: hydrogen contributes 2 multiplied by 1, which is 2, and oxygen contributes 1 multiplied by 16, which is 16, giving a total of 18 grams per mole. Percentage of hydrogen equals 2 divided by 18 multiplied by 100, which is 11.1 percent. Percentage of oxygen equals 16 divided by 18 multiplied by 100, which is 88.9 percent. Add them: 11.1 plus 88.9 equals 100, so the answer checks out. Notice that oxygen dominates the mass even though there are more hydrogen atoms, because each oxygen atom is much heavier.

This example teaches an important lesson about counting: number of atoms and mass contribution are different things. Water has twice as many hydrogen atoms as oxygen atoms, yet hydrogen is only about 11 percent of the mass. Students who guess from atom counts alone get this badly wrong. Always let the masses decide, not the atom counts. A good habit is to write the contribution beside each element before dividing, so the examiner can follow your method and award method marks even if one division slips.
bullets: H2O molar mass: 2 + 16 = 18 g/mol.
Hydrogen: 2 divided by 18 times 100 = 11.1 percent.
Oxygen: 16 divided by 18 times 100 = 88.9 percent.

sections.h2: Worked Example 2: Carbon Dioxide and Calcium Carbonate
paras: Question: Find the percentage of carbon in carbon dioxide, CO2. Molar mass: carbon 12 plus two oxygen atoms at 16 each, which is 32, giving 44 grams per mole. Percentage of carbon equals 12 divided by 44 multiplied by 100, which is 27.3 percent. Percentage of oxygen equals 32 divided by 44 multiplied by 100, which is 72.7 percent, and the total is 100 percent. Question: Find the percentage of calcium in calcium carbonate, CaCO3. Molar mass: calcium 40 plus carbon 12 plus three oxygen atoms at 48, giving 100 grams per mole. Percentage of calcium equals 40 divided by 100 multiplied by 100, which is 40 percent.

Calcium carbonate is a favourite exam example because its molar mass is a round 100, which makes the percentages easy to check. Carbon is 12 percent and oxygen is 48 percent, and 40 plus 12 plus 48 equals 100, confirming the working. When you meet a compound with a round molar mass, use it as a confidence check, but do not expect every compound to be so neat. For ammonia, NH3, the molar mass is 14 plus 3, which is 17, so nitrogen is 14 divided by 17 times 100, which is 82.4 percent, and hydrogen is 3 divided by 17 times 100, which is 17.6 percent. Practise one two-element and one three-element compound each day.
bullets: CO2: carbon 27.3 percent, oxygen 72.7 percent.
CaCO3: calcium 40 percent, carbon 12 percent, oxygen 48 percent.
NH3: nitrogen 82.4 percent, hydrogen 17.6 percent.

paras: The most common mistake is forgetting to multiply by the subscript, so H2O is treated as HO and CO2 is treated as CO, which changes every percentage. Another error is dividing by the atomic mass instead of the molar mass, which can give a percentage above 100 and should immediately warn you that something is wrong. A third error is forgetting to multiply by 100, leaving the answer as a decimal fraction such as 0.111 instead of 11.1 percent. Always end with the percent sign and a total check, because a missing percent sign can cost a mark even when the number is right.

In exams, show the molar mass working first, then each percentage on its own line, then the total check. If the question asks for only one element, still show the molar mass, then that one percentage, and you will earn method marks. Practise with compounds you already know, such as water, carbon dioxide, sodium chloride, and calcium carbonate, before trying longer formulas with brackets. Speed comes from the fixed five-step method, not from skipping steps, so keep every step visible until the method is automatic. More practice guides are on the [blog](/blog/).

points: Percentage equals element mass divided by molar mass times 100.
Multiply atomic mass by the subscript for each element.
Always find the molar mass before any percentage.
Percentages for all elements must add to 100.
Brackets multiply every atom inside them, as in Ca(OH)2.

faqs.q: What is percentage composition?
faqs.a: It is the mass of each element in a compound shown as a percentage of the total mass. It tells you how much of the compound's mass comes from each element.

faqs.q: How do I find the percentage of hydrogen in water?
faqs.a: Water has a molar mass of 18, and hydrogen contributes 2, so divide 2 by 18 and multiply by 100 to get 11.1 percent.

faqs.q: Why must percentages add to 100?
faqs.a: Because the elements together make up the whole compound. If your percentages do not add to about 100, one contribution, the molar mass, or a division is wrong.

faqs.q: What if the formula has brackets?
faqs.a: Multiply the subscript outside the bracket by every atom inside it. In Ca(OH)2 there are two oxygen atoms and two hydrogen atoms, not one of each.

title: Class 9 Chemistry: Valency and Chemical Formulae
desc: Master class 9 chemistry valency formulae with the crossover method, valency tables, polyatomic ions, and worked formula examples.
intro: The class 9 chemistry valency formulae topic is the key to writing correct chemical formulas instead of guessing them. Valency is the combining capacity of an element, and the crossover method lets you combine two valencies into a balanced formula quickly. This guide explains valency in simple words, shows the crossover steps with worked examples, covers polyatomic ions such as sulphate and ammonium, and warns you about the mistakes that make a correct idea into a wrong formula.

sections.h2: What Valency Means in Simple Words
paras: Valency is the number of bonds an atom can form, or the combining capacity it shows when it joins with other atoms. Hydrogen has a valency of 1, oxygen has a valency of 2, sodium has a valency of 1, calcium has a valency of 2, and aluminium has a valency of 3. These numbers come from how many electrons an atom needs to gain, lose, or share to reach a stable arrangement. You do not need to derive every valency from electron shells at this stage; learning the common valencies by heart, with understanding, is enough for Class 9 formula writing.

Valency is not the same as charge, though they are related. A sodium ion has a charge of plus 1 because it loses one electron, and its valency is 1. A calcium ion has a charge of plus 2 and a valency of 2. For negative ions, chloride has a charge of minus 1 and a valency of 1, while oxide has a charge of minus 2 and a valency of 2. When writing formulas, you use the size of the valency, not its sign, because the crossover method balances positive and negative combining capacities against each other. Keep a small valency table in your notebook for revision. See the [solved notes](/solved.html) for more Class 9 help.

sections.h2: The Crossover Method Step by Step
paras: Write the symbols of the two parts side by side, with the positive part, usually the metal or hydrogen or ammonium, on the left and the negative part on the right. Write each valency above its symbol. Then cross them over: the valency of the left part becomes the subscript of the right part, and the valency of the right part becomes the subscript of the left part. Finally, simplify the subscripts if both can be divided by the same number, and leave out any subscript of 1, because it is understood. This method works because it balances the total combining capacity on both sides.

For example, calcium has valency 2 and chlorine has valency 1, so crossing over gives Ca1Cl2, which is written as CaCl2. Aluminium has valency 3 and oxygen has valency 2, so crossing over gives Al2O3, which cannot be simplified further. Sodium has valency 1 and sulphate has valency 2, so crossing over gives Na2SO4, with the polyatomic ion kept together. Always check your finished formula by multiplying valency by subscript on each side: the totals should match, which confirms the formula is balanced. The [books page](/books.html) lists supporting textbooks.

diagram.caption: Cross the valencies over, then simplify if possible.

paras: Example 1: Sodium chloride. Sodium valency 1 and chlorine valency 1 cross over to give Na1Cl1, written as NaCl. Example 2: Magnesium oxide. Magnesium valency 2 and oxygen valency 2 cross over to give Mg2O2, which simplifies by dividing both subscripts by 2 to give MgO. Forgetting to simplify is a common error, because Mg2O2 is not the accepted formula even though the ratio is right. Example 3: Aluminium chloride. Aluminium valency 3 and chlorine valency 1 cross over to give Al1Cl3, written as AlCl3, meaning one aluminium atom combines with three chlorine atoms.

Example 4: Carbon dioxide. Carbon valency 4 and oxygen valency 2 cross over to give C2O4, which simplifies by dividing by 2 to give CO2. This simplification step is essential, and many students lose marks by stopping at C2O4. Example 5: Calcium oxide. Calcium valency 2 and oxygen valency 2 cross over to give Ca2O2, simplifying to CaO. Notice the pattern: whenever both valencies are equal, the formula simplifies to a one-to-one combination. Practise these five until the crossover feels like a single movement rather than four separate thoughts.
bullets: NaCl: valencies 1 and 1 give a one-to-one formula.
MgO: Mg2O2 simplifies to MgO by dividing by 2.
AlCl3: aluminium valency 3 crosses to three chlorines.
CO2: C2O4 simplifies to CO2 by dividing by 2.

paras: A polyatomic ion is a group of atoms that carries a charge and behaves as one unit in reactions, such as sulphate SO4 with valency 2, nitrate NO3 with valency 1, carbonate CO3 with valency 2, hydroxide OH with valency 1, and ammonium NH4 with valency 1. When a polyatomic ion needs a subscript greater than 1, you must put brackets around the whole ion before writing the subscript, because the subscript applies to the entire group. For example, calcium hydroxide is Ca(OH)2, meaning one calcium ion with two hydroxide groups, not CaOH2, which would be a different and wrong formula.

Worked examples help here. Aluminium sulphate: aluminium valency 3 and sulphate valency 2 cross over to give Al2(SO4)3, with brackets because sulphate needs the subscript 3. Ammonium chloride: ammonium valency 1 and chlorine valency 1 give NH4Cl, with no brackets needed because the subscript is 1. Sodium carbonate: sodium valency 1 and carbonate valency 2 give Na2CO3, again with no brackets because carbonate takes subscript 1. Always ask: does this ion need a subscript above 1? If yes, bracket it first, then write the subscript outside the bracket.
bullets: Ca(OH)2: brackets show two whole hydroxide groups.
Al2(SO4)3: brackets show three whole sulphate groups.
NH4Cl and Na2CO3 need no brackets because the subscript is 1.

paras: The most frequent mistake is writing the valency itself as the subscript of its own element, instead of crossing it over. Another is forgetting to simplify, leaving answers such as Mg2O2 or C2O4 instead of MgO and CO2. A third is dropping brackets around polyatomic ions, turning Ca(OH)2 into CaOH2, which changes the meaning completely. Students also mix up the order of symbols, putting the negative part first, which examiners may mark wrong even if the ratio is right, so keep the positive part on the left as the convention requires.

For revision, make a table with two columns: element or ion on the left and valency on the right, and test yourself by covering one column. Then practise ten formulas a day, mixing simple compounds, simplified compounds, and polyatomic ions, and always finish with the valency-times-subscript check. In exams, write the valencies above the symbols in rough work, cross them over visibly, and then write the final formula cleanly. That visible method earns marks for working and makes your own checking much easier. More guides are on the [blog](/blog/).

points: Valency is combining capacity, not charge itself.
Crossover: each valency becomes the other part's subscript.
Simplify subscripts when both share a common divisor.
Drop subscript 1; it is understood.
Bracket a polyatomic ion when its subscript is above 1.

faqs.q: What is valency?
faqs.a: Valency is the combining capacity of an atom or ion, meaning how many bonds it can form or how many hydrogen atoms it can combine with. Hydrogen has valency 1, oxygen has valency 2, and aluminium has valency 3.

faqs.q: How does the crossover method work?
faqs.a: Write the two symbols with valencies above them, then cross over: the left valency becomes the right subscript and the right valency becomes the left subscript. Simplify if both subscripts share a divisor.

faqs.q: Why is calcium hydroxide written Ca(OH)2?
faqs.a: Hydroxide is a polyatomic ion, OH, and it needs a subscript of 2. Brackets show that the 2 applies to the whole hydroxide group, not just to hydrogen.

faqs.q: Why does Mg2O2 become MgO?
faqs.a: Magnesium and oxygen both have valency 2, so crossing gives Mg2O2, but both subscripts divide by 2. The simplest whole-number ratio is MgO, which is the accepted formula.

title: Class 9 Chemistry: Gas Laws in Simple Words
desc: Learn class 9 chemistry gas laws simple with Boyle's and Charles's laws, balloon examples, and easy pressure-volume-temperature problems.
intro: The class 9 chemistry gas laws simple topic explains how gases change when you squeeze them, heat them, or let them expand. Boyle's law links pressure and volume, Charles's law links volume and temperature, and both laws come alive with balloon examples you can picture. This guide explains each law in plain words, shows the formula, works through simple numericals, and warns you about the temperature mistake that catches almost every student at least once.

paras: Gases are different from solids and liquids because their particles are far apart and move freely, so a gas fills its container and can be compressed into a smaller volume. Pressure is the force of gas particles hitting the walls of the container, volume is the space the gas occupies, and temperature measures how fast the particles move on average. When you change one of these, at least one other usually changes too, and the gas laws describe exactly how. Keeping one quantity fixed while studying the other two is the trick that makes each law simple.

For all gas law numericals, you must keep the amount of gas fixed and use the same units on both sides of the equation. Pressure can be measured in atmospheres or other units, but both pressures in one question must use the same unit. Volume can be in litres or cubic centimetres, but again both volumes must match. Temperature is the special case: gas laws require Kelvin, not Celsius, because Kelvin starts at absolute zero, where particle motion is at its minimum. Forgetting to convert Celsius to Kelvin is the single most common gas law error. See the [solved notes](/solved.html) for more revision.

sections.h2: Boyle's Law: Squeeze It, Pressure Rises
paras: Boyle's law states that at fixed temperature, the pressure of a fixed amount of gas is inversely proportional to its volume. In simple words, if you halve the volume, the pressure doubles, and if you double the volume, the pressure halves. The formula is P1V1 equals P2V2, where P1 and V1 are the starting pressure and volume and P2 and V2 are the new pressure and volume. This happens because squeezing the gas into a smaller space makes particles hit the walls more often, which increases pressure without changing temperature.

A balloon example makes it clear. Imagine a balloon with a volume of 4 litres at a pressure of 1 atmosphere. If you squeeze it gently to 2 litres without letting air escape and without changing temperature, the new pressure becomes 2 atmospheres, because 1 times 4 divided by 2 equals 2. If you instead let it expand to 8 litres, the pressure falls to 0.5 atmosphere. A real-world use is a syringe: pushing the plunger reduces volume and increases pressure, which is why medicine can be forced out. Remember the inverse pattern: one goes up, the other goes down. Check the [books page](/books.html) for supporting books.

diagram.caption: One law changes volume by pressure, the other by temperature.

sections.h2: Charles's Law: Heat It, It Expands
paras: Charles's law states that at fixed pressure, the volume of a fixed amount of gas is directly proportional to its temperature in Kelvin. In simple words, heating a gas makes it expand, and cooling it makes it shrink, as long as pressure stays the same. The formula is V1 divided by T1 equals V2 divided by T2, where temperatures must be in Kelvin. This happens because hotter particles move faster and push outward harder, so the gas needs more space to keep the same pressure against the container walls.

Picture a balloon left in warm sunlight: the air inside warms up, particles move faster, and the balloon swells slightly. Put the same balloon in a cold place and it shrinks, because slower particles need less space. A worked example: a gas occupies 300 cubic centimetres at 300 Kelvin. If it is heated to 600 Kelvin at fixed pressure, its new volume is 300 multiplied by 600 divided by 300, which is 600 cubic centimetres, exactly double, because the Kelvin temperature doubled. If you had used Celsius, 27 degrees and 327 degrees, without converting, you would have got a completely wrong answer.
bullets: Charles's law: V1/T1 = V2/T2 at fixed pressure.
Always convert Celsius to Kelvin by adding 273.
Doubling Kelvin temperature doubles volume at fixed pressure.

sections.h2: Worked Problems: Boyle's and Charles's Together
paras: Boyle's problem: A gas at 2 atmospheres occupies 6 litres. What is its volume at 3 atmospheres at the same temperature? Using P1V1 equals P2V2, we get 2 times 6 equals 3 times V2, so V2 equals 12 divided by 3, which is 4 litres. The pressure rose, so the volume fell, which matches the inverse pattern and confirms the answer makes sense. Always do this sense check: if pressure goes up, volume must go down in a Boyle's law question, and if your answer shows both rising, you have swapped the numbers.

Charles's problem: A gas occupies 200 cubic centimetres at 27 degrees Celsius. What is its volume at 127 degrees Celsius at fixed pressure? First convert: 27 plus 273 equals 300 Kelvin, and 127 plus 273 equals 400 Kelvin. Then V2 equals 200 multiplied by 400 divided by 300, which is about 267 cubic centimetres. Notice that the Celsius temperatures roughly quadrupled, but the Kelvin temperatures only rose by a third, so the volume rose by a third, not four times. That contrast shows why the Kelvin conversion is not a small detail but the heart of the calculation.
bullets: Boyle's example: 2 atm and 6 L become 4 L at 3 atm.
Charles's example: 200 cm3 at 300 K becomes 267 cm3 at 400 K.
Sense-check every answer against the law's pattern.

paras: The biggest mistake is using Celsius in Charles's law instead of Kelvin, which ruins an otherwise perfect method. The second mistake is mixing units, such as using litres for one volume and cubic centimetres for the other without converting. The third is forgetting which quantity is fixed: Boyle's law needs fixed temperature, while Charles's law needs fixed pressure, and naming the wrong law loses marks even if the arithmetic is right. Always write the law, the fixed quantity, the conversion to Kelvin if needed, and the substitution on separate lines.

For revision, draw two small graphs from memory: pressure against volume for Boyle's law falls as a curve, while volume against Kelvin temperature for Charles's law rises as a straight line. Sketching the shape helps you recall whether the relationship is direct or inverse under pressure. Practise two Boyle's and two Charles's problems a day, always converting temperature first, and you will stop making the Celsius mistake. Finish by explaining each law with a balloon example to a friend, because a law you can explain in plain words is a law you will remember in exams. More guides are on the [blog](/blog/).

Charles's law: volume and Kelvin temperature are directly proportional at fixed pressure.
Convert Celsius to Kelvin by adding 273 before using Charles's law.
Boyle's formula is P1V1 = P2V2; Charles's is V1/T1 = V2/T2.
Sense-check: pressure up means volume down in Boyle's law.

faqs.q: What is Boyle's law in simple words?
faqs.a: At fixed temperature, squeezing a gas into a smaller volume raises its pressure, and letting it expand lowers its pressure. Pressure and volume move in opposite directions.

faqs.q: What is Charles's law in simple words?
faqs.a: At fixed pressure, heating a gas makes it expand and cooling it makes it shrink. Volume changes in the same direction as temperature, measured in Kelvin.

faqs.q: Why must temperature be in Kelvin?
faqs.a: Kelvin starts at absolute zero, where particle motion is lowest, so volume is truly proportional to Kelvin temperature. Celsius starts at the freezing point of water, so the proportion does not hold in Celsius.

faqs.q: How do I convert Celsius to Kelvin?
faqs.a: Add 273 to the Celsius value. For example, 27 degrees Celsius becomes 300 Kelvin, and 127 degrees Celsius becomes 400 Kelvin.

title: Class 9 Chemistry: Solutions and Concentration
desc: Understand class 9 chemistry solutions concentration with solute, solvent, percent concentration, and worked problems explained step by step.
intro: The class 9 chemistry solutions concentration topic is about mixtures you meet every day: salt water, sugar syrup, and fizzy drinks are all solutions. A solution has a solute dissolved in a solvent, and concentration tells you how much solute is present. This guide explains the key words, the percent concentration formulas, and worked problems, so you can solve mass percent, volume percent, and simple dilution questions without confusion about which mass goes where.

paras: A solution is a homogeneous mixture, meaning it looks the same throughout and its composition is uniform in every part. The solute is the substance that dissolves, and the solvent is the substance that does the dissolving, usually present in the larger amount. In salt water, salt is the solute and water is the solvent. In a sugar syrup, sugar is the solute and water is the solvent. In air, which is a gaseous solution, oxygen and other gases are solutes dissolved in nitrogen, the main solvent gas. Naming solute and solvent correctly is the first mark in many questions, so always identify them before calculating.

Solutions can be solid, liquid, or gaseous, and the solvent decides the type. Brass is a solid solution of zinc in copper, fizzy drinks are liquid solutions with dissolved carbon dioxide gas, and air is a gaseous solution. A solution is different from a suspension, where particles settle out, and from a colloid, where tiny particles scatter light. In a true solution, the solute particles are so small that they do not settle, cannot be filtered out by ordinary filter paper, and do not scatter a beam of light in the same way. If a question asks why salt water is a solution, the answer is its uniformity and stability. See the [solved notes](/solved.html) for more guides.

Concentration describes how much solute is dissolved in a given amount of solution or solvent. A concentrated solution has a large amount of solute, while a dilute solution has a small amount. Concentration is not the same as amount: a large glass of weak sugar water may contain more total sugar than a small glass of strong sugar water, but the small glass is more concentrated because its sugar is packed into less water. This distinction matters in questions that ask you to compare two solutions, because you must compare ratios, not just total amounts.

At Class 9 level, percent concentration is the most common measure. Mass percent means grams of solute per 100 grams of solution, and volume percent means cubic centimetres of solute per 100 cubic centimetres of solution. The word solution in the denominator is crucial: mass percent divides by the mass of the whole solution, solute plus solvent, not by the mass of solvent alone. Students who divide by solvent mass get a higher, wrong percentage, especially when the solute mass is large. Always add solute and solvent masses first to find the solution mass. Check the [books page](/books.html) for textbooks.

diagram.caption: Follow this order so the denominator is always the whole solution.

paras: Question: What is the mass percent of salt in a solution made by dissolving 10 grams of salt in 90 grams of water? First find the solution mass: 10 plus 90 equals 100 grams. Then mass percent equals solute mass divided by solution mass multiplied by 100, which is 10 divided by 100 multiplied by 100, giving 10 percent. Question: What is the mass percent when 20 grams of sugar dissolve in 180 grams of water? Solution mass is 20 plus 180, which is 200 grams. Mass percent is 20 divided by 200 multiplied by 100, giving 10 percent again, even though the amounts are larger, because the ratio is the same.

A harder version asks for the solute mass from a percent. Question: How much salt is needed to make 250 grams of a 20 percent salt solution? Let the salt mass be the unknown: 20 equals salt mass divided by 250 multiplied by 100, so salt mass equals 20 multiplied by 250 divided by 100, which is 50 grams. The water needed is then 250 minus 50, which is 200 grams. This reverse question appears often, so practise both directions: percent from masses, and mass from percent and total. Always check that your solute mass is smaller than the solution mass, or something has gone wrong.
bullets: 10 g salt in 90 g water: solution 100 g, concentration 10 percent.
20 g sugar in 180 g water: solution 200 g, concentration 10 percent.
250 g of 20 percent solution needs 50 g salt and 200 g water.

sections.h2: Worked Example 2: Volume Percent and Dilution
paras: Volume percent works the same way with volumes instead of masses. Question: What is the volume percent of alcohol in a solution with 25 cubic centimetres of alcohol in 75 cubic centimetres of water? Solution volume is 25 plus 75, which is 100 cubic centimetres, so volume percent is 25 divided by 100 multiplied by 100, giving 25 percent. Remember that volumes are not always perfectly additive in real mixtures, but Class 9 questions treat them as additive unless told otherwise, so add them in the same way as masses.

Dilution means adding more solvent to lower the concentration without changing the amount of solute. If you have 100 grams of a 20 percent salt solution, it contains 20 grams of salt. Add 100 grams of water, and the solution mass becomes 200 grams, but the salt stays at 20 grams, so the new percent is 20 divided by 200 multiplied by 100, giving 10 percent. Dilution halves the concentration when you double the total mass, and this pattern is a useful sense check. Evaporation does the opposite: removing solvent raises concentration while solute mass stays the same.
bullets: 25 cm3 alcohol in 75 cm3 water: 25 percent by volume.
Dilution adds solvent, so solute mass stays the same.
Doubling solution mass by adding solvent halves the percent.

paras: The most common mistake is dividing by solvent mass instead of solution mass, which gives a percentage that is too high. Another is forgetting to multiply by 100, leaving a decimal such as 0.10 instead of 10 percent. Students also mix mass and volume, dividing grams by cubic centimetres, which gives a meaningless number unless the question explicitly asks for that ratio. Always check units first: grams with grams for mass percent, and cubic centimetres with cubic centimetres for volume percent. If the units do not match, convert or stop and re-read the question.

In exams, write solute, solvent, solution mass or volume, formula, substitution, and answer with the percent sign, each on a clear line. If the question gives percent and total and asks for solute mass, rearrange the formula before substituting numbers, so you do not get lost in arithmetic. Practise one mass percent, one volume percent, one reverse, and one dilution question each day for a week, and concentration problems will become routine. End by sorting five household mixtures into solute and solvent pairs from memory, since naming the parts correctly is half the skill. More guides are on the [blog](/blog/).
