Filtration traps particles that can shield germs.
Boiling reliably kills most bacteria, viruses and parasites.
Chemical treatment needs the exact instructed dose.
Clean, covered storage keeps purified water safe until drinking.

faqs.q: Does clear water mean safe water?
faqs.a: No. Many germs and dissolved chemicals are invisible, tasteless and odourless, so clear water from an unprotected source can still be unsafe without treatment.

faqs.q: Why filter water before boiling it?
faqs.a: Particles can shield germs from heat and chemicals and can clog treatment, so removing mud first makes boiling and disinfection work more reliably.

faqs.q: How long should water be boiled?
faqs.a: A full rolling boil for at least one minute is commonly recommended, longer at high altitude. Let it cool in a clean, covered container before drinking.

faqs.q: Why should drinking water be covered?
faqs.a: An uncovered container lets dust, insects and dirty hands contaminate treated water, undoing purification. A clean lid and tap or narrow opening prevent this.

faqs.q: Does boiling remove chemicals from water?
faqs.a: No, boiling kills germs but does not remove dissolved chemicals or salts, so chemically polluted water needs professional testing and treatment.

title: Science in Plants and Gardens
desc: Photosynthesis, pollination and compost in your garden: how plants grow, make food, attract pollinators and recycle nutrients, explained for students.
intro: A garden is a living science classroom. Roots drink water, leaves catch sunlight, flowers invite insects, and fallen leaves rot into rich soil that feeds the next generation of plants. Behind this quiet activity are powerful processes: photosynthesis, pollination, seed dispersal and decomposition. This article explores garden science through plants you can grow at home, from mint and chillies to marigolds and beans, and shows how simple observations and experiments can turn gardening into one of the most enjoyable ways to learn biology.

sections.h2: Photosynthesis: How Leaves Make Food From Air and Light
paras: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants make their own food. Inside leaf cells, a green pigment called chlorophyll captures sunlight, and the plant uses that energy to combine water from its roots with carbon dioxide from the air, producing sugars for growth and releasing oxygen as a by-product. The famous word equation is simple to remember: carbon dioxide plus water, using light energy, gives glucose plus oxygen. Without this process, almost all life on Earth would lack food and oxygen, because plants sit at the base of nearly every food chain.

Leaves are beautifully designed for this job. They are broad and flat to catch light, thin so gases can move in and out quickly, and full of tiny pores called stomata that let carbon dioxide in and oxygen and water vapour out. Veins carry water to leaf cells and sugars away to growing parts such as roots, stems and fruits. That is why plants kept in darkness grow pale and weak, and why a plant near a bright window leans toward the light: it is trying to capture more energy for photosynthesis.

sections.h2: Roots, Stems and the Plant Transport System
paras: Roots anchor the plant and absorb water and dissolved minerals from the soil through tiny root hairs, which greatly increase the absorbing surface. The water then travels upward through narrow tubes called xylem, while sugars made in the leaves travel to other parts through tubes called phloem. This transport system works like a plant's blood circulation, though it has no heart: water is pulled upward partly by evaporation from leaves, a process called transpiration, which creates a gentle pull through the whole plant.

Stems hold leaves up toward light and flowers up toward pollinators, while also carrying water and sugars between roots and leaves. Some stems store food, such as potatoes, which are swollen underground stems, while others, like sugarcane, store sweet sap. Gardeners use this knowledge when they water at the base of a plant rather than only wetting leaves, when they mulch soil to reduce evaporation, and when they avoid damaging roots during transplanting, because a damaged transport system starves the whole plant.

diagram.caption: Roots, leaves and sunlight work together to make food and support growth.

sections.h2: Pollination: Flowers, Bees and the Making of Seeds
paras: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the male part of a flower, the anther, to the female part, the stigma, and it is necessary for most flowering plants to produce seeds and fruit. Bees, butterflies, moths, birds and even wind act as pollinators, carrying pollen as they visit flowers for nectar. Flowers advertise themselves with bright colours, sweet scents and nectar rewards, and bees are especially effective because their hairy bodies pick up pollen and their regular flower visits move it between plants of the same kind.

After pollination, fertilisation follows inside the flower, and the ovary grows into a fruit containing seeds. That is why a garden without pollinators may flower beautifully but produce little fruit. Gardeners can help by growing a mix of flowers that bloom across seasons, avoiding spraying insecticides during flowering, and leaving some wild corners for insects to nest. A simple observation project is to sit quietly near flowers for ten minutes and record which insects visit, what colours they prefer, and how long they stay.
bullets: Pollen moves from anther to stigma during pollination.
Bees carry pollen on hairy bodies between flowers.
Fruit forms after pollination and fertilisation.

sections.h2: Compost: Recycling Garden Waste Into Rich Soil
paras: Compost is decayed plant and food material that returns nutrients to the soil, and it is made by microbes, fungi and small creatures such as earthworms. When leaves, vegetable peels and grass cuttings are piled with air, moisture and a mix of green and brown material, decomposers break them down into dark, crumbly humus. This humus improves soil structure, holds moisture, feeds plants slowly, and supports the soil life that keeps gardens healthy without heavy use of chemical fertilisers.

Good composting balances wet, nitrogen-rich green material such as fresh leaves and kitchen vegetable waste with dry, carbon-rich brown material such as dried leaves and paper. Turning the pile adds air, which decomposers need, and keeping it moist but not soggy speeds the process. Meat, dairy and oily foods are usually avoided in home compost because they attract pests and smell. After weeks or months, the finished compost smells earthy and can be mixed into garden beds before planting.

A home garden is an ideal place for fair experiments. You can grow the same bean seeds in sunlight and shade, in sandy and loamy soil, or with different amounts of water, changing only one factor at a time and measuring height every few days. Recording results in a table and drawing a simple graph turns gardening into real scientific investigation, teaching variables, measurement and fair testing far better than reading about them alone. Even a few pots on a balcony can host such experiments.

Gardening also teaches patience, care and respect for living things. Plants need regular water, protection from harsh sun and strong wind, and gentle handling of roots and stems. Harvesting herbs, chillies or tomatoes you grew yourself shows the full journey from seed to food. For more study material, explore the [books page](/books.html) and the [blog](/blog/) on this site, and start with one easy plant, observe it daily, and write down what surprises you most.

Xylem carries water up, phloem carries sugars around the plant.
Pollination moves pollen from anther to stigma for seed production.

faqs.q: What is photosynthesis?
faqs.a: Photosynthesis is the process in which green plants use sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make glucose for growth, releasing oxygen as a by-product.

faqs.q: Why do plants lean toward light?
faqs.a: Plants grow toward light so their leaves can capture more light energy for photosynthesis, a response called phototropism.

faqs.q: What is the difference between xylem and phloem?
faqs.a: Xylem carries water and dissolved minerals upward from roots to leaves, while phloem carries sugars made in leaves to growing parts of the plant.

faqs.q: Why do gardens need pollinators?
faqs.a: Most flowering plants need pollen transfer to produce seeds and fruit, and pollinators such as bees carry pollen between flowers as they collect nectar.

faqs.q: What makes good compost?
faqs.a: A balance of green, nitrogen-rich material and brown, carbon-rich material, plus air, moisture and time for decomposers to break it into dark, earthy humus.

title: Science in Sports: Cricket, Football and Running
desc: Spin, speed and balance behind every game: the physics of cricket, football and running, from friction and force to energy, reaction time and training.
intro: Sport feels like pure fun, but every run, kick, throw and catch is governed by physics and biology. A cricket ball swings because of air pressure, a football curves because of spin, a runner speeds up by pushing against the ground, and muscles turn food energy into motion. Understanding these ideas does not spoil the game; it makes watching and playing far more interesting, and it helps young athletes train smarter and stay safer. This article explores the science behind cricket, football and running, three sports loved across Pakistan and the world.

sections.h2: Force, Motion and Newton's Ideas on the Field
paras: Newton's laws explain much of sport in plain language. An object stays still or keeps moving steadily unless a force acts on it, which is why a ball rolls on until friction and air resistance slow it down. Force equals mass times acceleration, so a heavier ball needs a stronger push to speed up as quickly as a lighter one. Every action also has an equal and opposite reaction: when a runner pushes backward against the ground, the ground pushes the runner forward, and when a footballer kicks a ball, the ball pushes back on the foot.

Momentum, which combines mass and speed, explains why a fast, heavy player is harder to stop than a slow, light one, and why a goalkeeper must absorb the momentum of a hard shot with hands, arms and body. Impulse, the effect of force over time, explains why catching a fast ball with soft, moving hands hurts less than catching it stiffly: giving more time spreads the same momentum change over a longer period, reducing the peak force on your hands.

sections.h2: Cricket Science: Swing, Spin and Timing
paras: A cricket ball swings when air flows differently on its two sides. A shiny side lets air flow smoothly, while a rough side slows air and changes pressure, and the pressure difference bends the ball's path through the air. Bowlers polish one side and let the other roughen to increase this effect, and they also use seam position to disturb airflow. Reverse swing, seen with older balls, reverses the usual pattern because of complex airflow at higher speeds, which is why it puzzles even experienced batters.

Spin bowling uses friction and rotation. A spinner grips the ball so it rotates as it leaves the hand, and when it lands, friction with the pitch grips the spinning surface and changes direction. Topspin dips and bounces higher, backspin floats and skids lower, and sidespin turns the ball left or right. Batting timing is applied physics too: the batter must judge speed, bounce and line, move feet into position, and meet the ball with a bat angled to send it where fielders are not, all within a fraction of a second.

diagram.caption: Air pressure, spin, friction and timing shape every delivery and shot.

sections.h2: Football Science: Curves, Bounce and Kicking Power
paras: A curving free kick is a beautiful example of the Magnus effect. When a football spins in flight, it drags air around with it, speeding airflow on one side and slowing it on the other. The resulting pressure difference pushes the ball sideways, curving its path in the direction of the spin. Striking the ball off-centre with the inside or outside of the foot creates the spin, and the amount of curve depends on spin speed, ball speed and air conditions, which is why the same kick behaves slightly differently on a windy day.

Kicking power comes from the whole body, not just the foot. A run-up builds momentum, the planted foot gives balance and direction, the kicking leg swings like a pendulum from the hip, and the follow-through transfers energy smoothly into the ball. The angle of the kick decides height and distance: a low, driven pass uses a flatter strike, while a high clearance uses a strike lower on the ball. Ball bounce depends on air pressure inside the ball and the hardness of the surface, which is why a properly inflated ball bounces predictably and an under-inflated one feels dead.
bullets: Spin creates a pressure difference that curves the ball.
A run-up and follow-through add power to a kick.
Correct ball pressure gives a predictable bounce.

sections.h2: Running Science: Energy, Muscles and Breathing
paras: Running turns chemical energy from food into kinetic energy of motion. Muscles contract by sliding tiny fibres past each other, using energy released from glucose, and that contraction pulls on bones through tendons to move the legs. The faster you run, the more energy your muscles need, and the more oxygen your lungs and heart must deliver, which is why breathing quickens and heart rate rises during a sprint. Training improves this system: the heart grows stronger, muscles become more efficient, and the body learns to clear waste products faster.

Running technique is also physics. Short, quick steps with feet landing under the body waste less braking force than long, overreaching strides that land far ahead. Arms swing opposite to legs to balance rotation, and leaning slightly forward helps gravity assist forward motion without toppling. Good running shoes grip the surface, cushion impact and protect joints, but no shoe replaces gradual training: increasing distance or speed too fast is the commonest cause of strains, shin pain and stress injuries in young runners.

sections.h2: Balance, Reaction Time and Playing Safely
paras: Balance depends on keeping your centre of gravity above your base of support. A footballer with feet wide apart is harder to push over than one standing narrowly, and a batter with a stable stance can react faster because the body is already balanced. Reaction time is the delay between seeing an event and responding to it, and it improves with practice because the brain learns to recognise patterns, such as a bowler's action or a goalkeeper's movement, and prepare a response before the ball arrives.

Safety science protects players at every level. Warming up raises muscle temperature, increases blood flow and loosens joints, reducing injury risk, while cooling down and stretching help muscles recover. Helmets, pads, shin guards and mouthguards spread impact forces and protect vulnerable parts, and drinking water before, during and after play prevents dehydration, especially in hot weather. Rest days are part of training, not laziness, because muscles grow stronger during recovery. For more everyday science, visit the [blog](/blog/) and the [solved notes](/solved.html) on this site, and try timing your own reaction with a dropped ruler experiment.

Uneven airflow makes a cricket ball swing in flight.
Spin creates a pressure difference that curves a football.
Muscles turn food energy into motion through contraction.

faqs.q: Why does a cricket ball swing?
faqs.a: Air flows differently over the shiny and rough sides of the ball, creating a pressure difference that bends its path through the air.

faqs.q: Why does a spinning football curve?
faqs.a: Spin drags air around the ball, speeding airflow on one side and slowing it on the other, and the pressure difference, called the Magnus effect, pushes the ball sideways.

faqs.q: Why does a runner breathe faster when sprinting?
faqs.a: Muscles need more oxygen to release energy quickly during a sprint, so the lungs breathe faster and the heart pumps harder to deliver that oxygen.

faqs.q: Why does catching with soft hands hurt less?
faqs.a: Soft, moving hands spread the change in momentum over a longer time, reducing the peak force on the hands compared with a stiff, sudden catch.

faqs.q: Why is warming up important?
faqs.a: Warming up raises muscle temperature, increases blood flow and loosens joints, which prepares the body for effort and lowers the risk of strains and injuries.

title: Punjab Second Annual Exams Begin Today: First-Day Guide for 3 November 2026
desc: Punjab second annual exams begin today, Tuesday 3 November 2026. A first-day guide to timings, roll slips, centres and a calm plan for your first paper.
kw: Punjab second annual exams 3 November 2026 first day guide
intro: Today is the day thousands of Punjab students have been preparing for. The HSSC second annual examinations begin across the province on Tuesday 3 November 2026, with Part-II (12th class) theory papers running from 3 to 16 November 2026 under all nine Punjab boards. If you are appearing today, your job is simple: reach the right centre on time, carry the right documents, and attempt your paper with a clear head. This guide walks you through the first day step by step, using only verified board information, so that nothing about the morning surprises you.

paras: The second annual examinations are held province-wide through the Punjab Boards Committee of Chairpersons, covering all nine boards: Lahore, Rawalpindi, Gujranwala, Faisalabad, Multan, Sargodha, Sahiwal, Bahawalpur and DG Khan. Part-II theory papers run from 3 to 16 November 2026, and Part-I (11th class) theory papers follow from 17 to 28 November 2026. Practical examinations are scheduled later, from 1 to 11 December 2026. Knowing this overall shape matters because it tells you that today is the start of a two-week theory window, not a single-day event, and that your preparation should pace itself across the whole series.

Morning papers begin at 9:00 AM and evening papers at 2:00 PM, while on Fridays the evening paper starts at 2:30 PM. Check your own roll number slip for whether your paper is a morning or evening session, because the two shifts have very different travel and revision plans. A morning-paper student should plan to be up early, revised and travelling well before 9:00 AM, while an evening-paper student gets extra morning revision time but must still reach the centre comfortably before 2:00 PM. Never guess your session from a friend's slip, since centres and shifts can differ even within the same subject.

sections.h2: Before You Leave Home: The First-Day Checklist
paras: Your roll number slip is the most important item of the day. It tells you your centre, your seat and your paper timing, and examiners will ask for it before you enter the hall. Pack it the night before, along with your original identity documents if your board requires them, and the stationery your paper needs: pens, pencils, a ruler, a geometry box or calculator only where the paper allows them. Keep everything in one clear folder so you are not searching through a bag at the centre gate.

Check your centre address the night before and plan your route with extra time for traffic. If your centre is in an unfamiliar part of town, confirm the location with a family member or a classmate who has been there before, and keep a charged phone for navigation and contact. Eat a proper breakfast, drink water, and avoid starting any brand-new topic on the morning of the exam. First-day nerves are normal, and a calm, prepared start does more for your marks than a panicked last-minute cram session ever will.
bullets: Roll number slip, checked for centre name, paper and session timing
Pens, pencils, ruler and any paper-specific stationery allowed by the board
A water bottle and a light snack for the wait before the paper
Travel planned with extra time so you arrive before the gate closes

sections.h2: At the Centre: Seating, Instructions and First Minutes
paras: Arrive early and head straight to the seating plan or notice board, where your roll number will show your room and seat. Sit down, settle your stationery, and listen carefully to the invigilator's instructions about attendance, answer-book details and the use of extra sheets. Fill in your roll number and other required details on the answer book slowly and exactly as they appear on your slip, because a wrongly written roll number can cause real trouble later even when the answers themselves are good.

When the question paper is handed out, use the first few minutes to read the whole paper before writing anything. Mark the questions you know best, note the ones that carry the most marks, and decide your attempt order. Most students do best when they start with a question they are confident about, since an early success steadies the nerves and builds momentum for the harder questions that follow. Keep an eye on the clock from the start, and divide your time roughly in proportion to the marks each section carries.

sections.h2: A Calm Plan for the First Paper
paras: The first paper sets the tone for the whole series, so treat it as a warm-up as well as an exam. Write in a clear hand, keep your answers organised under the right question numbers, and show your working in numerical papers, because examiners award marks for method as well as final answers. If a question stalls you, move on and come back to it later rather than losing twenty minutes on one part while easier marks wait elsewhere in the paper.

In the last fifteen minutes, stop writing new answers and start reviewing. Check that every attempted question is numbered correctly, that no page is left blank by accident, and that your roll number appears wherever the answer book requires it. A short review at the end catches small slips that cost marks for no reason. After the paper, avoid long post-paper discussions about answers you cannot change, and instead rest briefly, eat well, and turn your attention to the next paper on your date sheet.

diagram.alt: First Exam Day, Step by Step
diagram.caption: A simple first-day routine for Punjab second annual candidates.

sections.h2: What Comes Next, and What Is Already Closed
paras: After today, the Part-II theory series continues until 16 November 2026, followed by Part-I theory from 17 to 28 November 2026 and practicals from 1 to 11 December 2026. Keep your date sheet somewhere visible at home, and tick off each paper as it passes, so that your revision always focuses on the next paper rather than the one already done. If you are a 12th class student, remember that the 11th class papers starting on 17 November do not concern you, and if you are in 11th class, your series has not started yet, so use these two weeks for focused revision rather than exam-day stress.

Two things are worth stating plainly so that no student is misled. First, the admission windows for these examinations, which ran from 24 September to 17 October, are now closed, so nobody should expect to apply fresh at this stage. Second, no supplementary result date has been announced by an individual board in the sources checked for today. A preliminary schedule reported in Dawn on 18 January 2026 puts a supplementary intermediate result around 12 January 2027, but that is only a reported schedule expectation, not a confirmed board announcement, and students should wait for their own board's notice before treating any date as final. title: Punjab Second Annual First-Week Plan: English, Maths, Biology and More
desc: A first-week plan for Punjab second annual exams, using BISE Multan date-sheet examples for English, Maths, Biology, Computer Science, Chemistry and Physics.
kw: Punjab second annual first week papers plan BISE Multan date sheet
intro: The first week of the Punjab second annual examinations is where good planning pays off most. With Part-II theory papers running from 3 to 16 November 2026, the opening days set your rhythm for the whole series, and the gaps between papers decide how much real revision you can fit in. This plan uses subject examples from the BISE Multan date sheet to show how a first week can look, but it comes with one warning that matters more than any timetable: every student must confirm their own board's date sheet, because subject dates can differ from board to board. Use the structure here, and fill in your own board's exact dates.

sections.h2: How to Read Your Date Sheet Before Planning Anything
paras: A date sheet is more than a list of dates. It tells you the order of your papers, the gaps between them, and whether each paper falls in the morning session at 9:00 AM or the evening session at 2:00 PM, with Friday evening papers at 2:30 PM. Start by writing out your own papers in order, with the gap in days before each one, and you will immediately see which papers have breathing room and which ones arrive back to back. That gap map is the real foundation of your plan, because a paper with a three-day gap can carry a full revision cycle, while a paper that follows the previous one by a single day needs short, targeted revision only.

The examples in this article come from the BISE Multan date sheet, and they are useful for showing the shape of a first week, but they are not a substitute for your own board's sheet. If your board places Chemistry before Computer Science, or your Physics paper falls on a different day, your plan must follow your board, not Multan's. Check your roll number slip and your board's published date sheet, and if the two ever disagree, ask your school or college office which one to trust. Planning from the wrong sheet is one of the few mistakes that can cost a whole paper.

In the BISE Multan examples, 12th class English Compulsory falls on 4 November, very early in the series. English is a paper where many students lose marks not on knowledge but on presentation and time management, so the revision for it should look different from a science paper. Practise one essay and one precis-style passage under timed conditions, revise the grammar rules that repeatedly appear, and read through your textbook lessons once more for the short questions. Keep a list of quotations, pair-of-words and correction items that you keep getting wrong, and drill only that list in the final day.

On the day itself, attempt the sections you are strongest in first, and leave enough time for the essay, which carries heavy marks and cannot be rushed in the last ten minutes. Write neatly, keep paragraphs short, and check spellings of common words as you go. An English paper rewards steady, organised writing far more than it rewards cramming new material at the last hour, so treat the day before it as a practice day, not a reading day. For general study guidance, the [solved notes](/solved.html) section and the [blog listing](/blog/) carry exam preparation articles that apply across subjects.

The Multan examples place Mathematics and Biology on 6 November, which means students of either stream face a heavy paper two days after English. For Mathematics, the final revision should be almost entirely practice: work through past-paper style questions from each chapter, write every step clearly, and keep a short formula sheet that you revise from memory rather than reading passively. The most common Mathematics mistakes are skipped steps, sign errors and unfinished questions, and all three are fixed by practice under time pressure, not by re-reading solved examples.

For Biology, the same two days should be spent on diagrams, definitions and the short questions that examiners repeat year after year. Draw each important diagram from memory at least once, label it fully, and practise writing definitions in your own words rather than memorising long paragraphs word for word. Biology answers score best when they are precise and well labelled, so spend your last revision hour on the diagrams and terminology that you find hardest to recall. Both streams should sleep properly the night before, because a tired mind makes exactly the small errors that cost marks in these papers.

sections.h2: Computer Science, Chemistry and Physics Across the Week
paras: Computer Science appears on 10 November in the Multan examples, giving students a four-day gap after the 6 November papers, which is generous by exam standards. Use the first two days of that gap for the chapters you find hardest, especially programming concepts and short questions, and the last two days for full practice papers and revision of definitions. Chemistry on 12 November follows a similar pattern: split the gap between physical, organic and inorganic portions, and practise numerical problems and chemical equations by writing them out, since Chemistry rewards students who can reproduce equations accurately under pressure.

Physics on 16 November closes the Part-II theory series in these examples, and it is the paper students most often underprepare because it comes last. Do not let the long gap breed laziness. Work through numerical problems chapter by chapter, revise derivations by writing them from memory, and practise the short questions that test understanding rather than memory. A useful rule for the whole week is to finish each day's revision by writing down tomorrow's plan, so that every morning starts with a clear task instead of a decision about what to study.

sections.h2: Rest, Health and the Warning That Protects Your Plan
paras: A first-week plan fails more often from exhaustion than from a lack of study. Eat regular meals, keep water nearby during revision, and protect at least six to seven hours of sleep each night, because the brain consolidates what it studied only during rest. Short breaks every hour keep concentration higher than marathon sessions do, and a walk or light exercise between papers helps more than an extra hour of tired reading. If you feel overwhelmed, scale the plan down rather than abandoning it: a smaller plan followed properly beats a perfect plan followed for one day.

Finally, repeat the warning that underpins this whole article. Every date in it, from English on 4 November to Physics on 16 November, is a BISE Multan example, given to show the shape of a first week. Your own board, whether Lahore, Rawalpindi, Gujranwala, Faisalabad, Sargodha, Sahiwal, Bahawalpur or DG Khan, may place your papers on different days. Confirm your own board's date sheet before you lock your timetable, and if anything about your centre or timing is unclear, check with your school or college office rather than relying on a friend's sheet. A plan built on your own verified dates is the only plan worth following.

title: Punjab 11th Class Second Annual: Two-Week Prep Plan Before 17 November
desc: Punjab 11th class second annual papers run 17 to 28 November 2026. A two-week prep plan with Multan date-sheet examples, revision blocks and practical dates.
kw: Punjab 11th class second annual prep plan 17 November 2026
intro: While 12th class students sit their papers from 3 November, 11th class students across Punjab have a valuable two-week window before their own second annual theory papers begin on 17 November 2026. Those two weeks are the difference between entering the hall prepared and entering it hoping, but only if they are used with a plan rather than drifted through. This article builds a two-week preparation plan around the verified structure of the series, using BISE Multan date-sheet examples for subject order, and it ends with the practical examinations that follow in December.

sections.h2: The Shape of the 11th Class Series
paras: The 11th class (Part-I) theory papers run from 17 to 28 November 2026 across all nine Punjab boards, Lahore, Rawalpindi, Gujranwala, Faisalabad, Multan, Sargodha, Sahiwal, Bahawalpur and DG Khan, with practical examinations following from 1 to 11 December 2026. Morning papers begin at 9:00 AM and evening papers at 2:00 PM, with Friday evening papers at 2:30 PM. Because the 12th class papers occupy the first half of November, 11th class students can watch the exam season begin around them while keeping their own focus on preparation, and that is an advantage if it is used calmly rather than anxiously.

In the BISE Multan examples, the 11th class order runs: English Compulsory on 18 November, Computer Science on 23 November, Mathematics or Biology on 25 November, and Physics on 27 November. Other subjects fill the days between and around these, and the exact order on your own board's sheet may differ, so treat these examples as a shape to plan around, not as your personal timetable. Write out your own board's full paper list first, then fit the two-week plan below to it.
bullets: Part-I theory: 17 to 28 November 2026
Practicals: 1 to 11 December 2026
Morning 9:00 AM, evening 2:00 PM, Friday evening 2:30 PM

sections.h2: Week One: Cover Weaknesses First (3 to 9 November)
paras: The first week of preparation should attack weaknesses, not strengths. List every subject you are appearing in, and under each one write the two chapters or topics you find hardest. Those weak topics get the morning slots of week one, when concentration is highest, while stronger material gets the afternoon. For English, this means practising essays, precis work and grammar items you repeatedly get wrong. For Mathematics, it means working problems from the chapters where your steps break down. For Biology, it means drawing the diagrams you cannot yet reproduce from memory.

By the end of week one, you should be able to say honestly that nothing on your syllabus is completely untouched. That does not mean everything is mastered, only that there are no blank areas left to panic about later. Keep a short daily log of what you revised and which questions you still got wrong, because that log becomes the revision list for week two. Students who study without a log often revise the same comfortable chapters three times while the weak ones stay weak, and week one exists to prevent exactly that.

sections.h2: Week Two: Practice Papers and Exam Conditions (10 to 16 November)
paras: Week two should feel like the exam itself. Sit down with past-paper style questions, a clock, and no notes, and practise full papers or full sections under timed conditions. For English, practise the essay and the comprehension passage within their time limits. For Mathematics and Physics, practise numerical sets and derivations by writing every step, since examiners award marks for method. For Computer Science, practise short questions and programming concepts until definitions come quickly. After each practice session, mark your work honestly and add every repeated mistake to a short error list.

The final two days of week two should taper, not intensify. Revise your error list, read through your formula sheets and definitions, and practise one more short paper for confidence, but do not start any brand-new chapter. The night before 17 November, prepare your roll number slip, stationery and centre route, and get a full night's sleep. Students who arrive rested and organised outperform students who arrive exhausted from a final all-nighter, even when the tired student studied more hours in total.

sections.h2: Subject Order: Using the Multan Examples Wisely
paras: If your board follows the Multan example order, English on 18 November comes first and deserves the heaviest early attention, because it opens your series and sets your confidence. Computer Science on 23 November then gives a gap of several days after English, which is ideal for splitting between programming concepts and short-question revision. Mathematics or Biology on 25 November is the heavy paper of the second week of exams, and Physics on 27 November closes the series, so the days between them should be protected for numerical practice and derivations rather than spent on already-strong material.

Whatever your board's actual order, apply the same principle: give the first paper extra preparation because it sets your tone, give heavy numerical papers the longest practice blocks, and keep the last paper's revision going right to the end instead of relaxing early. Check your own board's sheet as soon as it is available, and if any date differs from the examples here, rebuild your plan around your own dates immediately. A plan that matches your real timetable is worth far more than a beautiful plan built on another board's dates. For general preparation help, see [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [blog listing](/blog/).

sections.h2: After Theory: Practicals from 1 to 11 December
paras: Theory papers end on 28 November, but the series is not over. Practical examinations run from 1 to 11 December 2026, and students in science subjects should begin practical preparation during the theory weeks, not after them. Keep your practical notebooks complete and up to date, revise the experiments you performed during the year, and practise writing observations and results clearly. A practical notebook that is finished early removes a whole source of stress from the days after theory ends.

The gap between the last theory paper and the first practical is also the time to rest properly for a day or two before shifting into practical mode. Eat well, sleep properly, and then work through your practical syllabus subject by subject, confirming your practical centre and timing from your slip. Treat practicals with the same seriousness as theory, because their marks count just as much, and a well-prepared practical performance is one of the most reliable ways to lift an overall result.

faqs.a: Part-I (11th class) theory papers run from 17 to 28 November 2026 across all nine Punjab boards. Practical examinations follow from 1 to 11 December 2026.

faqs.q: What does the Multan example order look like for 11th class?
faqs.a: In the BISE Multan examples, English Compulsory falls on 18 November, Computer Science on 23 November, Mathematics or Biology on 25 November, and Physics on 27 November. Your own board's order may differ, so confirm your own date sheet.

faqs.q: How should I split the two weeks before 17 November?
faqs.a: Use the first week for your weakest chapters in morning slots and stronger material in the afternoon. Use the second week for timed practice papers, mark them honestly, and keep an error list for the final days.

faqs.q: When are the practical examinations?
faqs.a: Practical examinations run from 1 to 11 December 2026. Keep practical notebooks complete during the theory weeks so that the practical phase does not start with catch-up work.

faqs.q: Should I study all night before the first paper?
faqs.a: No. Taper revision in the final two days, prepare your slip and stationery the night before, and sleep properly. A rested student with a clear plan outperforms an exhausted student who crammed through the night.

title: BIEK Supplementary Exams: Mid-Series Revision Between Papers
desc: BIEK supplementary exams run 28 October to 21 November 2026. A mid-series revision plan for the days between papers, without burnout, in the afternoon shift.
kw: BIEK supplementary exams mid-series revision plan between papers
intro: The BIEK supplementary examinations are now past their opening week and into the middle of the series, running from 28 October to 21 November 2026. For students still appearing, the hardest part of this stage is not any single paper but the stretch between papers: revising the next subject while recovering from the last one, without burning out before the series ends. This article offers a mid-series revision plan built for that exact situation, using the verified timing and structure of the BIEK supplementary series, so that the days between papers work for you instead of wearing you down.

sections.h2: The Series You Are In the Middle Of
paras: The Board of Intermediate Education Karachi is holding its HSC Part-I and Part-II supplementary examinations from 28 October to 21 November 2026, in a single afternoon shift from 2:00 PM to 5:00 PM daily, with a reporting time of 1:30 PM. The date sheet was released on 23 October 2026 under press releases No. BIE/PR/2026/150 and 151, dated 22 October 2026. More than 21,000 students are appearing across 49 examination centres in Karachi, covering the Pre-Medical, Pre-Engineering, Science General, Commerce, Arts, Home Economics and special-category groups, under Chairman Faqir Muhammad Lakho.

The afternoon shift shapes everything about mid-series revision. Your mornings are free, your papers occupy the afternoon, and your evenings are for recovery and light preparation. Students who treat the morning as a second full school day and the evening as another study session quickly exhaust themselves, and exhaustion is the main enemy in the middle of a long series. The plan below treats the morning as the main revision block, the paper as the main event, and the evening as recovery plus only the lightest next-day preparation.

sections.h2: The Evening After a Paper: Recover First
paras: When you return home after a 2:00 to 5:00 PM paper, resist the urge to open the next subject immediately. Eat a proper meal, rest for at least an hour, and let the paper go. Long discussions about answers you cannot change only drain energy and raise anxiety, and they steal time from the sleep that consolidates what you already know. A short walk, a conversation with family, or simple rest does more for tomorrow's paper than an evening of tired, unfocused reading.

In the later part of the evening, spend no more than an hour on the next paper, and keep it light: glance at the chapter list, pick the three topics you will revise in the morning, and lay out your notes and stationery. This is planning, not studying, and it means the next morning starts with a decision already made. Then sleep at a regular time. A supplementary series is a marathon, and students who protect their sleep in the middle weeks are the ones still performing well in the final week.

sections.h2: The Morning Before a Paper: Short, Targeted Revision
paras: The morning before a paper is your main revision block, and it should be short and targeted rather than broad. Work through the three topics you chose the night before, practise the question types that appear most often in that subject, and write out anything you keep forgetting, such as formulas, definitions, diagrams or dates. For science papers, redraw key diagrams from memory and practise numerical steps. For commerce and arts papers, practise structuring answers and recalling definitions and explanations in your own words.

Stop revising at least an hour before you need to leave for the centre. Use that hour to check your admit card, which is available at admitcard.biek.edu.pk using your 16-digit challan number and matric roll number, confirm your centre, and travel so that you arrive by the 1:30 PM reporting time. Arriving calm and on time matters as much as the last hour of revision, because a rushed, anxious entry into the hall affects the first thirty minutes of the paper, which is when many students settle their rhythm.

sections.h2: Between Papers: The One-Day Gap Routine
paras: When you have a full day between two papers, split it into three blocks with real breaks. The morning block covers the weakest topics of the next paper, the afternoon block is for practice questions and writing answers under time, and the evening block is for light review and preparation of materials. Between blocks, take genuine breaks: eat, rest, step outside, and avoid screens that tire your eyes. Three focused blocks beat six unfocused hours, and the breaks are part of the plan, not a failure of it.

If the gap is only a single evening and morning, shrink the plan rather than skipping rest. One evening of planning plus one morning of targeted revision is enough to enter the paper prepared, provided you studied the subject properly during the year. Mid-series revision is about recall and confidence, not about learning a subject from scratch, and students who accept that do better than students who try to cover everything the night before and arrive exhausted. Keep your notes organised by paper so that switching subjects takes minutes, not an hour of searching.

sections.h2: Staying Steady Until 21 November, and What Comes After
paras: The series ends on 21 November 2026, and the final papers deserve the same steady routine as the first ones. Do not change your method in the last week, do not add new material, and do not compare your performance with other students' accounts of their papers, since those accounts are unreliable and unhelpful. Keep the same pattern: recover in the evening, revise in a targeted way in the morning, arrive by 1:30 PM, and attempt the paper calmly. Consistency is what carries students through a long series.

After the last paper, there is one fact to hold clearly: no supplementary result date has been announced, and a result can only come after the series ends on 21 November 2026. Do not trust any date circulating without an official BIEK notice, and check the official BIEK website for genuine announcements. In the meantime, rest properly, keep your admit card and any result-related documents safe, and use the waiting period to plan your next academic step in general terms rather than worrying about a date nobody has announced. For general study help, visit [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [blog listing](/blog/).

faqs.a: The HSC Part-I and Part-II supplementary exams run from 28 October to 21 November 2026 in one afternoon shift, 2:00 PM to 5:00 PM daily, with a reporting time of 1:30 PM.

faqs.q: How should I use the evening after a paper?
faqs.a: Eat, rest for at least an hour, and avoid long answer discussions. Later, spend at most an hour picking the next paper's three revision topics and laying out your notes, then sleep at a regular time.

faqs.q: What is the best morning routine before a paper?
faqs.a: Revise three targeted topics, practise the most common question types, and write out anything you keep forgetting. Stop at least an hour before leaving, check your admit card and centre, and arrive by 1:30 PM.

faqs.q: How do I handle a single day between two papers?
faqs.a: Split it into three blocks: morning weak topics, afternoon practice questions, and evening light review, with real breaks between them. If the gap is shorter, shrink the plan rather than skipping rest.

title: BIEK Part-I Results One Week On: Next Steps If You Did Not Pass All Papers
desc: BIEK Part-I results were announced 26 October 2026. One week on, here is what to check, what to ask your college, and the supplementary route in general terms.
kw: BIEK Part-I results 26 October 2026 next steps not passed all papers
intro: A week has passed since the Board of Intermediate Education Karachi announced its HSC Part-I Annual Examination 2026 results on 26 October 2026. For students who passed all their papers, the path is clear. For students who did not pass every paper, this first week after the result is the right time to stop worrying in general and start checking specific things: what exactly the gazette and marksheet say, which papers need attention, what your college advises, and what the supplementary route looks like in general terms. This article walks through those next steps one by one.

sections.h2: One Week On: What the 26 October Announcement Covered
paras: BIEK announced the HSC Part-I Annual Examination 2026 results on 26 October 2026 for the Pre-Medical, Science General, Commerce (Regular and Private), Arts (Regular and Private), Special Candidates (Arts Regular) and Home Economics groups. Pre-Engineering results had been announced earlier, on 2 October 2026. Results are available on the official BIEK website, biek.edu.pk, and through the official BIEK Android app. A week after the announcement is a good moment to check your result calmly, because the first-day rush, slow pages and shared confusion have settled, and you can read your own record carefully.

The gazettes behind the announcement are large documents: the Pre-Medical gazette runs to 178 pages and the Commerce gazette to 172 pages, according to result.pk. That size is worth knowing, because it explains why finding your entry takes patience, and why you should search by your roll number rather than scrolling. Your marksheet, when you receive it, is the document that matters most for the next steps, so keep it safe and make a copy or a clear photograph of it for your records.

sections.h2: The 40 Percent Rule: Understanding What Ungraded Means
paras: Under the rule applied by IBCC and the Sindh Universities and Boards Department, a paper in which a student scores under 40 percent is marked Ungraded, which means the paper is not passed. This is the single most important rule for students who did not pass all papers, because it tells you exactly which papers need action and which do not. A student who passed five papers and fell below 40 percent in one paper has one paper to address, not a whole year to repeat, and that distinction changes the whole plan.

Read your marksheet paper by paper and mark each result against the 40 percent line. Note the papers you passed, the papers marked Ungraded, and any paper where the marks look inconsistent with your expectations. If a paper's marks surprise you badly, note it separately and ask your college about the proper route for queries, since colleges handle student questions about results through official channels. Do not rely on rumours about rechecking or retotalling procedures that have not been announced for your case; ask the college office what applies to you.

sections.h2: Checklist: Gazette, Marksheet and College Questions
paras: Start with the gazette entry for your roll number and compare it with your marksheet when it arrives, checking that your name, roll number and subject marks match in both places. Any mismatch should be raised with your college promptly, with a copy of both documents in hand, because corrections are easiest when they are reported early and with evidence. Keep your admit card, marksheet and any result printouts together in one folder, since you will need them for every later step, from college queries to future examination forms.

Then visit your college office with three specific questions. First, which of my papers are recorded as Ungraded, and what does that mean for my next examination appearance? Second, what is the college's process and timetable for students in my situation? Third, what study support does the college offer for the papers I need to improve? Written answers to these questions are worth more than general reassurance, so note down what you are told and the name of the person who told you. For general study guidance, the [solved notes](/solved.html) section and the [blog listing](/blog/) offer exam preparation help across subjects.
bullets: Compare your gazette entry with your marksheet, roll number and subject marks included
List each paper as passed or Ungraded under the 40 percent rule
Ask your college about process, timetable and study support for your papers
Keep admit card, marksheet and result printouts together in one folder

sections.h2: The Supplementary Route in General Terms
paras: For students who did not pass all papers, the supplementary examination route is the usual next opportunity to clear the remaining papers, and it is worth understanding in general terms while waiting for specific announcements. Supplementary examinations are held for students who need to reappear in particular papers, and the current supplementary series running from 28 October to 21 November 2026 shows the shape of such a series: an afternoon shift, a published date sheet, and admit cards issued through the official BIEK channels. Your own appearance, however, depends on the official announcement that applies to your result, and that announcement has not been made for the 26 October Part-I cohort in the sources checked for this article.

That means two things. First, do not assume a date, a form deadline or a fee from another group's schedule; wait for the notice that names your examination. Second, use the waiting time productively by revising the Ungraded papers now, while the material is still fresh, rather than waiting for a form to appear before opening a book. Students who start revision early enter the supplementary series with confidence, while students who wait for paperwork often find the preparation time has shrunk. No recheck or supplementary date is invented in this article, because none has been announced for this cohort in the sources checked.

sections.h2: Planning the Next Few Weeks Without Panic
paras: A result that is not a full pass is disappointing, but it is not the end of an academic year, and it is far more common than students realise. Many students clear their remaining papers in the next appearance and continue without losing a year, especially when they treat the weak papers as a focused project rather than a general failure. Build a simple weekly plan: two or three study blocks per week for each Ungraded paper, regular practice questions, and one weekly review of what improved. Keep the plan small enough to follow every week, because a plan followed for six weeks beats an ambitious plan abandoned after one.

Talk to your teachers about the specific topics where you lost marks, and ask for short practice tests on those topics. Teachers can usually identify quickly whether the problem was understanding, presentation, time management or exam technique, and each problem has a different fix. If the problem was time management, practise timed papers. If it was understanding, revisit the chapters with a teacher's help. If it was presentation, practise writing structured answers. One week after the result, you have time to fix the real problem, and that is the most useful thing this week can give you.

title: BIEK Part-I Commerce and Arts Pass Rates Explained
desc: BIEK Part-I Commerce Regular passed about 41 percent and Arts Regular about 35 percent of appeared students. What passed all papers means, and how the groups compare.
kw: BIEK Part-I Commerce Arts pass rates explained 2026
intro: When the BIEK Part-I results were announced on 26 October 2026, the headlines naturally focused on the largest groups, but the Commerce and Arts figures tell their own important story. Commerce Regular and Arts Regular recorded the lowest pass-all-papers rates among the main groups, and understanding why those numbers look the way they do matters for students, parents and teachers alike. This article explains the verified figures, shows how the rates are calculated, and clarifies what passed all papers actually means, so that nobody mistakes a partial result for a failure or a pass-all rate for a whole-group failure rate.

sections.h2: The Verified Figures for Commerce and Arts
paras: For Commerce Regular, the verified figures are 23,549 registered, 22,693 appeared, and 9,332 who passed all seven papers. For Arts Regular, the figures are 11,171 registered, 10,678 appeared, and 3,748 who passed all six papers. These are the official counts behind the rates discussed here, and they come from the same 26 October 2026 announcement that covered the Pre-Medical, Science General, Commerce, Arts, Special Candidates and Home Economics groups. Commerce students sit seven papers, which is why their passed-all count refers to seven papers, while Arts students sit six.

It is worth noting the gap between registered and appeared in both groups. In Commerce Regular, about 856 registered students did not appear, and in Arts Regular the gap is about 493. Those students are counted in neither the appeared base nor the passed count, which is why pass rates are calculated against appeared students rather than registered ones. A rate calculated against registered students would look lower and would mix two different things: students who did not sit the examination and students who sat it but did not pass all papers.

The pass-all-papers rate is simply the number of students who passed every paper divided by the number who appeared, multiplied by one hundred. For Commerce Regular, that is 9,332 divided by 22,693, which comes to about 41 percent. For Arts Regular, it is 3,748 divided by 10,678, which comes to about 35 percent. Both of these rates are calculated from the verified figures above, and they are labelled as calculated here because the board's announcement gave counts, and the percentages are arithmetic derived from those counts.

The same calculation for the larger science groups gives useful context. Pre-Medical recorded 11,966 passes out of 24,544 appeared, which is about 49 percent, and Science General recorded 15,036 passes out of 30,386 appeared, which is also about 49 percent. These calculated rates show that Commerce at about 41 percent and Arts at about 35 percent sit below the science groups, but the gap is not enormous, and it certainly does not mean that the remaining students in those groups failed everything. That misunderstanding is the most common one, and the next section explains why.

sections.h2: What Passed All Papers Means, and What It Does Not
paras: Passed all papers means exactly what it says: the student passed every paper in the group, all seven for Commerce Regular and all six for Arts Regular. A student who passed five out of six papers is not counted in the passed-all figure, even though that student passed most of their papers and has only one paper to clear. This is why a pass-all rate of 35 percent does not mean that 65 percent of Arts students failed everything. It means that 65 percent did not pass every single paper, and within that group there is a wide range, from students who missed one paper to students who missed several.

The 40 percent rule sits behind this. Under the rule applied by IBCC and the Sindh Universities and Boards Department, a paper scored under 40 percent is marked Ungraded, meaning that paper is not passed. So a student with five passes and one Ungraded paper is a partial pass, not a full pass, and the supplementary route exists precisely for such students to clear the remaining paper. Parents reading a pass-all rate should therefore ask a second question: how many papers did my child pass, and which ones remain? That question is far more useful than the headline rate alone.

sections.h2: Why Commerce and Arts Rates Differ from Science Groups
paras: There is no single verified explanation for the gap between the groups in the announcement itself, and this article does not invent one. What can be said honestly is that the groups differ in structure: Commerce students must pass seven papers rather than six, which gives one more paper in which to fall below the line, and Arts students come from a wide range of college backgrounds and subject combinations. Subject difficulty, preparation time and college support all vary, and any one of them can move a group's rate by several percentage points. Students should therefore treat the group rate as background context, not as a judgment on their own ability.

A more useful comparison for an individual student is with their own record. If you passed most of your papers, your position is strong and your task is narrow: clear the remaining paper or papers with focused revision. If you missed several papers, your task is broader and deserves a conversation with your teachers about which topics caused the most trouble. Either way, the group rate does not decide your next step. Your own marksheet does, paper by paper, and the [solved notes](/solved.html) section offers general study help for the subjects you need to strengthen.

sections.h2: Reading Results Responsibly: Advice for Students and Parents
paras: First, read the marksheet, not just the headline. Count your passed papers, identify the Ungraded ones, and keep the marksheet safe with your admit card and result printouts. Second, ask your college what support is available for the papers you need to improve, and whether practice tests or revision classes are offered. Third, avoid comparing your result with group percentages in a way that discourages you, because a group rate describes thousands of students and says nothing about your next paper. Fourth, start revising the remaining papers now, while the material is fresh, rather than waiting for a supplementary notice, since no date for this cohort has been announced in the sources checked.

Finally, remember that the science-group context cuts both ways. Pre-Medical at about 49 percent and Science General at about 49 percent also mean that roughly half of appeared students in those groups did not pass all papers either. Partial passes are common across every group, and the system provides a route forward for them. A calm, paper-by-paper plan, built with your teachers and followed week by week, is the most reliable response to any result, whatever the group rate says. For more result guidance, visit the [blog listing](/blog/) and the [home page](/) for related articles.

title: After the Benazirabad 9th Result: Next Steps Toward Class 10
desc: BISE Shaheed Benazirabad announced the Class 9 result on 31 October 2026. Here is how to keep your marksheet safe and start Class 10 with strong study habits.
kw: Benazirabad 9th result next steps Class 10 31 October 2026
intro: The Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education Shaheed Benazirabad announced its Class IX (Part-I) Annual Examinations 2026 results for the Science and General Groups on 31 October 2026. For the thousands of students who appeared, the result closes one chapter and opens the next: Class 10, the year that ends with the matriculation examination. This article is not another announcement of the result. It is a practical guide to what comes after it: keeping your documents safe, reading your result honestly, and building the study habits that make Class 10 a strong year from the very first week.

sections.h2: The Result in Brief: What Was Announced on 31 October
paras: The announcement was made under Chairman Dr Asif Ali Memon and Controller Shah Muhammad Farooq Rashdi, and was reported by APP via The Nation on 1 November 2026. In the Science Group, 52,260 students registered, 51,546 appeared, and 41,425 were successful, giving an overall pass percentage of 79.02 percent. In the General Group, an overall pass rate of 52 percent was reported. The General Group cohort was small, and no registered or appeared counts for it were given in the retrieved report, so this article does not invent any.

Students can check their results through the board's official website, www.bisesba.edu.pk, and the board's Android application. If you have not yet seen your own detailed result, check it through those official channels rather than relying on forwarded lists or screenshots, which can carry errors. Your own marksheet is the document that counts, and the next section explains how to protect it.

sections.h2: Keep Your Marksheet Safe: The Document That Follows You
paras: Your Class 9 marksheet is not a piece of paper to file and forget. It is part of your academic record, and you will need it for school and board processes connected with Class 10 and beyond. As soon as you receive it, check that your name, roll number, subjects and marks are all correct, and raise any error with your school promptly, with the marksheet in hand. Then make a clear photograph or photocopy and store it separately from the original, so that a lost original does not become a crisis.

Store the original in a folder with your admit card and any other board documents, in a place where it will not get damp, torn or misplaced. Students often discover the value of this habit only when a form or a verification process asks for the marksheet months later, and by then a careless loss can mean weeks of trouble. A few minutes of care now saves that trouble entirely. This is also a good moment to note your strong and weak subjects from the marksheet, because Class 10 builds directly on Class 9 foundations.

sections.h2: Read Your Result Honestly: Strengths, Gaps and the 40 Percent Rule
paras: A result deserves an honest reading, subject by subject. Note the subjects where you scored comfortably, and note the ones where your marks were close to the line or below it. Under the new grading applied in this result, scoring under 40 percent in a paper means Ungraded, which means that paper is not passed. If any of your papers fall in that category, talk to your teachers about what went wrong and what the route forward is, rather than hoping the problem disappears in Class 10, because Class 10 work in the same subject will assume the Class 9 foundation.

An honest reading also means recognising genuine strengths. If you scored well in Science subjects, for example, that tells you something real about where your effort paid off, and it is worth protecting that strength in Class 10 rather than coasting on it. The students who improve most between Class 9 and Class 10 are usually not the ones who study the most hours, but the ones who fix specific gaps: a weak chapter in Mathematics, shaky grammar in English, or diagram practice in Biology. Name your gaps now, while the result is fresh, and Class 10 starts with a plan instead of a guess.

sections.h2: Starting Class 10: Habits That Work from Week One
paras: Class 10 rewards steady habits more than bursts of effort. Set a daily study routine that covers every subject across the week, with extra time for the subjects where Class 9 exposed a gap. Revise each day's classwork on the same day, keep your notebooks organised, and practise writing answers regularly rather than only reading notes. For science subjects, draw diagrams from memory and practise numerical problems by writing full steps. For languages, practise writing short answers and essays, and read the textbook lessons carefully rather than relying on summaries alone.

Two habits deserve special emphasis. First, ask questions in class the moment you do not understand something, because Class 10 topics build on each other and a gap left in week one becomes a bigger gap by month three. Second, test yourself weekly with short self-tests on what you studied, since testing reveals what you actually know far better than re-reading does. Students who build these two habits in the first month of Class 10 usually find the rest of the year far less stressful, because they never fall far behind. For general study help, see [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [blog listing](/blog/).

sections.h2: What Not to Invent: Admissions, Dates and Next Announcements
paras: It is tempting, after a result, to look for the next date immediately: admissions, classes, forms, examinations. This article deliberately gives no admission dates for Class 10, because none were included in the verified information for this result, and inventing one would mislead students and parents. Your school is the right source for Class 10 admission and class-start information, and you should follow its notice rather than any date circulating on social media or in forwarded messages.

The same caution applies to any claim about future board announcements. If a date or a process has not been published by BISE Shaheed Benazirabad through its official website or application, treat it as unverified. Students who act on rumoured dates waste time and worry; students who wait for official notices and use the meantime to study steadily are always better placed. Your next step is simple and entirely in your control: protect your marksheet, learn from your Class 9 result, and start Class 10 with habits that will carry you through the year.

title: Hyderabad Inquiry Report Window: What Students Waiting on Results Should Expect
desc: A Hyderabad inquiry committee must report within 30 days of its 23 October 2026 order. What that window means for students waiting on Class 9 and 11 results and certificates.
kw: Hyderabad board inquiry report window students waiting results certificates
intro: Students waiting on BISE Hyderabad results and certificates are living with an unusual kind of uncertainty: an inquiry is under way, a report is due within a window, and meanwhile their own results and documents are delayed. This article explains what the inquiry report window actually means for those students, what is verified and what is not, and what to do while waiting. It is written carefully, because the inquiry concerns allegations, not proven findings, and because no student should be named or judged in connection with it.

sections.h2: What Happened: Suspension, Committee and the 30-Day Window
paras: The Sindh government suspended the BISE Hyderabad Deputy Controller of the Top Secret Branch, Ijaz Ali Kaka, and formed a three-member inquiry committee under a notification issued by Universities Secretary Abbas Baloch and approved by Provincial Minister Muhammad Ismail Rahoo. The committee is headed by Professor Dr Arbeela Bhutto. Its report is due within 30 days of the order dated 23 October 2026. This article deliberately states the window as within 30 days of that order, rather than naming a confirmed calendar date, because the verified information gives the window, not a single date, and students should not treat a calculated date as an official deadline.

The scope of the inquiry is alleged irregularities in the Class XII (Intermediate Part-II) annual examination 2026 results, in the pre-medical and pre-engineering groups, covering position holders, top-10 and A-1 and A grade students, and the processes of checking, tabulation and announcement. These are allegations only. They are not proven findings, and the results have not been cancelled. Any report or message that presents the allegations as proven facts, or that names individual students, should be ignored, and students should not repeat such claims.

sections.h2: What the Window Means for Students Waiting on Class 9 and 11 Results
paras: The most direct effect on waiting students is delay. Sources have warned that the compilation of Class IX and XI results could be delayed further, and no Class IX or XI result date for Hyderabad is confirmed. That means students waiting for those results should not trust any date circulating without an official board announcement, and should not plan admissions, admissions-related steps or further study choices around a rumoured date. The waiting period is frustrating, but acting on an invented date causes more harm than waiting for the real one.

The reason for the delay is connected to the wider disruption at the board. According to a Tribune report of 27 October 2026, the chairman, controller and secretary posts at BISE Hyderabad lack permanent appointments and are held on additional charge or deputation, with BIEK Chairman Faqir Muhammad Lakho holding additional charge as Hyderabad chairman and Mehran University Assistant Professor Shakeel Laghari serving as controller on deputation. A board operating under additional charge and an ongoing inquiry moves more slowly than usual, and students should understand that the delay reflects administrative disruption, not any judgment about their own papers.

A separate but related problem affects students waiting for certificates: certificate issuance has been delayed by missing signatures. A certificate that is otherwise ready cannot be issued until the required signatures are in place, and when senior posts are held on additional charge, that step can stall. Students who need certificates for admission or employment should therefore plan for extra waiting time, keep their existing documents, such as marksheets and admit cards, safe and ready, and ask their school or college office what interim proof, if any, the board or institution accepts while a certificate is pending.

If you are in this position, keep a written record of your requests: the date you applied or enquired, the office you visited, and what you were told. That record is useful if you need to follow up, and it protects you against confusion when different offices give different answers. Do not pay any unofficial fee or use any unofficial channel that promises faster certificates, because no such channel is part of the official process, and unofficial payments create risk without any guarantee.

sections.h2: What Students Should Do During the Window
paras: First, rely only on official board announcements for dates, and check the board's official channels rather than social media forwards. Second, keep studying or revising in general terms for your next class or next examination, because waiting time spent on study is never wasted, whatever the inquiry's outcome. Third, if you are a Class 9 or 11 student waiting for a result, keep your school informed that you are waiting, so that the school can advise you as soon as genuine news arrives, and so that any school-level planning for the next class includes you.

Fourth, protect your privacy and that of others. Do not share or repeat lists of names connected with the inquiry, and do not treat any named student as guilty of anything, since the inquiry has made no findings and no student has been named in any verified source used here. Fifth, if the wait is causing real anxiety, talk to a teacher, a parent or a school counsellor rather than carrying it alone. Uncertainty is stressful, and asking for support is a sensible response, not a weakness. For general study help while you wait, visit [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [blog listing](/blog/).

sections.h2: What the Report Window Does Not Mean
paras: The report window does not mean that results will automatically appear when the window closes, and it does not mean that existing results will be cancelled. The committee's report is an input to a decision, and the government and board must then act on it, which can take further time. Students should therefore expect the window to end with a report, not necessarily with instant results, and should avoid disappointment by keeping that distinction clear. Equally, the window does not mean that every result is under suspicion. The inquiry's scope is specific to the alleged irregularities in the Class XII pre-medical and pre-engineering results, and it does not cast doubt on every student's paper.

What students can reasonably expect is information: the submission of a report within the stated window, and then official communication about what follows. Until that communication arrives, the safest course is patience plus preparation. Keep your documents ready, keep your studies going, and check official channels regularly. A calm, documented wait is the strongest position a student can hold while an inquiry runs its course.

title: Sindh Boards Roundup: 3 November 2026
desc: A roundup of Sindh board news on 3 November 2026: Punjab exams begin today, BIEK supplementary running, Benazirabad results, Hyderabad inquiry and STBB review.
kw: Sindh boards roundup 3 November 2026 BIEK Punjab Benazirabad Hyderabad STBB
intro: Tuesday 3 November 2026 is a busy day across Sindh and Punjab board news, with examinations beginning, examinations continuing, results settling in, an inquiry window running, and a curriculum review under way. sections.h2: Punjab Second Annual Exams Begin Today
paras: The biggest story of the day is the start of the Punjab HSSC second annual examinations. Part-II (12th class) theory papers begin today, Tuesday 3 November 2026, and run to 16 November 2026 across all nine Punjab boards: Lahore, Rawalpindi, Gujranwala, Faisalabad, Multan, Sargodha, Sahiwal, Bahawalpur and DG Khan. Students appearing today should carry their roll number slip, arrive early, and confirm their centre and session from their own slip rather than a friend's. On results, no individual board has announced a supplementary result date in the sources checked. More than 21,000 students are appearing across 49 centres. Admit cards are available at admitcard.biek.edu.pk using a 16-digit challan number and matric roll number. Students who did not pass all papers should read their marksheet paper by paper against the 40 percent Ungraded rule, ask their college about process and support, and begin revising weak papers now rather than waiting for a supplementary notice that has not yet been announced for their cohort.

sections.h2: Benazirabad Class 9 Result and the Hyderabad Inquiry Window
paras: BISE Shaheed Benazirabad announced its Class IX Annual Examinations 2026 results on 31 October 2026. In the Science Group, 52,260 students registered, 51,546 appeared and 41,425 were successful, an overall pass rate of 79.02 percent, while the General Group recorded an overall pass rate of 52 percent. Students can check results through the board's official website, www.bisesba.edu.pk, and its Android application. sections.h2: STBB Curriculum Review: Creativity, Critical Thinking and Tolerance
paras: The curriculum story of the day comes from the Sindh Textbook Board, where a curriculum review committee has held its first meeting on the directives of Sindh Minister for Education Syed Sardar Ali Shah, chaired by STBB Chairman Parvez Ahmed Baloch. After reviewing the 12th-grade Sindhi textbook, experts shared observations and suggested revisions in line with contemporary educational needs. The committee emphasised including critical thinking, creativity and tolerance in school curricula, and recommended a comprehensive review of all STBB publications.
