title: STBB Curriculum Review: Creativity, Critical Thinking and Tolerance in School Books
desc: A recent STBB curriculum review committee meeting pushed creativity, critical thinking and tolerance into school books. What it means for students, teachers and textbooks.
kw: STBB curriculum review creativity critical thinking tolerance school books
intro: School textbooks shape how millions of students think, and a recent meeting of the Sindh Textbook Board's curriculum review committee has put three qualities at the centre of that shaping: creativity, critical thinking and tolerance. The committee, chaired by STBB Chairman Parvez Ahmed Baloch and held on the directives of Sindh Minister for Education Syed Sardar Ali Shah, reviewed the 12th-grade Sindhi textbook, heard experts' observations, and recommended a comprehensive review of all STBB publications. This article explains what the review means, why those three qualities matter, and what students and teachers can expect as the revised curriculum arrives from the next academic year.

sections.h2: The Meeting: Who Met, What Was Reviewed, What Was Recommended
paras: The first meeting of the STBB curriculum review committee was held to evaluate educational textbooks, on the directives of Sindh Minister for Education Syed Sardar Ali Shah, and was chaired by STBB Chairman Parvez Ahmed Baloch. The committee reviewed the 12th-grade Sindhi textbook, and experts shared their observations and suggested revisions in line with contemporary educational needs. That choice of starting point matters: a 12th-grade language textbook is read by students at the threshold of adult life, and the values and thinking habits it models travel with them beyond school.

Two recommendations came out of the meeting. First, the committee emphasised the inclusion of critical thinking, creativity and tolerance in school curricula. Second, it recommended a comprehensive review of all STBB publications, not just the single textbook examined at this meeting. Together, those two points signal a programme rather than a one-off edit: every STBB book is to be examined against the same standards. This article describes the meeting as recent, because its report gives no exact date, and no date is invented for it here.

sections.h2: The Scale Behind the Review: 195 Titles and 52 Million Sets
paras: To understand why a curriculum review matters so much, consider the scale of STBB publishing. The STBB 2026-27 textbooks, published under the Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Textbook Series from Early Childhood to Grade 10, comprise 195 titles in Sindhi, Urdu and English, with 52 million sets, and distribution was inaugurated on 19 February 2026. A change to the approach of these books therefore reaches an enormous number of classrooms, and a review that touches all publications is one of the largest educational undertakings in the province.

Scale also explains why the revised curriculum is expected from the next academic year rather than immediately. Textbooks must be reviewed, revised, approved, printed and distributed, and that cycle cannot be rushed without risking errors. Students currently studying from existing books should therefore continue with their current textbooks and syllabi, since those remain the basis for current examinations. The review is a direction of travel for the books of the coming years, not a change to the paper a student will sit next week.

Creativity in a curriculum does not mean only drawing or art classes. It means textbooks that invite students to imagine alternatives, to write their own endings to a story, to design their own solutions to a problem, and to ask what else could be true. A science chapter that asks students to design a simple experiment practises creativity. A language lesson that asks for an original paragraph practises creativity. A social studies question that asks how a community problem could be solved in three different ways practises creativity.

For students, the practical way to build creativity now is to go beyond memorising the textbook answer. After finishing a lesson, try one extra task of your own: write a different ending, propose a different solution, or explain the idea to a classmate in your own words. Teachers can support this by rewarding original, well-reasoned answers even when they differ from the model answer, and by setting at least one open-ended question in class tests. Creativity grows when it is practised and praised, not when it is only mentioned in a policy document.

sections.h2: Critical Thinking and Tolerance: Thinking Clearly, Living Together
paras: Critical thinking means examining a claim before accepting it: asking what evidence supports it, what evidence counts against it, and whether a different explanation fits better. In school, it is practised whenever a student compares two accounts of an event, checks a statement against a source, or explains why an argument is weak. Textbooks that include questions asking students to evaluate, compare and judge, rather than only recall, are building this skill. Students can practise it today by asking, for every important claim in a lesson, what reason the book gives and whether that reason is strong.

Tolerance, in a curriculum, means learning to live respectfully with people who differ in religion, language, culture or opinion. The committee's emphasis on tolerance sits alongside a related verified development: Sindh Hindu religious textbooks have been approved for Hindu students in government schools, in Grades III to V, for the academic year 2026-27, following a Sindh Curriculum Council Executive Committee meeting on 20 April 2026 and a letter to the STBB chairman on 29 April 2026. Textbooks that present diversity fairly, and classrooms where different views are discussed respectfully, teach tolerance far more effectively than a single lesson about it. For study help across subjects, visit [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [blog listing](/blog/).

sections.h2: What Students and Teachers Should Do Now
paras: Students should not wait for new books to start thinking creatively, critically and tolerantly. The habits can begin with current textbooks: question claims, propose alternatives, discuss respectfully, and write original answers. When revised books arrive from the next academic year, students who already practise these habits will find the new material natural rather than strange. Parents can help by encouraging discussion at home, by asking children what they think about a lesson rather than only what they memorised, and by modelling respectful disagreement.

Teachers are the bridge between a review committee's recommendations and a classroom's reality. A teacher who sets one open question per lesson, who asks students to justify their answers, and who ensures every student is heard respectfully is already delivering the curriculum the committee described, whatever edition of the textbook is on the desk. The comprehensive review of all STBB publications will take time, and its success will ultimately be measured not by committee minutes but by whether classrooms feel more curious, more thoughtful and more respectful. That is a goal worth working toward starting today.

title: Maths Word Problems: Money and Shopping
desc: Learn to solve money word problems with easy steps: change, discount and total bill problems explained with worked examples for school maths.
intro: Money word problems feel easy because we all go shopping, yet many students lose marks on them in exams. The reason is rarely the calculation itself; it is reading the problem too fast and mixing up what is given and what is asked. A money problem usually hides a simple addition, subtraction, multiplication or division inside a small story about buying, paying, saving or getting change. If you slow down, underline the numbers, name what each number means, and decide the operation before touching your pencil, the story turns into a short calculation. This guide teaches you a steady method for change problems, discount problems and total bill problems, with worked examples you can copy into your practice notebook. You can also check our [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [books page](/books.html) for more practice material.

sections.h2: Read the Problem Like a Shopkeeper
paras: Before you calculate anything, read the whole problem twice and ask yourself three questions: what did the person buy, how much money did they have or pay, and what exactly is the question asking for. Many students start adding numbers the moment they see them, but a money problem often gives you one extra number you do not need, such as the number of shops visited or the colour of a bag. Circle only the numbers that belong to the question, and write a short note beside each one, for example price of one notebook, number of notebooks, or money given to the shopkeeper. This small habit prevents the most common error in money problems, which is using the right numbers in the wrong operation.

Next, decide the operation by thinking about the story, not by guessing. If things are being bought together, you add. If money is being returned, you subtract. If the same item is bought several times, you multiply. If a total amount is shared or split, you divide. Write the operation in words first, such as total cost equals price times quantity, and only then put in the numbers. Students who write the plan first almost never mix up addition and multiplication, because the plan forces them to think about what is happening in the story. Practice this on five problems a day, and the method will soon feel automatic in exams.

sections.h2: Change Problems: What You Get Back
paras: A change problem always follows the same two steps: first find the total cost of everything bought, then subtract that total from the money paid. Suppose Sara buys a pencil for 25 rupees and an eraser for 15 rupees, and she pays with a 100-rupee note. The total cost is 25 plus 15, which is 40 rupees. The change is 100 minus 40, which is 60 rupees. The most common mistake here is subtracting only one item from the money paid and forgetting the other, so always add all the items first and subtract once at the end. Writing the two steps on separate lines makes your working clear and earns full marks even if a small slip happens later.

Change problems get trickier when quantities appear, because you must multiply before you subtract. For example, if Ahmed buys 3 pens at 30 rupees each and pays with a 200-rupee note, the total cost is 3 times 30, which is 90 rupees, and the change is 200 minus 90, which is 110 rupees. Notice the order: multiplication first, then subtraction. A useful check is to add the change back to the total cost; the result must equal the money paid. In this case 110 plus 90 equals 200, so the answer is correct. This reverse check takes five seconds and catches most careless errors before you move on.

diagram.caption: Follow these four steps in order for every change problem.

sections.h2: Discount Problems: Less Than the Price Tag
paras: A discount means the shop reduces the price, so the customer pays less than the marked price. To solve a discount problem, first find the discount amount and then subtract it from the marked price. For example, a shirt marked at 800 rupees is sold at a discount of 100 rupees. The selling price is 800 minus 100, which is 700 rupees. Some problems give the discount as a percentage instead, such as 10 percent off. Ten percent of 800 is 80 rupees, so the selling price is 800 minus 80, which is 720 rupees. Always check whether the problem gives the discount in rupees or in percent, because the method changes completely.

A classic exam trap is asking for the discount amount when only the two prices are given. If a bag marked at 500 rupees is sold for 450 rupees, the discount is 500 minus 450, which is 50 rupees. Another trap is giving the selling price and the discount and asking for the marked price; here you must add, not subtract, because the marked price is higher than the selling price. For instance, if a toy is sold for 360 rupees after a discount of 40 rupees, its marked price was 360 plus 40, which is 400 rupees. Drawing a tiny number line with marked price, discount and selling price helps you see which operation to use.

sections.h2: Total Bill Problems: Adding Items and Quantities
paras: A total bill problem asks you to combine several purchases into one final amount, and it tests whether you can handle both addition and multiplication in the same question. The safe method is to make a small table with three columns: item, price of one, and quantity. Multiply across each row to get the cost of that item, then add the rows down to get the bill. For example, 2 notebooks at 60 rupees each cost 120 rupees, and 4 pencils at 10 rupees each cost 40 rupees, so the total bill is 120 plus 40, which is 160 rupees. A table keeps your working tidy and lets your teacher follow every step.

Watch out for problems that mix units, such as buying items in dozens or paying partly in cash and partly from savings. If eggs cost 20 rupees each and a dozen are bought, the quantity is 12, not 1, so the cost is 12 times 20, which is 240 rupees. If a bill of 850 rupees is paid with 500 rupees in cash and the rest from a wallet, the wallet amount is 850 minus 500, which is 350 rupees. Read every quantity word carefully, especially dozen, pair, packet and kilogram, because these words change the number you multiply by. After finishing, reread the question once to confirm you answered exactly what was asked.

The first common mistake is rushing the reading and using a number that the question never asked about, such as the age of the buyer or the number of shops. The second is forgetting to multiply when several identical items are bought, so a student adds the price once instead of three times. The third is subtracting in the wrong order in change problems, for example subtracting the money paid from the total cost, which gives a negative or impossible answer. The fourth is confusing discount with selling price, writing the discount amount as the final answer when the question asked what the customer actually paid. Each of these mistakes is avoidable with the slow, step-by-step method taught above.

Another frequent error is losing track of rupees and paisas, or mixing up the decimal point when prices include paisas, such as 45.50 rupees. Always line up decimal points in addition and subtraction, and treat 45.50 as 45 rupees and 50 paisas. Finally, never leave a money answer without its unit: write 60 rupees, not just 60. In exams, missing units and missing working both cost marks even when the final number is right. Build a habit of showing every step, labelling every amount, and doing the reverse check on change problems, and money word problems will become one of your most reliable sources of marks. For more study help, visit our [blog](/blog/) and [about page](/about.html).

Change equals money paid minus total cost; always add all items before subtracting.
Multiply price by quantity before adding items into a total bill.
A discount in rupees is subtracted directly; a percent discount must be calculated first.

faqs.q: What is the first step in solving a money word problem?
faqs.a: The first step is reading the whole problem twice and identifying what is bought, what each item costs, how much money is paid, and what the question actually asks. Many students fail because they start calculating before understanding the story. Write down each number with a short label, such as price of one pen or money given, and cross out any extra number the question does not need. This careful start makes the rest of the problem much easier.

faqs.q: How do I calculate change in a shopping problem?
faqs.a: First find the total cost of everything bought, multiplying price by quantity where needed, and then subtract that total from the money paid. For example, if items cost 140 rupees in total and you pay with a 500-rupee note, the change is 500 minus 140, which is 360 rupees. Always check your answer by adding the change back to the total cost; the result must equal the money paid.

faqs.q: What is the difference between discount and selling price?
faqs.a: The discount is the amount reduced from the marked price, while the selling price is what the customer actually pays after that reduction. If a shirt is marked at 800 rupees with a discount of 100 rupees, the selling price is 700 rupees. Students often write the discount amount as the final answer by mistake, so always reread the question to see whether it asks for the discount, the selling price, or the marked price.

faqs.q: How do I solve a total bill problem with several items?
faqs.a: Make a small table with item, price of one, and quantity, multiply across each row to find each item's cost, and then add all the rows to get the total bill. This method keeps your working organised and prevents the common error of adding a price once when several identical items were bought. After finding the total, reread the question to confirm you answered exactly what was asked, such as the bill or the change.

faqs.q: Why do I keep making mistakes in money problems?
faqs.a: Most mistakes come from rushing the reading, forgetting to multiply for quantities, subtracting in the wrong order, or confusing discount with selling price. Slow down, write a plan in words before calculating, show every step on separate lines, and use the reverse check for change problems. Practising five problems a day with this method will quickly turn money problems into easy marks in your exams.

title: Maths Word Problems: Time and Distance
desc: Master time and distance word problems: speed, journey time, and late-or-early problems explained with simple worked examples for school maths.
intro: Time and distance problems appear in almost every maths exam because they test whether you can connect three simple ideas: how far something travels, how fast it moves, and how long the journey takes. Students often know the formulas but still lose marks because they mix up units, forget to convert minutes into hours, or answer a different question from the one asked. The good news is that every time and distance problem uses the same three-way relationship, so once you learn to organise the given information, the problems become routine. This guide explains speed, journey time and late-or-early problems with worked examples, and shows you the checks that catch careless errors. You can find more practice in our [solved notes](/solved.html) and on the [books page](/books.html).

sections.h2: The Three Friends: Speed, Distance and Time
paras: Speed, distance and time are linked by one simple rule: distance equals speed multiplied by time. From this one rule you can find any of the three if you know the other two. Speed equals distance divided by time, and time equals distance divided by speed. A useful way to remember this is the triangle method: cover the quantity you want to find, and the remaining two show the operation. Cover distance and you see speed times time; cover speed and you see distance over time; cover time and you see distance over speed. Write this triangle at the top of your rough work before starting any problem.

The most important rule in these problems is that units must match. If speed is given in kilometres per hour, then time must be in hours and distance in kilometres. If time is given in minutes, convert it to hours by dividing by 60 before using it with a speed in kilometres per hour. For example, 30 minutes is 0.5 hours, and 45 minutes is 0.75 hours. Many students skip this conversion and get answers that are 60 times too big or too small. Always write the units beside every number, and convert first, calculate second.

A journey time problem usually gives you the distance and the speed and asks how long the trip takes. Divide the distance by the speed, and remember to convert the answer into hours and minutes if it comes out as a decimal. For example, a bus travels 120 kilometres at a speed of 40 kilometres per hour. The time is 120 divided by 40, which is 3 hours. If a car travels 150 kilometres at 50 kilometres per hour, the time is 150 divided by 50, which is also 3 hours. When the answer is a decimal like 2.5 hours, convert it properly: 2.5 hours means 2 hours and 30 minutes, not 2 hours and 50 minutes.

Some journey problems give the starting time and ask for the arrival time, which means you must add the journey time to the start time. If a train leaves at 8:15 in the morning and the journey takes 2 hours and 45 minutes, it arrives at 11:00. Add the hours first, then the minutes, and carry over 60 minutes as one hour whenever the minutes reach 60 or more. Practise adding times on a clock face in your head, because clock arithmetic is where most students slip. If the journey crosses noon, be careful with morning and afternoon labels, and write am or pm beside your final answer.

diagram.caption: Use these steps for any journey time question.

sections.h2: Late or Early: Comparing Two Journeys
paras: Late-or-early problems compare two journeys over the same distance at different speeds, and ask who arrives first or how many minutes late someone is. The method is to calculate each journey time separately and then subtract the smaller from the larger. For example, Ali walks 4 kilometres to school at 4 kilometres per hour, taking 1 hour, while his friend cycles the same distance at 8 kilometres per hour, taking half an hour. The cyclist arrives 30 minutes earlier. Always calculate both times fully before comparing; guessing from the speeds alone often leads to errors when distances differ.

A trickier version gives a fixed arrival time and asks what speed is needed to arrive on time. Suppose school is 6 kilometres away and a student must arrive in 30 minutes, which is 0.5 hours. The required speed is 6 divided by 0.5, which is 12 kilometres per hour. If the student walks at only 6 kilometres per hour, the journey takes 1 hour, so the student would be 30 minutes late. These problems reward students who write both journeys in a small table with columns for person, speed and time, because the table makes the comparison visible and prevents mixing up the two journeys.

sections.h2: Unit Changes: Minutes, Hours and Kilometres
paras: Unit conversion is the hidden skill inside time and distance problems, and it causes more lost marks than the formulas themselves. Remember the key conversions: 1 hour equals 60 minutes, 1 minute equals 60 seconds, and 1 kilometre equals 1000 metres. To change minutes into hours, divide by 60; to change hours into minutes, multiply by 60. For example, 90 minutes is 1.5 hours, and 2.25 hours is 2 hours and 15 minutes. When a speed is given in metres per second but the distance is in kilometres, convert one of them first so both match.

A common exam question asks for speed in kilometres per hour when distance is in metres and time in seconds, which needs two conversions at once. The safest route is to convert distance to kilometres and time to hours first, then divide. Alternatively, remember that multiplying a speed in metres per second by 3.6 gives kilometres per hour, and dividing kilometres per hour by 3.6 gives metres per second. Learn this 3.6 rule only after you understand the two-step conversion, because examiners often ask you to show the conversion working. Always write the unit beside your final answer, such as 40 kilometres per hour.

sections.h2: Common Mistakes in Time and Distance Problems
paras: The biggest mistake is using minutes directly with a speed in kilometres per hour without converting to hours, which gives an answer 60 times too large. The second is writing 2.5 hours as 2 hours and 50 minutes instead of 2 hours and 30 minutes, because the decimal part is a fraction of an hour, not minutes. The third is forgetting to add the journey time to the starting time when the question asks for arrival time, and instead giving only the journey time as the answer. The fourth is mixing up which quantity to divide by which, such as dividing speed by distance instead of distance by speed.

To avoid these errors, always start by listing what is given with units, then write the formula you will use, then convert units, and only then calculate. After finishing, do a sense check: a person walking cannot travel at 60 kilometres per hour, and a bus travelling 120 kilometres at 40 kilometres per hour cannot take 30 hours. If your answer looks impossible, recheck your conversions first, because that is where the error usually hides. With steady practice, time and distance problems become quick, reliable marks. Explore more guides on our [blog](/blog/) and [about page](/about.html).

points: Distance equals speed times time; cover one value in the triangle to find the formula.
Units must match: convert minutes to hours before using kilometres per hour.
A decimal like 2.5 hours means 2 hours and 30 minutes, not 2 hours and 50 minutes.
For late-or-early problems, calculate both journey times fully, then subtract.
Always sense-check your answer: impossible speeds or times signal a conversion error.

faqs.q: What is the formula for speed, distance and time?
faqs.a: Distance equals speed multiplied by time, and from this one rule you can find any value if you know the other two. Speed equals distance divided by time, and time equals distance divided by speed. A handy memory aid is the triangle: cover the value you want, and the remaining two show the operation. Always make sure the units match before calculating, converting minutes to hours when speed is in kilometres per hour.

faqs.q: How do I convert minutes into hours in a problem?
faqs.a: Divide the number of minutes by 60 to get hours. For example, 30 minutes is 0.5 hours, 45 minutes is 0.75 hours, and 90 minutes is 1.5 hours. This step is essential whenever speed is given in kilometres per hour, because using minutes directly gives an answer 60 times too large. To change hours back into minutes, multiply by 60 instead.

faqs.q: How do I find arrival time from a start time and journey time?
faqs.a: Add the journey time to the starting time, adding hours first and then minutes, and carrying over 60 minutes as one extra hour whenever the minutes reach 60 or more. For example, leaving at 8:15 in the morning for a journey of 2 hours and 45 minutes gives an arrival time of 11:00. Be careful with morning and afternoon labels when a journey crosses noon, and write am or pm beside your final answer.

faqs.q: What is a late-or-early problem in maths?
faqs.a: A late-or-early problem compares two journeys over the same or different distances and asks who arrives first or by how many minutes someone is late. Calculate each journey time separately using time equals distance divided by speed, then subtract the smaller time from the larger to find the difference. Writing both journeys in a small table with columns for person, speed and time helps you avoid mixing up the two journeys.

faqs.q: Why are my time and distance answers often wrong?
faqs.a: Most errors come from unit mistakes, such as using minutes with kilometres per hour, or misreading a decimal like 2.5 hours as 2 hours and 50 minutes. Other common errors are dividing the wrong way round and forgetting to add journey time to the start time when arrival time is asked. Listing given values with units, writing the formula first, converting units, and sense-checking the final answer will fix nearly all of these mistakes.

title: Maths Word Problems: Ratio in Recipes and Classes
desc: Learn ratio word problems with easy methods: sharing and mixing problems, ratios in recipes and classes, with worked examples for school maths.
intro: Ratio problems sound difficult, but they describe something you already do every day: sharing food fairly, mixing ingredients in a recipe, or comparing the number of boys and girls in a class. A ratio simply compares two or more quantities of the same kind, and the most important skill is splitting a total into parts according to that ratio. Once you learn the total-parts method, sharing problems, recipe problems and class problems all follow the same pattern. This guide explains ratios from the basics, works through sharing and mixing examples, and shows you the mistakes that cost marks. You can practise further with our [solved notes](/solved.html) and the [books page](/books.html).

paras: A ratio like 2:3 means that for every 2 parts of one thing, there are 3 parts of another thing, making 5 parts in total. The numbers in a ratio are not the actual amounts; they are the shares. If 2:3 describes the boys and girls in a group of 25 students, the total number of parts is 5, so each part is worth 25 divided by 5, which is 5 students. That gives 2 times 5, which is 10 boys, and 3 times 5, which is 15 girls. Notice that 10 plus 15 equals 25, which confirms the answer. This total-parts method is the key to nearly every ratio problem you will meet.

Ratios must compare quantities of the same kind and in the same units, and they should be written in simplest form. The ratio 10:15 simplifies to 2:3 by dividing both numbers by 5, just like simplifying a fraction. A common exam question gives you a ratio and one actual amount and asks for the other amount. For example, if the ratio of red to blue pens is 3:4 and there are 12 red pens, then one part is worth 12 divided by 3, which is 4 pens, so the blue pens number 4 times 4, which is 16. Always find the value of one part first; everything else follows from it.

sections.h2: Sharing Problems: Dividing a Total Fairly
paras: Sharing problems give you a total amount and a ratio, and ask how much each person or group receives. The method never changes: add the ratio numbers to find the total parts, divide the total amount by the total parts to find one part, then multiply by each share. For example, a prize of 500 rupees is shared between two friends in the ratio 3:2. The total parts are 5, so one part is worth 500 divided by 5, which is 100 rupees. The first friend receives 3 times 100, which is 300 rupees, and the second receives 2 times 100, which is 200 rupees. Add the shares back together to check: 300 plus 200 equals 500.

Sharing problems sometimes ask for the difference between two shares instead of the shares themselves. If 720 rupees is shared in the ratio 5:3, the total parts are 8, so one part is worth 90 rupees. The shares are 450 and 270 rupees, and the difference is 450 minus 270, which is 180 rupees. A shortcut is to subtract the ratio numbers first, 5 minus 3 equals 2 parts, and multiply by one part, 2 times 90 equals 180 rupees. Both routes give the same answer, but the shortcut only works once you have found the value of one part. In exams, show the full working so partial marks are available even if the last step slips.

diagram.caption: The total-parts method works for every sharing problem.

paras: Recipe problems use ratios to scale ingredients up or down, and they test whether you can keep the proportions correct. Suppose a recipe for 4 people uses flour and sugar in the ratio 3:1, with 300 grams of flour and 100 grams of sugar. For 8 people, you double everything, so you need 600 grams of flour and 200 grams of sugar, and the ratio stays 3:1. The trick is that scaling a recipe never changes the ratio; it only changes the actual amounts. If a problem asks how much sugar is needed when 450 grams of flour are used, note that one part is 150 grams, because 3 parts equal 450, so the sugar is 1 part, which is 150 grams.

Paint and mixture problems work exactly the same way. If blue and white paint are mixed in the ratio 2:5 to make 35 litres of paint, the total parts are 7, so one part is 5 litres. The mixture contains 2 times 5, which is 10 litres of blue paint, and 5 times 5, which is 25 litres of white paint. A common trap is giving the amount of only one ingredient and asking for the total mixture. If a mixture contains 10 litres of blue paint in the ratio 2:5, one part is 5 litres, so the total mixture is 7 times 5, which is 35 litres. Always identify whether the given amount is one share, one part, or the total.

sections.h2: Ratios in a Class: Boys, Girls and Groups
paras: Class problems often give the ratio of boys to girls and the total number of students, or the ratio and the difference between the numbers. For a class of 40 students with a boy-to-girl ratio of 3:5, the total parts are 8, so one part is worth 5 students. That gives 15 boys and 25 girls, and 15 plus 25 equals 40, which checks out. If instead the problem says there are 10 more girls than boys with a ratio of 3:5, the difference in parts is 2, so one part is worth 10 divided by 2, which is 5 students, giving the same 15 boys and 25 girls. The difference method is just the total-parts method applied to a difference.

Some class problems combine ratios with fractions or percentages, so keep the ideas separate in your working. If the ratio of boys to girls is 3:5, the fraction of the class that is boys is 3 out of 8, and the percentage is 37.5 percent. You do not need percentages to solve a ratio problem, but converting between ratio, fraction and percentage is a favourite exam question. Practise by taking one ratio, such as 2:3, and writing it as a fraction of each part, as a simplified ratio, and as percentages. This flexibility turns ratio questions from a feared topic into an easy source of marks.

The most common mistake is treating the ratio numbers as the actual amounts, for example writing that a 2:3 ratio means 2 boys and 3 girls when the class actually has 25 students. The second mistake is forgetting to add the ratio numbers to find total parts, and instead dividing the total by only one of the numbers. The third is mixing up the order of the ratio, giving the larger share to the wrong person, which matters when the problem names who gets which share. The fourth is failing to simplify a ratio when the question asks for the simplest form, leaving an answer like 10:15 instead of 2:3.

Another error is adding ratios together as if they were fractions, or adding a ratio to a total that includes something else, such as counting the teacher in a class ratio meant only for students. Always check that the total you divide matches what the ratio describes. Finally, label your shares clearly: write boys equals 15 and girls equals 25, not just two bare numbers. Clear labels make your answer easy to mark and easy to check. With the total-parts method practised daily, ratio problems become some of the quickest marks in the paper. Find more guides on our [blog](/blog/) and [about page](/about.html).

points: A ratio compares shares, not actual amounts; always find the value of one part first.
Sharing method: add ratio numbers for total parts, divide the total, then multiply by each share.
Scaling a recipe changes amounts but never changes the ratio itself.
For difference problems, divide the difference by the difference in parts to find one part.
Check every ratio answer by adding the shares back to the original total.

faqs.q: What is a ratio in simple words?
faqs.a: A ratio compares two or more quantities of the same kind by showing how many parts of each there are. For example, a ratio of 2:3 means that for every 2 parts of one thing there are 3 parts of another, making 5 parts in total. The numbers in a ratio are shares, not actual amounts, so to find real amounts you must first work out what one part is worth by dividing the total by the total number of parts.

faqs.q: How do I share an amount in a given ratio?
faqs.a: Add the ratio numbers to get the total parts, divide the total amount by the total parts to find the value of one part, and then multiply one part by each share in the ratio. For example, sharing 500 rupees in the ratio 3:2 gives total parts of 5, one part of 100 rupees, and shares of 300 and 200 rupees. Always check by adding the shares together; they must equal the original total.

faqs.q: How do ratio problems work in recipes?
faqs.a: A recipe ratio shows the proportions of ingredients, and scaling the recipe up or down multiplies every ingredient by the same factor without changing the ratio. If a recipe uses flour and sugar in the ratio 3:1 with 300 grams of flour, then using 450 grams of flour means one part is 150 grams, so the sugar needed is 150 grams. The key skill is finding the value of one part from whichever ingredient amount you are given.

faqs.q: What if a ratio problem gives the difference, not the total?
faqs.a: When a problem gives the difference between two shares, subtract the ratio numbers to find the difference in parts, then divide the given difference by that number to find one part. For example, if girls exceed boys by 10 in a ratio of 3:5, the difference in parts is 2, so one part is 5, giving 15 boys and 25 girls. Once you know one part, every other value follows by multiplication.

faqs.q: Why do students get ratio questions wrong?
faqs.a: The most common errors are treating ratio numbers as actual amounts, forgetting to add the ratio numbers for total parts, mixing up the order of the ratio, and failing to simplify the final ratio. Students also sometimes divide a total that does not match what the ratio describes, such as including the teacher in a student-only ratio. Labelling each share clearly and checking that shares add back to the total prevents nearly all of these mistakes.

title: Maths Word Problems: Percentage in Marks and Shops
desc: Solve percentage word problems easily: increase, decrease and pass-mark problems with worked examples for marks, prices and school maths exams.
intro: Percent means out of one hundred, and percentage problems appear everywhere in school maths: in exam marks, in shop discounts, in price increases, and in pass marks. Students often know that percent means per hundred but still struggle, because percentage problems ask for different things: sometimes the percentage itself, sometimes the amount it represents, and sometimes the original value before a change. The trick is to identify which of these three the question wants, and then use the right method. This guide works through marks, pass marks, increases and decreases with simple numbers you can follow step by step. More practice is available in our [solved notes](/solved.html) and on the [books page](/books.html).

sections.h2: Percent Means Out of One Hundred
paras: A percentage is a fraction with a denominator of 100, so 25 percent means 25 out of every 100, which is the same as the fraction one quarter. To find a percentage of an amount, multiply the amount by the percentage and divide by 100. For example, 20 percent of 300 is 20 times 300 divided by 100, which is 60. To find what percentage one number is of another, divide the first number by the second and multiply by 100. For example, 15 out of 60 as a percentage is 15 divided by 60 times 100, which is 25 percent. Learning both directions of this skill covers most percentage questions.

It also helps to memorise the common percentage-fraction pairs: 50 percent is one half, 25 percent is one quarter, 75 percent is three quarters, 20 percent is one fifth, and 10 percent is one tenth. These pairs let you solve many problems mentally. Ten percent of any number is found by dividing by 10, so 10 percent of 450 is 45, and 20 percent is double that, which is 90. When a problem uses a friendly percentage like 10, 20 or 25, use the fraction shortcut; when it uses an awkward percentage like 37 percent, use the multiply-and-divide-by-100 method and show your working carefully.

Marks problems usually ask for a percentage score: divide the marks obtained by the total marks and multiply by 100. If a student scores 72 out of 90, the percentage is 72 divided by 90 times 100, which is 80 percent. Simplify the fraction first when you can: 72 over 90 simplifies to 4 over 5, which is 80 percent, and simplifying before multiplying keeps the numbers small and avoids errors. If the total marks are 100, the marks themselves are the percentage, which is why many students find tests out of 100 the easiest to read.

Pass-mark problems work backwards: the pass percentage is given, and you must find the minimum marks needed. If a paper is out of 200 marks and the pass mark is 40 percent, the passing marks are 40 percent of 200, which is 80 marks. A student scoring 75 marks would fail by 5 marks, while a student scoring 95 marks would pass by 15 marks. A common trap is confusing the pass percentage with the pass marks themselves; always check whether the question asks for marks or for a percentage, and label your answer clearly so the examiner sees what you found.

diagram.caption: First identify what the question asks for, then pick the matching method.

paras: An increase problem gives an original value and a percentage increase, and asks for the new value. First find the increase amount, then add it to the original. For example, a book priced at 200 rupees rises by 10 percent. Ten percent of 200 is 20 rupees, so the new price is 220 rupees. A faster method is to multiply the original by 110 percent, which is 1.10 times 200, also giving 220 rupees. Both methods work, but the two-step method is safer for beginners because it shows the increase amount separately, which is often what the question asks for.

Increase problems also appear in marks and populations. If a class of 40 students grows by 25 percent, the increase is 10 students, so the new class size is 50. If a player's score rises from 60 to 75, the increase is 15, and the percentage increase is 15 divided by 60 times 100, which is 25 percent. Notice that the percentage increase is always calculated on the original value, never on the new value. This is the single most tested idea in increase problems, and remembering it will save you from the most common error in this topic.

sections.h2: Decrease Problems: Discounts and Falling Marks
paras: A decrease problem works like an increase problem in reverse: find the decrease amount and subtract it from the original. If a jacket priced at 1000 rupees is reduced by 20 percent, the decrease is 200 rupees, so the new price is 800 rupees. The shortcut is to multiply by 80 percent, which is 0.80 times 1000, also giving 800 rupees. Decrease problems in shops are the same as discount problems, so the skills from money word problems transfer directly here. Always confirm whether the question asks for the decrease amount or the new price, because these are different answers.

A classic exam trap is the double change: a price rises by 10 percent and then falls by 10 percent, and students expect it to return to the original price. It does not. A price of 100 rupees rising by 10 percent becomes 110 rupees, and then falling by 10 percent means subtracting 11 rupees, giving 99 rupees. The second percentage is calculated on the new, higher value, so the fall is bigger than the rise. Remembering that each percentage change applies to the current value, not the original, protects you from this trap and from similar questions about marks and populations.

The first common mistake is calculating a percentage on the wrong base value, especially in increase and decrease problems where the base changes after the first step. The second is forgetting to multiply by 100 when finding a percentage, giving an answer like 0.8 instead of 80 percent. The third is confusing the percentage with the amount, for example answering 20 percent when the question asked how many rupees the discount was. The fourth is mishandling percentages over 100 percent, which are perfectly valid for increases but impossible for a share of a fixed total like exam marks.

Another frequent error is rounding too early in multi-step problems, which changes the final answer by a mark or two. Keep full numbers through the working and round only at the end, and only if the question asks for rounding. Finally, always write the percent sign when the answer is a percentage, and write rupees or marks when the answer is an amount. A bare number with no unit loses marks even when the calculation is correct. Practise a mix of marks, shop and increase problems every week, and percentages will become a reliable strength. More help is on our [blog](/blog/) and [about page](/about.html).

points: Percent means out of 100: find a percentage of an amount by multiplying and dividing by 100.
Marks percentage equals marks obtained divided by total marks, times 100.
Pass marks equal the pass percentage of the total marks; check marks versus percent carefully.
Percentage increase or decrease is always calculated on the original value, not the new one.
After a rise and a fall of the same percent, the value does not return to the original.

faqs.q: How do I find a percentage of a number?
faqs.a: Multiply the number by the percentage and divide by 100. For example, 20 percent of 300 is 20 times 300 divided by 100, which is 60. For friendly percentages, use fraction shortcuts instead: 10 percent means divide by 10, 25 percent means divide by 4, and 50 percent means divide by 2. Both routes give the same answer, so choose the one that keeps your numbers simplest and show your working.

faqs.q: How do I calculate my percentage score in an exam?
faqs.a: Divide the marks you obtained by the total marks and multiply by 100. If you scored 72 out of 90, the calculation is 72 divided by 90 times 100, which is 80 percent. Simplify the fraction before multiplying when possible, because smaller numbers reduce errors. If the paper is out of 100 marks, your marks are already your percentage, which makes reading the result straightforward.

faqs.q: How do I find pass marks from a pass percentage?
faqs.a: Multiply the total marks by the pass percentage and divide by 100. For a paper out of 200 marks with a pass mark of 40 percent, the passing marks are 40 percent of 200, which is 80 marks. A student scoring below 80 fails, and the shortfall is found by subtracting their marks from 80. Always check whether the question asks for the pass marks or the pass percentage, because these are different answers.

faqs.q: What is the difference between percentage increase and percentage decrease?
faqs.a: Both are calculated on the original value, but an increase is added to the original while a decrease is subtracted from it. A price of 200 rupees rising by 10 percent becomes 220 rupees, while the same price falling by 10 percent becomes 180 rupees. Remember that a rise followed by a fall of the same percent does not return to the original value, because the second change applies to the new, changed value.

faqs.q: Why do percentage answers go wrong so often?
faqs.a: Most errors come from calculating on the wrong base value, forgetting to multiply by 100, confusing a percentage with an amount, or rounding too early in multi-step problems. Students also mix up increase and decrease, or give the change amount when the question asked for the new value. Writing the method first, labelling the answer with percent, rupees or marks, and rounding only at the end will fix nearly all of these mistakes.

title: Maths Word Problems: Area of Rooms and Fields
desc: Solve area word problems step by step: flooring, fencing and painting problems for rooms and fields, with worked examples for school maths.
intro: Area problems describe real jobs: laying tiles on a floor, putting a fence around a field, or painting the walls of a room. Students often know the area formula for a rectangle but still lose marks, because they confuse area with perimeter, mix up units, or forget to subtract doors and windows when painting. The secret is to draw a quick sketch, label the sides, and decide before calculating whether the question is about covering a surface or going around an edge. This guide works through flooring, fencing and painting problems with clear methods you can reuse in exams. Extra practice is available in our [solved notes](/solved.html) and on the [books page](/books.html).

sections.h2: Area and Perimeter Are Not the Same
paras: Area measures the surface covered inside a shape, while perimeter measures the distance around its edge, and confusing the two is the most common error in this topic. For a rectangle, area equals length multiplied by breadth, and perimeter equals twice the sum of length and breadth. A room 5 metres long and 4 metres wide has an area of 20 square metres and a perimeter of 18 metres. Notice the units: area is always in square units, such as square metres, while perimeter is in ordinary units, such as metres. Writing the unit correctly is itself worth marks and also acts as a check on your method.

Before calculating, ask yourself whether the job covers a surface or follows an edge. Flooring, tiling, carpeting and painting are area jobs, because they cover a surface. Fencing, skirting boards and borders are perimeter jobs, because they run around an edge. A question about a fence around a field needs the perimeter, while a question about grass seed for the same field needs the area. Many exam questions deliberately test this distinction by describing a field and asking about fencing, so underline the key verb: fence, surround and border mean perimeter, while cover, tile and paint mean area.

sections.h2: Flooring a Room: Tiles and Carpets
paras: Flooring problems usually give the room dimensions and the tile size, and ask how many tiles are needed. The method is to find the area of the floor and divide it by the area of one tile. For example, a floor 6 metres long and 4 metres wide has an area of 24 square metres. If one tile covers 1 square metre, then 24 tiles are needed. If tiles are smaller, convert carefully: a tile 50 centimetres by 50 centimetres covers 0.25 square metres, so the same floor needs 24 divided by 0.25, which is 96 tiles. Convert all lengths to the same unit before calculating, or the answer will be wrong by a large factor.

Carpet problems are simpler because carpet is usually sold by area, so you only need the floor area, plus sometimes the cost. If carpet costs 300 rupees per square metre and a room measures 5 metres by 4 metres, the area is 20 square metres and the cost is 20 times 300, which is 6000 rupees. A common trap is a room with an attached bathroom or a missing corner, which makes the floor an L-shape rather than a rectangle. Split an L-shape into two rectangles, find each area separately, and add them together. Drawing the split on your sketch makes this step obvious and prevents missing a section.

diagram.caption: Follow these steps for tiles, carpets and floor area questions.

paras: Fencing problems ask for the length of fence needed around a field, which is the perimeter, and sometimes the cost of that fence. For a rectangular field 40 metres long and 30 metres wide, the perimeter is twice the sum of 40 and 30, which is 140 metres. If fencing costs 50 rupees per metre, the total cost is 140 times 50, which is 7000 rupees. Watch for questions that leave a gap for a gate: if a 4-metre gate is left open, subtract it from the perimeter before calculating the cost, giving 136 metres of fence and a cost of 6800 rupees. Reading the gate detail is essential.

Some fencing problems involve several rows of wire, such as a field fenced with 3 rounds of wire. Here you must multiply the perimeter by the number of rounds before finding the cost. A field with a perimeter of 140 metres fenced with 3 rounds needs 420 metres of wire. Another variation gives the perimeter and one side and asks for the other side: if the perimeter is 100 metres and the length is 30 metres, then twice the breadth equals 100 minus 60, which is 40, so the breadth is 20 metres. Working backwards like this is a favourite exam style, so practise it until it feels natural.

sections.h2: Painting Walls: Subtracting Doors and Windows
paras: Painting problems ask for the area to be painted, which is usually the area of the walls minus the area of doors and windows that are not painted. Suppose a wall is 5 metres long and 3 metres high, giving an area of 15 square metres. If the wall has a door 2 metres by 1 metre, the door area is 2 square metres, so the paintable area is 13 square metres. For a room with four walls, calculate each wall separately or use the perimeter times the height, then subtract all doors and windows. Students who forget this subtraction overstate the paint needed and lose the mark.

Paint cost problems add one more step: multiply the paintable area by the cost per square metre, or divide by the coverage of one tin. If one tin of paint covers 10 square metres and the paintable area is 45 square metres, you need 45 divided by 10, which is 4.5 tins, so you must buy 5 tins because paint is sold in whole tins. Always round up when buying materials like tiles or paint tins; rounding down would leave the job unfinished. This practical rounding rule is easy to forget in an exam, but examiners test it deliberately.

The first common mistake is confusing area with perimeter, answering a fencing question with an area or a tiling question with a perimeter. The second is mixing units, such as multiplying metres by centimetres without converting, which gives an answer out by a factor of 100. The third is forgetting to subtract doors and windows in painting problems, or forgetting to subtract a gate in fencing problems. The fourth is rounding down when buying tiles or paint tins, leaving the job short. Each of these errors comes from rushing, not from a lack of knowledge.

To avoid them, always start with a sketch, label every side with its unit, and write whether the question needs area or perimeter before calculating. Convert all lengths to the same unit first, show the formula you are using, and finish with the correct square or ordinary unit. After finding the answer, do a sense check: a classroom floor cannot be 2 square metres, and a field fence cannot be 5 metres long. These quick checks catch most errors before you hand in your paper. More guides are on our [blog](/blog/) and [about page](/about.html).

points: Area covers a surface; perimeter runs around an edge — decide which one first.
Rectangle area equals length times breadth; perimeter equals twice length plus breadth.
Convert all lengths to the same unit before multiplying, or the answer will be wrong.
Painting area means wall area minus doors and windows; fencing means perimeter minus gates.
Round up when buying tiles or paint tins; rounding down leaves the job unfinished.

faqs.q: What is the difference between area and perimeter?
faqs.a: Area measures the surface inside a shape, while perimeter measures the distance around its edge. For a rectangle, area equals length multiplied by breadth and is measured in square units, while perimeter equals twice the sum of length and breadth and is measured in ordinary units. Flooring, tiling and painting are area jobs, while fencing and borders are perimeter jobs, so identifying the job correctly is the first step in every problem.

faqs.q: How do I find how many tiles are needed for a floor?
faqs.a: Find the area of the floor by multiplying its length by its breadth, find the area of one tile the same way, and divide the floor area by the tile area. For example, a floor of 24 square metres covered with tiles of 0.25 square metres needs 96 tiles. Convert all lengths to the same unit first, and round up the final tile count, because you cannot buy part of a tile and the job must be fully covered.

faqs.q: How do I solve a fencing problem with a gate?
faqs.a: First calculate the perimeter of the field, then subtract the width of the gate, because no fence is needed across the opening. For a field with a perimeter of 140 metres and a 4-metre gate, the fence length is 136 metres. If fencing costs a certain amount per metre, multiply the fence length by that rate. If several rounds of wire are used, multiply the perimeter by the number of rounds before finding the cost.

faqs.q: Why do painting problems subtract doors and windows?
faqs.a: Doors and windows are not painted, so their area must be removed from the wall area to find the true paintable area. Calculate each wall's area, add them together, then subtract the area of every door and window. Forgetting this step overstates the paint needed and loses the mark. After finding the paintable area, divide by the coverage of one tin and round up, because paint is sold in whole tins.

faqs.q: What mistakes should I avoid in area problems?
faqs.a: The most common mistakes are confusing area with perimeter, mixing metres and centimetres without converting, forgetting to subtract doors, windows or gates, and rounding down when buying materials. Always sketch the shape, label sides with units, state whether area or perimeter is needed, convert units first, and sense-check the final answer against the real size of the room or field described.

title: Maths Word Problems: Ages of Family Members
desc: Solve age word problems with confidence: ages now, after five years and five years ago, explained with worked examples for school maths exams.
intro: Age problems are a favourite exam topic because they look like stories about families but are really simple equations in disguise. The key idea is beautifully simple: everyone ages at the same speed, so the difference between two people's ages never changes. If a father is 30 years older than his son today, he will still be 30 years older in ten years, and he was 30 years older ten years ago. Once you understand this, problems about now, after five years and five years ago all follow the same method. This guide explains that method with worked examples your whole family can follow. More practice is in our [solved notes](/solved.html) and on the [books page](/books.html).

sections.h2: Ages Move Together: The Golden Rule
paras: The golden rule of age problems is that the difference between two ages stays constant over time. If Ali is 12 and his sister is 8, the difference is 4 years, and it will still be 4 years when Ali is 20 and his sister is 16. This rule lets you check your answers quickly: if your final ages give a different difference from the one in the question, something has gone wrong. It also lets you solve problems backwards, because knowing one person's age and the difference immediately gives you the other person's age at any point in time.

The second idea is that ages shift by the same amount for everyone. After five years, every person is five years older, so you add five to every age in the problem. Five years ago, every person was five years younger, so you subtract five from every age. Students often add five to only one person's age and forget the other, which breaks the golden rule and gives a wrong answer. A safe habit is to write a small table with columns for now, after five years and five years ago, and fill in every row before calculating anything.

Problems about now usually give a sum of ages or a ratio of ages and ask for each person's age. For example, a father and son have ages in the ratio 5:1, and the sum of their ages is 48 years. The total parts are 6, so one part is worth 8 years, giving the father 40 years and the son 8 years. Check: 40 plus 8 equals 48, and the difference is 32 years. Another common type gives the difference directly: if a mother is 26 years older than her daughter and their ages add up to 50, then twice the daughter's age equals 50 minus 26, which is 24, so the daughter is 12 and the mother is 38.

When a problem about now gives a multiple, such as a father being three times as old as his son, use the same parts method with the multiple as a ratio. If the father is three times as old as his son and their ages sum to 44, the ratio is 3:1, the total parts are 4, and one part is 11 years, so the son is 11 and the father is 33. Always check both the sum and the multiple in your answer. If either check fails, your working has an error, and rechecking the parts division usually finds it. Writing the checks beside your answer also earns method marks in exams.

diagram.caption: Use this method for now, future and past age questions.

paras: After-five-years problems describe a relationship that will hold in the future, and the key step is to add five to every age before setting up the equation. For example, a son is 10 years old and his father is 38. After five years, the son will be 15 and the father will be 43. A typical exam question reverses this: a father is now three times as old as his son, but after five years he will be only twice as old. Let the son's age now be x, so the father is 3x. After five years they are x plus 5 and 3x plus 5, and the equation 3x plus 5 equals twice x plus 5 gives x equals 5, so the son is 5 and the father is 15.

The most common error in future problems is adding the years to only one person, which destroys the constant difference and produces an impossible answer. Another error is writing the future relationship using present ages, for example setting the father's present age equal to twice the son's future age. To avoid this, write the future ages in a separate line of your working, clearly labelled after five years, and build the equation only from that line. If your answer gives a negative age or a father younger than his son, you know immediately that a step went wrong.

Five-years-ago problems work exactly like future problems but in reverse: subtract five from every age before building the equation. For example, a mother is now 34 and her daughter is 10. Five years ago, the mother was 29 and the daughter was 5. A typical exam question says that five years ago, a father was four times as old as his son, and today the father is 40. Five years ago the father was 35, so the son was 35 divided by 4, which is not a whole number, and that tells you the question must have different numbers; in a well-set question the division works out neatly. Real exam questions are designed to give whole-number answers, so a fraction is a warning sign.

Consider a proper example: five years ago, a father was 5 times as old as his son, and today the father is 45. Five years ago the father was 40, so the son was 40 divided by 5, which is 8 years old then, and 13 years old now. The check is that today the father is 45 and the son is 13, a difference of 32 years, and five years ago the difference was also 32 years, since 40 minus 8 equals 32. This difference check is your best friend in past problems. If the difference changes between your present and past ages, you have added or subtracted the years unevenly.

The first common mistake is shifting only one person's age when moving to the future or the past, which breaks the constant age difference. The second is mixing up present and future ages in the same equation, for example using the father's present age with the son's future age. The third is forgetting that ages must be whole numbers and positive; an answer like negative 3 years or a son older than his father is always wrong. The fourth is solving the equation correctly but answering the wrong question, such as giving the son's age when the question asked for the father's age in five years' time.

To avoid these traps, always write a table with rows for each person and columns for now, future and past, and fill it in completely before writing any equation. Solve the equation step by step, showing each line, and finish by checking the sum, the ratio and the constant difference. Finally, reread the question and confirm you answered exactly what was asked, including whether it wanted a present age or a future age. With this disciplined method, age problems become one of the most predictable and rewarding topics in the paper. Find more guides on our [blog](/blog/) and [about page](/about.html).

points: The difference between two people's ages never changes over time.
After five years, add five to every age; five years ago, subtract five from every age.
Use a table with rows for people and columns for now, future and past.
Check every answer against the sum, the ratio and the constant age difference.
Ages must be positive whole numbers; a negative or fractional age signals an error.

faqs.q: What is the golden rule of age problems?
faqs.a: The golden rule is that the difference between two people's ages never changes, because everyone ages at the same speed. If a father is 30 years older than his son today, he will still be 30 years older in ten years and he was 30 years older ten years ago. This rule gives you a powerful check: if your final ages show a different difference from the one in the question, your working contains an error, usually from shifting only one person's age.

faqs.q: How do I solve an age problem about five years from now?
faqs.a: Add five years to every person's age before building your equation, and use only the future ages in the relationship the question describes. For example, if a father is now three times as old as his son but will be twice as old after five years, write the son's present age as x, the father's as 3x, then set 3x plus 5 equal to twice x plus 5, giving x equals 5. Adding the years to only one person is the most common mistake in these problems.

faqs.q: How do five-years-ago problems work?
faqs.a: Subtract five years from every person's age before setting up the equation, exactly mirroring future problems. If a father is 45 today, he was 40 five years ago, and if he was then five times as old as his son, the son was 8 then and is 13 now. Check your answer with the constant difference: the father-son difference must be the same now as it was five years ago. If it changed, you shifted the ages unevenly.

faqs.q: How do I use ratios in age problems?
faqs.a: Treat the ratio like any sharing ratio: add the ratio numbers for total parts, divide the sum of ages by total parts to find one part, then multiply by each share. If a father and son are in the ratio 5:1 and their ages sum to 48, total parts are 6, one part is 8 years, so the father is 40 and the son is 8. Always verify both the sum and the ratio in your final answer before moving on.

faqs.q: Why do my age problem answers come out impossible?
faqs.a: Impossible answers, such as negative ages, fractional ages or a son older than his father, usually come from shifting only one person's age, mixing present and future ages in one equation, or setting up the equation from the wrong time period. Writing a table for now, future and past, filling every cell before calculating, and checking the constant age difference will catch these errors. Reread the question at the end to confirm you answered the age it actually asked for.

title: Maths Word Problems: Speed of Trains and Bikes
desc: Solve speed word problems with trains and bikes: who arrives first, unit conversions and journey comparisons, with worked examples for school maths.
intro: Speed problems with trains and bikes are exciting because they feel like real races, but they punish students who rush the units or compare the wrong quantities. A train travelling at 60 kilometres per hour and a bike at 15 kilometres per hour cannot be compared fairly unless they travel the same distance or the same time, and many exam questions deliberately mix these cases. The method is always the same: organise distance, speed and time for each vehicle, match the units, and only then compare. This guide works through who-arrives-first problems, unit conversions, and the common traps, with examples you can practise tonight. More help is in our [solved notes](/solved.html) and on the [books page](/books.html).

paras: Speed tells you how much distance is covered in one unit of time, so speed equals distance divided by time. A train covering 180 kilometres in 3 hours travels at 60 kilometres per hour, because 180 divided by 3 equals 60. A bike covering 30 kilometres in 2 hours travels at 15 kilometres per hour, because 30 divided by 2 equals 15. Comparing these two speeds is easy once both are in the same unit: the train is four times as fast as the bike. The danger comes when one speed is in kilometres per hour and the other in metres per second, because the numbers then look misleading until converted.

Always write the unit beside every speed, distance and time, and convert before comparing. A speed of 20 metres per second sounds slower than 60 kilometres per hour, but converting shows that 20 metres per second equals 72 kilometres per hour, which is actually faster. The conversion rule is simple: multiply metres per second by 3.6 to get kilometres per hour, and divide kilometres per hour by 3.6 to get metres per second. Practise this conversion until it is automatic, because examiners love mixing units in speed questions.

Who-arrives-first problems give two vehicles travelling the same distance at different speeds and ask which arrives first and by how much. Calculate each journey time separately with time equals distance divided by speed, then subtract. For example, two trains travel 240 kilometres: the express at 80 kilometres per hour takes 3 hours, while the local at 60 kilometres per hour takes 4 hours. The express arrives 1 hour earlier. The mistake to avoid is assuming the faster train always wins by a simple margin; the time difference depends on the distance too, so a small speed advantage over a long distance creates a big time gap.

Some questions add different start times, which changes the answer completely. If the slow train leaves one hour before the fast train on the same 240-kilometre route, the slow train arrives after 4 hours while the fast train, leaving an hour later, arrives after 3 hours of travel, which is also 4 hours after the slow train left. In this case they arrive together, even though their speeds differ. To handle start-time problems, convert every arrival into clock time: add each journey time to its own start time, and then compare the clock times. This method never fails, however tricky the question looks.

diagram.caption: Compare journeys fairly by converting everything to clock times.

paras: Bike problems often mix kilometres, metres, hours, minutes and seconds, because cycling speeds feel natural in both kilometres per hour and metres per second. A cyclist covering 900 metres in 60 seconds travels at 15 metres per second, which converts to 54 kilometres per hour by multiplying by 3.6. If the question gives distance in kilometres and time in minutes, convert the minutes to hours first: 45 minutes is 0.75 hours, so a 18-kilometre ride in 45 minutes means a speed of 18 divided by 0.75, which is 24 kilometres per hour. Writing each conversion as its own line keeps the working clean and checkable.

A favourite exam variation asks how far a bike travels in a given time at a given speed, which uses distance equals speed times time. A bike at 20 kilometres per hour for 30 minutes, which is 0.5 hours, covers 10 kilometres. Another variation asks how long a journey takes at a changed speed: if the same 10-kilometre ride is done at 25 kilometres per hour instead, the time is 10 divided by 25, which is 0.4 hours, or 24 minutes. Notice how 0.4 hours becomes 24 minutes by multiplying by 60, not by reading it as 40 minutes. Decimal-to-minutes conversion is tested again and again.

Overtaking problems describe a faster vehicle catching a slower one, and meeting problems describe two vehicles moving towards each other. For meeting problems, the key idea is that their speeds add up, because together they cover the distance between them. If a train at 70 kilometres per hour and another at 50 kilometres per hour move towards each other across 240 kilometres, they close the gap at 120 kilometres per hour, so they meet after 2 hours. The first train has then travelled 140 kilometres and the second 100 kilometres, and 140 plus 100 equals 240, which checks the answer beautifully.

For overtaking problems, the key idea is the opposite: subtract the speeds, because only the speed difference closes the gap. If a bike at 25 kilometres per hour starts 10 kilometres ahead of a bike at 35 kilometres per hour, the gap closes at 10 kilometres per hour, so the faster bike catches up after 1 hour. Students often add speeds in overtaking problems by mistake, which gives an answer that is far too quick. Remember the simple rule: towards each other means add the speeds, same direction means subtract them, and the rest of the method is the same distance-speed-time calculation.

The first common mistake is comparing speeds in different units without converting, which makes a slower vehicle look faster. The second is using minutes directly with kilometres per hour, giving an answer 60 times too large. The third is reading a decimal time like 0.4 hours as 40 minutes instead of 24 minutes. The fourth is adding speeds in an overtaking problem or subtracting them in a meeting problem. The fifth is ignoring different start times in who-arrives-first problems, which can reverse the winner entirely. Each of these mistakes is a reading and conversion error, not a formula error.

To avoid them, always list distance, speed, time and start time for every vehicle in a small table, convert all units before calculating, and finish by converting journey times into clock arrival times. Then sense-check: a bike cannot travel at 200 kilometres per hour, and a train journey of 240 kilometres cannot take 10 minutes. If an answer looks impossible, recheck the conversions first. With this disciplined approach, speed problems become fast, reliable marks. More guides are on our [blog](/blog/) and [about page](/about.html).
