points: Speed equals distance divided by time; always write the unit beside every value.
Convert metres per second to kilometres per hour by multiplying by 3.6, and reverse by dividing.
Who arrives first: find each journey time, add it to its start time, compare clock times.
Meeting vehicles add their speeds; overtaking vehicles subtract their speeds.
Convert decimal hours to minutes by multiplying by 60, never by reading the decimal as minutes.

faqs.q: How do I decide who arrives first in a race problem?
faqs.a: Calculate each vehicle's journey time using time equals distance divided by speed, add each journey time to that vehicle's own start time, and compare the resulting clock times. The earlier clock time wins, even if that vehicle is slower but started earlier. Ignoring different start times is the most common error in these problems, so always convert journey times into arrival clock times before comparing.

faqs.q: How do I convert metres per second to kilometres per hour?
faqs.a: Multiply the speed in metres per second by 3.6 to get kilometres per hour, and divide kilometres per hour by 3.6 to get metres per second. For example, 20 metres per second equals 72 kilometres per hour, which surprises many students because the number looks small before conversion. Always convert speeds to the same unit before comparing them, or the faster vehicle may appear slower.

faqs.q: What is the difference between meeting and overtaking problems?
faqs.a: In meeting problems, two vehicles move towards each other, so their speeds add together to close the gap. In overtaking problems, both move in the same direction, so only the difference of their speeds closes the gap. For example, trains at 70 and 50 kilometres per hour meeting head-on close at 120 kilometres per hour, while a bike at 35 catching one at 25 closes at only 10 kilometres per hour.

faqs.q: How do I convert 0.4 hours into minutes correctly?
faqs.a: Multiply the decimal part by 60, because one hour contains 60 minutes. So 0.4 hours equals 0.4 times 60, which is 24 minutes, not 40 minutes. Similarly, 2.5 hours is 2 hours and 30 minutes, and 0.75 hours is 45 minutes. This conversion is tested very often, so practise it until it feels automatic before your exam.

faqs.q: Why do speed problem answers often look impossible?
faqs.a: Impossible answers almost always come from unit errors: using minutes with kilometres per hour, comparing speeds in different units, adding speeds when they should be subtracted, or misreading decimal hours as minutes. Listing every vehicle's distance, speed, time and start time in a table, converting units before calculating, and sense-checking the final answer against real-world speeds will catch nearly all of these mistakes.

title: Maths Word Problems: Fractions of Pizza and Pocket Money
desc: Learn fraction word problems with food and money stories: parts of a whole, pizza slices and pocket money, with worked examples for school maths.
intro: Fractions describe parts of a whole, and the best way to understand them is through food and money: slices of a pizza, pieces of a chocolate bar, or parts of your pocket money spent and saved. Fraction word problems test whether you can find a fraction of an amount, add or subtract fractions, and handle the tricky case where a fraction is taken of what remains rather than of the original whole. Students lose marks mainly by applying a fraction to the wrong whole, so this guide teaches you to always ask: fraction of what. Worked pizza and pocket money examples make each method concrete. More practice is in our [solved notes](/solved.html) and on the [books page](/books.html).

sections.h2: A Fraction Is Part of a Whole
paras: A fraction has two parts: the denominator tells you how many equal parts the whole is divided into, and the numerator tells you how many of those parts you have. In the fraction three quarters, the whole is divided into 4 equal parts and you have 3 of them. To find a fraction of an amount, divide the amount by the denominator and multiply by the numerator. For example, three quarters of 80 rupees is 80 divided by 4, which is 20, times 3, which is 60 rupees. This divide-then-multiply method works for every fraction-of-an-amount problem, whatever the numbers.

It helps to visualise fractions with a simple bar or circle divided into equal parts, shading the parts the question mentions. Drawing takes only seconds and prevents the most common error, which is swapping the numerator and denominator. If a problem says a pizza is cut into 8 slices and Ahmed eats 3, the fraction eaten is 3 over 8, and the fraction remaining is 5 over 8, because 8 minus 3 equals 5 slices left. Always check that the fractions for eaten and remaining add up to the whole, which is 1, because 3 over 8 plus 5 over 8 equals 8 over 8, which is 1.

Pizza problems usually ask how much each person gets when a pizza is shared, or how much remains after some slices are eaten. If 3 pizzas are shared equally among 4 friends, each friend gets 3 over 4 of a pizza, because the total pizzas divided by the number of friends gives the share. If one pizza is cut into 12 slices and Sara eats 5 slices, she has eaten 5 over 12 of the pizza, and 7 over 12 remains. When slices are different sizes, the fraction only works if the parts are equal, so exam questions always state that the pizza is cut equally.

A harder pizza problem combines two fractions, such as eating one half of a pizza and then one quarter of what remains. After eating one half, one half remains, and one quarter of that remaining half is one eighth of the whole pizza, leaving three eighths. The trap is to add one half and one quarter to get three quarters eaten, which is wrong, because the quarter applies to the remaining half, not to the whole pizza. Always identify the whole for each fraction separately, and draw the pizza in stages if the problem has two steps.

diagram.caption: Always ask first: fraction of what whole.

sections.h2: Pocket Money Problems: Spending and Saving
paras: Pocket money problems apply fractions to money, and they test the same divide-then-multiply method. If Bilal receives 200 rupees and spends two fifths of it, he spends 200 divided by 5, which is 40, times 2, which is 80 rupees, leaving 120 rupees. If he then saves one half of what remains, he saves 60 rupees, because the second fraction applies to the remaining 120, not to the original 200. This two-step structure is the most tested pattern in fraction problems, and the phrase of what remains is the signal that the whole has changed.

Another common type gives the fraction spent and the amount left, and asks for the original pocket money. If Sara spends three quarters of her money and has 50 rupees left, the remaining fraction is one quarter, so one quarter equals 50 rupees, and the whole amount is 4 times 50, which is 200 rupees. Working backwards like this requires finding the remaining fraction first, which many students forget. Always write down both the spent fraction and the remaining fraction before calculating, because the remaining fraction is often the key to the whole problem.

Fractions of a remaining amount confuse students because the whole changes halfway through the problem, and each fraction must be applied to the correct whole. Consider a ribbon 24 metres long: first one third is cut off, leaving 16 metres, and then one quarter of the remainder is cut off, which is 4 metres, leaving 12 metres. The second fraction, one quarter, applies to 16 metres, not to 24 metres. If you mistakenly apply it to 24, you get 6 metres and a wrong final answer of 10 metres instead of 12. Writing the remaining amount after each step prevents this error completely.

A useful check is to track the remaining fraction as well as the remaining amount. After cutting one third, two thirds remain. After cutting one quarter of the remainder, three quarters of the remainder survive, which is three quarters of two thirds, or one half of the original. One half of 24 metres is 12 metres, confirming the step-by-step answer. Multiplying fractions like this is an advanced check, but even without it, the habit of rewriting the remaining amount after every step will carry you through the hardest fraction problems in your exams.

The first common mistake is applying a fraction to the original whole when the question says of the remainder, which changes the answer completely. The second is swapping the numerator and denominator, for example using 4 over 3 instead of 3 over 4. The third is adding fractions with different denominators without finding a common denominator, such as claiming one half plus one third equals two fifths. The fourth is forgetting that the parts must be equal for a fraction to make sense, which matters when a story mentions unequal slices. The fifth is leaving an answer as an improper fraction when the question expects a mixed number, or vice versa.

To avoid these errors, always start by naming the whole, draw a quick bar showing the parts, and write the remaining amount after each step in a multi-step problem. Simplify fractions only at the end unless the question asks for simplest form, and label your final answer with its unit, such as slices or rupees. With steady practice on pizza and pocket money stories, fractions stop feeling abstract and become a reliable source of marks. More guides are on our [blog](/blog/) and [about page](/about.html).

points: To find a fraction of an amount, divide by the denominator and multiply by the numerator.
Always ask: fraction of what — the original whole or the remaining amount.
After each step in a multi-step problem, rewrite the remaining amount before continuing.
Fractions for eaten and remaining parts must add up to the whole, which is 1.
Draw a quick bar or circle divided into equal parts to visualise any fraction problem.

faqs.q: How do I find a fraction of a number?
faqs.a: Divide the number by the denominator and multiply the result by the numerator. For example, three quarters of 80 is 80 divided by 4, which is 20, times 3, which is 60. This divide-then-multiply method works for any fraction and any amount, including money, lengths and quantities of food. Drawing a bar divided into equal parts helps you see why the method works and prevents swapping the numerator and denominator.

faqs.q: What does fraction of the remainder mean?
faqs.a: It means the fraction applies to whatever is left after an earlier step, not to the original whole. If you spend one half of 200 rupees, 100 rupees remain, and spending one quarter of the remainder means spending 25 rupees, not 50. The phrase of what remains is the signal that the whole has changed, so always rewrite the remaining amount after each step before applying the next fraction.

faqs.q: How do I share pizzas equally among friends?
faqs.a: Divide the total number of pizzas by the number of friends to find each share as a fraction. If 3 pizzas are shared among 4 friends, each friend gets 3 over 4 of a pizza. If a single pizza is cut into 12 equal slices and someone eats 5, they have eaten 5 over 12 of the pizza and 7 over 12 remains. The parts must be equal for the fraction to be valid, so exam questions always state that the pizza is cut equally.

faqs.q: How do I work backwards from a remaining amount?
faqs.a: First find the remaining fraction by subtracting the spent fraction from 1, then use the remaining amount to find the whole. If Sara spends three quarters of her money and has 50 rupees left, the remaining fraction is one quarter, so one quarter equals 50 rupees and the whole amount is 200 rupees. Writing down both the spent and remaining fractions before calculating is the key step students most often skip.

faqs.q: Why do fraction word problems go wrong?
faqs.a: Most errors come from applying a fraction to the wrong whole, especially in of the remainder problems, swapping numerator and denominator, or adding fractions with different denominators without a common denominator. Drawing a bar diagram, naming the whole for each fraction, rewriting the remaining amount after each step, and checking that parts add up to the whole will prevent nearly all of these mistakes.

title: Maths Word Problems: Averages of Marks and Runs
desc: Master average word problems: class averages, cricket averages and finding a missing score, with worked examples for school maths exams.
intro: An average is a single number that represents a whole group fairly, as if the total had been shared equally among everyone. Average problems appear in exams through class marks, cricket scores, heights, weights and daily earnings, and they test two skills: finding an average from a list, and working backwards to find a missing value from a known average. Both skills use one formula: average equals total divided by how many, and total equals average times how many. This guide explains both directions with class and cricket examples, plus the missing-score problems that students find hardest. More practice is in our [solved notes](/solved.html) and on the [books page](/books.html).

paras: The average of a set of numbers is found by adding all the numbers and dividing by how many numbers there are. If five students score 70, 80, 90, 60 and 100 marks, the total is 400 and the average is 400 divided by 5, which is 80 marks. Think of the average as sharing the total equally: if all five students had scored the same, each would have scored 80. This sharing idea explains why an average must always lie between the smallest and largest values in the set; an average outside that range is impossible and signals a calculation error.

The reverse formula is just as important: total equals average multiplied by how many. If the average of 6 numbers is 25, their total is 150. This reverse form is the key to missing-value problems, because it lets you find a total even when one value is unknown. For example, if the average of 4 numbers is 30, the total is 120, so if three of the numbers are 25, 35 and 30, the missing number is 120 minus 90, which is 30. Practise both directions until switching between them feels natural, because exams test both equally.

sections.h2: Class Averages: Marks of Many Students
paras: Class average problems often combine two groups, such as boys and girls, and ask for the combined average. The correct method is to find each group's total first, add the totals, and divide by the total number of students. For example, 10 boys average 70 marks, giving a total of 700, and 15 girls average 80 marks, giving a total of 1200. The combined total is 1900 and the combined number of students is 25, so the combined average is 76 marks. Notice that 76 is not the simple average of 70 and 80, which would be 75, because the groups have different sizes and the larger group pulls the average towards itself.

A common trap is averaging the averages directly, which only works when the groups are exactly equal in size. Another trap gives the combined average and one group's average and asks for the other group's average. If a class of 30 students averages 72 marks, the total is 2160. If 18 of them average 70 marks, their total is 1260, so the remaining 12 students total 900 marks, averaging 75 marks. Working through totals at every step keeps these problems organised. A table with columns for group, count, average and total makes the method visible and checkable.

diagram.caption: Totals are the bridge between averages and missing values.

paras: Cricket averages work the same way as class averages, but the context makes them more interesting. A batsman's average is the total runs divided by the number of times dismissed, and a bowler's average uses wickets instead. If a batsman scores 40, 60, 20 and 80 in four innings, the total is 200 and the average is 50 runs per innings. If the same batsman then scores 100 in the next innings, the total becomes 300 over 5 innings, and the new average is 60. Notice how one big score lifts the average, and one low score pulls it down, which is why averages change gradually over a long career.

Cricket problems often ask what score is needed to reach a target average. Suppose a batsman averages 45 runs over 10 innings, giving a total of 450 runs, and wants an average of 50 after 11 innings. The required total after 11 innings is 550 runs, so the batsman must score 100 in the next innings. This is the missing-value method applied to cricket: find the required total from the target average, subtract the current total, and the difference is the needed score. The same method answers how many runs a team needs in its last match to reach a tournament average.

Missing-score problems give an average and all but one value, and ask for the missing value. The method is: multiply the average by the count to get the total, add up the known values, and subtract to find the missing one. For example, the average of 5 test scores is 84, so the total is 420. If four scores are 78, 90, 85 and 82, their sum is 335, so the missing score is 420 minus 335, which is 85. Always verify by recomputing the average with the missing value included: 420 divided by 5 equals 84, confirming the answer.

A harder version asks what score is needed to raise an average to a target. If a student averages 70 over 4 tests, the total is 280, and to average 75 over 5 tests the total must be 375, so the fifth test score must be 95. Students sometimes try to average the averages or guess the difference, but the totals method is exact and reliable. Another variation removes a score and asks for the new average: subtract the removed score from the total, reduce the count by one, and divide again. Keeping totals at the centre of your working handles every variation of this problem type.

The first common mistake is averaging the averages of unequal groups directly, instead of combining through totals. The second is forgetting to change the count when a value is added or removed, for example dividing by 5 when there are now 6 values. The third is adding incorrectly when finding the total, a careless slip that ruins an otherwise perfect method; adding the numbers twice, in a different order, catches most slips. The fourth is giving an average that lies outside the range of the data, such as an average of 120 when all scores are below 100, which should trigger an immediate recheck.

Another error is confusing average with the middle value or the most common value, which are different ideas tested in later topics. For now, remember that average means total divided by how many, and that totals are your best tool for missing-value and combined-group problems. Always label your answer with its unit, such as marks or runs, and check that it falls between the smallest and largest values. With totals-based working, average problems become some of the most reliable marks in the paper. More guides are on our [blog](/blog/) and [about page](/about.html).

points: Average equals total divided by how many; total equals average times how many.
Combine groups through their totals, never by averaging the averages directly.
A missing value equals the required total minus the sum of the known values.
When a value is added or removed, both the total and the count change.
An average must always lie between the smallest and largest values in the set.

faqs.q: How do I find the average of a set of numbers?
faqs.a: Add all the numbers together and divide by how many numbers there are. For example, the scores 70, 80, 90, 60 and 100 total 400, and dividing by 5 gives an average of 80. Think of the average as sharing the total equally among everyone in the group. Always check that your average lies between the smallest and largest values, because an average outside that range is impossible and signals an error.

faqs.q: How do I combine averages from two groups?
faqs.a: Find each group's total by multiplying its average by its count, add the totals together, add the counts together, and divide the combined total by the combined count. For example, 10 boys averaging 70 give 700, and 15 girls averaging 80 give 1200, so the combined average is 1900 divided by 25, which is 76. Averaging the two averages directly gives 75, which is wrong, because the groups are different sizes.

faqs.q: How do I find a missing score from an average?
faqs.a: Multiply the average by the count to find the total, add up all the known values, and subtract that sum from the total. If the average of 5 scores is 84, the total is 420, and if four scores sum to 335, the missing score is 85. Verify by recomputing the average with the missing value included. The same totals method finds the score needed to reach a target average in the next test or innings.

faqs.q: How does a cricket batting average work?
faqs.a: A batting average is total runs divided by the number of times the batsman has been dismissed. If a batsman scores 40, 60, 20 and 80 in four innings, the total is 200 and the average is 50. To find the score needed to reach a target average, multiply the target average by the new innings count to get the required total, then subtract the current total. One big innings lifts the average, while one low innings pulls it down.

faqs.q: What mistakes should I avoid in average problems?
faqs.a: The most common mistakes are averaging averages of unequal groups, forgetting to update the count when a value is added or removed, and adding the numbers incorrectly when finding the total. Students also sometimes give an average outside the data range or confuse average with the middle value. Working through totals at every step, re-adding in a different order, and checking that the average sits between the minimum and maximum will prevent nearly all errors.

title: Maths Word Problems: Profit and Loss in a Shop
desc: Learn profit and loss word problems: cost price, selling price and profit percent explained with shop examples for school maths exams.
intro: Every shopkeeper buys at one price and sells at another, and the difference between those two prices is either a profit or a loss. Profit and loss problems test whether you can identify the cost price and the selling price, find the difference, and express it as a percentage of the cost price. Students lose marks mainly by calculating the percentage on the selling price instead of the cost price, or by mixing up which price is which. This guide explains cost price, selling price and profit percent with shop examples, and shows you the checks that keep your answers correct. More practice is in our [solved notes](/solved.html) and on the [books page](/books.html).

paras: The cost price is what the shopkeeper pays to buy an item, and the selling price is what the customer pays to buy it from the shop. If the selling price is higher than the cost price, the shopkeeper makes a profit; if it is lower, the shopkeeper makes a loss; if they are equal, there is neither profit nor loss. For example, a shopkeeper buys a toy for 400 rupees and sells it for 500 rupees, making a profit of 100 rupees, because 500 minus 400 equals 100. If instead the toy is sold for 350 rupees, the loss is 50 rupees, because 400 minus 350 equals 50. Profit and loss are always found by subtracting the smaller price from the larger, but you must label which one it is.

A common confusion is treating the marked price as the cost price, but these are different. The marked price is the price written on the tag, while the cost price is what the shopkeeper actually paid the supplier. A shopkeeper might buy a shirt for 600 rupees, mark it at 900 rupees, and sell it at a discount for 800 rupees, making a profit of 200 rupees on a cost price of 600. The marked price matters only for discount problems; for profit and loss, only the cost price and the selling price count. Always underline both prices in the question before calculating anything.

To find profit or loss, subtract the cost price from the selling price: a positive result is a profit, and a negative result means a loss of that amount. A shopkeeper buys 10 pens for 200 rupees and sells them for 300 rupees, making a profit of 100 rupees in total, or 10 rupees per pen. If the same pens are sold for 150 rupees, the loss is 50 rupees in total, or 5 rupees per pen. When quantities are involved, find the total cost price and the total selling price first, then subtract; working per item also works, but mixing total and per-item figures in one calculation is a frequent source of errors.

Some problems give the profit or loss and one price, and ask for the other price. If a book bought for 250 rupees is sold at a profit of 50 rupees, the selling price is 250 plus 50, which is 300 rupees. If a bag bought for 800 rupees is sold at a loss of 100 rupees, the selling price is 800 minus 100, which is 700 rupees. The rule is simple: add the profit to the cost price, or subtract the loss from the cost price, to get the selling price. Drawing a small diagram with cost price, selling price and the gap between them helps you see whether to add or subtract.

diagram.alt: Solving a Profit and Loss Problem
diagram.caption: Profit percent and loss percent are always calculated on the cost price.

paras: Profit percent is the profit expressed as a percentage of the cost price, never of the selling price. The formula is profit divided by cost price, multiplied by 100. If a toy bought for 400 rupees is sold for 500 rupees, the profit is 100 rupees, and the profit percent is 100 divided by 400 times 100, which is 25 percent. This is the single most tested rule in the topic, and examiners deliberately set questions where using the selling price gives a tempting but wrong answer: 100 divided by 500 times 100 would give 20 percent, which is incorrect. Always divide by the cost price.

Profit percent problems also work backwards: given the cost price and the profit percent, find the selling price. If a shirt costs 600 rupees and is sold at a profit of 20 percent, the profit is 20 percent of 600, which is 120 rupees, so the selling price is 720 rupees. The shortcut is to multiply the cost price by 120 percent, which is 1.20 times 600, also giving 720 rupees. The two-step method is safer for beginners because it shows the profit amount separately, which the question often asks for as well as the selling price.

sections.h2: Loss Percent and Selling at a Loss
paras: Loss percent follows the same rule as profit percent: loss divided by cost price, multiplied by 100. If a phone bought for 10000 rupees is sold for 9000 rupees, the loss is 1000 rupees, and the loss percent is 1000 divided by 10000 times 100, which is 10 percent. If the loss percent and the cost price are given, find the loss amount first and subtract it: a bicycle costing 5000 rupees sold at a loss of 8 percent loses 400 rupees, so the selling price is 4600 rupees. The shortcut is to multiply by 92 percent, which is 0.92 times 5000, also giving 4600 rupees.

A classic exam trap asks for the cost price when the selling price and the profit or loss percent are given. If a watch is sold for 1100 rupees at a profit of 10 percent, the cost price is not 1100 minus 10 percent of 1100. Instead, the selling price represents 110 percent of the cost price, so the cost price is 1100 divided by 1.10, which is 1000 rupees. The same logic applies to losses: a selling price of 900 rupees at a loss of 10 percent means the selling price is 90 percent of the cost price, so the cost price is 900 divided by 0.90, which is 1000 rupees. Learning this reverse method earns marks on the hardest questions.

sections.h2: Common Mistakes in Profit and Loss Problems
paras: The first common mistake is calculating profit or loss percent on the selling price instead of the cost price, which is wrong in every case. The second is confusing cost price with marked price, especially when a discount is also mentioned in the question. The third is mixing total and per-item figures, such as comparing the total cost of 10 pens with the selling price of one pen. The fourth is subtracting in the wrong order and calling a profit a loss, or giving a negative profit percent. The fifth is finding the profit amount correctly but stopping there when the question asked for the profit percent.

To avoid these errors, always start by writing cost price equals and selling price equals with their values, then state profit or loss, and only then calculate the percent. Check that a profit percent is positive when the selling price exceeds the cost price, and that a loss percent appears when it does not. Finally, reread the question to confirm whether it asked for the amount, the percent, or the missing price. With this method, profit and loss problems become steady, predictable marks. More guides are on our [blog](/blog/) and [about page](/about.html).

points: Cost price is what the shopkeeper pays; selling price is what the customer pays.
Profit equals selling price minus cost price; a lower selling price means a loss.
Profit percent and loss percent are always calculated on the cost price, never the selling price.
To find a selling price from a profit percent, add the profit to the cost price.
To find a cost price from a selling price, divide by 1 plus or minus the percent as a decimal.

faqs.q: What is the difference between cost price and selling price?
faqs.a: The cost price is the amount the shopkeeper pays to buy an item from a supplier, while the selling price is the amount the customer pays the shopkeeper. If the selling price is higher, the shopkeeper makes a profit; if it is lower, the shopkeeper makes a loss. The marked price on the tag is a third, different value that matters for discounts but not for profit and loss calculations, which use only cost price and selling price.

faqs.q: How do I calculate profit percent?
faqs.a: First find the profit by subtracting the cost price from the selling price, then divide the profit by the cost price and multiply by 100. For example, buying at 400 rupees and selling at 500 gives a profit of 100 rupees and a profit percent of 25 percent. Dividing by the selling price instead would give 20 percent, which is the most common error in this topic, so always divide by the cost price.

faqs.q: How do I find the selling price from a profit percent?
faqs.a: Find the profit amount as the given percent of the cost price, then add it to the cost price. If a shirt costs 600 rupees and is sold at a profit of 20 percent, the profit is 120 rupees and the selling price is 720 rupees. The shortcut is to multiply the cost price by 1.20, but the two-step method is safer because it shows the profit amount separately, which the question often asks for as well.

faqs.q: How do I find the cost price from a selling price and profit percent?
faqs.a: Remember that the selling price represents 100 percent plus the profit percent of the cost price. If a watch sells for 1100 rupees at a profit of 10 percent, the selling price is 110 percent of the cost price, so the cost price is 1100 divided by 1.10, which is 1000 rupees. For a loss, the selling price is 100 percent minus the loss percent, so divide by 0.90 for a 10 percent loss.

faqs.q: Why do profit and loss answers go wrong?
faqs.a: Most errors come from calculating the percent on the selling price instead of the cost price, confusing cost price with marked price, mixing total and per-item figures, or stopping at the profit amount when the question asked for the percent. Writing cost price and selling price explicitly, stating profit or loss before calculating the percent, and rereading the question at the end will prevent nearly all of these mistakes.

title: Class 6 English Vocabulary: 100 Useful Words
desc: Build Class 6 English vocabulary with everyday words, simple meanings and short example sentences grouped by school, home, nature and feelings.
intro: English feels hard only when the words feel new, so this general word list gives Class 6 students a friendly set of everyday words with simple meanings and short example sentences, grouped by theme so revision feels easy and useful, and it is not presented as an official answer key for any single lesson. Work through one group at a time, say each word aloud, copy its meaning, and write one sentence of your own, because that small habit turns a list into real vocabulary you can use in class, in homework and in daily conversation. You can also practise alongside the [solved notes](/solved.html) and [books](/books.html) pages on this site for extra reading material.

paras: Class 6 English becomes much easier when you know the words you meet every day at school and at home, because reading, writing and speaking all depend on the same small set of useful words, and the [solved notes](/solved.html) on this site show how simple words build clear sentences. Book means a set of printed pages for reading or study. For example, I keep my English book in my school bag every day.. Pencil means a thin tool used for writing or drawing. For example, She writes her homework neatly with a sharp pencil.. Bag means a container for carrying books and other things. For example, Ali carries his lunch and books in a strong bag.. Water means the clear liquid we drink every day. For example, Please drink enough water during the hot afternoon..

When you learn a word, always learn its meaning and one sentence with it, because a word without a sentence is easy to forget, while a word used in your own sentence stays in your memory for a long time and becomes ready for tests and class work. Door means the opening through which you enter a room. For example, Please close the door quietly when you leave the classroom.. Window means an opening in a wall that lets in light and air. For example, The teacher opened the window because the room felt warm.. Chair means a seat with a back, used by one person. For example, Every student sits on a chair during the lesson.. Table means a flat piece of furniture with legs. For example, We place our notebooks on the table before the lesson starts..

sections.h2: School Words You Use Every Day
paras: School words are the most useful words for a Class 6 student, because you hear them in every lesson, and once you know them well you can follow instructions, ask questions and write answers with confidence, just like the learners who practise with [books](/books.html) every week. Teacher means a person who teaches students in a school. For example, Our teacher explains every new lesson with simple examples.. Lesson means a period of learning or teaching. For example, Today's English lesson is about describing our school.. Notebook means a book of blank pages for writing notes. For example, Write the new words in your notebook after each lesson.. Classroom means a room where a class is taught. For example, The classroom looks clean because every student helps to keep it tidy..

Homework and questions are part of daily school life, so learn these words until you can use them without thinking, and practise them by writing two sentences of your own for each word before you move on to the next group. Homework means school work that you do at home. For example, I finish my homework before I watch television in the evening.. Question means a sentence that asks for information. For example, The teacher asked a question and every student tried to answer it.. Answer means a reply to a question. For example, Write your answer in a complete sentence, not in one word.. Friend means a person you like and trust. For example, My friend helps me learn new English words every day..

diagram.alt: How to Learn a New Word
diagram.caption: Follow these steps for every new word you meet.

paras: Home words help you talk about your family and your daily routine in English, and because you use these words at home every day, they are the easiest words to remember once you start saying them in real sentences with your family members. Kitchen means the room where food is cooked. For example, Mother cooks delicious food in our kitchen every evening.. Garden means a piece of land where flowers and plants grow. For example, We water the plants in our garden every morning.. Breakfast means the first meal of the day. For example, I eat breakfast with my family before going to school.. Mother means a female parent. For example, My mother wakes me early so I can revise my lesson..

Daily actions at home give you many chances to practise English, so name what you are doing in English while you do it, and soon these words will feel as natural as the names of the rooms in your own house. Brother means a boy or man who has the same parents as you. For example, My brother and I read our lessons together after school.. Clean means free from dirt. For example, Please keep your room clean and put your books in place.. Cook means to prepare food by heating it. For example, Father can cook rice and vegetables very well.. Sleep means to rest with your eyes closed. For example, Children should sleep early so they can wake up fresh..

Nature words describe the world outside your home, and Sindh gives you many examples every day, from rivers and fields to trees, birds and clouds, so try to name five things you see on your way to school in English each morning. River means a large natural stream of water. For example, The river flows slowly past the green fields near our village.. Mountain means a very high area of land. For example, Snow covers the top of the mountain during the winter season.. Flower means the coloured part of a plant. For example, The red flower in our garden smells sweet in the morning.. Rain means water that falls from clouds. For example, Rain makes the fields green and fills the ponds with water..

Weather and nature words also appear in reading passages and picture descriptions, so learn them with their colours, sounds and seasons, and use them in short descriptions of what you see from your window each day. Sun means the star that gives light and heat to the Earth. For example, The sun rises in the east and gives light to the whole village.. Tree means a tall plant with a trunk and branches. For example, Birds build their nests in the big tree near our school.. Bird means an animal with wings and feathers. For example, A small bird sings sweetly on the branch every morning.. Cloud means a white or grey mass of water in the sky. For example, Dark clouds gathered in the sky before the rain started..

Feeling words help you describe yourself and other people honestly, and action words like help and share teach good behaviour, so learn them together and use them when you talk about your day, your friends and your family. Happy means feeling pleased and glad. For example, I feel happy when I learn a new lesson well.. Kind means gentle and caring towards others. For example, A kind student helps a new student find the classroom.. Brave means not afraid in a difficult situation. For example, The brave boy crossed the road carefully and helped his sister.. Help means to make something easier for someone. For example, Please help your friend carry the heavy books to class..

End your practice by writing a short paragraph using five words from this list, then read it aloud to a family member, and keep revising from [blog](/blog/) and your notebook so the words grow into a strong vocabulary for Class 6 and beyond. Share means to give part of something to others. For example, Good friends share their books and pencils with each other.. Laugh means to make a happy sound when something is funny. For example, The children laugh happily when the teacher tells a funny story.. Careful means giving attention to avoid mistakes. For example, Be careful while writing, and check your spelling at the end.. Honest means truthful and fair. For example, An honest student always tells the truth, even when it is hard..

points: Learn words in theme groups, not in random order.
Always learn a meaning plus one example sentence.
Say each new word aloud and write it once.
Revise yesterday's words before learning new ones.
Use five new words in a short paragraph every week.

faqs.q: How many words should a Class 6 student learn each week?
faqs.a: Ten to fifteen new words per week is a healthy target for Class 6, because it leaves time to practise each word in sentences and to revise older words, while a much larger list usually leads to fast forgetting and confusion during tests and class work.

faqs.q: Is this list taken from one STBB lesson?
faqs.a: No, this is a general useful word list for the Class 6 level, grouped by everyday themes such as school, home, nature and feelings, and it is not presented as an official answer key or as the word list of any single lesson in any book.

faqs.q: What is the best way to remember a new word?
faqs.a: Read the word, say it aloud, learn its simple meaning, and then write your own sentence with it, because using the word yourself connects it to your memory far better than only reading it again and again from a list. Try the idea in class or homework this week, and note what felt easy and what still needs practice before your next revision.

faqs.q: Should I learn spellings at the same time?
faqs.a: Yes, copy each new word carefully once or twice and check its spelling against the list, because correct spelling helps in written tests, and a word you can spell correctly is usually a word you can also read and use confidently. Ask your teacher about any part that stays unclear, because a quick question now prevents a bigger confusion before the examination.

faqs.q: How can parents help with vocabulary practice?
faqs.a: Parents can ask the child to explain five words at dinner, listen to one short paragraph using new words, and praise correct sentences, because short daily praise and practice build confidence much faster than one long weekly revision session. Practise with a friend when possible, since explaining an idea to someone else is one of the strongest ways to remember it well.

title: Class 7 English Vocabulary: 100 Useful Words
desc: Grow Class 7 English vocabulary with textbook words, clear meanings and example sentences for reading, grammar, school life and thinking skills.
intro: Class 7 English asks for more than everyday words: reading passages grow longer, grammar terms appear in questions, and answers need thinking words like describe and explain, so this general list gathers useful textbook-level words with simple meanings and example sentences for the Class 7 level. It is not an official answer key for any single lesson, and every word here is chosen because it helps in reading, writing or class discussion. Learn one theme at a time, write your own sentence for each word, and revise weekly through the [solved notes](/solved.html) and [books](/books.html) pages for steady progress.

paras: Class 7 reading passages use longer texts than Class 6, so you need words that describe the parts of a book and the work you do with it, and the [solved notes](/solved.html) pages show how these words appear in real summaries and answers. Chapter means one part of a book. For example, We read the second chapter of the story in class today.. Paragraph means a group of sentences about one idea. For example, Write your answer in one clear paragraph with five sentences.. Summary means a short version giving only the main points. For example, Write a summary of the lesson in your own words.. Example means something that shows how a rule or idea works. For example, The teacher gave an example to explain the new rule..

When you meet a reading word, notice how it is used in the passage, copy the sentence into your notebook, and then try the same word in a sentence about your own school day, because that transfer from reading to writing is what builds real understanding. Exercise means a set of questions for practice. For example, Complete the exercise at the end of the chapter carefully.. Dictionary means a book that gives meanings of words. For example, Use a dictionary to find the meaning of a difficult word.. Sentence means a group of words that makes complete sense. For example, Every sentence in your answer should start with a capital letter.. Story means an account of real or imagined events. For example, The story teaches us that hard work always brings success..

Grammar words name the building blocks of sentences, so learning them helps you understand questions, follow grammar rules and correct your own writing, which is why every Class 7 student should know them before moving to harder work. Verb means a word that shows an action or state. For example, Run, read and sleep are all verbs in these sentences.. Noun means a word that names a person, place or thing. For example, Teacher, school and book are nouns in this sentence.. Adjective means a word that describes a noun. For example, The adjective tall describes the boy in the sentence.. Pronoun means a word used instead of a noun. For example, He and she are pronouns that take the place of names..

Tense and punctuation words also matter in every test, because they decide whether a sentence talks about the past, present or future, and whether it ends correctly, so practise them with short sentences of your own every day. Tense means the form of a verb showing time. For example, The present tense talks about actions happening now.. Punctuation means marks such as full stops and commas. For example, Use punctuation carefully so your sentences are easy to read.. Plural means the form of a word for more than one. For example, The plural of book is books, and of child is children.. Opposite means a word with the reverse meaning. For example, Hot is the opposite of cold in this pair of words..

diagram.alt: How to Master a Grammar Word
diagram.caption: Use this cycle for every grammar term you learn.

paras: School life words help you talk about places, people and routines in your school, and because you meet them every day, they are perfect for speaking practice with classmates during breaks and group work. Library means a room or building with books for reading. For example, I borrow story books from the school library every week.. Laboratory means a room for science experiments. For example, Students work carefully in the science laboratory.. Assembly means a gathering of students and teachers. For example, The morning assembly starts with a short prayer and news.. Principal means the head of a school. For example, The principal visits every classroom once a week..

Examination words can feel stressful, but knowing them early removes fear, because you understand what a timetable means, what revision involves and what a result shows, so you can plan your study calmly instead of worrying. Timetable means a plan showing times for lessons. For example, Our timetable shows English first on Monday morning.. Examination means a formal test of knowledge. For example, The examination will test reading, writing and grammar skills.. Revision means studying again to remember well. For example, Revision the night before the test helps you stay confident.. Result means the outcome of a test or examination. For example, Good results come from regular study, not from last-day worry..

Words about journeys, markets, weather and health connect English to life outside school, and when you learn them you can describe your town, your family routines and the seasons in simple, correct English sentences. Journey means a trip from one place to another. For example, Our journey to the city took two hours by bus.. Market means a place where goods are bought and sold. For example, Mother buys fresh vegetables from the market every week.. Neighbour means a person who lives near you. For example, Our neighbour is kind and helps us in difficult times.. Weather means the state of the sky and air. For example, The weather today is cool and pleasant for playing outside..

Health and habit words are equally useful, because they appear in essays, letters and health lessons, and they also help you talk about your own routine honestly, from exercise and sleep to food and daily habits. Season means one of the four parts of the year. For example, Summer is the hottest season in our part of the country.. Health means the state of being free from illness. For example, Good health comes from clean food, exercise and enough sleep.. Energy means the strength to do work or be active. For example, A good breakfast gives us energy for the whole school day.. Habit means something you do regularly. For example, Reading for twenty minutes daily is a very good habit..

Thinking words help you write better answers, because questions often ask you to describe, explain, compare or imagine, and if you know what each word asks for, you can shape your answer correctly instead of guessing, with extra practice from [blog](/blog/). Describe means to say what something is like. For example, Describe your school in five clear sentences.. Explain means to make an idea clear and easy to understand. For example, Please explain the rule with one simple example.. Compare means to show how two things are alike or different. For example, Compare summer and winter in four sentences.. Imagine means to form a picture in your mind. For example, Imagine a village with clean streets and happy children..

Finish by choosing one thinking word each day and writing a short answer with it, then checking your work for spelling and full stops, because steady daily practice builds the confident writing that Class 7 tests reward. Remember means to keep something in your mind. For example, Remember the meanings by revising them every evening.. Decide means to choose something after thinking. For example, Decide your study time and follow it every day.. Improve means to make something better. For example, Daily practice will improve your English writing quickly.. Respect means to show honour and care for others. For example, Respect your teachers, elders and classmates every day..

points: Learn reading words first, then grammar words.
A word is learned only when you can use it in a sentence.
Revise older words every week, not only new ones.
Use thinking words to match what a question asks.
Keep a personal word notebook with meanings and examples.

faqs.q: How is Class 7 vocabulary different from Class 6?
faqs.a: Class 7 vocabulary adds textbook and grammar words such as chapter, paragraph, tense and summary, because reading passages grow longer and questions start asking students to describe, explain and compare instead of only naming everyday things. Keep this answer beside your lesson notes, and read it once more before the next test so the idea stays fresh and ready.

faqs.q: Is this list from a specific Class 7 lesson?
faqs.a: No, this is a general word list for the Class 7 level, covering reading, grammar, school life and daily life, and it is not presented as an official answer key or as the vocabulary of any single lesson in any book. Use the idea in one real sentence or task today, because using knowledge turns it from a fact into a skill you own.

faqs.q: How can I remember grammar terms easily?
faqs.a: Learn each term with one short definition and one example sentence, then spot that term in your textbook the same week, because finding a term in real reading fixes it in memory far better than only memorising a definition. Revise older answers together with new ones, so new learning connects with what you already know instead of replacing it.

faqs.q: What should I do when I forget a word in a test?
faqs.a: Stay calm, use a simpler word with a similar meaning, and continue your answer, because a clear simple sentence earns more marks than a blank space, and you can revise the forgotten word properly after the test. Stay patient with slow progress, because steady small steps in English build more lasting skill than rushed cramming before tests.

faqs.q: How often should I revise my word notebook?
faqs.a: Revise new words the next day, again after three days, and once more at the end of the week, because spaced revision turns short-term learning into lasting vocabulary that stays ready for examinations. End each study session by recalling the main point aloud without looking, since recall practice strengthens memory far more than re-reading.

title: Class 8 English Vocabulary: 100 Useful Words
desc: Strengthen Class 8 English with stronger words for essays and letters: opinions, linking words, formal terms and society vocabulary with examples.
intro: Class 8 English rewards stronger writing: essays need opinions with evidence, paragraphs need linking words, and letters need formal respect, so this general list gathers stronger words for essays and letters with simple meanings and example sentences for the Class 8 level. It is not an official answer key for any single lesson, and its value lies in daily use: pick a theme, learn its words, and use them in one essay or letter each week. With steady practice through the [solved notes](/solved.html) and [books](/books.html) pages, these words become a natural part of your writing instead of a list you memorise and forget.

sections.h2: Words That Build a Strong Essay
paras: Class 8 essays need more than simple sentences: they need words that state an opinion, support it and finish clearly, and the [solved notes](/solved.html) pages show how such words turn scattered ideas into a well-organised essay. Opinion means what you think about something. For example, In my opinion, reading daily is the best habit for students.. Argument means a reason given to support an idea. For example, His argument for early study was strong and clear.. Evidence means facts that prove an idea is true. For example, Good essays give evidence, not only opinions.. Introduction means the opening part of an essay. For example, The introduction should tell the reader the main topic..

A clear conclusion matters as much as a good opening, because it reminds the reader of your main point and leaves a strong final impression, so practise ending every essay with one short paragraph that repeats your idea in new words. Conclusion means the final part that sums up ideas. For example, The conclusion repeated the main point in simple words.. Paragraph means a group of sentences about one idea. For example, Each paragraph of the essay should cover only one main idea.. Topic means the subject you write or talk about. For example, Choose a topic you know well before you start writing.. Title means the name given to a piece of writing. For example, A good title tells the reader what the essay is about..

Linking words join your ideas smoothly, so your essay reads like one connected piece instead of separate sentences, and examiners notice this flow because it shows clear thinking and careful planning behind your writing. However means used to show a contrast. For example, The task was hard; however, the students completed it well.. Therefore means used to show a result. For example, He studied daily; therefore, he passed with good marks.. Although means used to show a surprising contrast. For example, Although it rained, the students reached school on time.. Furthermore means used to add another point. For example, Furthermore, reading improves spelling and vocabulary..

Use linking words sparingly and correctly, because one well-placed however or finally is stronger than five linking words used without meaning, and every linking word must match the real connection between your two ideas. Finally means used to introduce the last point. For example, Finally, we should thank our teachers for their guidance.. Meanwhile means used to show things happening at the same time. For example, Meanwhile, the other students prepared their charts.. Instead means used to show a replacement or choice. For example, Instead of worrying, he made a simple study plan.. Otherwise means used to show what happens if not. For example, Revise daily; otherwise, you may forget the lesson..

diagram.alt: How to Build a Strong Paragraph
diagram.caption: Follow these steps for every essay paragraph you write.

paras: Strong verbs and quality words make essays and letters lively, because they show effort, character and results, and they help you describe people and actions with precision instead of repeating the same weak words again and again. Achieve means to reach a goal through effort. For example, With daily practice, she achieved excellent marks in English.. Improve means to make something better. For example, Reading aloud every day will improve your pronunciation.. Succeed means to reach a wanted result. For example, Students who plan well usually succeed in examinations.. Encourage means to give someone hope and confidence. For example, Teachers encourage students to ask questions freely..

Character words also help in essays about ideal students, good citizens and role models, so learn them with examples from real life, and use them when you describe people you admire in your class or family. Appreciate means to value and thank for something good. For example, We appreciate our teachers for their hard work every day.. Responsible means trusted to do a job well. For example, A responsible student completes homework on time.. Honest means truthful and fair in behaviour. For example, An honest student admits mistakes and learns from them.. Confident means sure of yourself in a calm way. For example, Practice makes a student confident during class presentations..

Essays in Class 8 often ask about society, environment and the future, so these words help you write sensibly about real problems and solutions, from pollution and community life to education and the duties of a good citizen. Environment means the natural world around us. For example, We must protect our environment by planting more trees.. Pollution means harmful substances in air, water or land. For example, Pollution harms health, so we must keep our streets clean.. Citizen means a member of a country or city. For example, A good citizen follows rules and helps neighbours.. Community means a group of people living together. For example, Our community works together to keep the school clean..

Future and knowledge words complete this group, because essays about progress need words for learning, freedom and growth, and these ideas appear again and again in school essays, speeches and letters. Freedom means the right to act and speak freely. For example, Freedom comes with responsibility towards other people.. Knowledge means facts and skills gained by learning. For example, Knowledge grows when students read, ask and practise daily.. Education means learning and teaching in schools. For example, Education opens doors to a better and brighter future.. Future means the time that is yet to come. For example, Hard work today builds a strong future for every student..

Letters need formal words that show respect and clarity, and learning them early helps Class 8 students write applications, requests and invitations correctly, with more examples on [blog](/blog/) and in solved letter guides. Address means the place where someone lives or works. For example, Write your address at the top of a formal letter.. Salutation means the greeting at the start of a letter. For example, Dear Sir is a common salutation in formal letters.. Subject means a short line stating the purpose. For example, The subject line tells the reader why you are writing.. Sincerely means used to close a formal letter politely. For example, End your application with Yours sincerely and your name..

End letter practice by writing one short application each week, checking the greeting, subject and closing carefully, because a neat formal letter shows respect for the reader and earns good marks in examinations. Request means asking for something politely. For example, I request you to grant me leave for two days.. Permission means allowing someone to do something. For example, Students must take permission before leaving the classroom.. Apology means saying sorry for a mistake. For example, A sincere apology can repair a small misunderstanding.. Invitation means asking someone to come to an event. For example, We sent an invitation to our parents for the school function..

points: Essay words state an opinion, support it, then conclude.
Use one linking word per idea, not one per sentence.
Formal letter words show respect and clarity.
Learn society words with real-life examples.
Write one essay or letter weekly using new words.

faqs.q: Why do Class 8 students need linking words?
faqs.a: Linking words join ideas smoothly, so an essay reads as one connected argument instead of separate sentences, and examiners reward this flow because it shows clear thinking, planning and control over English writing. Short daily practice works better than one long session, so revisit this point tomorrow and again at the end of the week for lasting progress.

faqs.q: Is this list from a specific Class 8 lesson?
faqs.a: No, this is a general word list for the Class 8 level, covering essay words, linking words, formal letter terms and society vocabulary, and it is not presented as an official answer key for any single lesson. Write the point in your own words in a notebook, because explaining it yourself shows whether you truly understand it or only recognise it.

faqs.q: How many new essay words should I learn weekly?
faqs.a: Eight to ten new words per week is enough if you use each one in a real sentence or paragraph, because words used in writing stay in memory, while long lists copied without use are forgotten quickly before tests. Try the idea in class or homework this week, and note what felt easy and what still needs practice before your next revision.

faqs.q: What makes an essay paragraph strong?
faqs.a: A strong paragraph starts with one main idea, supports it with a reason or example, links its sentences smoothly, and ends with a clear point, so the reader can follow your thinking without confusion or repetition. Ask your teacher about any part that stays unclear, because a quick question now prevents a bigger confusion before the examination.

faqs.q: How do I choose between formal and informal letter words?
faqs.a: Use formal words like salutation, subject and sincerely for teachers, officers and applications, and use friendly informal words only for close friends and family, because the reader and purpose decide the correct level of formality. Practise with a friend when possible, since explaining an idea to someone else is one of the strongest ways to remember it well.

title: Class 9 English Vocabulary: 100 Useful Words
desc: Master Class 9 board-exam English vocabulary: exam terms, grammar words, literature terms and study skills with meanings and example sentences.
intro: Class 9 is the first board-exam year for many students, so English vocabulary must cover the exact terms the paper uses: comprehension and precis, tense and voice, theme and moral, plus the study skills that turn knowledge into marks. This general list gives board-exam words with simple meanings and example sentences for the Class 9 level, and it is not an official answer key for any single lesson. Learn one theme at a time, practise one past-style question for each group, and revise through the [solved notes](/solved.html) and [books](/books.html) pages so the paper feels familiar when it arrives.

sections.h2: Board Exam Terms You Must Know
paras: Board examinations use fixed terms in their papers, so Class 9 students should know exactly what comprehension, precis, essay and letter questions ask for, and the [solved notes](/solved.html) pages show how these terms appear in real papers. Comprehension means understanding a passage and answering about it. For example, Read the comprehension passage twice before answering its questions.. Precis means a short, clear version of a longer passage. For example, A good precis keeps only the main ideas of the passage.. Summary means a brief account of the main points. For example, Write the summary in your own words, not by copying lines.. Essay means a piece of writing on one topic. For example, The essay question carries good marks, so plan it carefully..

Letter, application, dialogue and narration questions also follow fixed patterns, so learn their names and formats now, and practise one of each every month so the board paper holds no surprises for you. Letter means a written message to someone. For example, Write a letter to your friend about your school library.. Application means a formal written request. For example, Write an application to the principal for leave of two days.. Dialogue means a conversation between two people. For example, Write a dialogue between a student and a bookseller.. Narration means telling a story or events in order. For example, Narration questions test how clearly you can retell events..

sections.h2: Grammar Terms for the Board Paper
paras: Grammar terms decide marks in the board paper, because questions name them directly, and a student who confuses tense with voice, or speech with punctuation, loses marks on questions that are actually easy with clear terms. Tense means the verb form showing past, present or future. For example, Change this sentence from present tense to past tense.. Voice means active or passive form of a verb. For example, Change the sentence from active voice to passive voice.. Speech means direct or indirect reporting of words. For example, Change this direct speech into indirect speech carefully.. Punctuation means marks that organise written sentences. For example, Correct punctuation makes your writing clear and easy to mark..

Idiom, proverb, synonym and antonym questions reward students who learn them as pairs with sentences, because a meaning remembered without a sentence is often confused in the paper, while a sentence fixes the meaning firmly. Idiom means a phrase with a special meaning. For example, The idiom break the ice means to start friendly talk.. Proverb means a short saying with a wise meaning. For example, Slow and steady wins the race is a well-known proverb.. Synonym means a word with a similar meaning. For example, Happy is a synonym of glad in this sentence.. Antonym means a word with the opposite meaning. For example, Hot is an antonym of cold in this pair..

diagram.alt: How to Prepare for a Board Question
diagram.caption: Use this method for every board exam question type.

paras: Literature questions use words like theme, moral, character and setting, so learn them before the paper, because they tell you exactly what the examiner wants: the message, the people, the place or the events of a text. Theme means the main idea or message of a text. For example, The theme of the story is the value of hard work.. Moral means the lesson taught by a story. For example, The moral of the story is that honesty always wins.. Character means a person in a story or play. For example, The main character of the story is a brave young student.. Setting means the time and place of a story. For example, The setting of the story is a small village school..

Plot, stanza, poet and narrator complete the literature set, and they appear in poetry and story questions alike, so learn each one with a short example from a lesson you have already studied in class. Plot means the sequence of events in a story. For example, The plot moves quickly from a problem to its solution.. Stanza means a group of lines in a poem. For example, Each stanza of the poem describes one part of nature.. Poet means a person who writes poems. For example, The poet describes the morning with beautiful images.. Narrator means the person who tells a story. For example, The narrator tells the story from the view of a student..

Board success depends on study skills as much as on knowledge, because a good timetable, honest revision and calm concentration turn what you know into marks, while last-day panic wastes even well-prepared lessons. Revision means studying material again to remember it. For example, Daily revision keeps old lessons fresh before examinations.. Timetable means a plan showing when to study each subject. For example, Follow a simple timetable and give English time every day.. Practice means doing exercises repeatedly to improve. For example, Practice past paper questions to understand the paper pattern.. Preparation means getting ready for a test or task. For example, Good preparation starts weeks before the examination, not nights..

Concentration, confidence, accuracy and presentation are the quiet skills behind high marks, because they decide whether your knowledge reaches the paper neatly, completely and in the time allowed by the examiner. Concentration means full attention on one task. For example, Concentration improves when you study away from noise.. Confidence means belief in your own ability. For example, Confidence grows when you practise answers regularly.. Accuracy means being correct and exact. For example, Accuracy in spelling and grammar earns extra respect from checkers.. Presentation means how neatly work is shown. For example, Neat presentation with clear paragraphs impresses every examiner..

Question verbs tell you what to do: analyse, describe, discuss and explain are not the same task, and students who learn the difference write focused answers, with model answers on [blog](/blog/) showing each verb in action. Analyse means to examine something in detail. For example, Analyse the character of the hero in five sentences.. Describe means to say what something is like. For example, Describe the scene in the poem with clear details.. Discuss means to talk about ideas for and against. For example, Discuss the advantages of reading books daily.. Explain means to make an idea clear. For example, Explain the proverb with one real-life example..

Finish your board vocabulary with adjectives that add quality to answers, because a significant point, an effective method or an appropriate example sounds precise and mature, which is exactly the tone board examiners reward. Illustrate means to explain with an example. For example, Illustrate your answer with one example from daily life.. Significant means important and meaningful. For example, Reading daily has a significant effect on vocabulary.. Effective means producing the wanted result. For example, Regular revision is an effective way to prepare.. Appropriate means suitable for the situation. For example, Use appropriate words for a formal letter to the principal..
